title: Definitions
text:
(a) Notwithstanding the definitions already contained in CAR DEF, CAR AGA and CAR SMS, the
terms listed below have the following meaning within the context of this regulation:
(1) Aerodrome Emergency Plan Manual (AEP Manual). A manual that forms part of the
application for an Aerodrome Certificate or and is maintained pursuant to these
regulations. The Aerodrome Emergency Plan Manual, as determined by the aerodrome
operator, reflects the nature of emergency planning and management of aircraft and
non-aircraft emergencies at an aerodrome.
(2) Aerodrome Rescue and Firefighting Service Operations Manual (ARFFS Operations
Manual). A document, as determined by the Aerodrome operator or a Service Provider,
details the level of service delivery, organisation, risk management, operational
procedures and quality assurance of the rescue and firefighting service.
(3) Aerodrome Rescue and Firefighting Service Training Manual (ARFFS Training Manual).
A document, as determined by the Aerodrome operator or a Service Provider, details
the competency-based training and assessment policies and procedures of the rescue
and firefighting service.
(4) Aerodrome Rescue and Firefighting Service Fitness Manual. A document, as
determined by the Aerodrome operator or a Service Provider, details the medical and
physical fitness policies and procedures of the rescue and firefighting service.

(5) Aircraft Firefighting. The control or extinguishment of fire adjacent to or involving an
aircraft following accidents or incidents.
(6) Aircraft Rescue. Actions taken to save or set free persons involved in an aircraft
accident/incident by safeguarding the integrity of the aircraft fuselage from an external /
internal fire, to support self-evacuation and to undertake the removal of injured and
trapped persons.
(7) Accepted by the GCAA. Documented by the GCAA as suitable for the purpose intended.
Below is the list of documents to be accepted by the GCAA
(a) Aerodrome Emergency Plan Manual
(b) Aerodrome Rescue and Firefighting Service Training Manual
(8) Assessor. A person acceptable to the aerodrome operator to make judgements about
performance against the requirements of the training standards.
(9) Augmented reality (AR). An interactive experience that enhances the real world with
computer-generated perceptual information. Using software, apps, and hardware such
as AR glasses, augmented reality overlays digital content onto real-life environments and
objects.
(10) Certificate of conformity. Certificate of Conformity is a document issued by
manufacturers or an authorised testing centre, which certifies that the foam
concentrate supplied meet the required firefighting performance standards complies
with ICAO requirements. A certificate of conformity can be either in physical or
electronic form and should be readily available for audit/inspection by the GCAA.
(11) Certificate of competence. This refers to documentary evidence confirming an
individual has successfully demonstrated and achieved the necessary standard of
competence for that particular training. A certificate of competence can be either in
physical or electronic form and should be readily available for audit/inspection by the
GCAA.
(12) Competence. The ability to apply knowledge, skills and attributes (KSA) in performing to
the standards required in employment. This includes problems and meeting changing
demands.
(13) Competency-based training and assessment. Training and assessment that are
characterized by a performance orientation, emphasis on standards of performance and
their measurement, and the development of training to the specified performance
standards as defined in ICAO Doc 9868 PANS-TRG

(14) Crisis Management Centre (CMC). A focal point where an aerodrome operator ’s senior
management together with other senior management of mutual-aid supporting
agencies take overall responsibility for the multi-agency management of an incident,
establish a strategic framework and direction within which emergency operations centre
and other coordinating groups will work at an aerodrome.
(15) Critical Area Concept. The critical area is a concept for rescue of the occupants of an
aircraft. It seeks to control only that area of fire adjacent to the fuselage instead of
attempting to control and extinguish the entire fire. The objective is to safeguard the
integrity of the fuselage and maintain tolerable conditions for its occupants.
(16) Control time (aircraft fire). The time required to reduce the initial intensity of an aircraft
fire by 90 per cent.
(17) Debrief. A means of analysing an outcome of workplace/ training/exercise activity,
which confirms the success of the activity or identifies where there is an opportunity to
promote improvements to personal and organisational performance.
(18) Drainage time (foam). Refers to the rate at which foam solution drains from a foam
blanket may be a partial consideration in that foam blanket’s efficiency in progressively
controlling and extinguishing fires and subsequent post-fire security.
(19) Emergencies (aircraft-related).
(i) Aircraft accident (ACC). An emergency declaration made by Air Traffic Control
and/or Incident Command that an aircraft accident/crash which has occurred on or
in the vicinity of the aerodrome. This emergency declaration will trigger a full
emergency response action by both on and off aerodrome agencies as detailed in
the emergency plan.
(ii) Aircraft ground incident (AGI). An emergency declaration made by Air Traffic
Control and/or Incident Commander when an aircraft on the movement area is in
difficulty or is involved in an incident. The declaration will trigger the appropriate
aerodrome emergency response actions and will normally require the attendance
of on-aerodrome agencies as detailed in the emergency plan. Depending on the
severity and complexity of the incident, the situation may trigger a full emergency
response action similar to an aircraft accident as detailed in the aerodrome
emergency plan.
(iii) Full emergency (FEM). An emergency declaration made by Air Traffic Control
and/or Incident Commander upon notification by the Pilot-in-command that an
aircraft approaching the aerodrome is, or is suspected to be, in such trouble that

there is imminent danger of an accident (crash). The declaration of a full
emergency will trigger the appropriate aerodrome emergency response actions
and will require the full attendance of both on and off aerodrome agencies as the
emergency plan.
(iv) Local standby (LSB). An emergency declaration made by Air Traffic Control and/or
Incident Commander upon notification by the Pilot-in-command that an aircraft
approaching the aerodrome is known or is suspected to have developed some
defect, but the trouble is not such as would normally involve any serious difficulty
in effecting a safe landing. The declaration of a local standby will trigger the
appropriate aerodrome emergency response actions and normally require the
attendance of on-aerodrome agencies as per the emergency plan.
(v) Public health (PHE). An emergency declaration made by a responsible agency
where there is increased risk of travellers or cargo spreading a serious
communicable disease internationally through air transport and severe outbreak of
a communicable disease potentially affecting a large proportion of aerodrome
staff. This declaration triggers the appropriate actions to be taken by relevant on
and off aerodrome agencies as detailed in the aerodrome emergency plan and/or
communicable disease management plan.
(vi) Weather standby (WSB). An emergency declaration made by Air Traffic Control
and/or Incident Commander when weather condition has deteriorated to such an
extent as to render the landing of aircraft more difficult or more difficult to
observe. This declaration will trigger the appropriate actions to be taken by on-
aerodrome agencies as detailed in the emergency plan.
(vii) Acts of Unlawful Interference (AUI). An emergency declaration made by the
responsible agency i.e police authority or security agency in the case of any
unlawful act involving an aircraft in conjunction with local police/security agency.
This emergency declaration will trigger the appropriate emergency response
actions as detailed in the aerodrome security and/or emergency plan
(20) Emergencies (non-aircraft related).
(i) Domestic incident (DOM). An emergency declaration made by Air Traffic Control
and/or Incident Commander in the event of any fires, operational or medical
incident affecting aerodrome personnel, operations, facilities, infrastructure or in
response to calls from public or other agency on humanitarian grounds. The
declaration will trigger the appropriate emergency response actions by relevant

on-aerodrome agencies. Depending on the severity and scale of the incident, the
assistance of relevant off-aerodrome agencies may be required. Appropriate
emergency instructions should be detailed in the emergency plan.
(ii) Dangerous goods/hazardous material incident (DGI). An emergency declaration
made by Air Traffic Control and/or Incident Commander in the event of any
accidental release of dangerous goods affecting aerodrome building, facilities,
property, infrastructure or in response to calls from public or other agency on
humanitarian grounds. The declaration will trigger the appropriate emergency
response actions by on-aerodrome agencies as detailed in the emergency plan.
Depending on the severity and scale of the incident, the assistance of relevant off-
aerodrome agencies may be required.
(21) Emergency operations centre (EOC). A focal point for an aerodrome operator supported
by all those agencies concerned with an incident at an aerodrome to act together in a
concerted way, provides tactical coordination and support to the mobile command post.
(22) Emergency exercise. An exercise is a simulation of an emergency situation at an
aerodrome. Exercises have three main purposes: to validate plans (validation), to
develop staff competencies; and give them practice in carrying out their roles in the
plans (training); and to test well-established procedures (testing). Types of emergency
exercise:
(i) Full-scale.  A full-scale exercise is to ensure the adequacy of the aerodrome
emergency plan to cope with different types of emergencies.
(ii) Partial exercise. A partial exercise is to ensure the adequacy of the response to
individual participating agencies and components of the aerodrome emergency
plan.
(iii) Table-top. A test of the integration and capability of emergency response
resources without the expense and disruption of services incurred by other
emergency exercises.
(iv) Modular test. A modular test is to enable concentrated effort on specific
components of aerodrome emergency plan.
(23) Emergency planning order. A high-level statement detailing an order in dealing with an
emergency.
(24) Emergency planning instruction. An operational action or task to be taken to implement
the emergency planning order.

(25) Expansion ratio (foam). Refers to the amount of air entrained into a foam stream
governs its expansion, which in turn may affect the fluidity of the finished foam and
therefore the rate of spread over the surface of burning fuels.
(26) Extinguishing Agent. An extinguishing agent is to extinguish and/or suppress a fire on
which it is applied.
(i) A principal extinguishing agent is a type of foam for aircraft rescue and firefighting
primarily intended to provide an air excluding blanket which prevents volatile
flammable vapours from mixing with air or oxygen. Principal agent is to achieve
permanent control of fire, i.e. for a period of several minutes or longer.
(ii) Complementary extinguishing agent is a type of chemical powder or halocarbon
field to provide rapid fire suppression or quick knockdown but generally only offer
a transient control, which is available during application.
(27) Foam. An aggregation of small bubbles used to form an air-excluding, vapor-suppressing
blanket over the surface of a flammable liquid fuel.
(28) Foam Concentrate. A concentrated liquid foaming agent as received from the
manufacturer.
(29) Foam induction input-based testing. A method of testing of the foam solution method
by measuring the flow rate or volume of concentrate, or suitable substitute for
concentrate, and comparing this flow rate or volume to the flow rate or volume of water
used, then using those two numbers to calculate the proportions of concentrate and
water in the foam solution. This method involves the use of an external device/pump
connected to the vehicle to test the accuracy of the foam production system. (NFPA 440)
(30) Foam induction output-based testing. A method of testing the foam solution by
collecting a sample of the solution after aerating and dispensing it, and using
instruments and calculations to determine the sample’s proportions of concentrate and
water in the foam solution. This is standard method of testing the accuracy of the foam
production system. (NFPA 440)
(31) Frangible object. An object of low mass designed to break, distort or yield on impact so
as to present the minimum hazard to aircraft or vehicle. (Note. — Guidance on design
for frangibility is contained in the Aerodrome Design Manual (Doc 9157), Part 6.)
(32) Human factors principles. Principles which apply to aeronautical design, certification,
training, operations and maintenance and which seek safe interface between the human
and other system components by proper consideration to human performance.

(33) Human performance. Human capabilities and limitations which have an impact on the
safety and efficiency of aeronautical operations.
(34) Incident Management System (IMS). An internationally recognised safe and effective
system for managing an incident at an aerodrome. IMS is underpinned by the key
principles of national guidance, which supports the delivery of a safe, effective and
efficient operational response, using planned and systematic processes to minimise
personal and organisational risk.
(35) Internal Quality Assurance (IQA). A process which ensures the integrity and value of
management system, plans, procedures, qualifications and/or assessments throughout
their life cycle.
(36) Low Visibility Conditions (LVC). The meteorological conditions requiring approaches and
landings in Category II and Category III, take offs in RVR less than 550 metres or for
surface movements in meteorological conditions not permitting ATS to be carried out
with visual reference.
(37) Low Visibility Procedures (LVP). The measures required to support safe operations at an
aerodrome in Low Visibility Conditions (LVC).
(38) Maintenance of Competence (MoC). A structured learning framework that can be used
to maintain skills and assess the competence of Rescue and Fire Fighting Service
personnel.
(39) Manoeuvring Area. That part of an aerodrome to be used for the take-off, landing and
taxiing of aircraft, excluding aprons.
(40) Mobile Command Post (MCP). A mobile facility capable of rapid deployment to an
incident where an aerodrome incident commander in cooperation with mutual-aid
supporting agency heads assemble to receive and disseminate information and make
decisions pertinent to the rescue and firefighting operations at the scene of an
emergency at an aerodrome.
(41) Optimum visibility and surface conditions. Defined as daytime, good visibility, no
precipitation with normal response routes free of aircraft and surface contamination
(42) Proficiency Check. A formal assessment of competence carried out by an assessor at
predetermined intervals in order to ensure competence in critical functions.
(43) Qualified. Denotes fitness or fit for the purpose. This may be achieved through
fulfilment of the necessary conditions such as completion of required training, or
acquisition of a diploma or degree, or through the gaining of suitable experience. It, also,

includes the ability, capacity, knowledge or skill that matches or suits an occasion, or
makes someone eligible for a duty, office, position, privilege or status.
(44) Rescue and Fire Fighting Service (ARFFS). An international term describing a service
provider or a specialised aerodrome unit responsible to immediately respond, create
and maintain survivable conditions, to provide egress routes for aircraft occupants and
to initiate the rescue of those occupants unable to make their escape without direct aid
during an aircraft accident/incident at an aerodrome. A ARFFS is also known as an
aerodrome fire rescue service or aerodrome emergency services.
(45) Response Time. The time between the initial call to the ARFFS and the time when the
first responding vehicle(s) is(are) in position to apply foam at a rate of at least 50 per
cent of the discharge rate specified in the table on minimum usable amounts of
extinguishing agents appropriate to the level of aerodrome category.
(46) Standby Position. A pre-determined strategic location around the airfield within a safe
distance from the runway for ARFFS vehicles to take up forward readiness position to
respond immediately in the event of a full emergency or local standby declaration.
(47) Structured Learning Programme (SLP). A training programme that is organised in a
manner that enables individuals to achieve competency in a particular set of roles
and/or tasks according to their grade (Watchroom, Firefighter, Supervisor and
Manager).
(48) Task resource analysis (TRA). A risk-based approach method using both qualitative and
quantitative analysis supported by a workload assessment to determine the necessary
level of ARFFS staffing to perform identified tasks in real-time before mutual-aid
supporting agencies are needed based on credible worst-case aircraft accident or
incident scenarios at an aerodrome.
(49) Technology. Any other suitable method of communicating which may include using
telephone / video conferencing, that is not through the face-to-face medium.
(50) Training facilities analysis. A process to analyse the type and quantity of appropriate
facilities and equipment required for the implementation of a training programme to
ensure initial and continued competence.
(51) Training frequency analysis. A process to analyse how frequently training and
assessments in particular areas should be repeated within a programme of training, to
ensure continued competence.
(52) Training needs analysis. A process to identify and analyse the underpinning knowledge,
skills and attributes (KSA) required to carry out the tasks required of ARFFS personnel in

relation to their operational role (Watchroom, Firefighter, Driver, Supervisor and
Manager).
(53) Virtual Reality (VR). A realistic visual stimulus used in many modern training and
assessment scenarios as it confers a wide range of benefits in a safe and controlled
environment.

title: Organisational requirements
text:
INITIAL CERTIFICATION
(a) For initial aerodrome certification or initial landing area acceptance, a new applicant shall
comply with applicable organisational requirements stated in CAR AGA PART ADR.
CONTINUED VALIDITY
(a) For continued validity of an aerodrome certificate or landing area acceptance, an aerodrome
operator shall comply with applicable organisational requirements stated in CAR AGA PART
ADR.

(ACM.OPS.CERT)

title: Provision of services and/or activities
text:
(a) The services and/or activities under this SUBPART shall be provided at the aerodrome by the
aerodrome operator either directly or indirectly.
(b) Where the services and/or activities contained in this SUBPART are provided by a third party
either fully or partially, an aerodrome operator shall establish and implement safety oversight
of the provisions, in accordance with the operator’s safety management system, to ensure
compliance with the applicable requirements contained in this Regulation.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Provision of services and/or activities
text:
PROVISION OF SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) The services and/or activities contained in this SUBPART need to be provided at an
aerodrome. In some cases, these services and/or activities are not directly provided by the
aerodrome operator, but by a third-party organisation or combination of both. However, the
aerodrome operator, being responsible for the operation of the aerodrome should have
arrangements and interfaces with the third party to ensure that these services and/or
activities are provided according to the legal requirements.
(b) The method described above meets with the intention of an integrated Safety Management
System that helps the aerodrome operator to ensure the safety objective of the provision is
being met.

title: Crisis management
text:
CRISIS MANAGEMENT
(a) An aerodrome operator shall establish and implement a crisis management plan that:
(1) is commensurate with the aircraft operations and other activities conducted at an
aerodrome;
(2) provides for the strategic direction in dealing with crises occurring at an aerodrome or
in its surroundings; and
(3) contains procedures for periodic testing of the adequacy of the plan and for reviewing
the results in order to improve its effectiveness.

title: Crisis management
text:
ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING A CRISIS MANAGEMENT PLAN

(a) Where a crisis management centre is not located within the aerodrome, the activation of the
centre and key personnel must not cause any delay and compromise the strategic response to
the emergency.
(b) Arrangements are made for the aerodrome operator to co-chair the group if the crisis
management group is not lead by the aerodrome certificate holder.
(c) Developing health and safety arrangements are necessary for the strategic commander and
crisis management group especially in a protracted emergency.

title: Crisis management
text:
TESTING AND EXERCISING A CRISIS MANAGEMENT PLAN
(a) Testing and exercising of the crisis management plan should include:
(1) personnel and agencies detailed in the crisis management plan;
(2) core elements of the crisis management plan and establish how and when these
elements are tested;
(3) senior executives of the aerodrome operator actively participate in the exercises as per
their assigned roles and responsibilities in the crisis management plan; and
(4) records of testing and exercising and ensure such records are readily available for audit
and inspection by the GCAA.

title: Business continuity
text:
BUSINESS CONTINUITY PLANNING
(a) An aerodrome operator shall establish and implement a business continuity plan that:
(1) is commensurate with the aircraft operations and other activities conducted at an
aerodrome;
(2) provides for the partial or full closure of facilities and operations occurring at an
aerodrome or in its surroundings arising from crises; and
(3) contains procedures for periodic testing of the adequacy of the plan and for reviewing
the results in order to improve its effectiveness.

title: Business continuity
text:
BCP COMPETENT PERSON
(a) The Airport Business Continuity Planning (BCP) Competent Person should possess the
necessary knowledge, skills, and authority to manage business continuity efforts effectively,
and to ensure compliance with relevant standards, such as NCEMA 7000 and/or ISO 22301, as
well as national and international aviation regulations.
(b) To be effective in their role, the Airport BCP Competent Person must possess a strong
foundation of skills and expertise in both business continuity and aviation operations. Key
competencies include:
(1) Technical Knowledge: A deep understanding of business continuity management
principles, including NCEMA 7000 and/or ISO 22301, risk assessment methodologies,
and recovery planning techniques, is essential. Additionally, the Competent Person
must be familiar with airport operations, safety protocols, and regulatory requirements
specific to the aviation industry.
(2) Leadership and Decision-Making Skills: The Competent Person must demonstrate strong
leadership skills, with the ability to coordinate diverse teams and make critical decisions
under pressure. In times of crisis, they must be able to provide clear direction, resolve
issues quickly, and maintain control of the response efforts.
(3) Communication and Collaboration: Excellent communication skills are essential, as the
Competent Person must regularly engage with internal and external stakeholders,
ensuring clarity and consistency in the messaging around continuity planning and
response efforts. The individual must be able to collaborate effectively with all levels of
the organisation and external partners to ensure cohesive action during a disruption.
(4) Problem-Solving and Analytical Skills: The Competent Person must be adept at analysing
risks, identifying vulnerabilities, and developing effective solutions to mitigate them.
This requires the ability to think critically and remain flexible, adapting plans and
strategies as new risks emerge.
(5) Experience and Qualifications: Ideally, the Competent Person should hold relevant
certifications in business continuity (such as NCEMA 7000 and/or ISO 22301 Lead
Implementer or Manager certifications) and have prior experience in managing business

continuity or emergency planning efforts within complex operational environments
such as airports.

title: Business continuity
text:
BUSINESS CONTINUITY PLANNING COMMITTEE
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) The Airport Business Continuity Planning (BCP) Committee is responsible for overseeing and
implementing business continuity strategies to ensure airport operations continue
uninterrupted during disruptive events. Airports, as vital transportation and commerce hubs,
must be prepared to withstand various risks including natural disasters, cyber-attacks, and
operational disruptions. The Committee plays a key role in safeguarding the airport's
infrastructure, personnel, and services, ensuring both safety and efficiency during and after an
incident.
2. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
(a) The primary purpose of the Airport BCP Committee is to develop, implement, and monitor a
comprehensive business continuity management system (BCMS) tailored to the unique
challenges of the airport environment. This system is designed to mitigate disruptions,
maintain critical airport operations, and facilitate swift recovery to minimize downtime and
maintain passenger confidence and safety.
(b) The Committee's scope covers all areas of airport operations, including air traffic
management, passenger services, security, ground handling, baggage systems, cargo services,
fuel supply, and communication with external stakeholders such as airlines, regulatory
authorities, and emergency responders.
3. ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
(a) The Airport BCP Committee comprises senior management from key departments, including
but not limited to:
(1) operations,
(2) safety,
(3) security,
(4)  IT,
(5) communications, and
(6) human resources, as well as representatives from external partners such as airlines and
government authorities.

4. RISK IDENTIFICATION AND IMPACT ANALYSIS
(a) In compliance with NCEMA 7000 and ISO 22301 requirements, the Committee conducts a
detailed risk assessment to identify potential threats to airport operations. This includes
evaluating natural hazards (e.g., severe weather, earthquakes), technological risks (e.g., cyber-
attacks, system failures), and operational challenges (e.g., strikes, fuel shortages). A
comprehensive Business Impact Analysis (BIA) is carried out to understand the criticality of
various airport functions and the potential consequences of disruptions. Based on these
assessments, the Committee identifies priorities for recovery and sets recovery time
objectives (RTOs) for each operational area.
5. DEVELOPMENT OF THE BUSINESS CONTINUITY PLAN (BCP):
(a) The Committee leads the development of the airport's BCP, which outlines step-by-step
procedures for responding to and recovering from incidents. The plan includes detailed
strategies for maintaining essential functions such as airfield operations, terminal
management, passenger processing, and emergency services. The BCP is designed to be
flexible and adaptable, ensuring that it can respond to a variety of scenarios, whether they
involve immediate safety concerns or long-term infrastructure damage.
6. COORDINATION WITH STAKEHOLDERS:
(a) Airports rely on numerous external partners, including airlines, government agencies, and
service providers. The Committee ensures ongoing collaboration with these stakeholders,
fostering strong communication and shared continuity planning efforts. This coordination is
essential for a unified response during an emergency and for ensuring that external
stakeholders are aligned with the airport's recovery timelines and strategies.
7. RESOURCE ALLOCATION AND MANAGEMENT:
(a) The BCP Committee is responsible for identifying and allocating the resources needed to
ensure the airport can respond effectively during an incident. This includes maintaining access
to backup systems, emergency supplies, and trained staff prepared to implement continuity
measures.
8. TRAINING, AWARENESS, AND PREPAREDNESS:
(a) The Committee ensures that all airport staff are aware of the BCP and their respective roles
during a disruption. This involves regular training programs, simulations, and emergency drills
that test the airport's ability to respond to incidents in real time.
9. PLAN TESTING AND EVALUATION:

(a) Continuous testing and review of the airport's BCP are key responsibilities of the Committee.
The plan is tested through a variety of exercises, such as live simulations of operational
disruptions, IT system failures, and emergency evacuations. After each test, the Committee
evaluates the effectiveness of the response and recovery efforts, identifies areas for
improvement, and updates the BCP accordingly. Regular reviews also ensure that the plan
remains current.

title: Business continuity
text:
ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING A BUSINESS CONTINUITY PLAN
(a) Guidance in establishing and implementing a business continuity plan can be referred to
either:
(1) UAE National Business Continuity Management System AE/SCNS/NCEMA 7000. This
document is developed for the concerned organizations in all sectors to comply with
The National Standard For Business Continuity Management System by implementing
the requirements of this standard, thereby enhancing the capacity of the UAE business
community to cope with emergencies and crises, and this standard enables employees,
through the training programs and applied models, to achieve comprehensive
knowledge in business continuity management in accordance with the concept of vital
functions in the organization; and/or

(2) ISO 22301 Security and resilience Business continuity management systems
Requirements. ISO 22301 is the international standard for Business Continuity
Management Systems (BCMS). It provides a framework for organizations to plan,
establish, implement, operate, monitor, review, maintain, and continually improve a
documented management system to protect against, reduce the likelihood of, and
ensure recovery from disruptive incidents. This standard is crucial for organizations to
enhance their resilience against various unforeseen disruptions, ensuring continuity of
operations and services. It helps in identifying risks, preparing for emergencies, and
improving recovery time.

title: Emergency planning
text:
AERODROME EMERGENCY PLANNING
(a) An aerodrome operator shall establish and implement an emergency plan that is in
accordance with aerodrome certification requirements stated in CAR AGA PART ADR, that
ensure:
(1) the plan commensurate with the type of aircraft operations and other activities
conducted at an aerodrome;
(2) sufficient emergency planning arrangements are provided at an aerodrome;
(3) the plan provides for the command, control, coordination and communication of the
actions to be taken in an emergency occurring at an aerodrome or in its vicinity;
(4) the plan coordinates the response or participation of all existing agencies which, in the
opinion of the aerodrome operator, could be of assistance in responding to an
emergency; and
(5) the plan observes human factors principles to ensure optimum response by all existing
agencies participating in emergency operations.
(b) The aerodrome emergency plan shall be submitted to the GCAA for acceptance, as part of the
initial certification and subsequent changes to the emergency plan shall be managed
according to the aerodrome operator’s safety management system.

title: Emergency planning

CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS
(a) An aerodrome emergency plan is an essential component of the aerodrome operator’s overall
safety management system in demonstrating the level of emergency preparedness and
readiness in planning and dealing with the onset and aftermath of aviation emergencies
occurring at an aerodrome and its immediate vicinity. The emergency plan is an essential
document for the initial and continued validity of an aerodrome certificate or landing area
acceptance, in accordance with CAR AGA PART ADR Certification Requirements.

title: Emergency planning
text:
PURPOSE AND OBJECTIVE OF EMERGENCY PLANNING
(a) Aerodrome emergency planning is the process of preparing an aerodrome to cope with an
emergency occurring at an aerodrome or in its vicinity. The objective of aerodrome
emergency planning is to minimize the effects of an emergency, particularly in respect of
saving lives and maintaining aircraft operations.

(b) The aerodrome emergency plan sets forth the procedures for coordinating the response of
different aerodrome agencies (or services) and of those agencies in the surrounding
community that could be of assistance in responding to the emergency.
(c) The emergency plan is a critical component of the overall aerodrome’s safety management
system and its effectiveness heavily relies on the plan’s commensurability with the size,
complexities, risks and hazards of the types of aircraft operations and other operational
activities conducted at an aerodrome. The efficacy of the plan is dependent on
comprehensiveness of the emergency orders/instructions, response protocols and risk
mitigation measures.
(d) To be operationally sound, a comprehensive aerodrome emergency plan (see Figure-1) should
consider:

Figure-1: Comprehensive aerodrome emergency planning framework
(1) preplanning BEFORE an emergency;
(i) “Before the emergency” considerations include planning for the handling of all
factors that could bear upon effective emergency response. Preplanning should
define the organizational authority and the responsibilities for developing, testing
and implementing the emergency plan.
(2) operations DURING the emergency;
(i) “During the emergency” considerations depend on the stage, nature and location of
the emergency. The situation may change as the rescue work progresses. (For
example, while the aerodrome fire chief or designee would normally be the first
person in command of the emergency forces, this officer may thereafter become
one of several staff officers as other responding officers from other agencies assume
their specified roles at the command post under the jurisdiction of the designated
“on-scene” commander.); and
(3) support and documentation AFTER the emergency:
(i) “After the emergency” considerations may not carry the urgency of preceding
events, but transitions of authority and responsibility at the scene need to be
thoroughly discussed and planned in advance. Some personnel, who in early stages
PRE-PLANNING
BEFORE THE
EMERGENCY
OPERATIONS DURING
THE EMERGENCY
SUPPORT AND
DOCUMENTATION
AFTER THE
EMERGENCY

have a direct operational assignment, subsequently may be required to remain on
the scene and may assume a supportive role (i.e. police/security personnel, rescue
and firefighting personnel, aerodrome operator and public works). Thus, it is also
necessary to pre-plan for such supportive services, and to consider problems related
to restoring or maintaining protective services to permit continuation of normal
aerodrome/aircraft operations which may have been disrupted by the emergency.
The need to communicate the termination of the emergency to supporting agencies
(hospitals, ambulances, etc.) so they can return to “normal” operation should also
be considered. Documentation of the various operations in an emergency is an aid
to the gathering and organizing of data for various post-accident/incident reports. It
also can provide the structure for a critique of the emergency and can be used as a
format for improving the procedures and arrangements in the emergency plan.
(e) In some cases, the aerodrome emergency plan is part of an organisation’s integrated Crisis
Management Plan, and the responsibility for its development is assigned to another
organisation, different from the aerodrome certificate holder. However, this does not prevent
the aerodrome operator from preparing its own local emergency plan describing the actions
that should be taken during an emergency, in cooperation with the organisation, which are
responsible for the overall crisis plan.
(f) Irrespective of whose responsibility is the establishment and implementation of an emergency
plan covering emergencies at or in the surroundings of an aerodrome, the emergency plan
should ensure that there are provisions for:
(1) orderly and efficient transition from normal to emergency operations;
(2) delegation of authority;
(3) assignment of emergency responsibilities;
(4) authorising key personnel for actions contained in the plan;
(5) coordination of efforts to cope with the emergency; and
(6) safe continuation of aircraft operations or return to normal operations as soon as
possible.
(g) Further guidance material in establishing aerodrome emergency planning is given in the ICAO
Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 7 – Aerodrome emergency planning.

title: Emergency planning
text:
PLANNING AND TAILORING THE AERODROME EMERGENCY PLAN

(a) An aerodrome emergency plan is an important aspect of the aerodrome operator ’s safety
management system. An emergency plan should be appropriately scaled and relevant to the
hazards and risks arising from the different types of aircraft operations and operational
activities conducted at an aerodrome. Considerations for the planning and tailoring the
aerodrome emergency plan can be achieved by:
(1) Understanding Operations: Thoroughly understand the types of aircraft operations and
activities conducted at an aerodrome. This includes the types and sizes of aircraft, the
volume of traffic, cargo operations, passenger services, and any special activities such as
maintenance or training flights.
(2) Risk-Based Approach: Use a risk-based approach to identify and assess potential
hazards and threats specific to the aerodrome's operations. This ensures that the
emergency plan addresses the most significant risks and is tailored to the specific
operational environment. Conducting a risk/hazard analysis can assist an aerodrome
operator in this aspect.
(3) Considering Aircraft Types and Sizes: The emergency plan should account for the
different types and sizes of aircraft e.g. fuel-based, electric, hydrogen, etc, that operate
at an aerodrome. Larger aircraft may require more extensive firefighting resources and
medical support, while smaller aircraft might have different evacuation and rescue
requirements.
(4) Traffic Volume: Higher traffic volumes increase the likelihood of incidents and
necessitate more robust emergency response capabilities. The plan should include
provisions for managing multiple simultaneous incidents and ensuring sufficient
resources are available. Periodic assessment of traffic volume may be necessary.
(5) Passenger Services: If the aerodrome handles large numbers of passengers, the
emergency plan should include specific measures for mass evacuation, crowd control,
and providing medical care and shelter to affected individuals.
(6) Cargo Operations: For aerodromes with significant cargo operations, the plan should
address potential hazards associated with hazardous materials, large freight loads, and
specialized cargo handling equipment.
(7) Special Activities: If the aerodrome supports special activities such as fuelling,
maintenance, training, or military operations, the emergency plan should incorporate
procedures to handle specific risks associated with these activities, such as training
accidents or hazardous material spills during maintenance.

text:
AERODROME EMERGENCY PLANNING COMMITTEE
1. ESTABLISHING AN AERODROME EMERGENCY PLANNING COMMITTEE
(a) Depending on the size, complexity of the aerodrome and availability of different mutual aid
agencies, aerodrome operator may consider further dividing the AEPC into two main groups -
strategic level attended by senior management personnel and operational level attended by
working level personnel, to manage the committee proceedings effectively. Forming sub-
committees to further support the works of the AEPC may be consider including, but are not
limited to:
(1) a review committee;
(2) an exercise committee; and
(3) a welfare committee, etc.
2. RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE AEPC
(a) The AEPC is primarily responsible for assisting the aerodrome operator in:
(1) preparing, accepting, and maintaining the AEP for the aerodrome;
(2) developing emergency response arrangements based on the identification and
availability of emergency resources at, and in the vicinity of the aerodrome;
(3) establishing an exercise programme to periodically test the AEP; and
(4) revising and updating the AEP.
3. REPRESENTATION ON THE AEPC
(a) The AEPC should include representation from:
(1) local police service
(2) local fire service
(3) Local hospital or ambulance service;
(4) air traffic control;
(5) ground handling services; and
(6) any other agencies that may be required to assist in an emergency, as appropriate.
(b) Airlines and other support agencies should also be considered for inclusion on the AEPC

4. FREQUENCY OF AEPC MEETINGS
(a) At least once a year, the AEPC is to meet to review the adequacy of the AEP, and following
each occasion of:
(1) the plan being activated;
(2) a test or exercise being held; and
(3) where the currency and procedural validity of the AEP needs to be addressed.
(b) A senior member of the aerodrome operator should chair the AEPC meetings, and a Terms of
Reference should be established to ensure all committee members have a common
understanding of their roles and responsibilities.
(c) A record of meeting should be documented and retained by the aerodrome operator for a
minimum period of five years.

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY PLAN DOCUMENT

(a) In order to ensure that an aerodrome emergency plan document fully serves its purpose, it
should include the following:
(1) clear incident command and control policies and procedures.
(2) examples of emergencies are: aircraft emergencies, sabotage including bomb threats,
unlawfully seized aircraft, dangerous goods occurrences, building fires, natural disaster
and public health emergencies.
(3) examples of public health emergencies are increased risk of travellers or cargo
spreading a serious communicable disease internationally through air transport and
severe outbreak of a communicable disease potentially affecting a large proportion of
aerodrome staff.
(4) details of tests for aerodrome facilities and equipment to be used in emergencies such
as emergency operations centre, mobile command centre, firefighting vehicles and
equipment, communication means, first aid medical supplies, etc., including the
frequency of those tests;
(5) details of exercises to test emergency plans, including the frequency of those exercises;
(6) a list of organisations, agencies, and persons of authority, both on and off-aerodrome,
for site roles; their telephone and fax numbers, e-mail and addresses, and the radio
frequencies of their offices;
(7) the establishment of an aerodrome emergency planning committee to review incidents,
discuss tactics, liaison, co-operative training, exercise planning, etc;
(8) the appointment of an aerodrome incident commander for the overall emergency
operation; and
(9) details of the off-aerodrome areas for which the aerodrome ARFFS will provide a
response, and the size and nature of the response.

title: Emergency planning
text:
CONTENTS OF EMERGENCY PLAN DOCUMENT
(a) This guide is to assists an aerodrome operator in developing the contents of an aerodrome
emergency plan.
1. EMERGENCY PLAN
The purpose of the aerodrome emergency plan document is to provide all the required
information to agencies and staff involved in an emergency. The document should be structured

in such a manner, that the required information is easily identifiable. For that purpose, the
structure of the aerodrome emergency plan should be as follows:
2. COVER PAGE
The cover page has the title of the plan. It should include a date and identify the jurisdiction(s)
covered by the plan.
3. ACCEPTANCE PAGE
The GCAA’s acceptance is included in this page.
4. IMPLEMENTATION PAGE
Implementation page introduces the plan, outlines its applicability, and indicates that it
supersedes all previous plans. It should include a delegation of authority for specific modifications
that can be made to the plan and by whom they can be made without the senior official’s
signature. It should also include a date and should be signed by the Accountable Manager.
5. AMENDMENT RECORDS
Each update or change to the plan should be tracked. The record of changes, usually in table
format, contains, at a minimum, a change number, the date of the change, the name of the
person who made the change, and a summary of the change. Other relevant information could be
considered.
6. DISTRIBUTION RECORDS
The record of distribution, usually in table format, indicates the title and the name of the person
receiving the plan, the agency to which the recipient belongs, the date of delivery, and the
number of copies delivered. Other relevant information could be considered. The record of
distribution can be used to prove that tasked individuals and organizations have acknowledged
their receipt, review, and/or acceptance of the plan. Copies of the plan can be made available to
the relevant stakeholders.
7. TABLE OF CONTENTS
The table of contents should be a logically ordered and clearly identified layout of the major
sections and subsections of the plan that will make finding information within the plan easier.
8. INTRODUCTION – PURPOSE, SCOPE AND OVERVIEW
Purpose.
The purpose sets the foundation for the rest of the AEP. The basic plan’s purpose is a general
statement of what the AEP is meant to do. The statement should be supported by a brief synopsis
of the basic plan and annexes.
Scope.

The AEP should also explicitly state the scope of emergency and disaster response and the entities
(e.g., departments, agencies, private sector, citizens) and geographic areas to which the plan
applies.
Situation Overview.
The situation section characterizes the “planning environment,” making it clear why an AEP is
necessary. The level of detail is a matter of judgment; some information may be limited to a few
specific annexes and presented there. At a minimum, the situation section should summarize
hazards faced by the jurisdiction and discuss how the jurisdiction expects to receive (or provide)
assistance within its regional response structures. The situation section covers a general
discussion of:
• Relative probability and impact of the hazards
• Geographic areas likely to be affected by particular hazards
• Vulnerable critical facilities (e.g., nursing homes, schools, hospitals, infrastructure)
• Dependencies on other jurisdictions for critical resources
• The process used by the jurisdiction to determine its capabilities and limits in order to
prepare for and respond to the defined hazards
• The actions taken in advance to minimize an incident’s impacts, including short- and
long-term strategies.
9. CONCEPT OF OPERATIONS
AEP stakeholders need to be able to visualize the sequence and scope of the planned emergency
response. The CONOPS section is a written or graphic statement that explains in broad terms the
aerodrome operator ’s intent with regard to an emergency operation. The CONOPS should
describe how the response organization accomplishes a mission or set of objectives in order to
reach a desired end-state. Ideally, it offers clear methodology to realize the goals and objectives
to execute the plan. This may include a brief discussion of the activation levels identified by the
jurisdiction for its operations centre. The CONOPS should briefly address direction and control,
alert and warning, and continuity matters that may be dealt with more fully in annexes. CONOPS
is especially important for aerodrome dealing with multiple runway incidents. See guidance at GM

title: PERSONS OF AUTHORITY — SITE ROLES
text:
To include, but not limited to, the following, according to local requirements:
• On-aerodrome:
o Aerodrome ARFFS chief fire officer or the most senior ARFFS officer is the incident
commander (IC);
o Aerodrome authority;
o Police and security — Officer-in-charge; and
o Medical coordinator.
• Off-aerodrome:
o Local fire service chief fire officer or the most senior fire officer - the IC will be
designated as required from within the pre-arranged mutual aid emergency
agreement;
o Police and security service — officer-in-charge;
o Ambulance and medical service — officer-in-charge; and
o Other government authorities.
10. PLAN DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE

This section discusses the overall approach to planning and the assignment of plan development
and
maintenance responsibilities. This section should, at least, include:
• Describe the planning process, participants in that process, and how development and
revision of different “levels” of the AEP (plan, annexes, etc) are coordinated during the
preparedness phase;
• Assign responsibility for the overall planning and coordination to a specific position; and
• Provide for a regular cycle of training, evaluating, reviewing, and updating of the AEP.
11. SUPPORTING ANNEXES
What follows is a discussion of the purpose and potential content of supporting annexes to the
emergency plan. For consistency, the recommended structure for all annexes is the same as that
of the plan.
• Incident command structure;
• Alerting and notification structure;
• Communication network;
• Grid map;
• Community map;
• Water response map (if any); and
• Other enclosures.

title: Emergency planning
text:
1. TYPES OF EMERGENCIES
(a) At least the following types of emergencies may be included in the aerodrome emergency plan:
(1) Aircraft emergencies – within aerodrome and its immediate vicinity;
(2) Aircraft ground incidents;
(3) Sabotage, including bomb threats;
(4) Unlawfully seized aircraft;
(5) Dangerous goods occurrences;
(6) Building fires;
(7) Natural disasters; and
(8) Public health emergencies.
2. AIRCRAFT EMERGENCIES

(a) The aircraft emergencies for which services may be required are generally classified as:
(1) ‘Aircraft Accident’: an aircraft accident which has occurred on or in the aerodrome
surroundings;
(2) ‘Full Emergency’: an aircraft approaching the aerodrome is, or is suspected to be, in such
trouble that there is imminent danger of an accident; and
(3) ‘Local Standby’: an aircraft approaching the aerodrome is known. or is suspected to have
developed some defect, but the trouble is not such as would normally involve any serious
difficulty in effecting a safe landing; and
(4) ‘Aircraft Ground Incident’: where an aircraft on the ground is known to have an emergency
situation other than an accident, requiring the attendance of emergency services; and
(5) ‘Weather Standby: when weather conditions are such as to render a landing difficult or
difficult to observe.
3.  DOMESTIC EMERGENCY
(a) The classification ‘Domestic Emergency’ is given to any non-aircraft related emergencies such as
fire or emergency involving building, structural, road/baggage tunnel, fuel storage facility,
maintenance hangar, road traffic collision, etc.:
(1) On the aerodrome not included in the categories above.
(2) Outside the aerodrome boundary (other than aircraft accidents) which is liable to constitute
a danger to flying or aerodrome property.
(3) Which the Aerodrome Rescue and Fire Fighting Service should attend:
(i) according to an agreement with the local fire authority;
(ii) in response to calls for the public or police on humanitarian grounds.
4. OTHER EMERGENCY DUTIES
(a) The principal objective of the Aerodrome Rescue and Fire Fighting Service (ARFFS) personnel and
equipment is to deal with aircraft accidents and rescue of people involved. Equipment and
techniques recommended are generally directed towards this goal. However, aerodrome ARFFS
personnel may be called upon to perform other duties that occur such as weather standbys
(sometimes confined to standbys in conditions of poor visibility), domestic fires, special services
or to provide precautionary cover during hazardous operations, e.g. fuel flow tests.
(b) Aerodrome operator s should include the action to be taken by the ARFFS and external
emergency services in the event of such calls being received in the emergency plan.
5. UNLAWFUL ACTS OF INTERFERENCE

(a) Action to be taken in the case of any unlawful act will be contained in the aerodromes
contingency plan which will be drawn up in conjunction with the local Police Authority.
6. OFF-AERODROME ACCIDENTS
(a) The aerodrome operator should ensure that emergency orders contain details of the action to
be taken in the case of aerodrome accidents occurring outside the aerodrome boundaries
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
1. EMERGENCY ORDERS AND INSTRUCTIONS
(a) A set of emergency orders and instructions should be developed to ensure prompt response of
rescue and firefighting, law enforcement, police/security, medical services, other agencies on
and off the aerodrome and other competent, trained, expert personnel, sufficient to meet all
unusual conditions.
Note: - Emergency orders are high-level statements of actions and emergency instructions are
detailed course of actions to carry out the orders.
2. AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT ON THE AERODROME
(a) General
The aerodrome emergency plan should be implemented immediately upon an aircraft accident
occurring on the aerodrome. For this type of emergency, responding agencies are expected to take
action as described below.
(b) Action by air traffic services
(1) Initiate emergency response by using the crash alarm communication system.
(2) Notify the rescue and firefighting service and provide information on the location of the
accident, grid map reference and all other essential details, including time of the accident
and type of aircraft. Subsequent notification may expand this information by providing
details on the number of occupants, fuel on board, aircraft operator, and any dangerous
goods on board, including quantity and location, if known.
(3) Close the affected runway and minimize vehicle traffic on that runway to prevent
disturbance of accident investigation evidence.
(4) If required, initiate communications to the police and security services, operator, and
medical services in accordance with the procedure in the aerodrome emergency plan.
Provide the contacts with grid map reference, rendezvous point and/or staging area and
aerodrome entrance to be used.
(5) Issue the following Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) immediately:

(i) “Aerodrome rescue and firefighting service protection unavailable until (time) or
until further notice. All equipment committed to aircraft accident.”
(6) Verify by written checklist that the actions above were completed, indicating notification
time(s) and name of person completing action.
(c) Action by aerodrome rescue and firefighting services
(1) A request to respond to an aircraft accident on the aerodrome will normally be issued by the
air traffic services.
(2) When, however, a call is received from any other person, an accident is observed, or there is
reason to consider that an accident is imminent, the aerodrome rescue and firefighting
service will take action in the same manner as if the air traffic services had originated the
request. The air traffic services will then be informed of the nature of the request/call and of
the response initiated.
(3) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services shall:
(i) proceed via fastest access routes to the site indicated by air traffic services;
(ii) advise mutual aid fire department(s) while en-route of the following:
(A) rendezvous point;
(B) staging area;
(iii) human resources and equipment required for support, if known;
(iv) any other pertinent information; and
(v) immediately establish a well identified command post. This is a temporary post
until the mobile command post is available and operative.
(4) The aerodrome incident commander is the responsible officer in charge until the emergency
has been stabilized.
(5) An aircraft/structural fire is unique because of the fire control problems with the presence
of highly flammable fuel and the high structures normally found on an aerodrome. Control
of the combined aircraft/structural fire will be predicated on mutual aid emergency
agreements.
(6) Prior agreement should be reached between the on-aerodrome rescue and firefighting
service and the off aerodrome mutual aid fire departments as to which is best equipped to
fight fires in aircraft hangars or other aerodrome structures.
(7) Additionally, there should be prior agreement as to which agency will be in command when
an accident involves an aircraft and an aerodrome structure.
(d) Action by police and security services

(1) The first security/police officer to arrive, in co-ordination with the on-scene commander, will
assume security responsibility, immediately establish free traffic lanes on ingress and egress
roads for emergency vehicles, and request reinforcements as needed. This officer shall
remain in command of security until relieved by the law enforcement authority who has
jurisdiction over the area.
(2) Security personnel should establish an ambulance route to the triage area to enable those
vehicles to proceed to the area, load and depart in an orderly line. The route should provide
for the continuous, unobstructed flow of emergency vehicles without blockage or reversal
into the casualty pick up area.
(3) Security personnel and police will be needed to handle traffic in the vicinity of the accident
site, to admit authorized emergency personnel, to keep unauthorized persons from the
accident site, and to assume custody of personal effects removed from the aircraft.
(4) Normal traffic should be routed away from or around the accident site.
(5) The emergency site shall be cordoned off as soon as possible to exclude intruders, press,
sightseers, onlookers and souvenir hunters. Appropriate markings shall be prominently
displayed to advise all persons of possible hazards which may cause them serious injury
should they encroach on the area.
(6) Communications between all security check points and the command post and/or
emergency operations centre should be implemented as soon as possible.
(7) Notification of other agencies as shown in Figure-2 should be carried out as soon as possible.

Figure-2: Chart showing notification of agencies
(8) Identifying arm bands, site passes, or I.D. tags should be issued by the controlling authority
and monitored by the security police officer and the security police team.
(9) Special security provisions are necessary to protect the flight data and cockpit voice
recorders. Additional security should be effected to protect any mail involved, secure any
dangerous goods which may be present, or to protect personnel from exposure to
radioactive materials.
(e) Action by aerodrome operator

(1) The aerodrome operator will go to the accident site and, when required, set up an easily
identifiable mobile command post. The mobile command post should be sufficiently staffed
by senior representatives capable of making decisions involving:
(i) aerodrome operations;
(ii) security operations;
(iii) medical operations;
(iv) aircraft operations; and
(v) aircraft recovery operations.
(2) The aerodrome operator will review the action checklist to verify that:
(i) the aerodrome emergency operations centre has been activated;
(ii) mutual aid police procedures have been initiated and secondary notification calls
have been made;
(iii) mutual aid fire departments have been notified and escort has been provided for
their access to the accident site and staging areas designated;
(iv) d) medical and ambulance services have been alerted and their arrivals at the
designated rendezvous point or staging area have been verified;
(v) the affected aircraft operator has been notified and information obtained
concerning any dangerous goods on board the aircraft (e.g. explosives, compressed
or liquified gases, flammable liquids or solids, oxidizers,
(vi) poisonous substances, infectious substances, radioactive materials or corrosives),
and this information has been passed on to appropriate participants;
(vii) liaison has been established with air traffic services concerning the closure of
aerodrome areas, designation of emergency response corridors, issuing of voice
advisories and NOTAM advising of reduced aerodrome rescue and firefighting
protection;
(viii) government aircraft accident investigation authorities have been notified;
(ix) the meteorological department has been notified to make a special weather
observation;
(x) arrangements have been made for the immediate survey and photography of the
affected runway to identify the location of crash debris;
(xi) arrangements have been made to secure the crash debris pending release by the
investigating agencies;
(xii) airspace reservation co-ordination offices (air traffic flow control office), if any,
have been advised of reduced aerodrome capabilities; and

(xiii) if fatalities are involved, the Medical Examiner has been notified and temporary
morgue facilities designated.
(3) In conjunction with mutual aid police, the aerodrome operator should:
(i) designate rendezvous points and staging areas for the inner and outer perimeters;
(ii) assign security personnel at the staging area and/or rendezvous point to escort
vehicles so as to ensure the orderly flow of emergency vehicles, particularly
ambulances, to and from the accident site; and
(iii) assign staging areas for escort vehicles and ambulances to ensure rapid dispatch.
(4) After consulting with the chief fire officer in charge, the aerodrome operator shall co-
ordinate the activities of mutual aid rescue personnel and direct their activities to maximize
their efforts.
(5) The aerodrome operator should also arrange the availability of the following services as
required:
(i) portable emergency shelter for use by other than medical services;
(ii) lavatories;
(iii) drinking water;
(iv) ropes, barriers, etc.;
(v) food service;
(vi) mobile or portable lighting;
(vii) portable heating system;
(viii) cones, stakes, and signs;
(ix) machinery, heavy equipment, extraction tools;
(x) hydraulic extraction tools and shoring materials; and
(xi) communications equipment, such as megaphones, portable telephones, etc.
(6) The aerodrome operator will provide the initial briefing for the aerodrome public
information officer and will then co-ordinate with the public information officer of the
aircraft operator involved, when appropriate, any press releases and statements to the
press.
(7) Upon concurrence of the chief fire officer, police/security chief and the medical co-
ordinator, the aerodrome operator 's on-scene commander will notify all participating
mutual aid organizations upon termination of the aerodrome emergency.
(f) Action by medical services
(1) It shall be the responsibility of the medical co-ordinator to supervise the medical services
and to:

(i) verify the notification of mutual aid medical and ambulance services and their
subsequent arrival at the rendezvous point or staging area;
(ii) organize the necessary actions for triage, treatment of the casualties, and their
eventual evacuation by appropriate means of transportation;
(iii) control the flow of casualties and ensure, together with the transportation officer,
the dispatch of the casualties to the appropriate hospitals by all available means of
transportation;
(iv) maintain an accurate list of the casualties including their names and their final
disposition;
(v) co-ordinate the transportation of the uninjured to the designated holding area
with the aircraft operator concerned;
(vi) provide medical evaluation of ambulatory and uninjured survivors;
(vii) arrange for the replenishment of medical supplies, if necessary; and
(viii) organize, with the police, reception facilities for the dead.
(g) Action by hospitals
(1) Appoint a hospital co-ordinator responsible for the following:
(i) immediately provide and transport doctors and medical teams skilled in trauma
care to the accident site upon
(ii) notification of the emergency;
(iii) provide medical care to the casualties when they arrive at the treatment area; and
(iv) ensure that sufficient doctors and nurses, operating rooms, intensive care units,
surgical teams, blood and
(v) blood volume expanders are available for emergency situations, including aircraft
accidents.
(h) Action by aircraft operators
(1) The senior aircraft operator representative will report to the mobile command post to co-
ordinate the aircraft operator activities with the person in charge. In the event the aircraft
operator is not an aerodrome tenant, the aerodrome operator should designate the most
capable operator on the aerodrome to handle emergencies involving transient aircraft until
such time as the aircraft operator involved can arrive at the scene.
(2) The senior representative of the aircraft operator will provide information regarding
passenger load, flight crew complement and the existence of any dangerous goods together
with their loading position. Dangerous goods include explosives, compressed or liquified
gases (which may be flammable or toxic), flammable liquids or solids, oxidizers, poisonous

substances, infectious substances, radioactive materials and corrosives. Information
concerning dangerous goods should be relayed, as soon as possible, to the chief fire officer
and the medical co-ordinator.
(3) The senior aircraft operator representative shall make arrangements for transportation of
uninjured persons from the accident site to the designated uninjured holding area.
Transportation of the “walking injured” from the scene should be permitted only after
consultation with the medical co-ordinator.
(4) The aircraft operator staff shall proceed to the designated uninjured holding area. The
senior aircraft operator representative at the uninjured holding area will appoint qualified
receptionists, registrars, and welfare co-ordinators from the staff.
(5) The aircraft operator representative who is in command of the uninjured holding area will
oversee those operations by making arrangements for additional medical services (if
required), commissary items, clothing, telephone facilities, etc.
(6) The receptionists should meet the transporting vehicles as they arrive from the scene of the
accident and direct the passengers to the registrars' tables where they will be processed.
The receptionists should know where toilet facilities are located. Migration from the holding
area should be prevented until each person transported to the holding area is identified and
processed according to the aerodrome emergency plan.
(7) The registrars will record the passenger's name on the manifest and determine desired
reservation requirements, i.e. hotel accommodations, air transportation or other modes of
transportation, etc. Registrars should list any persons to be notified of the passenger's
physical and/or mental condition and potential plans. The registrar will then place an
identification tag or sticker on the passenger. The registrars will direct the passengers to the
welfare co-ordinators when registration has been completed. See Figure-3 for a sample of
registrar form.
