(8) Welfare co-ordinators and mental health specialists trained in stress management should:
(i) give support and comfort to relatives and friends of passengers and crew members
on board the aircraft;
(ii) register relatives and friends waiting at an aerodrome for information about
persons on board; and provide care, comfort, and assistance to the “walking
injured”, uninjured survivors and responding personnel (if required).
(9) The aircraft operator or its representative will provide notification of the aircraft accident to:
(i) health and welfare agencies;
(ii) customs, where applicable;
(iii) immigration, where applicable;
(iv) post office; and
(v) environmental agencies, where applicable.
(10)  A senior aircraft operator official will be responsible for the initial notification of relatives
and friends.

(11)  News releases by aircraft operators will be prepared in co-ordination with the aerodrome
public information officer and liaison officers from other agencies involved in the accident.
(12)  The aircraft operator or its’ appointed person/organisation is responsible for the removal of
the wrecked or disabled aircraft, but only after receiving authorization from the aircraft
accident investigation authority. For further information, refer to ICAO Airport Services
Manual (Doc 9137), Part 5 — Removal of Disabled Aircraft.
(i) Action by government authorities
(1) The following government authorities may be required to take appropriate action as
indicated in their emergency plan:
(i) government accident investigation personnel;
(ii) health and welfare;
(iii) post office;
(iv) customs;
(v) immigration;
(vi) agriculture;
(vii) public works; and
(viii) environmental agencies.
(j) Action by the media/public information officer
(1) All press personnel will be directed to a designated press staging area for press personnel
authorized to cover an aerodrome emergency. At this area the following will be provided:
(i) briefing;
(ii) communications; and
(iii) transportation service to and from the accident site, when permissible.
(2) Only members of the press, free-lance reporters and photographers wearing a valid press
card will be admitted to the briefing area, to the designated press staging area, or
transported to the scene of the accident.
(3) In general, responsibility for news releases concerning an aircraft emergency should be that
of:
(i) a public information officer designated by the aerodrome operator; and
(ii) the representative of the aircraft operator involved.
(4) Under no circumstances will the press or any other personnel not involved in life saving or
firefighting operations be permitted inside security lines until all rescue operations have
been completed. Establishment of security lines should consider the interests of media
coverage as much as rescue operations permit.

3. AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT OFF THE AERODROME
(a) General
The aerodrome emergency plan, as well as the mutual aid emergency agreement, should be
implemented immediately upon an aircraft accident occurring off the aerodrome. For this type of
emergency, responding agencies are expected to take action as described below.
(b) Initial notification
Initial notification of an off-aerodrome accident normally will be made by a witness to the local
police, fire department, or Alarm and Dispatch Centre, if available. The Alarm and Dispatch Centre is
the centralized notification system for any emergency situation that alerts appropriate responding
agencies, depending on the nature of the emergency.
(c) Action by air traffic services
(1) Initiate emergency response by using the alarm communications system. See Figure-4:
Sample Notification Chart for Off Aerodrome Aircraft Accident.
(2) Notify the emergency services having jurisdiction over the area, providing information on
the location of the accident, giving grid map reference and all other essential details. These
details should include the time of accident and the type of aircraft involved. Subsequent
notification may expand this information by giving details on the number of occupants, fuel
on board, aircraft operator, if appropriate, and any dangerous goods on board, including
quantity and location, if known.
(3) Initiate notification of the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service, police and security
services, aerodrome authority, and medical services in accordance with the procedure in the
aerodrome emergency plan, giving grid map reference.
(4) If required, issue the following NOTAM as soon as possible:
(i) “Aerodrome rescue and firefighting service reduced to category (indicate category
number) or zero aerodrome rescue and firefighting category until further notice.”
(5) Confirm that the actions above were completed, by written checklist, indicating notification
time(s) and name of person completing action.
(d) Action by aerodrome rescue and firefighting services
(1) Notification of an aircraft accident off the aerodrome will normally be received from the air
traffic services, local police or local fire departments. Designated vehicles will be sent in
accordance with the existing mutual aid fire department agreement.
(2) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services shall:

(i) proceed via the most suitable access routes to the off-aerodrome accident site in
co-ordination with the local police responsible for ingress and egress roads;
(ii) co-ordinate with mutual aid fire department(s); and
(iii) while en-route, exchange information with the fire department having jurisdiction
over the area concerning:
(A) rendezvous point and/or staging area;
(B) human resources and equipment responding; and
(C) any other pertinent information.
(3) The senior aerodrome rescue and firefighting service officer will report to the senior fire
officer of the local fire authority having jurisdiction over the area and will request
instructions.
(4) Prior agreement should be reached between the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service,
the local fire department in command, and mutual aid fire departments as to which is best
equipped to fight fires involving aircraft and/or structures. Additionally, there should be
agreement as to which agency will act in command when an accident involves both an
aircraft and an aerodrome structure.
(e) Action by police and security services
(1) The first security/police officer to arrive will immediately assume security responsibility,
establish free traffic lanes on ingress and egress roads for emergency vehicles, and request
reinforcements as needed. He shall remain in command of security until relieved by the
appropriate law enforcement authority who has jurisdiction over the area.
(2) Traffic flow and site security are the primary responsibility of police and security personnel.
They should notify the appropriate communications centre of the location of the accident
and available means of access and egress. After consultation with the on-scene commander,
they should initiate traffic control measures in order to aid responding emergency vehicles.
(3) Security personnel and police will be needed to handle traffic in the vicinity of the accident
site and to prevent disturbance of material scattered over the accident site.
(4) The emergency site shall be cordoned off as soon as possible to exclude intruders, press,
sightseers, onlookers and souvenir hunters. Appropriate markings should be displayed
prominently, advising all persons of possible hazards that may cause serious injury should
they encroach on the area. In order to prevent ignition of fuel vapours, flares should not be
used within a distance of approximately 100 m of the accident site.
(5) Communications between all security check points and the command post and/or
emergency operations centre should be implemented as soon as possible.

(6) Notification of other agencies as shown in Figure-4 should be carried out as soon as possible.
(7) Identifying arm bands, site passes, or I.D. tags should be issued by the controlling authority
and monitored by security and police officers.
(8) Special security provisions are necessary to protect the flight data and cockpit voice
recorders, to protect mail, to secure any dangerous goods which may be present, and to
protect personnel from exposure to radioactive materials, if necessary.
(f) Action by aerodrome operator
(1) Agreements for emergency mutual aid with the surrounding community enable the
aerodrome operator to take the following actions:
(i) respond to the accident site;
(ii) activate the aerodrome crisis management centre, emergency operations centre
and the mobile command post (if required);
(iii) extend as much emergency aid as requested by the jurisdiction agency in
command of the off-aerodrome accident/incident;
(iv) notify the aircraft operator involved;
(v) notify other agencies; and
(vi) provide medical equipment and personnel.
(g) Action by medical services
(1) Local fire authority and other local authorities normally will be responsible for organizing the
medical response. However, the medical response from the on-aerodrome medical service
should also be applicable to mass casualty accidents occurring off the aerodrome.
(2) According to the mutual aid emergency agreement with the surrounding community, the
aerodrome operator may provide, if requested and if available, a part of its medical
equipment, supplies (i.e. first aid equipment, stretchers, body bags, mobile shelters, etc.)
and assistance of first-aid personnel at the accident site.
(h) Action by hospitals
(1) Ensure that sufficient doctors, nurses, and operating room, intensive care, and surgical
teams are available for emergency situations, including aircraft accidents.
(2) Provide medical care to the injured when they arrive.
(i) Action by aircraft operators
(1) The senior representative of the aircraft operator or a designee will report to the command
post to co-ordinate the aircraft operator activities with the person in charge.
(2) The senior representative of the aircraft operator will provide information regarding
passenger load, flight crew complement and the existence of any dangerous goods together

with their loading position. Dangerous goods include explosives, compressed or liquified
gases (which may be flammable or toxic), flammable liquids or solids, oxidizers, poisonous
substances, infectious substances, radioactive material or corrosives. Information
concerning dangerous goods should be relayed, as soon as possible, to the chief fire officer
and the medical co-ordinator.
(3) The senior aircraft operator representative shall make arrangements for transportation of
uninjured persons from the accident site to the designated uninjured holding area.
Transportation of the “walking injured” from the scene should be permitted only after
consulting with the medical co-ordinator.
(4) The aircraft operator staff shall proceed to the designated uninjured holding area. The
senior aircraft operator representative at the uninjured holding area will appoint qualified
receptionists, registrars and welfare co-ordinators from staff.
(5) The aircraft operator representative who is in command of the uninjured holding area will
oversee those operations by making arrangements for additional medical services (if
required), commissary items, clothing, telephone facilities, etc.
(6) The receptionists should meet the transportation vehicles as they arrive from the scene of
the accident and direct the passengers to the registrars' tables where they will be processed.
The receptionists should know where support facilities are located, i.e. toilet facilities,
telephones, clothing, drinking water, etc.
(7) The registrars will record the passenger's name on the manifest and determine desired
reservation requirements, i.e. hotel accommodations, air transportation or other modes of
transportation, etc., and any persons to be notified of the passenger's physical and/or
mental condition and potential plans. The registrar will use an identification tag or sticker, to
place on the passenger. The registrars will direct the passengers to the welfare co-ordinators
when registration has been completed.
(8) The aircraft operator will provide notification of the aircraft accident to:
(i) state licensing and accident investigation authorities, as required;
(ii) health and welfare agencies;
(iii) customs, where applicable;
(iv) immigration, where applicable;
(v) post office; and
(vi) environmental agencies.
(9) A senior aircraft operator representative will be responsible for the initial notification of
relatives and friends.

(10)  News releases by aircraft operators will be prepared in co-ordination with the aerodrome
public information officer and liaison officers from other agencies involved in the accident.
(11)  The aircraft operator or its appointed person/organisation is responsible for the removal of
the wrecked or disabled aircraft, but only after receiving authorization from the aircraft
accident investigation authority. For further information refer to ICAO Airport Services
Manual (Doc 9137), Part 5 — Removal of Disabled Aircraft.
(j) Action by government authorities
(1) The following government authorities, after being notified, may be required to take
appropriate action as indicated in their emergency plans:
(i) government accident investigation personnel;
(ii) health and welfare;
(iii) post office;
(iv) customs, immigration and agriculture; and
(v) environmental agencies.
(k) Action by the public information officer
(1) The responsibility for news releases concerning an off-aerodrome emergency should be that
of:
(i) the representative of the aircraft operator;
(ii) a public information officer designated by the particular government authority in
command; and
(iii) a public information representative designated by the aerodrome operator.
(2) Only members of the press, reporters, and photographers wearing valid passes will be
admitted to the briefing area, permitted to the designated press staging area, or transported
to the scene of the emergency.
(3) In general, responsibility for news releases concerning an aircraft emergency should be that
of:
(i) a public information officer designated by the aerodrome operator; and
(ii) the representative of the aircraft operator involved.
(4) Under no circumstances should the media or any other personnel not involved in the
firefighting, rescue or emergency medical care be permitted inside security lines until all
rescue operations have been completed and the area is declared safe for entry by the on-
scene commander/chief fire officer.

4. FULL EMERGENCY
(a) General
The agencies involved in the aerodrome emergency plan should be alerted to “full emergency”
status when it is known that an aircraft approaching the aerodrome is, or is suspected to be, in such
trouble that there is a possibility of an accident.
(b) Action by air traffic services
(1) Notify the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service to stand by at the predetermined ready
positions applicable to the planned runway and provide as many of the following details as
possible:
(i) type of aircraft;

(ii) fuel on board;
(iii) number of occupants, including special occupants — handicapped, immobilized,
blind, deaf;
(iv) nature of trouble;
(v) planned runway;
(vi) estimated time of landing;
(vii) aircraft operator, if appropriate; and
(viii) any dangerous goods on board, including quantity and location, if known.
(2) Initiate notification of the mutual aid fire department(s) and other appropriate organizations
in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the aerodrome emergency plan, providing, if
necessary, the rendezvous point and aerodrome entrance to be used.
(c) Action by other agencies
(1) The specific responsibilities and roles of the various agencies corresponding to an aircraft
accident on the aerodrome can be paralleled for “full emergency” as required by local
operating requirements.
5. LOCAL STANDBY
(a) General
(1) The agencies involved in the aerodrome emergency plan should be alerted to “local
standby” status when an aircraft approaching the aerodrome is known or is suspected to
have developed some defect but the trouble is not such as would normally involve any
serious difficulty in effecting a safe landing.
(b) Action by air traffic services
(1) Notify the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service to stand by as requested by the pilot,
or stand by as local aerodrome agreements require at the predetermined ready positions
applicable to the runway to be used. Provide as many of the following details as possible:
(i) type of aircraft;
(ii) fuel on board;
(iii) number of occupants, including special occupants — handicapped, immobilized,
blind, deaf;
(iv) nature of trouble;
(v) planned runway;
(vi) estimated time of landing;
(vii) aircraft operator, if appropriate; and

(viii) any dangerous goods on board, including quantity and location, if known.
(c) Action by other agencies
(1) The specific responsibilities and roles of the various agencies corresponding to an aircraft
accident on the aerodrome can be paralleled for “local standby” as required by local
operating requirements.
6. AIRCRAFT GROUND INCIDENTS
(a) General
(1) The agencies involved in the aerodrome emergency plan should be alerted to “aircraft
ground incident” status when an aircraft on the movement area is in difficulty or is involved
in an incident (whether or not another aircraft, vehicle or personnel is concerned).
(b) Action by air traffic services
(1) Notify the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service to stand by as requested by the pilot,
or stand by as local aerodrome agreements require at the predetermined ready positions
applicable to the runway to be used. Provide as many of the following details as possible:
(i) type of aircraft;
(ii) fuel on board;
(iii) number of occupants, including special occupants — handicapped, immobilized,
blind, deaf;
(iv) nature of trouble;
(v) planned runway;
(vi) estimated time of landing;
(vii) aircraft operator, if appropriate; and
(viii) any dangerous goods on board, including quantity and location, if known.
(c) Action by other agencies
(1) The specific responsibilities and roles of the various agencies corresponding to an aircraft
ground incident on the aerodrome are dependent on the severity of the incident as required
by local operating requirements.
7. NON-AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT-RELATED AERODROME EMERGENCIES
(a) General
(1) Procedures and techniques developed for responding to non-aircraft accident-related
aerodrome emergencies should be similar to the techniques in handling aircraft accident
emergencies. It should be recognized that medical and fire emergencies can arise at any
location where large numbers of persons work or congregate. This problem can be severe at

aerodromes because of the exposure associated with commonplace activities, such as
arriving and departing passengers and sightseers, and the use of public service facilities (i.e.
automobile movement and parking areas, restaurants, bars, baggage handling and storage
areas, etc.). Additionally, aerodromes can be selected by malcontents as locations to
demonstrate their anger against any group or activity.
(2) The diverse character of persons travelling by air suggests the need for the aerodrome
operator to arrange to have available emergency medical services to treat conditions such as
cardiac arrest, abdominal pains, burns, cuts, abrasions, and other medical problems. Such
conditions may require immediate care facilities and detailed mutual aid plans with outside
agencies.
8. UNLAWFUL ACTS AGAINST CIVIL AVIATION
(a) General
(1) Detailed information on procedures for dealing with unlawful interference is given in the
Aerodrome Security Plan. The subsequent responsibilities and roles of the various agencies
for responding to an emergency should be developed, as required, in accordance with
Aerodrome Security Plan requirements and procedures. For further guidance refer to ICAO
Security Manual.
(2) An aircraft which is subjected to a threat of sabotage or unlawful seizure should be parked
at an isolated aircraft parking position until the act of unlawful interference is terminated.
Such an area should be located at least 100 m away from other aircraft parking positions,
buildings or public areas as specified in ICAO Annex 14. In such cases it may be necessary to
evacuate passengers without the aid of loading ramps provided at the passenger terminal.
Motorized loading ramps may be available which could be driven to the site; otherwise,
built-in aircraft stairs or the aircraft slides may be used.
9. OCCURRENCES INVOLVING DANGEROUS GOODS
(a) General
(1) Detailed information on procedures for dealing with Occurrences Involving Dangerous
Goods is given in the ICAO Emergency Response Guidance for Aircraft Incidents involving
Dangerous Goods (Doc 9481).
(2) Many types of dangerous goods can be shipped by air. These include explosives, compressed
or liquified gases (which may be flammable or toxic), flammable liquids or solids, oxidizers,
poisonous substances, infectious substances, radioactive material or corrosives. Packages
containing dangerous goods may be found in aerodrome cargo buildings, on aircraft loading

ramps, in aircraft cargo compartments, etc. Rescue and firefighting personnel need to be
aware of the potential hazards of any dangerous goods and be prepared to deal with related
emergencies. Accidents involving aircraft carrying dangerous goods present special rescue
and fire control problems, although the existence of such cargoes may not be immediately
known. Aircraft operators should report without delay the presence, or possible presence, of
dangerous goods on board aircraft involved in an accident. Packages containing dangerous
goods can be identified by the distinctive diamond-shaped dangerous goods labels. Rescue
and firefighting personnel should familiarize themselves with the various labels.
(3) If a package containing radioactive materials ruptures and spillage occurs, the vehicles or
persons that come near or cross through the area may become contaminated. If radioactive
material is disturbed, winds or a thermal column from an aircraft fire could carry and spread
the radioactive material over a great distance, endangering a wide area. Provision for
decontamination of responding personnel and equipment should be included in emergency
planning procedures. If packages containing radioactive material are damaged, the
assistance of radiological experts will be required without delay. The most appropriate
organization able to provide such assistance should be determined. This may well be one of
the specialist agencies.
(4) Where broken containers are found which could cause injury to or affect the health of
exposed aircraft occupants or rescue personnel (particularly from radioactive, aetiological,
or toxic materials), special precautions should be taken. Personnel trained to deal with the
special problems involved shall be utilized. If damaged packages of dangerous goods are
found, especially if they are radioactive, infectious or poisonous materials, precaution
should be taken to safeguard the health of exposed aircraft occupants and rescue personnel.
Fire fighters and other rescue workers should be trained to deal with the special problems
that could arise.
(5) In the event radioactive materials are suspected, the following general procedures should be
followed:
(i) the nearest nuclear energy facility, hospital with a radiological unit, military base or
local fire authority organization should be required to dispatch immediately a
radiological team to the accident site;
(ii) persons coming in contact with radioactive material should be segregated until
examined by radiological team physicians;
(iii) suspected material should be identified but not handled until it has been
monitored and released by authorized personnel. Clothing and tools used at the

accident scene should be segregated until released by a radiological emergency
team;
(iv) food or drinking water suspected of contamination should not be used;
(v) only properly attired rescue and firefighting personnel should remain on the scene;
all other persons should be kept as far from the scene as possible; and
(vi) all hospitals shall be notified immediately that radioactive materials are involved so
they can establish radioactive decontamination areas in the hospital.
(6) The basic regulations for the carriage of radioactive materials by all forms of transport are
published by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). These regulations form the
basis for many national regulations.
(7) Food or drinking water suspected of contamination by aetiological or toxic materials should
not be used.
(8) The public health and veterinary authorities should be informed immediately.
(9) Any casualty or person exposed to dangerous materials should be removed from the scene
of the occurrence and transported to the appropriate medical facilities for suitable
treatment as soon as possible.
(10)  Many publications are available which deal with the handling of dangerous goods. These
include ICAO's Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air (Doc
9284), the International Air Transport Association's Dangerous Goods Regulations, the
International Atomic Energy Agency's Regulations for the Safe Transport of Radioactive
Materials and Emergency Response Planning for Transport Accidents Involving Radioactive
Materials. Particularly useful to fire departments would be the United States National Fire
Protection Association's Fire Protection Guide on Hazardous Material.
10. NATURAL DISASTER
(a) General
(1) The natural disasters to which aerodromes may be subjected include storms, floods,
earthquakes, and seismic sea waves. The vulnerability of an aerodrome to any of these will,
in good measure, be affected by geography, since the more dangerous occurrences are
often defined by certain areas or belts. While nothing can be done to avert them, there are
actions that can be taken to minimize damage and expedite restoration of aircraft
operations.

(2) Development of weather patterns, prediction and tracking of movement of storms, and
notification to the public of potential danger will normally be carried out by a meteorological
service in the area.
(3) The aerodrome emergency plan should provide for initial protective measures, emergency
supplies pertinent to local disaster exposure, personnel shelter, and post-storm clean up and
restoration. Aircraft operations will usually be impossible for several hours before and after
the storm.
(4) As soon as severe storm warnings are received, all owners of aircraft based or located at an
aerodrome should be notified. Warnings should be issued to all aircraft pilots en route to
the aerodrome. Aircraft owners and pilots should be responsible for their aircraft. If
possible, all aircraft on the ground should be evacuated to aerodromes outside the storm
area. Aircraft in flight should be advised to divert to an alternate destination. Aircraft on the
ground that cannot be dispersed should be put under cover or tied down so as to face into
the approaching winds.
(5) Power interruptions are common during a natural disaster, either by damage to generating
plants or by destruction of transmission lines. Aerodromes located in severe storm areas
should take measures to ensure minimum interruption to power supply, either by providing
standby engine generators or dual sources of commercial power.
(6) Specific personnel assignments for building protection to collect or secure all loose objects
that may be blown about by the winds should be made in the aerodrome emergency plan. It
may be necessary to fill and place sandbags if there is any possibility of flooding.
(7) Natural disasters require large quantities of specific equipment for use in earthquakes,
floods, tsunamis, etc. A survey of the quantity and type of emergency supplies available
from each individual agency should be made to provide a consolidated list of supplies
available for the region.
11. EMERGENCIES AT AERODROMES BORDERING WATER AREAS
Many aerodromes are located adjacent to large bodies of water which requires additional
emergency services. Aircraft may sink rapidly making the danger of drowning or hypothermia a
major problem for the occupants. Some aircraft are not equipped with life vests, rafts or inflatable
slides. Floatation devices sufficient to carry the number of occupants of the largest aircraft regularly
using the aerodrome should be carried on amphibious rescue vehicles capable of rapid deployment.

RENDEZVOUS POINTS

(a) A rendezvous point is a prearranged reference point, i.e. road junction, crossroad, main
access/entry point or other specified place, to which personnel/vehicles responding to an
emergency situation initially proceed to receive directions to staging areas and/or the
accident/incident site.
(b) The following Rendezvous Points will be used by the Local Authorities - Fire, Police and
Ambulance Services:
(c) Specifications for Rendezvous Point Signs
(1) The signs should be designed in accordance with local road transport authority requirements
and recognised by Local Emergency Services - Police, Fire and Ambulance. The sizes given
are the minimum likely to allow them to be recognised easily by attending local emergency
services.
(2) Rendezvous Point (RVP) Signs
(i) Rendezvous Point signs should be displayed at the point(s) designated by the
Aerodrome Emergency Plan as the rendezvous point(s) for all responding
Emergency Services. Signs should be clearly visible from any direction from which
responding Emergency Service vehicles/personnel are likely to approach when
attending aircraft accidents/incidents within the response area defined by or cross-
referenced in the Aerodrome Manual. See Figure-5.
(ii) Signs should have nominal dimensions 1000 mm x 1000 mm and comprise bright,
white letters ‘EMERGENCY SERVICES RENDEZVOUS POINT’ on a contrasting green
background. (The white lettering may also be retro-reflective.) The sign should
have a bright, contrasting yellow border of 25 mm dimensions. (The border may
also be retro-reflective).

Figure-5: Examples of an Emergency Services Rendezvous Point and Directional Signs
(3) Rendezvous Point Directional Arrow Signs

(i) Sufficient signs bearing RVP directional arrows should be placed in such a manner that
‘off-aerodrome’ Emergency Service vehicles/personnel responding to an incident on the
aerodrome are directed expeditiously to any previously designated RVP. See Figure-5
for examples.
(ii) Sign(s) should be placed within and around the aerodrome perimeter so that they are
visible and legible from any practicable direction of approach.
(iii) Sign(s) should have nominal dimensions 525 mm x 625 mm and comprise a bright,
white arrow and the letters ‘RVP’ on a contrasting green background. The sign should
have a bright, contrasting yellow border of 25 mm dimensions. (The lettering and
border may also be retro-reflective).
(iv) Where appropriate, RVP signs and RVP Directional Arrow signs should be illuminated.

title: Emergency planning
text:
MANAGING AIRCRAFT EVACUATION
(a) In the event of an aircraft accident or incident on operational runway or active movement
area, passengers and crew members who are able to evacuate from the aircraft are
susceptible to the risk of injury if they are not quickly move away from the aircraft to a safe
area. There were actual cases where evacuating passengers from aircrafts had strayed into
the runway or active movement area. While it is expected that an aerodrome ARFFS will be
the first arriving unit at the scene, they will however be actively engaged in trying to suppress
any resulting fires or dealing with immediate hazards and rescuing those injured passengers
and crew. In order to facilitate the safe evacuation process of passengers and crew at an
aircraft accident scene, some aerodromes have implemented passenger evacuation
management systems (PEMS). The aerodrome ARFFS or other first arriving unit at the scene
can facilitate the immediate evacuation of passengers and crew to a designated safe location,
normally sited upwind and uphill from the incident scene.
(b) A passenger evacuation management system (PEMS) has emerged as a recent innovation at
certain aerodromes, serving to facilitate the lead and guide evacuated crew and passengers
from the impacted aircraft to a relatively safe and secure area. They differ in design from one
aerodrome to another, but primarily they are illuminated signs with a loud speaker capability
(visual and audible directions) and are carried on the rear of dedicated ARFFS vehicles and/or
airfield operations vehicles. These large signs and loudspeaker giving verbal instruction “ALL
PASSENGERS ASSEMBLE HERE” are located at safe and secure area selected by the PEMS
officer within the boundary of inner and outer cordon, where it is can be easily visible and

heard by the evacuating passengers and crew. Figure-6 shows an example of an aircraft
passenger evacuation management system mounted on an airfield operations vehicle
deployed at an aircraft accident scene.
(c) Sufficient emergency planning procedures should be established for evacuated aircraft
passengers and crew to be guided and directed towards these vehicles. Passengers and crew
who require medical treatment should be assisted or carried to this location for triage by the
responding ambulance crews.

Figure-6: Example of siting an aircraft passenger evacuation management system.

title: Emergency planning
text:
GENERAL
(a) A system for locating and reaching each accident site in minimum time, with sufficient rescue,
firefighting and medical equipment, should be employed at each aerodrome. A detailed grid
map(s) will be beneficial in this regard. The grid maps should reflect a distance of at least 1
000 m beyond the threshold and the aerodrome perimeter. Studies of the ICAO Accident

Incident Data Reporting (ADREP) System show that a large (more than 25 percent) portion of
accidents occurred on the area (1 000 m long and 60 m width) beyond the runway end.
(b) A detailed grid map(s) of the aerodrome and its vicinity (with date of revision) should be
provided in the emergency operations centre. Similar small-size maps should be available in
the control tower, fire station, rescue and fire fighting vehicles and all other supporting
vehicles responding to an emergency. Copies should also be distributed to the agencies
involved in the plan.
(c) It is preferable that two (2) grid maps be provided; one map should depict the confines of
aerodrome access roads, location of water supplies, rendezvous points, staging areas, etc (See
Figure-7 for a sample of aerodrome grid map). The other map should include surrounding
communities and depict appropriate medical facilities, access roads, rendezvous points, etc.
within a distance of approximately 8 km from the centre of the aerodrome. See Figure-8 for a
sample of aerodrome community grid map.
(d) It is absolutely essential that where more than one grid map is used, the grids do not conflict;
they should be immediately identifiable to all participating agencies. Use of different colour
grids as in Figures-7 & 8 preclude misinterpretation of grid maps.
(e) The grid map which shows the available medical facilities should contain information on
potential bed availability and medical specialities at the different hospitals. Each hospital
should be individually numbered and treatment specialty indicated with distinct data such as
beds, personnel, etc.
(f) It is essential that whenever the grid map is revised, an updated copy should be provided to
all participating agencies and the old map destroyed.

Figure-7: Example of an aerodrome grid map

Figure-8: Example of an aerodrome community map

title: Emergency planning
text:
INCIDENT MANAGEMENT
(a) A management system for dealing with an incident should be established and implemented at
the aerodrome that includes:

(1) a scalable command and control structure for the type of emergency detailed in the
emergency plan, the agency assigned to each emergency, specify the roles and
responsibility of these agencies necessary to deal with each emergency; and
(2) procedures for inter and intra operability of all mutual-aid agencies required to deal
with the different emergencies at the aerodrome and its immediate vicinity.

title: Emergency planning
text:
INCIDENT MANAGEMENT
(a) This guidance document is to assist an aerodrome operator in establishing and implementing
a comprehensive incident management system at an aerodrome.
(b) The guidance document contains three sections including:
(1) Section A – Aerodrome incident command. This section explains the framework of
incident command at an aerodrome.
(2) Section B – Aerodrome incident command competence. This section explains the
necessary knowledge, skills and understanding in the application of incident command
at an aerodrome.
(3) Section C – Mutual-aid emergency services interoperability plan. This section explains
the interoperability plans and procedures when working with mutual-aid emergency
services needed to support the aerodrome operator s and emergency response services
during an aviation incident.
INTRODUCTION
1. The aim of this document is to establish a national aerodrome incident management system
by providing suitable guidance to aerodrome operator s, emergency planners and emergency
response services, collectively known as Aerodrome Emergency Response Organisation
(AERO), to establish and implement a robust incident management system at an aerodrome.
2. This document supplements the UAE National Response Framework in dealing with any
aviation incidents at an aerodrome or in its immediate vicinity. It is essential for all
commanders at strategic, tactical and operational levels, emergency response services
personnel, aerodrome operations personnel and any other personnel involved in responding
to aviation incidents to understands the contents of this document.
3. References for the development of this document are derived from:
• UAE National Response Framework
• UK National Operational Guidance on Incident Command

• UK National Operational Guidance on Incident Command – knowledge, skills and
competence
• UK Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Principles (JESIP)
4. Operational response is hazardous and varied. Some incidents need only simple actions and
procedures to be dealt with effectively and safely, as risks are low. Others are more
challenging and may quickly increase in size, complexity and duration.
5. The document contains three sections including:
• Section A – Aerodrome incident command. This section explains the framework of
incident command at an aerodrome.
• Section B – Aerodrome incident command competence. This section explains the
necessary knowledge, skills and understanding in the application of incident command at
an aerodrome.
• Section C – Mutual-aid emergency services interoperability plan. This section explains the
interoperability plans and procedures when working with mutual-aid emergency services
needed to support the aerodrome operator s and emergency response services during an
aviation incident.
6. Given the interdependencies of the materials contained in this document, it is important that
this document should be read in its entirety.

title: AERODROME INCIDENT COMMAND
text:
A. THE INCIDENT COMMAND SYSTEM AND THE ROLE OF INCIDENT COMMANDERS
1. The incident command system is an all-hazards approach, providing a progressive, scalable
and flexible system of operational command, control and organisation. The system is
designed to help an incident commander manage and fulfil their incident plan. It encourages a
controlled and systematic approach to resolving incidents.
2. The key components of the incident command system include:
• Clear, defined and visible lines of command
• Manageable spans of control
• A communications infrastructure
• Appropriate responsibility and authority
• Clearly defined and understood roles and responsibilities
• Sectorisation of the incident

3. It is the role of incident commanders to effectively and safely organise resources to obtain the
best resolution to an incident. It is the role of all personnel, who may attend or are involved
with an incident, to be familiar with the requirements of the incident command system and
know how to operate safely and effectively in it. This applies equally to those who will
perform a command role and those who will be operating under the command of others,
including the fire control room.
4. Incident command and support activities start on receipt of the emergency call to the fire
control room and continue to the conclusion of the incident.
5. Operations on the incident ground should be well-organised and controlled. The incident
command system provides the incident commander with a clear framework to help them
structure, organise and manage an emergency. It can be adapted to all sizes and types of
incident and helps incident commanders to deploy and use resources effectively.
6. The incident command system will only be successful when applied with good command skills.
It is not the incident command system that achieves the outcome; it is how the incident
commander makes and applies sound operational decisions within it.
7. The incident command system allows the incident commander to use health and safety
arrangements, policies or procedures, which are tailored to the characteristics of an incident
and the objectives of the incident plan. This helps to achieve a balance between risk and
benefit.
8. Incident commanders should be aware of becoming overburdened and having too broad a
span of control. This can result in ineffective leadership, poor decision-making and poor
communications, leading to a failure of situational awareness. Incident commanders should
consider the issues of team dynamics to get the best from the resources available to them.
9. Aerodrome emergency response organisation has a responsibility to provide their incident
commanders with the necessary training, equipment and resources to effectively apply the
incident command system to any incident.
B. COMMAND SKILLS AND THE ROLE OF THE INCIDENT COMMANDER
1. The use of command skills by incident commanders is as important as the effective
implementation of the incident command system, policies and procedures. Command skills
complement these technical skills and together are critical for assertive, effective and safe
incident command.

2. In exceptional circumstances, if no policies or procedures exist, or if following them could be a
barrier to resolving an incident, a commander should use their command and technical skills
to inform their professional judgement and apply operational discretion if appropriate.
3. Command skills are social, personal and cognitive skills that come under the heading of
human factors. They enable commanders to function effectively when in charge of an
incident. The safety-critical command skills are:

4. In a hazardous, fast-moving, emotion-charged and pressurised situation, an incident
commander is expected to be able to cope and competently perform their role even if
information about the incident is incomplete. To achieve this, they should use their command
skills proficiently to gather and interpret information, and to decide on, communicate and
implement a plan. If an incident commander omits or performs a command skill poorly, this
may lead to dangerous consequences.
5. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should recognise the importance of incident
commanders having effective command skills. Without good command skills, a commander
will lack the ability to successfully implement their technical knowledge to command an
incident. A failure to effectively use a command skill may expose personnel or others to
unacceptable risks and cause harm, but when performed well contribute to safe and effective
operations.
6. For example, if a commander fails to demonstrate assertive, effective and safe leadership this
may result in others not trusting their judgement or competence. This may adversely affect
the communication, co-ordination and co-operation of personnel or members of other
agencies; in turn, this may place personnel and others at greater risk of being harmed.
Leadership
Situational
awareness
Decision-
making
Interpersonal
communication
Personal
resilience
Teamwork

7. The application of command skills and the implementation of the incident command system
may be regarded equally as control measures to ensure safe and effective incident command.
8. Incident commanders should have a range of qualities, and effectively use command skills, to
deal with the wide-ranging nature of incidents. Assertive and effective incident commanders:
• Are confident and self-aware
• Are well-trained and competent
• Have sound situational awareness
• Are able to lead, direct and instruct others
• Can communicate effectively
• Are able to plan and implement
• Can apply sound judgement and effective decision-making
• Are able to adapt to changing and challenging situations
• Are calm and controlled
9. An incident commander should possess the technical knowledge and command skills to
underpin their judgements, decisions and behaviours. Incident command: Knowledge, skills
and competence provides detailed information for the role, based on research and incident
ground observations.
10. The application of these skills on the incident ground is key to incident ground safety and the
implementation of an effective operational plan. Services should have safe systems of work to
support incident commander decision-making at incidents to reduce the risk of human factors
affecting safety.
11. The effective practice of these skills is enhanced within a learning culture that encourages
empowerment and the acceptance of responsibility and accountability. This includes systems
and processes to actively monitor the performance of command skills by incident
commanders in training and at operational incidents.
12. Post-incident reviews and safety event investigations should examine the use of command
skills by incident commanders to highlight the impact of human factors on operational
outcomes. Similarly, a service’s operational policies and procedures should be consistent with
its approach to incident command. Its command ethos should be clearly articulated to help
ensure incident commanders are aware of the service's expectations.
C. SELECTION, TRAINING AND REVALIDATION OF INCIDENT COMMANDERS
1. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should establish robust selection processes to
identify suitable personnel to be developed for the role of incident commander. The

processes should ensure that people who perform incident command functions are capable of
doing so under the expected pressures of incidents and can deal with situations where there
is sustained pressure and stress.
2. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should ensure they appropriately train, assess
and revalidate their incident commanders, to ensure they understand, have practised and
revalidate the skills they need for command. Aerodrome emergency response organisation
should also equip incident commanders with the operational knowledge that is required to
resolve the full range of foreseeable incidents.
3. Section B - Incident command competence provides detailed information on these topics,
including:
• Selection of effective incident commanders
• Training for incident commanders
• Command competence
• Validation and revalidation of commanders
D. LEGISLATION
1. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should assure themselves that all relevant
legislation and regulations for their area are considered when developing policies, procedures
and training. Legislation and regulations may affect operational decisions; some of the key
pieces for incident command include:
• Civil Aviation Law
• Civil Aviation Regulations
• Civil Defense Act
• National Response Framework
• National Business Continuity Management Standards
• National Occupation Health and Safety Management System Standard
E. RISK MANAGEMENT PLAN
1. Emergency planning and management are critical elements of the overall aerodrome
aerodrome operator’s safety management system. Each aerodrome emergency response
organisation should develop their strategic direction through their risk management plan. To
determine the extent of their firefighting capability, strategic managers will consider their
statutory duties and the foreseeable risk within their area.

2. Work to identify risk and prepare operational plans should consider all stakeholders, including
local emergency planning groups and the aerodrome emergency response organisation risk
management plan.
F. RESOURCING
1. As part of their risk management plan each aerodrome emergency response organisation
should consider the resources they need to mobilise to an incident to support effective
incident command at operational events.
2. For incident command the risk management plan should include:
• The role and level at which incidents will be commanded, for example, Level 1 incident,
crew manager and watch manager
• The types of equipment to provide command support functions, such as command boards
and control units, and the size of incidents at which each will be used
• The arrangements for command teams and any support vehicles
• The need for competent and skilled officers to be available for command support and
functional or support sectors, such as water, foam or inter-agency liaison
G. RESPONSIBILITY OF AERODROME EMERGENCY RESPONSE ORGANISATION
1. Aerodrome emergency response organisations are responsible, under legislation and
regulations, for developing policies and procedures and to provide information, instruction,
training and supervision to their personnel about foreseeable hazards and the control
measures used to reduce the risks arising from those hazards.
2. This guidance sets out to provide Aerodrome emergency response organisation with sufficient
knowledge about the potential hazards their personnel could encounter when attending
incidents. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should ensure their policies,
procedures and training cover all of the hazards and control measures contained within this
guidance.
H. INTRAOPERABILITY AND INTEROPERABILITY
1. Other agencies should base their expectation of the aerodrome emergency response
organisation response to multi-agency incidents on the incident command system contained
in this guidance. Therefore, adoption of this guidance will support intraoperability and
interoperability.

2. Using common language and components will ensure aerodrome emergency response
organisation can more effectively resolve local, cross-border and national incidents.
INTRAOPERABILITY
3. Clearly defined roles, particularly the specialist roles performed by personnel from dedicated
departments such as fire control or hazardous materials, will support intraoperability and the
establishment of effective command teams.
4. Risk management plans, and other pre-planning, should consider incidents that may involve
working with the resources or assets of other Aerodrome emergency response organisation,
or the National Resilience capabilities.
INTEROPERABILITY
5. Interoperability is delivered through the mutual-aid emergency services interoperability plan
detailed in Section C. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should be aware of the
aspects of interoperability that exist when identifying, assessing and preplanning for all
incident types and eventualities they may attend.
6. In addition to the community risk register, personnel have a wealth of local knowledge of risks
or potential scenarios areas that would benefit from a multi-agency response.
7. It is essential that all components of Aerodrome emergency response organisation, including
fire control personnel, operational planning departments and incident commanders, identify
and liaise with relevant partner agencies. This ensures that in the event that they are required
to respond to different incident types, all agencies are fully aware of the assistance available
to maximise effectiveness in saving lives and reducing harm.
8. It is possible that other agencies who attend an incident will have risk-critical information.
Incident commanders should request risk-critical information in the joint agency briefing as
well as sharing any information they have. They should ensure this information flows
throughout the incident.
9. As well as the common agreed principles contained within MAESIP, there is a legal framework
to share information between responders in an emergency situation. There may also be
formal information sharing agreements (ISAs) between agencies.
MUTUAL-AID EMERGENCY SERVICES INTEROPERABILITY PLAN (MAESIP)
10. The MAESIP framework advocates the use of the M/ETHANE model for information gathering
and sharing between emergency responders, their control rooms and other agencies.

11. This model should be used when passing information between emergency responders, their
control rooms and other agencies so that shared situational awareness can be established:
• Major incident declared?
• Exact location
• Type of incident e.g. explosion or building collapse
• Hazards present, potential or suspected
• Access - routes that are safe to use
• Number, type and severity of casualties
• Emergency services now present and those required
12. The broader principles of intraoperability and interoperability at the pre-incident stage are
captured above, and the principles will be augmented by the on-scene interoperability
information contained in the Section C.

title: AERODROME INCIDENT COMMAND COMPETENCE
text:
A. INTRODUCTION
1. This section complements and supports Section A - Incident command, providing the detail
required for assertive, effective and safe incident command to be practised and applied.
2. The content aims to support aerodrome emergency organisation when establishing a robust
emergency response for incident command. It is an essential guide for the safe systems of
work required at incidents and provides essential reading for all commanders, operational
personnel and fire control personnel.
3. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should have simple and straightforward policies
and procedures that identify legal considerations in place. They should also have systems and
processes in place to prepare commanders at all levels to understand, interpret and apply the
incident command system appropriately to every incident.
4. The incident command system provides commanders with a clear framework to structure,
organise and manage an incident. It can be adapted to all sizes and types of incident and will
help them deploy and use resources in an efficient and safe way. The incident command
system allows commanders to use health and safety arrangements, including operational
procedures, tailored to the characteristics of an emergency. This helps commanders to
achieve an appropriate balance between the benefit of undertaking planned actions, and the
risks associated with them.

5. Operational response is hazardous and varied. Some incidents may need only simple actions
and procedures to deal with them effectively and safely, as risks are low. Others are more
challenging and may quickly increase in size or complexity, or become protracted.
6. The incident command system should commence from when the first call is received about an
incident and remain in place until the last appliance leaves an incident. During that time, it is
used to:
• Identify tasks and hazards
• Assess risk
• Manage and review control measures
7. Usually, the last activity at the incident ground is to hand over responsibility for health and
safety to the appropriate person or agency.
8. Commanding operational incidents is different to managing controlled and defined situations
or workplace scenarios. Commanders need a range of qualities, together with command skills,
to deal with the wide-ranging nature of emergencies.
9. Assertive and effective commanders:
• Are confident and self-aware
• Are well trained and competent
• Have sound situational awareness
• Are able to lead, direct and instruct others
• Can communicate effectively
• Are able to plan and implement
• Can apply sound judgement and effective decision-making
• Are able to adapt to changing situations
• Are calm and controlled
10. Aerodrome emergency response organisations have a responsibility to apply selection
processes to ensure that personnel who are responsible for performing command functions
are capable of doing so. Commanders should be able to demonstrate clear potential to deal
with stressful situations where there is sustained pressure. Once appointed they should
periodically be required to demonstrate competence in their role.
11. Aerodrome emergency response organisations should appropriately train and assess their
commanders. They should continually ensure that relevant personnel understand and have
sufficient time and facilities to practise the skills they need for command. Training should
provide commanders with the operational knowledge and understanding needed to resolve

the full range of reasonably foreseeable incidents and enable them to adapt to those that are
not.
12. A framework of competence for commanders should aim to equip them with:
• Appropriate behaviours
• Command skills
• Knowledge of policies and procedures
• An understanding of their responsibilities for the health, safety and welfare of others
• Familiarity with relevant legislation
THE SAFETY MAXIM
1. There is a balance between ensuring emergency response personnel safety and carrying out
the role of the emergency response service. This is known as the Safety Maxim, and is as
follows:
2. "At every incident the greater the potential benefit of emergency response actions, the
greater the risk that is accepted by commanders and personnel. Activities that present a high
risk to safety are limited to those that have the potential to save life or to prevent rapid and
significant escalation of the incident.”
3. The Safety Maxim acknowledges that firefighters operate in hazardous environments whilst
recognising the legal duty to ensure, as far as is reasonably practicable, the safety of everyone
our operations may affect and the professional dilemma of maintaining safety and taking
action to effect a rescue or mitigate an emergency.
4. This Safety Maxim will apply at every incident. It describes how an incident commander will
consider the benefits of our activities and the risks to those involved. This should not
necessarily be seen as a balance of one against the other, but more as an assessment of
whether the benefit is worth the risk; for example, where lives are in danger, the benefit of
saving life is high, then a higher risk to firefighters may be accepted.
5. Where the incident has high risk but with low benefit, commanders should only tolerate a
limited risk to firefighters. Activities in the hazard area are unlikely to take place until the risk
is reduced. An example might be a property where fire is confirmed with no persons missing
and the fire has not ventilated. Here the crews are unlikely to enter the building until
ventilation has been carried out and the risk of backdraught reduced. There is still benefit to
be gained in saving the building once the higher risks have been reduced.

6. At some apparent high risk, low benefit incidents, additional information may emerge, which
means the benefit increases. An example of this would be where people are later reported to
be missing in a fire.
B. COMMAND COMPETENCE
1. Aerodrome emergency response organisation commanders can be called upon at any time to
respond to a wide range of emergency situations; they are expected to work in complex,
dynamic and hazardous environments.
2. In responding to such incidents, services should ensure that individuals undertaking a
command role have the necessary knowledge, skills and attributes. Command competence is
the ability for a commander to effectively, safely and assertively demonstrate this in practice;
they should recognise the risks in operational activities and apply the right measures to
control and manage those risks, as they bring an incident to conclusion.
3. Competence is described as “...the combination of training, skills, experience and knowledge
that a person has and their ability to apply them to perform a task safely. Other factors, such
as attitude and physical ability, can also affect someone’s competence”. They also state that
‘Competence in health and safety should be seen as an important component of workplace
activities, not an add-on or afterthought’.
4. The incident command system (ICS) is an all-hazards approach to aerodrome emergency
response organisation incident management. Due to the complexity and hazardous
environment in which they work, to demonstrate competence commanders need to have an
effective understanding of the National Operational Guidance for Incident command, and the
roles of those working within the complete ICS.
5. Commanders should have a detailed understanding of the application of command principles
and practice for the levels of command both above and below their area or responsibility. To
ensure they can safely and effectively function within the overall command structure, they
should also have a good understanding of the breadth of incident types they may be
presented with.
OPERATIONAL STANDARDS FOR INCIDENT COMMAND
6. Aerodrome emergency response organisations need to select individuals with the potential to
achieve the required operational standards. They should have an effective system for the
training and development of personnel in place.

7. At key points during training and development, individuals should be assessed and validated
against the operational standards that are relevant to their roles. Once the individual has
demonstrated the effective appropriate knowledge, skills and attributes in the training
environment, aerodrome emergency response organisation should assess their competence
through an appropriate operational effectiveness framework.
SELECTION OF INCIDENT COMMANDERS
8. When selecting operational commanders, aerodrome emergency response organisation
should first ensure that candidates have the potential to demonstrate the necessary
knowledge, skills and attributes that are required to undertake a command role.
9. There are well-established methods for progression that exist in roles requiring operational
sector competence, from initial firefighter training through supervisory, middle, senior and
strategic roles. However, aerodrome emergency organisation may wish to consider attracting
diverse skills and experience from direct entry candidates, or those in non-operational roles
when filling management vacancies. This may include the potential for some roles being
considered for command duties.
10. Aerodrome emergency organisation may wish to consider individuals for command roles,
where the individual has not previously undertaken operational duties. In this situation it will
be necessary to undertake a risk assessment and gap analysis to determine if the candidate
has the potential to demonstrate assertive, safe and effective command, within the overall
ICS. In doing so, aptitude, for assimilation of technical knowledge, and attributes that support
command skills should be assessed, together with prior learning or experience, which may be
transferable.
11. While this does not guarantee future competence, the process should provide a basis for
undertaking a training needs analysis (TNA). This gap analysis should enable Aerodrome
emergency organisation to establish the development activities required, and the associated
resource requirements, of implementing such activities.
12. Where candidates are being considered for command roles at initial, intermediate or
advanced command (Levels 1, 2 or 3), development programmes for those without previous
operational and command experience are likely to be extensive. This is due to the wide-
ranging, complex, dynamic and hazardous environments a commander is required to operate
in at the scene of an incident.
13. Where entry is considered at Levels 2 or 3, significant development may be at the lower
command levels, and candidates may also require initial firefighter training. In all cases where

candidates are being considered for an operational role at command Levels 1, 2 or 3, they
should meet the relevant health and fitness standards adopted by their service.
14. Where candidates are being considered for Level 4 strategic command roles, development
programmes should also ensure a clear understanding of the application of command
principles and practice for initial, intermediate and advanced levels of command.
15. Aerodrome emergency organisation should seek to validate the knowledge, skills and
attributes of candidates following appropriate training, development and support for all levels
of command. Operational assurance assessments to confirm the demonstration of
competence should be carried out following suitable exposure of candidates to operational
incidents.
16. Carrying out validation and assessment of competence should satisfy Aerodrome emergency
organisation that the candidates will deliver an assertive, safe and effective, all-hazards
command to safeguard the public and operational personnel.
TRAINING, DEVELOPMENT AND ASSESSMENT
17. Aerodrome emergency response organisations should take account of the competence of
relevant employees when conducting risk assessments, to assist in deciding what level of
information, instruction, training and supervision is required. Aerodrome emergency
organisation should have arrangements in place to effectively train and develop commanders,
for entry into each level of command roles and ongoing maintenance. Initial knowledge
acquisition may be achieved through consideration of command qualifications.
Notwithstanding this, appropriate assessments of commanders should be carried out.
18. Aerodrome emergency organisation should have a robust method for assessing commanders
and recording the outcome of the assessment; this may require implementing an appropriate
assessment system. Any system used should be compatible with the aerodrome emergency
response organisation’s systems for operational effectiveness, assurance, performance and
review.
19. The incident command system (ICS) operates within a wider framework of policies and an in-
depth understanding of operational issues that should be considered by all personnel. The key
elements of effective incident command are in three functional areas:
• Command skills – considers the knowledge, skills and understanding required by an
incident commander, and the importance of developing and maintaining such
competencies

• Safety management – the principal consideration of the incident commander is the safety
of their personnel; when developing their tactical plans, the incident commander should
achieve an appropriate balance between the benefit of undertaking planned action and
the associated risks
• Organisation at an incident – this gives the incident commander a recognised system from
which to work, when organising and using personnel and resources at an incident
20. In consideration of these functional areas, the following provides some context for each level
of command. All personnel, from firefighter, require the full range of knowledge and core
skills, as well as having an understanding of the ICS.
21. An operational incident commander at a relatively small-scale incident needs a highly-detailed
knowledge and understanding of all operational considerations. As the wider political or social
implications factor less in the resolution of smaller-scale incidents, there is less emphasis on
these and more on the operational requirements to resolve the incident.
22. A tactical commander at an intermediate or advanced level requires a balance of skills, which
incorporate not only the detailed understanding and capability of operational breadth,
capacity capability, but also how these interface in the wider context of political,
environmental and societal aspects of the incident.
23. In contrast, a strategic manager at a major incident, involving strategic command needs a
detailed understanding of the political, social and environmental implications the incident
may generate. The operational knowledge and understanding of strategic managers does not
need to be as technically detailed as that of an operational incident commander.
24. Strategic commanders need to understand the capabilities and limitations of operational
knowledge and skills, and be able to apply incident command skills in a complex, multi-agency
environment while also considering the potential political impact.
25. In considering the above, key aspects of operational deployment that will require candidates
to demonstrate competence include:
• Technical skills – personnel and commanders having the required knowledge, skills and
understanding to perform their routine duties
• Command and control – having the required knowledge, skills and understanding to
perform their duties on the incident ground
• Management and leadership skills – in the sense of setting direction, managing their
allotted activities, prioritising and balancing the demands of the role and developing their
confidence and resilience

• Working with others – problem- solving and dealing with change in an organised, safe and
systematic way
• Multi-agency collaboration – working as part of a team and in partnership with other
agencies to save life, reduce harm and safeguard communities
26. When considering assessments, the following provides a brief overview of key aspects for
candidates at each command level.
27. Initial commanders (Level 1) should:
• Have a comprehensive understanding of the core skills of operational personnel
• Have a thorough knowledge of their service's policies, procedures, capabilities and
limitations
• Demonstrate command and control of personnel at all operational incidents
• Be capable of making critical decisions in pressured situations to ensure the deployment
of additional resources as an incident escalates
• Demonstrate they can develop their own specialist knowledge and skills
• Demonstrate they can use specialist knowledge and draw on the skills of others
28. Intermediate and advanced tactical commanders (Level 2 and Level 3) should:
• Have a working understanding of the core skills of operational personnel
• Have a thorough knowledge of their service's policies, procedures, capabilities and
limitations
• Have a comprehensive knowledge of the command skills of their operational commanders
• Demonstrate command and control at complex and escalating incidents
• Demonstrate effective working at a multi-agency level
• Demonstrate they can develop their own specialist knowledge and skills
• Demonstrate they can use specialist knowledge and draw on the skills of others
29. Strategic commanders (Level 4) should:
• Have a thorough knowledge of their service's policies, procedures, capabilities and
limitations
• Be capable of providing strategic support at complex and escalating operational incidents
• Be capable of operating in a multi-agency environment
• Demonstrate they can develop their own specialist knowledge and skills
• Demonstrate they can use, and when required, manage the specialist knowledge and
skills of others

30. In addition to command competencies, Level 2, Level 3 and Level 4 commanders are required
to acquire, demonstrate and maintain specialist skills commensurate with their role. This may
include working as a tactical adviser (TacAd) within the command structure for the following
fields:
• National Inter-agency Liaison Officer (NILO)
• Urban search and rescue (USAR)
• High volume pumps (HVP)
• Flood response
• Hazardous materials
• Chemical, Biological, Radioactive, Nuclear (explosive) (CBRN(e))
• Radiation protection
• Marine
• Waste fires
• Communications
• Fire investigation
31. Aerodrome emergency response organisation should have assessment systems in place to
validate candidates and also confirm competence for each of these specialist roles.
C. VALIDATION AND REVALIDATION
1. The ability to lead and resolve operational incidents safely is a key attribute for individuals
who are charged with incident command responsibilities. Aerodrome emergency organisation
should assure themselves that command skills are maintained.
2. Incident commanders are expected to work in challenging and high-pressure situations. It is
therefore important to ensure that incident commanders are provided with the opportunity
to develop and maintain incident command skills. Personnel also have a responsibility
towards their own continuous development.
3. Aerodrome emergency organisation need to ensure commanders have the time and
opportunity to engage in incident command practice and development.
4. Command validation and revalidation should:
5. Ensure consistent standards of maintenance of competence are applied to incident
commanders across all levels
6. Provide evidence that officers have the required knowledge and command skills for their level
of command

7. Provide evidence that officers are consistently performing incident command at the required
level
8. Provide an auditable trail of incident command skills and development
9. Encourage continuous improvement through the uptake of professional development
opportunities
PRINCIPLES OF VALIDATION AND REVALIDATION
10. Validation of command competence should be established at operational incidents, following
an individual completing training, development and validation in simulated environments.
11. Following an individual being established as competent, an ongoing cycle of operational
deployment and continuous training and development should be used to revalidate
commanders to ensure they maintain competence.
12. Revalidation should be undertaken by all personnel who have incident command
responsibilities and are competent in their role; this should form part of the training needs
analysis (TNA) and training frequency assessment processes. It should also apply to any
personnel who have been assessed to perform incident command duties in a temporary
capacity.
13. Incident commanders should be revalidated against the level at which they are operating in a
command capacity. Where personnel are in development, the processes to move from
development to competent in role should apply.
14. If personnel are commanding at a level above their substantive role, Aerodrome emergency
organisation should have a procedure to assure themselves that an individual has the
appropriate knowledge and skills to do so; this should be in line with any training needs
analysis process that is in place.
15. To effectively revalidate incident command competence, several key component areas should
be examined in the process, as shown in the table below. To maintain command competence
all three areas of the incident command revalidation process should be passed.
