OPERATIONAL
13. The operational commander will control and deploy the resources of their respective service
within a functional or geographical area and implement direction provided by the tactical

commander. As the incident progresses and more resources attend the scene, the level of
supervision will increase in proportion.
TACTICAL
14. The tactical commander will be located where they can maintain effective tactical command
of the operation. Invariably the aerodrome emergency response organisation incident
commander will be in attendance at the scene. If a Tactical Co-ordinating Group (TCG) is
established, either the incident commander or a nominated liaison officer should attend
meetings. The TCG may be located remote from the incident.
STRATEGIC
15. The strategic commander in overall charge of each service is responsible for formulating the
strategy for the incident. Each strategic commander has overall command of the resources of
their own organisation, but will delegate implementation decisions to their respective tactical
level commanders.
16. The aerodrome emergency response organisation ordinarily structures incidents without
using strategic command. However, if agencies form a SCG or RRP, the aerodrome emergency
response organisation should structure the levels below as Tactical and Operational.
17. Depending on the circumstances, different emergency services may choose to command from
different locations. The aerodrome emergency response organisation incident commander
may choose to command from an established command location at or near to the scene of
operations.
18. If aerodrome emergency response organisation representative is required to attend a
meeting at an off-site command location, this should be either the incident commander or a
nominated member of the incident command team. The designation and responsibilities of
command reside with the on-scene incident commander.
19. The person attending an off-site meeting needs to be empowered to make decisions on
behalf of their service. If the command authority remains on-scene, communication between
the two service representatives needs to be robust.
20. Incident commanders should be aware that when working with military personnel they use
the terms operational and tactical in the reverse of the aerodrome emergency response
organisation incident command system.
N. RISK ASSESSMENT

1. The aerodrome emergency response organisation operates within a framework that uses
trained personnel, safe systems of work and specialist equipment. The incident commander
should reduce risks as far as reasonably practicable.
INDIVIDUAL RISK ASSESSMENT
2. Individual risk assessment helps personnel remain safe when working unsupervised. There
will be circumstances where personnel may encounter unexpected or unforeseen situations.
Individual risk assessment is the process a firefighter carries out to identify hazards and
determine the level of risk they will accept. The outcomes of an individual risk assessment
inform and influence their decisions.
DYNAMIC RISK ASSESSMENT

3. Dynamic risk assessment (DRA) describes the assessment of risk in a rapidly changing
environment at an incident where decisions are sometimes made in fast-moving situations,
with incomplete or inaccurate information. It is a process not a control measure. The outcome
of the DRA will contribute to the incident plan. It helps to inform whether personnel should
be operating in the hazard area, which in turn determines the tactical mode.

4. DRA is the continuing assessment of risk in a rapidly changing environment at an incident. It is
a process of quickly determining the nature of the risk and what the response should be. It
confirms the response is appropriate by taking into account the benefit and risk. This
assessment should determine the reasonably practicable measures which should be taken to
manage the risk.
5. The person undertaking the DRA should also apply the statutory requirements for risk
assessment, which will assist the incident commander in making informed decisions.
1. EVALUATE THE SITUATION, INCLUDING DECIDING WHO MIGHT BE HARMED AND HOW
To identify hazards and suitable control measures the incident commander will first need to
consider:
• Operational risk information available from site visits, fire safety plans, standard
operational procedures and crews on scene
• Information available from the owner or responsible person at the scene
• The nature of the tasks to be carried out
• The significant hazards presented by the incident
• Who might be harmed and how, based on the risks presented to:
o The public, including casualties
o Personnel
o Other emergency responders
o The environment
• The resources that are available, for example, competent personnel, appliances and
equipment, specialist advice.
2. BENEFITS OF ACTIONS PROPORTIONATE TO RISK
Once they identify what they are going to do, they need to make a judgement about the benefits
and risks. Are the benefits of the outcomes proportional to the risks for those involved?
• If YES, proceed
• If NO, then consider how else the incident may be dealt with
3. SELECTING SYSTEMS OF WORK
Commanders will need to consider the possible systems of work and choose the most appropriate
for the situation. Are the proposed control measures reasonably practicable and achievable?
4. DECLARING THE TACTICAL MODE

The outcome of this assessment will contribute to the incident plan. This will include a decision
about whether personnel should work in the hazard area, which will require the appropriate
tactical mode to be announced. The declaration of a tactical mode is a simple method of
recording the outcome of the incident commander's risk assessment.
5. TACTICAL CONTROL
When proceeding with a task a commander will need to make sure that:
• Individuals and teams understand their objectives
• They have allocated clear responsibilities
• People understand the safety measures and procedures
6. ADDITIONAL ALTERNATIVE CONTROL MEASURES
Commanders will still need to eliminate, reduce or contain any remaining risks to an acceptable
level by introducing additional or alternative control measures, such as:
• Appropriate procedures and methods of work
• Additional personal protective equipment (PPE), for example, safety glasses or safety
harnesses
• The deployment of Breathing apparatus
• Specialist personnel or equipment, for example, urban search and rescue USAR, aerial
appliances or water rescue
As the incident develops, changing circumstances may require the original course of action to be
revised, for example:
• Firefighting tactics may change from defensive to offensive, or vice versa
• New hazards and their associated risks may arise for example, the effects of fire on
building stability
• Existing hazards may present different risks
• Personnel may experience fatigue
7. REVIEW
Incident and sector commanders need to manage safety by monitoring the situation. This
monitoring should include a regular review of how effective the existing control measures are.
As the environment changes, the incident commander should review the risk assessment. Even
when a safe system of work is in place the incident commander should take into account changing
priorities as this may alter the risk or the perception of risk. Refer to Decision control process.

A change of plan will need to be put in place with minimal delay. Incident commanders should
declare the revised tactical mode, make sure they communicate the change and continue with the
DRA process.
ANALYTICAL RISK ASSESSMENT
6. As the incident progresses, or becomes more complex, it requires a more detailed and formal
record of the significant findings of the risk assessment. This is referred to as analytical risk
assessment (ARA).

7. Having carried out the DRA and established a tactical mode, an incident commander should
be aware of the immediate hazards, who is at risk and the control measures necessary to
protect them. This assessment should determine the reasonably practicable measures that
personnel should take to control the risk.
8. This initial assessment now forms the basis of a more detailed incident risk assessment known
as an ARA. This should be completed and recorded on all occasions when the recorded DRA is
not sufficient.
9. An incident commander should ensure an ARA is carried out as soon as time or resources
permit. Responsibility for carrying out the risk assessment within a sector may be delegated
to sector commanders. However, the incident commander still retains responsibility for
approving the tactical mode.

10. The person who completes the ARA should be competent. They need to bring their findings to
the attention of the incident or sector commander. These should include details of any
hazards, risks and control measures.
11. In addition, the key findings of the ARA should be shared with all responders that are at the
incident ground and the fire control room. This information may form part of the multi-
agency decision-making process at the incident.
12. Incident or sector commanders should review the ARA whenever the risk to personnel
changes and at suitable intervals. It is for each service to decide what a suitable interval is;
however the incident commander can vary the interval after consulting any sectors or safety
sector. One example of this kind of static incident is a controlled burn at a barn fire.
13. Reviewing the risk assessment may confirm the existing control measures and tactical mode
are correct. It may also show the incident needs extra control measures or a change in tactical
mode. Incident commanders should make sure changes are announced and new actions
happen without delay. The new situation is also the basis for any future risk assessment.
14. Where there is a formal debrief, the use of the ARA forms can help show the risks known at
the time. The suitability of the risk assessment should also be reviewed at this time.

15. Aerodrome emergency organisation should keep ARAs for audit and periodic review. They
should also be considered for training and guidance development.

ENVIRONMENTAL RISK ASSESSMENT
16. Incident commanders should conduct an assessment of the environmental risk at incidents
they attend. This will help them to identify the potential risks posed by aerodrome emergency
response organisation actions on the environment and the control measures that can be
applied to reduce or, where possible, prevent environmental damage.
17. Incident commanders should conduct an assessment of the environmental risk at incidents
they attend. This will help them to identify the potential risks posed by fire service actions on
the environment and the control measures, which can be applied to reduce or, where
possible, prevent environmental damage.
18. An environmental risk assessment should identify:
• Nearby population
• Livestock
• Location of local watercourses
• Location of sensitive habitats and their proximity to the incident
• Incident location in relation to sensitive groundwater.
• Local drainage
• Polluting materials
• Type of media being used
• Quantity of firewater run-off being produced
• Volume/properties of any spilt materials
19. For smaller incidents the environmental risk assessment may be included as part of the
dynamic risk assessment. For larger, more protracted incidents or where a known risk to the
environment has been identified, a formal environmental analytical risk assessment should be
completed and recorded.
20. Any risk to the environment either known or suspected should be communicated to those
attending the incident and where appropriate, the relevant agencies.
O. TACTICAL MODE
OFFENSIVE MODE
1. This is where aerodrome emergency response organisation personnel are working in the
hazard area and exposed to greater risk, because the incident commander has decided it is
appropriate following their risk assessment. This may apply to an individual sector or to the
whole incident when every sector is in offensive mode.

2. Offensive mode is likely to be the common mode of operation. Examples of offensive mode
include:
• An aircraft or property fire where personnel enter the aircraft or building for rescue and
firefighting
• Personnel dealing with an incident outside an aircraft or building but still operating in the
hazard area
• Personnel dealing with a road traffic collision and working on the airside roadway
• Personnel entering an industrial site for firefighting or to isolate machinery
• Withdrawing personnel from a hazardous area because the risk has increased
3. In the last example, although personnel are being withdrawn they are still in the hazard area
and the tactical mode is still offensive. It would not change to defensive mode until all
personnel have left the hazard area and been accounted for. Use the message ‘tactical
withdrawal of responders in progress’ or ‘emergency evacuation of responders in progress’ to
timestamp the decision of the incident commander’s dynamic risk assessment, including the
need to change to defensive mode.

DEFENSIVE MODE
4. This is where commanders deal with an incident from a defensive position. In defensive
mode, the identified risks are unacceptable and outweigh the potential benefits. No matter
how many extra control measures could be put in place at that particular time, the risks
remain too great to commit personnel into the hazard area.

5. Defensive mode does not indicate that operational activity is not taking place. However, it
does indicate that personnel are not working in the hazard area.
6. Examples of defensive mode include:
• Firefighting outside a hazard area
• Standing by awaiting expert advice, before committing crews
• Standing by in a safe area while other services deal with an incident, for example, a
terrorist related incident

TACTICAL MODES WHEN SECTORS ARE IN USE
7. Examples of announcement of No Overall Tactical Modes
8. Communication with the fire control room may also be the method of recording significant
findings from a risk assessment. If this is the case it should include sufficient information
about why the mode is appropriate. For example:
• ‘Crews in offensive mode: persons reported or saveable life’
• ‘Crews in offensive mode: saveable property’
• ‘Crews in offensive mode: environmental protection’
• ‘Crews in defensive mode: awaiting isolation of power cables’
9. All incidents need a tactical mode and it should be kept current. The frequency of
announcements is for each aerodrome emergency response organisation to determine.
10. Communication examples when changing from offensive to defensive tactical mode

11. Communication should be timely, without detracting from risk critical operations, and include
sufficient information demonstrating the need to change from offensive to defensive tactical
mode, for example:
• ‘Offensive mode: all persons accounted for, tactical withdrawal of responders in
progress’... followed by;
• ‘Defensive mode: all crews withdrawn’
Or:
• ‘Offensive mode – emergency evacuation of responders, signs of structural collapse’ ...
followed by;
• ‘Offensive mode – emergency evacuation of responders in progress, crews committed to
assist in evacuation’...followed by;
• ‘Defensive mode – all personnel accounted for, roll call complete’

title: MUTUAL-AID EMERGENCY SERVICES INTEROPERABILITY PLAN (MAESIP)
text:
A. INTRODUCTION
1. Major incidents are commonly defined as events that require an extraordinary allocation of
resources, either due to their location, severity, type, and/or number of victims. The
management of these incidents, varied by nature as they are, usually involves responders
coming together from

2. multiple rescue services. Agencies might even have to come from different jurisdictions or
geographies.
3. Inter-service cooperation, in this context, is necessary but rarely simple. That’s because
responding agencies will bring their own competencies, experiences, systems, and
terminology.
4. Merging everything together, particularly during a severe incident, is difficult, one of the
challenges to optimal resource allocation and effective incident management.
5. Starting with the Incident Command System (ICS) in the late 1970s, however, major incident
command, control, and coordination frameworks have emerged to tackle the variegated
challenges associated with multiagency cooperation, e.g., limited spans of control, the need
for clearer lines of command, as well as inability to communicate effectively across
organisations.
6. What’s been developed and refined serves the purpose, therefore, of directing different
actions in an affected region. Resultant frameworks seek to organise command and scene
assessment, such that an individual structure becomes the mode of handling an incident, and
local directors within that region conform to the structure in place.
7. One such framework is the JESIP Joint Doctrine, an interoperability framework, which
standardises multiagency working. JESIP models and principles themselves, the most salient
of which this guide will lay out, have become the standard for interoperability in the U.K. The
Mutual-Aid Emergency Services Interoperability Plan (MAESIP) adopts the JESIP principles to
ensure incident management during emergencies at an aerodrome are safely and effectively
coordinated.
B. MAESIP PRINCIPLES
1. MAESIP focus is on improving multi-agency response to major incidents. The framework is
scalable, with models of joint working that can be applied to any type of multi-agency
incident.
2. The most important principle outlines how multiple agencies can work jointly, in all phases of
an incident, irrespective of scale and whether the incident was spontaneous or pre-planned.
Principle  Description Notes
Co-locate Co-locate with other
emergency responders as
soon as practicably possible
at a single, safe, and easily
identified location.
• Benefits of co-location include improved
communication and understanding that
support joint working.
• Co-location supports responders to
jointly agree upon objectives and develop

a coordinated plan to effectively resolve
an incident.
Communicate Communicate using clear
language, free from
technical
jargon and abbreviations.
• Meaningful and effective communication
between emergency responders and
other organisations underpins effective
joint working.
• The “talk not tell” process involves
control room personnel passing
information and asking other
organisations what their response to the
incident will be. This is achieved by:
o Sharing information from all
available sources along with
immediate resource availability and
decisions
o Nominating a point of contact in
each control room and establishing
a method of communication
between all of them
o Co-ordinating the setting up of
multi-agency interoperable voice
communications for responders and
operational working if necessary.
Coordinate Coordinate by agreeing on
the lead organisation.

Identify priorities, resources,
capabilities, and limitations
for an effective response,
including the timing of
further meetings
• Coordination involves control rooms and
responders of all levels discussing the
available resources and activities of each
responder organisation, agreeing to
priorities, and making joint decisions
throughout the incident.
• Coordination underpins joint working by
avoiding potential conflicts, preventing
duplication of effort, and minimising risk.
• For effective co-ordination, however, one
organisation generally needs to take a
lead role. To decide who the lead should
be, factors such as the phase of the
incident, the need for specialist
capabilities and investigation, during
both the response and recovery phases
should be considered.
Jointly
understand
risk
Jointly understand risk by
sharing information about
the likelihood and potential
impact of threats and
hazards, so as to agree upon
appropriate control
measures.
• By jointly understanding risks and their
associated mitigating actions,
organisations can promote the safety of
responders and reduce the impact that
risks may have on members of the public,
infrastructure, and the environment.
• But as different responder organisations
may see, understand, and treat risks
differently, each organisation should
carry out their own risk assessments,

then share the results, so that they can
plan control measures and contingencies
together more effectively.
• Individual dynamic risk assessment
findings may be used to develop the
analytical risk assessment for the
incident.
Shared
situational
awareness
Establish shared situational
awareness by using
M/ETHANE and the Joint
Decision Model.
• Shared situational awareness is a
common understanding of the
circumstances, immediate consequences,
and implications of the emergency, along
with an appreciation of the available
capabilities and the priorities of the
responder organisations.
• Achieving shared situational awareness is
essential for effective interoperability.
And establishing shared situational
awareness is important for developing a
Common Operating Picture (COP) at all
levels of command, between incident
commanders, and between control
rooms.
• Communications between control rooms
greatly assists the creation of shared
situational awareness in the initial stages
and throughout the incident.

C. SHARED SITUATIONAL AWARENESS
1. Communicating to commanders before they arrive on scene as well as throughout the
incident also helps. The organising process, however, should include identifying risks and
hazards. The following considerations have been singled out:

Is it clear who the lead
organisation is at this
point? If so, who is it?
What information and
intelligence does each
organisation hold at
this point?
What hazards and risks
are known by each
organisation at this
point?
What assets have been,
or are being, deployed
at this point and why?
How will the required
agencies continue
communicating with
each other?
At what point will
multi-agency
interoperable voice
communications be
required, and how will
it be achieved

2. And that’s where standardised methodologies for sharing information with the aim of
contributing to shared situational awareness come in. The most import of these in the
emergency management context is M/ETHANE.
D. M/ETHANE MESSAGE
1. M/ETHANE is an established reporting framework, which serves as a popular method for
passing incident information between emergency services and control rooms in a consistent
manner.
M/ETHANE Framework
M
Major incident declared.
Has a major incident (aircraft accident) been declared? Advise major incident
“standby” or “declared.” For incidents falling below the major incident
threshold M/ETHANE becomes an ETHANE message.
E
Exact location of the incident.
What is the exact location and geographical area of the incident? Examples:
Runway / taxiway location, grid reference, road names, landmarks, etc.
T
Type of incident.
What kind of incident is it? With brief details, could include aircraft
crash/incident, building fires, chemical spill, road traffic collision, etc.
H
Type of Hazards.
What hazards or potential hazards can be identified? Present and potential.
A
Location of Access/egress.
What are the best routes for access and egress? Routes to the incident and
potential rendezvous points.
N
Number of casualties.
How many casualties are there, and what condition are they in? An estimate
in the first instance, then upgraded with their severity/type.
E
Emergency services required.
Which, and how many, emergency responder assets and personnel are
required or are already on-scene? Present and those required, including
specialist input.

E. STAGES OF RESPONSE TO A MULTI-AGENCY INCIDENT
1. The importance of the M/ETHANE mnemonic and reporting model is that it brings structure
and clarity to the initial stages of managing a major incident.

2. During these early stages, it will take time for operational structures, resources and protocols
to be established. Some, if not much, of the required information may not be available.
3. All of this puts undue pressure on the first responders and early control rooms.
4. Add to that, incident commanders may lack the necessary resources to deal with the incident.
And so, a common approach, such as M/ETHANE, will be required.
5. According to the Joint Decision Model, there should be periodic consideration of the major
incident designation by responders. This helps to establish whether a developing situation has
indeed become a major incident.
6. Each responder organisation will then send a M/ETHANE message to its control room. Those
organisations should then share it with relevant responder organisations as soon as possible.
7. It’s imperative, though, that when the first resources arrive on the scene, they consider their
own safety. This will involve sending a M/ETHANE message so that situational awareness can
be established quickly.
8. The information received through multiple M/ETHANE messages will gradually accumulate to
support shared situational awareness in those responding to the incident and between
control rooms.
F. DEVELOPING A COMMON OPERATING PICTURE
1. It is incumbent on responders to develop a common operating picture (COP). A COP is defined
as a common overview of an incident, which is created by assessing and fusing information
from multiple sources. The overview developed then gets shared between appropriate
command, control, and co-ordinating groups to support joint decision making.
2. Although a common point of reference, the COP should evolve with the incident, to
sufficiently summarise the below:
3. There is no set format for the COP. The COP should, however, reflect local requirements and
practices. And whatever form the COP takes, it should be user-friendly, easy to navigate, and
geared to the requirements of busy decision makers under pressure.

G. JOINT DECISION MODEL
1. This is where the Joint Decision Model (JDM) comes in. The JDM, depicted below, is designed
to help responding agencies make effective decisions during dynamic circumstances.
• When using the JDM, the priority is to gather and assess information and intelligence.
Responders should work together to build shared situational awareness, recognising that
this requires continuous effort as the situation, and responders’ understanding, will
change over time.
• Understanding the risks is vital to establishing shared situational awareness, as it enables
responders to answer the three fundamental questions: what, so what, and what might?
But once the process of building shared situational awareness has begun, the desired
outcomes should be agreed to as the central part of a joint working strategy.
• If a Crisis Management Group is convened to this effect, that CMG will agree and share
the joint strategy for the multi-agency response. The strategic command teams from each
organisation should then review and amend their single-agency strategy to be consistent
with the joint strategy and support them in achieving the jointly defined outcomes, or
overarching aim.
• Deciding how all agencies will work towards the desired outcome reflects the available
capabilities, powers, policies, and procedures (means) and the arising options,
constraints, and contingencies (ways).
• Identifying options and contingencies comes next. Some options, however, will not be
viable, either difficult to implement, technically or logistically infeasible, or illegal and/or
What does it
all mean and
what effects
will it have?
What might
happen next or
in the future?
What is
happening
now and
what is
being done
about it?

ethically indefensible. Such options, though, should still be logged with rationale as to
why they were not achievable.

2. At this point, the JDM advises responders to take action after they’ve mulled over the
appropriate considerations. Responders should also list the various stages taken to reach that
decision.
3. This is just a cursory picture of the JDM. Further considerations include:
Stages of Joint-Decision Making (JDM)
Stage  Consideration
Working together
saving lives reducing
harm
This is the most important consideration throughout the decision-
making process. All joint decisions should be made with reference to
the overarching or primary aim of any response to an emergency – to
save lives and reduce harm.
Gather
information and
intelligence

At any incident, no single responder organisation can appreciate all the
relevant dimensions of an emergency straight away. A deeper and
wider understanding will only come from meaningful communication
between responder organisations, with the product of those
communication,
i.e., intelligence, subjected to the following tests:
o Evaluation, to determine its significance
o Risk assessment, to determine the need for it to be acted on
• Analysis, to identify critical links and associations that assist
understanding of the incident
Assess threat and
risk and develop a
working strategy
This analytical stage involves responders jointly assessing the situation,
including any specific threats, hazards, and the risk of harm. It’s rare,
however, for a complete or perfect picture to exist for a rapid onset
incident. A working strategy, as such, should therefore be based on the
Assess

develop a
working

Consider

& review
what

&

information available and reviewed on a continual basis. When
developing that working strategy, responders should apply decision
controls, share single service risk assessments, and record and
agree the joint assessment of risk.
Further steps to take include:
• Identify hazards. This begins with the initial call to a control room
and continues as first responders arrive on scene. Information
gathered by individual agencies should be disseminated to all first
responders, control rooms and partner agencies effectively.
• Dynamic risk assessment. Individual agencies carry out dynamic
risk assessments, reflecting the tasks and objectives to be
achieved, the hazards identified and the likelihood of harm from
those hazards. The results should then be shared with all agencies
involved.
• Identify tasks. Each individual organisation should identify and
consider their specific tasks, according to their role and
responsibilities. These tasks should then be assessed in the
context of the incident.
• Apply risk control measures. Each organisation should consider
and apply appropriate control measures to ensure any risk is as
low as reasonably practicable. The hierarchy of control should be
considered when agreeing a coordinated control measure
approach: elimination, substitution, engineering controls,
administrative controls, and personal protective clothing and
equipment.
• Have an integrated, multi-agency operational response plan. The
outcomes of the hazard assessments and risk assessments should
be considered when developing this plan, within the context of
the agreed priorities for the incident. If the activity of one
organisation creates hazards for a partner organisation, a solution
should be implemented to reduce the risk to as low as reasonably
practicable.
• Record decisions. The outcomes of the joint assessment of risk
should be recorded, together with the jointly agreed priorities
and the agreed multi-agency response plan, when resources
permit. This may not be possible in the early stages of the
incident, but post-incident scrutiny focuses on the earliest
decision-making.
Consider powers,
policies, and
procedures
A common understanding of relevant powers, policies, and procedures
is essential to ensure that the activities of responder organisations
complement each other. And so, this stage relates to any relevant
laws, procedures, or polices that may have an impact on the response
plan and the capabilities available to be deployed.
Identify options and
contingencies
Finally, contingency arrangements should be put in place to address
reasonably foreseeable events that may occur from actions taken or
not taken. But these potential options or courses of action should be
evaluated, considering the following:
o Suitability. Does it fit with the strategic direction?
o Feasibility. Can it be done with the available resources?
o Acceptability. Is it legal, morally defensible, and justifiable?

Whatever the option chosen, though, responders should be clear on
what they need to carry out. Procedures for communicating any
decision to defer, abort, or initiate a specific tactic should also be
clearly agreed.

H. DECISION MAKING SUPPORT
1. Thoroughly assessing the information received helps to ensure quality and suitability for the
task at hand. This is critical to ensuring that joint decision making is based on the best possible
information, which can only happen by identifying where critical uncertainties lie.
2. Once decisions have been made and actions agreed to, information should be relayed in a
structured way. That way it can be easily understood by those who will carry out actions or
support activities. This process is commonly known as briefing.
3. As incidents develop past their initial stages, or if they are protracted and require a handover
of responsibility, a more detailed briefing tool should be used.
4. The mnemonic IIMARCH, short for Information, Intent, Method, Administration, Risk
Assessment,
5. Communications, and Humanitarian Issues, is commonly used in these circumstances, so that
information can be briefed in appropriate detail.
6. When using IIMARCH to prepare a briefing it is helpful to consider the following:
• Brevity is important – if it is not relevant, leave it out
• Communicate using unambiguous language free from jargon and in terms people will
understand
• Check that others understand and explain if necessary
• Consider whether an agreed information assessment tool or framework has been used
7. The IIMARCH template below may help commanders in preparing a brief. When using
IIMARCH, it is helpful to consider the following:
IIMARCH template for incident briefing
Element Key questions and considerations Action
I Information
What, where, when, how, how many,
so what, what might?
Timeline and history (if applicable),
key facts reported using M/ETHANE

I Intent
Why are we here, what are we trying
to achieve?
Strategic aim and objectives, joint
working strategy

M Method
How are we going to do it?
Command, control and co-ordination
arrangements, tactical and
operational policy and plans,
contingency plans

A Administration
What is required for effective,
efficient and safe implementation?
Identification of commanders, tasking,
timing, decision logs, equipment,
dress code, PPE, welfare, food,
logistics

R Risk assessment
What are the relevant risks, and what
measures are required to mitigate
them?
Risk assessments (dynamic and
analytical) should be shared to
establish a joint understanding of risk.
Risks should be reduced to the lowest
reasonably practicable level by taking
preventative measures, in order of
priority. Consider the hierarchy of
controls.
Consider Decision Controls

C Communications
How are we going to initiate and
maintain communications with all
partners and interested parties?
Radio call signs, other means of
communication, understanding of
inter-agency communications,
information assessment, media
handling and joint media strategy

H Humanitarian issues
What humanitarian assistance and
human rights issues arise or may
arise from this event and the
response to it?
Requirement for humanitarian
assistance, information sharing and
disclosure, potential impacts on
individuals’ human rights

8. Finally, the matter in which information is shared is also important to support joint decision-
making. It is recommended using a common information sharing platform, preferably digital,
to share and manage information collaboratively.
9. Responder organisations may use various supporting processes and sources to provide
information, including any planned intentions; this supports joint decision-making.
10. All decisions, the rationale behind them and subsequent actions, should be recorded in a joint
decision log. Recording of decisions is critical and where possible should be undertaken by a
trained loggist or scribe. A sample joint decision log template is provided below:

11. Using a digital platform helps with automating aspects of sourcing, combining, analysing, and
displaying data.
12. Certain advanced emergency management platforms carry both information sharing and full-
lifecycle emergency management capabilities. Using these platforms have the added benefit
of providing incident management dashboards, as well as the capability to create both
M/ETHANE reports and IIMARCH briefings.
13. A truly digital EOC suited for aerodrome emergency response organisations, these platforms
have been designed for industry best practice, such as ICS and JESIP. This means, in close, that
the platforms boast powerful workflows which go the critical last mile to automate key
response steps, making it easier for practitioners of JESIP models and principles to
collaborate, communicate, and coordinate to improve their response to major incidents.

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY COMMAND FACILITIES
(a) Emergency command facilities should be provided at the aerodrome including:
(1) a fixed emergency operation centre as part of the aerodrome facilities that is readily
available for use during an emergency and is responsible for the tactical command and
coordination of the response to an emergency;
(2) a mobile command post that is capable of being moved rapidly to the scene of an
emergency and is responsible for the operational command, control and coordination
of all responding agencies at the scene of the emergency;
(3) provision of sufficient communication equipment and resources for use at these
facilities; and
(4) provision of sufficient competent persons assigned to assume control of the emergency
operation centre and the mobile command post.

text:
ESTABLISHING AND MANAGING EMERGENCY OPERATIONS CENTRE
1. INTRODUCTION

(a) This document provides guidance on the establishing and managing an Aerodrome Emergency
Operations Centre (EOC) during emergencies at the aerodrome. It is based on International
Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards and recommended practices. The EOC plays a
critical role in coordinating multi-agency responses, ensuring the continuity of airport
operations, and effectively managing crisis situations. This guidance is intended for use by
senior airport management, emergency response coordinators, and regulatory authorities.
2. GENERAL
(a) A fixed emergency operations centre should be available to deal with emergency situations at
each aerodrome. Certain emergency situations will require a mobile command centre at the
scene, normally under the direction of the aerodrome incident commander.
3. DESIGN AND FEATURES OF AN EMERGENCY OPERATIONS CENTRE
(a) The main features of an emergency operation centre are:
(1) its fixed location;
(2) it acts as tactical command, co-ordination and communication centre for supporting the
aerodrome incident commander in the mobile command centre for aircraft
accidents/incidents, unlawful seizure of aircraft and bomb threats; and
(3) it is operationally available 24 hours a day.
(b) The design of the emergency operations centre should be fit for purpose and where
necessary, sufficient supporting facilities are provided to support its various functions.
(c) The location of the emergency operations centre should provide a clear view of the
movement area and isolated aircraft parking position, wherever possible.
(d) The mobile command centre will usually be sufficient to co-ordinate all operational command
and communication functions. The emergency operations centre is a designated area on the
aerodrome which is usually used in supporting and co-ordinating operations in
accidents/incidents, unlawful seizure of aircraft, and bomb threat incidents.
(e) The emergency operation centre should have the necessary equipment and personnel to
communicate with the appropriate agencies involved in the emergency, including the mobile
command centre, when this is deployed. The communication and electronic devices should be
checked daily and regularly tested.
Note. — General guidelines on development and management of an emergency operations centre
(EOC) can be refer to ASTM E2668 and E2915.
4. STRUCTURE AND ROLES WITHIN THE EOC

The Airport EOC should follow a hierarchical command structure with clearly defined roles to ensure
seamless coordination during an emergency. Key personnel and their respective responsibilities are
as follows:
 EOC Director / Manager (Silver Commander)
 Responsibility: Overall command of the EOC, ensuring the effective implementation of
the AEP. Acts as the central decision-maker and is responsible for coordination
between the Bronze Commander (BC) and the Gold Commander (GC).
 Duties:
(i) Serve as the focal point for communication with external agencies and government
bodies.
(ii) Direct resource allocation, personnel assignments, and logistical support.
(iii) Ensure timely situational reports (SITREPs) to senior airport management and
stakeholders.
(iv) Ensure compliance with regulatory requirements and maintain command during
the entirety of the emergency.
 Operations Officer / EOC Support
 Responsibility: Manages tactical operations within the EOC and ensures information
flow between on-scene responders and EOC Director/Manager.
 Duties
(i) Coordinate real-time operations with the IC.
(ii) Oversee deployment of resources, including emergency services, medical teams,
and security.
(iii) Ensure adherence to predefined response protocols and timelines.
 Logistics Officer
 Responsibility: Management of all logistical aspects, including resource mobilisation,
transportation, and supply chain coordination.
 Duties:
(i) Track and deploy required resources such as equipment, personnel, and vehicles.
(ii) Maintain a record of resource availability and needs.
(iii) Coordinate staging areas for incoming support teams and resources.
 Planning Officer
 Responsibility: Anticipate operational needs and develop strategies for prolonged
incidents.
 Duties:

(i) Collect and analyse data to assist in forecasting potential escalation of the incident.
(ii) Prepare and revise action plans in alignment with the IC’s operational directives.
(iii) Maintain documentation of key decisions and provide updates to the EOC
Director/Manager.
 Communications Officer
 Responsibility: Ensure the functionality of all communication systems and manage the
dissemination of information between the EOC, on-site teams, and external agencies.
 Duties:
(i) Monitor radio communications and ensure the proper use of standardised ICAO
phraseology.
(ii) Ensure communication channels (radio, satellite, digital) are secure and fully
functional.
(iii) Coordinate with air traffic control (ATC) and other agencies to facilitate clear
information flow.
 Public Information Officer (PIO) / Media Officer
 Responsibility: Manage public communications, including media relations and social
media updates.
 Duties:
(i) Develop and disseminate accurate information regarding the emergency.
(ii) Liaise with airport management to ensure unified messaging across agencies.
(iii) Act as the main point of contact for media briefings and public inquiries.
 Safety Officer
 Responsibility: Oversee safety procedures and ensure the protection of all personnel
involved in the response.
 Duties:
(i) Monitor on-site and EOC safety protocols.
(ii) Coordinate with the IC and relevant safety bodies to mitigate risks.
(iii) Investigate and address any safety violations or incidents.
5. COMPETENCIES OF KEY PERSONNEL
Personnel assigned to the EOC must possess the necessary expertise to handle complex and dynamic
emergency situations. Each role requires the following competencies:

 EOC Director / Manager: Strategic leadership, decision-making under pressure, advanced
coordination skills, comprehensive understanding of airport operations, regulatory compliance,
and crisis management.
 Operations Officer: In-depth knowledge of emergency response protocols, quick tactical
decision-making, operational oversight, and field coordination.
 Logistics Officer: Expertise in resource management, inventory control, transport logistics, and
supply chain resilience.
 Planning Officer: Strong analytical and forecasting abilities, familiarity with emergency planning
tools, and experience in developing action plans.
 Communications Officer: Proficiency in radio communication systems, ICAO standard
phraseology, and secure communication practices.
 PIO: Media relations expertise, clear communication skills, and the ability to handle sensitive
information under public scrutiny.
 Safety Officer: Risk assessment, incident investigation, and application of safety management
systems in high-pressure environments.
6. WRITING AND RECORDING CRITICAL INFORMATION
Effective record-keeping and information management are essential for situational awareness and
decision-making during emergencies. Key practices include:
 Incident Logs: Maintain continuous logs detailing actions, communications, and decisions taken
during the emergency. Logs should be updated in real-time and reviewed periodically by senior
EOC personnel. (See Table 1 for example of EOC incident log entries)
 Information to be recorded in the EOC Incident Log includes:
(i) Date and Time: Precise timestamps for all actions, decisions, communications,
and events.
(ii) Incident Description: Brief summary of the emergency situation (e.g., type of
aircraft, flight number, nature of the incident, location).
(iii) Activation Time: Time the EOC was officially activated for the incident.
(iv) Notification Details: Record of who initially reported the incident and through
which communication channel (e.g., ATC, on-site personnel, external agencies).
(v) Key Personnel Activation: Names, roles, and activation times of key personnel
(e.g., EOC Manager, Operations Officer, Communications Officer).
(vi) Initial Assessments: Any early evaluations or assessments provided by
responders (e.g., damage, injury severity, risk level).

(vii) SITREPs (Situation Reports): Regular updates on the incident’s progress and
evolving conditions, including input from field units and on-scene Incident
Commander (IC).
(viii) Resource Requests and Deployment: Details of resources requested (e.g.,
firefighting units, medical teams, equipment) and time of dispatch.
(ix) External Agency Coordination: Record of all interactions with external agencies
(e.g., police, fire services, medical services), including requests for support and
confirmation of their arrival on scene.
(x) Critical Decisions: Document all major decisions made by the EOC Manager and
senior personnel, including the rationale behind them.
(xi) Instructions Issued: All instructions passed to on-scene responders (Bronze
Command) or external agencies, along with confirmation of receipt.
(xii) Public Information Releases: Record of press releases, media statements, and
public information issued by the Public Information Officer (PIO).
(xiii) Health and Safety Updates: Safety issues encountered, and measures taken to
protect response personnel and the public.
(xiv) Communication Logs: Record of all significant communications between the EOC,
Gold Command, Bronze Command, and other relevant parties (e.g., ATC, airline
representatives).
(xv) Significant Events: Chronological recording of important developments, including
containment of the emergency, casualties, infrastructure damage, etc.
(xvi) Incident Escalation or De-escalation: Log any changes in the incident status (e.g.,
from minor to major emergency or vice versa) and the reasons for escalation or
de-escalation.
(xvii) Termination of Emergency: Time and rationale for the decision to terminate
emergency operations.
 To ensure accuracy, clarity, and consistency, information in the EOC incident log should
follow these principles:
(i) Use Clear and Concise Language: Write in a precise, objective manner, avoiding
vague terms. Include essential details while avoiding unnecessary information.
Use plain language to ensure all readers understand the log entries.
(ii) Maintain Chronological Order: Record all entries in real-time as events unfold.
Ensure each entry is timestamped accurately.

(iii) Identify Personnel by Title/Role:  Always use the specific title or role of the
personnel involved (e.g., "EOC Manager," "Bronze Command") to avoid
confusion.
(iv) Log Key Decisions and Actions: For every significant decision, include a clear
description of what was decided, why, and by whom. Record the actions taken,
who executed them, and when.
(v) Ensure Accountability: Sign each log entry with the name or initials of the person
recording the information. Note who issued specific instructions and the
recipient.
(vi) Record External Communications: Document all communications with external
agencies (e.g., police, fire, airlines) and include the name or agency and the
content of the communication.

Table 1: Example of EOC Incident Log Entries

an emergency due to suspected engine fire during approach. EOC

incident and request additional medical support from the city’s

Confirmed by Bronze Command.

 Recording Information: Each entry must include:
(i) Time: Precise time when the action occurred or decision was made.
(ii) Description of the Event: A brief yet thorough explanation of what happened,
what decisions were made, and what actions were taken.
(iii) Signoff/Initials: The person making the entry should sign or initial it, ensuring
accountability and traceability.
 This approach ensures an organised, real-time record of all critical information, aiding
in response coordination and post-incident review.
 SITREPs: Regularly updated situation reports must be distributed to all relevant agencies and
airport management. These reports should summarise operational status, resource needs, and
critical developments.
 Action Plans: Document the emergency action plans, including roles and responsibilities,
resource allocations, and timelines. Ensure all updates are promptly communicated to relevant
stakeholders.
 Resource Tracking: Maintain an inventory of deployed resources, including personnel,
equipment, and supplies. Accurate tracking ensures efficient use and replenishment during
prolonged incidents.
7. USE OF STANDARD RADIO PHRASEOLOGY
The use of standardised communication is critical to avoid confusion during an emergency. The
following standard phraseology terms stated in the aerodrome emergency plan, must be used by all
EOC and response personnel (see Table 2):
 Standby: Await further instructions.

 Roger: Message received and understood.
 Affirmative/Negative: Yes/No responses to avoid ambiguity.
 Mayday: Indicates a life-threatening emergency.
 Pan-Pan: Urgent situation that is not immediately life-threatening.
 Clear: Communication channel is free for further transmissions.

8. ACTIVATION AND TERMINATION OF THE EOC
 Activation
 Activation of the EOC is triggered by defined events, including but not limited to:
(i) Notification of a major aircraft incident.
(ii) Declaration of an emergency by ATC or the BC/GC.
(iii) Significant threats to airport operations or public safety.
 The Silver or Gold Commander must initiate the activation process, which includes
notifying key personnel, setting up communication channels, and deploying initial
response teams.
 Termination

 Termination of the emergency response is determined by the Gold or Silver Command
in consultation with the IC.
 A formal announcement of termination should be made, followed by a structured de-
escalation process that returns airport operations to normal while ensuring any ongoing
impacts are managed.
 Post-incident debriefs and evaluations are essential to document lessons learned,
assess response efficacy, and revise the AEP as necessary.
9. ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
 Coordination with External Agencies
 Establish Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with external response agencies (fire,
police, medical) to ensure cohesive collaboration during emergencies.
 Regular joint exercises should be conducted to ensure familiarity with inter-agency
coordination protocols.
 Information Flow and Technology Integration
 Leverage technology such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS), CCTV, and digital
communication platforms for real-time situational awareness.
 Ensure redundancy in critical communication systems to prevent failures during the
response.
 Staff Rotation and Welfare
 Prolonged incidents may require staff rotations to avoid fatigue. Plan for adequate shift
changes and provide mental health support for EOC personnel.
 Security Protocols
 Implement strict access control to the EOC during emergencies to ensure the protection
of sensitive information and avoid unauthorised personnel disruptions.
10. CONCLUSION
(a) Establishing and managing an EOC during aircraft emergencies requires comprehensive
planning, robust training, and well-defined roles to ensure a coordinated and effective
response. By adhering to the guidance outlined in this document, airports can significantly
improve their preparedness and operational resilience during emergencies. This guidance
should be regularly reviewed and updated in alignment with evolving international best
practices and airport-specific needs.

title: Emergency planning
text:
ESTABLISHING AND MANAGING MOBILE COMMAND POST
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) Aircraft emergencies present significant challenges that require coordinated responses from
multiple agencies. In such incidents, the Mobile Command Post (MCP), commonly referred to
as the Bronze Command, plays a critical role in ensuring the effective on-scene management
of resources and operational activities. This document provides comprehensive guidance on
the management of MCP operations during aircraft emergencies, based on International Civil
Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards and recommended practices, to ensure a unified and
effective response.
(b) This document aims to provide aerodrome operators, emergency responders, and crisis
management teams with a structured approach for establishing and managing a Mobile
Command Post (Bronze Command) during an aircraft emergency. It focuses on key aspects
such as command structure, communication protocols, resource management, and
interagency coordination.
(c) The guidance applies to all categories of aerodromes managing aircraft emergencies, with
specific emphasis on operations at international airports. The document aligns with ICAO
Annex 14, Volume I, and ICAO Document 9137 Part 7.
2. DESIGN AND FEATURES OF A MOBILE COMMAND POST
(a) The mobile command post is a facility located at the scene of an incident, normally at the
outer cordon, where operational commanders from mutual aid agencies assemble to receive
and disseminate information and make decisions pertinent to the rescue and firefighting
operations. The main features of the MCP are:
(1) it is a mobile facility capable of being rapidly deployed;
(2) it serves as operational command, co-ordination and communication centre for aircraft
accidents/incidents;
(3) it is operational during aircraft accidents/incidents; and
(4) it is correctly located with respect to wind and terrain conditions.
(b) In the event of any accident/incident, a designated, recognizable and readily visible mobile
command centre is a high priority item. It should be established as quickly as possible,
preferably at the same time as the initiation of fire control and rescue activities. A continuity
of command should be maintained so that each agency reporting to the mobile command
centre can be sufficiently briefed on the situation before assuming control of its individual
responsibilities.

(c) The design and size of the mobile command centre should be fit for purpose and should
contain the necessary communication equipment and personnel to communicate with all
agencies involved in the emergency, including the emergency operations centre. The
communication and electronic devices should be checked each month and regularly tested.
(d) In order to eliminate confusion and missed transmissions, since several different agencies are
working together in the command post utilizing several radio frequencies and telephones, it is
essential that the volume of noise be reduced by utilizing headsets or sound absorbent
partitions for each participant.
(e) Maps, charts, and other relevant equipment and information should be immediately available
at the mobile command centre.
(f) The mobile command post should be easily recognizable by provision of an elevated
distinguishing marker, such as a chequered flag, coloured traffic cone, balloon or rotating
light. See Figure-9 for example of a mobile command post.
(g) Depending on the scale and magnitude of an incident, it may be necessary to establish a
forward/sub-command post at the inner cordon to allow direct and immediate oversight of
rescue and firefighting operations. When this is required, one location should be designated
as a “master” command post with sufficient communications to the forward/sub-command
post.

Figure-9: Example of a mobile command post

3. AIRPORT INCIDENT COMMAND BOARD

(a) The Airport Incident Command Board (AICB) serves as a crucial tool for managing and
coordinating responses to aircraft accident/incident that may occur at an airport or within its
immediate vicinity (see Figure-10 as an example of an AICB). The aim and objectives of an
Airport Incident Command Board typically include:
(1) To provide a structured framework for effectively managing and coordinating responses
to incidents within the airport premises.
(2) To ensure the safety and security of responders, passengers, employees, and airport
facilities.
(3) To minimize disruptions to airport operations and restore normalcy as quickly as
possible.
(b) AICB main objectives are:
(1) Establish Command Structure: Define clear roles and responsibilities for personnel
involved in incident response, including representatives from various airport
departments, emergency services, and relevant stakeholders.
(2) Enhance Communication: Facilitate efficient communication channels among all
stakeholders involved in the incident response, ensuring timely dissemination of
information and coordination of activities.
(3) Coordinate Resources: Identify and allocate necessary resources, such as personnel,
equipment, and materials, to effectively manage the incident and support response
efforts.
(4) Ensure Safety and Security: Prioritize the safety and security of individuals and property
affected by the incident, implementing appropriate measures to mitigate risks and
hazards.
(5) Manage Information: Collect, analyse, and disseminate relevant information regarding
the incident, including its nature, scope, and potential impact, to inform decision-
making and response strategies.
(6) Implement Incident Action Plans (IAPs): Develop and execute comprehensive IAPs
outlining specific objectives, tactics, and timelines for managing the incident and
achieving established goals.
(7) Monitor and Evaluate Progress: Continuously monitor the progress of response efforts,
assess the effectiveness of implemented strategies, and make necessary adjustments to
optimize resource utilization and address emerging challenges.

(8) Coordinate with External Agencies: Collaborate with external agencies, such as local
emergency services, government agencies, airlines, and other airports, as needed, to
enhance response capabilities and facilitate mutual aid agreements.
(9) Facilitate Recovery and Restoration: Develop strategies and initiatives to facilitate the
recovery and restoration of airport operations and infrastructure following the
resolution of the incident, including post-incident debriefings and lessons learned
exercises.
(c) By adhering to these objectives, the Airport Incident Command Board aims to effectively
manage incidents, mitigate potential risks, and safeguard the continuity of airport operations
while ensuring the safety and well-being of all stakeholders involved.

Figure-10: Example of an airport incident command board

4. ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE MOBILE COMMAND POST (BRONZE COMMAND)
(a) Role of the MCP: The Mobile Command Post serves as the on-scene operational hub for
managing an aircraft emergency. It is responsible for:
(1) Coordinating operational-level responses by on-scene emergency services lead by the
Airport Incident Commander

(2) Managing on-scene resources, including fire and emergency services, medical teams,
law enforcement, and security.
(3) Providing situational updates to the higher command levels (Silver and Gold
Commands).
(4) Ensuring effective communication among all involved agencies.
(b) Responsibilities of Bronze Command: Bronze Command is responsible for executing the
incident management plan at the operational level, ensuring that the strategies developed by
Silver Command are carried out effectively. Specific responsibilities include:
(1) Deployment of resources as per the incident action plan.
(2) Monitoring and ensuring the safety of operational personnel.
(3) Liaising with the Airport Incident Commander to report on progress, challenges, and
resource needs.
(4) Managing interagency coordination and ensuring that each service understands their
role and responsibilities.
5. ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION OF THE MOBILE COMMAND POST
(a) Site Selection and Setup: The location of the Mobile Command Post must be strategically
selected to provide a clear line of sight of the incident site and accessibility to essential
resources. Key factors in selecting an MCP location include:
(1) Proximity to the emergency scene without compromising responder safety.
(2) Adequate space for personnel, communication equipment, and operational tools.
(3) Availability of access routes for emergency vehicles and logistics support.
(b) The MCP should be equipped with the necessary communication systems, including radio,
satellite, and secure internet connections, as well as visual aids such as maps, operational
plans, and tracking boards.
(c) Operational Structure: The Mobile Command Post should follow a structured command
system in line with the Aerodrome Incident Command System (ICS). Key roles include:
(1) Airport Incident Commander / Bronze Commander: Overall in charge of the
operational response.
(2) Logistics Officer: Responsible for ensuring the availability and distribution of resources,
including personnel and equipment.
(3) Operations Officer / Bronze Support: Coordinates the tactical response of fire services,
medical teams, and law enforcement.

(4) Liaison Officer: Facilitates communication and coordination with other agencies and
stakeholders.
(5) Safety Officer: Monitors and ensures the safety of all personnel on-site.
(6) Communication Officer: Ensure the functionality of all communication systems and
manage the dissemination of information between the MCP, EOC, on-site teams, and
external agencies.
(d) Resource Management: Effective resource management is critical for the success of MCP
operations. Bronze Command must:
(1) Conduct a thorough assessment of resource availability and deploy them as per the
incident action plan.
(2) Ensure that resources are used efficiently and prevent overcommitment, which could
lead to operational fatigue.
(3) Keep a detailed log of resource allocation and usage for accountability and future
reference.
(e) Communication Protocols: Clear, concise, and continuous communication is essential for
effective management of aircraft emergencies. The MCP must establish and maintain
communication with:
(1) Silver Command (Tactical): To receive tactical instructions and provide tactical updates.
(2) Gold Command (Strategic): For policy-level decisions, if required.
(3) On-site Units: Fire services, medical teams, law enforcement, and other responders to
ensure the alignment of operational activities.
(f) The communication systems must be reliable and should include redundancies such as backup
radios, satellite phones, and manual dispatch systems.
(g) See Table 3 for example of standard MCP phraseology for aircraft emergency scenarios and
Table 4 for example of MCP incident log entries.

6. INTERAGENCY COORDINATION
(a) Multi-Agency Coordination: Aircraft emergencies often involve multiple agencies working
together. Effective interagency coordination ensures that:

(1) Each agency’s role is clearly defined in the incident action plan.
(2) Agencies maintain their own command structures but operate under the unified
command framework established by the MCP.
(3) Regular interagency briefings are held to update all responders on the current status of
operations, emerging risks, and changes in strategy.
(b) Joint Incident Action Plan: The MCP is responsible for implementing the Joint Incident Action
Plan, which outlines the tactical objectives, operational strategies, and resource deployment
for the aircraft emergency. The plan should be developed with input from all responding
agencies and must include:
(1) Objectives: Clear and measurable goals for each phase of the emergency response.
(2) Tactical Assignments: Specific tasks assigned to each unit, such as fire suppression,
casualty evacuation, or perimeter security.
(3) Contingency Plans: Secondary actions to be taken in case of unexpected developments,
such as adverse weather or secondary incidents.
7. SAFETY AND WELFARE OF PERSONNEL
(a) Personnel Safety: Bronze Command has a primary responsibility to ensure the safety and
welfare of all operational personnel. This involves:
(1) Conducting regular dynamic risk assessments and hazard identification at the incident
site.
(2) Implementing safety measures such as personal protective equipment (PPE),
decontamination protocols, and safe zones.
(3) Monitoring fatigue levels and mental health of responders, ensuring adequate rest
periods and psychological support where necessary.
(b) Incident Termination and Demobilisation: The MCP will oversee the safe demobilisation of all
personnel and resources at the conclusion of the emergency. This includes:
(1) Accounting for all personnel and equipment.
(2) Conducting a post-incident briefing to evaluate the response and identify areas for
improvement.
(3) Ensuring the site is handed over to the appropriate authority for investigation or
recovery efforts.
8. POST-INCIDENT REVIEW AND REPORTING
(a) Debriefing: Once the emergency has been brought under control, a debriefing session should
be conducted at the MCP with all involved agencies. This debrief should cover:

(1) A summary of the incident and the response operations.
(2) Identification of any operational challenges encountered.
(3) Recommendations for improving future MCP operations.
(b) Reporting: A formal incident report should be prepared by Bronze Command detailing the
MCP’s activities, resource usage, and coordination efforts. This report must be submitted to
Silver Command and the Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) within a stipulated timeframe.
9. CONCLUSION
(a) Effective management of the Mobile Command Post (Bronze Command) during aircraft
emergencies is essential for the success of the overall incident response. This guidance
document, based on ICAO standards and best practices, provides a comprehensive framework
for the setup, operation, and coordination of MCP activities. By following this structured
approach, aerodrome operators and emergency responders can ensure a coordinated,
efficient, and safe response to aircraft emergencies.

COMMUNICATION SYSTEM
(a) A communication system should be provided at the aerodrome that:
(1) link the crisis management centre, the emergency operations centre and the mobile
command post with each other and with the relevant responding agencies are
provided;
(2) ensure adequacy of the communication system in accordance with the emergency plan
and consistent with the particular requirements of the aerodrome; and
(3) where an aerodrome operates more than one operational runway, a communication
system is capable to support multiple emergencies. Where necessary, a communication
needs assessment should be conducted.

title: Emergency planning
text:
1. COMMUNICATION SERVICES
(a) Arrangements for two-way communications should be made for all aerodrome agencies
involved in an emergency. The plan also should include the maintenance of a sufficient
communication network with off-aerodrome agencies responding to an emergency. The plan
calls for the mobile command centre and emergency operations centre to have the capability

of continuous communication with all participating agencies. Backup modes of
communication should be identified during the planning process.
2. COMMUNICATION NETWORK
(a) Communication network for use during an emergency should be accepted by the UAE
telecommunication authority to be used at an aerodrome.
(b) A co-ordinated communication network is of vital importance to any major operation
involving agencies from more than one jurisdiction.
(c) A co-ordinated communication network should consist of a sufficient number of radio
transceivers, telephones and other communication devices to establish and maintain a
primary and a secondary means of communication. These networks should link the
emergency operations centre and the command post with each other as well as with all
participating agencies.
(d) The operational communication network should provide a primary and, where necessary, an
alternate means for effective direct communications between the following, as applicable:
(1) The alerting agency (control tower or flight service station, aerodrome manager, fixed-
base operator, or airline office) and the rescue and firefighting (RFF) units serving the
aerodrome.
(2) Air traffic control tower and/or flight service station, the appropriate ARFFS watchroom
and the RFF crews en-route to an aircraft emergency and at the accident/incident site.
(3) Appropriate mutual aid agencies located on or off the aerodrome, including an alert
procedure for all auxiliary personnel expected to respond.
(4) The RFF vehicles, including a communication capability between crew members on each
RFF vehicle.
3. COMMUNICATION EQUIPMENT
(a) It is important to provide serviceable communication equipment in sufficient quantity to
ensure rapid response of personnel and equipment to an emergency. The following
communication equipment should be available for immediate use in the event of an
emergency.
(b) A sufficient number of portable, two-way radios should be available to provide each
participating agency with the ability to communicate with the command post.
(c) Strict communication discipline should be employed to prevent jamming of emergency
frequencies. Each agency should operate on its own frequency, and there should be a
designated command frequency.

(d) Radios should be available at the command post to provide direct communication with the
aircraft or ground controllers should it become necessary. These radios should be equipped
with headsets to reduce the confusion and noise from multiple frequencies in use at the time.
(e) Direct communications may also be established with the pilot or the aircraft cockpit by use of
cockpit-to ground lines. This requires a proper connector, wire, microphone, and headset. Co-
operation and co-ordination between the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service and the
individual aircraft operator(s) are needed to establish this type of communication capability.
Normally, this communication capability results from the use of a ground service headset that
is plugged into a wheel well interphone jack.
(f) A sufficient number of telephone lines (both listed and unlisted) or cellular phones should be
available at the command post to provide direct communication with agencies outside the
aerodrome, as well as within the aerodrome. Direct lines save time and reduce the probability
of overloading radio communication channels.
(g) Medical facilities and ambulances need communications capability in order to take advantage
of advance life support systems within the medical community.
(h) A dedicated vehicle equipped with necessary communication equipment and self-contained
electrical power may be a definite asset to a good communication system. A well-equipped
communication vehicle is an indispensable part of an efficient, well-managed command post.
Planning should always include a qualified vehicle driver/operator.
(i) It is desirable to install recording devices with time insertion units at the operations centre
and/or mobile command centre to ensure that all communications are recorded for later
analysis. It is also desirable to record all emergency communications, including printed
communication.
(j) In the event of a temporary lapse of communications, appropriate contingency measures or
runners should be assigned to the command post to augment other modes of communication.
Portable megaphones should also be available.
4. APRON AND TERMINAL AREA EMERGENCIES
(a) A communications system should be established by the aerodrome operator s, or the aircraft
operators, in order to provide rapid response of the emergency equipment to accidents and
incidents occurring in the terminal areas. Apron accidents include aircraft cabin fires,
refuelling spills and fires, aircraft and vehicle collisions and medical emergencies.

(b) As many apron personnel as possible, but at least all supervisory personnel, should be
equipped with two-way radios in order to establish direct communication with a central
notification facility.
(c) All aircraft loading gates or jetways should be equipped with telephones at both boarding and
apron levels.
(d) Emergency telephone numbers should be prominently displayed at apron areas.
5. TESTING AND VERIFICATION
(a) The communication system should be tested each day to verify the operability of all radio and
telephone networks.
(b) A complete and current list of interagency telephone numbers should be available to all
agencies and to personnel responsible for the aerodrome/community emergency plan. These
phone numbers should be verified monthly to ensure they are correct. Updated lists should be
distributed to all emergency plan participants on a continual basis.

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES AND EQUIPMENT
(a) Sufficient medical services and supplies should be provided at an aerodrome. Provision of
medical services will generally not present great difficulties at a large aerodrome or
aerodromes near a large city, as the human resources and material will normally be available.
It is necessary to develop the co-ordination with the emergency medical assistance system in
the region. The medical co-ordinator appointed to the aerodrome should be responsible for
the provision and checking of medical supplies.
(b) Provision of medical services may present some difficulties at small aerodromes not located
near populated areas.
(c) These aerodromes, however, should have available emergency medical services to provide
sufficient medical care in the event of an aircraft accident, taking into account the largest
aircraft using the aerodrome.
(d) A medical inventory of the aerodrome community area should be part of the aerodrome
emergency plan. Consideration should be given to:
(1) human resources on and off the aerodrome, i.e. doctors, teams qualified in
occupational first aid, stretcher bearers and nurses; and
(2) medical equipment and services on and off the aerodrome, i.e. hospitals and
ambulances.
(e) At aerodromes where the above resources are only available from areas beyond the
immediate aerodrome community, the aerodrome emergency plan should be integrated with
wider emergency plans to obtain the necessary response, possibly using helicopters to
transport medical services and equipment to the crash site.

EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES AT AERODROMES
(a) Basis for recommendations.
(1) Emergency medical services at aerodromes are based on the concept that medical
personnel and a medical facility commensurate with the size of the aerodrome have
been established at an aerodrome and that mutual aid emergency agreements have
been developed. Sufficient medical supplies should be maintained at an aerodrome
facility to deal with routine medical emergencies which normally occur at an aerodrome
(on-the-job injuries, heart attacks, etc.) plus possible aircraft accidents.
(2) Emergency medical training of aerodrome personnel. All personnel assigned to rescue
duties and “public-contact” aerodrome employees should be given first aid and CPR
(cardiopulmonary resuscitation) training.
(3) Rescue and firefighting personnel should have the ability to stabilize seriously injured
casualties. At least two full-time members per shift of the aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service or other on-aerodrome personnel should be trained to an
emergency medical treatment level as determined by the local medical authority. In
addition, it is recommended that as many rescue and firefighting personnel as is
practicable receive training to meet minimum standards of medical proficiency and
preferably to the level of personnel highly qualified in first aid or the equivalent.
Accordingly, they should have sufficient medical equipment at their immediate disposal
to initiate stabilization until full medical services are available at the site or until
transportation of casualties to sufficient medical facilities is provided.
(b) Occupation first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
(1) Rescue and firefighting personnel should be trained in occupational first aid (OFA) and
cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) as taught by the medical authority, accepted
medical person or organisation. Periodic exercises and drills in OFA and CPR techniques
are mandatory to maintain proficiency.
(2) The everyday medical problems at an aerodrome can serve to promote and ensure a
sufficient level of medical proficiency of aerodrome-based emergency personnel. It
should be noted, however, that proficiency in emergency medical techniques can be
maintained only through constant practical application. Unless operations include
providing advanced life-support systems on a day-to-day basis, proficiency will decline
or disappear.
(3) Aerodromes may enlist volunteers from aerodrome employees other than rescue and
firefighting personnel to provide an immediate response to assist casualties resulting

from emergencies. Volunteers should be trained by accredited agencies in first aid and
rescue response duties. In case of an emergency, they should initially be under the
supervision of the first commander at the scene, i.e. the chief fire officer, until the
arrival of the medical co-ordinator. Each appropriate authority should address the
issues of compensation and liability.
(c) Emergency medical supplies and equipment.
(1) The aerodrome operator should arrange to have sufficient medical supplies, available
on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome, to treat the passenger and crew capacity of the
largest aircraft normally using the aerodrome. Experience has shown, however, that
more than one aircraft can be involved in an aircraft accident. Consequently, medical
supplies to handle this possibility should be considered. The type and quantity of such
supplies should be determined by the principal medical authority for the aerodrome
using the statistical information given in Table 5 below.

Note: These figures are taken from ICAO based on the assumption that the maximum number of
surviving casualties at an aircraft accident occurring on or in the vicinity of an aerodrome is
