(2) Statistical data collected from aircraft accidents indicates that about 75 per cent of the
aircraft occupants are expected to be surviving casualties. It can be expected that
requirements for care of these will be distributed as follows:
(i) 20 per cent — Immediate care (Red — Priority I)
(ii) 30 per cent — Delayed care (Yellow — Priority II)
(iii) 50 per cent — Minor care (Green — Priority III)
A table of the estimated maximum number of casualties resulting from an aircraft accident
occurring at an aerodrome is given in Table-1.
(3) The aerodrome should have available stretchers, blankets, backboards and/or
immobilizing mattresses, preferably stored on a suitable vehicle (e.g. trailer) which can
be transported to the accident site. Blankets are needed to alleviate casualties'
exposure to shock and possible adverse weather conditions. Since trauma victims in an
aircraft accident sometimes sustain severe spinal injuries, backboards and cervical
collars should be used when removing such casualties from the aircraft in order to
minimize the possibility of further spinal injury. The backboards should be of a type
designed to fit through access ways and aisles of commercial and business aircraft. They
should have restraining straps available so that the patient can be secured to the board.
A cleat should be attached to the underside of the backboard to facilitate lifting by
carrying personnel.
(4) Sufficient emergency oxygen and respiratory equipment should be available to treat
smoke inhalation victims.
(5) Since the majority of non-accident-related medical emergencies at aerodromes involve
coronary difficulties, advanced life support systems should be readily available.
(6) Mobile emergency hospitals or inflatable tents or shelters can be used for on-site
treatment of immediate care (Priority I — Red) and delayed care (Priority II — Yellow)
casualties. These units should be readily available for rapid response. The casualties can
be treated at the scene, stabilized and be available for transportation to the
appropriate hospital.
(7) A resuscitation type ambulance can be used as an ideal shelter for an immediate care
(Priority I — Red) casualty.
(8) Inflatable tents should have sufficient ventilation and lighting when possible. A large
tent can normally accommodate about ten (10) serious cases and can be carried on a
large all-purpose vehicle along with other necessary medical equipment.

(9) To cope with an emergency involving a large aircraft, it is recommended that the
general emergency medical supplies and equipment described in Table-2 be available at
an aerodrome or be available from outside sources. Table-2 has been prepared to cope
with the largest type of aircraft at present being used for commercial air transport
operations, i.e. A380, B747, DC-10, Airbus. If only operations by smaller aircraft are
planned for the foreseeable future, the specified medical supplies and equipment
should be adjusted to comply with reasonable requirements for the largest aircraft
expected to operate at an aerodrome.
(10) The following material describes some of the items included in Table 6:
(i) Immobilizing mattresses (also called vacuum mattresses): This apparatus consists
of a plastic bag designed like a mattress and filled with very small balls. An
aspirator (mechanical or other) is used to take out the air so that the mattress is
crushed by atmospheric pressure and becomes as rigid as plaster. A human body,
partly enveloped before compressing the mattress, is completely wrapped. Head,
limbs and backbone thus become immobilized, allowing any type of
transportation through the use of lateral rope loops. The apparatus is permeable
to x-rays. Although the dimensions are variable, its length varies generally
between 1.80 and 1.90 m and its width between 0.80 and 0.90 m.
(ii) Backboards. These are classified as long and short backboards. The approximate
dimensions for a long backboard are 1.90 x 0.5 m. Although a backboard of 1.90
m, some backboards of 1.85 m length should be available to manoeuvre through
the smallest aircraft emergency exits of 51 cm wide and 91.5 cm high. A 7.5 cm
wide velcro retaining strap is normally required for legs. hips, upper torso and
head. The appropriate dimensions for a short backboard is. A 7.5 cm wide velcro
retaining strap is normally required for lower and upper torso.
Table 6: List of general emergency medical supplies and equipment
Description Quantity
Triage labels 500
Stretchers, adaptable to the most commonly used ambulances 100
Immobilizing mattresses for backbone fractures 10
Splints, either conventional or inflatable, for the various types of fractures 50
First-aid kits, each containing a set of 10 tags, haemostatic pads, tourniquets,
respiratory tubes, scissors, dressings, sterile burn packs

Resuscitation chests containing material for on-site intubation, infusion and
oxygenation for about 20 casualties
Electrocardiographic or electro-radioscopic apparatuses 2 or 3
Manual or mechanical respirators 2 or 3
Intravenous infusion packs (normal saline or haemocoel) with giving sets 10
Suction devices 2 or 3
Entonox analgesic cylinders 2
Plastic body bags / temporary storage for the deceased 300-500

(d) Emergency medical communication system.
(1) Communications is a primary requisite of an aerodrome emergency medical plan. The
aerodrome medical service communication system should ensure sufficient
communication during emergencies to disseminate warning information and obtain
support operations. Without communications the hospital cannot know the number
and type of casualties it will be receiving, ambulances cannot be directed to the
facilities most capable of rendering the needed care, supplies available from outside
sources cannot be called for, and medical personnel cannot be directed to the point
where they are needed most.
(2) The participating hospitals should have the capability of communicating with one
another by means of a two-way communication network. Ideally, each hospital should
have the capability of either calling other individual hospitals or, if the occasion arises,
calling all other hospitals simultaneously. This capability is invaluable for hospitals
experiencing an emergency such as a requirement for a certain blood type or an item of
equipment in short supply. It is also recommended that the medical co-ordinator be
able to communicate with participating hospitals directly.
(e) Emergency medical transportation facilities.
(1) The dispatch of casualties to hospitals from the accident site should take into
consideration the hospital(s) medical personnel on staff, medical specialties and beds
readily available. Ideally, each aerodrome should have available at least one on-call
ambulance for routine medical emergencies. Written agreements with off-aerodrome
based ambulances should be prepared to provide for emergency transportation
services.

(2) Airborne transportation equipment, i.e. helicopters and fixed wing aircraft, should be
considered for emergency evacuation or for transport of medical services and
equipment from hospitals to the accident site.
(3) Since it may be necessary to transport many casualties to appropriate off-aerodrome
medical facilities, ambulances arriving at the scene should report to the rendezvous
point or staging area and then to the designated transportation officer. This officer will
be responsible for ascertaining the number of casualties who will need transportation,
the number and type of ambulance units necessary, and the availability and capacity of
each medical facility receiving casualties. In the event of a multi-casualty accident, the
transportation officer (or members of the team) will also supervise the actual loading,
recording of names and injuries of casualties, and routing of the individual vehicles and
casualties to hospitals.
(4) In major emergency situations, other means of transportation may be substituted for
ambulances. Vans, buses, automobiles, station wagons or other suitable aerodrome
vehicles may be used. Immediate transportation for moving of the uninjured or
apparently uninjured to a designated holding area should be available.
(5) A grid map (with date of latest revision) of the aerodrome and surrounding area should
be provided for all rescue vehicles. All medical facilities should be depicted prominently
on the grid map
AERODROME MEDICAL CARE FACILITIES (MEDICAL CLINIC AND/OR FIRST-AID ROOM)
(a) General factors influencing need.
(1) There are many general factors which influence the need for an aerodrome first-aid
room or an aerodrome medical clinic. Factors to be taken into consideration include:
(i) the number of passengers served annually and the number of employees based on the
aerodrome;
(ii) the industrial activity on the aerodrome property and in the surrounding
community;
(iii) the distance from sufficient medical facilities; and
(iv) mutual aid medical services agreements.
(2) Generally, it may be recommended that an aerodrome medical clinic be available when
the aerodrome employees number 1 000 or more and that a first-aid room be available
at every aerodrome. The aerodrome medical care or first-aid room personnel and
facilities should be integrated with the aerodrome emergency plan.

(3) The aerodrome medical clinic, in addition to providing emergency medical care to the
aerodrome population, may extend emergency care to communities surrounding the
aerodrome, if these communities have no emergency facilities of their own.
(4) The aerodrome medical clinic may be included in the community emergency services
organization and planning. In the event of a large-scale non-aerodrome local
emergency, the aerodrome medical clinic may function as the co-ordination site for
direction of incoming medical assistance.
(b) Location of aerodrome medical care facilities.
(1) The facilities should be readily accessible to the aerodrome terminal building, to the
general public and to emergency transportation equipment (i.e. ambulances,
helicopters, etc.). Site selection should avoid the problem of having to move injured
persons through congested areas of the aerodrome terminal building, while providing
access to the facility by emergency vehicles by a route that as far as is feasible can
bypass normal public access roadways to and from the aerodrome. This suggests that
the medical care facility be located so that access can be gained from the air side of the
aerodrome terminal building as this provides control over unauthorized vehicles
interfering with emergency equipment.
(c) Aerodrome medical care facility personnel.
(1) The number of trained personnel and degree of expertise needed by each individual will
depend on the particular aerodrome's requirements. The staff of the aerodrome
medical clinic should form the nucleus for the medical services planning for the
aerodrome emergency plan (and be responsible for implementation of the medical
portion of the plan). It is recommended that an aerodrome first-aid room be staffed
with at least highly qualified first-aid personnel.
(2) In general, it is recommended that during the principal hours of aerodrome activity at
least one person trained to deal with the following be on duty:
(i) cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR);
(ii) bleeding from a traumatic source;
(iii) Heimlich manoeuvre (choking);
(iv) fractures and splinting;
(v) burns;
(vi) shock;
(vii) emergency childbirth and immediate care of newborn, including prematures;

(viii) common medical conditions which may influence the outcome of injury (allergies,
high blood pressure, diabetes, pace-maker, etc.);
(ix) basic measures for treatment and protection subsequent to spills or leaks of
radioactive materials, toxic, or poisonous substances;
(x) treatment of emotionally disturbed persons;
(xi) recognition and first aid for poisons, bites, and anaphylactic shock; and
(xii) transportation techniques for injured persons.
(3) This person should have authority to order hospitalization, if necessary and to arrange
any needed transportation.
(4) The aerodrome operator should obtain the advice and direction of a consulting
emergency medical care physician as to the allotment and design of equipment for the
first-aid room commensurate with the anticipated needs of the particular aerodrome.
(5) The aerodrome medical clinic equipment and the medical supplies have to be
determined by the physician or the group of physicians in charge of the clinic. It should
be remembered that responding to an aircraft emergency may be the main problem.
(6) The aerodrome medical care facility should be sufficiently equipped to handle cardiac
arrest and other types of injuries and illnesses associated with industrial medicine. If
drugs are maintained, provision should be made to ensure full security.
(7) Sufficient emergency oxygen and respiratory equipment should be available to treat
smoke inhalation victims.
(8) Since the majority of non-accident related medical emergencies at aerodromes involve
coronary problems, advance life support systems including oxygen, oxygen regulators,
and other elements for cardiopulmonary care should be readily available. In addition,
first-aid kits (containing drugs, a wide selection of bandages and splints, blood
transfusion equipment, and burn and maternity kits), chains, ropes, crow-bars, and
metal cutters should be available.
AERODROMES WITHOUT A MEDICAL CARE FACILITY
(a) At aerodromes without a medical care facility (medical clinic or first-aid room), the aerodrome
operator should make arrangements to have available sufficient personnel trained in
advanced first aid to cover all active hours of aerodrome operation. Equipment for first aid
work at these aerodromes should consist, at minimum, of an emergency medical care bag.
(b) This bag should be readily available to be carried on a designated aerodrome emergency
vehicle and should contain at least:

(1) one plastic sheet (1.80 m × 1.80 m) with four spikes;
(2) seven haemostats (one package of three, one package of four);
(3) two field dressings (one 45 cm × 56 cm, one 56 cm × 91 cm);
(4) ten abdominal pads (five packages of two);
(5) forty 10 cm × 10 cm gauze pads (four packages of ten);
(6) two tourniquets;
(7) one artificial airway;
(8) three disposable airways (one each No. 2, No. 4, No. 5);
(9) one bulb syringe with two catheters (No. 12, No. 14 FR);
(10) two large bandage scissors;
(11) twenty disposable syringes with No. 25 GA 1.6 cm needle;
(12) twelve ace bandages (two 15 cm, four 7.5 cm, six 5 cm);
(13) twelve alcohol sponge packages;
(14) four rolls of gauze bandage (two 7.5 cm, two 5 cm);
(15) two rolls of adhesive tape;
(16) four vaseline gauze dressings (15 cm × 91 cm);
(17) box of 100 band-aids;
(18) one blood pressure cuff and gauge;
(19) two clipboards (22 cm × 28 cm);
(20) six pencils;
(21) sufficient supply of casualty identification tags (see Appendix 8);
(22) one set of inflatable splints;
(23) one resuscitube;
(24) one short spine board;
(25) one flashlight;
(26) two cervical collars;
(27) one bite-stick wedge;
(28) one disposable obstetric kit; and
(29) one immobilizing mattress.

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY FACILITIES
(a) The aerodrome should provide a designated area for passengers in order to assemble and
process those who were not injured, or apparently were not injured, during an emergency or

times of disruption. Depending on local circumstances, this area should also be able to take
care of injured passengers. The area selected should provide for both passenger stabilization
and secure protection from the news media.
(b) Taking care of passengers and providing them with all necessities including food and
beverages, warm clothing, etc. is of major importance. Holding together all groups involved in
the accident and in the recovery phases of an accident makes it easier for all parties to control
the flow of information both to passengers and to relatives.
(c) A reception centre should be established in order to accommodate and facilitate the presence
of governing agencies, aircraft operator representatives, health care agencies, police, customs
or any other organization involved. The reception centre will be the natural point of contact
for families, friends, meeters and greeters to get in contact with passengers.
(d) When considering areas where the various functions for caring of survivors can take place,
thought should be given to, at minimum, the following factors:
(1) Security of the area;
(2) Access/egress;
(3) The size of the area;
(4) Facilities such as seating, toilets, etc.;
(5) Telephones/facsimile machines;
(6) Refreshments, etc.;
(7) Processes that need to be undertaken within areas such as triage, medical and welfare;
(8) Wheelchair and stretcher access;
(9) Identification of all persons, including passengers;
(10) Areas for relatives, friends and authorized personnel;
(11) Location and availability of various supplies such as first-aid kits, blankets, stretchers,
etc.;
(12) Power supply for equipment; and
(13) Removal and distribution of luggage and personal effects.
(e) The reception centre and areas where equipment is located should be shown in the AEP. The
list of information that should be kept in an emergency kit at reception centres is as follows:
(1) All personnel of the centre should have knowledge of the location of the emergency kit.
The kit should contain writing pads or forms on which to list the following information
for each passenger:
(i) Name, address and home telephone number of the passenger;

(ii) Name and telephone number of the person to be notified of the passenger’s
condition;
(iii) Arrangement requests of the passenger (i.e., future flight, hotel, transportation
within the local area, etc.); and
(iv) Where the passenger can be contacted during the next 72 hours.
(2) The kit should also contain adhesive name tags to identify passengers who have been
processed and those for whom arrangements have been made.
(3) Telephone numbers for the following resources should be available in the emergency
kit:
(i) Doctors to attend to minor injuries: Each aircraft operator should have a letter of
agreement with a physician(s) who will respond to a designated holding area;
(ii) Hotels where passengers can be billeted: It is beneficial to place passengers in the
same hotel, or at least in groups at hotels;
(iii) Linguists, who should be available on a 24-hour basis and preferably people who
work on the aerodrome, for quick response. (Local schools and private language
departments can also be contacted);
(iv) Caterer (if commissary items are required);
(v) All local reservations offices of aircraft operators;
(vi) Ambulance companies, in case a passenger unexpectedly requires transportation;
(vii) Taxicab companies; and
(viii) Emergency telephone numbers to be disseminated on radio and television, so
that families of the casualties may telephone and receive information.
(4) A current copy of a recognized airline guide should be available in the emergency kit.
Local airline schedules would be most helpful for registrars who will be making
reservation arrangements on future flights.
(f) Consideration needs to be given to arrangements for the release of survivors from the
Reception Centre, as follows:
(1) Reconciliation with relatives;
(2) Survivors without waiting relatives; and
(3) Survivors waiting for other survivors.
(g) Friends and Relatives Reception Centre
(1) A secure and comfortable area should be provided for the assembly of friends and
relatives, located landside in a discreet and comfortable location which is secure and
out of the eye of the public. There, these persons can be registered as legitimate friends

and relatives of the passengers involved in the accident/incident. This is the first place
that families and friends are taken to provide for their basic needs, to record details of
the family and to provide information updates.
(2) The Care of Relatives Plan should be automatically activated when the emergency
operational response to the following emergencies is activated:
(i) Aircraft crash on-aerodrome; and
(ii) Aircraft crash off-aerodrome, where the aircraft originated from or was destined
for the aerodrome.
(3) A senior official of the aircraft operator will be responsible for the initial notification of
relatives and friends.
(h) Reunion and Exit Centre
(1) A secure and comfortable area for the exit of uninjured passengers and their
reunification with friends and relatives should be established. This may include a private
area where friends and relatives will receive information of a passenger’s status.
(i) Survivor Reception Centre
(1) In the transportation area(s), the Incident Command Post should control and record the
transportation of every survivor.
(2) For uninjured survivors, the aerodrome operator , aircraft operator (where involved) or
other predesignated agency selected for the purpose is responsible for:
(i) Interviewing the uninjured and recording their names, addresses, phone numbers
and where they can be reached for the next 72 hours;
(ii) Notifying relatives or next of kin where deemed necessary;
(iii) Co-ordinating efforts with the designated international relief agency (Red Cross,
etc.);
(iv) Preventing interference by unauthorized persons or those not officially
connected with the operation in progress; and
(v) Keeping contact data for every survivor so that the emergency response process
can be continued.
(j) Survivor Repatriation Centre
(1) A survivor repatriation centre is a facility that helps individuals who have survived
traumatic events at aerodromes and in need repatriation assistance.
(2) For uninjured survivors, the aerodrome operator, aircraft operator (where involved) or
other predesignated agency selected for the purpose is responsible for:
(i) medical care;

(ii) counselling;
(iii) legal aid;
(iv) accommodation;
(v) travel arrangements; and
(vi) other necessary resources to support their return to the home country or
intended destination safely.
(k) Aircraft Operator Roles and Responsibilities
(1) The aircraft operator is normally the best entity to establish whether or not a person
has been involved in an aircraft accident. UAE legislation requires each aircraft operator
to maintain a passenger manifest. It is important for the aircraft operator to establish
strict control on the dissemination of passenger manifest to prevent release to
unauthorised persons/organisations. The aircraft operator is also required to establish
family assistance plan in accordance with UAE regulation UAE National Aviation Disaster
Family Assistance Plan regulation for the provision of family assistance in the event of
an accident. The plan covers necessary safety and well-being support, crisis counselling,
etc. For detailed information on the UAE aviation disaster family assistance plan, refer
to Civil Aviation Regulations Family Assistance Plan (CAR FAP).
(2) The aircraft operator is required to provide a high level of protection of passengers by
establishing common rules on care and assistance to passengers in the event of denied
boarding, cancellation, delay and diversion of flights. Aircraft operators are required to
establish regulations and policies required to implement effective coordination and
control of the efforts to provide a passenger welfare programme. This regulation
requires aircraft operators flying to/from and diverting to aerodromes located in the
United Arab Emirates implement a passenger welfare programme, which can be part of
their business continuity plan, and ensure that the programme is implemented,
supervised and audited as necessary. For further guidance on the provision of
passenger welfare programme, refer to Civil Aviation Regulations Passenger Welfare
Programme (CAR PWP).
(3) The aircraft operator should have suitably qualified and trained persons available to
answer inquiries concerning the passengers involved. In general, aircraft operators have
an extensive and comprehensive emergency plan for handling accidents. These plans
should be synchronized with the emergency plans of the aerodrome to minimize any
reduction of effectiveness of deployed resources.
(4) The Airline Coordinator.

(i) Normally this would be the senior representative from the airline whose aircraft
had the accident. In the event of a charter or non-scheduled flight, the
representative of the airline designated to provide ground services for that flight
should take charge. In the event of an overflight or carrier without personnel
based at an aerodrome, representative authority would have to be determined
by those responding. The person in charge should have radio communication to
the airline operations or other designated emergency centre. Telephones should
be available in the holding areas. The person in command oversees the overall
airline operations, making arrangements for additional medical services if
required, commissary items, and so forth.
(ii) The receptionist should meet the transportation vehicles as they arrive from the
scene of the accident and direct the passengers to the registrars’ tables where
they will be processed. The receptionist should know where toilet facilities are
located.
(5) Registrars.
(i) The registrars should have emergency kits available to them. Two people should
constitute one registrar team. Several teams can be required to process the
passengers swiftly and efficiently. One member should enter the passenger’s
name on the manifest and determine what reservation requirements are desired
(hotel accommodations, another flight, transportation, etc.) and any persons to
be notified of the passenger’s condition and plans. The other member of the
registrar team should make out an ID tag or sticker (available from the
emergency kit) and place it on the passenger. This action can assist in identifying
the passenger when accommodations have been made and, more important, will
indicate that the passenger has been processed. The registrars should direct the
victims to the welfare coordinators when their registration is completed. See
Figure-3 for an example of a registrar form.
(ii) Welfare coordinators are the nucleus of psychological first aid. They should
attempt to stimulate passenger discussion. Special attention should be given to
those who do not join in the discussion. In giving psychological first aid, welfare
coordinators should note that some persons become more disturbed than others.
Giving those persons sympathetic understanding can be the first step toward
helping them. Overwhelming victims with pity could only increase their fear and
feelings of helplessness. A person who exhibits bodily trembling, rapid breathing,

rapid pulse, shortness of breath, and so forth, should be engaged in conversation,
and professional medical attention should be requested as soon as available.
(iii) A sizable personnel force can be provided by most aircraft operators; however,
there can be a problem at aerodromes with a small operation. As a result, a
mutual aid assistance programme of all airline personnel (and, if necessary, other
aerodrome tenants based at an aerodrome) should be established. Training can
be acquired from local mental health care and Red Cross units. This training is not
extensive but would provide education for passenger service in an emergency. In
addition to caring for the victims evacuated from an accident site, training also
should include a simulated exercise of a traumatic situation that could develop in
the gate area of the terminal building.
(6) Emergency Kits.
(i) Each airline should prepare an emergency kit that can be readily available to all
airline personnel during all hours of operation. This kit should never be placed in
an office that is locked during certain hours of the day. All station personnel
should have knowledge of the location of the emergency kit. The contents of the
kit should include the following:
(A) Tablets or forms to record the victims’ names, addresses, and home phone
numbers; name and phone number of person to be notified of passenger’s
condition; accommodation request of passenger (i.e., future flight, hotel,
transportation within the local area). See Figure-3 for an example of a
registrar's form.
(B) Stick-on, adhesive-type name tags to identify passengers who have been
processed and to identify victims when accommodations have been made
(C) Telephone numbers of the following:
(D) Doctors to attend to minor injuries. Each airline should have a letter of
agreement with physicians who will respond to a designated holding area.
(E) Hotels where victims can be billeted. It is beneficial to place victims in the
same hotel or at least in groups at hotels.
(F) Linguists, preferably ones who work on the aerodrome premises, for quick
response.
(G) Caterer, if commissary items are required.
(H) All airline reservations offices.
(I) Ambulance companies, in case a victim requires hospitalization.

(J) Taxi/cab companies.
(K) A current copy of the Official Airline Guide (OAG). Local airline schedules
can be helpful for registrars who will be making arrangements on future
flights.

title: Emergency planning
text:
CARE OF AMBULATORY SURVIVORS
(a) The aerodrome operator, aircraft operator (where involved), or other predesignated agency
selected for the purpose is responsible to:
(1) select the most suitable holding area for the particular emergency from those
predesignated in the aerodrome emergency plan;
(2) provide for the transportation of the uninjured from the accident site to the designated
holding area;
(3) arrange for doctor(s), nurse(s) or teams qualified in first aid to examine and treat the
supposedly uninjured, especially for nervous traumatism (shock) and/or smoke
inhalation, where pertinent;
(4) furnish a full passenger and crew manifest for accountability purposes;
(5) interview the uninjured and record their names, addresses, phone numbers, and where
they can be reached for the next 72 hours;
(6) notify relatives or next of kin, where deemed necessary;
(7) co-ordinate efforts with the designated international relief agency (Red Cross, etc.); and
(8) prevent interference by unauthorized persons or those not officially connected with the
operation in progress.
(b) Prearrangement should be made for the immediate transportation by bus or by other suitable
transport of the “walking injured”/ambulatory from the accident site to the designated
holding area. This plan should be implemented automatically following notification of the
emergency. A nurse or a person trained in first aid should accompany these people to the
holding area. Each and every passenger and crew member should be examined for nervous
traumatism (shock) and smoke inhalation. Cold or inclement weather may require additional
provisions for their protection and comfort.
(c) Occupants departing an aircraft using evacuation slides may be barefoot or without proper
wearing apparel.
(d) Where the aircraft accident occurred in water, swamps or desert areas, these people may be
deplorable and uncomfortable conditions. These problems should be anticipated by having

supplies of clothing, footwear, and blankets readily available. It may be necessary to establish
a special holding area which can supply warmth and clothing to prevent hypothermia, heat
related illness and be used for examination purposes, before these persons are transported to
the designated ambulatory holding area.

title: Emergency planning
text:
TRIAGE AND MEDICAL CARE
IMMEDIATE NEED FOR CARE OF INJURED PERSONS IN AIRCRAFT ACCIDENTS
(a) In the aftermath of an aircraft accident, many lives may be lost and many injuries aggravated if
immediate medical attention is not provided by trained rescue personnel. Survivors should be
triaged, given available emergency medical aid as required, and then promptly evacuated to
appropriate medical facilities.
TRIAGE PRINCIPLES (ALL EMERGENCIES)
(a) “Triage” is the sorting and classification of casualties to determine the order of priority for
treatment and transportation. Casualties should be classified into four categories:
(1) Priority I: Immediate care (RED)
(2) Priority II: Delayed care (YELLOW)
(3) Priority III: Minor care (GREEN)
(4) Priority IV: Deceased (BLACK)
(b) The first qualified, medically trained person to arrive at the site should immediately begin
initial triage. This person(s) will continue performing triage until relieved by a more qualified
person or the designated aerodrome triage officer.
(c) Victims should be moved from the triage area to the appropriate care holding areas before
definitive treatment is rendered. Casualties should be stabilized at the care holding areas and
then transported to an appropriate facility.
(d) Every effort should be made to ensure that Priority I casualties are treated first and receive
ambulance transportation priority when stabilized. This is the responsibility of the triage
officer.
(e) Triage is most efficiently accomplished in place. However, the conditions at an accident scene
may demand the immediate movement of casualties before triage can be safely
accomplished. In that case, the casualties should be moved the shortest distance possible,
well away from firefighting operations, and upwind and uphill from the scene.

(f) Triage of casualties should include the use of casualty identification tags to aid in the sorting
of the injured and their transportation to a designated hospital. This technique is especially
suited to multilingual situations.
STANDARDIZED CASUALTY IDENTIFICATION TAGS AND THEIR USE
(a) Need for standardized tags. Casualty identification tags should be standardized through colour
coding and symbols to make the tag as simple as possible. Tags help to expedite the treatment
of mass casualties in a triage situation and thus permit more rapid evacuation of the injured to
medical facilities.
(b) Tag design. Standardized tags should be designed to require only minimal information to be
entered thereon, be usable under adverse weather conditions, and be water resistant. An
example of such a tag is illustrated in Figure-11 below. In this tag, numerals and symbols
indicate the medical priority classification of casualties as follows:

Figure-11: Example of a triage tag
(1) Priority I or immediate care: RED tag (Roman numeral I; rabbit symbol);
(2) Priority II or delayed care: YELLOW tag (Roman numeral II; turtle symbol);

(3) Priority III or minor care: GREEN tag (Roman numeral III; ambulance with X symbol);
(4) Priority IV or deceased: BLACK tag
(c) Where tags are unavailable, casualties may be classified by using Roman numerals on
adhesive tape or by placing marks directly on the forehead or on other exposed skin areas to
indicate priority and/or treatment needs. Where marking pens are unavailable, lipstick can be
used. Felt tipped pens are not advisable as they may smear in rain, sand or hail and freeze in
low temperatures.
CARE PRINCIPLES
(a) Stabilization of the seriously injured should be accomplished at the accident site. The
immediate transportation of the seriously injured before stabilization should be avoided.
(b) In accidents occurring on or adjacent to the aerodrome, rescue and firefighting personnel are
generally the first emergency personnel on the scene. These personnel should be aware that it
is imperative that seriously injured casualties be located and stabilized as quickly as possible.
In cases where fire control or prevention does not require the efforts of all rescue and
firefighting personnel, available persons should immediately commence casualty stabilization
under the direction of the most qualified trauma-trained individual on the scene. First
response rescue vehicles should carry initial supplies of casualty-care equipment, including
artificial airways, compresses, bandages, oxygen and other related equipment used for the
stabilization of smoke inhalation casualties and severe trauma. Sufficient oxygen should be
available for use on rescue and firefighting personnel. However, oxygen should not be used in
areas where fuel spills or fuel-soaked clothing is present due to the explosion hazard.
(c) Actions taken during the first few minutes of medical treatment should stabilize the casualties
until more qualified medical care is available. When specialized trauma teams arrive, more
sophisticated medical care (i.e. cardiopulmonary resuscitation, etc.) will be provided.
(d) The triage procedure and subsequent medical care should be placed under the command of
one authority, the designated medical commander, upon this officer's arrival. Prior to this, the
command of triage should be assumed by the individual designated by the commanding
rescue and firefighting chief and should continue until relieved by the predesignated medical
co-ordinator.
(e) The medical commander has responsibility for all medical aspects of the incident and should
report directly to the aerodrome incident commander. The medical commander’s primary
function will be administrative, not as a participant of the medical team treating the injured.

(f) As a means to easily identify and distinguish the medical co-ordinator, a white hard hat and
highly visible white coat or vest should be worn, with “MEDICAL COMMANDER” displayed
front and back in reflective red lettering (see Figure-12).

Figure-12: Example of a medical commander tabard
(g) Care of Priority I (Immediate care) casualties. This type of casualty includes:
(1) major haemorrhages;
(2) severe smoke inhalation;
(3) asphyxiating thoracic and cervico-maxillo-facial injuries;
(4) cranial traumata with coma and rapidly progressive shock;
(5) compound fractures;
(6) extensive burns (more than 30 per cent);
(7) crush injuries;
(8) any type of shock; and
(9) spinal cord injuries.
(h) The following actions are recommended:
(1) first aid (clearing of the wind pipe, stopping of haemorrhages by means of haemostatic
pads, and positioning
(2) the casualty in the recovery position;
(3) resuscitation;
(4) oxygen administration, except in areas of fuel or fuel soaked clothing; and
(5) placing the injured under shelter pending transportation.
(i) Care of Priority II (Delayed care) casualties. This type of casualty includes:
(1) non-asphyxiating thoracic trauma;
(2) closed fractures of the extremities;
(3) limited burns (less than 30 per cent);

(4) cranial trauma without coma or shock; and
(5) injuries to soft parts.
(j) Care of casualties sustaining injuries which do not need immediate emergency medical
treatment to sustain life can be delayed until Priority I casualties have been stabilized.
Transportation of Priority II casualties will be performed following minimum on-site care.
(k) Care of Priority III (Minor care) casualties. This type of casualty includes minor injuries only.
Certain accidents/incidents will occur where passengers have either minor or no injuries, or
appear not to be injured. Because these casualties can interfere with other priorities and
operations, it is important that they be transported from the accident/incident site to the
designated holding area where they should be re-examined.
(l) It is important that provisions be made for the care, comfort, and identification of Priority III
casualties. This should be provided through aerodrome operations, the aircraft operator (where
involved), or international relief organization (Red Cross, etc.). Specific treatment areas should
be predesignated for this purpose, such as an empty hangar, a designated area in a passenger
terminal, a fire station, or other available sites of sufficient size (hotel, school, etc.). Any such
area selected should be equipped with heating or cooling systems, electric light and power,
water, telephones and toilet facilities. A number of such preselected sites should be available so
that, when an accident occurs, the most advantageous site can be selected based on both travel
distance and space needs (number of casualties involved). All aircraft operator personnel and
aerodrome tenants should know the location of such designated facilities.
CONTROL OF THE FLOW OF THE INJURED
(a) The injured should pass through four areas which should be carefully located and easily
identified. See Figure-13 below.
(1) Aircraft survivor and crew collection area — location where initial collection of the
aircraft survivors and crew from the incident area is accomplished. Need for the
establishment of this area will be dependent upon the type of accident and the
circumstances surrounding the accident site. Custody of casualties is normally
transferred from the rescue and firefighting personnel to medical services at this point.
The rapid deployment of an aircraft passenger evacuation management system (PEMS)
will provide effective aid by leading and guiding passengers and crew to safe and secure
area. In most cases, however, this transfer will occur at the triage area.
(2) Triage area — The triage area should be located at least 90 m upwind of the accident
site to avoid possible exposure to fire and smoke. If necessary, more than one triage

area may be established. Where necessary, secondary triage area/facility may be
considered to protect the survivability of casualties due to ambient heat and humid
conditions.
(3) Care area — Initially, there will be a single care area. Subsequently, this area should be
subdivided into three subareas according to the three categories of injured, i.e.
Deceased (Priority 0), Immediate care (Priority I), Urgent care (Priority II), Delayed care
(Priority III), and Uninjured Holding Area. Care areas can be colour coded for
identification purposes (Red — Immediate, Yellow — Urgent, and Green — Delayed).
The use of coloured tents, tarpaulin ground sheets, traffic cones, flags, etc., may be
used.
(4) Transportation area — A transportation area is made up of one or more staging areas
for the recording, dispatching and evacuation of injured and uninjured survivors should
be located between the triage area and the egress road. The transportation area should
be safe and facilitates rapid movement of vehicles without causing a traffic congestion
at the scene. A coordinator should be designated at each staging area to control and
coordinate the safe movements of vehicles. If there is more than one transportation
area, it is essential to have communications between them.

Figure-13: Triage and medical care at an aircraft accident scene
(5) Ambulance staging area
(6) Ground transportation staging area

(7) Emergency vehicles staging area
(b) Mobile facilities for the stabilization and treatment of Priorities I and II casualties are
recommended. Ideally these facilities should be operational in less than thirty (30) minutes.
Their design should therefore permit rapid conveyance to the site and rapid activation to
receive casualties. These facilities should consist of:
(1) conventional or resuscitation ambulances. A resuscitation ambulance is an ideal shelter
for a Priority I casualty. The casualty may be treated there and subsequently conveyed
directly to a hospital;
(2) red tents to accommodate Priority I casualty - serious or extremely urgent cases. These
facilities, with provisions for integrated heating and lighting, can be transported to the
scene together with all the necessary medical equipment;
(3) yellow tents to accommodate Priority II casualties. Transportable mobile hospitals or
ambulances can be used for stabilization treatment for all casualties; and
(4) green tents to accommodate Priority III casualties or uninjured survivors. Ground
transport or airside buses or vans can be used to house these survivors.

title: Emergency planning
text:
CARE OF DECEASED AND FATALITIES
(a) Evidence should be preserved when caring for the deceased/fatalities during an aircraft
accident. It is important to realize that an undisturbed site will produce the most reliable
evidence for determining cause and/or future corrective action that may help prevent a
similar accident.
(b) The plan should include contingencies that address management of the fatalities at the scene
of the emergency.
(c) The plan needs to designate the person(s) responsible for contacting and co-ordinating with
the forensic doctor. Rescue and firefighting personnel and other rescue personnel should
understand the basic need for and the techniques and procedures used in aircraft accident
investigation. Whenever possible, the wreckage should remain undisturbed until the arrival of
the appropriate accident investigation authority.
(d) Areas immediately surrounding the location of the fatality should be completely secured.
Areas in which a large number of fatalities or dismembered bodies are located should be left
undisturbed until the arrival of the forensic doctor and the aircraft accident investigator or a
designee.

(e) A sufficient supply of disposable plastic gloves and leather gloves should be available for
stretcher bearers removing the remains of the fatalities. Although disposable plastic gloves
are acceptable, they are easily cut or torn by aircraft wreckage and debris. Leather gloves do
not rip or tear but do absorb body fluids and decrease the sense of touch. it is suggested that
one plastic and one leather glove be worn by the individual stretcher bearer or two bearers
can work as a team. All gloves should be burned following use in gathering body parts.
(f) If it becomes necessary to move bodies or parts of the wreckage, photographs should be
taken showing the relative position of bodies and parts within the wreckage and a sketch of
their respective positions should be made prior to removal. In addition, tags should be affixed
to each body or body part displaced and corresponding stakes or tags should be placed where
the body parts were found in the wreckage. A journal should be kept of all tags issued. Special
precautions should be taken to avoid disturbing anything in the cockpit area. Should any flight
controls be required to be displaced, photographs, drawings, or notes should be taken before
displacement.
(g) The fatalities should be extricated and personal effects removed from the wreckage prior to
the arrival of the forensic doctor or appropriate authority only to prevent their destruction by
fire or for other similar compelling reasons.
(h) When bodies should be moved, previously mentioned precautions should be taken. Provisions
should be made to obtain sufficient body bags to contain all bodies as well as personal effects.
(i) Body bags are normally available from major local suppliers of caskets, funeral directors and
their equipment and supply firms, and from nearby military facilities. Stocks of body bags at
each aerodrome are desirable.
(j)  Body identification and determination of cause of death is conducted with the concurrence of
the GCAA designated for this duty. This operation is generally conducted with the co-
operation of forensic teams and other specialists.
(k)  Accidents which result in a large number of fatalities will overload normal morgue facilities. In
areas where delay or temperature may contribute to the deterioration of tissue, refrigerated
storage should be available. This may be provided either by a permanently located cooler or
refrigerated semitrailers. The area for post-mortem examination should be located near the
refrigerated storage and be arranged to provide a high level of security. This should be a
suitable working area with electricity and running water, large enough for initial body sorting.
(l)  The morgue should be isolated in an area remote from places where relatives or the general
public have access.

(m)  After identification has been made of the fatality, efforts to contact next of kin should
commence. Agencies such as aircraft operators, public service organizations (i.e. international
relief agencies and police), or clergy should be utilized.
(n)  The aircraft accident investigation team has the GCAA and the need to require autopsies and
toxicological analyses of flight crew members, and in special cases, passengers. The need for
these tests should be determined prior to the release of bodies.
(o) As soon as practical after the emergency, all participants in the firefighting and rescue effort
should be debriefed. Their observations should be recorded by the proper authorities.
Sketches, diagrams, photographs, movie films, and tape and video recordings made on the
accident site as well as appropriate details on the tagging of bodies and body parts removed
from their positions are invaluable tools for investigators.
(p)  The forensic officer in charge should wear a dark brown hard hat and vest or other apparel,
with “FORENSIC OFFICER” displayed front and back in distinctive lettering (see Figure-14).

Figure-14: Example of a Forensic Officer Tabard

text:
RISK-BASED APPROACH TO MULTIPLE RUNWAY OPERATIONS
(a) Adopting a risk-based thinking approach to emergency planning at these aerodromes provides
a safe and proactive approach to identify, assess, and prioritize risks based on their probability
and potential impact. This approach allows aerodromes to allocate their resources effectively,
focusing on the most significant risks that require immediate attention. It also enables a
continuous improvement cycle, where aerodromes can monitor and review their emergency
plans, update risk assessments, and learn from incidents and near misses to enhance their
overall preparedness.
(b) By adopting risk-based thinking, aerodromes can ensure that their emergency plans are
grounded in a solid understanding of the potential risks they may face and are designed to
minimize their impact. A risk-based thinking approach to aerodrome emergency planning
brings the following benefits:
(1) improves overall aerodrome incident management governance framework;
(2) enhances safety management system at an aerodrome;
(3) establishes safe and proactive culture of continuous improvements;
(4) assists with statutory and regulatory compliance;
(5) assures consistency of delivering of emergency response actions from on and off
aerodrome agencies;
(6) strengthen stakeholders’ inter-operability, intra-operability and confidence; and
(7) business resilience plans.
(c) The risk-based approach strategy covers all aspects of aerodrome emergency preparedness,
including risk assessment, response planning, and continual improvement. It entails
identifying potential hazards, determining their probability and impact, prioritizing risks, and
developing risk criteria. It also includes the formulation of emergency response processes, the
specification of roles and duties, the construction of communication protocols, and the

execution of training and drills. The work also emphasizes the importance of continuous
monitoring and review of emergency plans, updating risk assessments as new information
becomes available, and learning from incidents and near misses to adopt essential
adjustments. By addressing these essential areas, this work seeks to create a thorough and
strong framework for aerodrome emergency preparedness.
(d) It is understood that managing multiple emergencies at an aerodrome will cause severe strain
to the incident management system, resources and personnel. If not meticulously planned,
such situation may cause the overall incident management system to collapse. When planning
for such emergencies, the emergency plan should not solely base on the provision of
aerodrome rescue and firefighting category of the aerodrome but also consider other
pertinent factors. The emergency plan should consider a risk-based approach when planning
for such emergencies. A concept of emergency operations detailing the appropriate level of
emergency response at an aerodrome should be developed. An emergency response model
should be scalable and adaptable to any emergency without compromising the principal
objective of an aerodrome emergency planning.
(e) Assessment for multiple emergencies at an aerodrome should consider the emergency plan’s
adequacy to cope with another emergency situation occurring on the other operational
runway/s whilst managing the first emergency at other runway. When conducting such
assessment, the support and inputs from other aerodrome agencies – air traffic services,
airfield operations, ground handling companies, aerodrome medical facility, etc, may be
necessary.
(f) Aerodromes may consider applying the principles and guidelines outlined in the ISO 31000
risk-based thinking framework to enhance emergency planning processes at these
aerodromes. This framework delves into the various aspects of risk-based thinking, including
the identification and assessment of risks in emergency scenarios, the development of risk
mitigation strategies, and the continuous improvement of emergency preparedness measures
(see Figure-15). The research will consider the challenges and considerations specific to large
aerodromes, as well as the roles and responsibilities of stakeholders involved in the
implementation of the risk-based thinking approach.

Figure-15: Risk-based approach for multi-runways operations
(1) Establishing the context of credible worst-case aircraft emergency scenarios at airports with
multiple runways involves a comprehensive process of identifying, analysing, and preparing
for the most severe and plausible emergency situations that could occur at the airport. This
process is essential for effective risk management and emergency response planning in
complex airport environments.
(i) Understanding Airport Dynamics: This involves a deep understanding of the
operational complexities of airports with multiple runways. Factors like runway
layout, traffic volume, types of aircraft, and airport usage (commercial, cargo,
military) play significant roles.
(ii) Scenario Identification: Identifying worst-case scenarios requires considering a
range of potential emergencies. This could include multiple aircraft incidents
occurring simultaneously, severe weather events, terrorist threats, or catastrophic
mechanical failures.
(iii) Risk Assessment: Evaluating the likelihood and potential impact of each identified
scenario. This assessment takes into account historical data, current airport
operations, and foreseeable changes in aviation trends.

(iv) Vulnerability Analysis: Determining how susceptible the airport's infrastructure,
operations, and safety measures are to these scenarios. This analysis helps in
identifying critical areas that need strengthening.
(v) Stakeholder Consultation: Engage with a wide range of stakeholders, including
airline operators, emergency services, local authorities, and airport staff, to gain
diverse perspectives on potential worst-case scenarios.
(vi) Resource Evaluation: Review the resources available for handling such scenarios,
including emergency response teams, equipment, and communication systems.
Identify any gaps in resources that could hinder an effective response.
(vii) Regulatory and Best Practice Alignment: Ensure that the scenarios and subsequent
plans align with national and international regulatory requirements and industry
best practices.
(2) Identifying all relevant risks arising from aircraft emergencies at airports with multiple
runways involves examining a range of factors that could potentially contribute to or
exacerbate emergency situations. Identifying these risks is a critical step in developing
comprehensive safety and emergency response strategies for airports with multiple
runways. Each risk requires specific attention in planning, training, and resource allocation to
ensure preparedness and effective management in emergency situations.
(i) Runway Incursions and Collisions: With multiple runways, the risk of runway
incursions (unauthorized aircraft, vehicle, or person on a runway) and collisions
increases, particularly during high traffic periods or poor visibility conditions.
(ii) Air Traffic Congestion: High traffic volumes can lead to increased risk of mid-air or
ground collisions, especially during take-offs, landings, and taxiing.
(iii) Crosswind and Weather Hazards: Multiple runways often mean varied orientations,
which can be challenging during crosswinds or severe weather, increasing the risk of
runway excursions or accidents.
(iv) Communication Breakdowns: Effective communication between air traffic control,
pilots, and ground crews is crucial. Miscommunication can lead to serious incidents,
especially in complex multi-runway environments.
(v) Emergency Response Complexity: Coordinating emergency response in a multi-
runway airport can be complicated due to the size and complexity of the airport
layout, potentially delaying critical response efforts.

(vi) Navigational Challenges: Pilots navigating busy, multi-runway airports, especially
those unfamiliar with the layout, can face increased risks of error, contributing to
potential emergencies.
(vii) Mechanical Failures: Aircraft emergencies related to mechanical failures can have
amplified effects at busy airports, where a single incident can disrupt numerous flights
and pose risks to other aircraft.
(viii) Terrorist Threats and Security Breaches: Larger airports with multiple runways may
be more attractive targets for terrorist actions or security breaches, posing significant
risks to safety.
(ix) Environmental and Wildlife Hazards: Wildlife strikes or environmental concerns, like
fog or ice, can be more challenging to manage across multiple runways, increasing the
risk of accidents.
(3) Analysing the risks associated with aircraft emergencies at airports with multiple runways
involves a detailed examination of both the complexities and magnitude of potential
emergencies. This process is crucial for effective risk management and emergency response
planning. By analysing these aspects, airports can develop targeted strategies to mitigate
risks and prepare effective emergency response plans. This analysis is dynamic, requiring
regular updates to reflect changes in airport operations, traffic patterns, and emerging
threats.
(i) Complexity of the Airport Layout: Airports with multiple runways have intricate
layouts that can complicate emergency responses. The analysis includes
understanding runway intersections, taxiway configurations, and potential
bottlenecks that could impact emergency access and evacuation routes.
(ii) Air Traffic Volume and Patterns: High traffic volumes increase the likelihood of
runway incursions or collisions. Risk analysis considers peak traffic times, types of
aircraft (commercial, cargo, private), and flight schedules to assess potential
emergency scenarios.
(iii) Nature of Emergencies: The analysis covers a wide range of emergencies, from
aircraft malfunctions, crashes, and runway overruns to external threats like
terrorism or natural disasters. Each type of emergency has unique risks and
requires specific response strategies.
(iv) Magnitude and Severity: The potential impact of each emergency scenario is
assessed in terms of severity. This includes potential casualties, infrastructure
damage, and disruption to airport operations. Larger-scale emergencies, like a

major crash or terrorist attack, have far-reaching consequences that need
comprehensive response plans.
(v) Interdependent Systems: Airports operate with interlinked systems including air
traffic control, ground handling, and emergency services. Risk analysis examines
how an emergency in one area can cascade and affect other operations.
(vi) Resource Availability and Response Time: Assessing the availability and readiness
of emergency resources (firefighting equipment, medical personnel, evacuation
facilities) and the response time is crucial. Delays in response can exacerbate the
situation, especially in large-scale emergencies.
(vii) External Factors: Factors such as weather conditions, geographical location
(proximity to urban areas), and external emergency support services are also
considered. For instance, an airport near a city might face different risks and have
different resources compared to a remote airport.
(4) Evaluating the risks in terms of their impact and severity on an aerodrome operating
multiple aircraft emergencies involves a comprehensive analysis of potential incidents and
their consequences. By thoroughly evaluating these risks, airport emergency planners can
prioritize areas for improvement in their emergency response plans, ensuring that they are
prepared to effectively manage and mitigate the impacts of various emergency scenarios.
(i) Assessing Probability and Impact: The first step is to assess the likelihood of
various emergencies, such as aircraft collisions, system failures, or natural
disasters, and their potential impact on airport operations and safety.
(ii) Safety of Personnel and Passengers: Evaluating risks involves prioritizing the safety
of passengers, crew, and ground staff. High-severity scenarios include those with a
high potential for causing injuries or fatalities.
(iii) Operational Disruption: The analysis includes how emergencies might disrupt
operations. High-impact risks are those that could lead to significant delays,
cancellations, or diversion of flights, especially during peak operational times.
(iv) Infrastructure Damage Assessment: This involves estimating the potential damage
to airport facilities, including runways, terminals, and navigation aids. Severe risks
are those that could cause extensive damage, requiring significant time and
resources for repair.
(v) Resource Availability for Emergency Response: Evaluating whether the airport has
sufficient resources (personnel, equipment, medical facilities) to handle multiple
emergencies simultaneously is crucial. A lack of resources constitutes a higher risk.

(vi) Environmental and Economic Impact: Consideration of the environmental
repercussions, such as fuel spills, and the broader economic impact of airport
shutdowns or damage to aircraft and facilities is also part of the risk evaluation.
(vii) Reputation and Public Perception: Understanding the potential impact on the
airport's reputation and public trust, especially in the event of severe emergencies
or perceived poor handling of the situation.
(viii) Cascading Effects: Particularly in an aerodrome with multiple runways and
high traffic volumes, the risk evaluation considers the potential for cascading
effects, where an incident in one area can exacerbate issues in another.
(5) Establishing appropriate control measures for managing risks in airport emergency
situations, especially at aerodromes operating with multiple runways, involves a strategic
and multi-faceted approach. By implementing these control measures, an aerodrome can
effectively manage the risks associated with multiple aircraft emergencies, minimizing
impact and ensuring the safety and well-being of passengers, staff, and the surrounding
community.
(i) Enhanced Surveillance and Monitoring Systems: Implement advanced systems for
real-time monitoring of air traffic and runway operations. This helps in early
detection and management of potential emergencies.
(ii) Robust Emergency Response Plan: Develop a comprehensive emergency response
plan that includes protocols for various types of emergencies. Ensure this plan is
regularly reviewed and updated.
(iii) Dedicated Emergency Response Teams: Establish specialized teams trained to
handle different emergency scenarios, including firefighting, medical response, and
hazardous material containment.
(iv) Effective Communication Systems: Set up reliable communication networks
between air traffic control, ground staff, emergency services, and external
agencies. Clear and quick communication is crucial during emergencies.
(v) Regular Training and Drills: Conduct routine emergency drills and training for all
relevant personnel. This ensures preparedness and effective execution of
emergency plans.
(vi) Infrastructure Preparedness: Ensure that the airport infrastructure supports
emergency responses. This includes clear emergency access routes, well-equipped
medical facilities, and designated evacuation areas.

(vii) Resource Availability: Maintain a readily available supply of emergency resources
such as firefighting equipment, medical supplies, and evacuation vehicles.
(viii) Collaboration with External Agencies: Establish partnerships with local
authorities, hospitals, and other relevant organizations for coordinated emergency
responses.
(ix) Public Information and Guidance Systems: Have systems in place for timely and
accurate dissemination of information to the public and guidance for evacuation or
other safety measures.
(x) Post-Emergency Recovery Plans: Develop plans for rapid recovery and resumption
of normal operations following an emergency, including infrastructure repair and
support for affected individuals.
(xi) Psychological Support Services: Offer psychological support services for
passengers, staff, and responders’ post-emergency.
(6) Communicating and consulting with all relevant stakeholders on their preparedness and
readiness for airport emergencies, especially at aerodromes with multiple runways, is a
critical aspect of comprehensive emergency management. By maintaining open lines of
communication and actively involving all stakeholders in preparedness and readiness
activities, an airport can ensure a coordinated and effective response in the event of an
emergency.
(i) Identify Stakeholders: First, identify all relevant stakeholders involved in airport
operations and emergency response. This includes airport management, airline
operators, air traffic control, emergency response teams, local authorities, and
potentially affected community groups.
(ii) Regular Meetings and Workshops: Organize regular meetings and workshops with
stakeholders to discuss and review emergency plans. These meetings provide
opportunities for stakeholders to understand their roles, raise concerns, and offer
suggestions.
(iii) Clear Communication Channels: Establish clear and reliable channels of
communication. This could be through regular emails, a dedicated intranet,
newsletters, or emergency alert system.
(iv) Joint Emergency Drills: Conduct joint emergency drills involving all stakeholders.
These drills not only test the readiness of each party but also enhance coordination
and communication among them.

(v) Feedback Mechanism: Implement a feedback mechanism after drills and real
emergencies. Encourage stakeholders to provide insights into what worked well
and what needs improvement.
(vi) Training Programs: Offer training programs tailored to different stakeholders.
Training should cover specific responsibilities, communication protocols, and
emergency procedures.
(vii) Information Sharing: Share relevant information, such as changes in airport
operations, new risks identified, and updates in emergency procedures, with all
stakeholders. Ensure that the information is accessible and easy to understand.
(viii) Collaborative Decision-Making: Involve stakeholders in decision-making processes
related to emergency preparedness. This collaborative approach ensures that
different perspectives and expertise are considered.
(ix) Community Engagement: Engage with the local community, especially those living
near the airport. Inform them about emergency procedures and how they might be
impacted in an emergency situation.
(x) Review and Update Contact Lists: Regularly update contact lists to ensure that all
stakeholders can be reached quickly in an emergency.
(xi) Transparent Reporting: Maintain transparency in reporting the state of
preparedness and readiness. Share reports and updates on training exercises,
equipment status, and response capabilities.
(7) Monitoring the relevancy of control measures in the context of airport emergency
management, particularly for aerodromes with multiple runways, is vital to ensure ongoing
effectiveness and adaptability to changing circumstances. By actively monitoring and
updating control measures, an aerodrome can maintain a high level of preparedness and
ensure that its emergency response strategies remain effective, relevant, and aligned with
the evolving nature of risks and airport operations.
(i) Regular Review and Assessment: Schedule periodic reviews of all control
measures. This involves assessing their effectiveness in recent drills or actual
emergencies and determining if they meet current operational needs.
(ii) Stakeholder Feedback: Collect and analyse feedback from all stakeholders,
including airport staff, emergency response teams, airline operators, and local
authorities. Their insights can reveal practical challenges and areas for
improvement.

(iii) Benchmarking Against Industry Standards: Compare your control measures with
industry standards and best practices. This benchmarking can highlight areas
where your measures may be outdated or need enhancement.
(iv) Updating Risk Assessments: As new threats emerge and airport operations evolve,
regularly update your risk assessments. Ensure that your control measures align
with the latest risk profiles.
(v) Technological Advancements: Stay informed about technological advancements in
airport safety and emergency response. Incorporate relevant technologies to
enhance your control measures.
(vi) Training Efficacy: Evaluate the effectiveness of training programs in preparing staff
for emergencies. Adjust training content and methods based on performance in
drills and real incidents.
(vii) Incident Analysis: After any emergency incident, conduct a thorough analysis to
understand what worked well and what didn’t. Use these insights to refine your
control measures.
(viii) Regulatory Compliance: Ensure that all control measures comply with current
regulations and legal requirements. Regulatory changes may necessitate updates
to your measures.
(ix) Change Management: Be prepared to manage changes effectively. When a control
measure is updated, communicate changes clearly to all stakeholders and provide
necessary training.
(x) Continual Improvement Process: Adopt a culture of continual improvement,
encouraging suggestions for enhancements and innovations in control measures.
(xi) Emergency Response Plan Testing: Regularly test the entire emergency response
plan. This not only checks the efficacy of individual control measures but also their
collective effectiveness in a simulated emergency situation.
(8) Regularly reviewing and updating control measures and the emergency plan is a critical
process for ensuring the ongoing effectiveness of airport emergency management,
especially in complex environments like aerodromes with multiple runways. By regularly
reviewing and updating control measures and the emergency plan, an aerodrome can
maintain a state of readiness and ensure its response strategies are robust, effective, and
aligned with the current operational environment and emerging risks.
(i) Scheduled Reviews: Set a regular schedule for reviewing the emergency plan and
its associated control measures. Depending on the complexity of the airport

operations and the frequency of changes in risk factors, this could be annually,
biannually, or following significant changes in operations or infrastructure.
(ii) Incorporate Stakeholder Input: Involve all relevant stakeholders in the review
process. This includes airport management, airline representatives, emergency
response teams, air traffic control, local authorities, and potentially affected
community groups. Stakeholder meetings or surveys can be effective ways to
gather feedback.
(iii) Analyse Recent Incidents and Drills: Use data and insights from recent emergency
situations and drills to assess the effectiveness of current control measures.
Identify any weaknesses or areas where the response could be improved.
(iv) Assess Changes in Risk Environment: Evaluate any new risks or changes in the
operational environment. This might include new types of aircraft using the
airport, changes in traffic volume, construction projects, or evolving external
threats.
(v) Update Based on Technological Advancements: Keep abreast of technological
advancements that can enhance emergency response and management.
Incorporating new technologies might involve updating procedures, training, or
equipment.
(vi) Regulatory Compliance: Ensure that the emergency plan and its control measures
comply with current regulations and industry standards. Regulatory changes might
necessitate updates to the plan.
(vii) Training and Competency Assessments: Review the effectiveness of training
programs and conduct competency assessments. Ensure that all personnel are
sufficiently trained for their roles in emergency response.
(viii) Documentation and Communication: Update all documentation related to the
emergency plan and control measures. Communicate any changes clearly to all
involved parties. This might involve revising manuals, updating digital resources,
and conducting briefings or training sessions.
(ix) Plan for Continuous Improvement: Adopt a continuous improvement approach to
emergency management. Encourage feedback and suggestions from all levels of
staff and stakeholders.
(x) Test the Updated Plan: Once updates are made, test the revised emergency plan
through drills and simulations. This testing phase is critical for ensuring that the

changes are effective and that all participants understand their revised roles and
responsibilities.
(xi) Review External Partnerships: Reassess the roles and effectiveness of external
partners, such as local emergency services, hospitals, mutual aid agencies, etc.
Ensure that these relationships and protocols remain effective and relevant.

ADDITIONAL AERODROME HAZARDS
(a) Where there are additional hazards resulting from supporting facilities and operational
activities at the aerodrome, the emergency plan should include:
(1) sufficient emergency orders and instructions to deal with emergencies arising from
these hazards.; and
(2) where the rescue and firefighting service is expected to deal with these additional
hazards, determine the additional amount of extinguishing agents, number of
personnel, vehicles and equipment required, as these requirements may exceed the
promulgated level of aerodrome fire protection.

ADDITIONAL AERODROME HAZARDS
The business of managing an aerodrome may generate other hazards in addition to those created by
the types of aircrafts operating at an aerodrome. Some aerodromes handle vast amounts of cargo
and, in some instances, chemicals and specialized hazardous materials including radioactive
substances. Aerodromes may have significant large fuel storage installations which in themselves
may present considerable hazards. Re-assessment of the additional amounts of extinguishing agents
and number of personnel required to deal with such emergencies must be conducted.

title: Emergency planning
text:
COORDINATION WITH OTHER AGENCIES AND ORGANISATIONS
(a) The aerodrome emergency plan should describe the procedures for coordinating the response
of different aerodrome agencies organisations or services (e.g. ground handlers, airlines,
security services) and those agencies in the surrounding community that could be of
assistance in responding to an emergency.
(b) Emergency mutual aid agreements should be established to define responsibilities and/or
liabilities of each external agency responding to an emergency. These agreements should
include the following:
(1) clarification of the political and jurisdictional responsibilities of the several agencies
(e.g. police, local firefighting services, local authorities, accident investigation bodies,
etc.) that could be involved in order to avoid problems when an emergency occurs;
(2) establishment of the command authority; i.e. a single on-the-scene commander (with
designated alternates if necessary);
(3) designation of communication priorities at the accident site;
(4) organisation of emergency transportation facilities under (a) pre-designated
coordinator(s);
(5) predetermination of the legal authorities and liabilities of all cooperating emergency
personnel; and
(6) pre-arrangements for use of portable and heavy rescue equipment from available
sources.
(c) The aerodrome emergency plan should be implemented similarly at an aircraft
accident/incident whether it is an on or an off-aerodrome.

title: Emergency planning
text:
MUTUAL AID EMERGENCY AGREEMENTS

(a) The close proximity of an aerodrome to surrounding communities and the possibility of an off-
aerodrome aircraft accident give rise to the need for mutual aid emergency agreements.
(b) A mutual aid emergency agreement should specify initial notification and response
assignments. It should not specify the responsibilities of the agency concerned as this will be
contained in the emergency plan. See Figure-16 for a sample of emergency mutual-aid
agreement.

Figure-16: Example of emergency mutual-aid agreement
(c) Mutual aid emergency agreements should be prearranged and duly authorized. The
aerodrome operator may have to act as co-ordinating agency if more complicated
jurisdictional or multi-agency agreements are necessary. This guidance is to assist the
preparation of mutual aid emergency agreements with local fire authority for accidents
occurring on and off the aerodrome.
(d) Procedure for local fire authority — aircraft accident on-aerodrome:
(1) When a response is initiated, local fire authority shall proceed directly to the
rendezvous point or staging area at an aerodrome. An escort will be provided by
aerodrome police/security from the rendezvous point or staging area to the accident
site.

(2) It is imperative that mutual aid fire department(s) members recognize that unless the
aerodrome is closed to flight operations, unescorted movement on aerodrome property
is extremely dangerous and may result in conflict with aircraft movements.
(e) Upon arrival at the accident site:
(1) The most senior officer of the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service receiving
mutual aid has full authority at the scene;
(2) fire department mutual aid communications shall be carried out on the pre-designated
communication channel; and
(3) communication transmissions will be prefaced by aerodrome rescue and
firefighting/local fire department call number.
(f) Procedure for local fire authority — aircraft accident off-aerodrome:
(1) A call to an off-aerodrome aircraft accident will normally be received from air traffic
services or police. Should that not be the case, the local fire authority shall notify air
traffic services or police via radio or telephone that an accident has occurred and give
the approximate location on the grid map.
(g) Upon arrival at the accident site, the local fire authority shall:
(1) ensure that the mutual aid emergency agreement is initiated;
(2) establish a command post (This may be a temporary post until the aerodrome operator
mobile command post is available and operative.); and
(3) ensure that all communications are on the designated aircraft accident channel.
(h) The local fire authority shall advise air traffic services or police of the following:
(1) exact location of the accident site;
(2) location of the command post;
(3) specific location/rendezvous points on the grid map to which fire units should respond;
and
(4) any request for specialized equipment if necessary.
