title: Emergency planning
text:
IMPLEMENTING EMERGENCY EXERCISE PLAN
(a) Implementation of the emergency exercise plan includes but not limited to pre-exercise
planning and preparation, safety assessment, exercise evaluation, after exercise review, post
exercise report, etc.
(b) In ensuring safe and effective conduct of the emergency exercise plan, aerodrome operator
should provide the necessary procedures, resources and personnel.
(c) Follow-up actions after the emergency exercise include, but not limited to: regulatory
observations, exercise post-mortem briefings/meetings, stakeholders’ engagements, reviews
of recorded transcripts, interviews, site inspection, etc.
(d) Clear and valid justifications must be provided for any extension request to the emergency
exercise.

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY EXERCISE ARRANGEMENTS
(a) Emergency exercise arrangements should include:
(1) before the exercise,
(i) confirm the logistics and transport arrangements of the full-scale emergency
exercise with the GCAA, at least, 7-days in advance, including the date, time,
location, and a brief description of the exercise scenario;
(2) during the exercise,
(i) brief the GCAA on overview of the exercise, any updates or changes to the
exercise plan, safety protocols and emergency procedures relevant to the
exercise;
(ii) ensure that the GCAA has unrestricted access to all areas of the exercise that are
relevant to their evaluation including exercise site, command centres, reception
centres, exercise personnel, etc;
(iii) facilitate real-time communication between the GCAA, exercise participants and
coordinators to ensure that the GCAA can observe critical moments of the
exercise and assess the effectiveness of emergency response procedures;
(iv) implement and enforce all safety measures outlined in the exercise plan;
(3) after the exercise,
(i) conduct a post exercise evaluation within 14-days and review meeting with
relevant exercise evaluators and participants within 30 days;
(ii) submit a detailed exercise report to the GCAA within 30 days after the exercise
review meeting including:
(A) summary of the exercise, including objectives and outcomes,
(B) analysis of performance against objectives,
(C) any deviations from the exercise plan and the reasons for those deviations,
(D) action plan including corrective and preventive actions, addressing GCAA
feedback, findings and observations identified during the exercise; and
(E) maintain records of the full-scale emergency exercise, including all
planning documents, execution details, and post-exercise evaluations, for a
minimum of five years. These records should be made available to the
GCAA during audit, inspection or upon request.

title: Emergency planning
text:
DEFERMENT OF EMERGENCY EXERCISES
(a) Following an aircraft accident or serious incident occurring at the aerodrome, the aerodrome
operator may consider the deferment of the planned full-scale, partial, and/or modular
emergency exercises at the aerodrome. Deferment considerations should include:
(1) a detailed assessment of all actions taken by the responding on and off aerodrome
agencies during the aircraft accident referenced against the relevant emergency orders
and instructions contained in the emergency plan;
(2) supporting reports, transcripts, log records, and other relevant evidences. and
(3) a management of change according to the operator’s safety management system,
including approval by the Accountable Manager.
(b) Where the exercise deferment is approved by the Accountable Manager, the aerodrome
operator should immediately notify the GCAA in writing and ensure a full-scale emergency
exercise is conducted within 12-months., or as determined by the GCAA.

title: Emergency planning
text:
MANAGING AERODROME EMERGENCY EXERCISE PLAN
1. INTRODUCTION

(a) The objective of this guidance is to ensure that aerodrome operators adopt a formalised, risk-
based, and quality-assured approach to the management of their emergency exercise
programmes. The scope covers full-scale exercises, modular or component-based tests, and
table-top simulations that form part of the aerodrome emergency preparedness cycle.
(b) The exercise monitoring system must be embedded within the aerodrome’s SMS to support
performance monitoring, identification of systemic gaps, enhancement of inter-agency
coordination, and compliance with regulatory expectations.
2. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND VALIDATION OF EXERCISE PLAN
(a) The aerodrome operator must establish a systematic process for the review, revision, and
validation of the emergency exercise or modular testing plan. This process must be
documented within the SMS and include:
(1) Clear exercise objectives aligned with risk scenarios from the aerodrome emergency
plan (AEP);
(2) Defined roles and responsibilities for planning, control, and evaluation teams;
(3) Stakeholder consultation and integration of feedback from previous exercises or
incidents;
(4) Use of standardised planning tools, timelines, and resource templates;
(5) Pre-exercise briefings and pre-mortem analysis of anticipated challenges.
(b) The exercise plan should be validated through senior-level review to ensure it reflects current
operations, infrastructure, stakeholder roles, and updated regulatory expectations.
3. DOCUMENTATION AND CONTROL PROCESS
(a) All documents related to the exercise programme i.e. plans, scripts, participant lists,
evaluation checklists, debrief reports, and lessons learned, must be managed under a
controlled documentation system, consistent with the SMS documentation policy.
(b) Version control must be applied to exercise plans, ensuring that updates are properly
recorded, approved, and communicated to all stakeholders. All documentation must be stored
in accordance with records management procedures and made available for audit or
inspection by the GCAA.
(c) Exercise debriefs and post-incident reports should be compiled promptly following the
exercise and must include a summary of findings, gaps identified, recommendations for
improvement, and an implementation tracking matrix.
4. QUALITY ASSURANCE AND AUDIT PROCESS

(a) The aerodrome operator must implement a quality assurance mechanism to monitor the
planning and execution of exercises. This includes:
(1) Conducting internal audits on the adequacy of exercise planning and stakeholder
coordination;
(2) Monitoring compliance with planned exercise timelines, objectives, and scope;
(3) Verifying the corrective and preventive action plans arising from previous exercise
reports;
(4) Reviewing the consistency of exercises with regulatory requirements and safety
performance indicators.
(b) Findings from these quality assurance processes should be reported to the appropriate safety
forum and integrated into the aerodrome’s continuous improvement and risk assessment
processes.
5. APPROVAL PROCESS
(a) The emergency exercise plan, including its schedule, scope, and objectives, must be formally
approved by the Accountable Manager or by a delegated senior executive, prior to the
conduct of the exercise.
(b) The approval must confirm the adequacy of resources, stakeholder coordination, and strategic
alignment of the exercise with broader safety objectives and operational context.
(c) Delegation of approval authority must be documented and consistent with the aerodrome’s
organisational governance framework and SMS roles and responsibilities.
6. SUBMISSION TO THE GCAA
(a) A copy of the approved emergency exercise plan or modular testing schedule, along with the
planned dates and scope of the exercise, must be submitted to the GCAA at least 30 days in
advance of the proposed exercise date.
(b) Following the exercise, the aerodrome operator must provide the GCAA with:
(1) A copy of the exercise evaluation report;
(2) The corrective action plan, including timelines and responsible persons;
(3) Evidence of implementation and tracking of improvement actions.

title: Emergency planning
text:
DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENTS AND 1 000 METRES RESPONSE AREA
(a) An aerodrome operator shall ensure the emergency plan includes the ready availability of, and
coordination with, appropriate specialist rescue services to be able to respond to emergencies

where an aerodrome is located close to water, difficult terrain, and/or swampy areas and
where a significant portion of approach or departure operations takes place over these areas.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
RESPONSES TO EMERGENCIES IN DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENTS AND 1 000 METRES AREA
(a) For land aerodrome located close to water, swampy areas, or difficult terrain, the emergency
plan should include the establishment, testing and assessment at regular intervals of a pre-
determined response for the specialist rescue services.
(b) For a water aerodrome, the emergency plan should consider the particular hazards associated
with seaplane operations, including:
(1) passenger evacuation into a further life-threatening environment, e.g., deep water; the
onset of hypothermia, and its associated effects, during and following prolonged
immersion in cold water; and
(2) the immediate toxicity and respiratory effects on survivors in the water following the
ingestion of floating fuel and oils and their associated vapours, and fire suppressant
foams, powders and gases;
(3) contain sufficient provisions for water rescue and fire response; and
(c) An assessment on the approach and departure areas within 1 000 m from the runway
threshold should be conducted to determine the options available for intervention in the
event of an aircraft accident at these areas.
(d) Where response to emergencies occurring in difficult environments and those areas within
1000 m from the runway threshold, falls outside the direct responsibility of the aerodrome
operator and is provided by specialised rescue services operated by public or private agencies
under separate federal or local regulations, the aerodrome operator should ensure:
(1)  such services and response arrangements are appropriately coordinated with the
aerodrome emergency plan; and
(2)  prearranged procedures are established for the timely alerting, activation,
mobilisation, and coordination of the responsible specialist rescue services during an
emergency.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
AIRCRAFT ACCIDENTS IN THE WATER
(a) Where aerodromes are situated adjacent to large bodies of water (such as sea, rivers or lakes)
or where they are located on coastlines, special provisions should be made for rescue and

firefighting operations in the event of an aircraft accident/incident in the water. Specialized
equipment for rescue and firefighting may include fire/rescue vessels, aircushion vehicles,
helicopters, coastal patrol vessels, or amphibious vehicles.
(b) Consideration of unusual terrain and water conditions such as tidal flats and swamps dictates
the choice of the unique types of vehicles most suitable to these conditions. Helicopters, air-
cushion, and amphibious vehicles as well as conventional watercraft may be found to provide
this specialized service.
(c) In developing the water rescue service, consideration should be given to public services (such
as marine search and rescue units, harbour police, or fire departments) and private rescue
services (such as rescue squads, power and communication companies, offshore oil field
operators, or shipping and waterway operators) that may be available and are capable of
rendering assistance. A signal system for alerting private or public services in time of
emergency should be prearranged.
(d) Many aircrafts do not carry personnel flotation devices on board, especially those not
engaged on extended flights over water. Such flotation devices should be available in numbers
sufficient to meet the needs of the maximum passenger capacity of the largest aircraft
normally using the aerodrome. Where the largest aircraft are equipped for scheduled over-
water operation, the aerodrome may reduce the amount of personnel flotation devices.
(e) Probability of fire. Where accidents occur in the water, the possibility of fire is normally
reduced because of the suppression of ignition sources by the water contact and the cooling
of heated surfaces. In a situation where fire is present, control and extinguishment will require
the availability of specialized equipment.
(f) Spillage of fuel on water surfaces. It should be anticipated that the impact of the aircraft
hitting the water might rupture fuel tanks and lines. It is thus reasonable to assume that
quantities of fuel will be found floating on the surface of the water. Vessels having exhausts at
the waterline may present an ignition hazard if operated where this condition is present.
Where fire is present, approach should be made after considering wind direction and velocity
and water current. Fire may be moved away from the area by using a sweeping technique
with hose streams. Foam and other extinguishing agents should be used where necessary.
Wind and water currents should be considered to deal effectively with floating fuel and to
prevent it from moving into areas where it would be hazardous to rescue operations. As soon
as possible, pockets of fuel should be broken up or moved with high volume nozzles,
neutralized by covering them with foam or a special inert material, or boomed to contain the

fuel in a safe area prior to absorption, dilution, or removal. With preplanning, the water
pollution control authorities may provide emergency assistance during this operation.
(g) Rescue vessels. Rescue vessels should be capable of shallow water operations. Vessels
powered by jet-type propulsion eliminate the dangers of propellers puncturing inflatable
equipment or injuring survivors during rescue operations. Vessels powered by conventional
propellers may prevent the hazards of puncture and injury by being equipped with fan-type
guards or cowls. Inflatable vessels may be punctured by wreckage or barnacles.
(h) If the water environment is subject to freezing, vehicles suitable for operation on ice (i.e.
hovercraft, swamp vessels, etc.) should be available.
(i) Vessels and other rescue vehicles should be so located that they can be brought into action in
minimum time. Special boathouses or launching ramps should be provided in order to reduce
response time.
(j) Vessels should be of such size as to efficiently carry the flotation equipment required with
sufficient space for the crew. Sufficient working space should be provided to permit rapid
dispersal of the flotation devices. Inflatable life rafts should be the prime flotation equipment
carried; there should be a sufficient quantity on hand to accommodate the maximum
passenger load of the largest aircraft normally using the aerodrome. Once this flotation
equipment has been distributed, there should be sufficient space to accommodate a limited
number of litter cases brought aboard in the rescue process.
(k) Sufficient two-way radio equipment should be provided in all rescue vessels in order to permit
communications with other rescue units, such as helicopters, air cushion or amphibious
equipment, and water-land based units.
(l) A minimum of two floodlights should be provided for night operations.
(m) Radar reflectors should be used to facilitate navigation and rendezvous efforts.
(n) Even though occupied sections of the aircraft may be submerged, the possibility remains that
enough air may be trapped inside to maintain life. Entry by divers should be made at the
deepest point possible.
(o) Organizing diving units/use of divers. Diving units should be dispatched to the scene. When
available, helicopters can be used to expedite the transportation of personnel divers to the
actual area of the crash. Rescue personnel or divers who may be called for this type of service
should be highly trained in surface and underwater search and recovery techniques. In areas
where there are no operating governmental or municipal underwater search and recovery
teams, agreements may be made with private diving clubs. In all operations where divers are

in the water, standard diving flags should be flown and vessels operating in the area should be
warned to exercise extreme caution (see Figure-18).

Figure-18: Standard diver / Alpha flag when personnel or divers are working on the water.
(p) It should be anticipated that victims are more apt to be found downwind or downstream from
the accident site. This should be taken into consideration in planning the operation. Where
only the approximate location of the crash is established upon arrival, divers should use
standard underwater search patterns and mark the locations of the major parts of the aircraft
with marker buoys. If sufficient divers are not available, dragging operations should be
conducted from surface craft. In no instance should dragging and diving operations be
conducted simultaneously.
(q) A command post should be established at the most feasible location on an adjacent shore.
This should be located in a position to facilitate implementing the aerodrome/community
emergency plan (see Figure–19).

Figure-19: Responding to aircraft accident in the water

text:
UNIFIED AIRPORT EMERGENCY PLANNING
(a) The principal aim of a Unified Aerodrome Emergency Planning (UAEP) is to establish an
integrated, consistent, coordinated, and efficient framework for managing emergencies across
multiple aerodromes operated by a single aerodrome operator. This approach seeks to

enhance the collective safety and security of passengers, staff, and infrastructures by ensuring
that all aerodromes within the network are prepared to respond effectively to a wide range of
emergencies, while also optimizing resources, standardizing procedures, and facilitating
seamless communication and coordination.
(b) A Unified Airport Emergency Plan (UAEP) is a comprehensive and integrated emergency
management strategy that applies to multiple aerodromes operated by the same operator
under the same jurisdiction. The purpose of a UAEP is to create a consistent and coordinated
approach to handling emergencies across all the aerodromes within the network. This plan
integrates the incident management system, emergency orders, instructions, resource
allocation, communication protocols, and stakeholder coordination into a single unified and
cohesive framework.
(c) The requirements contained in this section detail the development, implementation, and
maintenance of a Unified Aerodrome Emergency Plan (UAEP) that encompasses all
aerodromes under the aerodrome operator’s control within the same jurisdiction.
(d) A Unified Airport Emergency Plan (UAEP) approach offers numerous benefits, however there
are conditions where this approach may not be applicable or implementable to some
aerodrome, such as significantly different local regulatory environments, large geographical
separation, complex stakeholder structures, conflicting incident command structures,
different emergency preparedness maturity levels, political and administrative complexities,
etc.

title: Emergency planning
text:
DETERMINING SUITABILITY OF UNIFIED AERODROME EMERGENCY PLANNING
Determining the suitability of an aerodrome operator to adopt a Unified Airport Emergency Planning
(UAEP) approach involves a comprehensive safety assessment evaluating several factors to ensure
that this strategy aligns with the operator’s capabilities, stakeholders’ emergency preparedness
levels, the characteristics of the aerodromes, and the regulatory environment (see Figure-20 on
conducting unified airport emergency planning assessment). The aerodrome operator should:
(a) Assess Operational Characteristics
(1) Evaluate the size, complexity, and operational focus of the aerodromes. If the
aerodromes vary significantly (e.g., a mix of large international hubs and small regional
aerodromes), a unified approach may require careful adaptation to ensure it meets the
needs of each airport.

(2) Consider the types of operations at each aerodrome, such as passenger services, cargo
handling, or specialised operations (e.g., military, VIP services). A unified plan should be
flexible enough to cover diverse operational contexts.
(b) Evaluate Regulatory and Legal Requirements
(1) Review the regulatory environment across the aerodromes. If the aerodromes are in
different countries or regions with distinct regulatory requirements, a unified approach
may face challenges in ensuring compliance across all jurisdictions.
(2) Assess the legal implications of adopting a unified plan. Ensure that the plan can meet
the legal obligations of each aerodrome, including liability considerations and
compliance with local laws.
(c) Analyse Risk Profiles
(1) Identify risks that are common across all aerodromes in the network, such as aviation
accidents, security threats, or natural disasters. A unified plan is more suitable if these
risks are similar and can be addressed collectively.
(2) Determine if there are unique risks at specific aerodromes that may require specialized
planning. The plan should be adaptable to include local annexes that address these
unique challenges without compromising the overall unity of the approach.
(d) Examine Resource Availability
(1) Assess the potential for sharing resources such as emergency equipment, personnel,
and expertise across the aerodromes. A unified approach is more feasible if resources
can be effectively pooled and redistributed as needed.
(2) Consider whether the infrastructure at each aerodrome can support a unified approach,
particularly in terms of communication systems, emergency facilities, and command
centres.
(e) Evaluate Incident Management Structure
(1) Determine the existing incident management structure of the aerodrome operator. If
the operator already has a centralized incident management system, a unified approach
may be easier to implement. Conversely, if the management is highly decentralized,
adopting a unified plan may require significant restructuring.
(2) Assess the level of alignment among stakeholders, including local airport authorities,
emergency services, and external partners. A unified plan requires strong coordination
and collaboration across all parties involved.
(f) Consider Geographical Factors

(1) Evaluate the geographic proximity of the aerodromes. A unified approach is more
suitable if the aerodromes are located within a reasonable distance of each other,
facilitating resource sharing and coordinated responses.
(2) Consider the environmental conditions at each aerodrome, such as climate, terrain, and
proximity to water bodies. If these conditions vary widely, the unified plan must be
flexible enough to accommodate different environmental challenges.
(g) Assess Communication Systems
(1) Ensure that the communication systems used across the aerodromes are compatible
and can support a unified emergency response. If significant upgrades or changes are
required, consider whether this is feasible within the operator’s budget and timeline.
(2) Evaluate the potential for integrating technology platforms across the aerodromes to
support real-time communication, data sharing, and coordination during emergencies.
(h) Review Training and Preparedness Levels
(1) Assess whether existing training programs can be standardized across all aerodromes. If
there are large disparities in training and preparedness levels, the operator may need to
invest in harmonising these before implementing a unified plan.
(2) Determine the readiness of the aerodromes to participate in joint emergency exercises,
which are critical for testing the effectiveness of a unified plan.
(i) Conduct Operational Readiness and Testing
(1) Consider piloting the unified plan at a few aerodromes to test its effectiveness before
full-scale implementation. This can provide valuable insights and allow for adjustments
based on real-world experience.
(2) Gather feedback from all stakeholders, including airport staff, emergency responders,
and regulatory bodies, to assess the suitability of the unified approach.

title: Emergency planning
text:
DEVELOPING UNIFIED AERODROME EMERGENCY PLAN
(a) Developing the unified emergency plan should include:
(1) consideration of a modular approach, with a central core document applicable to all
aerodromes and individual annexes for each aerodrome;
(2) a comprehensive risk assessment using a recognized methodology to identify and
mitigate risks effectively;
(3) a unified incident management system with clear definitions of roles, responsibilities,
and reporting lines;
(4) a centralised resource inventory system that tracks all emergency response resources,
including personnel, equipment, and supplies, across the network;
(5) mutual aid agreements with local emergency services and other aerodrome
stakeholders within the operator’s network to ensure resource availability during major
emergencies; and
(6) a comprehensive management of change programme, in accordance with the
operator’s safety management system.

title: Emergency planning
text:
DEVELOPING UNIFIED AERODROME EMERGENCY PLAN
(a) For the Unified Aerodrome Emergency Plan (UAEP) to be coordinated and effective, the plan
must be carefully designed to ensure that multiple aerodromes under a single operator with
the same jurisdiction can respond efficiently and consistently to emergencies.
(b) To provide an assurance on the efficacy of the plan, it is important that the aerodrome
operator should not be too eager to unify too many aerodromes under its control. It is
strongly recommended that the aerodrome operator starts with less than 3 aerodromes
under its management control.  Once the plan reaches an acceptable level of maturity and the
emergency preparedness at other aerodromes have demonstrated positive levels, the
aerodrome operator can consider adding more aerodromes to the plan.
(c) This guidance provides a structured approach to developing a UAEP, ensuring it is integrated,
comprehensive, adaptable, and aligned with regulatory standards (See Figure-21).

Figure-21: Developing unified aerodrome emergency plan process flow
1. INITIAL PLANNING AND SCOPING
(a) Define the Scope and Objectives
(1) Identify the airports to be covered by the UAEP and outline the specific objectives of
the plan, such as enhancing safety, ensuring regulatory compliance, and optimizing
resource use across the network.
(2) Establish clear goals, such as reducing response times, improving coordination, and
standardizing emergency procedures.
(b) Stakeholder Engagement
(1) Identify key stakeholders, including airport management, emergency services,
regulatory authorities, airlines, and local communities.
(2) Engage stakeholders early in the planning process to gather input, build consensus, and
ensure that the plan reflects the needs and expectations of all parties involved.
2. RISK ASSESSMENT AND HAZARD IDENTIFICATION
(a) Conduct a Comprehensive Risk Assessment
Identify common risks across all airports (e.g., aircraft accidents, fire, severe weather) and
unique risks specific to individual airports (e.g., proximity to hazardous materials, geographic
vulnerabilities).
Use risk assessment methodologies like SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities,
Threats) analysis, Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), or Failure Modes and Effects Analysis
(FMEA) to evaluate potential hazards.

(b) Prioritize Risks
(1) Prioritize risks based on their likelihood and potential impact. Focus on high-priority
risks when developing emergency procedures.
3. DEVELOPING CORE EMERGENCY ORDERS AND INSTRUCTIONS
(a) Standardized Procedures
(1) Develop standardized emergency response procedures that apply uniformly across all
airports. These procedures should cover key scenarios such as aircraft incidents,
security breaches, natural disasters, and medical emergencies.
(2) Ensure that procedures are aligned with national and international regulations.
(b) Local Adaptations
(1) Create localized annexes within the UAEP that address site-specific risks and
operational nuances at each airport. These annexes should be flexible enough to
accommodate local conditions while maintaining overall consistency.
(c) Resource Management
(1) Outline procedures for the efficient allocation and sharing of resources, including
personnel, equipment, and facilities. Establish protocols for mutual aid between
airports within the network.
4. UNIFIED COMMAND AND CONTROL STRUCTURE
(a) Unified Incident Management System (IMS)
(1) Implement an IMS that provides a clear chain of command and defines roles and
responsibilities during an emergency. Ensure that the ICS is compatible across all
airports within the network.
(2) Design the IMS to be scalable, allowing it to adapt to incidents of varying magnitude,
from minor disruptions to large-scale crises.
(b) Centralized Coordination
(1) Establish a central emergency coordination centre that can provide strategic oversight
and support during emergencies. This centre should facilitate communication, resource
allocation, and decision-making across all airports.
5. UNIFIED COMMUNICATION PROTOCOLS
(a) Unified Communication Systems

(1) Develop standardized communication protocols that ensure seamless information flow
between airports, emergency services, and other stakeholders. Include provisions for
real-time data sharing and collaboration.
(2) Ensure that communication systems are compatible across all airports and that backup
systems are in place in case of primary system failures.
(b) Public and Stakeholder Communication
(1) Develop a public communication strategy to provide timely and accurate information to
passengers, staff, and the community during emergencies. Ensure that messages are
consistent across all airports.
(2) Engage with external stakeholders, including local governments and emergency
services, to coordinate communication and response efforts.
6. TRAINING AND EXERCISES
(a) Unified Training and Proficiency Checks Programmes
(1) Develop training programs that ensure all personnel across the airport network are
familiar with the UAEP and their specific roles within it. Standardize training to maintain
consistency while allowing for local adaptations.
(2) Include training on the ICS, communication protocols, and emergency procedures.
(b) Joint Emergency Exercises
(1) Plan and conduct joint emergency exercises involving multiple airports to test the
effectiveness of the UAEP. These exercises should simulate a range of scenarios,
including those that require inter-airport coordination.
(2) Use the exercises to identify gaps in the plan and areas for improvement.
7. COMPLIANCE AND REVIEW
(a) Regulatory Compliance
(1) Ensure that the UAEP meets all relevant regulatory requirements, both national and
international. Regularly review the plan to ensure ongoing compliance with updated
regulations.
(b) Continuous Improvement
(1) Establish a process for regularly reviewing and updating the UAEP based on lessons
learned from incidents, exercises, and feedback from stakeholders.
(2) Conduct post-incident reviews after real emergencies to assess the effectiveness of the
plan and make necessary adjustments.

8. DOCUMENTATION AND RECORD-KEEPING
(a) Comprehensive Documentation
(1) Maintain detailed documentation of the UAEP, including the core plan, local annexes,
training records, and exercise reports. Ensure that all documents are accessible to
relevant personnel.
(2) Use version control to track updates and changes to the plan, ensuring that all
stakeholders are working from the most current version.
(b) Accessibility
(1) Ensure that the UAEP is easily accessible to all relevant personnel at each airport.
Consider digital platforms or secure cloud storage to facilitate quick access during
emergencies.

title: Emergency planning
text:
MANAGING THE UNIFIED AERODROME EMERGENCY PLAN
(a) The aerodrome operator should ensure that the unified aerodrome emergency plan (UAEP) is
implemented in agreement with the GCAA and all AEP stakeholders identified in the
aerodrome emergency planning framework. This agreement must be documented, traceable,
and approved through a collaborative process that ensures the plan's operational feasibility,
regulatory compliance, and interoperability across all response agencies.
(b) The UAEP should reflect a consolidated response structure, with clearly defined roles,
responsibilities, communication protocols, and resource commitments agreed upon by the
relevant stakeholders, including but not limited to:
(1) Rescue and Firefighting Services (RFFS);
(2) Air Traffic Services (ATS);
(3) Airport Police or Security Services;
(4) Emergency Medical Services;
(5) Law Enforcement Authorities;
(6) Airlines and Ground Handlers;
(7) Airport Tenants and Terminal Operators;
(8) Civil Defense Authority;
(9) Public Health Authority; and
(10) Local agencies, etc.
(c) The plan should be approved by the Accountable Manager or a delegated senior executive.

(d) Any updates, changes, or revisions to the unified aerodrome emergency plan that affect the
roles, responsibilities, or response coordination should be communicated in advance to the
AEP stakeholders for revalidation and re-endorsement, as appropriate.
(e) The UAEP should be fully integrated into the aerodrome operator’s Safety Management
System (SMS), ensuring that its maintenance, testing, and improvement are subject to
continuous safety assurance mechanisms, including hazard identification, safety risk
assessment, and emergency exercise feedback.

title: Emergency planning
text:
MANAGING THE UNIFIED AERODROME EMERGENCY PLAN
(a) The concept of a unified aerodrome emergency plan refers to a singular, harmonised
emergency response framework that aligns the objectives, procedures, and resource
mobilisation of all agencies and entities involved in emergency response at the aerodrome.
Unlike fragmented or agency-specific response plans, the UEP ensures interoperability, clarity
of command, and efficient coordination.
(b) The process of agreeing to and implementing the UAEP should begin with a collaborative
planning cycle, typically conducted through a structured Emergency Planning Committee (EPC)
or equivalent multi-agency coordination group. This committee should:
(1) Identify risks and operational scenarios that require joint response;
(2) Review existing protocols and align them with ICAO, EASA, and national regulatory
standards;
(3) Develop integrated procedures, communication flows, and staging logistics;
(4) Conduct a joint validation review before submission to the GCAA for agreement.
(c) It is good practice to maintain a Stakeholder Agreement Register, which tracks the date,
scope, and signatory for each stakeholder involved in the emergency plan. Where feasible,
this should be digitised and incorporated into the aerodrome’s documentation management
system.
(d) In addition to documentation, joint emergency exercises are a critical method for reinforcing
and evaluating the effectiveness of the UEP. Exercise feedback should be formally recorded
and actioned through the SMS process. The results of such exercises may trigger updates to
the UEP, which would in turn require re-engagement with the GCAA and affected
stakeholders.

(e) Stakeholders should be given access to the current version of the UEP via a secure platform,
and awareness sessions should be conducted to ensure their personnel understand their
roles. These sessions should be documented and monitored for effectiveness.
(f) The UEP must also account for non-aviation emergencies (e.g., pandemics, natural disasters,
hazardous material spills), reflecting the full scope of potential emergencies that could affect
operations at the aerodrome.
2. RECORD KEEPING AND OVERSIGHT
(a) All correspondence, approvals, versions, and stakeholder engagement activities related to the
UEP should be retained by the aerodrome operator for a minimum of five years or as
prescribed by national regulation.
(b) These records should be made available during audits, certification reviews, or investigations.
(c) The aerodrome operator should assign responsibility for UEP document control and
stakeholder communication to the designated AEP Competent Person.

PROVISION OF SERVICES AND/ACTIVITIES
(a) An aerodrome operator shall:
(1) ensure rescue and firefighting services, facilities and equipment are provided at an
aerodrome;
(2) where an aerodrome is located close to water, swampy areas, or difficult terrain, and
where a significant portion of approach or departure operations takes place over these
areas, ensure specialist rescue services and firefighting equipment appropriate to the
hazard and risk are available; and
(3) establish and implement policies and procedures relating to the administration and
management of a rescue and firefighting service at an aerodrome.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROVISION OF RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
1. INTRODUCTION

(a) The requirements under this Section places an obligation on the aerodrome operator to
ensure that aerodrome operator complies with all relevant requirements in this regulation.
(b) This guidance provides to the aerodrome operator on this issue, since ARFFS provision can
take one of two forms.
(c) The ARFFS is an integral part of the aerodrome operator ’s own organisation. However, there
may be instances where the ARFFS is provided by an organisation external to the aerodrome
operator ’s own organisation, for example by other fire service or a private contractor.
Guidance for these two circumstances is set out below.
3. WHERE THE ARFFS IS AN INTEGRAL PART OF THE AERODROME OPERATOR
(a) In this case the ARFFS is an integral part of the aerodrome operator’s organisation. Thus, the
ARFFS is covered by the aerodrome operator ’s Safety management system (SMS).
(b) In this case the ARFFS manual forms a natural part of the aerodrome manual system. Some of
the information required in ARFFS manual relating to organisational structure would naturally
be placed in the part of the aerodrome manual dealing with such matters.
4. WHERE THE ARFFS IS NOT PART OF THE AERODROME OPERATOR
(a) In this case the ARFFS is basically a contractor to the aerodrome operator, and consequently
there should be a written agreement either a contract or Service Level Agreement (SLA)
between the two parties.
(b) Even if the ARFFS is provided by a contractor, the requirement to comply with Sub Part D
requirements, and to support the aerodrome operator appropriately, is a mandatory element
of the aerodrome certificate. It is recommended that the ARFFS service provider includes a
statement of compliance as part of the agreement.
Note. - The contract or SLA should be included in the Aerodrome Manual. Where confidentiality
clauses exist, essential details of the agreement must be included.
(c) Since the responsibility for ensuring that the ARFFS complies with the requirements in this
Regulation rests with the aerodrome operator, all issues related to the ARFFS will be handled
through the aerodrome certificate holder.
(d) Apart from any business-related material, the agreement should at least include provisions for
the following issues:
(1) The level of service provided
(2) In terms of the promulgated level of aerodrome category and hours of service. This is a
important issue and is stated in the aerodrome manual.

(3) Procedures for changes in the level of service
(4) This should cover any need to increase the level of service and arrangements in case of
depletion of the ARFFS available. Changes of a permanent character affect the
aerodrome manual.
(5) The organisational structure of the ARFFS service provider
(6) As it pertains to the service provided for the aerodrome. Include names and
responsibilities of the senior persons.
(7) Minimum staffing levels
(8) For the RFF categories covered by the agreement as determined by a task resource
analysis.
(9) Arrangements for the integration of ARFFS SMS and Aerodrome SMS
(e) Unless the ARFFS is covered by the aerodrome operator’s SMS, there is a need to ensure
appropriate integration between the two systems. Some elements that should be in place
include, but are not limited to:
(1) ARFFS representation in the aerodrome safety committee, local runway safety team
and other relevant safety groups.
(2) Sharing of deviation reports and findings, including any follow-up actions.
(3) Arrangements for auditing the ARFFS
(4) As part of its safety management system, the aerodrome operator has an obligation to
perform audits of the ARFFS in accordance with its quality assurance requirements. This
is also one of the means by which the aerodrome operator can be assured that the
ARFFS complies with the requirements of this Section.
(5) The aerodrome operator should make available all relevant manuals documents and
records, including personal training records for the staff concerned. Similarly, the
aerodrome operator will need to make arrangements for these documents and records
to be made available to the GCAA by the Aerodrome operator during regulatory audits
and as otherwise required by the GCAA.
(6) Arrangements for dealing with audit findings
(7) Arrangements to ensure that any findings identified by the aerodrome operator or
raised by the GCAA will be sufficiently dealt with through the aerodrome certificate
holder. This is to ensure that follow-up actions resulting from the audits referred to
above will be implemented, complied with and can be monitored.
(8) Arrangements for supplying the ARFFS manuals and other documentations to the GCAA

(9) Arrangements should be made to provide ARFFS manual and other documents, through
the aerodrome operator, to the GCAA as required.
(10) Participation in Emergency Planning Arrangements
(i) The aerodrome operator should make available all suitable resources to engage
with emergency planning arrangements including the emergency planning
committee, specialist rescue services where it has been determined and to take a
lead in emergency exercises.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROVISION OF RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING SERVICE
(a) Rescue and firefighting service should come under the administrative control of the
aerodrome operator, that is responsible for ensuring that the service provided is organised,
equipped, staffed, trained and operated in such a manner as to fulfil its proper function and
achieve compliance with this regulation.
(b) Requirements for a rescue and firefighting service to deal with incidents involving building,
fuel storage facility and other non-aircraft related emergencies at an aerodrome are not
included in this Section. Where rescue and firefighting service is required to response to such
incidents at the aerodrome, additional quantities of extinguishing agents, personnel, vehicles
and equipment should be determined.
(c) Policies and procedures relating to the administration and management of the rescue and
firefighting service should be established and implemented at an aerodrome.
(d) Key information on the provision of ARFFS should be documented in the Aerodrome Manual.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROVISION OF RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING SERVICE
(a) Public or private organizations, suitably located and sufficiently equipped, may be designated
to provide the rescue and firefighting service at an aerodrome.
(b) The principal objective of a rescue and firefighting service (ARFFS) is to save lives in the event
of an aircraft accident or incident occurring at, or in the immediate vicinity of, an aerodrome.
The main purposes of an RFF service are:
(1) to create and maintain survivable conditions,
(2) to provide egress routes for occupants; and
(3) to initiate the rescue of those occupants unable to make their escape without direct
aid.

(c) The RFF service should assume at all times the possibility of and need for extinguishing a fire
which may:
(1) exist at the time an aircraft is landing, taking off, taxiing, parked, etc.; or
(2) occur immediately following an aircraft accident or incident; or
(3) occur at any time during rescue operations.
(d) The rupture of fuel tanks in an aircraft crash and the consequent spillage of highly volatile
fuels, and other flammable liquids used by aircraft, present a high degree of probability of
ignition if these liquids come into contact with hot metal parts of the aircraft or because of
sparks caused by the movement of wreckage or disturbance of the electrical circuit. Fires may
also occur through the discharge of accumulated electrostatic charges at the time of ground
contact or during fuelling operations. A distinctive characteristic of aircraft fires is their
tendency to reach lethal intensity within a very short time. This presents a severe hazard to
the lives of those directly involved and can hamper rescue or evacuation efforts.
(e) For this reason, the provision of sufficient and special means of dealing promptly with an
aircraft accident or incident occurring at, or in the immediate vicinity of, an aerodrome
assumes primary importance because it is within this time frame that there are the greatest
opportunities of saving lives.
(f) The extent of aircraft fires which may affect rescue is influenced largely by the quantity and
disposition of fuel carried by the aircraft and the location of any fuel released as a result of the
accident or incident.
(g) Emergency exits and their ability to be opened from the inside and outside of an aircraft is of
primary importance in rescue and evacuation operations. The provision of special tools for
rescue crews in order to gain access to the interior of a fuselage is essential. However, their
use can only be regarded as an extreme measure to be taken whenever normal means of
access (including emergency exits) are unavailable or unsuitable for use.
(h)  The most important factors bearing on effective rescue in a survivable aircraft accident is:
(1) the training received;
(2) the effectiveness of the equipment; and
(3) the speed with which personnel and equipment, designated for RFF purposes, can be
deployed.
(i) The proposals set out hereunder concerning these services are intended as a general guide, to
be applied to the fullest extent practicable.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
ADMINISTRATION OF RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING SERVICE
(a) To ensure safe and effective administration of the ARFFS, a clearly defined organizational
structure is essential to support the mission of ARFFS, which is to save lives. A well-structured
organization should be able to define:
(1) how things will be done in the organization;
(2) who does what and who answers to whom (operational – firefighters, drivers &
watchroom operators, supervisors – crew, watch & station commanders & managers –
unit commanders & deputy/chief fire officers);
(3) how everyone interacts and what they do within the organization to support the
mission; and
(4) clear chain of command during an incident.
(b) The organizational structure also defines the span of control of managers and supervisors at
incidents, identifying a direct relationship between organizational structure and incident
command.
(c) This guidance provides examples of organizational structures and roles and responsibilities
within both simple and complex management structures in the ARFFS arena. A structure is
necessary to clearly define the roles of everyone involved so that they understand their
responsibilities and how they contribute to achieving the organization’s goals.
(d) The formal organisational structure of the ARFFS should be depicted in an organizational chart
to:
(1) show the relationships between all ranks;
(2) define their roles;
(3) show lines of authority; and
(4) clearly indicate the path of communication in terms of information flow and reporting
relationships.
(e) The ARFFS will generally have a hierarchical structure that can be simple or complex. Every
organization has different manning levels to suit their operational needs; however, the
hierarchical lines of authority, communication paths, flow of control, management and
supervisory tiers are similar. See Table 9 showing different ARFFS rank-based organisational
structure for the different aerodrome categories. See Table 10 on guidance on minimum duty
personnel for aerodrome categories.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
CONTENTS OF RFFS MANUAL
1. REQUIREMENTS
(a) The ARFFS should provide, for compliance by its personnel, an ARFFS Manual for the services
listed in its description and which complies with this regulation.
(b) A guidance in developing an ARFFS manual is provided below.
INTRODUCTION
This document provides guidance to Aerodrome operator developing an aerodrome ARFFS
manual in achieving compliance with Part E of this regulation.
(a) An aerodrome ARFFS manual should describe the policy, organisation, capability, facilities,
equipment and operational procedures of the ARFFS, that include:
(1) a statement signed by the Accountable Manager or an appropriate delegated person on
behalf of the organisation confirming that the manual:
a. defines the organisation and demonstrates its means and methods for ensuring
continuing compliance with this and any other applicable Part; and
b. is required to be complied with by its personnel at all times; and
(2) a rank-based organisation chart showing lines of authority and responsibility; and

(3) in the case of withdrawal or transfer of service, the transitional arrangements, and
(4) the establishment of ARFFS and any transitional arrangements; and
(5) where a higher category is available by prior arrangement the procedure necessary to
upgrade the facility including, where necessary, actions to be taken by other
departments; and
(6) a policy and procedures indicating how depletion of the ARFFS is to be managed including
the extent to which operations are to be restricted, how pilots are to be notified and the
maximum duration of any depletion; and
(7) objectives for each RFF category provided, including a description of:
a. amounts and type of extinguishing media provided; and
b. discharge rates; and
c. number of foam-producing appliances;
d. number of supporting appliances;
e. number of specialised appliances; and
f. staffing levels (minimum and optimum); and
g. numbers and levels of managers and supervisors; and
(8) a statement describing the process of recruitment and selection of RFF personnel; and
(9) policies and procedures by which RFF personnel selected for operational duties are
initially and continually assessed as fit and capable of their duties; and
(10)  the processes by which the initial and continued maintenance of competence of RFF
personnel according to the assigned tasks, including occupational first aid training; and
(11)  details of the training facilities available for initial and recurrent maintenance of
competence on the aerodrome or sourced externally; and
(12)  details of the specific requirements and assessment to determine the provision of
personal and respiratory protective equipment; and
(13)  the safety accountabilities of all personnel to be promulgated or referred to in the
Aerodrome Manual; and
(14)  details of the type and operational capability of the fire vehicles employed for each RFF
category required; and
(15)  details of specialist equipment such as rescue craft, emergency appliances, hose layers,
appliances with aerial capability, etc, where the ARFFS provides these, and procedures to
be followed if these facilities are temporarily unavailable; and

(16)  policies or letters of agreement, where the ARFFS is reliant upon other organisations to
provide equipment, which is essential for ensuring safe operation of the aerodrome (such
as water rescue) and contingency plans in the event of non-availability are described; and
(17)  details of the rescue and medical equipment stowed on the fire vehicles and where
rescue and medical equipment is held other than on the RFF vehicles a statement
indicating its location and how it is to be transported to an incident site; and
(18)  details of both the principal and complementary extinguishing agent to be provided; and
(19)  the availability of additional water supplies following an aircraft accident and details of
the policy and procedures to be followed in the event of circumstances that requires
isolation or depletion of supplies; and.
(20)  details of the radio communication system to be provided; and
(21)  a statement describing the process for the testing, inspecting and maintenance of
extinguishing media, rescue and medical equipment, specialist equipment, vehicles and
radio communication systems; and
(22)  details of the fire station(s) facilities and location; and
(23)  details of the crash maps to be used by the ARFFS, external emergency services and ATS
in the event of an aircraft accident or incident on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome; and
(24)  procedures for monitoring the aircraft movement areas for the purpose of alerting RFF
personnel including:
a.  how RFF personnel are alerted throughout the range of functions (training,
extraneous duties, etc.) and geographical locations from where they may be
expected to respond; and
b. how the adequacy of the response time capability throughout their functions and
locations is tested, monitored and maintained; and
c. how RFF personnel engaged in extraneous duties are managed to ensure that
response capability is not affected; and
(25)  where a ARFFS is expected to respond to incident on landside, the policy and procedures
include management of the effects on continued aircraft operations; and
(26)  procedures indicating how accidents within 1,000 metres of the threshold of each
runway, and other difficult environs where they exist, are to be accessed; and
(27)  where a ARFFS is expected to respond to domestic fires or special services, procedures
for managing the impact of this upon the normal aircraft RFF response; and

(28)  where an aerodrome accepts freight aircraft, medical flights or movements not required
to use a certificated aerodrome, company objectives regarding RFF category; and
(29)  arrangements for ensuring the adequacy of responses in non-optimum conditions i.e. low
visibility procedures; and
(30)  procedures to notify changes in operational status with the aeronautical information
services responsible for the AIP and the aerodrome operator or operator; and
(31)  the procedures regarding the keeping of a watchroom log; and
(32)  details of the emergency access roads and gates provided; and
(33)  details of the systems and procedures regarding the quality management system; and
(34)  details of the systems, procedures, and programmes regarding the safety management
system; and
(35)  details of procedures for managing aircraft and non-aircraft incidents within aerodrome
and its vicinity.

(a) The ARFFS should make available enough copies of the ARFFS Manual for one to be readily
accessible by all personnel who may need to refer to it.
(b) The ARFFS should take all reasonable steps to ensure that each member of the ARFFS personnel:
(1) is aware of the contents of every part of the ARFFS Manual which is relevant to his/her
duties as such; and
(2) undertakes his/her duties in conformity with the relevant provisions of the Manual.
(c) If any prescribed subject is not included in the ARFFS Manual because it is not applicable to the
ARFFS at an aerodrome, the ARFFS should state in the Manual the reason for non-applicability of
that subject.
(d) The ARFFS should alter or amend the ARFFS Manual, whenever necessary, to maintain the
accuracy of the information in it.
(e) The ARFFS should notify the aerodrome operator or operator as soon as practical of any
significant changes that the ARFFS wishes to make to the ARFFS Manual.
(f) The ARFFS should comply with any directive issued by the GCAA to the aerodrome operator or
operator requiring alteration or amendment of the ARFFS Manual.
2. DOCUMENTATION
(a) The ARFFS should have immediate access to current copies of the relevant technical manuals
and any other document necessary for the provision and operation of the services listed in its
ARFFS Manual.

Note. - Documents may be in hardcopy or electronic and accessible to all personnel requiring
access. Full unrestricted access should be provided to the GCAA when requested.
(b) The ARFFS should establish a procedure to control all the documentation required by paragraph
(a) which ensure that:
(1) all incoming documentation, including amendments, are reviewed and actioned as required
by authorised personnel;
(2) all documentation is reviewed and authorised before issue;
(3) current issues of all relevant documentation are available to personnel at all locations where
they need access to such documentation for the provision and operation of ARFFS;
(4) all obsolete documentation is removed promptly from all points of issue or use;
(5) any obsolete documents retained as archives are suitably identified as obsolete;
(6) changes to documentation are reviewed and accepted by authorised personnel who should
have access to pertinent background information upon which to base their review and
acceptance;
(7) safety-significant changes are assessed in accordance with the safety management system;
and
(8) the current version of each item of documentation can be identified to preclude the use of
out-of-date editions.
3. WATCHROOM LOG
(a) The ARFFS should ensure that a logbook, with sequentially numbered pages, is kept at each
ARFFS station.
(b) The procedure should ensure that:
(1) the logbook is maintained by the senior person on duty, or the person on watch at a
nominated operating position;
(2) the logbook is maintained throughout the hours of watch of the station;
(3) all entries include the time of entry;
(4) the person responsible for maintaining the logbook signs On Watch, and effects transfer of
responsibility by successive On Watch entries; and
(5) logbook entries are:
(i) in chronological sequence and in ink;
(ii) without erasure, defacement, or obliteration; and
(iii) corrected by drawing a single line through the erroneous information and initialling the
correction.

(6) actual times of opening and closing watch are recorded in the logbook, together with the
reason for every variation from published hours of service;
(7) the operational category is stated at the beginning of each watch and any changes in the
operational status recorded and that the operational status and any changes to it is
confirmed by the senior officer in-charge of the watch signing the log; and
(8) logbooks are retained for a period of 5 years from the date of final entry.
4. RECORDS
(a) The ARFFS should establish systems and procedures to identify, collect, file, store securely,
maintain for at least 5 years, access and dispose of records necessary for:
(1) the operational provision of ARFFS; and
(2) the purpose of assisting with any accident or incident investigation.
(b) The ARFFS should compile, maintain and retain records in the following areas, but not limited to:
(1) ARFFS personnel:
(i) training received; and
(ii) competency and performance evaluations.
(2) ARFFS vehicle(s):
(i) commissioning/initial performance testing; and
(ii) initial certification and recurrent foam system testing; and
(iii) initial certification and recurrent complementary agent system testing; and
(iv) regular inspection; and
(v) maintenance; and
(3) Ancillary equipment:
(i) maintenance; and
(ii) inspections; and
(iii) tests; and
(4) Extinguishing agents:
(i) foam certification of conformity to ICAO; and
(ii) complementary agent conformity to ISO; and
(5) Watchroom log; and
(6) Incidents/accidents reports; and
(7) Safety management reports/assessments;
(8) Internal quality assurance reports/assessments; and
(9) Any other record required by the aerodrome operator  and/or the GCAA.
