title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
1. FEATURES COMMON TO ALL AIRCRAFT EMERGENCIES
(a) Upon notification from air traffic control announcing an aircraft emergency, the required
equipment is dispatched to the scene of the accident or to the predetermined standby
positions. Once the call has been received, all subsequent RFF action will be the responsibility
of the aerodrome RFF service officer-in-charge.
(b) Runway standby positions for RFF vehicles in anticipation of an emergency may be
predetermined, and documented to provide the best possible coverage.
(c) For emergencies involving gear malfunction or tire difficulty, there is always a possibility of the
aircraft veering off the runway and possibly hitting emergency equipment. In such cases, it is
preferable for the emergency equipment to be located near the point of touchdown and then
to follow the aircraft down the runway after ground contact.
(d) Response by RFF equipment to off-aerodrome accident(s) should be done in accordance with
off aerodrome response procedures and existing mutual aid agreement(s). Communication
should be maintained between RFF vehicles, the fire station and air traffic control. Wherever
possible, mutual aid resources should monitor predetermined frequencies.
(e) Additional resources should be dispatched when the accident site is known to be beyond
normal fire protected zones (underground water mains and hydrants) or where water relays
may be required. Prearrangements should be made to assure that additional supplies of
extinguishing agents are brought to the accident scene.
(f) Pre-incident planning of off-aerodrome conditions should be made to prevent delays at time
of emergency. Significant factors should be charted on the grid maps carried in RFF vehicles.
(g) All personnel operating directly in the involved area of the crash should be provided with
sufficient protective clothing. The training of rescue personnel should stress the value and the
limitations of their protective equipment to avoid a false sense of security and to recognize
that they could unwittingly lead the occupants of the aircraft through a dangerous
atmosphere.
(h) Lines to be used in fire attack should be charged after equipment is properly positioned. If no
fire is visible, all equipment should be staged for immediate response if necessary.
(i) Should spill of a flammable liquid occur without fire breaking out, it is important to eliminate
as many ignition sources as possible while the spill is being neutralized or covered with foam.
Engine ignition sources should be made inert or cooled. There may be enough residual heat in

turbine aircraft engines to ignite fuel vapours up to 30 minutes after shutdown or 10 minutes
on piston engines.
(j) A continuous water supply is essential and is usually not available at all points. Provisions
should be in place to ensure that the required fire flow be maintained. It is important that pre-
arrangements also include additional emergency resources.
(k) Rescue operations should be accomplished through regular doors and hatches wherever
possible but RFF personnel should be trained in forcible entry procedures and be provided
with the necessary tools.
Note. — In a number of cases, misuse of forcible entry tools has resulted in unnecessary fuel spills
increasing the fire hazard.
(l) Rescue of aircraft occupants is a priority and should proceed with the greatest possible speed.
Evacuation of injured occupants from a dangerous environment in the fire-threatened area
should be done with care so as not to aggravate their injuries.
(m) Broken fuel, hydraulic fluid (flammable type), alcohol and oil lines should be plugged or
crimped, when possible, to reduce the amount of spill and extent of fire.
(n) If the source of heat and fire cannot be controlled, fuel tanks exposed but not involved should
be protected by appropriate agents to prevent involvement or explosion.
(o) Aircraft windows maybe used for rescue or for ventilation. Some are designed to be used as
emergency exits. On all aircraft these exits are identified and have latch release facilities on
both the outside and inside of the cabin.
(p) Cabin doors may be used as emergency exits except when they are not operationally
available. With some exceptions these doors open outwards. When exits are used for
ventilation they should be opened on the downwind side.
(q) The “No Smoking” rule should be rigidly enforced at the scene of the accident and in the
immediate vicinity.
2. FIGHTING AIRCRAFT FIRES
(a) The primary mission of the RFF service is to control the fire in the critical area to be protected
in any post-accident fire situation with a view to permitting the evacuation of the aircraft
occupants. Equipment and techniques recommended are generally directed toward this goal.
(b) The ARFFS officer-in-charge when responding to aircraft accident/incident is expected to deal
with the following fires:
(1) Combustible material fires.
(2) Fuel spill fires.

(3) Hot brakes and wheel fires.
(4) Rocket engine fires.
(5) Confined engine fires (piston).
(6) Confined turbine engine fires (jet).
(7) Titanium fire control.
(8) Magnesium fire control.
(9) Fire situations involving rear mounted aircraft engines.
(10) Fire situations involving avionics compartment or flight deck.
(11) Fire situations involving galley or overhead compartment.
(12)  Fire situations involving aircraft battery fires including lithium-ion batteries.
(c) External fires
(1) The priority is to create a survivable condition inside the aircraft, for passengers and
crew who have not been able to evacuate safely.
(2) On arrival, appliance positioning is critical, there are no specific instructions regarding
this matter, however the following points should be considered:
• so that personnel can clearly see the aircraft and evacuating passengers
• so that appliances do not obstruct escape slides either in use, or slides that may
be required later
• in a manner which ensures they are unlikely to be unaffected by any sudden
movement or collapse of the aircraft (aircraft swing – caused by the collapse of
an undercarriage or weather conditions)
• clear of known hazard areas such as rim/tyre disintegration zones, engine
intakes and exhausts, propellers, aircraft weapon systems etc
• upwind and uphill
• RFFS drivers should be aware of pooling or running fuel.
(3) It is essential that the integrity of the fuselage is maintained; therefore, firefighting
activities should be directed towards sweeping fire away from fuselage and protecting
the escape chutes/routes that are likely to be used. By sweeping fire away from the
fuselage the risk of fire penetration is greatly reduced and the fuselage will cool.
(4) External fires can penetrate the fuselage within a minute of starting, depending upon
the intensity and the location of the fire in relation to the fuselage. Therefore, external
fires need to be controlled rapidly and entry into the fuselage made as quickly as is
reasonably practical.

(5) In a fire and/or life risk situation, fuel spillages should be covered by an aspirated foam
blanket and maintained until there is no further possibility of accidental ignition. Once
all firefighting and rescue operations are complete, a decision will need to be made to
stop re-applying foam and maintaining the foam blanket, for the following reasons:
• it covers hazards such as ruts in the ground and sharp debris, creating
• additional hazards for emergency responders
• it covers body parts and makes disaster victim identification difficult
• it creates an additional environmental impact
• it makes post-crash investigation difficult.
(6) Escape slides and exits should be protected throughout the incident by hose lines.
(7) As soon as the major fire is under control/out, at least one charged line should be
maintained on each side of the aircraft ready for immediate use in case the fire
suddenly escalates or reignite.
(8) At any time during the incident, it is possible that the aircraft or part of the aircraft may
collapse. Therefore, it is essential that personnel are vigilant throughout the incident
and safety officers are designated as per the incident command system.
(9) During the incident all personnel within the inner cordon, will wear full personal
protective equipment, and the appropriate level of respiratory protective equipment as
instructed by the Incident Commander.
(d) Internal fires
(1) Fires involving the interior of modern passenger aircraft are hazardous and complex.
Large passenger carrying aircraft will have the capacity to carry more than four hundred
passengers (more with the introduction of the A380). Within the cabin area of the
aircraft there will be a substantial fire loading. Fires can develop very rapidly if not dealt
with, filling the cabin with dense toxic smoke and hampering any escape from the
aircraft.
(2) The conditions likely to be encountered on the inside of an aircraft with an internal fire
include dense toxic smoke, extreme levels of heat and humidity. Personnel are likely to
experience difficulty in advancing through the cabin due to debris, casualties and the
collapse of the aircraft interior fittings.
(3) Internal fires pose numerous potential hazards for firefighters.
Aircraft structural collapse

(4) In serious internal fire situations, there is an ever-present risk from the fuselage
collapsing. Generally, the collapse will occur at the rear of the mainplane, where large
portions of the fuselage are unsupported. Personnel working on the exterior of the
aircraft must be conscious of where appliances and equipment are positioned.
Personnel inside the aircraft must advance with care and ensure their means of egress
is maintained.
(5) The floor of the aircraft fuselage may also be weakened and collapse with no warning,
therefore caution must be exercised when moving through the fuselage.
Evacuating passengers and crews
(6) If not controlled, evacuating passengers and crew may hamper firefighting and rescue
operations. Evacuated passengers may attempt to re-enter the aircraft if they discover
that their family or friends have not yet escaped. The exercise of firm control over those
who have evacuated safely is therefore of paramount importance. The use of aircraft
passenger management systems (PEMS) is recommended.
Dense toxic smoke and flammable vapours
(7) Fires involving the furnishing of an aircraft will produce large quantities of toxic smoke
and flammable vapours. The expedient location and extinguishment of any fire is
essential if passengers are to survive. The fuselage must be ventilated without delay.
This will allow hot toxic gases and smoke to be replaced by fresh air and therefore
greatly improve the chance of survival.
(8) The application of foam to the fuselage (internal fires only) is to be avoided as the foam
blanket acts as a heat insulator and prevents the internal fire from burning through the
fuselage and ventilating the aircraft.
Pressurised and live electrical systems
(9) ARFF Service personnel working inside may be exposed to pressurised systems and live
electrical circuits. Therefore, personnel will be required to wear full personal protective
equipment and breathing apparatus and correct search procedure must be adhered to
at all times.
Rapid development of fire
(10) Because of the rapid build-up of heat, large volumes of explosive flammable vapours
will be released. This has the potential for a flashover and backdraft, therefore tactics
for the reduction of a flashover and backdraft should be adopted.

Hazardous materials
(11) At all incidents involving aircraft there is a danger of aviation fuel, hydraulic fluid, cargo
(possibility of numerous hazardous materials) and polymer composite, alloys etc. These
all pose a potential hazard and a comprehensive assessment of risk will be required and
personnel exposure kept as low as reasonably practicable. ARFF Service personnel must
be provided with the appropriate personal protective equipment and respiratory
protective equipment.
(e) Internal firefighting and search procedures
(1) ARFF Service should be familiar with the interior of an aircraft. It is vital to personnel
working inside the aircraft that firefighting, search and rescue operations are
methodical.
(2) ARFF Service personnel entering an aircraft for firefighting operations must, as a
minimum, be wearing full personal protective equipment including breathing
apparatus. They should also have with them a charged line (45mm) with a hand-
controlled branch.
(3) Entry into the aircraft may be difficult and escape slides may need to be removed prior
to the firefighting teams entering the fuselage. The use of aircraft stairs, fire service
ladders or a stable platform is necessary.
(4) ARFF Service personnel tasked with firefighting should use a water spray to cool and
drive the smoke towards a venting point further along the fuselage (opened by external
crews if not already opened by passengers).
(5) It is important to vent the fuselage of toxic fumes and smoke as personnel proceed
along the fuselage, thus creating a survivable atmosphere. It may not be physically
possible to remove all survivors to fresh air, because of the potentially large numbers of
passengers involved.
(6) Therefore, ARFF Service personnel should not be distracted from their task by
passengers that require rescuing, extinguishing the fire and ventilating the fire gases
will potentially save more lives. Before venting takes place, guard branches should be
strategically positioned at the ventilation points.
(7) Ventilating an aircraft fuselage can be achieved in a number of ways:
• utilising prevailing wind conditions
• utilising hose lines and coned spray water jets to forcibly push fire gases towards
ventilation points

• use of positive pressure ventilation fans as per ARFF Service standard operating
procedures, this is not always possible due to the height of the aircraft from the
ground
• internal fires – being allowed to burn through the fuselage, this will self-
ventilate the aircraft.
(8) Hose management will be challenging for teams entering the aircraft due to the
confined space, internal layout and post-crash debris.
(9) Subsequent breathing apparatus teams may be tasked to carry out rescue operations.
These teams will need to risk assess the requirements for firefighting media, as hose
management and cramped conditions will play a major part of the efficiency of this
task.
(10) On wide bodied aircraft it will be necessary to use at least one team in each aisle. On
some aircraft firefighting/rescue operations may need to be carried out on upper and
lower decks. The use of thermal imaging cameras may assist in the location of casualties
(thermal imaging cameras do not replace the need for correct search procedures).
(11) The searching of the aircraft should be done in a methodical manner and in a way that
subsequent teams can assist or re-enter and continue with the search.
(12) The use of seat counting and simple laminated charts depicting seat layouts can be
useful in identifying casualties and as a reference point for subsequent rescue teams.
(13) The water supply to personnel working inside the aircraft must be maintained at all
times. Should any team working inside lose their water supply they would be seriously
at risk. Therefore, during the incident, it is vital to monitor the availability of water
supplies.
(14) As in all fire ground operations good communication between personnel is essential.
(15) Below are some examples of possible internal firefighting scenarios for narrow bodied
and wide-bodied aircraft.

3. RESCUE TACTICS AND ASSOCIATED EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS

(a) Before attempting to specify the tactics and equipment to be used in rescue operations
following an aircraft accident, it will be necessary to identify the tasks to be performed. First,
the term rescue should be taken to include protection of the routes followed by occupants of
the aircraft who are able to escape from the aircraft.
(b) The activities external to the aircraft may include firefighting, the blanketing of fuel wetted
areas adjacent to the aircraft, the assistance in the effective use of the emergency escape
equipment deployed from the aircraft and the provision of lighting where this would expedite
the evacuation of the aircraft and the assembly of its occupants in a safe area. It will be
obvious that entry to the aircraft at this time should not be attempted by any of the routes
which are in use by escaping occupants. It will also be obvious that evacuation from the
aircraft and any operations within the fuselage cannot be conducted effectively if a fire
situation exists which imperils the occupants or the rescue forces.
(c) While the rescue of all occupants may be considered as the primary objective, the overall
requirement is to create conditions in which survival is possible and in which rescue
operations may be conducted. For this reason, it may be essential to commence firefighting
operations before attempting to rescue any one of the occupants, as failure to suppress the
fire or render a fuel wetted area safe from fire may preclude the survival of everyone aboard.
4. ACCIDENTS INVOLVING DANGEROUS GOODS
(a) Dangerous goods are articles or substances which are capable of posing significant risk to
health, safety or property when transported by air. For the purposes of air transport, they are
divided into nine classes (in the ICAO Technical Instructions (Doc 9284) reflecting the type of
hazard they present to transport workers and emergency response personnel.
(b) The nine classes of dangerous goods are:
(1) Class 1 Explosives
(2) Class 2 Gases: compressed, liquefied, dissolved under pressure or deeply refrigerated
(3) Class 3 Flammable liquid
(4) Class 4 Flammable solids; substances liable to spontaneous combustion; substances
which, in contact with water, emit flammable gases
(5) Class 5 Oxidizing substances; organic peroxides
(6) Class 6 Toxic and infectious substances
(7) Class 7 Radioactive materials
(8) Class 8 Corrosive

(9) Class 9 Miscellaneous dangerous articles or substances which, during air transport,
present a danger not covered by other classes. Examples: magnetized material;
acetaldehyde ammonia; expandable polystyrene beads and lithium batteries.
Note. — The order in which these classes are listed does not imply a relative degree of hazard.
(c) In some classes, dangerous goods are further divided into divisions. The division is expressed
by placing a decimal point after the class number and reflecting the number of the division,
i.e. Division 6.1. In these cases, reference is made only to the division and not to the class, e.g.
Division 5.2, not Class 5, Division 2.
(d) As a condition for transporting dangerous goods by air, the ICAO Technical Instructions
prescribe certain actions that should be taken to advise transport workers and emergency
response personnel of the hazards presented by the dangerous goods transported. These
hazards are communicated principally through markings and labels applied to the package of
dangerous goods and through the provision of certain information in transport documents
that accompany a shipment.
(e) Package markings and labels.
(f) Transport documentation.
(g) Information by pilot-in-command in case of in-flight emergency
(h) Many types of dangerous goods (e.g. flammable liquids) would be consumed in large aircraft
fires and consideration of the possible types and amount of cargo aboard an aircraft suggests
a potential for an even greater hazard. RFF personnel should use proper procedures and
operations in response, (i.e. scene size-up/assess the situation), to ensure they are protected
from the effects of dangerous goods. As with any fire, however, personal protective clothing,
including breathing apparatus (as a minimum), should always be worn. As far as possible, RFF
personnel should stay position upwind and out of smoke, fumes and dust.
(i) On cargo-carrying aircraft, hazardous freight is usually placed in unit load devices, which are
aircraft containers, aircraft pallets, and which may be secured with a net. These containers are
then loaded aboard the aircraft. Some air carriers use specially modified unit load devices for
transporting certain dangerous goods on the main deck of freighter aircraft. These containers
may have special colours and include an integral fire suppression capability. Unit load devices
containing dangerous goods will have a small tag wired to the outside or placed in a plastic
window, indicating which of the nine hazard classes, previously listed, are shipped inside. The
tag will usually have a “red striped” border. Special discharge nozzles located inside the
container are coupled to a portable extinguisher by a connection on the exterior of the unit.

Flight personnel can manually discharge extinguishing agent into the container without having
to open it. Certain dangerous goods should be accessible to the crew in flight in case of a leak
or fire. As a general rule, most dangerous goods on the main deck of cargo aircraft are loaded
in the most forward location.
5. ACTS OF UNLAWFUL INTERFERENCE
(a) An aircraft which is subjected to a threat of sabotage or unlawful seizure should be parked at
an isolated aircraft parking position located on an area at least 100 m away from other aircraft
parking positions, buildings or public areas until the act of unlawful interference is terminated.
In such cases, it may be necessary to evacuate passengers without the use of loading ramps
provided at the passenger terminal. Motorized loading ramps may be available which could be
driven to the site, or emergency evacuation stairs or the aircraft’s slides could be used.
Detailed information on procedures for dealing with unlawful interference is given in the ICAO
Air Traffic Management Security Manual (Doc 9985 — Restricted).
(b) Chemical, biological and radioactive (CBR) threats. Although all dangerous goods are required
to be clearly labelled and packed, there could be scenarios where substances are unknown
and that they may be unlawfully released in an aircraft or within the aerodrome premises.
CBR threats, considered as security-related incidents, should be handled by specialised
emergency response agency and may be out of the capability of RFF services. Where RFF
service is also assigned to handle CBR threats, RFF personnel should be trained and equipped
with the basic equipment to detect the nature of such substances. These include any
chemical, biological or radioactive personal protective equipment and detectors.
6. POST-ACCIDENT PROCEDURES
(a) Rescue units should familiarize themselves with all regulations, national and local, regarding
movements of wreckage and disposal of human remains and the preservation of evidence. It
is also important to understand the techniques and procedures used in aircraft accident
investigation. After fire suppression and survivor rescue have been completed, the following
procedures should be observed.
(b) Removal of bodies of fatality injured occupants remaining in the wreckage after the fire has
been extinguished or controlled should be accomplished only by or under the direction of
responsible medical authorities. Premature body removal has, in many cases, interfered with
identification and destroyed pathological evidence required by the medical examiner, coroner
or air accident investigation authority.

(c) If extrication of casualties from aircraft wreckage is necessary, the position and seat number
in which the survivors were located in the aircraft should be recorded at the earliest
opportunity. Where casualties are located at positions away from the wreckage, the positions
should be marked by a stake with a label identifying the victim and the seat. In all cases, the
casualties should have an identifying label attached to them stating where they were found
and in which seat. Similarly, personal belongings should remain attached. Apart from gaining
information which may assist in the accident investigation, the careful recording of all these
data may assist in the identification of casualties.
(d) If circumstances permit, the area should be photographed for future reference prior to any
body removal activity. Photographs are advantageous tools to aid investigators and should be
given as soon as practicable to the appropriate agency having responsibility for the accident
investigation. To this end, it may be desirable to appoint an RFF photographer so that the
scene can be photographed for future accident investigation purposes.
(e) The wreckage of an aircraft involved in an accident, including controls, shall not be disturbed
(moved) until released for removal by the investigational authority having jurisdiction. If the
aircraft, parts, or controls should be moved because they directly present a hazard to human
life, efforts should be made to record their original condition, positions, and locations, and
due care should be afforded to preserve all physical evidence. If circumstances permit,
photographs should be taken showing the location and position of all major components
marked on the ground. Details on removal of disabled aircraft can be found in the ICAO
Airport Services Manual (Doc 9137), Part 5 — Removal of Disabled Aircraft.
(f) On completion of the initial rescue operation, it is important that the RFF personnel exercise
as much care as possible to ensure their movements do not destroy evidence which may be of
value in the investigation. For example, movement of ambulance and RFF vehicles should not
be made along the wreckage trail if alternative access is possible.
(g) The location of mail sacks and pouches should be observed and this information given to
postal authorities. If necessary, the mail should be protected from further damage.
(h) Aviation fuels and hydraulic fluids may cause dermatitis by contact with the skin. RFF
personnel who have had these fluids spilled on them should be washed thoroughly with soap
and water as soon as possible. Wet clothing and uniforms should be changed and
decontaminated promptly.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
OPERATIONAL ARFFS COMMUNICATIONS

1. INTRODUCTION
(a) This guidance document outlines the recommended radio communication phraseology for
Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting (ARFFS) operations during various aircraft emergencies. The
guidance is developed based on ICAO requirements and international best practices. Effective
and clear communication is critical for ensuring the safety of both the emergency response
teams and the affected passengers and crew during an aircraft emergency. The phraseology
provided will assist ARFFS personnel in managing incidents with precision, coordination, and
clarity.
(b) In ARFFS operations, the Airport Bronze Commander / Incident Commander (ABC / AIC) holds
responsibility for overall command and control of the incident. Callsigns should be assigned
clearly to ensure all ARFFS personnel are aware of the command structure.
(c) These callsigns should remain consistent throughout the incident to avoid confusion and to
facilitate proper coordination between teams.
(d) The examples provided in this guidance is non-exhaustive and ARFFS commanders need to
adapt where required.
2. STANDARD CALLSIGNS FOR ARFFS
(a) In aircraft emergency situations, the use of standardised callsigns is crucial for ensuring clear
and efficient communication among all units involved in the response. These callsigns allow
for precise identification of the role and location of each ARFFS (Aerodrome Rescue and
Firefighting Services) team member, vehicle, or command structure. This document outlines
the standard callsigns used by ARFF personnel during emergency operations, based on ICAO
recommendations and best practices in the aviation emergency response domain.
(1) Hierarchy of Command: The "Command" or "Bronze Command" callsigns refer to the
highest levels of control, usually the Incident Commander or the Mobile Command Unit.
All sectors and units report directly to these command posts.
(2) Sector Callsigns: The incident may be divided into sectors (Alpha, Bravo, etc.), and
sector leaders take on the responsibility for coordinating all actions within their
assigned area of the incident. All units operating in a sector must report to the Sector
Commander.
(3) Vehicle-Specific Callsigns: Vehicles such as fire appliances, foam tenders, and water
tenders are identified by their vehicle type followed by a number (Fire One, Foam
Tender Two, etc.) to distinguish them.

(4) Specialised Teams: Specialised teams, such as Breathing Apparatus (BA) teams, Rapid
Intervention Teams (RIT), and Hazardous Materials (Hazmat) teams, are also assigned
callsigns that correspond to their role in the emergency response.
(5) Medical and Evacuation Teams: Medical and evacuation teams are given specific
callsigns to differentiate them from firefighting units, ensuring that medical support is
prioritised and evacuation efforts are well-coordinated.
(b) The use of standardised callsigns is critical for maintaining clarity and coordination during an
aircraft emergency. Each callsign clearly identifies the role, vehicle, or team function, allowing
the Incident Commander to efficiently manage resources and personnel. Ensuring familiarity
with these callsigns through regular training and exercises is essential for smooth and
effective ARFF operations during real-world emergencies. (See Table 11: Examples of Standard
Callsigns for ARFF Personnel During Aircraft Emergencies)

3. INCIDENT SECTORISATION
(a) For effective management of large-scale aircraft incidents, the incident site should be divided
into sectors. This approach is especially important for wide-body and multi-deck aircraft
emergencies. Typical sector names may include:
(1) Forward Sector: Front of the aircraft
(2) Rear Sector: Rear of the aircraft
(3) Left Sector (Port side): Left side of the aircraft
(4) Right Sector (Starboard side): Right side of the aircraft
(5) Main deck: Single deck or lower deck (for multi-deck aircraft)

(6) Upper deck: for multi-deck aircraft
(7) Aisle: middle, left or right
(8) Under-wing Sector: Area beneath the aircraft wings
(9) Cargo compartment: Forward, mid or aft section
(10) Engines: Use number starting from port side of aircraft i.e. 1, 2. 3, 3 or tail mounted
(11) APU: auxiliary power unit
(12) Avionics: Avionic, battery compartment, etc
(b) Communications should consistently use these sector names when referring to specific areas
of the aircraft. For example, "Sector Alpha to Command, conducting internal search
operations on the upper deck."
(c) Table 12 provides examples of a structured approach to radio communication for the
sectorisation of an aircraft emergency. Incident sectorisation is crucial for the effective
management of ARFFS operations, and clear, precise communication ensures that all teams
remain coordinated and informed. By following these standardised communication protocols,
ARFFS personnel can safely and efficiently manage the various tasks associated with an
emergency response. Regular drills and training on sectorisation communication are essential
for maintaining proficiency and preparedness.

protocols will ensure smooth coordination, safety, and efficiency in ARFFS operations. Regular
training on these communication standards, as well as periodic drills, is strongly
recommended to ensure proficiency and readiness among ARFFS personnel.

5. BREATHING APPARATUS (BA) OPERATIONS
(a) ARFFS personnel involved in internal firefighting or rescue operations will often need to
operate in confined and smoke-filled spaces, requiring the use of breathing apparatus (BA).
Effective communication during these operations is critical for maintaining safety and
situational awareness (see Table 17: Example of BA operations communications)
(1) Entering a Hazardous Area: “BA Team [Number] entering Sector [Name] for search and
rescue.”
(2) Location Updates: “BA Team [Number], located in [area], conducting search.”
(3) Air Supply Status**: “BA Team [Number], air supply at [percentage].”
(4) Exiting Hazardous Area: “BA Team [Number] exiting, all clear.”
(b) The BAECO should communicate regularly with BA teams and the IC to track the progress of
internal operations, air supply levels, and team statuses.

6. AIRCRAFT INTERNAL SEARCH AND RESCUE OPERATIONS
(a) Internal search and rescue operations are vital for locating and evacuating trapped passengers

(1) Narrow-Body Aircraft: “BA Team [Number] entering forward section, initiating cabin

(2) Wide-Body Aircraft: “BA Team [Number] entering lower deck, commencing search in

(3) Multi-Deck Aircraft: “BA Team [Number] proceeding to upper deck, searching for
trapped occupants.”
(b) Clear communication regarding the specific area of the aircraft being searched is necessary to
ensure comprehensive coverage and coordination between teams.

7. PILOT COMMUNICATION USING DISCRETE EMERGENCY FREQUENCY 121.6 MHZ
(a) During an emergency, it may be necessary for the ARFFS IC to communicate directly with the
flight crew using the discrete emergency frequency 121.6 MHz. The IC should request
clearance from Air Traffic Control (ATC) before using this frequency to avoid interference. (See
Table 19: Example of ARFFS Communication with Aircraft Pilot Using Discrete Emergency
Frequency 121.6 MHz)
(1) Request for Clearance: “Command to Tower, requesting clearance to communicate on
emergency frequency 121.6 MHz.”
(2) Establishing Contact: “Command to [Flight Number], this is ARFFS Command. Please
confirm current status.”

(3) Instructions to Flight Crew: “ARFFS Command to [Flight Number], we are initiating an
emergency evacuation; confirm passenger status and cockpit conditions.”
(b) Coordination between ARFFS command and the flight crew is critical for understanding the
internal situation and guiding the response.

8. EVACUATION COMMUNICATION
(a) In the event of an evacuation, ARFFS personnel must provide clear instructions to passengers
and ensure safe evacuation routes are established. Communication should be concise and
authoritative to manage the evacuation effectively.
(1) Initiating Evacuation: “Command to all sectors, initiating passenger evacuation. Direct
passengers to assembly points via safe exits.”
(2) Sector-Specific Instructions: “Sector Bravo, passengers evacuating via right-side exits,
confirm status.”
(3) Evacuation Progress Updates: “Sector Alpha, all passengers clear from forward section.”
(b) Continuous updates on evacuation progress should be provided to the IC to track the
situation.
(c) Table 20 provides example of standard ARFFS phraseology during aircraft evacuation
procedures. By following these communication protocols, ARFFS teams can ensure the safe
and efficient evacuation of passengers in an organised manner. These standardised phrases
are essential for maintaining situational awareness and ensuring that the incident command
team receives real-time updates from all sectors, allowing them to make informed decisions
during an emergency evacuation.

9. EMERGENCY WITHDRAWAL
(a) In situations where an emergency withdrawal of ARFFS personnel is required (e.g., imminent
danger of explosion), clear communication is crucial to ensure the safety of all responders.
(1) Initiating Withdrawal: “Command to all units, emergency withdrawal. Repeat,
emergency withdrawal. Clear the area immediately.”
(2) Sector Confirmation: “Sector Alpha to Command, all personnel clear from forward
section.”
(3) Final Withdrawal Confirmation: “Command to all sectors, confirm all personnel clear.”
(b) The IC should only give the “all clear” signal once confirmation is received that all personnel
have withdrawn to a safe location.
(c) Table 21 provides examples of standardised radio communication phraseology for the
emergency withdrawal of ARFFS personnel. Adhering to these protocols ensures the safe and
orderly evacuation of responders from hazardous environments, while also maintaining clear
lines of communication with the Incident Commander. Accountability, coordination, and real-

time updates are critical during such operations to ensure the safety of all ARFFS personnel
and prevent unnecessary risks. Regular training and drills are recommended to ensure ARFFS
teams are proficient in emergency withdrawal communication procedures.

10. ESCALATION AND DE-ESCALATION OF EMERGENCIES
(a) Managing the escalation or de-escalation of an emergency is a dynamic process, and
communication must reflect the changing circumstances of the incident.

(1) Escalation: “Command to all units, emergency status elevated to major. Request
additional resources and standby teams.”
(2) De-escalation: “Command to all units, de-escalating to recovery operations. Stand down
non-essential teams.”
(b) Changes in emergency status should be communicated immediately to ensure all responding
units adjust their actions accordingly.
(c) Table 22 provides examples of standardised radio communication phraseology for managing
the escalation, de-escalation, and termination of an emergency during ARFFS operations.
These structured communication protocols are vital for maintaining situational awareness,
ensuring proper resource management, and confirming personnel safety throughout the
different phases of emergency response. Regular training on these communication practices is
essential for maintaining proficiency and readiness among ARFFS personnel.

11. CONCLUSION
(a) This guidance document has provided a standardised approach to ARFFS incident command
radio communication phraseology during aircraft emergencies. Adhering to these
communication protocols based on ICAO standards will enhance the coordination, safety, and
efficiency of ARFFS operations during critical incidents. Continuous training and regular review
of these communication practices are recommended to ensure all personnel are proficient
and familiar with their roles during aircraft emergencies.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESCUE OPERATIONS IN DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENTS
(a) Suitable rescue equipment and services should be provided at the aerodrome where the area
to be covered by the service includes water, swampy areas, desert or other difficult
environment that cannot be fully served by conventional wheeled rescue and firefighting
vehicles. This is particularly important where a significant portion of approach/departure
operations takes place over these areas.
(b) Adequate rescue equipment should be carried on vessels or other vehicles such as helicopters
and amphibious or air cushion vehicles, capable of operating in the area concerned. The
vehicles should be so located that they can be brought into action quickly to respond to the
areas covered by the service.
(c) At an aerodrome bordering the water, vessels or other vehicles are located on the aerodrome
and convenient launching or docking sites should be provided. If these vehicles are located off

the aerodrome, they should preferably be under the control of the aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service or, if this is not practicable, under the control of another competent public
or private organization working in close coordination with the aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service (such as police, military services, harbour patrol or coast guard).
(d) Rescue vessels or other vehicles should have as high a speed as practicable so as to reach an
accident site in minimum time. To reduce the possibility of injury during rescue operations,
water jet-driven vessels are preferred to water propeller driven vessels unless the propellers
of the latter vessels are ducted. Vehicles used in this service should be equipped with life rafts
and life preservers related to the requirements of the larger aircraft normally using the
aerodrome, with two-way radio communication, and with floodlights for night operations. If
aircraft operations during periods of low visibility are expected, it may be necessary to provide
guidance for the responding emergency vehicles.
(e) Rescue personnel designated to operate the equipment should be trained and competent in
providing rescue services in the appropriate environment.
(f) When drawing up the detailed plan for the conduct of search and rescue operations in
accordance with national or local search and rescue authority, emergency plan should
coordinate with the relevant rescue coordination centres to ensure that the respective limits
of their responsibilities for an aircraft accident within the vicinity of an aerodrome are clearly
delineated.
(g) Coordination between the rescue and firefighting service at an aerodrome and public
protective agencies, such as local fire brigade, police force, coast guard and hospitals, should
be achieved by prior agreement for assistance in dealing with an aircraft accident.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESCUE OPERATIONS IN DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENTS
(a) At aerodromes where a significant proportion of aircraft arrivals and departures takes place
over water, swampy areas or other forms of difficult terrain in the immediate vicinity of the
aerodrome and where conventional RFF vehicles may not be capable of an effective response,
the aerodrome operator or an appropriate rescue agency should ensure the availability of
special procedures and equipment to deal with accidents which may occur in these areas.
These facilities need not be located on, or be provided by, the aerodrome if they can be made
immediately available by off-aerodrome agencies as part of the aerodrome emergency plan.
In all cases, the aerodrome operator or an appropriate rescue agency should determine and
specify in advance the response area for which it undertakes to provide a rescue service.

(b) In producing its detailed plan, the aerodrome operator or an appropriate rescue agency
should have regard to the services and facilities already provided by the search and rescue
organization in accordance with National Search and Rescue Plan, to ensure that the separate
responsibilities for an aircraft accident in the vicinity of the aerodrome are clearly delineated.
All operations, and any exercises conducted to test operational efficiency, should involve the
relevant rescue coordination centre, to ensure the effective mobilization of all resources.
Matters dealing with services and facilities necessary to provide practical and economical
search and rescue coverage of a given area are described in the International Aeronautical
and Maritime Search and Rescue (IAMSAR) Manual (Doc 9731), Volume I — Organization and
Management.
(c) The objectives of each operation should be to create conditions in which survival is possible
and from which the total rescue operation can succeed. This concept anticipates that the
initial, rapid response attendance may have to provide a preliminary level of succour while
awaiting the arrival of a larger rescue force. The first stage would have as its objective the
removal of immediate hazards to survivors, their protection, including the first-aid treatment
of injuries, and the use of communications equipment to identify the locations to which
additional rescue forces should respond. The emphasis will be on rescue and need not include
any firefighting capability.
(d) If a fire situation has occurred in the impact stage of an accident, the inevitably extended
response times of the first vehicles are likely to preclude effective firefighting operations. The
scale of provision of rescue equipment should be related to the capacities of the larger aircraft
using the aerodrome.
(e) The types of difficult terrain for which special rescue facilities may be required include:
(1) the sea or other large bodies of water adjacent to the aerodrome;
(2) swamps or other similar surfaces, including the estuaries of tidal rivers;
(3) mountainous areas; and
(4) desert areas.
(f) The equipment to be deployed in effecting a rescue operation will vary with the environment
in which the operation is to be conducted. The training required by the personnel delegated
to these duties will similarly reflect the terrain conditions. In all situations the basic equipment
may include:
(1) communications equipment, which may include equipment for visual signals. Ideally the
use of a transmitter on the distress frequency will provide a link with air traffic control
and the emergency operations centre;

(2) navigation aids;
(3) medical first-aid equipment;
(4) life-support equipment, including life-jackets in marine situations, shelter, foil blankets
and drinking water;
(5) lighting equipment; and
(6) lines, boat hooks, megaphones and tools, e.g. wire cutters and harness knives.
(g) The types of vehicle available for rescue operations in difficult terrain may include:
(1) helicopters;
(2) hovercraft;
(3) boats, of a number of types and capacities;
(4) amphibious vehicles;
(5) tracked vehicles; and
(6) all-terrain vehicles, including those employing ground-effect to minimize wheel-
loadings.
(h) Guidance on the capabilities of these types of vehicles is detailed under ICAO Doc 9137
Airport Services Manual Part 1, Chapter 13.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
LEVEL OF PROTECTION
(a) An aerodrome operator shall:
(1) provide level of protection at an aerodrome for rescue and firefighting commensurate
with the level of aerodrome category irrespective of the number of aeroplane
movements;
(2) determine the aerodrome category from Table-23 and shall be based on the longest
aeroplanes normally using the aerodrome and their fuselage width;
(3) after selecting the category appropriate to the longest aeroplane’s overall length, that
aeroplane’s fuselage width is greater than the maximum width in Table 23, column 3,
for that category, ensure the category for that aeroplane is actually be one category
higher;
(4) during anticipated periods of reduced activity, ensure level of protection available is no
less than that needed for the highest category of passenger aircraft planned to use the
aerodrome during that time irrespective of the number of movements; and
(5) for changes in the level of protection normally available at an aerodrome for rescue and
firefighting, notify the appropriate air traffic services units and aeronautical information

services units to enable those units to provide the necessary information to arriving and
departing aircraft; and
(6) in addition to (e), when such change in the level of protection has been corrected, the
appropriate air traffic services units and aeronautical information services units are
notified accordingly.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DETERMINING LEVEL OF PROTECTION
(a) The level of protection provided at an aerodrome for rescue and firefighting should be equal
to the largest aircraft using the aerodrome irrespective of the number of movements, as
determined at Table-23.
(b) The aerodrome category for rescue and firefighting should be based on the overall length of
the longest aircrafts normally using the aerodrome and their maximum fuselage width.
(c) The aerodrome category specified in Table-23 should be determined by categorizing the
aircrafts using the aerodrome, by first evaluating their overall length and second, their
fuselage width
(d) If after selecting the category appropriate to an aircraft’s overall length that aircraft’s fuselage
width is greater than the maximum width in column (3) for that category, the category for
that aircraft should be one category higher.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DETERMINING LEVEL OF PROTECTION
(a) The level of protection to be provided at an aerodrome should be based on the dimensions of
the aircrafts normally using the aerodrome regardless of their frequency of operations.
(b) The aerodrome category for RFF should be based on the overall length of the longest aircrafts
normally using the aerodrome and their maximum fuselage width. The aerodrome category
should be determined using Table-23 by categorizing the aircrafts using the aerodrome, by
first evaluating their overall length and second, their fuselage width. If after selecting the
category appropriate to an aircraft’s overall length that aircraft’s fuselage width is greater
than the maximum width in column (3) for that category, then the category for that aircraft is
actually one category higher. For examples in determining the appropriate level of aerodrome
category refer to ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 1, Chapter 2.
(c) Aerodromes that additionally serve other types of operations (for example, general aviation
and/or aerial work) may consider providing information in the aeronautical information
publication (AIP) regarding the level of protection to be provided for these types of
operations.
(d) Either a take-off or a landing constitutes a movement. Movements of scheduled, non-
scheduled and general aviation operations should be counted in determining the aerodrome
category.
(e) The level of protection at aerodromes used for all-cargo, training, testing and out of service
aircraft operations may be reduced in accordance with Table 24. This is based on the need to
protect only the area around the cockpit of the aircraft in the critical area concept. Using this
rationale, the aerodrome category for all-cargo, training, testing and out of service aircraft
operations may be reduced by providing enough water quantity Q1 for the control of fire.
Information on the critical area concept and the method by which the scale of extinguishing
agents has been related to the critical area may be found in ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services
Manual Part 1, Chapter 2.4.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
LEVEL OF PROTECTION FOR MULTI-RUNWAY OPERATIONS
When determining the appropriate level of rescue and firefighting protection required at
aerodromes with multi-runway operations, rescue and firefighting services, facilities and equipment

should commensurate with the specific operational demands of each runway are provided, whilst
maintaining overall safety and efficiency.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DETERMINING LEVEL OF PROTECTION FOR MULTI-RUNWAY OPERATIONS
This guidance outlines a methodology for aerodromes that operate two or more runways for
assessing and deploying rescue and firefighting resources based on runway-specific requirements,
traffic patterns, and potential risks. This guidance provides a comprehensive framework for
determining the level of rescue and firefighting protection required for aerodromes with multi-
runway operations. By following this guidance, aerodrome operators are able to ensure that each
runway is adequately protected, that resources are allocated efficiently, and that response times
meet regulatory standards. Regular risk assessments, training, and compliance audits will help
maintain high levels of safety and operational effectiveness in the complex environment of multi-
runway airports (see Figure-22).

Figure-22: A methodology for determining level of protection for multi-runway operations
(a) Critical Aircraft Determination
(1) The aerodrome operator should identify the critical aircraft type for each runway, based
on the largest aircraft (in terms of fuselage length and width) that regularly uses that
runway.
(2) The identified critical aircraft should be used to determine the appropriate RFF category
for each runway, as per the requirements set forth in these regulations. The RFF

category will guide the minimum requirements for the number and type of firefighting
vehicles, agents, and personnel necessary for adequate protection.
(b) Runway Operations and Resource Allocation
(1) The aerodrome operator should conduct a thorough assessment of the operational
characteristics of each runway. This assessment should consider factors such as:
(i) The type and volume of aircraft operations on each runway.
(ii) The potential for simultaneous operations on multiple runways.
(iii) The distance between runways and the feasibility of sharing RFF resources.
(2) Based on the operational assessment, the aerodrome operator should allocate RFF
resources to each runway as follows:
(i) Dedicated Resources: Each runway should have dedicated RFF resources that can
respond within the required timeframes within the response time of two
minutes.
(ii) Shared Resources: In cases where runways are in close proximity and
simultaneous operations are unlikely, shared resources may be deployed.
However, these resources must be able to meet the response time requirements
for any of the runways they cover.
(3) Supplemental Resources: Additional resources should be allocated to runways with
higher traffic volumes, larger aircraft, or increased risk factors, as determined by the
risk assessment.
(c) Response Time and Coverage
(1) The aerodrome operator should ensure that ARFFS resources can reach any point on
each runway within three minutes from the time of alarm. This applies to the first
responding vehicle as well as the full complement of ARFFS resources.
(2) During all operational hours, every runway should be covered by the designated RFF
resources. If a runway is temporarily closed or has reduced operations, resource
allocation may be adjusted accordingly, provided full protection is restored prior to the
runway’s return to full operational status.
(d) Risk Assessment and Management
(1) As part of the task resource analysis, the aerodrome operator should conduct a
comprehensive risk assessment to evaluate the specific risks associated with each
runway. This assessment should consider:
(i) The frequency and type of aircraft movements on each runway.
(ii) The likelihood and impact of simultaneous operations on different runways.

(iii) Environmental conditions, such as weather patterns and visibility.
(iv) Any unique hazards associated with the airport’s layout or surrounding area.
(2) The results of the risk assessment should inform the allocation of RFF resources and the
development of operational procedures. The aerodrome operator should regularly
review and update the risk assessment, particularly following significant changes in
runway operations, traffic patterns, or infrastructure.
(e) Inter-Agency Coordination and Communication
(1) The aerodrome operator should establish clear and effective communication protocols
between RFF services, air traffic control (ATC), airside operations, and other relevant
emergency services. These protocols should ensure coordinated responses to incidents
and effective resource deployment across all runways.
(2) Regular training sessions and emergency drills should be conducted to ensure that all
stakeholders are familiar with the ARFFS procedures and response protocols. These
exercises should simulate various incident scenarios, including simultaneous runway
operations, to test the effectiveness of the coordination and communication strategies.
(f) Documentation and Reporting
(1) The aerodrome operator should develop and maintain an ARFFS plan that details the
allocation, positioning, and operational procedures for all ARFFS resources across the
airport’s runways. This plan should be regularly reviewed and updated to reflect any
changes in operations or risk factors.
(2) The aerodrome operator should maintain detailed records of all RFF responses,
including response times, the resources deployed, and the outcomes of each incident.
This data should be used to evaluate the effectiveness of the RFF plan and to identify
areas for improvement.
(g) Compliance Monitoring and Review
(1) The aerodrome operator should conduct regular audits to ensure that ARFFS resource
allocation, response times, and operational procedures comply with these regulations.
These audits should be coordinated with the relevant national regulatory authorities.
(2) Feedback from audits, incident reports, and training exercises should be used to
continuously improve the RFF protection strategy. The aerodrome operator should
implement changes as needed to ensure ongoing compliance these requirements and
to enhance overall safety.

RE-CATEGORISATION OF PROTECTION LEVEL
(a) Notwithstanding GM AMC1 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.010(a) Rescue and firefighting, during
anticipated periods of reduced activity, the airport category may be reduced to that of the
highest category of commercial air transport aircraft planned to use the airport during that
time irrespective of the number of movements.
(b) The level of protection at aerodromes used for all-cargo aircraft operations may be reduced in
accordance with Table 24 below. This is based on the need to protect only the area around
the cockpit of an all-cargo aircraft in the critical area concept. Using this rationale, the
aerodrome category for an all-cargo aircraft may be reduced by providing enough water
quantity Q1 for the control of fire. Information on the critical area concept and the method by
which the scale of extinguishing agents has been related to the critical area may be found in
ICAO Doc 9137-AN/898 Airport Services Manual Part I — Rescue and Firefighting.
(c) The level of protection at aerodromes for aircrafts operating on non-commercial flights
without fare-paying passengers e.g flight crew training, flight testing, non-static display and
out of service operations may be reduced in accordance with Table 24.
(d) Where an aerodrome caters to different aircraft operations, the highest level of protection is

movements specified in AMC1 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.010 Rescue and firefighting.

text:
CHANGES IN LEVEL OF PROTECTION FOR DIFFERENT AIRCRAFT SITUATIONS
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) This guidance is to assist aerodrome certificate holders in assessing the appropriate level of
protection as part of their safety management system, deemed acceptable by aircraft
operators using the aerodromes for differing purposes. This guidance, however, does not
relieve the aerodrome operator from the obligation to ensure that an acceptable level of
protection is available for the aircraft intended to be used.
2. BASIC CONCEPTS
(a) For flight planning purposes, an aircraft operator should utilise an aerodrome in the United
Arab Emirates whose ARFFS category, as required by ACM.OPS.CERT.E.010 Rescue and
firefighting, matches or exceeds the aircraft’s ARFFS category. The current provisions relate to
the level of aerodrome protection to be provided for the largest passenger aircraft using an
aerodrome, hence this level of protection does not take into account aircrafts for which the
aerodrome is selected as an alternate aerodrome.
(b) If an aerodrome is exposed to a temporary reduction of its ARFFS capability, the requirements
stated in ACM.OPS.CERT.E.010 Rescue and firefighting applies.
3. MINIMUM ACCEPTABLE AERODROME ARFFS CATEGORY
(a) In principle, the published ARFFS category at each aerodrome should be equal to or better
than the aircraft’s ARFFS category. When establishing acceptable levels of rescue and
firefighting categories to be provided for different aircraft situations, the aerodrome operator
may consider the criteria stated in Table 25 below.

Note 1. — Alternate aerodrome is an aerodrome to which an aircraft may proceed when it becomes
either impossible or inadvisable to proceed to or to land at an aerodrome of intended landing where
the necessary services and facilities are available, where aircraft performance requirements can be
met and which is operational at the expected time of use. Alternate aerodromes include:
• A Take-off alternate is an aerodrome at which an aircraft would be able to land should this
become necessary shortly after take-off and it is not possible to use the aerodrome of
departure.
• An en-route alternate is an aerodrome at which an aircraft would be able to land in the event
that a diversion becomes necessary while en-route.
• A Destination alternate is an aerodrome at which an aircraft would be able to land should it
become either impossible or inadvisable to land at an aerodrome of intended landing
• The aerodrome from flight departs may also be an en-route or a destination alternate
aerodrome for that flight

(b) Intended operations to aerodromes with ARFFS categories below the promulgated levels
specified in AMC1 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.010 Rescue and firefighting, should be coordinated
between aerodrome operator  and aircraft operator.
(c) For departure and destination aerodromes, the acceptable level of ARFFS protection should
be equal or exceed the values specified in Table 25.
(d) For flight planning purposes, the acceptable aerodrome ARFFS category at a selected alternate
aerodrome may equal or exceed the values specified in Table 25.
(e) Notwithstanding (a), an aerodrome ARFFS category below the protection levels defined in
Table 25 may be acceptable if other considerations prevail such as:
(1) achieving ARFFS principal objective,
(2) emergency planning arrangements,
(3) aerodrome conditions,
(4) runway characteristics,
(5) weather conditions,
(6) length of diversion;
(7) non-scheduled / occasional flight, or
(8) temporary downgrades exceeding 72 hours.
(f) In addition to (e), variation to the protection levels defined in Table 25 for the type of aircraft
operations may be acceptable based on:
(1) specific risk assessment conducted by the aerodrome operator as part of its safety
management system,
(2) used for a group of aerodromes selected for same purpose, for a given aircraft type,
(3) 72-hour threshold for ARFFS temporary downgrades may not be relevant for a single
flight to or from the aerodrome concerned, and
(4) is time-limited or within specified duration.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) An aerodrome operator shall:
(1) provide both principal and complementary extinguishing agents at an aerodrome;
(2) ensure amounts of water for foam production and the complementary agents provided
on the rescue and firefighting vehicles are in accordance with the appropriate
aerodrome category, except that for aerodrome categories 1 and 2 up to 100 per cent
of the water may be substituted with complementary agent;

(3) for the purpose of agent substitution at aerodrome categories 1 and 2 mentioned in (b),
1 kg of complementary agent is taken as equivalent to 1.0 L of water for production of a
foam meeting performance level A;
(4) ensure quantity of foam concentrates separately provided on rescue and firefighting
vehicles for foam production is in proportion to the quantity of water provided and the
type of foam concentrate selected;
(5) ensure discharge rate of the foam solution mentioned in (d) is not less than the rates as
determined by the aerodrome category; and
(6) ensure complementary agents comply with the appropriate specifications of the
International Organization for Standardization (ISO).
(b) From 1 July 2026, provisions of environmental-sustainable extinguishing agents shall apply to
new builds or replacement of existing systems or part thereof.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
FOAM HEALTH, SAFETY, AND ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES
1. GENERAL
(a) There has been a significant shift in the emphasis on environmental and health concerns
associated with legacy foam products. The purpose of this information is to provide the
aerodrome operator with high-level information and information on suggested solutions to the
questions being asked about firefighting foam health, safety, and environmental issues.
(b) In general, the chemicals contained in legacy fluorinated foams, such as AFFF, AR-AFFF, FFFP,
etc. (i.e., fluorinated surfactants which are classified as PFAS), have come under significant
health and environmental scrutiny.
(c) The approach of dilution and release into the environment and/or wastewater treatment
systems is obsolete and unacceptable going forward for all fluorinated foams. International,
federal, state, and local jurisdictions are limiting the use of legacy AFFF as a result of these
concerns.
(d) International civil aviation authorities are also researching and implementing new restrictions on
the use of these legacy products.
(e) Current international standards that cover foam fire suppression agents and systems are being
revised to address these new trends and to allow for flexibility going forward.
(f) Currently, the criteria for defining an environmentally/toxicologically acceptable alternative is
still changing. Once defined, the industry will also need to define the testing and metrics needed

to validate the acceptability of such criteria. With that said, there has been a significant shift to
the use of synthetic fluorine-free foam (SFFF).
(g) The following are key issues that should be evaluated when using existing legacy fluorinated
foams, switching to AFFF C6 foams, or switching to SFFF foams.
(1) Firefighter health and safety. First responder exposure should be minimized using safer work
practices and personal protective equipment. In addition, procedures should be developed
for rinsing if the foam comes into contact with a person’s eyes or skin.
(2) Collection of firefighting foam after use. Industry best practice is that all foams and fire
water/foam runoff should be contained, collected, and disposed of based on federal, state,
and local requirements and the most current technical information as suggested in the
references listed. Foam discharge is more easily handled where there is an in-place
collection capability, i.e., primary and secondary containment. This situation might be found
in warehouses, tank farms, and firefighting training facilities. Where these facilities are not
available, temporary diking is an alternative where time and resources permit. The overall
environmental impact of foam discharge requires additional evaluation and development of
generally recognized guidance. Until recognized guidance is promulgated, users should rely
on manufacturers’ data and guidance from national environmental authorities and agencies.
In all situations, discussions with the environmental regulatory authorities are appropriate.
Work is continuing to identify appropriate policy and criteria to protect facilities that have
typically been protected by foam suppression systems. These efforts are focusing on
identifying applicable codes and standards, analysing environmental impact, evaluating
alternatives, and revisiting containment options.
(3) Disposal of firefighting foams. Currently, high-temperature incineration by an accredited
environmental firm should be considered the default for disposing of legacy AFFF products
(concentrates, solutions, and effluents).
(4) Procedures for decontaminating legacy equipment and acceptable levels of cleanliness.
Trying to determine how clean is clean continues to be an issue and might need to be
determined based on regulators’ direction or manufacturers’ information. Unless equipment
is properly cleaned, it might allow the new foam to continue to contaminate the
environment. Clean levels might be in the parts per billion to trillion range. Testing and
metrics will also need to be defined to validate the level of cleanliness.
(h) The environmental/health concerns associated with these chemicals are challenging for both
toxicologists and regulators, requiring continued research and updated regulatory requirements
that are still changing. Any users of firefighting foam should research the latest procedures and

precautions for their use and disposal prior to placing them into service. The following are two
organizations that have developed technically up-to-date and accurate information on this
subject.
2. DISCHARGE SCENARIOS.
(a) The following are examples of scenarios that might include the use of foam, which are presented
here to provide the user with ideas on how to handle these types of situations. The examples
are not intended to be complete, as the science on how to handle these scenarios is changing
very rapidly. The discharge of a foam-water solution is most likely to be the result of one of the
four following scenarios:
(1) Manual firefighting or fuel-blanketing operations
(2) Training
(3) Foam equipment system and foam fire apparatus tests
(4) Fixed system releases
(b) These four scenarios include events at such places as aircraft facilities, firefighter training
facilities, and special hazards facilities (such as flammable/hazardous warehouses, bulk
flammable liquid storage facilities, and hazardous waste storage facilities).
3. FIREFIGHTING OPERATIONS.
(a) Fires occur in many locations and under many different circumstances. In some cases, it is
possible to collect the foam solution used to douse a fire after it has been put out; and in others,
such as in marine firefighting, it is not. These incidents include aircraft rescue and firefighting
operations, vehicular fires (i.e., cars, vessels, train cars), structural fires involving hazardous
materials, and flammable liquid fires. A foam-water solution that has been used in firefighting
operations will probably be heavily contaminated with the fuel or fuels involved in the fire. It is
also likely to have been diluted with water discharged for cooling purposes.
(b) In some cases, the foam solution used during fire department operations can be collected.
However, it is not always possible to control or contain the foam; therefore, a non-persistent
foam such as SFFF, should be considered. This could be a result of the location of the incident,
size of incident, or the circumstances surrounding the incident.
(c) Event-initiated manual containment measures are usually executed by the responding fire
department to contain the flow of a foam-water solution when conditions and manpower
permit. Those operations include the following measures:

(1) Blocking sewer drains. This is a common practice used to prevent contaminated foam-water
solution from entering the sewer system unchecked. It is then diverted to an area suitable
for containment.
(2) Portable dikes. These are generally used for land-based operations. They can be set up by
fire department personnel during or after extinguishment to collect runoff.
(3) Portable booms. These are used for marine-based operations in the absence of better
techniques and are set up to contain foam in a defined area. These operations generally
involve the use of floating booms within a natural body of water. The boom contains the
foam bubbles, but as the bubbles drain, the foam solution might not be contained and could
spread into the rest of the body of water.
4. TRAINING.
(a) There are specially designed training foams available from most foam manufacturers that
simulate firefighting foam during live training but do not contain fluoro-surfactants. These foams
are biodegradable, have minimal environmental impact, and can be safely treated at a local
wastewater treatment plant. Because they do not contain fluoro-surfactants, training foams also
have reduced burn back resistance that allows for more repeat fire training sessions. Firefighters
and other foam users should work with the GCAA having jurisdiction (AHJ) to ensure that the use
of training foams meet all the local and application-specific live training requirements. In some
cases, training foams can also be used as substitutes for legacy fluorinated foams in vehicle and
equipment testing.
(b) Training should be conducted under circumstances conducive to the collection of spent foam.
Some fire training facilities have elaborate systems designed and constructed to collect foam
solution, separate it from the fuel, treat it, and, in some cases, reuse the treated water. At a
minimum, most fire training facilities collect the foam solution for discharge to a wastewater
treatment facility. Training can include the use of special training foams or actual firefighting
foams. Training facility designs should include containment systems.
5. SYSTEM TESTS.
(a) Testing primarily involves engineered, fixed foam fire-extinguishing systems. Two types of tests
are generally conducted on foam systems: acceptance tests, which are conducted pursuant to
installation of the system, and maintenance tests, which are usually conducted annually to
ensure the operability of the system.
(b) In the execution of both acceptance and maintenance tests, only a small amount of foam
concentrate should be discharged to ensure the correct concentration of foam in the foam-

water solution. Designated foam-water test ports can be designed into the piping system so that
the discharge of foam-water solution can be directed to a controlled location. The controlled
location can consist of a portable tank that would be transported to an accepted disposal site by
a licensed contractor. The remainder of the acceptance test and maintenance test should be
conducted using only water.
(c) NFPA 11 explicitly recognizes proportioning test methods that limit or eliminate the need to
discharge foam concentrate. These methods are permitted in Chapter 12.6.4 of NFPA 11.
6. FIXED SYSTEM RELEASES.
(a) This type of release is generally uncontrolled, whether it is the result of a fire incident or a
malfunction in the system. The foam solution discharge in this type of scenario can be dealt with
via event-initiated operations or engineered containment systems. Event-initiated operations
encompass the same temporary measures that would be taken during fire department
operations: portable dikes, floating booms, and so forth. Engineered containment is based
mainly on the location and type of facility and would consist of holding tanks or areas where the
contaminated foam-water solution would be collected, treated, and disposed of properly.
7. FIXED SYSTEMS.
(a) Facilities can be divided into those without an engineered containment system and those with
an engineered containment system.
8. FACILITIES WITHOUT ENGINEERED CONTAINMENT.
(a) Given the absence of any past requirements for containment, many existing facilities have
allowed foam-water solution to flow out of the facility and evaporate into the atmosphere or
percolate into the ground. Steps should be taken to avoid this as part of future foam
management planning. The choices for containment of foam-water solution at such facilities fall
into two categories: event-initiated manual containment measures and installation of
engineered containment systems. Selecting the appropriate option depends on the location of
the facility, the risk to the environment, the risk of an automatic system discharge, the
frequency of automatic system discharges, and any applicable rules or regulations.
(b) Event-initiated manual containment measures are the most likely option for existing facilities
without engineered containment systems. This can fall under the responsibility of the
responding fire department and include such measures as blocking storm sewers, constructing
temporary dikes, and deploying temporary floating booms. The degree of such measures should
be dictated by the facility’s location, as well as the available resources and manpower.

(c) The installation of engineered containment systems is an option for existing facilities. There are
cases, however, that might warrant the design and installation of such systems.
9. FACILITIES WITH ENGINEERED CONTAINMENT.
(a) Any engineered containment system will usually incorporate an oil/water separator. During
normal drainage conditions (i.e., no foam solution runoff), the separator functions to remove
any fuel particles from drainage water. However, when foam-water solution is flowing, the
oil/water separator should be bypassed so that the solution is diverted directly to storage tanks.
(b) The size of the containment system should be dependent on the duration of the foam-water
flow, the flow rate, and the maximum anticipated rainfall. Most new containment systems only
accommodate individual facilities. However, some containment systems can accommodate
multiple facilities depending on the topography of the land and early identification during the
overall site planning process.
(c) The specific type of containment system selected should also depend on the location, desired
capacity, and function of the facilities in question. The available systems include earthen
retention systems, belowground tanks, open-top inground tanks, and sump and pump designs
(i.e., lift stations) piped to aboveground or in-ground tanks. Storing spent foam below ground is
not advisable due to the potential for leaks. Regular checks can reduce the risk of leaks, but even
a small leak over time could result in contaminated soil.
(d) The earthen retention designs consist of open-top earthen berms, which usually rely on gravity-
fed drainage piping from a protected facility. They allow the foam-water solution to be collected
in an impermeable liner. Legacy foams should not be contained using earthen retention, as the
soil can become contaminated.
(e) Closed-top, belowground storage tanks usually consist of a gravity-fed piping arrangement and
can be suction pumped out.
(f) Open-top, belowground storage tanks are usually lined concrete tanks that can rely on gravity-
fed drainage piping or a sump and pump arrangement. These can accommodate individual or
multiple facilities. They should also accommodate the maximum anticipated rainfall.
(g) Aboveground tanks incorporate a sump and pump arrangement to closed, aboveground tanks.
Such designs usually incorporate the use of one or more submersible or vertical shaft, large-
capacity pumps. These can accommodate individual or multiple facilities.
10. NEW FACILITIES.
(a) The decision to design and install a fixed foam-water solution containment system is dependent
on the location of the facility, the risk to the environment, the possible impairment of facility

operations, the design of the fixed foam system (i.e., automatically or manually activated), the
ability of the responding fire department to execute event-initiated containment measures, and
any pertinent regulations.
(b) Where conditions warrant the installation of engineered containment systems, there are a
number of considerations. They include the size of the containment system, the design and type
of containment system, and the capability of the containment system to handle individual or
multiple facilities. Engineered containment systems can be used where foam extinguishing
systems are installed in facilities that are immediately adjacent to a natural body of water. These
systems might also be prudent at new facilities, where site conditions permit, to avoid
impairment of facility operations.
