title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
TRANSITION FROM EXISTING FOAMS TO ENVIRONMENTAL-SUSTAINABLE EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
FOR AERODROMES
1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
(a) This guidance is issued to provide a structured and comprehensive framework for aerodrome
operators to transition from the use of traditional firefighting foams, particularly those
containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), to environmentally sustainable
extinguishing agents. The transition is aligned with international regulatory trends and best
practices, aimed at reducing environmental impact while maintaining fire safety standards.
(b) The guidance applies to all aerodrome operators and is intended to ensure compliance with
updated environmental protection standards.
2. REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS
(a) Compliance with Environmental Standards
(1) Operators are required to transition to foams that are compliant with internationally
recognised environmental standards, such as those established by the International
Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and local environmental agencies. All newly adopted
extinguishing agents must be fluorine-free, biodegradable, and demonstrate minimal
toxicity to aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems.
(b) Performance Standards
(1) The selected environmentally sustainable extinguishing agents must meet the
operational performance requirements set out in ICAO Annex 14, Volume I

(Aerodromes). Agents should be certified for their effectiveness in controlling Class A
and B fires, particularly those involving aviation fuel.
(c) Transition Timeline
(1) Operators must develop a transition plan with a full transition to environmentally
sustainable extinguishing agents.
3. OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
(a) Risk Assessment and Planning
(1) Prior to the transition, operators must conduct a comprehensive risk assessment to
evaluate the potential impacts of switching to new extinguishing agents. This
assessment should include:
(i) Firefighting Capability: Testing the new agents for compatibility with existing
firefighting infrastructure, including vehicles, discharge systems, and foam
delivery mechanisms.
(ii) Environmental Impact: Assessing the local environmental conditions and ensuring
that the selected agents pose no harm to nearby ecosystems, water sources, or
soil quality.
(iii) Personnel Training: Updating training programmes to ensure that fire and
emergency services personnel are proficient in the use of the new extinguishing
agents, including safe handling, storage, and application.
(b) Testing and Validation
(1) All environmentally sustainable extinguishing agents must undergo a thorough testing
process prior to full deployment. This includes:
(i) Operational Testing: Conduct live fire drills to evaluate the effectiveness of the
agents under real-world conditions, ensuring they meet the minimum
extinguishing performance for aviation-specific fires.
(ii) Equipment Compatibility: Ensure that the agents are compatible with existing
firefighting systems, including nozzles, pumps, and foam proportioning
equipment. Any necessary modifications to equipment must be identified and
implemented prior to the transition.
(iii) Environmental Monitoring: Establish a monitoring programme to track the
environmental impact of the new agents, including potential runoff into water
bodies or impact on surrounding flora and fauna.
4. PHASED IMPLEMENTATION

(a) Phase 1: Evaluation and Procurement
(1) Operators should initiate the transition by evaluating available environmentally
sustainable extinguishing agents and selecting products that meet both performance
and environmental criteria. Procurement contracts should include provisions for long-
term supply and warranties on environmental compliance.
(b) Phase 2: Infrastructure and Equipment Modification
(1) Where necessary, modifications to existing firefighting systems should be undertaken to
ensure compatibility with the new agents. This may include recalibrating foam
proportioning systems, updating discharge nozzles, and ensuring that storage tanks are
compliant with the handling requirements of the new agents.
(c) Phase 3: Training and Operational Testing
(1) All personnel involved in fire suppression operations must be retrained in the use of the
new agents. This includes fire and emergency services personnel, maintenance crews,
and response team supervisors. Operational testing through live drills should be carried
out to validate the effectiveness of the new agents in a controlled environment.
(d) Phase 4: Full Deployment
(1) Once all testing, training, and infrastructure adjustments have been completed,
operators are required to fully implement the environmentally sustainable
extinguishing agents. The date of full implementation must be reported to the CAA, and
all stocks of legacy foams containing harmful substances must be appropriately
disposed of, following environmental disposal regulations.
5. REPORTING AND DOCUMENTATION
(a) Transition Plan must include:
(1) A timeline for the transition.
(2) A summary of the selected environmentally sustainable extinguishing agents.
(b) Risk assessments and mitigation measures.
(1) Training programmes for personnel.
(2) Infrastructure modifications, if required.
(c) Progress Reporting
(1) Operators must provide bi-annual progress reports to the CAA detailing the status of
the transition. These reports must include any challenges encountered and adjustments
made to the original plan.
(d) Final Compliance Report

(1) Upon full implementation, operators are required to submit a final compliance report,
including certification of the extinguishing agents, records of training completion, and
evidence of successful operational testing. This report must also document the proper
disposal of legacy foams.
6. CONCLUSION
(a) The transition to environmentally sustainable extinguishing agents represents a critical step in
enhancing fire safety while safeguarding the environment. Aerodrome operators are expected
to follow this guidance diligently to ensure a smooth transition, minimise environmental
impact, and uphold the highest standards of fire and emergency response.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PRINCIPAL AGENTS
(a) Principal agent provided at an aerodrome should either be a foam meeting performance level
B or C.
(b) Amounts of water for foam production and the complementary agents provided on the rescue
and firefighting vehicles should be in accordance with the aerodrome category as determined
at Tables 26 and 27.
(c) For aerodrome categories 1 and 2, up to 100 per cent of the water substituted with a
complementary agent should be based on equivalency of a foam meeting performance level A
i.e., 1 litre to 1 kg:
(1) replacement of water for category 1 aerodrome – 350 kg of complementary agent; or
(2) replacement of water for category 2 aerodrome – 1 000 kg of complementary agent;
(d) Quantity of foam concentrates separately provided on rescue and firefighting vehicles for
foam production should be n proportion to the quantity of water provided and the foam
concentrate selected.
(e) Amount of foam concentrate should be sufficient to supply at least two full loads of such
quantity of water for a 6 percent induction and four loads for a 3 per cent induction, where
sufficient additional water supplies are immediately available to ensure a rapid replenishment
of the water content carried.
(f) Discharge rates of the foam solution and complementary agents should not be less than the
rates shown in Tables 26 and 27.
(g) Foam solution concentration should be:

(1) for nominal 6 percent concentrates, the concentration is between 5.5 percent and 7.0
percent for turret and ground sweep nozzles and between 5.5 percent and 8.0 percent
for hand line and under truck nozzles; or
(2) for nominal 3 percent concentrates, the concentration is between 2.8 percent and 3.5
percent for turret and ground sweep nozzles and between 2.8 percent and 4.0 percent
for hand line and under truck nozzles.
(h) When selecting the type of foam concentrate to be used at an aerodrome, considerations
should include:
(1) environmental-sustainable type;
(2) firefighting performance meets or exceeds ICAO requirements;
(i) Where non-environmental sustainable type of foam is used at an aerodrome, policies and
procedures should be established to contain, mitigate and dispose any run-offs arising from
rescue and firefighting operations, testing and training activities in accordance with local
environmental laws and regulations.
(j) A foam certificate of conformity should be provided to demonstrate that the foams are
manufactured and tested in accordance with ICAO requirements or any other equivalent
international standards acceptable to the GCAA.
(k) Where training foams are used at the aerodrome, appropriate actions should include:
(1) segregate training foams away from operational foams to prevent mix-up; and
(2) rescue and firefighting personnel should be adequately informed on the firefighting
properties and performance of the training foams.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
1. TYPES AND AMOUNTS OF EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) Principal agents (foam) produce a permanent control, i.e., for a period of several minutes or
longer. Complementary agents (dry powder or other gaseous agent) have rapid fire

suppression capability but offer a “transient” control which is usually only available during
application.
(b) The complementary extinguishing agent should be:
(1) dry chemical powders (classes B and C powders); or
(2) other extinguishing agents with at least the same or better firefighting capability.
(c) When selecting dry chemical powder for use with foam, care should be exercised to ensure its
compatibility. If in doubt, a full performance testing should be conducted.
(d) Characteristics of the extinguishing agents are available in ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services
Manual Part 1 Chapter 8.
2. AMOUNTS OF EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) The amounts of water for foam production and the complementary agents to be provided on
the RFF vehicles should be in accordance with the aerodrome category determined in Tables
26 and 27, except that for aerodrome categories 1 and 2, up to 100 per cent of the water may
be substituted with a complementary agent.
(b) The amounts in Tables 26 and 27 are the minimum amounts of extinguishing agents to be
provided and are based on the average overall length of aircrafts in a given category. If the
aircraft operating at an aerodrome is larger than the median aircraft, the amounts should be
recalculated.
(c) The amounts in Tables 26 and 27 have been determined by adding the quantity of
extinguishing agents which are required to obtain a one-minute control time in the practical
critical area and the quantity of extinguishing agents which are required for continued control
of the fire thereafter and/or for possible complete extinguishment of the fire. Control time is
the time required to reduce the initial intensity of the fire by 90 per cent. Information on the
critical area concept and the method by which the scale of extinguishing agents has been
related to the critical area may be found in ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 1,
Chapter 2.4.
(d) The quantity of foam concentrates separately provided on vehicles for foam production
should be in proportion to the quantity of water provided and the foam concentrate selected.
The amount of foam concentrate should be sufficient to supply at least two full loads of such
quantity of water where sufficient additional water supplies are immediately available to
ensure a rapid replenishment of the water content carried.
(e) The amounts of water specified for foam production are predicated on an application rate of
5.5 L/min/m2 for a foam meeting performance level B and 3.75 L/min/m2 for a foam meeting

performance level C. These application rates are considered to be the minimum rates at which
control can be achieved within one minute.
(f) The amounts of foams given in Table 28 have been determined on the assumption that the
foams meet minimum specifications accepted by the GCAA. Guidance on basic characteristics
of foams is contained in ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 1, Chapter 8.
(g) At aerodromes where operations by aircrafts larger than the average size in a given category
are planned, the quantities of water shall be recalculated and the amount of water for foam
production and the discharge rates for foam solution shall be increased accordingly.
(h) Table 28 provides guidance on the calculation of the quantities of water and discharge rates
based on the largest overall length of aircraft in a given category. The table is based on the use
of performance level B foam with an application rate of 5.5 L/min/m2. The formulae indicated
in Table 28 are used only for the recalculation of quantities in accordance with paragraph (g)
above.
(i) There may be aerodromes that use more than one type of performance level foams, such as a
combination of level B and C foams, which could lead to error in quantity calculation or
replenishment. Due to these reasons, the use of a combination of different performance level
foams at an aerodrome is therefore discouraged.
(j) For the purpose of replacing water for foam production by complementary agents for
Categories 1 and 2 aerodromes, 1 kg of a complementary agent should be based foam
meeting performance level A equivalency (1 litre to 1 kg). Higher equivalencies for
complementary agents may be used if results of tests conducted on the complementary
agents used by the aerodromes have indicated higher efficiencies than those recommended.
When any other complementary agent is used, the substitution ratios need to be recalculated.

3. DISCHARGE RATES
(a) The discharge rates of the foam solution should not be less than the rates shown in Tables 26
or 27. The recommended discharge rates are those required to obtain a one-minute control
time on the practical critical area and have therefore been determined for each category by
multiplying the practical critical area by the application rate. The discharge rate of the foam
solution is thus equal to the water quantity Q1 in a control time of one minute.
(b) The discharge rates of complementary agents should be no less than the rates shown in
Tables 26 or 27.
4. TRAINING FOAMS
(a) Where the manufacturer can demonstrate that the training foam produces identical test
results to those expected to be obtained by the operational firefighting foam, it may be used
to conduct the foam production performance and in-service testing.
(b) Where training foams do not comply with any recognized international standards, they should
be quality assured by the manufacturer. They will be formulated to imitate the operational
foams, for induction, drainage and expansion properties. However, their firefighting

properties may be reduced. RFF personnel should understand this feature of training foams
before they are used.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
CRITICAL AREA FOR CALCULATING QUANTITIES OF WATER
(a) The critical area is a concept for rescue of the occupants of an aircraft. It differs from other
concepts in that, instead of attempting to control and extinguish the entire fire, it seeks to
control only that area of fire adjacent to the fuselage. The objective is to safeguard the integrity
of the fuselage and maintain tolerable conditions for its occupants. The size of the controlled
area required to achieve this for a specific aircraft has been determined by experimental means.
(b) There is a need to distinguish between the theoretical critical area within which it may be
necessary to control the fire and the practical critical area which is representative of actual
aircraft accident conditions. The theoretical critical area serves only as a means for categorizing
aircraft in terms of the magnitude of the potential fire hazard in which they may become
involved. It is not intended to represent the average, maximum or minimum spill fire size
associated with a particular aircraft. The theoretical critical area is a rectangle having as one
dimension the overall length of the aircraft and as the other dimension a length which varies
with the length and width of the fuselage.
(c) From experiments performed it has been established that for an aircraft with a fuselage length
equal to or greater than 24 m, in wind conditions of 16 to 19 km/h and at right angles to the
fuselage, the theoretical critical area extends from the fuselage to a distance of 24 m upwind
and 6 m downwind. For smaller aircraft a distance of 6 m on either side is sufficient. To provide
for a progressive increase in the theoretical critical area, however, a transition is used when the
fuselage length is between 12 m and 24 m.
(d) The overall length of the aircraft is considered appropriate for the theoretical critical area as the
entire length of aircraft should be protected from burning. If not, the fire could burn through the
skin and enter the fuselage. Also, other aircraft such as T-tail aircraft often have engines or exit
points in this extended portion.
(e) The formula for the theoretical critical area AT thus becomes:
Overall length Theoretical critical area AT
L < 12 m  L × (12 m + W)
12 m ≤ L < 18 m  L × (14 m + W)
18 m ≤ L < 24 m  L × (17 m + W)

L ≥ 24 m  L × (30 m + W)
Note: where L = the overall length of the aircraft, and W = the maximum width of the aircraft
fuselage.
(f) As mentioned earlier, in practice it is seldom that the entire theoretical critical area is subject to
fire and a smaller area, for which it is proposed to provide firefighting capacity, is referred to as
the practical critical area. As a result of a statistical analysis of actual aircraft accidents, the
practical critical area AP has been found to be approximately two-thirds of the theoretical critical
area, or
AP = 0.667 AT
(g) The quantity of water for foam production can be calculated from the following formula:
Q = Q1 + Q2
Where: Q = the total water required
Q1 = the water for control of the fire in the practical critical area, and
Q2 = the water required after control has been established and is needed for such factors as the
maintenance of control and/or extinguishment of the remaining fire.
(h) Factor K1 is the water required for control in the practical critical area (Q1), may be expressed by
the following formula:
K1 (Q1 = A × R × T)
Where: A = the practical critical area
R = the rate of application, and
T time of application.
(i) The amount of water required for Q2 cannot be calculated exactly as it depends on a number of
variables.
(j) The factors considered of primary importance are:
(1) maximum gross mass of the aircraft;
(2) maximum passenger capacity of the aircraft;
(3) maximum fuel load of the aircraft; and
(4) previous experience (analysis of aircraft RFF operations).
(k) Factor K2, when plotted on a graph, are used to calculate the total amount of water required for
each aerodrome category. The volume of water for Q2, as a percentage of Q1, varies from about
0 per cent for category 1 aerodromes to about 190 per cent for an aerodrome category 10.

(l) The graph mentioned in the preceding paragraph gives the following approximate values for
aircrafts representative of each aerodrome category:

2 27
3 30

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
INITIAL FOAM PRODUCTION PERFORMANCE TESTING
(a) Initial foam production performance testing for a rescue and firefighting vehicle should
include:
(1) a vehicle is first acquired for operational use at an aerodrome (acquisition may mean
new, second-hand purchase, leasing, transfer or hire of a vehicle); or
(2) an operational vehicle after significant maintenance, refurbishment or component
replacement that could affect a change in the foam quality or foam production system.
This also includes a change of foam-making branches, nozzles or monitors. Only those
parts of the system that could have been affected by the work undertaken or the
component change should also be tested.
(b) An initial foam production performance testing for a rescue and firefighting vehicle should
include:
(1) the induction percentage for all foam-making devices;
(2) the expansion ratio from all foam-making devices;
(3) the quarter drainage time from all foam-making devices;
(4) the jet range of the main monitor/high reach extendible turret; and
(5) the spray pattern of the main monitor/high reach extendible turret.

(c) For rescue and firefighting vehicles equipped with foam monitors capable of producing foam
while on the move, the tests should include an assessment of this capability. Where both a
high and low discharge capability are provided on larger monitors, this provision is tested
based on the OEM instructions.
(d) Foam induction systems should be induced with a tolerance of +/-10% of the desired
induction percentage at optimum working conditions. Premixed foam systems, if used, should
have foam concentrate introduced to within a tolerance of 1.0 to 1.1 times the
manufacturer’s desired induction rate.
IN-SERVICE FOAM PERFORMANCE TESTING
(e) For operational rescue and firefighting vehicles, in-service foam performance testing should
include:
(1) on-going testing of the capability of the foam production system; and
(2) periodic checks not exceeding 12-months to ensure induction accuracy and monitor
discharge distance.
(f) Foam specimen for checking the induction percentage should be collected during normal
procedural “spot” tests or training. Premixed foam units, when used at categories 1 and 2
aerodromes, are maintained and hydraulically pressure tested in accordance with the
intervals set by the OEMs. Only foam concentrates suitable for use in premixed form should
be used in these kinds of pressure vessels.
(g) For optimum foam firefighting and burn-back performance, foam-making test equipment
should produce the acceptable performance levels including:
(1) expansion ratio ranges from 6 to 10 for film forming foams and synthetic foams; and
(2) drainage times in excess of 3 minutes for film forming foams and synthetic foams,
preferably 5 minutes or more;
(h) In-service testing of the foam performance of rescue and firefighting vehicle should be:
(1) conducted by a competent person or organisation;
(2) where the test is conducted by a third party, the results should be validated against the
performance requirements; and
(3) records are maintained for audit and inspection by the GCAA.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
FOAM PRODUCTION PERFORMANCE TESTING
1. GENERAL

(a) The foam performance test method is based on criteria detailed in ICAO Doc 9137 Airport
Services Manual Part 1, Chapter 8.1. Any other test method having equivalent or better
criteria to ICAO requirements acceptable to the GCAA can be considered.
2. FIRE TEST METHOD
(a) Objective: To evaluate the ability of a foam concentrate to:
(1) extinguish a fire of: 4.5 m2, - performance level B or 7.3 m2, - performance level C
(2) resist burn-back due to exposure to fuel and heat.
(b) Equipment required:
(1) A circular fire steel tray of: 4.5 m2 – performance Level B or 7.32m2 – performance Level C
(2) The vertical wall should be 200 mm;
(3) Equipment or access to facilities to enable accurate recordings of:
a. air temperature;
b. water temperature; and
c. wind velocity;
(4) Fuel: 100 L of Avtur (Jet A1) for performance level B tests or 157 L of Avtur (Jet A1) for
performance level C tests.
Note 1. — Avtur Jet A or kerosene with similar specifications may be used if accepted by the
appropriate authority.
Note 2. — As some aviation kerosene may contain additives, it is recommended that testing
agencies utilize a pure kerosene test fuel in order to maintain and establish repeatable test
results.
(5) branch pipe, straight stream, air aspirating nozzle;
(6) suitable stop watch;
(7) circular, burn-back pot, measuring 300 mm (internal diameter), 200 mm high, 2 L of gasoline
or kerosene; and
(8) protective screen between tray and equipment, for protection against radiant heat, is
acceptable.
(c) Testing conditions:
(1) air temperature (EC) ≥ 15 C;
(2) foam solution temperature (EC) ≥ 15 C;
(3) wind velocity (m/s) ≤ 3;

(4) the test should not be carried out in conditions of high level of precipitation, if performed
outdoors.
3. FOAM TESTING PROCEDURE
See Table 29 for a sample of foam production performance testing.
Table 29: Foam production performance testing checklist
AERODROME NAME:
FIRE STATION/SUB-STATION:
VEHICLE MODEL, TYPE AND LICENSE NUMBER:
DATE AND TIME:
TESTING CONDITIONS:
TEST PROCEDURES RECORD RESULT
(a) Position the chamber holding the premix foam upwind of the
fire with the nozzle horizontal at a height of 1 m above the
upper edge of the tray and at a distance that will ensure that the
foam will fall into the centre of the tray.

(b) Test the foam apparatus to ensure:
(1) nozzle pressure; and
(2) discharge rate.

(c) When testing:
(1) For performance level B foam, place 100 L of water and 100
L of fuel into a 4.5 m2 tray
(2) for performance level C foam, place 157 L of water and 157 L
of fuel into a 7.32 m2 tray.

(d) Position the protective screen, if required.
(e) Test the foam apparatus to ensure a nozzle pressure of
approximately 7 bar and a discharge rate of 11.4 L/min.

(f) Record the air, kerosene, water and foam premix temperature
and check it is in the correct range.

(g) Record the wind velocity and check it is in the correct range.

(h) Ignite fuel and allow 60 seconds pre-burn from full involvement.
Note 1.— Full involvement shall be obtained in less than 30
seconds after the beginning of ignition.
Note 2. — Ignition method shall forbid putting a solid or liquid
substance into the kerosene, for example, ignition with a gas
burner is acceptable.

(i) Apply foam continuously while maintaining the nozzle pressure
and an application rate of 11.4 L/min for 120 seconds.

(j) Record extinction time (in seconds).
(k) Place burn-back pot in centre of fire tray.
(l) Ignite burn-back pot 120 seconds after the end of the
application of foam.

(m) Record when 25 per cent of the fuel area is re-involved with fire.
FOAM PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS
For each performance level, a foam concentrate should be considered acceptable if below
minimum requirements are achieved.
(a) if the time to extinguish the fire from the overall surface of the
tray is equal to or less than 60 seconds

(b) if the reignition of 25 per cent of the tray surface is equal to or
longer than 5 minutes.
Note. —  for testing person or organisation: At the 60 seconds
time, minute flames (flickers) visible between the foam blanket
and the inner edge of the tray are acceptable.

(c) do not spread in a cumulative length exceeding 25 per cent of
the circumference of the inner edge of the tray

(d) are totally extinguished during the second minute of foam
application.

FINAL RESULT PASS  FAIL 
REMEDIAL ACTIONS (IF ANY):
TESTED BY: Name, Designation and Signature
VERIFIED BY: Name, Designation and Signature
ACCEPTED BY: Name, Designation and Signature

4. OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS.
(a) The quality of foam produced by an RFF vehicle system may be affected by the characteristics
of the local water supply. It is important to acquire an sufficient clear water supply. No
corrosion inhibitors, freezing point depressants or other additives should be used in the water
supply without prior consultation with, and the acceptance of, the foam concentrate
manufacturer.
(b) Foam can be applied to fires in two distinct forms. Solid streams are used where the range of
application is essential or where the stream may be deflected from a solid object to distribute
it in the fire area. Solid streams should be employed with care at an aircraft accident where
survivors are evacuating the aircraft and escape slides may be in use. Dispersed patterns may
be employed to deliver foam at shorter ranges to a fire area, combining greater coverage with
the more effective surface application of the foam. Dispersed patterns are particularly
valuable in protecting firefighters from radiated heat. Monitors are directional control devices
which deliver larger capacity streams from nozzles. Low level application allows the operator
to see the position of the monitor, therefore minimizing the waste of agents. In some vehicles,
standard water nozzles are employed to produce “fog foam”, mainly from side-line deliveries.
While these nozzles are effective in achieving rapid knockdown, they may not be pre-
calibrated to produce foams of the specified qualities and these may not have the degree of
performance associated with fully-aspirated foams that normally provide a longer duration
and reignition (burn-back) protection.
(c) Equipment such as high reach extendable turrets (HRET) and low-level high-performance
monitors can provide the operator with greater flexibility in directing the foam stream. HRET
can be defined as a device, permanently mounted with a power-operated boom or booms,
designed to supply a large-capacity, mobile, elevated water stream or other fire extinguishing
agents, or both. The extendable turret places the nozzle well forward and below the operator,
thus eliminating foam overspray and providing a clearer view of the effectiveness of agent

application. The ability to position the nozzle nearer to, or in alignment with, the target allows
more precise aiming, reduces disruption from wind and helps to conserve agent.
(d) RFF vehicles equipped with HRET may incorporate penetrating technology that provides the
vehicle operator the ability to deliver extinguishment agent through an adjustable nozzle or
rigid probe in and around the aircraft and into the passenger or cargo compartments. Such
technology provides the ability to pierce through the fuselage or aircraft components,
affording the operator greater flexibility when it comes to the strategies and tactics of aircraft
interior firefighting. The piercing action of the rigid tip allows agent application to the seat of
the fire, which may be inaccessible to hand-line operations such as in the case of cargo
aircraft, tail-equipped aircraft engines, and auxiliary power units (APUs).
(e) Other suitable manual or hand-held penetrating technologies may include the following:
(1) manual piercing or hand-held penetrating nozzles, given a safe working platform and
proper protection, can deliver many of the same firefighting tactics and strategies
described for HRETs;
(2) hand-held skin penetrating agent applicator tool (SPAAT) is one of a variety of manual
penetration tools available to firefighters; and
(3) ultra-high pressure water streams have been developed using a narrow-gauge water
stream to “cut” a small hole through the aircraft skin to apply agent into the interior of
an aircraft. The ultra-high pressure water streams pierce the outer structure with high
pressure water and aggregate enabling an exterior attack on the involved structure.
Once the outer structure is penetrated, the ultra-high pressure sends a mist into the
thermal layer which cools the interior, dropping temperature from 800°C to 100°C in a
matter of seconds. This technology allows the operator to attack fire from a safe
exterior position without the firefighter entering the interior of a structure.
(f) The use of high reach extendible penetrating technology equipment to suppress aircraft
interior and cargo fires should be carefully evaluated as there may be concerns regarding its
efficacy and safety, in particular to safety of passengers. Where such equipment is provided,
policies and procedures on its safe operations should be established and RFF personnel are
trained and competent in the use of such equipment.
(g) Where an RFF vehicle is equipped with an internal self-calibration foam induction system, the
frequency of foam performance test may be extended to every three years provided:
(1) an internal self-calibration system accuracy check is conducted bi-annually;
(2) a high-pressure output discharge (splash test) from vehicle monitor, bumper and HRET
is conducted quarterly;

(3) a foam sample lab test is conducted annually; and
(4) where an RFF vehicle returns from a major maintenance, repair or de-calibration to the
foam induction system, a full foam performance system test should be conducted.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
COMPLEMENTARY AGENTS
(a) Discharge rate of complementary agents should be no less than the values shown in Tables 26
or 27.
(b) Complementary extinguishing agent provided at an aerodrome should be a dry chemical
powder suitable for extinguishing hydrocarbon fires.
(c) Dry chemical powders should comply with the specifications of the International Organization
for Standardization (ISO) or any other equivalent international standard acceptable to the
GCAA.
(d) Where alternative complementary agent is considered in replacement of a dry chemical
powder, an assessment should be conducted including practical testing, to demonstrate
having equal level or better firefighting performance.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
COMPLEMENTARY AGENTS
(a) Complementary agents do not generally have any substantial cooling effect on liquids or
materials involved in fire. In a major fire situation, extinguishment achieved by complementary
agents may well only be transient and danger of “flashback” or reignition may occur when foam
is not available to secure a fire. They are particularly effective on concealed fires (e.g. engine
fires) in aircraft freight holds and beneath wings, where foams may not penetrate and on
running fuel fire situations, on which foams are ineffective. They are known as complementary
agents because while they may have the capability of rapid-fire suppression (when applied at a
sufficient rate), it is generally necessary to apply a principal agent simultaneously or at least
before flashback can occur in order to achieve permanent control. Considerably improved
complementary agents have become available in recent years, and constant studies are still
being made in both the dry chemical and halocarbon fields.
(b) Due regard should be made to the problems which may arise when large quantities of
complementary agents are discharged rapidly. A dense cloud of the agent may impede aircraft
evacuation or rescue operations by limiting the visibility and affecting the respiration of those
exposed to the effects.

(c) Dry chemical powders.
(1) These are available in a number of formulations, each consisting of finely divided chemical
products which are combined with additives to improve their performance. The dry chemical
powders normally provided for aircraft RFF applications are not specifically designed or
intended for use on flammable metal fires, which require specialized agents. In aircraft RFF
operations dry chemical powders are normally of the “BC” type, indicating their
effectiveness against fires involving flammable liquids and those of an electrical origin. In
addition, dry chemical powders should comply with the specifications of the International
Organization for Standardization (ISO 7202). Operational applications are usually in one of
the following methods:
(i) they are effective against fires in inaccessible locations and for running fuel fires,
where foams are largely ineffective; and
(ii) at a high rate of application in the role of a principal agent, they may well be an
acceptable practice at aerodromes with extreme climatic conditions. When large
quantities of dry chemical powders are discharged rapidly, limited visibility will also
reduce the effective placement of foam in a dual-agent attack to those areas
where the dry chemical powder has achieved “knockdown”.
(d) It should be noted that dry chemical powder can be highly corrosive when applied to metal
surfaces and electrical componentry.
(e) Halogenated hydrocarbons.
(1) In line with the 1987 Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, the
production of halon 1211, 1301 and 2402 has been banned since 1994.
(2) The United States Environmental Protection Agency has evaluated substitutes for the ozone-
depleting chemicals that are being phased out as part of its Significant New Alternatives
Policy (SNAP).
(3) Halons are therefore no longer discussed in this document but may still be found in some
aircraft fixed installations.
(f) Carbon dioxide (CO2).
(1) Carbon dioxide is traditionally used in aircraft RFF operations in two ways:
(i) as a means of rapid knockdown for small fires or as a flooding agent in reaching
concealed fires in areas inaccessible to foam. It should not be used on fires
involving flammable metals; and
(ii) CO2, is most effective at high rates of delivery, achieved through “low pressure’’
systems.

(2) CO2 gas is only 1.5 times the weight of air and is therefore seriously affected in outdoor
applications by the wind and the convection currents associated with a fire.
(3) CO2 should comply with the specifications of the International Organization for
Standardization (ISO 5923).
(g) Alternative complementary agents having equivalent performance acceptable to the GCAA can
be considered for use at an aerodrome, provided full practical testing is conducted. Alternative
complementary agent should comply with the specifications of the International Organization
for Standardization.
(h) Further guidance on complementary agents is given in ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual
Part 1, Chapter 8.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESERVE SUPPLY
(a) Reserve supplies of principal and complementary agents equivalent to 200 per cent of the
quantities of these agents identified in Tables 26 or 27 should be provided near or on a fire
station/s for rapid replenishment of rescue and firefighting vehicles.
(b) For complementary agent, sufficient propellant gas should be included to utilize this reserve
agent.
(c) Where a delay in the supplies of extinguishing agents and increase in training activities are
anticipated, additional amount of reserve supplies should be determined and increased
accordingly.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
SUPPLY AND STORAGE OF EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) The quantities of the various extinguishing agents to be provided in the RFF vehicles should be
in accordance with the aerodrome category and Tables 26 or 27. This will permit an
immediate complete recharge of the vehicles, if necessary, subsequent to an emergency and
retention of a second complete recharge should another emergency occur before aerodrome
stocks can be replenished. For the purpose of determining quantities of reserve supply, the
quantities of foam concentrate carried on fire vehicles in excess of the quantity identified in
Tables 26 or 27 can be considered contributing to the reserve.
(b) Additionally, category 1 and 2 aerodromes that have replaced up to 100 per cent of the water
with a complementary agent, based on foam meeting performance level A equivalency (1 litre
to 1 kg), should hold a reserve supply of a complementary agent of 200 per cent.

(c) Where a major delay in the replenishment of the supplies is anticipated, the amount of
reserve supply should be increased as determined by, among others, the following
considerations:
(1) location of RFF service (may be remote);
(2) availability of supplies;
(3) training and competency requirements;
(4) vehicle and equipment testing regimes;
(5) delivery times; and
(6) customs considerations.
(d) Rescue and firefighting vehicle foam tanks should be kept full at all times when the vehicle is
in operational service because partially filled tanks will create stability problems when the
vehicle is cornering at speed. Furthermore, serious sludging problems can occur where protein
foam is carried through oxidation and agitation if there is an air space above the surface of the
foam.
(e) The conditions of storage are mainly specified by manufacturers or suppliers including the
intended shelf lives, but the aim should be:
(1) Foam concentrate should avoid extremes of temperature and be kept in climate-
controlled storage environment. Use stocks in order of receipt. Keep concentrate in
manufacturers’ containers or a suitable on-site bulk storage facility until required for
use, where applicable. Where either foam concentrate drums, bladders or large above-
ground tanks are used, they should be suitably contained in case of a spill. Where more
than one type of foam concentrate is in use, foam concentrate containers should be
suitably marked.
(2) Dry chemical powders. Use stocks in order of receipt. Replace and seal the lids of any
partly used containers ensuring the powder is kept dry and free from contaminates

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE OBJECTIVES
(a) An aerodrome operator shall ensure:
(1) rescue and firefighting service achieves response times to operational runway and
movement areas in optimum visibility and surface conditions;
(2) any vehicles, other than the first rescue and firefighting service responding vehicle(s),
required to deliver the amounts of extinguishing agents as determined by the

appropriate aerodrome protection category for continuous agent application, arrive
within the determined duration from the initial call;
(3) fire station/s including appropriate facilities to accommodate rescue and firefighting
vehicles, equipment and personnel is/are provided at an aerodrome;
(4) communication and alerting systems including a direct communication between the
rescue and firefighting service, air traffic service and the aircraft crew during an
emergency are provided at an aerodrome; and
(5) minimum number of rescue and firefighting vehicles and vessels are provided at an
aerodrome, in accordance with Table 30; and
(6) minimum types and quantities of rescue equipment are provided at an aerodrome.
Table 30: Minimum number of rescue and firefighting vehicles
Aerodrome
category
Minimum number of rescue and
firefighting vehicles
Minimum number of rescue and
firefighting vessels

2 1 1

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE TIME
(a) For land aerodromes:
(1) the operational objectives of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding two minutes to any point of each operational runway in
optimum visibility and surface conditions;

(2) the operational objectives of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding three minutes to any other part of the movement area in
optimum visibility and surface conditions, and
(3) any vehicles, other than the first responding rescue and firefighting vehicles specified in
Table 30, required to deliver the amounts of extinguishing agents specified in Tables 26
or 27, deliver continuous agent application and arrive no more than one minute after
the first vehicle/s.
(b) For water aerodromes:
(1) the operational objective of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding three minutes to any point of each operational runway in
optimum visibility and surface conditions;
(2) the operational objective of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding four minutes to any other part of the movement area in
optimum visibility and surface conditions; and
(3) any vessels, other than the first responding rescue and firefighting vessels specified in
Table 30, required to deliver the amounts of extinguishing agents specified in Tables 26
or 27, deliver continuous agent application and arrive no more than one minute after
the first vessel/s.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE TIME CONDITIONS
(a) Response time is considered to be the time between the initial call to the rescue and
firefighting service, and the time when the first responding vehicle(s) or vessel(s) is (are) in
position to apply foam at a rate of at least 50 per cent of the discharge rate specified in in
Tables 26 or 27.
(b) For land aerodrome, optimum visibility and surface conditions are defined as daytime, good
visibility, no precipitation with normal response route free of surface traffic and
contamination, e.g. water, sand, etc.
(c) For water aerodrome, optimum visibility and surface conditions are defined as daytime, good
visibility, normal response route free of surface traffic and not exceeding Beaufort Sea State 2.
Note. —  The Beaufort scale is an empirical measure that relates wind speed to observed
conditions at sea. Beaufort Sea State 2 refers to light breeze, wind speed (6 knots / 6-11 km/h),

wave height (0.3–0.6 m) and small wavelets still short but more pronounced with crests have a
glassy appearance but do not break.
(d) Additional guidance on response time is available in the ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services
Manual Part 1.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE TIME VERIFICATION
(a) In order for a rescue and firefighting service to maintain its response time objectives, the
aerodrome operator may consider conducting verification tests under the following
conditions:
(1) where there is new ARFFS personnel or existing personnel returning from long absence;
(2) where there is new ARFFS vehicle or existing vehicles returning from major
maintenance that may affect its operational performance;
(3) where there are major changes to aerodrome infrastructures and/or operating
environments; and
(4) where there are major changes to operational policies and procedures.
(b) The response location and routes should be selected and agreed in close coordination with Air
Traffic Control and should not cause any major disruption to aerodrome operations.
(c) Response time verification should include all RFF vehicles as per aerodrome category and each
vehicle discharging short burst of water through the vehicle’s monitor at the correct operating
pressure, immediately upon arrival at a nominated location (runway, taxiway, aircraft stand,
etc).
(d) The response time verification should be initiated, in close coordination with Air Traffic
Control, using the normal emergency response activation procedures detailed in the AEP, and
the time required from the activation to the production of water at the nominated location
should be recorded including the arrivals of first and last vehicles.
(e) The response timing verification should be conducted under strict controlled conditions and
safely performed during optimum visibility and surface conditions so that the rescue and
firefighting vehicles are not disrupted during the verification and the vehicles can be quickly

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
SUPPLEMENTARY AERODROME WATER SUPPLY SYSTEMS
(a) The guidance on aerodrome water supply systems is intended to support ARFFS operations at
any aerodrome. This guidance does not include water supply systems intended to support
aerodrome structural fire protection functions. Guidance for the water requirements for fire
protection of aerodrome structural facilities such as aerodrome terminals, aircraft hangers, air
cargo terminals, fuel farms, etc., should be refer to the local UAE fire code and/or NFPA 419 -
Guide for Master Planning Aerodrome Water Supply Systems for Fire Protection.
(b) Supplementary water supplies, for the expeditious replenishment of RFF vehicles, should be
prearranged. The objective of providing additional water supplies at sufficient pressure and
flow is to ensure rapid replenishment of aerodrome RFF vehicles. This supports the principle
of continuous application of extinguishing media to maintain survivable conditions at the
scene of an aircraft accident for far longer than that provided for by the minimum amounts of
water set out in Tables 26 or 27.
AERODROME FIRE HYDRANT SYSTEM
(a) All of the components for an aerodrome fire hydrant supply system should meet the
requirements of and be installed in accordance with the local UAE fire code or NFPA 24,
"Installation of Private Fire Service Mains and Their Appurtenances". The valves, hydrants, and
pumps should be designed to operate as intended at temperature conditions applicable for
the geographic region. The installation should include freeze protection, if necessary.
(b) Piping Layout. A gridded or a looped water distribution system is preferred over a single water
main. The emergency capacity of the system should be based on the ARFFS vehicle refill
standards and any domestic or industrial service that will have concurrent demands. Avoid
installing water lines under future sites for aerodrome buildings, maintenance facilities,
embankments, or heavy traffic areas such as runways and taxiways. Provide anti-surge
components as needed to protect piping from surge and water hammer damage. When
feasible, the aerodrome water distribution system should be fed with water at two or more
widely separated and isolatable inlets.
(c) Valves. Locate valves for optimum control and to limit size of the inoperative area during
system checks, repairs, modifications, or expansions.
(d) Hydrants.
(1) All hydrants installed in support of an ARFFS water supply system should be accepted by
the local UAE fire authority or an accepted testing organisation.

(2) The availability of hydrants in proximity to aprons is necessary. Where hydrants are
located close to hangers, terminal buildings, and passenger gates, the location should
be identified with a reflective sign at least 4.5 M above their position. Hydrants should
be strategically located on loops or grids readily accessible to ARFFS vehicles. Optimum
hydrant spacing is approximately 90 M. Spacing should not be more than 150 M apart
along the periphery of aprons which are used for aircraft parking and passenger loading
and unloading.
(3) Hydrant station locations should not constitute a hazard to aircraft or ground vehicle
movements. This placement should also safeguard hydrants against aircraft or ground
service vehicular damage and vandalism.
(4) Hydrants installed along runway shoulders or other strategic locations are intended
only as resupply points. They do not replace self-propelled ARFFS equipment. Runway
or taxiway hydrant systems should be conspicuously marked, and be of recessed or
flush type. Additionally, such systems will need special winter maintenance to insure
identification of their positions for inspection, test, maintenance, and emergency use.
(e) Fire Service Pumps. Fire service pumps are needed to boost the normal municipal water
system pressure to the levels needed for ARFFS emergencies as well as for multi-story
aerodrome structures and aircraft hangers. An effective emergency pumping system has the
following characteristics:
(1) Fire pumps are installed to conform to local UAE fire code or NFPA 20, "Standard for the
Installation of Centrifugal Fire Pumps."
(2) The number of pumps is sufficient to supply the total water demand at the required
pressure with the largest individual pump inoperative.
(3) The pump power source is highly reliable, i.e., each pump is individually driven. Avoid
the dependence of all pumps driven by a common source, such as a public electric
utility. For electric motor driven pumps, a backup engine generator with an automatic
transfer device is available in case of an electrical failure.
(4) The pump arrangement allows either manual or automatic operations.
(5) Pressure reducing components are provided to protect domestic piping from surge
pressures or water hammer damage.
(6) A regular inspection schedule and a preventive maintenance programme is in place.
(7) A strategic arrangement of valves and discharge headers is provided to ensure the
continuous availability of water during single or group pump maintenance operations.

(8) Suction lines to all fire pumps from reservoirs are sized to permit full water flow
requirements.
(9) The pump house is a detached building of fire resistive construction. Site location does
not constitute a hazard to aircraft operations. If pumps are housed within another
structure, the pump room is sectioned off by an enclosure having a minimum four-hour
fire rating.
(10) Spare pumps are operational and are on-line during emergencies.
WATER SUPPLY VEHICLES
(a) Vehicle Capacity.
(1) The water payload of an ARFFS vehicle is a function of the aerodrome ARFFS category.
The latter is based on the longest passenger aircraft serving the aerodrome. The ability
of any ARFFS water supply system to efficiently refill these vehicles is a primary
consideration in assessing system acceptability.
(2) Aerodrome categories are used to quantify the amount of water and the minimum
number of vehicles needed to transport it.
(3) The operational capacity for a given ARFFS vehicle is a function of the total water
requirements for that aerodrome category and the required number of vehicles needed
to transport and apply that quantity of water.
(b) Vehicle Tank Fill Connections.
(1) The tank fill performance standard for modern ARFFS vehicles specifies that the tank fill
connections be sized to permit the filling of the water tank in no more than two
minutes when the available water supply provided at the tank intake connection is at a
pressure of 5.5 bar.
(c) Fill Supply Flow Rate.
(1) To take full advantage of existing vehicle technology, the water system connections
designated as ARFFS vehicle fill stations should, wherever practical, be sized and have
the volume capacity to support that standard.
(2) As an illustration, a 7,600 litres capacity vehicle would need a minimum flow of 3,800
litres per minute. Using the individual vehicle fill requirements thus derived, a cost-
effective water supply system can be designed for any unique fleet of ARFFS vehicles.
WATER TANKS
(a) Water can be acquired from a public water system, man-made reservoirs, or natural sources.
Public water systems are generally a reliable primary source for ARFFS service operations.

Man-made reservoirs include a variety of devices such as: gravity tanks, pressure tanks, wells,
and in or above ground level reservoirs. Natural sources such as lakes, rivers, and springs may
also be accessible to the aerodrome. Whichever water source is chosen, the aerodrome
operator should identify the source as being able to support the present and forecasted water
requirements of the ARFFS service as well as the domestic water service demands of the
aerodrome. When selecting the water source to support an overall aerodrome fire protection
programme, the following should be considered:
(1) Public Water System. Generally, a reliable primary water supply source. The
disadvantages of this source include: lack of control over water sharing, physical
condition of the system, the scheduling of service interruptions, and system component
make-up, such as pressure reducing valves or water meters. Also, booster pumps are
often required to overcome restricted flows and/or to increase pressure during fire
service operations.
(2) Man-made Reservoirs.
(i) Elevated gravity tanks provide a dependable delivery of water. However, the
need for high pressures and flow rates during fire service operations may restrict
their use because of the extra cost of fire pumps or other practical
considerations. If employed, their height and location should not constitute an
aerodrome hazard. If selected, they should be properly sized to support the
needed flow rates and shall be installed and maintained in accordance with local
UAE fire code or NFPA 22, "Standard on Water Tanks for Private Fire Protection."
It should be noted that elevated facilities located on the aerodrome need to be
shown on the Aerodrome Layout Plan.
(ii)  In- or above ground level water reservoirs intended for ARFFS support can be
located on or off the aerodrome, but should be under the aerodrome operator 's
control to assure availability. Any reservoir should be divided into approximately
equal sections to allow continuous service during routine maintenance, repairs,
or expansions to the reservoir. As an additional safeguard, automatic supervision
of the water level in the reservoir is recommended. Installation of reservoirs shall
also be in accordance with local UAE fire code or NFPA 22. It should be noted that
when man-made reservoirs or natural bodies of open water are located on or
near aerodrome property, and will remain uncovered, consideration should be
given to the design of the reservoir such that attraction to wildlife is minimized.

Designs of the water body should be linear to facilitate covering if wildlife begins
to use the collected water.
(iii) Wells are subject to recedence. In some areas high volume use results in salt
water intrusion. This not only presents increased corrosion problems, it also
affects the usefulness of the water for foam production, except for military
specification AFFF or other foam concentrates known to be compatible with
either fresh- or saltwater. Before placing reliance on well water supplies, local
water table trends should be analysed for potential recedence, contaminants,
and saltwater intrusion.
(3) Natural Supply Sources.
(i) These are usually located beyond the physical control of the aerodrome. Other
disadvantages include: the effects of seasonal rain fall variations, new land
developments which increase water demands, and possible alterations of the
source. In addition, industrial pollutants or other contaminants, may affect the
usefulness of the water for foam production and/or cause damage to ARFFS
vehicles, pumping equipment, and/or the associated water supply distribution
network.
WATER SUPPLY SOURCES EVALUATION.
(a) A viable water source is one that has the capacity to support ARFFS water flow requirements.
To determine the best water source, analyse the alternatives on the basis of cost-
effectiveness and operational requirements. To avoid costly future expansions or corrective
measures, the selected source should be able to accommodate current needs as well as
projected expansions. The analysis should examine at least the following:
(1) Control. Validation of the aerodrome operator 's authority to maintain control over the
water source. The concept of "control" should include reliable "access" both in terms of
access rights to use the water and to have both the rights and the means to gain
physical access with ARFFS vehicles. The later could involve easements for vehicle
traffic. The arrangements for control/access may be critical in case of normal
distribution system failure and vehicle shuttle operations are needed as a backup
system.
(2) Capacity. Verification of the capacity of the potential source to supply the flow rates
and pressures needed to support both normal domestic and industrial obligations and

emergency ARFFS service demands. If insufficient, plans and procedures to curtail other
users during ARFFS operations should be considered.
(3) Seasonal Moisture Accumulations. An evaluation of the effects of drought and flood on
the reliability of potential water sources.
(4) Future Requirements. An assessment of the potable water requirements of any
population centres that may share the source. Consider the increases in population on-
and around the aerodrome which may expand significantly over time and develop
estimates for increased water demand.
(5) Water Quality. Identify any actual and potential water contamination, e.g., chemicals or
particulates and assess their effect on ARFFS operations.
(6) Backup Source. Identify any existing backup source or examine the feasibility of
providing a secondary water source to be used in the event of an interruption in the
main water supply. This is particularly important when hydrants are the primary source
of ARFFS vehicle refill. Contingency plans should be developed to provide the necessary
water resupply when the hydrant system is inoperative due to scheduled service as well
as for unscheduled interruptions.
AERODROME WATER SUPPLY SYSTEM READINESS.
(a) Oversight.
(1) Responsibility for assuring proper operation, maintenance, and testing of an ARFFS
vehicle fill source and the associated distribution system should rest with a single
agency or authority.
(2) Depending on the actual source, and/or its physical location, that authority could be
aerodrome management, a private water company, or the local municipal utilities
department.
(b) Operational Checks.
(1) Periodic testing of subsystem components as well as the total water supply system is
essential to both prove the operational readiness of the system and to train new
personnel or maintain the currency of those responsible for system operation under
emergency conditions.
(2) In addition, ARFFS personnel should be fully familiar with the operation of any portion
of the water supply system under aerodrome jurisdiction. The following schedule of
operational checks is recommended:

(i) Initiate and maintain a leak detection programme to detect and repair leaks that
may develop in any portion of the buried water system that lies near the air
operations surfaces. Undetected leaks could result in pavement undermining and
subsequent collapse.
(ii) Perform a turnover test for both the primary and the spare fire water pumps at
least once a week. Conduct full flow tests at least once per year. Run up each
internal combustion engine (including any spares) used to drive fire water pumps
weekly for at least one-half hour.
(iii) Flush test all hydrants annually. Operate all main and subsystem valves in the
water supply system through at least one full cycle (open/close/open or
close/open/close) at least once annually.
(iv) Conduct a daily inspection of all subsystem isolation valves to ensure that
inadvertent system outages do not go undetected in the event that unauthorized
valve closures occur.
(v) Conduct a full flow test immediately after any significant change, modification or
repair has been made to the aerodrome ARFFS water supply system; or, to any of
the major subsystems. This test is needed to ensure that the original design
parameters have not been degraded or that the anticipated improvements have
been attained.
(c) System Outage Reporting.
(1) The aerodrome operator should develop and implement an operating procedure that
assures ARFFS service notification of any reduction in the ARFFS water supply capability,
either in pressure or volume.
(2) In the case of an unscheduled interruption, the notification should be immediate and
should include information as to the extent or areas of the aerodrome affected, the
estimated time to system restoration, and any emergency procedures instituted by the
water supply system operator.
(3) For scheduled interruptions due to maintenance or system modifications, notification
should, whenever practical, precede the interruption by 24 hours.
(4) The RFF service should also be notified promptly of system restoration so that
appropriate system tests may be conducted.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EMERGENCY ACCESS ROADS AND GATES

(a) Emergency access roads should be provided on an aerodrome where terrain conditions permit
their construction so as to facilitate the achievement of minimum response times.
(b) Particular attention should be given to the provision of ready access to approach areas up to 1
000 m from the runway threshold or at least from the threshold to the aerodrome boundary.
(c) Where the aerodrome is fenced, access to outside areas should be facilitated by the provision
of emergency gates or frangible barriers.
(d) Emergency access roads and any associated bridges should be capable of supporting the
heaviest vehicles, which will use them and be constructed so as to be effectively available in
all weather conditions.
(e) Roads within 90 m of a runway should be constructed to prevent surface erosion and the
transfer of debris to the runway.
(f) Sufficient vertical clearance should be provided from overhead obstructions for the largest
rescue and firefighting vehicles. Wherever possible, roads should permit the passage of
vehicles in both directions.
(g) When the surface of the road is indistinguishable from the surrounding area, or in areas
where sand or vegetation may obscure the location of the roads, edge markers should be
placed at intervals of about 10 m.
(h) Where an emergency access road, normally provided with a gate or frangible barrier, leads
emergency vehicles on to a public road, the exterior face of the gate or barrier should be
marked to indicate its purpose, with a prohibition of vehicle parking in its immediate vicinity.
(i) Suitably designed corners, with sufficient radii for the manoeuvring of RFF vehicles, should be
provided to facilitate the departure of responding vehicles through the aerodrome fence
emergency gates or barriers.
(j) Combined facilities of emergency access road and gate or barrier should be subject to regular
inspection and physical tests where necessary, to prove the proper functioning of any
mechanical element, to ensure their availability in an emergency.
(k) Where access gates are non-frangible and secured by other mechanical means, access
through the gate(s) should be readily available, such as, but not limited to, the provision of
keys to the gates to be kept in the rescue and firefighting vehicles.

title: Rescue and firefighting

CONDITIONS
(a) In meeting the operational objective as nearly as possible in times of traffic/apron congestion
or in less than optimum conditions of visibility and conditions, especially during low visibility
operations, suitable guidance, equipment and/or procedures should be provided for rescue
and firefighting services including:
(1) establish and implement plans and procedures with air traffic control to direct ground
vehicle movement in case of accident or incident; and
(2) provide airfield charts, navigational equipment and tracking system for the rescue and
firefighting service.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
MAINTAINING RESPONSE CAPABILITY DURING TRAFFIC CONGESTION, NON-OPTIMUM
CONDITIONS OR AERODROME WORKS
(a) In order to meet the operational response objective as nearly as possible during traffic/apron
congestion, in less than optimum conditions of visibility, especially during low visibility
operations or aerodrome works at airside, suitable guidance, equipment and/or procedures
for RFF services should be provided. These may include navigation equipment installed in the
RFF vehicles such as:
(1) a driver enhanced vision system (DEVS) with on-board navigation equipment utilizing
the global navigation satellite system to provide the driver with the vehicle’s location
thus serving as an aid in navigating to the accident sites;
(2) tracking using digital radio datalink to assist the vehicle driver in locating and navigating
to the accident site, thereby reducing driver communications workload and improving
situational awareness; and
(3) low visibility enhanced vision using a forward looking infrared (FLIR) device (or other
comparable state-of-the-art low visibility enhanced vision technology) by sensing
thermal radiation instead of visible light to improve visual awareness in a smoky, foggy
or dark environment.

(b) RFF vehicles should approach any aircraft accident or incident by the quickest route
commensurate with safety, although this might not necessarily be the shortest distance to the
incident site. Traversing through unimproved areas can take longer than travelling a greater
distance on paved surfaces, therefore a thorough knowledge by ARFFS personnel of the
topography of the aerodrome and its immediate vicinity for all weather conditions is
paramount. The use of grid maps and careful selection of routes is essential for success in
meeting the response objectives.
(c) Consideration should be given to the provision and use of technical equipment, e.g. surface
movement radar, infrared vision systems, taxiway centreline lighting, vehicle positioning
equipment and other navigation aids that could enhance ARFFS response to the location of an
accident or incident site in low visibility conditions.
(d) Once low visibility operations have been initiated it may be necessary to restrict the operation
of vehicles in the aircraft manoeuvring area. Procedures developed for ATC to assist the ARFFS
in case of an accident or incident should be put in place.
(e) ARFFS and associated external emergency response personnel should be made aware of the
existence of any areas that may, from time to time, become impassable because of weather
or other conditions, and of the location of obstacles both permanent and temporary.
(f) Operational procedures should be developed through which air traffic control (ATC) stop or
divert all aircraft and non-essential traffic that conflicts with responding ARFFS vehicles. ARFFS
personnel should continuously monitor the minimum visibility operating conditions in order to
maintain response capability under such conditions.
(g) In addition, other suitable provisions should be considered such as bypass access roads as well
as the provision of ground movement guidance instructions from air traffic control based on
surveillance radar, accident site location by air traffic control and a collision avoidance facility
either from equipment installed in the vehicles or provided by surveillance radar from air
traffic control. For the guidance of the RFF vehicles from their station(s) or standby position(s)
to the accident site, rescue and firefighting vehicles should move in a convoy directed by air
traffic control.

title: Rescue and firefighting

MAINTAINING RESPONSE CAPABILITY DURING SPECIAL EVENT
(a) Where a rescue and firefighting service is required to support any special event conducted at
an aerodrome, participation should be planned and managed in accordance with the
aerodrome operator ’s safety management system.

(b) The participation of a rescue and firefighting service at a special event should not affect its
capability to respond to any emergencies at an aerodrome.

(a) A special event conducted at an aerodrome may include, but not limited to diplomatic or VVIP
visit, water salute commemorative event, testing/opening of a new facility, airside
promotional campaigns/celebrations, etc.
(b) Sufficient planning considerations for a special event include establishing procedures or
agreements with relevant stakeholders, conducting risk assessments, preparing personnel and
equipment, event rehearsal, exercising/testing, etc.
(c) Consult relevant stakeholders on the conduct of a special event. Depending on the nature and
scale of the special event, it may be necessary to develop plans and procedures including
obtaining the necessary acceptances. Preparatory drills/exercises may be conducted to test
the plans and procedures.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
FIRE STATION AND FACILITIES
(a) A fire station should be provided to accommodate rescue and firefighting vehicles, personnel
and associated equipment including:
(1) satellite fire station, whenever the response time cannot be achieved from a single fire
station; and
(2) the fire station/s is strategically located so that the access for rescue and firefighting
vehicles into the runway area is direct and clear, requiring a minimum number of turns.
(b) A watchroom should be provided at a fire station including:
(1) where there is more than one fire station is provided at an aerodrome, a main fire
station including its watchroom should be designated as the master watchroom; and
(2) the watch room is continuously manned by trained and competent person.
(c) A fire station should be a self-contained facility including:
(1) provision of appropriate facilities for the garaging of vehicles and its associated
equipment with adequate protection against inclement weather;
(2) availability of administration, domestic and accommodation facilities for rescue and
firefighting personnel – operational, supervisors and managers; and

(3) provision of additional operational facilities and services that are necessary to ensure
their continuous ability for effective and immediate response in an emergency.
(d) Acceptance of the GCAA should be obtained prior to construction of a new fire station or
changes made to existing fire station infrastructure including its operating environment at an
aerodrome, in accordance with CAR AGA PART ADR ADR.OR.H.070 requirements.
