title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
FIRE STATION AND FACILITIES
1. GENERAL
(a) In the past there has been a tendency to provide only the minimum level of accommodation
for the RFF vehicles, little more than garage space, with equally sparse facilities for their
crews. Experience has shown that these standards of provision are not conducive to
operational efficiency in terms of either the vehicles or the personnel who are to operate
them. A study of the operational requirement has emphasized the importance of correctly
sited fire stations, supported by efficient communications systems, as a prerequisite for the
immediate and effective response by RFF services.
(b) Properly constructed and appointed fire stations can make an important contribution to the
morale and efficiency of these services. Further, response times are likely to be reduced by
undertaking in the planning stage a study of traffic patterns, procedures, previous accident
experience and the probable response paths of RFF vehicles. The following paragraphs discuss
some of the design and site factors, which are considered to be significant in this context.
2. LOCATION
(a) The location of the fire station is a primary factor in ensuring that recommended response
times can be achieved; that is, two minutes and not more than three minutes to the end of
each runway in optimum conditions of visibility and surface conditions. Other considerations,
such as the need to deal with structural fires or to undertake other duties, are of secondary
importance and should be subordinated to the primary requirement. At some aerodromes it
may be necessary to consider the provision of more than one fire station, each located
strategically in relation to the runway pattern. Aircraft accident studies have shown that a
large proportion of accidents and incidents occur on, or close to the runway/accidents in or
beyond runway end safety area locations often produce the more serious consequences in
terms of fire situations and casualties.

(b) Where more than one fire station is provided, each may contain one or more vehicles from
the total fleet. This divides the overall quantity of extinguishing agents available into units
capable of initiating immediate fire suppression activities on arrival at the accident site. It is
usual, with more than one fire station, to designate one as the master (or main) station,
providing the master watchroom, and the other stations as satellites.
(c) RFF vehicles should have direct and safe access to the movement area that caters to the size
of the fire vehicle(s) being deployed and be capable of reaching the extremities of this area
within the recommended response time. When a new station is to be provided, vehicle
response trials should be run to determine the optimum location in relation to potential
accident sites. Due consideration should be given to the future development plans of the
aerodrome as these may increase the distances over which responses should be made.
(d) All fire stations should be located so that access to the runway area is direct, requiring the RFF
vehicles to negotiate the minimum number of turns. Additionally, the location should ensure
that the vehicle running distances are as short as possible in relation to the runway(s) the fire
station is intended primarily to serve. The ability to reach standby positions without delay is
important. The placement of the watchroom, if provided, in each fire station should ensure
the widest possible view of the movement area including aircraft approaches and departures.
The installation of closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras may be considered in watchrooms
to enhance their view.
3. DESIGN AND CONSTRUCTION
(a) Each fire station should be a self-contained RFF service, with appropriate facilities for the
garaging of vehicles, accommodation of crew members and the provision of operational
services that are necessary to ensure their continuous ability for effective and immediate
response in an emergency. Facilities for the major maintenance of fire vehicles need not be
included provided that these exist elsewhere, on, or in close proximity to, the aerodrome. The
range and extent of facilities may vary between those necessary in the main fire station and
those appropriate to a satellite station, but in general should include:
(1) sufficient accommodation for the garaging of fire vehicles, which may include other
specialist vehicles such as aerial vehicles or water rescue craft and for the conduct of in-
service (minor) maintenance;
(2) domestic and administrative facilities for the personnel required to operate these fire
vehicles;

(3) communications and alarm systems which will ensure the immediate and effective
deployment of fire vehicles in any emergency; and
(4) appropriate storage and technical support facilities as are necessary to protect and
maintain the equipment and reserves of extinguishing agents held at each fire station or
nearby facility.
(b) In meeting these basic requirements, it is desirable to consider not only design features, but
also constructional details since experience has shown that inadequacies in either respect can
add to the time taken to receive a call and respond to an emergency, as well as introducing
problems in the day-to-day use of a fire station. Some features, which are considered to be
important in ensuring the functional efficiency of fire stations, are outlined below.
(c) Vehicle housing.
(1) A series of bays providing sufficient space for each vehicle and a surrounding area in
which personnel can work conveniently. A minimum clearance of 1.2 m should be
provided around each fire vehicle. The minimum clearance area should consider and
allow for the way in which fire vehicle cabin doors and locker doors open as well as
rear-mounted fire vehicle engine cowlings that may open outwards for engine access.
The dimensions of each bay, including the working area, should have regard not only to
the vehicles currently in service, but also to future models which may be acquired to
meet increases in the aerodrome RFF service category.
(2) The floors of the fire vehicle bays should provide for any increase in fire vehicle weights,
lengths and or widths which new equipment may impose. The surface finish of floors
should be resistant to oil, grease, foam concentrates, etc. and be easily cleaned. This
can be achieved by having a non-slip tiled surface or a hard-top sealed concrete finish.
The floors should slope down towards the doors, where a transverse drain, with heavy
gauge cover, can receive surface water from the bays and the forecourt.
(3) The doors to the bays should be of the quick action type and of robust design,
incorporating, where possible, windows to improve the natural lighting within the bays.
Bay doors may be manually operated or equipped with automatic opening devices,
which may include remote operation from the watchroom or in association with the
operation of the station alarm bells or alerts. Provision should be made for manual
operation in the event of the malfunctioning of any automatic device. The size of the
door opening should allow sufficient clearance for the vehicles.
(d) Forecourt.

(1) The forecourt should be of sufficient size to permit fire vehicles to manoeuvre and
should be provided with floodlighting for night-time activities.
(2) A slope to the bay entrance drain should accommodate fire vehicle cleaning and other
surface water.
(3) Within the bays there should be sufficient lighting and, in appropriate cases, heating, to
maintain a temperature of at least 13°C. In the UAE, where high ambient temperatures
are prevalent some form of climate control should be considered.
(4) Electrical systems of appropriate design will also be required where fire vehicles are
fitted with engine heaters, battery charging devices or other protective equipment.
(5) Installations should be provided to convey exhaust fumes from each vehicle to the
external atmosphere, thus avoiding contamination within the vehicle bays during
periodic engine runs or rapid deployment of fire vehicles from the bays.
(6) All connections of services to fire vehicles should be designed to achieve immediate and
safe disconnections without delaying the response of fire vehicles to an emergency.
(e) Domestic and administrative requirements.
(1) Domestic facilities should include accommodation for personnel, consisting of a locker
room, mess room, washroom, drying room, with consideration to administrative rooms
(offices), training facilities, and fitness facilities.
(2) The locker room should provide sufficient space for the personnel to change and store
their clothing as well as other personal items Seating should also be provided.
(3)  The mess room should be fitted with chairs and tables and provide facilities for the
preparation of meals and food storage. Power to any cooking facilities including gas
supplies should be automatically turned off on activation of the alerting systems.
(4) A drying room should allow personnel to dry wet clothing quickly.
(5) The extent of administrative accommodation will depend on the range of technical
control and administration duties to be performed in a particular fire station.
(6) Classroom should provide tables (desks) and chairs, a magnetic whiteboard (or
blackboard), as well as appropriate library facilities relevant to the functionality.
Consideration may be given to electronic resources such as data viewers, screens and
computers.
(7) Fitness facilities or equipment should be inside a climate controlled or at least, well
ventilated environment. Consideration should be given to providing fitness equipment
conducive to the development and maintenance of anaerobic, aerobic flexibility and
strength fitness.

(8) Where there are female RFF personnel, separate domestic and administrative facilities
should be provided at the fire station.
(f) Supporting facilities requirements.
(1) These are facilities which can contribute to the efficiency of RFF services by preserving
equipment and extinguishing media, ensuring its prompt availability and in providing
test, inspection, maintenance and training opportunities.
(2) Storage space is required for fire hoses, with suitable racking and ventilation and may
include hose repair equipment and the hose record board.
(3) Drying facilities for fire hose is required in certain climates and may be in the form of a
drying tower or rack or an enclosed heating installation.
(4) Storage is required for extinguishing media, such as foam concentrate and
complementary agents, and particular attention should be given to ensuring that
temperatures are kept within the levels specified for each agent.
(5) Suitable facilities for containment should also be provided for stored foam concentrates
in the event of spillage or leakage. Advice in respect of appropriate storage
temperatures can be obtained from suppliers.
(6) A general workshop, where maintenance and repairs can be performed, will make a
valuable contribution towards the efficient and economical operation of the service.
(7) A fire station should be provided with a hydrant capable of delivering water at an
appropriate rate for rapid replenishment of vehicles.
(8) Appropriate facilities for the testing of fire hose and vehicles, for the rapid
replenishment of vehicles after use and for training purposes should be readily
available.
(9) Facilities for transferring foam concentrates from containers and complementary
agents to fire vehicles expeditiously should be provided.
(g) Watchrooms.
(1) In all fire stations there should be a central point for the reception of emergency calls,
from which fire vehicles may be dispatched for responses of all kinds and resources can
be mobilized and directed.
(2) A watchroom should be sited in a position which overlooks as much of the movement
area as possible. It may be necessary to elevate the watchroom to provide the
maximum degree of surveillance.
(3) Special provisions may be necessary to soundproof the watchroom and to deal with the
consequent ventilation and climate control problems which soundproofing may create.

(4) Tinted windows or sunshades may be required in some locations to minimize the
effects of direct or indirect exposure to the sun and other external elements such as
concrete surfaces and climatic conditions.
(5) Provision will be necessary to vary the intensity of watchroom lighting to permit
external vision when the watchroom is in use at night. The communications facilities
required in watchrooms are detailed in GM AMC7 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.020 Rescue and
firefighting, where a distinction is made between the requirements for the master
watchroom and watchrooms in satellite fire stations.
(6) Where a watchroom is located at a different facility other than a fire station at an
aerodrome, it should be provided with sufficient day/night runway and movement area
monitoring system, discrete ARFFS communication system, emergency notification and
alerting system and appropriate contingency measures in the event of system failure.
(h) General aspects.
(1) In addition to the particular requirements considered above there are a number of
general items, applicable to all fire stations, which can contribute to their efficient
operation and the well-being of personnel. Except where it may be necessary to elevate
a watchroom for operational reasons, it is desirable to provide all accommodation on
one level.
(2) It is important, in preparing the original plan, to make some provision for expansion to
correspond with the growth of the aerodrome. If the plan meets this situation by
providing the domestic accommodation to one side of the vehicle bays, an additional
benefit will be the exclusion of exhaust fumes from this accommodation when the
vehicles are running. Fire vehicle bays with access from the rear will aid the movement
of fire vehicles by providing a drive-through facility.
(3) The parking of fire vehicles should be such that the failure of any one should not
prevent others from making an immediate response. The high noise levels to which
some fire stations may be exposed may require some measure of soundproofing in the
domestic accommodation in addition to the watchroom.
(4) Additional attention to ventilation and climate control may also become necessary in
ensuring the comfort and efficiency of the occupants.
(5) All fire stations should be connected to a secondary (standby) electrical power supply to
ensure the continuous availability of essential equipment and facilities.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
COMMUNICATION AND ALERTING SYSTEM
(a) A discrete communication system should be provided linking a fire station with the air traffic
control tower, any other fire station on the aerodrome and the rescue and firefighting
vehicles.
(b) An alerting system for rescue and firefighting personnel, capable of being operated from that
station, should be provided at a fire station, any other fire station on the aerodrome and the
air traffic control tower.
(c) Provisions of communication and alerting system should be provided to ensure consistent
with the individual requirements of each aerodrome including:
(1) a direct communication between air traffic control and the fire station/s to ensure the
prompt dispatch of rescue and firefighting vehicles in the event of an aircraft
emergency;
(2) a communication between air traffic control and the rescue and firefighting personnel
enroute to, or in attendance at, an aircraft accident/incident;
(3) suitable guidance to the rescue and firefighting vehicles during low visibility conditions,
navigational equipment and communication assistance;
(4) communication between the fire station, or the main station, where more than one fire
station and rescue and firefighting vehicles;
(5) communication between the rescue and firefighting vehicles and its personnel;
(6) emergency alarm systems to alert auxiliary personnel and appropriate organizations
located on or off the aerodrome;
(d) At aerodrome with multiple operational runways, a communication needs assessment should
be conducted to determine the appropriate communication and alerting systems required to
support the possibility of managing multiple emergencies.
(e) A fire station watchroom communication and alerting system should be provided including:
(1) trained and competent personnel at an aerodrome to monitor aircraft movements and
facilitate all fire station communications between air traffic control, rescue and
firefighting services, on and off aerodrome agencies during an emergency; and
(2) where there is more than one fire station watchroom at an aerodrome, designate a
master watchroom linking all fire station communication and alerting systems.

(f) A discrete emergency frequency Channel 121.6 MHz should be provided at an aerodrome for
direct communication between rescue and firefighting services with the flight crew of an
aircraft in an emergency on the ground.
(g) An officer in-charge of the aerodrome rescue and firefighting service should be designated a
callsign of “Airport Incident Commander” when communicating with air traffic control tower
and flight crew of aircraft having an emergency on the ground.
(h) Rescue and firefighting vessels or other specialized vehicles intended for use in water,
swampy areas or other difficult terrain should be provided with two-way radio equipment.
(i) Special attention should be given to the selection of communication radio units intended for
use in marine applications or other difficult environments, particularly to their protective
containment systems; and
(j) Policies and procedures should be established and implemented to ensure rescue and
firefighting personnel designated to communicate with air traffic control tower, aircraft flight
crew and rescue and firefighting vehicles, are trained and competent in appropriate level of
aviation language proficiency and air-ground communications.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
COMMUNICATION AND ALERTING SYSTEM FACILITIES
(a) The efficiency of an RFF service is significantly dependent on the reliability and effectiveness
of its communication and alarm system. In addition, the successful conduct of the total
firefighting and related rescue operation will be facilitated by the system for alerting and
mobilizing other participating emergency support personnel. The importance of prompt and
clear communications cannot be over-emphasized.
(b) Consistent with the individual requirements of each aerodrome there should be provision for:
(1) direct communication between air traffic control (or other activating authority provided
by the aerodrome authority) and the aerodrome fire station(s) to ensure the prompt
dispatch of RFF vehicles in the event of an aircraft emergency;
(2) communication between air traffic control and the RFF crews en-route to, or in
attendance at, an aircraft accident/incident. To provide guidance to the RFF vehicles
during low visibility conditions, some form of navigational assistance may be required;
(3) communication between the fire station, or the main station, where more than one is
provided, and the RFF vehicles;
(4) communication between the RFF vehicles, including where necessary, a system to
provide intercommunication between the crew members of an RFF vehicle; and

(5) emergency alarm systems to alert auxiliary personnel and appropriate organizations
located on or off the aerodrome.
(c) Additionally, a direct communication should be provided between the RFF services and the
flight crew of an aircraft in an emergency on the ground.
FIRE STATION COMMUNICATIONS
(a) In considering the scope of fire station communications, two important factors need to be
considered.
(b) The first is the extent of the workload in the watchroom when an aircraft accident or incident
occurs. The range of communication facilities will naturally be related to this workload and if
some part of the emergency mobilization can be undertaken elsewhere, at an aerodrome
telephone exchange room or emergency operations centre, for example, then the fire station
watchroom can be more effectively equipped and operated in its primary role.
(c) The second consideration relates to those aerodromes operating more than one fire station.
Where two or more stations are provided it is usual to designate one as the main station and
its watchroom as the master watchroom, which is continuously staffed. A satellite station may
also have a watchroom with fewer facilities commensurate with its subordinate role and
usually staffed only until the satellite’s vehicles respond to a call.
(d) In discussing fire station communications, it is essential to differentiate between the minimum
requirements in main and satellite fire stations and to identify the systems which can serve
both.
(e) Calls to the aerodrome fire station(s) for attendance at an aircraft accident/incident normally
originate from air traffic control. Air traffic control should be linked with the main fire station
by a direct telephone line not passing through any intermediate switchboard so as to avoid
delays. This line is usually provided with a distinctive buzzer in the watchroom and is
safeguarded against buzzer defects by a warning light. This line can be linked to the alarm
system in the main and satellite fire station(s) so that the initiation of a call by air traffic
control simultaneously alerts all personnel. The alarm system may also be used to activate RFF
vehicle room doors. A separate switch for activating the alarm system should be provided in
each fire station watchroom.
(f) Fire stations should be provided with a public address system so that details of the
emergency, giving location, type of aircraft involved, preferential routing for RFF vehicles, can
be conveyed to crew members. Control of this system would normally be located in the

master watchroom,  which would also have a switch for silencing the alarm system to avoid
any interference with the effective use of the broadcast facility.
(g) Some calls for emergency services may reach the main fire station from the aerodrome
telephone switchboard and it is usual to have a special telephone circuit for these priority
calls. As some of these calls will be of lower priority than that associated with an aircraft
accident/incident, e.g. response to fuel spills, special services, etc., it is not necessary to link
this circuit with the alarm system. The alerting and directing of these responses can be
controlled from the master watchroom. A separate telephone circuit, for calls of a non-
emergency nature, should also be provided in each watchroom.
(h) Where the master watchroom is required to mobilize off-aerodrome support services for
aircraft-related or other emergency situations, direct telephone circuits with appropriate
priority indications should be provided to the appropriate control centres.
(i) Satellite fire station watchrooms should be linked to the master watchroom by a direct
telephone line. The satellite fire station should be served by the public address and alarm
system operated by the master watchroom as well as having the ability to activate the alarm
system and make public address broadcasts within its station. A grid reference map(s) should
be displayed.
(j) In many instances, the master fire station watchroom tends to become overloaded with
alarms, switches, buzzers, coloured lights, radio equipment, public address system, etc. The
watchroom should be designed in such a way as to minimize the workload on the watchroom
attendant during an emergency call. The objective should be to set out the watchroom in such
a manner that a call can be received and dealt with by a minimum of movement on the part of
the watchroom attendant. Grid reference maps, etc., should be placed directly in front of the
watchroom attendant’s position. Details on the design of the fire station watchroom can be
found in GM AMC6 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.020 Rescue and firefighting.
(k) All telephone and radio equipment in each watchroom should be regularly monitored for its
serviceability and arrangements should exist for emergency repair and maintenance of this
equipment. The continuity of electrical supplies to fire stations should be ensured by
connection to secondary power supplies.
RFF VEHICLE COMMUNICATIONS
(a) When RFF vehicles leave their fire stations and enter the manoeuvring area, they come under
the direction of air traffic control. These vehicles should be equipped with two-way radio
communications equipment, through which their movements can at all times be subject to

direction by air traffic control. The choice of a direct air traffic control/fire service frequency,
monitored in the master watchroom, or a discrete aerodrome fire service frequency, relaying
air traffic control instructions and fresh information, will be a matter for the aerodrome or
appropriate authority to determine, based on local operational and technical considerations.
A discrete frequency minimizes the extent to which fire service activities involve an air traffic
control channel at a busy aerodrome. It is important to provide the fire service with the
facility to communicate with flight crew members in certain types of incidents, particularly
where undercarriage situations are involved or aircraft evacuation may be proposed.
Technical solutions are available to permit both a discrete frequency and an aircraft “talk-
through” facility, subject to air traffic control acceptance. All transmissions should be recorded
once an emergency situation has been declared.
(b) The radio equipment on RFF vehicles should accommodate communication between vehicles,
en-route to, and in operation at, an aircraft accident. Within individual vehicles there should
be an intercommunication system, particularly between drivers and monitor operators, to
optimize the deployment of the vehicles at an accident. The provision of a communication
facility within an appliance should recognize the likelihood of high noise levels and this may
require the use of noise-cancelling microphones, headsets and loudspeakers for effective
intercommunication.
(c) The RFF vehicles should be provided with communication equipment capable of
communicating directly with an aircraft in an emergency situation using an aeronautical radio
frequency. The aeronautical radio frequency permits the RFF service and the aircraft to
communicate with each other directly allowing the RFF crew to issue critical information
regarding the exact nature of, and the hazards associated with, an emergency in progress
along with recommendations for actions. Where provided, the aeronautical radio frequency
may be selected by air traffic control and notified to the aircraft and the RFF service. The
requirements and responsibilities for the utilization of a radio frequency between the RFF
service and the flight crew of an aircraft in an emergency situation should be detailed in a
procedure agreed to between the air traffic services and the aerodrome operator .
(d) Communications between the flight crew, air traffic control and the RFF service should be
maintained throughout the emergency response. Due to the critical and timely nature of the
information transmitted on this frequency, transmissions should be limited to air traffic
control, the pilot of the aircraft and the officer-in-charge of the RFF operations. The officer-in-
charge of the RFF operations should delay transmissions to the aircraft until cleared by air
traffic control, unless the nature of the transmission is critical to emergency operations.

(e) One of the prerequisites for effective communication between the RFF service and the flight
crew of the aircraft is language proficiency. Steps should be taken to ensure that the rescue
and firefighting crew, in particular the officer-in-charge of the RFF operations, demonstrates
knowledge of the ICAO language designated for use in air-ground communications and the
ability to speak clearly so as not to adversely affect radio communication.
(f) Standard operating procedures (SOP) explaining the use of the dedicated radio frequency
should be developed outlining why, when and how it should be used.
(g) At the accident site, the officer-in-charge of RFF operations callsign “INCIDENT COMMANDER”
may leave the vehicle and make observations on foot, and can then direct and inform crew
members in all aspects of fireground operations using a portable megaphone. This equipment
may also serve a subsidiary role in communications with aircraft crew members, the
occupants of the aircraft and other persons responding to the accident.
(h) Rescue vessels or other specialized vehicles intended for use in water, swampy areas or other
difficult terrain should also be provided with two-way radio equipment. Special attention
should be given to the selection of units intended for use in marine applications, particularly
to their protective containment systems.
OTHER COMMUNICATION AND ALERTING FACILITIES
(b) The mobilization of all parties and agencies required to respond to an aircraft emergency on a
large aerodrome will require the provision and management of a complex communications
system. The requirement is examined in the Aerodrome Services Manual (Doc 9137), Part 7 —
Aerodrome Emergency Planning, Chapter 12. Part 7 covers all aspects of aerodrome
emergency planning of which communications is a vital element, and which should be subject
to individual consideration by aerodrome authorities in relation to local facilities.
(c) Where auxiliary personnel, not on standby duty, are required to respond to an emergency, an
audible alarm (siren or air horn) should be provided which can be clearly heard in appropriate
areas above normal noise level and all wind conditions. Personnel responding to alarm signals
of this nature should have access to a telephone number, from which more precise
information as to the nature of the emergency and their response requirement can be
acquired and to appropriate transport facilities to achieve this response.
(d) Direct communication between the RFF personnel and the flight crew during an emergency
does not necessarily involve speech only as the possible use of hand signals, in particular at
smaller aerodromes, may be considered. Table 31 contains standard emergency hand signals

for emergency communication between the RFF personnel and the cockpit and/or cabin crews
of the incident aircraft.
Table 31: Standard ARFFS emergency hand signals
Hand Signal Meaning

FIRE SIGNAL
Moving the right-hand or wand in a "fanning" motion
from shoulder to knee, while at the same time pointing
with the left-hand/wand to the area of fire (which
might be an engine, APU, brake, or elsewhere).

RECOMMEND EVACUATION SIGNAL
Signalling that an Evacuation is Recommended. Used
when an evacuation is recommended by the person
making the signal. The signalling arm or wand is
extended horizontally from the body, with the hand
upraised at eye level and the palm turned towards the
signaller, away from the pilot. Then a beckoning gesture
is made angling the arm backward from the elbow. The
non-beckoning arm is held against the body.

RECOMMEND STOP SIGNAL
Signalling a Recommendation that Activity, or Progress
is Stopped (including evacuation if in progress). Used to
get pilots to immediately stop any activity that is in
progress; this could be aircraft movement or even
evacuation, if an evacuation is already in progress.
Crossed arms, at the wrists, above and in front of the
head

EMERGENCY CONTAINED SIGNAL
Signalling that the Emergency is Contained. Used when
there is no outside evidence of dangerous conditions or
"All Clear". Start with arms or wand extended outward
and down at a 45-degree angle. Then move arms
inward below waistline simultaneously until wrists
crossed, then extend outward to starting position.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING VEHICLES
(a) Rescue and firefighting vehicles should be:
(1) capable of conveying and delivering, at least, the minimum quantities of extinguishing
agents specified in Tables 26 or 27, according to the aerodrome category, taking into
account the response time objectives;
(2) capable of carrying full load with maximum traction and mobility on surfaces in
optimum weather conditions and able to operate over all types of terrain on or around
the aerodrome, at a speed commensurate with safety;
(3) fitted with a monitor capable of a range appropriate to the largest of aircraft operating
at an aerodrome, and be measured using aspirated foam;
(4) fitted with monitors that are capable of:
(i) producing foam on the move at slow speed at optimum monitor operating
pressure;
(ii) conducting stationary discharge tests to establish the firefighting foam discharge
patterns produced and the maximum range attainable by the monitor nozzle
under wind conditions of 8 km/h or less with the monitor tilted upward to form a
30-degree angle with the horizontal to determine maximum discharge range;
(iii) discharging foam onto a paved surface at the specified pressure, in both the
straight stream and fully dispersed nozzle settings. (Note. - For purposes of
defining the edge of the pattern, any foam less than 12.7 mm in depth is
disregarded. The distance from the monitor to the end of the effective foam
pattern is measured);

(5) provided with searchlights or floodlights to illuminate the scene of an aircraft accident
at night;
(6) fitted with a bumper monitor/turret as option, and under appliance protection is
permitted, if these are of a non-aspirating type, and consideration is given to integrity
of the foam blanket;
(7) discouraged manual monitor operations by the driver when vehicle is in motion, other
than when side-lines are in operation;
(8) provided with a cabin for the safe conveyance of the crew to an aircraft accident with
sufficient space to facilitate the donning of protective clothing and respiratory
equipment;
(9) provided safe stowage of equipment and the storage of loose equipment within the
vehicle cabin is discouraged; and
(10) clearly marked by a single conspicuous colour, either red or yellowish green.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DESIGN AND CHARACTERISTICS OF VEHICLES
1. DESIGN
(a) Guidance on minimum characteristics of rescue and firefighting vehicles is given in the ICAO
Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 1 – Rescue and firefighting or NFPA 414 Standard for
Aircraft Rescue and Fire-Fighting Vehicles.
(b) Rescue and firefighting vehicles should be sufficiently designed and capable of conveying and
delivering at least the minimum quantities of extinguishing agents according to the
aerodrome category. The response time requirements should also be taken into account. The
vehicles may also carry some of the rescue equipment. The selection of a vehicle of a
particular capacity will be dependent on whether it is a replacement for a vehicle which is
obsolete or redundant or whether it is a component of a fleet to be deployed at a new
aerodrome. In the latter case the consideration of its compatibility with existing vehicles does
not arise.
(c) The acquisition of a new rescue and firefighting vehicle provides an opportunity to consider
not only its contribution as a replacement, but also the extent to which it may be specified so
as to accommodate any future RFF categorization, as may be required by changes in the
volume of traffic or the introduction of longer aircraft. The anticipated “operational life” of a
vehicle, with reasonable care and maintenance, will be at least ten years, and an assessment

of the probable growth of traffic in this period should be a factor in the specification of a
vehicle.
(d) When designing rescue and firefighting vehicles with liveries or Battenburg markings, the
following requirements should be considered:
(1) liveries are graphic designs on rescue and firefighting vehicles that are intended to
identify the vehicle's respective RFF service, improve visual identification, and
differentiate emergency vehicles from regular traffic;
(2) Battenburg design uses a regular pattern and the contrast between a light and a dark
colour to increase conspicuity for the human eye. The lighter colour is daylight-
fluorescent (such as fluorescent-yellow) for better visibility in daytime, dusk and dawn.
For night-time visibility, the complete pattern is retroreflective; and
(3) when selecting liveries or Battenburg markings to be used on rescue and firefighting
vehicles, sufficient precautions should be taken to ensure patterns and markings do not
have camouflage effect i.e. concealing a vehicle's outline, particularly in front of a
cluttered background and cause confusion to passengers and crew of incident aircraft,
on and off aerodrome emergency responders.
2. COMPATIBILITY OF NEW VEHICLES AND VESSELS WITH EXISTING FLEET
(a) In acquiring a new vehicle, it will be natural to seek the incorporation of all improvements
available from current technology. In securing these advantages it is essential to examine the
extent to which they may impose new problems to personnel in the RFF and support services.
In most cases, the new problems are capable of resolution by additional training and the
provision of appropriate support equipment.
(b) The value of a compatibility study lies in the early recognition of problem areas and the
provision of solutions. As an example, at the simplest level, the introduction of firefighting
delivery hoses, with jackets composed of synthetic materials rather than natural fibres,
demands specialized repair equipment. At a more significant level, the incorporation of
power-assisted control systems and electronic devices in automotive or firefighting
applications is desirable since they are compact, efficient and reliable, increasing the
contribution to be made by individual operatives at an aircraft accident. They will, however,
require particular levels of skill in their maintenance and repair.
(c) Training will be essential to acquaint support personnel with appropriate procedures, which
may include the provision of specialized tools, instruments or maintenance facilities.
Wherever power-assisted controls are provided in foam production and delivery systems, a

manual-override facility should also be provided to permit foam production in the event of
the failure of any power-assisted function. A system for monitoring the availability of power-
assisted functions, to be used as part of the vehicle’s daily inspection procedure, is desirable.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE PROGRAMME
(a) A preventive maintenance programme should be established and implemented for rescue and
firefighting vehicles or vessels that includes:
(1) periodic performance testing to ensure continued effectiveness of the vehicles or
vessels and its associated equipment in meeting the required response objectives
throughout the life of the vehicle or vessel;
(2) keeping and maintaining maintenance records throughout the lifespan of the vehicles
or vessels;
(3) conducting regular inspections on all vehicles or vessels including every aspect of their
structure, systems and operational functions;
(4) availability of reserve vehicles or vessels to maintain the appropriate level of aerodrome
protection when any of the regular vehicles or vessels are temporarily unavailable due
to maintenance requirements or becoming unserviceable; and
(5) ensuring reserve vehicles or vessels are able to meet the operational response time
objectives and operating specification/performance required in respect of the level of
service provided.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE OF RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING VEHICLES
1. GENERAL
(a) A maintenance programme, including preventive maintenance where appropriate, should be
established to maintain facilities in a condition which does not impair the safety, regularity or
efficiency of air navigation.
(b) Due to the ever-increasing complexity of specialized aviation fire vehicles, rescue vessels and
their associated rescue equipment, a programme of regular and ongoing preventive
maintenance is paramount to ensure availability and reliability. A robust maintenance
programme would also maximize the lifecycle of both fire vehicles, vessels and rescue
equipment.
2. PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE
(a) To ensure ongoing reliability and peak performance of any fire vehicle/vessel or item of rescue
equipment is maintained, and to ensure that rescue and firefighting (RFF) services are
provided at the required levels, all RFF vehicles, vessels and rescue equipment need to have
regular preventive maintenance conducted on them.
(b) To ensure that the maintenance can be conducted correctly, provision of the following is a
necessity:
(1) maintenance personnel;
(2) maintenance procedures;
(3) defect reporting system;
(4) designated maintenance work areas;
(5) tools;
(6) spare parts; and
(7) storage of maintenance records.
(c) A maintenance programme should take into account the following activities:
(1) original equipment manufacturer (OEM) maintenance recommendations;
(2) local environmental conditions, for example tropical heat versus cold winters;
(3) national or local regulatory requirements — for example certification of pressure
vessels, hoses,
(4) roadworthiness certificates; and
(5) regular performance testing.

3. MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES
(a) Maintenance procedures should be implemented to ensure a standardized manner in which
fire vehicles are maintained. Maintenance procedures should cover:
(1) activities to be undertaken to ensure that disruption to RFF services are minimized. For
example; bringing reserve fire vehicles into operational service to maintain category
levels, or conducting maintenance during breaks in aircraft movements where a vehicle
may be taken out of service without affecting category levels;
(2) the frequency of maintenance services;
(3) activities to be undertaken at each type of maintenance service as recommended by
the original equipment manufacturer (OEM). For example, visual check, inspections &
measurements;
(4) activities to be undertaken at each type of maintenance service as recommended by
national or local regulations;
(5) arrangements for technical support from the OEM or the OEM’s local agent;
(6) spare parts that should be held on site to enable regular maintenance to be conducted,
for example, filters, belts, drier cartridges, lubricants, coolants, wiper blades; generically
common spare parts should be held on site to minimize downtime, such as switches,
light globes, relays, circuit breakers, bolts, nuts, washers, O-rings and seals;
(7) arrangements with OEM and local suppliers for all other parts to ensure downtime is
kept to a minimum;
(8) tire replacement requirements;
(9) environmental procedures including appropriate disposal procedures for old parts as
well as used lubricants and coolants;
(10) any special measures to ensure safety of maintenance personnel such as procedures for
working at heights, confined space entry and working with high pressure liquids/gases;
and
(11) the method of reporting and documenting any defects that have been identified with
the fire vehicles or rescue equipment by operational and maintenance personnel.
4. PERFORMANCE TESTING — FIRE VEHICLES/VESSELS
(a) While an ARFFS fire vehicle may pass its initial acceptance test for compliance against its
specification, there is no guarantee that it will continue to do so throughout its service life. All
ARFFS fire vehicles have parts that wear with time and as a result performance is lost. To
ensure that the fire vehicle continues to have the ability to respond, and discharge firefighting

agents at the required amounts, regular performance testing should be undertaken including
quantitative checks of:
(1) acceleration (0 – 80km/h for RFF vehicles);
(2) top speed;
(3) braking distance;
(4) turning radius (man overboard manoeuvre for RFF vessel);
(5) flow rate from high and low flow deliveries;
(6) foam admixing percentages;
(7) monitor/high reach extendible turret throw; and
(8) compressed air foam systems (if any).
(b) Records of any performance tests undertaken should be retained, as it is a record of the fire
vehicle continuing to meet the specifications, and allows future review if performance starts
to deteriorate. Where multiple fire vehicles of the same type are stationed at the same
location or operated by the same organization, it allows prediction of when the same
performance deterioration may occur on other fire vehicles.
5. MAINTENANCE DOCUMENTATION
(a) A complete set of maintenance documentation should be delivered with the fire vehicle and
rescue equipment during the procurement process. As a minimum this should include:
(1) operating procedures;
(2) maintenance procedures;
(3) fault diagnosis and troubleshooting;
(4) adjustment procedures;
(5) removal/replacement of parts and repairable assemblies;
(6) instructions for disassembly and reassembly of repairable components;
(7) tolerances, specifications and capacities;
(8) illustrations and exploded views;
(9) schematic drawings, for example, electrical wiring circuits, pneumatic circuits, chassis
air circuits or hydraulic circuits;
(10) special tools needed for repairing and adjusting; and
(11) spare parts catalogue providing exploded views of the entire fire vehicle.
(b) It is important that the technical documentation is in a format that can be easily read,
understood and followed.

(c) Any schematic drawings should be a sufficiently large enough size to enable them to be easily
read. This is very important for fault diagnosis whereby any circuits can be traced. As a
minimum, all drawings should be of A1 size or similar. It is a good idea to laminate these so
that they can be kept clean of grease and still be read at a later time.
6. MAINTENANCE RECORD KEEPING
(a) A comprehensive set of maintenance records should be kept for each fire vehicle.
(b) Keeping individual sets of maintenance records is also beneficial for each of the larger and
more complex items of rescue equipment, for example, hoses, can be grouped together,
however each item of equipment should be readily identifiable via a unique numbering
system.
(c) Keeping such documentation has several benefits:
(1) provides a historical record of the maintenance of the fire vehicle/equipment — which
may be an organizational requirement for legal or compliance reasons;
(2) provides evidence for any warranty claim that may be made against the OEM;
(3) can be referred to in the future (if a similar fault occurs); and
(4) provides evidence for any surveillance audit that may be undertaken for regulatory
compliance.
(d) Maintenance and calibration certificates should be maintained in a register for all special tools
and test equipment.

text:
PROCUREMENT PROGRAMME
(a) A procurement programme should be established and implemented for new rescue and
firefighting vehicles or vessels that includes:
(1) a detailed assessment of the operational requirements when considering new
technology and advancements in the design of rescue and firefighting vehicles or
vessels; and

(2) a formal specification process that provides a phased approach and considers the
preliminary, preparation of specification, and additional contractual considerations;
(3) operational readiness and testing process of new rescue and firefighting vehicles or
vessels prior to operational duties; and
(b) The procurement programme of new rescue and firefighting vehicles or vessels should include
the training of rescue and firefighting personnel assigned to drive and operate these vehicles
or vessels including its associated equipment.
(c) Rescue and firefighting personnel should be competent in the functions and operations of
new vehicles or vessels including all associated equipment, prior to assigning these vehicles or
and vessels for operational duties.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
TYPES AND QUANTITIES OF RESCUE EQUIPMENT
 Due to complex nature of an aircraft incident on land or water, it may be necessary to
consider other suitable type and quantity of rescue equipment to be provided at the
aerodrome in order to achieve the ARFFS principal objectives.
 To establish the scope, types and quantities of rescue equipment applicable to the range of
aerodrome categories, a thorough assessment should be conducted at each location to ensure
that the equipment levels maintained are commensurate with what is required. Table 32
provides the range of rescue equipment normally applicable to the aerodrome categories. The
option exists, where more than one vehicle will attend an aircraft accident, to consider the
disposition of the rescue equipment to several vehicles. Further guidance on the types and
quantities of rescue equipment to be provided at an aerodrome is given in the ICAO Doc 9137
Airport Services Manual Part 1 – Rescue and firefighting.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING PERSONNEL
(a) An aerodrome operator shall, in accordance with CAR AGA PART ADR ADR.OR.H. Personnel
Requirements:
(1) appoint a competent person with the authority and responsibility to oversee and
manage a rescue and firefighting service at an aerodrome;
(2) ensure sufficient number of rescue and firefighting personnel including supervisors and
managers are readily available at an aerodrome;
(3) complete a task resource analysis to determine the minimum number of rescue and
firefighting personnel required and the level of staffing is documented in the
Aerodrome Manual;
(4) ensure personnel assigned for rescue and firefighting duties are trained and competent
to perform their duties in safe and efficient manner;
(5) establish, implement and maintain training and proficiency check programmes for
rescue and firefighting personnel including training in human performance and team
coordination;
(6) ensure personnel assigned for rescue and firefighting duties participate in live fire drills
commensurate with the types of aircraft and type of rescue and firefighting vehicles
and equipment in use at an aerodrome, including pressure-fed fuel fires;
(7) ensure personnel assigned for rescue and firefighting duties shall be fit to perform their
duties in safe and efficient manner;
(8) ensure personnel assigned for rescue and firefighting duties are provided with personal
protective equipment; and
(9) these personnel are trained and competent in the use of personal protective equipment
to enable them to perform their assigned duties in safe and effective manner.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECKS REQUIREMENTS
(a) Training and proficiency checks requirements for rescue and firefighting personnel are
specified in CAR AGA PART TRAINING.
(b) Guidance material to design training programmes on human performance and team
coordination can be found in the ICAO Doc 9683 Human Factors Training Manual.
(c) Fires associated with fuel discharged under very high pressure from a ruptured fuel tank are
known as “pressure-fed fuel fires”.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RFFS COMPETENT PERSON
(a) A formal process should be established and implemented for the selection and appointment
of the RFFS competent person.
(b) The RFFS competent person should:
(1) have appropriate skill, knowledge and experience based on the scale of aerodrome
rescue and firefighting operations;
(2) have direct reporting to the Accountable Manager and acts as the principal
communicator to the GCAA, with the authority and responsibility to:
(3) be responsible for establishing and effectively managing all aspects of rescue and
firefighting services, facilities and equipment as per the requirements of this regulation;
(4) be the principal communicator with the GCAA in relation to aerodrome rescue and
firefighting services;
(5) ensure that Aerodrome Certificate requirements are met, and that the aerodrome
operates in accordance with the regulatory requirements in the provision of RFFS;
(6) ensure rescue and firefighting services, facilities and equipment commensurate with
the sizes, types and frequency of aircraft in accordance with the aerodrome and
regulatory requirements;
(7) assess the feasibility of continuing aerodrome operations in an emergency situation;
and
(8) establish and implement necessary policies and procedures for the safe and effective
management of aerodrome emergencies and training activities.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RFFS OPERATIONAL PERSONNEL
(a) Sufficient trained and competent personnel including supervisors and managers should be
designated and are readily available to ride the rescue and firefighting vehicles and to operate
the equipment at maximum capacity.
(b) Rescue and firefighting personnel should be deployed in a way that minimum response times
can be achieved and that continuous agent application at the appropriate rate can be fully
maintained.
(c) Considerations should be given for rescue and firefighting personnel to use hand lines, ladders
and other rescue and firefighting equipment normally associated with aircraft rescue and
firefighting operations.
(d) Where the available rescue and firefighting personnel display limited capacity to use initiative,
the deficiency should be mitigated by the provision of additional supervisory staff who will be
responsible for exercising command and control over their crews.
(e) Where rescue and firefighting personnel are assigned to drive and operate rescue and
firefighting vehicles or vessels at the aerodrome, these personnel should be suitably qualified

and authorised to drive and operate the types of vehicles or vessels, in accordance with local
transport laws and regulations.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DETERMINING RFF STAFFING LEVELS
(a) The aerodrome operator should ensure sufficient number of rescue and firefighting personnel
including supervisors and managers, is provided at the aerodrome including:
(1) a minimum staffing level commensurate with the level of aerodrome protection
determined by a task resource analysis;
(2) an optimum staffing level appropriate to the size and complexity of the aerodrome
operations;
(3) staffing levels are approved by the Accountable Manager or delegated executive; and
(4) immediately notifying the GCAA in writing on changes to the staffing levels.
(b) Where the GCAA determines that the staffing level is insufficient to meet the promulgated
level of protection, the aerodrome operator should:
(1) conduct a systematic review of the task resource analysis and current staffing
arrangements, taking into account the RFF category, aerodrome risk profile, and the
response objectives; and
(2) revise and implement the required number of personnel including supervisors and
managers, in order to maintain command, control, and oversight of ARFFS activities.
(c) Policies and procedures should be implemented for managing changes to the task resource
analysis, according to the aerodrome operator’s safety management system, including:
(1) a systematic process to review, revise, and validate the task resource analysis;
(2) a documentation control process;
(3) quality assurance and audit process;
(4) an approval process by the Accountable Manager or a delegated executive; and
(5) updating the GCAA on any changes to the staffing levels.
(d) Policies and procedures should be implemented for the recruitment, selection and promotion
of rescue and firefighting personnel including supervisors and managers.
(e) Where rescue and firefighting personnel are assigned for other additional duties in the
aerodrome, suitable arrangements should be made for their immediate mobilization in the
event of an emergency.

(f) Wherever possible, rescue and firefighting personnel assigned for additional duties should
travel in their assigned vehicle and maintain constant radio contact with the fire station or air
traffic control.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DETERMINING NUMBER OF RFF PERSONNEL
(a) It is important that sufficient number of ARFFS personnel including supervisors and managers
are provided at an aerodrome, commensurate with the promulgated aerodrome category to
ensure safe and effective ARFFS. See guidance at GM2 AMC1 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.005(a) Rescue
and firefighting.
(b) To ensure a sufficient number of ARFFS personnel including supervisors and managers is
provided at an aerodrome, it is essential for ARFFS to determine both the minimum and
optimum level of personnel. Other than ensuring a minimum number of ARFFS personnel is
readily available on duty, there is also a need to establish an optimum number of personnel to
ensure an appropriate level of resilience is maintained at an aerodrome in case of shortfall
due to leaves, trainings, other exigency of service, etc.
(c) A task resource analysis (TRA) is a risk-based approach to establish a justification as to the
minimum number of qualified/competent personnel required to deliver an effective ARFFS to
deal with an aircraft incident/accident. If ARFFS is expected to attend structural incidents and
road traffic accidents in addition to aircraft incidents/accidents, due regard should be given to
the inability of not meeting required response times and robust procedures should be
introduced accordingly. The following items will assist in determining the basic contents of a
TRA:
(1) Description of aerodrome(s) including the number of runways;
(2) Promulgated ARFFS categories (Aeronautical Information Publication);
(3) Response time criteria (area, times and number of fire stations);
(4) Current and future types of aircraft movements;
(5) Operational hours;
(6) Current ARFFS structure and establishment;
(7) Current level of personnel;
(8) Incident command structure;
(9) Level of supervisory and managerial personnel;
(10) ARFFS qualifications/competence (training programmes and facilities);
(11) Extraneous duties (to include domestic and first aid response);

(12) Communications and ARFFS alerting system including extraneous duties;
(13) Appliances and extinguishing agents available;
(14) Specialist equipment— rescue boat, hovercraft, water carrier, hose layer, extending
boom technology, rescue stair, aerial ladder, etc;
(15) First aid — role responsibility;
(16) Medical facilities — role responsibility;
(17) Pre-determined attendance: local authority services — police, fire and ambulance, etc.;
(18) Incident task analysis — feasible worst-case scenarios) (workload assessment) (human
performance/factors. To include: mobilization, deployment to scene, scene
management, firefighting, suppression and extinguishment, application of
complementary agent(s), post fire security/control, personnel protective equipment,
rescue team(s), aircraft evacuation and extinguishing agent replenishment, effects of
ambient temperature; (Note. — The aim is to identify any pinch points within the
current workload and proposed workload.)
(19) Appraisal of existing ARFFS provision;
(20) Future requirements. Aerodrome development and expansion;
(21) Aerodrome emergency plan and procedures; and
(22) Enclosures could include: aerodrome maps, event trees to explain tasks and functions
conducted by the ARFFS, etc.).
(d) When developing a task resource analysis, the following phase approach should be
considered:
(1) For aerodrome categories 1 – 5, a TRA may be structured using a three-phase approach
(see Table 33).

Table 33: Developing a task resource analysis using a three-phased approach
PHASE 1 – AIMS AND OBJECTIVES
The aims and objectives of the ARFFS should clearly identify the required tasks that personnel are
expected to carry out.
Aims
Phase 1 - Aims and
objectives
Phase 2 -
Development of
credible scenario
Phase 3 - Task
resource analysis

(a) To maintain a dedicated ARFFS of qualified and competent fire and rescue personnel
equipped with vehicles and specialist equipment to make an immediate response to an
aircraft incident/accident on or in the immediate vicinity of the aerodrome within the
specified response time criteria.
(b) To identify any pinch points within the current workload and proposed workload. For
small ARFFS units, identified pinch points may have to be covered by alternative
resources.
Tasks Objectives
(1) Meet the required response time
(2) Extinguish an external fire
(3) Protect escape slides/ exit routes
(4) Assist in the self-evacuation of the aircraft
(5) Create a survivable environment
(6) Rescue trapped personnel
(7) Maintain post-fire security/control
(8) Preserve evidence
PHASE 2 – SCENARIO(S) DEVELOPMENT
Identify a selection of representative realistic and feasible aircraft accidents/incidents that may
occur at an aerodrome. It is also important to consider aircraft at the high end of the ARFFS
category to enable analysis of the upper limits of the ARFFS response. This can be achieved by:
(a) analysis of accidents around the world;
(b) consideration of the accident/incident history at an aerodrome;
(c) brainstorming ideas using a representative team from the aerodrome;
(d) statistical analysis of previous accidents at aerodromes.
In order that the feasible accident scenario can be modelled/simulated, a major factor is to
consider the probable location for the most realistic accident type that may occur, taking into
account the aerodrome’s particular location, environment, runway and taxiway configuration,
etc., which may present specific risks.
The team may have identified that the following elements contribute to a worst-case location:
(1) Response time;
(2) Route to the accident site (on or off paved surfaces);
(3) Terrain;

(4) Crossing procedures for active runway(s);
(5) Communications;
(6) Supplementary water supplies;
(7) Adverse weather conditions – e.g. Low Visibility Procedures, fog, sandstorms, rain/hail;
(8) Daylight and darkness;
From the above analysis a location or a number of locations may be identified, in agreement with
the aerodrome operator , the TRA facilitator and, if necessary, the regulator.
PHASE 3 – TASK AND RESOURCE ANALYSIS
Led by the TRA facilitator, the TRA team evaluates the accident scenario(s) developed in Phase 2
in a series of table top exercises/simulations.
The TRA objective should be to identify in real-time, and in sequential order the minimum number
of RFF personnel required at any one time to achieve the following:
(1) Receive the message and dispatch the ARFFS (the dispatcher may have to respond as part
of the minimum riding strength)
(2) Respond utilising communications; taking appropriate route and achieving the defined
response time
(3) Position appliances/vehicles in optimum positions and operate RFF appliances effectively
(4) Use extinguishing agents and equipment accordingly
(5) Deploy equipment accordingly
(6) Instigate Incident Command Structure
(7) Assist in passenger and crew self-evacuation
(8) Access aircraft to carry out specific tasks if required, e.g. firefighting, rescue etc.
(9) Support and sustain the deployment of fire-fighting and rescue equipment
(10) Support and sustain the delivery of supplementary water supplies
(11) Need to replenish foam supplies
The results of the analysis should be recorded in a table, spreadsheet or other suitable format.
The TRA may be set out in a table that times each task and identified the resource required for
each step of the response.

(1) For aerodrome categories 6 – 10, a TRA should be structured in a six-phase approach (see
Table 34).

Table 34: Developing a task resource analysis using a six-phased approach.
PHASE 1 – AIMS AND OBJECTIVES
(1) The aerodrome operator should be clear as to the aims and objectives for the RFF
services, and the required tasks that personnel are expected to carry out.
PHASE 2 – FORMATION OF A TRA TEAM
(1) Identify a selection of representative realistic, feasible accidents that may occur at an
aerodrome. This can be achieved by a statistical analysis of previous accidents on
aerodromes and by analysing data from international, national and local sources.
PHASE 3 – TYPES OF AIRCRAFT
(1) Identify the types of aircraft commonly in use at an aerodrome; this is important as the
type of aircraft and its configuration has a direct bearing on the resources required in
meeting Phase 1. It may be necessary to group the aircraft types in relation to common
aircraft configurations for ease of analysis or identify precise aircraft type that may have a
unique configuration.
PHASE 4 – DEVELOPMENT OF CREDIBLE SCENARIO
(1) Every aerodrome is unique in that the location, environment, runway and taxiway
configuration, aircraft movements, aerodrome infrastructure and boundary, etc., may
present specific additional risks.
(2) In order that the feasible accident scenario can be modelled/simulated, a major factor is
to consider the probable location for the most realistic accident type that may occur.
(3) To confirm the location of the scenario, it is important that a facilitator using a team of
experienced fire service personnel, who have knowledge of the aerodrome and the
locations in which an aircraft accident is likely to occur, evaluate the scenario.

(4) The role of the facilitator is to seek agreement in identifying the credible worst-case
locations and, by using a scoring system place, these locations in order of relevance and
priority. The team should determine why the locations have been identified and provide a
rationale for each location. One methodology would be to award a weighted number to
each location, then total the numbers in relation to each identified location.
(5) An additional time delay for any of the factors listed above should be estimated and
recorded, then the location with the highest additional response time could be identified
as the worst-case location.
(6) It is important to note that the location of an accident could have an impact on the
resources and tasks that will be required to be carried out by RFF personnel.
(7) From the above analysis, a location or a number of locations could be identified, in
agreement with the aerodrome operator  and the TRA facilitator.
PHASE 5 – COMBINATION OF AIRCRAFT TYPES
(1) Phase 5 combines the accident types to be examined as described in Phase 2, with the
aircraft identified in Phase 3 and the locations as described in Phase 4; the accident types
should be correlated with the possible location. In some cases, this could be in more than
one location on an aerodrome, for which a task and resource analysis needs to be carried
out.
(2) The above information is to be built into a complete accident scenario that can be
analysed by experienced supervisors and firefighters for the task and resource analysis in
Phase 6.
PHASE 6 – TASK RESOURCE ANALYSIS
(1) By using a TRA facilitator with teams of experienced aerodrome managers, supervisors
and ARFFS personnel the accident scenario(s) developed in Phase 5 is subject to a task
and resource analysis carried out in a series of table top exercises/simulations.
(2) When carrying out a task and resource analysis, the principal objective should be to
identify in real time and in sequential order the minimum number of RFF personnel
required at any one time to achieve the following:
• receive the message and dispatch the RFF service (the dispatcher may have to
respond as part of the minimum riding strength);
• respond utilizing communications, taking appropriate route and achieving the
defined response criteria;

• position appliances/vehicles in optimum positions and operate RFF appliances
effectively;
• use extinguishing agents and equipment accordingly;
• instigate incident command structure — supervisors;
• assist in passenger and crew self-evacuation;
• access aircraft to carry out specific tasks if required, e.g. firefighting, rescue;
• support and sustain the deployment of firefighting and rescue equipment;
• support and sustain the delivery of supplementary water supplies; and
• need to replenish foam supplies as needed.
(3) The task and resource analysis should identify the optimum time when additional
resources will be available to support/augment and/or replace resources supplied by RFF
services (aerodrome emergency plan). It can also provide vital evidence to support the
level of RFF vehicles and equipment.
(4) In order to start a task and resource analysis the required category of the aerodrome
should be identified as required by the regulatory authority. This should confirm the
minimum number of vehicles, and the minimum extinguishing agent requirements and
discharge rates, this should also determine the minimum number of personnel required
to functionally operate the vehicles and equipment.
(5) The results of the analysis should be recorded in a table or spreadsheet format and should
be laid out in a method that ensures that the following is recorded:
• receipt of message and dispatch of the RFF response;
• time — this starts from the initial receipt of call and the timeline continues in
minutes and seconds until additional external resources arrive or the facilitator
decides an end-time;
• list of assessed tasks, functions and priorities achieved;
• the resources (personnel, vehicles and equipment) required for each task should
be defined;
• comments to enable team members to record their findings; and
• identified pinch points.

(2) Conclusion. A task analysis should be as detailed as necessary. The aim is to itemize the
knowledge and practical skills (doing) involved in carrying out the task or function effectively
and to the correct the standard of competence based on a qualitative analysis. Having
gathered the appropriate data and agreed to the outcome, the TRA should enable an ARFFS
to confirm and subsequently provide the correct level of vehicles, equipment and personnel.
It would also enable the ARFFS to develop a training specification, and a learning
programme can then be designed around role and task. When planning a task and resource
analysis, ask the following questions:
a) What is done?
b) Why is it done?
c) When is it done?
d) Where is it done?
e) How is it done?
f) Who does it?
(3) It is often difficult to assess the overall effectiveness of a complete unit by observation only.

effectiveness of individual units and any element(s) of the emergency arrangements.
Documentary evidence relating to previous accidents or exercises may also assist in
establishing if the current ARFFS is staffed at an appropriate level. The overall objective is to
be satisfied that the ARFFS is organized, equipped, staffed, trained and operated to ensure
the most rapid deployment of facilities to the maximum effect in the event of an accident.
The above process can also be used to identify equipment shortages and training needs for
personnel required to deal with identified tasks.
(e) Further guidance on the developing a task resource analysis is given at ICAO Doc 9137 Airport
Services Manual Part 1 – Rescue and firefighting.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
DETERMINING NUMBER OF PERSONNEL FOR MULTI-RUNWAY OPERATIONS
(a) In addition to GM1 AMC3 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.025(a) Rescue and firefighting, this guidance
provides a structured methodology for determining the minimum number of rescue and
firefighting (RFF) personnel required at airports with multi-runway operations. The process
leverages Task Resource Analysis (TRA) to ensure that personnel resources are aligned with
operational needs, safety requirements, and regulatory standards.
(b) This methodology provides a robust framework for determining the minimum number of
rescue and firefighting personnel required for multi-runway airport operations. By
systematically analysing tasks, developing operational scenarios, and validating requirements
through testing and continuous monitoring, airport operators can ensure that they have the
necessary personnel to maintain safety and operational efficiency. Regular reviews and
adjustments will ensure that the personnel levels remain aligned with evolving operational
needs and regulatory standards.  The objectives of this approach are:
(1) To identify the critical tasks associated with rescue and firefighting operations at multi-
runway airports.
(2) To determine the necessary personnel required to effectively carry out these tasks.
(3) To ensure compliance with applicable regulatory requirements while optimizing
resource allocation.

Figure-23: A methodology for determining the minimum number of personnel required at airports
with multi-runway operations

Identification
Step 2: Task
Analysis
Step 3:
Operational
Scenario
Development
Step 4: Calculation
of Minimum
Personnel
Step 5: Validation
and Testing
Step 6: Ongoing
Monitoring and

STEP 1: TASK IDENTIFICATION
(a) Identify all tasks that rescue and firefighting personnel must perform, including:
(1) Emergency Response Tasks: Fire suppression, rescue operations, medical assistance,
hazardous material containment, and evacuation procedures.
(2) Routine Operations: Daily equipment checks, vehicle maintenance, training, and drills.
(3) Support Tasks: Coordination with air traffic control (ATC), ground operations, and
emergency services.
(b) Assign tasks to specific runways based on typical operations and incident scenarios. For
example, emergency response tasks are linked to runways handling larger aircraft or higher
traffic volumes.
STEP 2: TASK ANALYSIS
(a) Define Task Requirements. For each identified task, determine the following:
(1) Time: Estimate the time required to complete each task, considering both average and
peak workload scenarios.
(2) Personnel: Identify the number of personnel needed to execute each task effectively,
including specialists (e.g., drivers, medical responders) and support staff.
(3) Equipment: Determine the equipment needed for each task and the personnel required
to operate it.
(b) Assess Simultaneous Operations. Consider the potential for simultaneous operations across
multiple runways, which may require concurrent task execution. Identify tasks that may
overlap or require additional personnel during peak periods or complex incidents.
STEP 3: OPERATIONAL SCENARIO DEVELOPMENT
(a) Develop Operational Scenarios. Create a range of operational scenarios, including:
(1) Routine Scenarios: Daily operations under normal conditions.
(2) Emergency Scenarios: Worst-case incidents, such as a large aircraft fire or multi-runway
emergencies.
(3) Peak Traffic Scenarios: High traffic periods where multiple runways are in use
simultaneously.
(b) Simulate Personnel Requirements. For each scenario, simulate the personnel requirements
based on the task analysis. Ensure that all critical tasks are covered, and consider the impact
of simultaneous operations on personnel needs.
STEP 4: CALCULATION OF MINIMUM PERSONNEL

(a) Establish Base Personnel Numbers. Calculate the base number of personnel required for each
runway, ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements for the RFF category. Include
personnel needed for:
(1) Primary Response Teams: Immediate responders to incidents on each runway.
(2) Support Teams: Personnel for coordination, communication, and logistical support.
(b) Adjust for Scenario Demands. Adjust the base personnel numbers to account for:
(1) Simultaneous Operations: Ensure sufficient personnel are available for concurrent
incidents on multiple runways.
(2) Peak Workload: Increase personnel numbers for high traffic periods or complex
emergencies.
(3) Environmental Conditions: Factor in additional personnel for adverse weather or other
challenging operational conditions.
STEP 5: VALIDATION AND TESTING
(a) Conduct Drills and Simulations. Implement drills and simulations to test the adequacy of the
determined personnel numbers under various operational scenarios. Evaluate performance
metrics such as response time, task completion, and coordination efficiency.
(b) Review and Refine. Analyse the results of drills and simulations to identify any gaps or areas
where personnel numbers may need adjustment. Refine the personnel requirements based
on this feedback.
STEP 6: ONGOING MONITORING AND ADJUSTMENT
(a) Continuous Monitoring. Establish a system for ongoing monitoring of RFF operations, focusing
on key indicators such as response times, personnel availability, and incident outcomes.
(b) Periodic Review. Regularly review and update the personnel requirements to reflect changes
in airport operations, traffic patterns, regulatory standards, or after-action reviews from
incidents and exercises.
STEP 7: DOCUMENTATION AND COMPLIANCE
(a) Document the Methodology. Maintain comprehensive documentation of the methodology
used to determine the minimum number of RFF personnel. This should include task analyses,
scenario simulations, drill results, and any adjustments made.
(b) Ensure Regulatory Compliance. Regularly review the personnel numbers to ensure they meet
all applicable regulatory requirements. Update documentation and practices as necessary to
remain in compliance.

RECRUITMENT AND SELECTION OF RFF PERSONNEL
(a) A robust structured process for the recruitment, selection and promotion of RFF personnel is
important for the provision of a professional ARFFS, hence it is necessary to establish and
implement clear policies and procedures at an aerodrome for the following roles:
(1) new hires;
(2) existing personnel; and
(3) direct entry personnel (refers to any internal or external personnel who has the
qualifications, competencies and experiences to be directly employed at the
appropriate grades)
(b) Personnel recruited and selected for RFF services are categorised as operational (firefighters,
drivers & watchroom operators), supervisory (crew, watch & station commanders) and
managerial (unit commanders, deputy and chief fire officers). See guidance at GM2 AMC1

assessment of a fire situation and, above all, should be well trained and fully qualified. Every

(d) RFF supervisors and managers responsible for the organization, management and training of
the RFF service should be experienced, qualified and competent leaders. The capabilities of
