title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
MEDICAL FITNESS PROGRAMME
1. SELECTION OF PERSONNEL
(a) Regard should be given to the arduous nature of rescue and firefighting activities. Personnel
selected for these duties should be free from any physical disability which may impair their
performance or which may be aggravated by prolonged exertion.
(b) RFF personnel should have at least average strength and have no abnormalities, which could
reduce their physical powers during a rescue. Any conditions liable to be induced or
aggravated by smoke, dust, heat, irritants or fumes (e.g. asthma) should be considered a
disqualification).
2. MEDICAL EXAMINATIONS
(a) Personnel who are employed for rescue and firefighting duties at Categories 3-10 aerodromes
should have an initial examination before recruitment and undergo further examinations at
five-yearly intervals up to the age of 40 (If fitness is in doubt, frequency should be increased),
then at two-yearly intervals up to the age of 50 and annually thereafter for those above age of
50.
(b) RFF personnel should have at least average strength and have no abnormalities, which could
reduce their physical powers during a rescue. Any conditions liable to be induced or
aggravated by smoke, dust, heat, irritants or fumes (e.g. asthma) shall be considered a
disqualification).
(c) An ECG is to be carried out at the initial examination. At subsequent examinations an ECG may
be carried out if the examiner considers it necessary.
(d) Personnel should not be overweight. A suggested maximum is 20% above ideal weight, i.e. a
Body Mass Index of 30. Exceptions may be made for persons of heavy muscular build.

(e) The hazardous nature of the job makes most types of medication inadvisable. For example,
antihistamines and tranquillizers may cause drowsiness and a slowing of reaction time.
Persons who use antihistamines should be assessed unfit.
3. MEDICAL REQUIREMENTS
(a) Persons employed for rescue and firefighting duties should meet the following medical
assessment requirements as shown at Table 39 below.

(3) The use of contact lenses is not permitted.

4. MEDICAL FITNESS STANDARDS FOR RFF PERSONNEL PERFORMING SPECIALISED DUTIES
(a) Rescue and firefighting personnel assigned to perform specialised rescue duties such as water
or dive rescue, should be subjected to additional medical fitness assessment in accordance
with applicable requirements detailed in NFPA 1582 Standard on Comprehensive
Occupational Medical Programme for Fire Departments.
5. DISQUALIFICATIONS
(a) There are certain medical conditions or disabilities that may render a person unsuitable or
disqualified for operational rescue and firefighting duties. In such case, an aerodrome
operator should seek the confirmation from an occupational medical person/organisation.
The fitness standard and review committee should formally review the medical case and
decide on the temporary or permanent removal of the medical case from operational duties.
(1) History of epilepsy, gastric or duodenal ulcer or mental instability
(2) Hearing in either ear less than 6 m for ordinary conversational voice or any evidence of
labyrinthine disturbance.

(3) Patent perforation of one or both ears, otitis media, or gross nasal sepsis or obstruction.
Healthy perforation of one or other eardrum may be acceptable provided there is no
serious hearing loss of chronic discharge.
(4) Hernia or hydrocele.
(5) Serious varicose veins giving rise to symptoms.
(6) Serious chronic skin disease.
(7) Chronic bronchitis or asthma or other disabling disease of the lungs.
(8) Organic disease of the cardiovascular system.
(9) Albuminuria, unless shown to be simple orthostatic with proof of normal renal function.
(10) Personnel with glycosuria should normally be rejected, but if they are able to furnish
satisfactory evidence of normal sugar metabolism (e.g. from a hospital, clinic or
specialist) they may be accepted.
(11) Organic nervous disorder of any kind, a history of vertigo or any condition, which would
impair a candidate’s sense of balance.
(12) Significant obesity: Obese - Class I (BMI 30 to 34.9); Severe Obese - Class II (BMI 35 to
39.9); Morbid Obese - Class III (BMI > 40).
(13) Pregnancy
6. OTHER MEDICAL STANDARDS
(a) Other equivalent medical fitness standards suitable for rescue and firefighting personnel may
be considered provided that a safety assessment including practical testing, is conducted by an
authorised medical person/organisation.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PHYSICAL FITNESS PROGRAMME
1. IMPORTANCE OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
(a) As the nature of RFF operations involves periods of intense physical activity, all RFF personnel
have to possess a minimum level of physical fitness and medical fitness to be able to perform
the tasks associated with these operations. Physical fitness and medical fitness is often
described as the overall physical condition of the body, which can range from peak condition
for performance at one end of the spectrum to extreme illness or injury at the other. The key
fitness components for RFF are generally aerobic fitness, anaerobic fitness, flexibility and
medical fitness. Optimum physical fitness and medical fitness for RFF personnel would mean

that a firefighter is able to carry out RFF activities safely, successfully and without undue
fatigue.
(b) Aerobic fitness is the ability to continue to exercise for prolonged periods of time at low to
moderate or high intensity. This is typically what limits the ability to continue to run, cycle or
swim for more than a few minutes and is dependent upon the body’s heart, lungs and blood
to get the oxygen to the muscles (VO2) providing the sustained energy needed to maintain
prolonged exercise. Typical aerobic activities include walking, jogging, cycling, rope skipping,
stair climbing, swimming, or any other endurance activities.
(c) Anaerobic fitness works differently to aerobic fitness. It is an activity that requires high levels
of energy and is done for only a few seconds or minutes at a high level of intensity. The term
anaerobic means “without oxygen”. Participation in anaerobic activities leads to anaerobic
fitness, which may be defined as higher levels of muscular strength, speed and power.
Examples of anaerobic activities include heavy weight lifting, running up several flights of
stairs, sprinting, power swimming, or any other rapid burst of hard exercises.
(d) Flexibility refers to the ability to move the limbs and joints into specific positions at the end of
their normal range of movement. Flexibility is important as it will allow the body to work in
cramped positions without unduly stressing the muscles, tendons and ligaments and may
reduce the risk of injury. Flexibility is best developed using slow controlled stretching
exercises.
2. PHYSICAL FITNESS EVALUATION PROGRAMME
(a) The physical fitness of rescue and firefighting personnel should be evaluated, at least, once a
year. Where more regular intervals are necessary, a physical fitness evaluation programme is
necessary.
(b) The evaluation should be anti-discriminatory, non-punitive or non-competitive. The results of
the evaluation may be used to establish the person’s baseline or measured against the
person’s previous assessments.
(c) A physical fitness evaluation should be conducted following significant absence, illness or
injury prior to a return to operational duty. A medical evaluation may be necessary prior to
physical fitness evaluation.
(d) The physical fitness evaluation should include:
(1) a pre-evaluation health questionnaire; and
(2) an evaluation of aerobic, anaerobic and flexibility capabilities.
3. PRE-EVALUATION PROCEDURE

(a) RFF personnel should complete a pre-assessment screening questionnaire to identify
contraindications for participation in the fitness assessment.
(b) If RFF personnel have an incapacitating medical problem or a chronic medical condition, the
physical fitness assessment should be postponed until the personnel have been assessed as fit
by an occupational medical physician. In such circumstances, the RFF personnel should be
assessed as unfit and where necessary, place on non-operational duty until medically cleared
by the medical physician.
4. PHYSICAL FITNESS ASSESSMENT FOR LAND-BASED RFF PERSONNEL
(a) All RFF personnel are required to undertake physical fitness tests which aim to assess the level
of fitness, strength and manual dexterity as well as level of confidence in simulated exercises.
(b) The three types of fitness tests shown at Table 40 are designed to reflect operational practice
and may change from time to time. Candidates will be asked to complete a Medical Screening
Form prior to undertaking many of these tests, this is to ensure that individuals are fit enough
to undertake them.

5. PHYSICAL FITNESS ASSESSMENT FOR WATER-BASED RFF PERSONNEL
(a) The watermanship skills assessment is based on NFPA 2500, Standard for Operations and
Training for Technical Search and Rescue Incidents and Life Safety Rope and Equipment for
Emergency Services.
(b) There are five tests that evaluate stamina and comfort in the water, each rated by points and
to be conducted at an Olympic-size pool (50-metres length x 25-metres width x 2-metres
deep) or equivalent (see Table 41). Where such tests are conducted in open water, a safety
risk assessment and site inspection should be conducted to ensure safety of rescuers and test
integrity.
(c) A candidate should successfully complete all stations and score a minimum of 12 points to
pass the test. The test should be completed consecutively with not more than 15 minutes
intervals between each test.

6. OTHER ALTERNATIVE FITNESS STANDARDS
(a) An aerodrome operator may propose alternative fitness standards having equal to or
stringent requirements for rescue and firefighting personnel provided that a safety
assessment including practical testing, is conducted by an authorised medical
person/organisation and submitted to the GCAA.
7. MANAGING FITNESS FAILURES
(a) There can be a variety of reasons for a need to maintain fitness. Most firefighters will reach a
point in their career when fitness levels decline. However, evidence indicates that although
fitness does decline with age this can be mitigated in part by maintaining a healthy lifestyle
and training regime.
(b) Some firefighters however may need more assistance if they are to be able to maintain their
safe operational fitness level.
(c) Arising from a particular issue - access to a physiotherapy service may be beneficial and a
phased return to work with access to fitness support can ensure a quicker return to full
firefighting duties. Encouragement should be given to access a rehabilitation programme to
assist with returning to work/full duties.
(d) It is important that both the firefighter and the Aerodrome operator are aware of their
responsibilities and work together to best achieve a positive outcome.
(e) Aerodrome operator and firefighters will recognise that regular periodic monitoring is
necessary to assist the individual, identify the current position and to monitor sufficient
progress.
(f) Despite a firefighter being aware throughout their career of the importance of maintaining
the required fitness level for their role and actively working towards doing so with the support

of their RFF Service Provider, it may be that a firefighter is unable to do so due to genuine
medical or physical reason endorsed by an authorised medical authority or person. In such
circumstances redeployment to non-operational role is an option that should be considered.
(g) Following discussion this may be redeployment in role or, with the agreement of the
firefighter, Aerodrome operator may also wish to consider if there are any other suitable
redeployment options available within the organisation / service, or in extreme cases, removal
from the service. Figure-24 provides a risk assessment flow chart in managing fitness failures.

Figure-24: Fitness risk assessment flow chart

Note. — Fitness Standard and Review Committee will assess and decide the next course of actions on
operational suitability of those personnel with repeated fitness failures and certified medically unfit
for duty. Fitness records are maintained for audits and inspections.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROTECTIVE CLOTHING AND RESPIRATORY PROTECTION
(a) Rescue and firefighting personnel should:
(1) be provided with fit for purpose protective clothing, as a minimum: a firefighting suit,
helmet, boot, glove and flash hood; and readily available for immediate use for these
personnel to perform the assigned operational duties safely and effectively;
(2) where rescue and firefighting personnel are assigned for specialised rescue duties,
additional protective clothing and equipment are provided, commensurate with the
risks and hazards at the incident;
(3) be provided with fit for purpose respiratory equipment (breathing apparatus) when
working at high-risk irrespirable atmosphere in which fire, smoke and any environment
that is immediately dangerous to life and health, are present during an operational
incident, overhaul operations and training; and
(4) when assigned to wear respiratory equipment at operational incidents and training
activities, maintain sufficient facemask seal in accordance with national occupational
safety and health regulations.
(b) Training and proficiency checks programme for rescue and firefighting personnel required to
use protective clothing and respiratory equipment should be established and implemented.
(c) Policies and procedures for rescue and firefighting personnel wearing protective clothing and
respiratory equipment activities should be established and implemented at operational
incidents and training activities.
(d) Where necessary, radio communication equipment should be provided to rescue and
firefighting personnel wearing respiratory equipment at operational incidents.
(e) A procurement programme for protective clothing and respiratory equipment should be
implemented to ensure such clothing and equipment are fit for purpose and designed for use
at aircraft incident.

(f) A preventive maintenance programme for protective clothing and respiratory equipment
should be implemented including:
(1) the provision of suitable facilities for the storage, maintenance and cleaning of the
equipment; and
(2) associated facilities, plants and equipment for the storage, maintenance and cleaning of
the equipment are constructed, inspected and maintained, in accordance with the local
occupational safety and health regulations.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROTECTIVE CLOTHING
(a) Fit for purpose refers to a personal protective equipment (PPE) that is manufactured and
capable of performing the task it was designed for. Properly design PPE is fundamental to
firefighter safety and performance. Ensuring that PPE fits well is not merely a matter of
comfort but enhances firefighters’ ability to carry out their duties safely and effectively while
helping minimize the risk of accidents and injuries. Ill-fitting gear can impede movement,
restrict flexibility, decrease work capacity, and compromise overall functionality, posing
potential hazards on the fireground.
(b) Special rescue duties may include other operational incident where the use of different type
of PPE is required e.g chemical protective clothing, etc.
RESPIRATORY PROTECTION
(a) A standard issued respiratory equipment (self-contained breathing apparatus) for rescue and
firefighting personnel operating at operational incident and training activity consists of a
backplate, body harness, full facemask, pressure gauge, regulator, pressure reducer, two
200/300-bar air cylinder (main & spare), a 6-m personal line and torchlight.
(b) Where rescue and firefighting personnel wears a respiratory equipment, a facemask fit
assessment is conducted to ensure positive pressure within the facemask is achieved. Failure
to achieve a good facemask seal may impair the efficiency of the equipment and cause a
safety hazard to the wearer when working at irrespirable environment.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PERSONAL PROTECTIVE CLOTHING
(a) It is essential that all personnel operating at an operational incident e.g aircraft fires are
provided with protective clothing which will ensure the wearer is able to perform the assigned
duties. This clothing provided should be fit for purpose, maintained and readily available for

instant use. This specification should therefore have regard for three important factors in
determining the types of clothing to be provided and the conventions specified in respect of
its use during hours of duty. These are:
(1) the extent to which it is necessary to wear continuously all, or some elements of, the
protective clothing so as to ensure immediate response when a call for attendance at
an aircraft accident is received. Some forms of protective clothing create dressing
problems which cannot easily be solved within the crew compartment of a moving
vehicle;
(2) assuming that some elements of the protective clothing should be worn at all times
during a tour of duty, there will be significant effects on the wearers in locations with
high ambient temperatures. This is due to the nature of protective clothing and its
inevitable restriction on the loss of body heat through natural ventilation processes.
This suggests that there may have to be a compromise solution between the ultimate
degree of protection offered by some forms of clothing and a lesser, but acceptable,
form of protection which can be provided by clothing specifically designed for use in
areas with high ambient temperatures. This compromise does not expose wearers to
unacceptable risk but does ensure that immediate response to an operational incident
is feasible; and
(3) in all protective clothing considerations, it is essential to recognize the problems which
will arise for aesthetic and hygienic reasons if clothing has to be shared on an
“impersonal issue” basis. The costs of protective clothing may be regarded as
reasonable grounds for requiring certain elements, e.g. protective suits, to be used
successively by a number of operatives in the course of a tour of duty. Apart from the
practical difficulties of ensuring that each wearer is provided with clothing of the
correct size, in these circumstances there may well be strong personal objections to this
practice. One solution is the acquisition of relatively inexpensive uniforms, some of
which require a special form of undergarment for complete protection, which can be
worn in part throughout hours of duty without discomfort. Sufficient protection can be
provided and clothing issues may then be possible on a personal basis, ensuring correct
sizing and eliminating the personal difficulties described above. With reasons stated
above, the sharing of protective clothing amongst RFF personnel is highly discouraged
and each personnel should be issued with appropriately sized protective clothing
including spare, where required.

(b) Protective clothing is distinct from ordinary rescue and firefighting service uniforms (see
Figure-25) and is worn at operational incidents e.g., firefighting, overhauling, fire investigation
activities, and training activities. It is designed to provide the firefighter with protection from
radiated heat and from injuries arising from impact or abrasion during operational incident,
activities and training. A measure of protection from the ingress of water is also desirable
particularly in low temperature operations. A typical protective uniform consists of a helmet,
with visor, a suit, either in one piece or in a jacket and trousers combinations, boots, gloves
and flash hood. The desirable characteristics of each component are described below.
Figure-25: Examples of a station/work uniform and personal protective clothing

(c) Helmets.
(1) Helmets should provide sufficient protection from impact, be resistant to penetration
and electrical conductivity and should not be susceptible to deformation due to heat
absorption. A moveable visor, resistant to abrasion, impact, and radiant heat should
offer a wide angle of vision. A jet-style helmet is most preferred as it provides sufficient
protection to the head, neck and chest may also form part of the helmet if not

otherwise provided by the protective suit. The helmet should not give the wearer a
sense of isolation and should permit both speech and the reception of audible signals or
words of command. Ideally, the helmet should be capable of use in conjunction with
respiratory protection equipment and of incorporating radiotelephone receiver
installations. Where helmets incorporate radiotelephone receivers, the helmet should
carry a distinctive number to identify the wearer, applied in a contrasting colour and
reflective medium. Helmet should be of different colour to differentiate different
rank/authority at operational incidents and during trainings. See guidance at GM2

title: ARFFS administration.
text:
(d) Protective suits. Protective suits can be classified into two categories, proximity suits and
structural firefighting suits.
(1) Proximity suits, designed to permit firefighters to approach, and suppress, a fire
situation, are not intended to provide the level of protection necessary for entering
active fire areas. Suits with acceptable protective characteristics are provided in one-
piece overall designs and in two-piece jacket and trousers combinations. Materials of
construction vary widely, having regard to the climatic and other considerations in the
location of intended use. The comments in paragraph (a) above are relevant in the
selection of proximity suits by the aerodrome or appropriate authority but there are
basic criteria which should be applied before acquisition whenever proximity suits are
being assessed.
(2) The suit should provide sufficient thermal insulation, should resist radiant heat and
occasional direct flame contact and be impervious to solid, liquid and gas. The garments
should be lightweight, provide freedom of movement, be comfortable in extended
periods of wear and easy to don without assistance. The fabrics employed should not
be bulky and should be resistant to tearing and abrasion. They may be coated in a
reflective medium or lined to minimize the effects of radiated heat on the wearer.
(3) Fastenings should be easily secured by the wearer, sufficient to maintain their security
under stress and resistant to damage by heat or flame contact. Seams should be
waterproof and any pockets should have drainage holes in the lower corners.
(4) The entire suit should be capable of being cleaned without reducing its protective
qualities. Maintenance and minor repairs should be within local capabilities and not
require the return of suits to a manufacturer or distributor.
(e) Boots.

(1) Uppers should be of a tough, flexible, heat-resistant material and extend to the mid-calf
or knee level. Soles should be of a non-slip material, which may include synthetic
materials, resistant to heat, oil, aircraft fuels or acids. Toe caps and soles may be
reinforced with steel. The use of rubber boots in this application is not recommended.
(f) Gloves.
(1) These should be of the gauntlet type to provide wrist protection and their construction
should permit the wearer to operate switches, fastenings and hand tools. The nature of
firefighting operations indicates that the back of the glove should have a reflective
surface to minimize radiated heat effects and that the palm and fingers should be
provided in a material resistant to abrasion and penetration by sharp objects. All seams
should be resistant to penetration by liquids.
(g) Flash hoods.
(1) Intended use for firefighting operations and associated activities such as rescue work,
assistance during disasters. Flash hood is designed to be worn next to the skin to give a
specified level of protection against accidental contact with flame. The flash hood is for
use as secondary protection against heat and flame and should be worn with another
protective head gear.
(h) Protection requirements. As a general guide, the protective clothing, when correctly worn,
should offer at least the same level of protection as a structural firefighting suit. The exact
level of protection should be decided with regard to operational considerations and risk
assessment. Guidance relative to firefighting suits is available, as some examples, in the
following standards:
(1) ISO 11613: Protective clothing for firefighters — Laboratory test methods and
performance requirements;
(2) EN 469: Protective clothing for firefighters — Requirements and test methods for
protective clothing for firefighting;
(3) NFPA 1971 Standard on protective clothing for structural firefighting; and
(4) ISO 15538:2001 Protective clothing for firefighters — Laboratory test methods and
performance requirements for protective clothing with a reflective outer surface.
(5) For personal protective equipment for personnel performing water rescue operations
refer to NFPA 1952, Standard on Surface Water Operations Protective Clothing and
Equipment.
(i) Sufficient facilities for the cleaning, maintenance and storage of protective clothing should be
provided at a fire station. These facilities should be well-ventilated and sheltered from direct

sunlight. Some form of climate control environment is preferred. Cleaning and maintenance of
protective clothing should adhere to suit manufacturer or supplier recommendations. See
guidance at GM AMC5 ACM.OP.D.010(d) Fire station and facilities. ISO 23616 provides
detailed guidance on cleaning, inspection and repair of firefighters' personal protective
equipment (PPE).
(j) The health and safety of all personnel working at operational incident and during training are
critical to the success in achieving the operational objectives. Strict policies and procedures on
the safe use and operations of protective clothing should be established and implemented,
including decontamination protocols, inspection and replacement programmes. Whenever
there is a sign of deterioration and its protective performance is in doubt i.e after an incident
or during an investigation, protective clothing should be immediately withdrawn from
operations and its continued safe use is risk assessed.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPIRATORY EQUIPMENT (BREATHING APPARATUS) — GENERAL REQUIREMENTS
(a) Rescue and firefighting personnel entering any environment in which fire is present during an
aircraft incident, as well as during overhaul operations, should be protected with self-
contained respiratory equipment. This applies equally to aircraft that comprise aluminium and
composite fibre materials.
(b) The cabin interior of modern passenger aircraft comprises synthetic materials which, during
fire or charring, will produce dangerous toxic gases. Such gases include carbon monoxide,
hydrogen chloride, chlorine, hydrogen cyanide and carbonyl chloride (phosgene). Firefighters

required to enter a smoke-filled cabin or other toxic environment will need self-contained
respiratory equipment of an accepted design for the anticipated environment.
(c) Increasingly, composite fibre material is being used in the construction of modern aircraft and
in particular replacing the external aluminium skin. Composite fibre, if involved in fire, can
produce dangerous substances such as hydrogen cyanide, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen
sulphide, hydrogen fluoride, acrolein and nitrogen dioxide. RFF personnel required to operate
inside high risk and toxic environments will need self-contained breathing apparatus of an
accepted design (see Table 42 on international standards on personal protective clothing and
respiratory equipment and Figure-26 for example of a self-contained breathing apparatus
unit).
(d) Composite fibre, if involved in high impact, such as an aircraft crash landing without the
presence of fire, may become damaged to the extent minute particles of composite fibres are
released into the atmosphere. Firefighters required to enter an area where minute particles of
composite fibre are present will need self-contained breathing apparatus or, as a minimum,
full face respirators with the appropriate filtration filters.
(e) It is essential to ensure that the respiratory equipment selected is sufficient in terms of its
basic function, and its operational duration for the tasks involved. Industrial smoke masks and
certain types of limited capacity compressed air equipment are unlikely to meet the stringent
requirements of these operations.
(f) It is essential to develop and maintain a high level of competence in those firefighters
appointed to wear respiratory equipment. This competence should include the most stringent
procedures for the inspection, testing and maintenance of the equipment. If the highest
standards are not achieved and maintained by regular training, the equipment can become
ineffective and present a serious hazard to the wearer.
(g) Wherever self-contained respiratory equipment is operated, sufficient arrangements should
be made for the recharging of air cylinders with pure air and a quantity of spare parts should
be hand-held to ensure the continuous availability of the service.
