title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPIRATORY EQUIPMENT (BREATHING APPARATUS) — OPERATIONAL GUIDANCE
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) Breathing apparatus (BA) enables firefighters to breathe safely in otherwise irrespirable
atmospheres. Using BA is one of the control measures likely to be employed as part of the
overall incident plan for any incident involving fire and hazardous materials.
(b) This guidance document defines how breathing apparatus procedures should be used at
operational incidents. BA command and control procedures provide a clear framework for
operational activities to function effectively, structured around the incident command system.
The procedures will allow efficient, effective and safe working practices to be adopted and can
be adapted to all sizes and types of incidents that require the use of BA.
(c) This guidance document is adopted from the UK National Operational Guidance Programme –
Foundation of Breathing Apparatus. Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services may refer to
the following website for updates to the document - https://nfcc.org.uk/
2. SCOPE

(a) This document describes in detail the principles underpinning the planning, use and command
and control of BA. It also describes the responsibilities of relevant personnel when BA is
implemented as a control measure. The tactical guidance in this document will assist
aerodrome rescue and firefighting services with:
(1) Developing safe work procedures
(2) Managing BA operations
(3) Defining specific roles and responsibilities in relation to BA
(4) Intra-operability at large or cross-border incidents where more than one Aerodrome
rescue and firefighting services is in attendance
(5) Interoperability at incidents where other emergency responders are in attendance
3. OPERATONAL PRE-PLANNING
(a) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services are required to identify risks and collect
information indicating where there may be hazards to personnel. This may include
information gained under aerodrome rescue and firefighting service legislation, industrial on-
site plans and risk-based geographical information. Information collected may be used for
developing plans and for briefing BA wearers.
(b) Information gathered during pre-planning should identify locations that may require
additional control measures and therefore enhanced operational resources, such as
guidelines, extended duration BA, airline equipment or thermal imaging cameras. The
strategic siting and arrangements for mobilising suitable resources to implement these
additional control measures should also be identified during this process.
(c) To ensure the safety and effectiveness of communications with BA teams, local planning
arrangements should identify where there may be limited penetration of radio signals into
buildings and into structures below ground. Steps may be taken at this preplanning stage to
enhance the effectiveness of radio communications and telemetry within structures.
4. BREATHING APPARATUS PROCEDURES
Pre-incident Procedures
(a) All personnel have responsibilities for the organisation, planning and implementation of
breathing apparatus procedures before, during and following incidents. Arrangements should
be in place to ensure that on deployment, BA wearers are sufficiently prepared and equipped
to carry out the tasks they are given.
(b) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services should:

(1) Ensure that personnel required to wear BA are fit (as set out in local procedures) to
carry out that role
(2) Ensure that personnel required to wear BA are suitably trained and practised in the
procedures detailed in this document
(3) Ensure that suitable and sufficient testing, maintenance and servicing arrangements are
in place for BA equipment, including associated ancillary equipment
(4) Provide the means to log and record BA set and associated equipment test results
Role and Responsibilities of the Nominated ARFFS Personnel
(a) The BA supervisor/manager will:
(1) Ensure that the appropriate tests of BA and associated equipment are carried out and
that test records are accurately maintained
(2) Ensure that defective equipment is removed and reported as defective and that
replacement equipment is obtained as soon as possible
(3) Ensure that BA and associated equipment is maintained in a clean, safe and serviceable
condition and is available for operational use
(4) Nominate suitably qualified and competent individuals to wear BA
(5) Nominate a suitably qualified and competent individual to assume the duties of BA
entry control operative
(6) Nominate any other role required for the management of BA operations
(b) The nominated BA entry control operative will:
(1) Examine and test the BA entry control board to ensure serviceability Examine the BA
tabard(s)
(2) Ensure the availability of BA ancillary equipment
(3) Ensure the availability and operation of emergency air supply equipment (if provided)
Check and, where practicable, adjust the BA entry control board clock to the correct
time Report any defects or omissions to the supervisory manager
(c) The nominated BA wearer will:
(1) Ensure that before using BA, the apparatus is checked to ensure it is functioning
correctly by carrying out the tests prescribed by the aerodrome rescue and firefighting
service in accordance with manufacturers’ instructions. A BA set that fails a test must
not be worn until the reason for the failure is rectified.
(2) As soon as practicable after completing the appropriate tests, record the outcome in
accordance with aerodrome rescue and firefighting service procedures

(3) Ensure that their competencies for their BA role and associated tasks are maintained
Report any defects or omissions to the supervisory manager
(4) Be aware of all nominated BA command and control roles and personnel, including the
BA team leader, the person responsible for the BA ECP and the BA entry control
operative Achieve and maintain a satisfactory face-fit seal before deployment.
Deployment of Breathing Apparatus Wearers
(a) The BA Incident Commander (BIC) will only deploy breathing apparatus after identifying the
operational outcomes and objectives to be achieved. They must make a suitable and sufficient
assessment of the risks involved using all the information and local intelligence available,
including:
(1) Risk assessments
(2) Site-Specific Risk Information (SSRI)
(3) Local aerodrome rescue and firefighting services standard operational procedures
(4) Other local or circumstantial information
(b) BIC should give consideration to:
(1) Immediate dangerous to life and health (IDLH) conditions
(2) Prevention of significant escalation of an incident
(3) Size and complexity of the incident, and specifically the requirement for BA operations
(4) Long-term operational objectives and short-term specific or critical tasks to be achieved
Resources immediately available at the incident
(5) The full extent of resources required to fully execute the overall incident plan
(6) Estimated time of arrival of necessary additional resources
(7) Hazards and risks associated with the incident
(8) Structural integrity of the aircraft, building or risk area
(9) Location of suitable points of entry
(10) Safety and welfare of BA wearers
(11) Means of escape for BA wearers
Requirement for appropriate BA emergency arrangements
(a) The appropriate level of BA command and control procedures and safe work procedures
outlined in this document should be used at all incidents where BA is deployed. Incident
command system principles and practices should be adhered to at all times.
(b) BA will only be used on the instruction of, or with the authority of, the incident commander.
Only the incident, operations or sector commander may nominate BA entry control

operatives. During an incident, the incident commander may delegate authority to deploy BA
wearers to operations or sector commanders. However, operational personnel have the right
to request BA for respiratory protection, such as when a sudden change of wind direction
affects a pump operator and the crew’s safety would be compromised by leaving the pump
unattended. In such instances, the firefighter should inform the incident commander and BA
entry control operative, who should initiate the appropriate BA entry control procedures
whilst the firefighter dons BA. Such requests should be considered as part of the normal risk
management process.
(c) Procedures for briefing and debriefing BA wearers and teams are critical to establish safe work
procedures and maintain firefighter safety. Full and effective briefing and debriefing of BA
teams should therefore take place every time BA is deployed.
(d) Suitable, sufficient and resilient means of communication methods should be established at all
times to ensure the effectiveness and safety of BA wearers. Communications between the BA
entry control points, BA wearers and, where established, command support are essential.
(e) Suitable and sufficient firefighting equipment must be provided whenever BA teams are
committed to a risk area involving fire or a flammable atmosphere.
Breathing Apparatus Operational Procedures at All Incidents
(a) Breathing apparatus must be worn at incidents to provide respiratory protection for
firefighters working in oxygen-deficient, toxic and hazardous atmospheres.
(b) The level of supervision required should be subject to the situation and circumstances of any
incident. It should take the size and complexity of BA operations at the incident into
consideration, along with the hazards and risks presented to BA wearers.
(c) The guidance in this section should be followed on every occasion that BA is worn at an
operational incident. Additional guidance relating to individual activities is described in later
sections of this document.
(d) BA shall be donned and doffed in ‘safe air’ only. BA teams will consist of no less than two BA
wearers. One BA team member should be a competent firefighter and all BA wearers must be
trained in the use of BA.
(e) The exception to the above is where a single BA wearer is deployed in a low-risk situation (as
described in this document) and supported by the local standard operational procedures and
training of the individual aerodrome rescue and firefighting service.
(f) The BA team should normally remain as a team for the entire time they are deployed.
However, in exceptional circumstances and following a suitable and sufficient risk assessment,

the BA team leader may decide to split a team of four into two teams of two for a specific
task, such as the rescue of multiple casualties. This decision should take account of the:
(1) Requirement for each team to be equipped with firefighting media to ensure personal
protection where there is, or is likely to be, a fire or flammable atmosphere
(2) Provision of sufficient communications equipment
(3) Remaining cylinder contents of team members
(4) Physiological nature of the tasks being undertaken
(5) Ability, based on the competence of BA wearers, to appoint a team leader for each
team (see minimum BA team competencies)
(6) Any alteration to the size of the BA team(s), the initial briefing or the name(s) of the
team leaders should be relayed immediately to the person responsible for the BA entry
control point.
Role and Responsibilities of ARFFS Personnel when Managing the Use of Breathing Apparatus
(a) The incident commander shall be responsible for:
(1) Determining, on the basis of a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, whether BA is
required to deal with the incident.
(2) Ensuring that resources are sufficient to deal with the size and complexity of BA
operations
(3) Requesting suitable resource provision for additional BA teams, particularly where the
need for BA emergency resources is foreseeable.
(4) Determining, on the basis of a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, the appropriate
procedures and level of BA command and control
(5) Ensuring that all personnel are aware which BA entry control procedures are in use
(6) Communicating the level of BA entry control procedures to watchroom control
(7) Adopting any other appropriate safety precautions and personal protective equipment
for specific risks (e.g. chemical-protective clothing) required in conjunction with BA
(8) The siting and number of BA entry control points Implementing BA ECP support
arrangements
(9) Nominating and briefing, or specifically delegating the responsibility to a suitably
qualified person to nominate and brief, a person responsible for establishing each BA
ECP to manage and monitor the implementation of BA entry control procedures

(10) Communicating the location of all BA entry control points to the operations and/or
sector commanders, all BA entry control operatives, the BA sector commander and
command support
(11) Nominating and briefing safety officers on their specific role requirements, including BA
operations
(12) Establishing and communicating responsibilities for suitable and sufficient briefing and
debriefing of BA teams in accordance with the principles and procedures set out in this
document
(13) Ensuring that a structured and comprehensive handover takes place and all relevant
information is transferred and understood when personnel responsible for managing a
BA ECP are replaced
(14) Establishing suitable and sufficient systems and processes for logging and recording all
relevant BA command and control information
(15) Determining, applying and communicating the appropriate structural search procedures
where appropriate
(16) Assessing the need for, and authorising the use of, BA guidelines
(17) Determining the need for BA line communications
(18) Determining the need for and detailing the specific duties of the BA sector commander
Determining BA wearer welfare requirements and establishing suitable arrangements
where a BA sector commander has not been appointed
(19) Implementing the appropriate procedures in cases of BA wearer distress Ensuring
appropriate BA emergency arrangements
(20) Appropriate provision of relief BA teams at BA entry control points in a timely fashion
where a BA sector commander has not been appointed
(21) Ensuring that each BA team is equipped with the means to communicate with the
person responsible for the BA entry control point
(22) Arrangements for communicating with the people responsible for the BA entry control
points via the command structure
(23) Ensuring that a single level of BA entry control is applied to the whole incident
(b) The BA entry control operative (ECO) shall be responsible to:
(1) Monitor the time to activation of the low pressure warning device
(2) Set up and operate a BA entry control board or unit in a position nominated by the
incident commander
(3) Log on BA wearers who are to be committed to the risk area

(4) Monitor the displayed cylinder pressure of all telemetry radio units logged on to BA
entry control boards or units
(5) Ensure that appropriate action is taken if the cylinder contents of a BA wearer do not
correspond with the BA wearer’s time of whistle or low-pressure warning
(6) Initiate BA emergency procedures if appropriate
(7) Log off BA wearers leaving the risk area through the BA ECP from their BA entry control
boards/units
(c) The BA team leader shall be responsible to:
(1) Ensure that the team is fully briefed by the person responsible for the BA ECP before
deployment to the risk area
(2) Ensure appropriate firefighting equipment is provided and tested before entering the
risk area where there is, or is likely to be, a fire or flammable atmosphere
(3) Monitor working conditions, assess the potential physiological effects and the impact
this may have on working duration
(4) Continually assess the level of risk and determine when to withdraw, based on those
risk assessments
(5) Co-ordinate gauge checks and ensure that every BA wearer returns to the BA ECP
before their low-pressure warning device activates
(6) Test communications equipment with the BA entry control operative or BA
communications operative.
(7) Ensure that the required radio channel is selected and locked if possible
(8) Provide regular updates to the BA ECP operative on the progress of the team and any
other information relevant to the incident commander, such as conditions, layout and
hazards
(9) Determine when a team of four may be split into two teams of two
(10) The BA team leader is responsible for the conduct of the team in the risk area. The team
leader should base decisions on:
(i) Nature of tasks being performed
(ii) Training and experience gained from previous incidents
(iii) Information received by communications from outside the risk area Sensory
perception inside the risk area (e.g. noise, temperature)
(iv) Information from BA and associated equipment (e.g. gauges, whistles, alerts,
thermal imaging cameras)
(v) Information from other team members

(d) The BA wearer shall be responsible for:
(1) Managing their own air at all times in accordance with their briefing Ensure that they
fully understand their brief, tasks and instructions, where and how they are required to
enter the risk area, any identified hazards and any limitations on the duration of wear
as determined by the person responsible for the BA entry control point
(2) On instruction from the person responsible for the BA entry control point, starting up
the BA set, completing required apparatus pre-entry checks and proceeding to the BA
ECP Ensure an adequate face-fit seal is established in “safe air”
(3) Handing the BA tally to the BA entry control operative before entering the risk area,
ensuring the tally is placed in the BA entry control board with the ‘time in’ completed
(4) Ensuring that appropriate personal protective equipment is worn correctly
(5) Testing all firefighting equipment before entering the risk area where there is, or is
likely to be, a fire or flammable atmosphere
(6) Checking cylinder contents immediately before entering the risk area.
(7) Calculating and selecting the required turn-around pressure in agreement with the
person responsible for the BA ECP and the BA team leader
(8) Carrying out safe movement and search and rescue techniques at all times, maintaining
close personal contact
(9) Performing safe and effective firefighting where there is, or is likely to be, a fire or
flammable atmosphere
(10) Monitoring the pressure gauge and prompt other members of the team to monitor
theirs when in the risk area
(11) Monitoring air consumption closely to enable safe withdrawal to the BA ECP before the
low-pressure warning device activates
(12) Carrying out gauge checks more frequently when working hard
(13) Maintaining contact and regular verbal communication with the BA team leader and
other members of the BA team. Updating them on any relevant information, including
hazards and landmarks
(14) Working as part of a team, sharing workloads to maximise working duration Memorise
the route in and out of the risk area
(15) Transmitting and receiving radio messages to the BA ECP if required to do so by the BA
team leader
(16) Constantly monitoring conditions and re-evaluate risk, and inform the team leader of
the need to withdraw, if required

(17) Informing the BA team leader of the pressure at which the BA team will need to start
exiting the risk area
(18) Immediately reporting to BA ECP on exiting the risk area. Collect the BA tally from the
BA entry control operative
(19) Assisting the team leader with debriefing as required, ensuring that any information
that may be of use to subsequent teams entering the risk area, or to the incident
commander, is communicated to the person responsible for the BA entry control point
(20) If applicable, drawing a basic plan (or use available plans) to identify the route, hazards
and location of any casualties. Clearly marking areas that have been searched to assist
subsequent BA teams
(21) After wearing a BA:
(i) Ensure they, and other team members, are not suffering any effects of heat
related conditions Relax personal protective clothing following a suitable and
sufficient risk assessment
(ii) Cool down and hydrate
(iii) Rest and recuperate
(iv) Report any accidents, injuries or near-miss events in accordance with local
aerodrome rescue and firefighting service policies and procedures
(v) As soon as possible after wearing BA, clean and wash hands to reduce the risk of
contamination from the risk area. avoid contact of BA or personal protective
equipment with the skin and mouth
(vi) Ensure that apparatus is thoroughly cleaned, fitted with a fresh cylinder and
tested as required. Any defects found during routine testing or during use must
be reported according to aerodrome rescue and firefighting service procedures.
Breathing Apparatus Entry Control Procedures
(a) BA entry control procedures are designed to provide a consistent method for the safe and
effective command and control and management of BA operations and to ensure the safety of
firefighters.
(b) BA entry control must be fully aligned with incident command system principles and practices.
BA entry control procedures and provisions should be proportionate to the scale and
complexity of the BA operations at an incident, the overall incident plan and any known or
reasonably foreseeable hazards and risks to BA wearers.

(c) The BA ECP is the designated position at which BA deployment and command and control is
managed and forms an integral part of the incident command structure.
(d) Disciplined adherence to BA entry control procedures, briefings and instructions is critical to
the safety and effectiveness of BA operations and BA teams.
(e) The BA entry control procedure adopted will be consistent throughout the entire incident and
will not vary for different BA entry control points.
(f) All relevant emergency responders should be made aware of the BA entry control procedures,
and any additional procedures, in use at the incident, particularly those in a position of
command.
(g) The level of BA entry control in use should be communicated to fire control rooms to enable
monitoring officers to gather relevant information.
(h) Suitable and sufficient systems and processes for logging and recording all relevant BA
command and control information should be established prior to deploying BA wearers.
Additional operational procedures and relevant command decisions should be recorded in an
incident log as soon as practicable.
(i) Establishing and maintaining effective communications between the BA ECP and the BA team
is essential, as is exchanging timely and regular information throughout the command team.
(j) Personnel qualified by virtue of a suitable and sufficient local aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service development process can carry out the role of BA entry control operative,
although overall responsibility for BA entry control rests with the incident commander.
(k) BA entry control operatives must be nominated for each BA entry control board. The BA entry
control operative will undertake specific tasks in relation to BA entry control only (BA entry
control operative role and responsibilities), under the command and direction of the person
responsible for the BA entry control point.
(l) The allocated tasks of BA wearers should be confirmed, communicated and recorded before
deployment. BA wearers deployed into risk areas should be informed of their tasks, such as
firefighting, search and rescue, guideline laying or other specific tasks. Following a suitable
and sufficient assessment of risk, tasks may be combined, for example, firefighting and search
and rescue.
Designation and Siting of BA entry control points (ECP)
(a) ECP should be established in a safe position, in safe air, near the scene of operations.
(b) The working platform of an aerial appliance should not be used as a site for an ECP.

(c) ECPs should be designated and identified at the incident by means of suitable referencing
using the phonetic alphabet. The first BA ECP established at the incident will be designated
‘Alpha’, the second ‘Bravo’, and so on.
(d) BA teams deployed from the ECP will be identified by a sequential numbering system. For
example, at BA ECP Alpha, the first BA team will be designated ‘BA team Alpha 1’, the second
team ‘BA team Alpha 2’, and so on.
Bridgehead or Forward Entry Control Point (FECP)
(a) This arrangement allows an incident to be dealt with by deploying BA wearers from a safe-air
environment within a structure while being as close as practical to the scene of operations.
This may be considered necessary by an incident commander where there is a need to
establish a BA ECP at a distance from the first point of access to a building or risk area, such as
in high-rise building or large, complex structure.
(b) The location of the BA ECP in these circumstances will be determined by the incident
commander based on the incident plan and the outcome of a risk assessment.
(c) Some of the factors that should be taken into account when determining the location of a
bridgehead or forward BA ECP are:
(1) The potential for an escalation of the incident
(2) The safe-air environment necessary to start up BA
(3) The best access to and egress from the scene of operations Crew safety and welfare
(4) Effective communications with BA wearers
(5) Effective communications with the incident commander
(6) The level of supervision and support necessary for the BA entry control operative The
distance from the initial point of access to the BA entry control point
Stage 1 Breathing Apparatus Entry Control
(a) Stage 1 BA entry control procedures are used to monitor the safety of BA wearers at incidents
where the numbers of BA wearers is small and BA operations are limited and not complex.
(b) Stage I BA entry control procedures apply where:
(1) The nature of BA operations is limited and not complex
(2) The incident requires no more than one BA entry control point
(3) The incident requires no more than six BA wearers to be deployed to the risk area at
any one time
(4) BA guidelines are not required

(c) The BA team must receive and confirm their understanding of a clear briefing and instructions.
The briefing should include, for example, the task to be achieved, information regarding
hazards, risks and control measures, methods of communication and emergency
arrangements. Under Stage 1 BA entry control, the incident commander should ensure
suitable and sufficient emergency arrangements.
Stage 2 Breathing Apparatus Entry Control
(a) Stage 2 BA entry control procedures apply when a greater level of control is required to
manage and monitor the safety of BA wearers in complex BA operations, or where the criteria
for Stage 1 have been exceeded.
(b) Stage 2 BA entry control procedures apply where:
(1) The nature of BA operations are complex and require a greater degree of control and
supervision
(2) The incident requires more than one BA entry control point
(3) The incident requires more than six wearers to be deployed to the risk area at any one-
time BA guidelines are required
(c) Under Stage 2 BA entry control, the incident commander and BA entry control operatives
should ensure suitable and sufficient emergency arrangements are established at all BA entry
control points. See Emergency arrangements.
(d) Each ECP should establish and maintain communications with all other BA entry control points
at the incident.
(e) The initial BA entry control operative should, where possible, remain in place when moving
from BA Stage 1 to Stage 2. A nominated person with the appropriate level of managerial
authority, training and experience should supervise the BA entry control operative.
(f) When an existing BA entry control operative at a BA entry control board is replaced, this
should be done at a time when no BA wearers are committed through that particular board. A
structured exchange of information should take place between BA entry control operatives
under the strict supervision of the person responsible for the BA entry control point.
(g) The incident commander should determine the need for additional resources to manage the
BA entry control points and associated functions.
Breathing Apparatus Entry Control Point Supervision
(a) The incident or sector commander should consider the need to implement an appropriate
level of supervision as the risks and demands of the incident increase. It may therefore be
necessary to appoint a manager to provide additional BA ECP supervision. This manager will

be known as the BA ECP Supervisor and should have the appropriate level of managerial
authority, training and experience to ensure that they can effectively manage the required
resources dictated by the incident plan.
(b) The BA ECP supervisor provides a greater degree of control and co-ordination between
incident command, incident sectors, additional BA entry control points and other agencies
where necessary (including neighbouring fire and rescue services). In practice, the BA ECP
supervisor will perform co-ordination and logistical tasks associated with BA ECP operations.
This will enable the BA entry control operative to focus on the monitoring of BA wearers
deployed within the risk area.
(c) The BA ECP supervisor shall be responsible to:
(1) Receive a detailed brief and implement the incident, operations or sector commander’s
incident plan for breathing apparatus operations
(2) Brief and debrief all BA wearers
(3) Regularly update the incident, operations or sector commander on BA operations
undertaken from the BA entry control point
(4) Ensure that a co-ordinated search is carried out in liaison with the search co-ordinator
and that a record is kept of areas that have been searched or require searching
(5) Ensure that sufficient, fully equipped BA emergency teams are rigged and standing by at
the BA entry control point
(6) Determine the time and/or cylinder pressure at which a BA team is expected to return
to the BA entry control point
(7) Supervise BA communications for the BA entry control point
Breathing Apparatus Sector
(a) The purpose of establishing a breathing apparatus sector is to provide additional support for
co- ordinating BA resources and logistics, particularly where the incident is large or complex or
where there is more than one Stage 2 BA entry control point.
(b) The BA sector commander should have the appropriate level of managerial authority, training
and experience to ensure that they can effectively manage the logistical requirements of a BA
sector. The full extent of their role will depend on the complexity of the incident and the
number of BA wearers deployed. Where necessary, the BA sector commander may be
supported by assistants.
(c) The location of the BA sector should be communicated to all relevant emergency responders.

(d) Where a BA sector is in place, BA entry control operatives should establish and maintain
effective communications with the BA sector commander and report all relevant information,
including information from BA team briefings and debriefings, and submit requests for
resources and support in a timely manner.
(e) The BA sector commander will:
(1) Be appointed by, and report to, the incident commander
(2) Be clearly identified by suitable wording on their sector commander tabard
(3) Provide BA emergency team resource requirements to BA entry control points
(4) Be responsible for BA resources and logistics
(5) Be responsible for BA wearers’ welfare, and establish appropriate rest and recuperation
areas
(6) Operate within the command support structure and work alongside and closely with
other command support colleagues
(7) Establish and maintain communications with all BA entry control points
(8) Identify the location of each BA ECP and record the name of each BA entry control
operative
(9) Establish and record the availability of BA, associated equipment and personnel at the
incident
(10) Take account of any time variations between BA entry control board clocks
(11) Establish and record the requirements for relief teams of BA wearers
(12) Ensure that there are sufficient BA wearers to comprise the relief teams required by
each BA entry control point, and ensure they arrive at the BA ECP at least five minutes
before required
(13) Maintain suitable and sufficient records
Rapid/Initial Deployment Breathing Apparatus Procedures
(a) Suitable and sufficient pre-planning, including task and resource analysis, will assist incident
commanders in deploying the appropriate resources required to provide safe work
procedures applicable to an incident that may require breathing apparatus. In circumstances
where immediately available resources are unable to deliver the full incident plan but where
there is an opportunity to preserve life or take action that will prevent an incident
deteriorating, rapid/initial deployment of BA may be used under strict criteria.

(b) Rapid/initial deployment will only be undertaken on the instructions of the incident
commander following a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks versus the likely
benefits.
(c) Under rapid/initial deployment protocols, no more than two BA wearers will be in the risk
area.
(d) The incident commander may personally adopt the role of monitoring BA wearers following a
suitable and sufficient risk assessment.
(e) As soon as resources become available, Stage 1 BA entry control procedures must be
implemented as a minimum level of control.
(f) In addition to duties outlined in BA Operational Procedures – all incidents, the following
responsibilities apply:
(1) The incident commander will:
(i) Initiate the use of rapid/initial deployment BA procedures following a suitable
and sufficient assessment of the risks versus the likely benefits.
(ii) Inform watchroom control that rapid/initial deployment procedures are in use
(iii) Request further resources to establish the appropriate level of BA entry control
(iv) Ensure arrangements for communication between BA wearers, the person
monitoring BA wearers and the incident commander
(v) Implement appropriate BA entry control procedures as soon as resources allow
(2) The monitoring crew member will:
(i) Establish and maintain communications with BA wearers and the incident
commander
(ii) Record ‘time in’ on the BA entry control board
(iii) Ensure that BA tallies with suitable and sufficient details are placed in the BA
entry control board, automated rapid/initial deployment board, or telemetry is
established
(iv) Undertake other essential duties as required
(v) Provide a handover to any subsequent BA entry control operative
(3) BA wearers will:
(i) Ensure that all BA tallies and gauges are checked and that tallies are placed in the
BA entry control board, with ‘time in’ recorded by themselves or through an
automated board.

Single Breathing Apparatus Wearer Procedures
(a) In certain circumstances, it may be appropriate to deploy a single breathing apparatus wearer
to carry out a specific task. Stage 1 BA entry control procedures apply when deploying a single
BA wearer.
(b) The use of single BA wearers is only permissible when:
(1) Operations are not inside an aircraft, building or structure
(2) Limited to perform low-risk activities only
(3) The BA wearer’s gauge has been checked and their cylinder contents recorded
(4) The wearer’s BA tally has been placed in a BA entry control board with suitable and
sufficient details entered
(5) The BA wearer can be removed quickly from the risk area
(6) The BA wearer can always be seen by the incident commander or other nominated
crew member
(c) The incident commander will:
(1) Initiate the use of Stage 1 single deployment BA procedures following a suitable and
sufficient assessment of risks versus likely benefits
(2) Inform the watch/control room that Stage 1 single deployment procedures are in use
(3) Establish arrangements for communication between the BA wearer, the person
monitoring BA wearer and the incident commander
(d) The BA entry control operative will:
(1) Receive the tally of the BA wearer and check that the name of the wearer and the
cylinder pressure at the time they enter the risk area are correct
(2) Enter the ‘time in’ on the tally
(3) Record BA wearer’s entry and monitor the estimated air supply
(4) Place the tally in a slot on the BA entry control board
(e) The monitoring crew member will:
(1) Maintain visual contact with the BA wearer
(2) Monitor the activities and working environment of the BA wearer
(3) Establish and maintain communications with the BA wearer and incident commander
(f) The BA wearer will:
(1) Not enter any aircraft, building or structure
(2) Remain in view of the monitoring crew member
(3) Maintain communication with the monitoring crew member

Re-entry into a Risk Area Procedure
(a) It may sometimes be necessary for breathing apparatus teams to re-enter a risk area to
perform a specific task after they have withdrawn, reported to the BA ECP and closed down
their sets. Re-entry will only take place for a limited and defined period to achieve a specific
task or tasks within the physiological and psychological capabilities of the BA wearer.
(b) Re-entry can only be allowed where the incident commander is satisfied that:
(1) The BA team is still under the control and supervision of the BA entry control operative
(2) The re-entry is for a clearly defined, specific task which should not involve firefighting
(other than to ensure personal protection of the BA wearers)
(3) The cylinder contents of all BA wearers are sufficient for the task (this does not involve
fitting a fresh cylinder, which would constitute a new entry)
(4) The pressure gauges of all BA wearers register a pressure that provides a minimum of
15 minutes’ working duration
(5) The fitness and well-being of the BA wearers is adequate for the task to be undertaken
(6) The BA entry control operative must record fresh details for all the BA team members
involved in a re- entry procedure. This should include annotating the BA entry control
board appropriately with the words ‘re-entry’ or RE.
(7) Re-entry should not take place for team members wearing extended duration BA owing
to the additional weight of the extended duration BA set, the longer durations required
and the additional physiological burdens involved.
(c) The incident commander will:
(1) Determine the requirement for the identified specific task Confirm that the identified
task is for a limited duration
(2) Determine, following a suitable and sufficient assessment of risk, whether any specific
task is within the physiological and psychological capabilities of BA wearers
(d) The BA entry control operative will:
(1) Where a BA team re-enters a risk area, ensure that the cylinder contents of all BA
wearers are sufficient for the specific task; in all cases, the cylinder should be at a
pressure that provide a minimum of 15 minutes’ working duration
(2) Record fresh details for all BA team members
(e) The BA wearer will:
(1) Confirm their fitness to carry out the identified task
(2) Receive and confirm their understanding of a briefing before deployment

Breathing Apparatus used in conjunction with Aerial Access Vehicles/Platforms and Ladders
(a) Where the incident commander deems it necessary for aerial access platform cage operators
and personnel working on ladders to wear breathing apparatus, the appropriate BA entry
control procedure must apply.
(b) When a single BA wearer is operating from a working platform or head of a ladder, they must
remain in communication with the appliance operator or person footing the ladder and not
leave the head of the ladder or cage to enter any building or risk area.
(c) Where a BA team uses a ladder or cage as a means of access to a building or structure, a BA
entry control point should be established at ground level in a safe area.
Search and Rescue within Aircraft and Structures
(a) A primary function of aerodrome rescue and firefighting service is to save life and it may be
necessary for personnel to search aircraft, buildings or structures using breathing apparatus as
an essential control measure. A logical and methodical search procedure, including a
retraceable route for safe egress, is essential for BA wearers progressing through buildings or
structures with restricted visibility.
(b) The incident commander must establish full awareness of the working environment, including
fire conditions, fire development, levels of visibility and nature of hazardous materials, to
ensure that the most appropriate search plan is implemented. Wherever possible, the
incident commander should obtain risk information, including aircraft, building and structural
plans, which will enable operational planning for using BA at the incident.
(c) BA wearers observing the search criteria and the nature and parameters of the operational
brief in a disciplined way is critical to the safety and effectiveness of search and rescue
operations.
(d) Search and rescue procedures involving the use of BA should be planned following a suitable
and sufficient assessment of risk. At larger and more complex incidents, the incident
commander may determine a need for a strategic overview of the various search and rescue
activities in each sector and at each BA entry control point. They may then appoint a
dedicated search co-ordinator who will establish manageable spans of control, identify areas
to be searched and produce suitable search plans.
(e) The BA entry control operative should maintain plans and search records at the BA entry
control point. These and all other information relating to the operation should be duplicated
at command support.

(f) BA teams should ensure that details of areas searched are communicated to the BA entry
control operative, who will communicate with the incident, operations or sector commander.
A comprehensive search and rescue record can then be established at command support,
which will preclude duplication of search and rescue activity. The quality and effectiveness of
the BA team’s debriefing processes are therefore critical to the safety and effectiveness of the
overall search plan.
(g) Tactical ventilation should be considered when carrying out procedures for the search and
rescue of casualties as it may significantly improve conditions for casualties and BA wearers.
However, tactical ventilation must only be carried out following a suitable and sufficient risk
assessment and on direct instruction from the incident commander or delegated commander.
(h) The incident commander must provide clear, unambiguous briefings and instructions to BA
wearers. This will include the route to be used by BA team(s) when progressing through the
building or structure and the search and rescue method or procedures to be employed.
Disciplined and systematic observance of the search brief by BA wearers is essential. They
must assume responsibility for confirming their understanding of the briefing and instructions
and, once deployed, follow their instructions without variation, except in extreme
circumstances involving life-threatening situations.
(i) A BA team will work together, remain as a team at all times and maintain close personal
contact unless a larger team decides to split.
(j) In larger compartments, multiple BA teams may be committed in a co-ordinated way to
ensure that the entire compartment is searched and BA team safety is maintained.
(k) BA search teams operating within a structure where there is, or is likely to be, a fire or
flammable atmosphere must be equipped with suitable and sufficient firefighting media. The
means by which firefighting provision is deployed may be either:
(l) Carried by each BA team deployed within the risk area
(m) Carried by a specifically nominated firefighting BA team who maintain close personal contact
with the BA search team at all times
(n) The incident commander should ensure sufficient personnel are deployed to ensure that BA
teams do not have to separate to manage hose lines while operating inside an aircraft or
structure.
(o) When negotiating specific obstacles such as doors, chairs, stairs, walls and vertical ladders, BA
team members may separate briefly but should only be separated by the distance created by
the obstacle. It is imperative to maintain line of sight, close contact and/or verbal
communication at all times.

(p) The BA wearer will:
(1) Confirm the search procedure to be followed
(2) Maintain regular gauge checks
(3) Remain in close personal contact with other members of the team
(4) Maintain personal protection techniques
(5) Maintain communication with the BA team leader
Briefing and Debriefing of Breathing Apparatus Team Procedures
(a) It is essential that every breathing apparatus team is fully briefed at the BA ECP by the
appropriate person.
(b) The brief should at least contain:
(1) The designated BA team call sign
(2) The nature and layout of the aircraft, building or structure to be searched
(3) The specific area to be searched
(4) The hazards and risks presented
(5) Existing control measures
(6) The search procedures to be employed and equipment to be used
(7) The level of BA command and control procedures in use
(8) The location and tasks of any other BA teams
(9) Any relevant air-management criteria Communications provisions
(10) BA emergency and contingency arrangements
(11) Debriefing requirements
(12) All other relevant information
(c) The brief for a BA search team may require them to start the search at the point of entry:
(1) At a location beyond the point of entry where there is the greatest danger for casualties
(2) Where the likely seat of a fire is located
(3) At some other designated point within the building or structure.
(d) The BA team must follow all appropriate safe work procedures, search and rescue procedures
and personal safety techniques in reaching the designated point for the start of the search
and during the search itself.
(e) Suitable plans of the structure, annotated with areas still to be searched and those already
searched, landmarks (orientation reference points) and hazards identified, should be
produced wherever possible. These plans can provide additional information that may be

used during briefing and debriefing BA wearers to enhance the safety and effectiveness of BA
search and rescue teams.
(f) On completion of any BA deployment, the team should be fully debriefed at the BA entry
control point by the nominated and appropriate person. The essential elements of the
debriefing should also be recorded.
Recording
(a) Key information should be recorded appropriately. A suitable and sufficient record of search
and rescue instructions and briefings to breathing apparatus teams, debrief intelligence and
any other relevant operational and planning information should be maintained at the BA entry
control point. This risk-critical information impacts directly on the effective command and
control of any incident involving BA and the tasks allocated to subsequent BA teams.
(b) Records should be maintained, not just for the duration of the incident but for subsequent
audit, training and investigation purposes. These provide a contemporaneous record of the
instructions given to BA teams and information gained at the debrief on completion.
Action on Locating Casualties
(a) Information on the size, number and location of casualties in a risk area must be confirmed if
possible. This will influence decisions on BA team size, suitable equipment and priorities. For
example, if there are a number of casualties or a particularly large person needs rescuing, it
may be necessary to deploy a larger BA search and rescue team with appropriate evacuation
equipment alongside firefighting teams providing protection.
Summoning Assistance
(a) Wherever possible, radio communications should be used to summon assistance. If radio
communications are not available, BA wearers may gain the attention of other team members
or BA teams by slow, loud and regular handclapping. These actions do not constitute a distress
signal.
Breathing Apparatus Guidelines
(a) The deployment of breathing apparatus guidelines should be determined on the basis of a
suitable and sufficient assessment of risk and in accordance with the incident plan. The
incident commander should also consider using alternative or simultaneous operational
tactics to assist in aerodrome rescue and firefighting service operations and enhance
firefighter safety. These may include adopting tactical ventilation techniques and/or additional
access points.

(b) Stage 2 BA entry control procedures and appropriate BA emergency arrangements must be
established before BA guideline operations can start.
(c) The term ‘guideline’ defines the special line which is used either as ‘a main guideline’ to
facilitate an initial search and to indicate a route between an entry control point and the
scene of operations, or, alternatively, as ‘a branch guideline’, where is it necessary to traverse
or search more than six metres off a main guideline. The method of use of the line for either
purpose is the same.
(d) The purpose of a BA guideline is to enable:
(1) BA teams to locate the scene of operations
(2) BA teams to enter and search large or complex buildings or structures
(3) Subsequent BA teams to locate other BA teams
(4) A BA team in a risk area to retrace their steps to the BA entry control point
(e) The use of BA guidelines can be divided into two operational practices:
(1) Laying guidelines
(2) Following or searching off guidelines
(f) The BA guideline laying team has sole responsibility for laying the guideline along an access or
egress route; they should not be drawn into other activities. A guideline laying team should
therefore be supported by a firefighting team where there is, or is likely to be, a fire or
flammable atmosphere.
(g) BA guideline laying and search teams should not enter a risk area where there is, or is likely to
be, a fire or flammable atmosphere, without appropriate firefighting media. This equipment
may be carried by the search team themselves, or preferably by support firefighting BA teams
working closely with them.
(h) The guideline laying team should not operate ahead of any firefighting BA team because the
firefighting BA team will adopt fire suppression techniques to render the environment safe. If
the firefighting BA teams have to withdraw, the BA guideline laying team should also
withdraw.
(i) Additional support BA teams should be deployed in conjunction with a guideline laying or
search and rescue BA team for actions such as:
(1) Fire fighting and gas cooling
(2) Hose management
(3) Thermal imaging camera use
(4) Protecting the BA guideline laying team’s means of escape
(5) Support for casualty retrieval

(j) A main guideline leading from a BA ECP should be designated A or B, using a tally. The
relevant tally must be attached securely to the line before the BA team enters the risk area.
The following information must be written on a BA tally before entering the risk area:
(1) Location name
(2) Set number permanently marked
(3) Cylinder contents in litres permanently marked
(4) Space for name
(5) Space for cylinder pressure
(6) Space for time in
(7) Duration and no fresh records are required
(8) The Tally is attached to the DSU
(9) Space for dosimeter reading in and out
(k) The BA guideline should be secured to an immovable object outside the risk area in safe air
before any BA team enters the risk area, unless the guideline is being used to extend an
existing main guideline.
(l) Sufficient information must be communicated to subsequent BA teams to ensure they follow
the correct guideline.
(m) To avoid confusion and maintain manageable lines of communication and spans of control, no
more than two guideline routes are permitted to be in use at any single BA entry control
point.
(n) Only one guideline may be laid along a search route. However, two guidelines may be laid
near to a building or structure’s entry point, either side of a route, before they split into
clearly defined search areas.
(o) Guidelines should not cross over each other inside a building or structure or share tie-off
points. If two guidelines converge, one of them should be terminated and secured to a tie-off
point two metres or more from where the guidelines would have met.
(p) A guideline may consist of a number of lines joined together. However, consideration must
always be given to how long BA wearers can work, the physiological environment, the
distance to be covered (particularly if rescues are necessary) and the potential for incident
escalation.
(q) Incident commanders should use building plans and/or external reconnaissance to assess the
internal distances BA wearers may be required to travel.

(r) Where a guideline is being extended, the BA team leader must inform the BA entry control
operative, who will then ensure a suitable and sufficient record is maintained and inform the
sector/operations/incident commander as appropriate.
Branch Guidelines
(a) Branch guidelines should be used where the distance of the area of search from the main
guideline is greater than the length of one personal line (6-metres). No more than four branch
guidelines can be deployed from a single BA entry control point.
(b) The branch guideline should be referenced according to its main guideline and the number of
the branch guideline; for example, main guideline A, branch guideline 1. Any branch guideline
tally must be secured to the line before the BA team enters the risk area.
(c) If a branch guideline needs to be extended, following a suitable and sufficient risk assessment
based on information from the BA team leader, a record of the extension will be made and
maintained.
(d) The incident (or nominated) commander will:
(1) Determine the use of BA guidelines on the basis of a suitable and sufficient assessment
of risk Consider the use of alternative or simultaneous operational tactics
(2) Ensure that Stage 2 BA entry control procedures are applied to the whole incident
Regularly review the use of BA guidelines
(3) Ensure use of additional BA support teams in conjunction with guideline laying teams
Inform all relevant personnel that guidelines are in use
(4) Implement appropriate BA emergency procedures as necessary.
(5) Inform watchroom control rooms that BA guidelines are in use
(e) The BA entry control operative will:
(1) Record, monitor and log guideline use, including identifying which guideline each team
is laying, following or searching from
(2) Attach BA main and branch guideline tallies to the appropriate lines
(3) Ensure that all deployed BA wearers are made aware of any guidelines laid behind
them.
 Compartment Firefighting Activities
(a) Appropriate firefighting procedures should be employed whenever breathing apparatus teams
are firefighting in compartments. Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services must provide
training in appropriate firefighting techniques and media to all BA wearers.

(b) Firefighting tactics must take into account the effects and proximity of BA wearers within the
risk area.
Air management
(a) Air management is essential to the safe and effective operation of breathing apparatus
operations. It begins when BA wearers go under air, i.e. after they have been briefed and have
confirmed receipt of instructions.
(b) It is essential that BA wearers return to the BA ECP either before the low pressure warning
device or whistle activates or by a pre-determined time of return specified in the briefing and
instructions. Following deployment, BA wearers are responsible for their own air
management.
(c) The BA team leader will:
(1) Ensure that every BA wearer returns to the BA ECP before their low pressure warning
device or whistle activates
(2) Inform the BA entry control operative immediately if they become aware that this
cannot be achieved
(d) The BA wearer will:
(1) Read their own gauge and make calculations
(2) Take responsibility for informing the BA team leader of the pressure at which they will
need to start exiting the risk area
(3) Make the BA team leader aware of their gauge readings on a regular basis, so that work
can be shared evenly in the team to maximise the remaining working duration
(4) Inform the BA team leader of any variation in their expected air consumption rate
(e) The rate of consumption of air of open circuit breathing apparatus can vary over a wide range.
(f) This range of variation depends upon a number of factors, which include the work rate of the
wearer, their physique and the environmental conditions in which they are working.
(g) To enable the duration of open circuit breathing apparatus to be estimated an average
consumption rate of 40 litres per minute can be used.
• FULL DURATION - The period during which the breathing apparatus is expected to provide
respiratory protection from the moment the cylinder valve is open until the cylinder contents
are exhausted.
• WORKING DURATION - The period during which the breathing apparatus is expected to
provide respiratory protection from the moment the cylinder valve is opened until the low-
pressure warning whistle sounds.

• SAFETY MARGIN - The period during which the low-pressure warning whistle operates.
• Formula for calculating the duration of breathing apparatus is as follow:
D = P X C – 10 / N X 40
Where D = The remaining working duration (in minutes)
P = The pressure in the cylinder (bars)
N = The maximum filled pressure of the cylinder (bars)
C = The capacity (in litres) of the cylinder when pressurised to N bars.
Airlines
(a) An airline supplies air to the wearer from a cylinder located remotely from the wearer.
(b) Specific operating procedures apply to the command, control and deployment of airline
equipment, which must only be used by properly trained and competent personnel.
Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services must ensure that their procedures align with this
document and any other technical procedures that are in place covering the operation of
airline equipment.
(c) Subject to aerodrome rescue and firefighting service risk assessments, it may be appropriate
for aerodrome rescue and firefighting services to use airline equipment as a safe means of
providing a breathing apparatus capability.
(d) An airline may be appropriate:
(1) Where extended air supply to self-contained breathing apparatus wearers is required
(2) Where the use of self-contained BA may not be suitable or is less effective
(e) These incidents include but are not limited to:
(1) Incidents in the open, where airlines are used to provide a breathable atmosphere
without the weight of a self-contained BA set
(2) Specialist operations that involve restricted access to the working area
(f) In accordance with the system of operating when wearing self-contained BA, airline teams will
comprise a minimum of two BA wearers.
(g) Each airline team will be equipped with suitable communications that will enable each team
to communicate with the airline BA entry control point.
(h) The use of airlines reduces the overall weight imposed on a BA wearer and can provide a
limitless supply of air. However, the physiological limitations of the wearer should be
considered whenever airline equipment is used.
(i) An airline is susceptible to mechanical damage that could compromise the air supply to the
wearer. Appropriate care and protective arrangements must be maintained.

(j) The incident commander should be aware of the location of all airline BA entry control points,
and while it is permissible for self-contained BA wearers to use the same BA entry control
point, a separate BA entry control board with a dedicated BA entry control operative must be
established and maintained.
(k) The location of the airline BA ECP should take into account the previous guidance regarding
BA entry control points. The incident commander will also take account of the:
(1) Length and amount of airline required
(2) Number of personnel required to operate it
(3) Distance to the scene of operations
(l) The incident commander will:
(1) Determine the requirement for the use of airline equipment
(2) Identify the location of airline BA entry control points
(m) The BA wearer will:
(1) Manage the laying and recovery of the airline to ensure effective progress at an incident
Working in Pressurised Atmospheres
(a) There are broadly two types of environments where pressurised atmospheres may be
encountered. These are referred to here as ‘elevated pressures’ and ‘commercial workings’
(b) The task of firefighting and rescuing people in pressurised workings is principally the
responsibility of the on-site contractor. The aerodrome rescue and firefighting service would
continue to respond to a call to pressurised workings and might stand by to give advice and
provide backup facilities if necessary. Where, subject to any prior agreement and
arrangement, it is reasonably foreseeable that a aerodrome rescue and firefighting service
may be requested to support a contractor’s emergency arrangements, the limitations of its
breathing apparatus and associated equipment must be taken into account.
Withdrawal of breathing apparatus wearers
(a) The decision on when to withdraw from a risk area is extremely important. The main aim is to
ensure that all breathing apparatus teams return to the BA ECP before the estimated
activation of their low-pressure warning devices.
(b) The incident commander and BA team leader’s duties include ensuring that BA wearers are
not exposed to an unacceptable level of risk. BA wearers are responsible for ensuring that BA
team leaders are made aware of any relevant developments that might require an early
withdrawal from the risk area.
(c) The timing of withdrawal from a risk area must take into account:

(1) The specific instructions of the incident commander
(2) The potential for physiological and psychological stress or distress as a result of
environmental conditions or workload, including high temperatures, humidity and
casualty rescue
(3) The physiological conditions or depth of penetration into the risk area, such as in
aircraft fuselage, tunnels, confined spaces, etc
(4) A deteriorating situation such as fire growth or signs of collapse.
(5) Any relocation of the BA entry control point
(d) BA team leaders should not rely solely on pressure readings when reaching a decision on
when to withdraw their team; they should take into account information received from all
sources. BA team leaders must withdraw their team if any member:
(1) Has an uncontrolled loss of pressure
(2) Appears to be unwell, confused or in discomfort, especially when exposed to rapid
temperature increase.
(3) Has a gauge that is faulty or unreadable
(4) Has been exposed to an irrespirable atmosphere due to BA failure
(5) Has a low-pressure warning device that is activating
(6) Reaches the pressure gauge reading pre-determined by the person responsible for the
BA entry control point
(7) Has insufficient time for decontamination procedures to be carried out before the low-
pressure warning device activates
(e) BA team leaders must also withdraw their team if:
(1) An emergency evacuation signal sound.
(2) There is a loss of firefighting media (where applicable)
(3) The BA team experiences a sustained and unexpected loss of communications
(4) Conditions in the risk area have deteriorated to the extent that BA team members are
exposed to an unacceptable level of risk (following a risk assessment or on the advice of
team members)
(f) The BA entry control operative should immediately be informed of any decision to withdraw
prematurely from a risk area. This decision should then be relayed to the incident, operations
or sector commander.
(g) BA teams should ensure that they have provision for firefighting or gas cooling where there is,
or is likely to be, a fire or flammable atmosphere, as they make their way out of the risk area.
Firefighting media may only be left in areas unaffected by fire or fire gases within a structure.

However, BA teams may decide to leave other equipment in the hazard area to reduce the
workload when withdrawing as long as this does not compromise the safety of the BA team or
other teams in the hazard area.
Communications

(a) Suitable and sufficient communications procedures must be established and maintained
between the command team, the BA ECP and all BA teams throughout the duration of their
deployment.
(b) Communications equipment used with BA should be suitable for use within flammable
environments, complying with the requisite level of intrinsic safety.
(c) Communication between BA teams and the BA entry control operative is essential to the
effective command and control of an incident and the safety and welfare of BA wearers. All
relevant information should be shared.
(d) The BA team briefing should be given to all team members. It should include all information
relevant to the team’s task and safety, including emergency procedures. Regular
communication between BA team members is essential to ensure the safety of personnel and
the exchange of information within the BA team.
(e) When BA teams in the risk area come into contact with each other, team leaders should
exchange all relevant information.
(f) Where radio communications are used, a dedicated BA communications channel (s) should be
specified and used. However, at less complex incidents where the use of BA commuincations

is minimal and manageable, a general channel may be used for all hand-held radio
communications.
(g) In normal circumstances, the BA team leader should instigate all communications between
the BA team and the BA entry control point. However, in an emergency, any BA team member
may send a message.
(h) BA team members should be debriefed as soon as practicable after leaving the risk area.
Debriefing should include any information that could assist in resolving the incident or
improving safety for BA teams. Essential and risk-critical information must be communicated
to the incident commander as soon as possible and before debriefing.
(i) Where assistance with BA communications becomes necessary at the BA entry control point,
the incident commander should make the appropriate resources available.
(j) Normally, BA communications between teams will be via the BA entry control operative.
However, circumstances may arise where BA teams need to communicate directly with other
teams by radio. In such cases, teams should identify themselves and the team(s) they wish to
contact through their unique incident BA team call sign (see designation of BA ECP and BA
teams). As long as radio traffic is kept to a minimum, this should not prevent risk-critical
information from being passed between BA teams.
(k) Where communications are more complex and a greater level of control and supervision is
required, the incident, operations or sector commander may need to appoint a BA
communications operative. BA communications operatives should be considered under Stage
2 BA entry control.
(l) The incident commander should consider using line communications equipment:
(1) Where a high degree of intrinsic safety is required and cannot be provided through
hand-held radio and electronic communications equipment
(2) Where incidents require deep penetration into structures, such as basements and
tunnels Where incidents are likely to be of long duration
(3) Where BA guidelines are required
(4) Where airline equipment is in use without BA being worn
(m) The BA communications operative will:
(1) Report to, and take instruction from, the person responsible for the BA entry control
point, and work alongside the BA entry control operative
(2) Send and receive messages, liaising with the BA entry control operative and the person
responsible for the BA entry control point
(3) Provide appropriate communications equipment

(4) Maintain a position close to the BA entry control operative
(5) Carry out a communications check with BA teams before entering the risk area Monitor
BA teams’ progress in the risk area
(6) Inform and update the person responsible for the BA ECP of any unexplained
breakdown in communications with BA teams
Telemetry

(a) The purpose of telemetry in aerodrome rescue and firefighting service operations is to allow
live and relevant data to be transmitted and received between a remote monitoring point and
the breathing apparatus wearer.
(b) To maximise the signal power of a radio frequency transmission, aerodrome rescue and
firefighting services should follow the relevant guidance from telemetry system providers and
may consider, where appropriate, enhancing signal strength by using a ‘leaky feeder’ and/or
repeater units.
(c) This document is based on the minimum functionality of telemetry equipment. Individual
aerodrome rescue and firefighting services will need to develop their own procedures for their
equipment, and should seek to ensure that telemetry BA command and control and BA
equipment procedures for using telemetry are interoperable as far as is reasonably
practicable.
(d) In the event of a loss of contact or breakdown in telemetry communications, the procedures
followed by individual aerodrome rescue and firefighting services must consider other ways to
communicate with BA teams.

(e) Arrangements must be put in place to manage and operate the available telemetry, and to
monitor information received via telemetry at the BA ECP throughout the duration of BA
deployment.
(f) Depending on the scope and scale of the expected BA deployment and in accordance with the
incident plan, additional support to the person responsible for the BA ECP may be considered.
(g) The incident commander will:
(1) Decide whether emergency selective evacuation is appropriate
(2) Ensure that any decision to conduct an emergency total evacuation of all personnel is
communicated to all telemetry BA entry control operatives
(3) Ensure that the appropriate action, based on individual aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service standard procedures, is taken in the event of an unexpected and
sustained loss of telemetry
(h) The BA entry control operative will:
(1) Monitor the time to activation of the low pressure warning device
(2) Set up and operate a telemetry BA entry control board or unit in a position nominated
by the incident commander
(3) Log on telemetry-equipped BA wearers who are to be committed to the risk area
(4) Monitor the displayed cylinder pressure of all telemetry radio units logged on to
telemetry BA entry control boards or units
(5) Ensure that appropriate action is taken if the cylinder contents of a BA wearer do not
correspond with the BA wearer’s time of whistle or low-pressure warning
(6) Revert to manual BA entry control procedures if the telemetry signal is lost Initiate BA
emergency procedures if appropriate
(7) Log off BA wearers leaving the risk area through the BA ECP from their telemetry BA
entry control boards/units
(i) The BA team leader will:
(1) Test telemetry equipment with the BA entry control operative
(2) Ensure that the appropriate telemetry signal is transmitted by each member of the BA
team when leaving the risk area
(3) Ensure that the whole BA team is withdrawn if any member of the team receives an
emergency evacuation signal (total or selective)
(4) Ensure that each BA wearer acknowledges receipt of the evacuation signal (depending
on the telemetry system employed)
(j) The BA wearer will:

(1) Shut down the BA set and collect the BA tally from the BA entry control operative
Welfare of Breathing Apparatus Wearers

(a) Research has established that heat-related conditions are the greatest single source of
performance limitation and physiological threat to firefighters’ wellbeing when undertaking
firefighting and search and rescue activities in a built environment. The ability of BA wearers
to make critical decisions and sound judgements based on risk assessment may also be
affected by heat-related conditions.
(b) BA wearer welfare, safety and effectiveness should be addressed before, during and post-
deployment.
(c) Wearing breathing apparatus and personal protective equipment restricts the body’s ability to
regulate body temperature. This situation is exacerbated when the BA wearer is working in
hot and humid conditions. Apart from general tiredness associated with fatigue in an
operational environment, it could also result in:
(1) Poor judgement
(2) Reduced capacity for effective communication Poor co-ordination
(3) Reduced visual perception Reduced vigilance
(4) Slower reaction times Lack of concentration
(d) Incident commanders, anyone with delegated responsibility for BA wearer welfare and all BA
wearers must be alert to the signs and symptoms of heat-related conditions. Recognising
these signs and symptoms is part of the risk assessment process that helps determine
whether a person is fit to be deployed in BA at an incident. In addition, all personnel have a
responsibility to ensure that they arrive fit for duty.

(e) Further research has shown that regular training in BA increases an individual’s ability to cope
with the additional physiological demands that may be involved. However, the effects of heat-
related conditions on an individual cannot be completely removed by training alone, and
aerodrome rescue and firefighting services should therefore adopt the following guidance.
(f) Personnel have a responsibility to ensure that they are physiologically and psychologically fit
to wear BA. The welfare of BA wearers should be addressed and appropriately resourced on
every occasion that BA is deployed.
(g) Where possible, firefighters selected as BA wearers should not carry out other functions
requiring high levels of physiological effort, such as transporting equipment upstairs during
high-rise incidents. If personnel have already worked with BA at an incident and are to be
redeployed in BA, they should be given time to rest and recuperate.
(h) Where possible, action should be taken to improve the working conditions of BA teams
deployed in risk areas, for example, by using tactical ventilation or cooling techniques to
reduce temperatures.
(i) Recognising the physiological load and psychological effects imposed on BA teams and their
need for rest and recovery, plans should be made for relief BA teams. Incident commanders
should be aware of the hazards associated with wearers being recommitted.
(j) At an incident where BA operations are likely to be arduous or of long duration, establishing a
rest and recovery area should be considered, supervised by a manager who will be
responsible for managing rest, recuperation and refreshments for BA wearers. The rest and
recovery area should be in a safe and suitable location that is clean, dry, cool and remote from
the immediate scene of operations.
(k) Where refreshments are provided for crews at hazardous materials incidents, eating and
drinking is only permitted under the direction of the hazardous materials adviser or scientific
adviser where available.
(l) Appropriate health and safety recording systems must be maintained for BA wearers who
have experienced heat-related illness and injury.
(m) Incident commanders should consider the physiological and psychological effects those
previous activities may have on an individual or team’s wellbeing and their ability to
undertake their tasks safely when deployed to use BA.
(n) Individuals should be aware of their own personal fluid requirements and consume adequate
amounts of water throughout the day to remain hydrated.

(o) Where possible, all BA team members should share tasks, roles and functions and, where
appropriate, BA team leaders should consider team and task rotation. The designated BA
team leader should always maintain a leadership role within the BA team.
(p) All BA wearers should monitor team members for signs of heat-related conditions such as
dizziness, nausea, abdominal pain or a burning sensation of the skin. Under such
circumstances, the whole BA team should immediately withdraw from the risk area.
(q) Where appropriate and following a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, dressing down of
personal protective equipment should take place away from the scene of operations to allow
body heat to vent, reducing the physiological burden. This should be a standard pre- and post-
deployment procedure.
(r) To optimise recovery between BA deployments and maximise performance and safety before
being redeployed, BA wearers should be given a period of time to rest and rehydrate. Table 43
(below) offers guidance on rest and rehydration periods; however, the time given should be
based on the task undertaken, duration and conditions encountered by wearers.

CONDITIONS
