(s) Particular attention should be given to firefighters who have been working in confined spaces
with limited ventilation, such as basements or ships’ holds. If the work has been particularly
arduous, recovery time should be extended.
(t) Once the recovery period has elapsed or clearance has been given to leave the rest area, BA
wearers should report to the incident, operations or sector commander for redeployment.
(u) The incident commander will:
(1) Consider the physiological and psychological effects that previous activities may have
on an individual or BA team’s wellbeing and their ability to safely undertake their task
when deployed to use BA
(v) The BA entry control operative will:
(1) Acting on the instructions of the incident commander, restrict the length of exposure in
difficult or strenuous conditions and determine an earlier time of exit from the risk area

(2) Monitor BA team members for signs of heat-related conditions such as dizziness,
nausea, abdominal pain or a burning sensation of the skin following their withdrawal
from the risk area.
(w) The BA team leader will:
(1) Monitor working conditions and be aware of potential physiological effects that may
cause a heat-related condition to team members
(2) Monitor team members for signs of a heat related condition such as dizziness, nausea,
abdominal pain, or a burning sensation of the skin
(3) In the event of any of these symptoms being observed, initiate the immediate
withdrawal of the whole team from the risk area
(x) The BA wearer will:
(1) Monitor themselves and other BA team members for signs of a heat-related condition
such as dizziness, nausea, abdominal pain or a burning sensation of the skin.
(2) Inform the BA team leader should they display any of the symptoms of a heat-related
condition
Emergency Arrangements

(a) Emergency procedures provide effective arrangements for prompt and effective emergency
assistance to breathing apparatus wearers in distress.

(b) Consideration must be given to providing suitable and sufficient emergency arrangements
whenever BA is deployed at incidents. The full nature and extent of those emergency
arrangements should be proportionate to all reasonably foreseeable risks to BA wearers.
(c) The need for emergency teams will depend on the nature of the risk and the situation that is
being dealt with which may result in additional resource implications. During the initial stages
of operations, as part of their incident plan, incident commanders must consider whether BA
emergency arrangements (including the potential need for BA emergency teams) will be
required.
(d) Establishing BA entry control should include considering and providing emergency
arrangements. Minimum emergency arrangements are detailed for Stage 2 BA entry control,
but their nature and extent must be determined in line with the incident plan and be suitable,
sufficient and proportionate to the risks and foreseeable emergency events at the incident.
(e) Where BA emergency teams are deemed necessary under BA entry control procedures
(excluding Stage 2), steps should be taken to ensure their availability as soon as possible. The
nature and extent of emergency arrangements will be dictated by circumstances and
determined on the basis of risk.
Table 44: Summary of Minimum BA Emergency Arrangements
SUMMARY OF MINIMUM BA EMERGENCY ARRANGEMENTS
STAGE 1 BA ENTRY CONTROL
(a) The full extent of the BA emergency arrangements must be determined on the basis of a
risk assessment
(b) Arrangements may or may not involve the provision of BA emergency team(s)
(c) Where the provision of BA emergency teams is considered necessary but resources are not
immediately available, the incident commander should consider restricting BA operations
pending their arrival
STAGE 2 BA ENTRY CONTROL
(a) The full extent of BA emergency arrangements must be determined on the basis of a risk
assessment
(b) The minimum provision under Stage 2 is one BA emergency team per BA entry control
point, rigged and standing by throughout the time BA is in use

(c) A separate BA entry control/telemetry board should be provided to accommodate the
deployment of BA teams acting as additional BA emergency teams; they should be marked
accordingly at the BA entry control point
(d) Where additional resources are not immediately available, the incident commander should
restrict BA operations pending their arrival

(f) In situations where BA emergency teams are in place, their deployment should be considered
when any of the following conditions arise, or have the potential to arise, subject to a suitable
and sufficient assessment of risk by the person responsible for the BA entry control point:
(1) A wearer fails to return to the BA ECP before the pre-determined activation time of
their low-pressure warning device or whistle and cannot be contacted to confirm their
safety and wellbeing
(2) A distress signal is heard or received by a telemetry device (unless it can be established
immediately that this is an accidental activation)
(3) When audible or visual indicators suggest that a BA wearer is in distress or imminent
distress or danger: for example, owing to structural collapse or fire conditions
(4) Prolonged and unexplained breakdown in communications
(5) At the request of a BA wearer in the risk area
(6) Depending on the nature of the BA emergency, and to ensure suitable protection of the
BA emergency team, the person responsible for the BA ECP may identify the need to
deploy firefighting, hose management and casualty handling BA teams in addition to
the first BA emergency search and rescue team.
(7) Where BA wearers require – or appear to require – emergency assistance, the person
responsible for supervising the BA ECP should take immediate steps to contact all BA
teams in the risk area who may be affected. Other BA teams in the risk area should be
given information that may allow them to help affected wearers exit the risk area
safely. Radios, telemetry and other means of electronic communication, where
available, may assist in identifying the team and wearers.
Note: None of the above precludes anyone with responsibilities or duties at the BA ECP from
initiating a BA emergency radio message where necessary.
(8) Once a BA emergency has been declared, watchroom control room must be informed
immediately. The radio message must include the phrase ‘BA emergency’.

(9) Contingency arrangements should include suitable protection for BA emergency teams
entering risk areas containing potentially flammable, explosive or other hazardous
materials. Consideration should be given to support arrangements for deployed BA
emergency teams, taking into account the extreme physiological demands placed on BA
wearers tasked with assisting or rescuing colleagues in distress.
(10) The level and type of personal protective equipment provided for the BA emergency
team will be determined by the requirements of the incident and the risk assessment.
(11) The cylinder capacity and duration of the BA sets allocated to emergency teams must
be at least equivalent to the highest capacity and duration of those of the BA wearers to
whom the emergency arrangements relate.
(12) BA emergency teams standing by should be close to the BA ECP and receive regular and
relevant updates, such as briefings to BA teams, information on hazards and the layout
of the risk area, and details of areas searched.
(13) BA emergency teams should rig, but not don or start up, in BA and stand by at the BA
ECP ready for immediate deployment until instructed otherwise.
(14) A separate BA entry control/telemetry board should be provided at the BA ECP to
record the deployment of BA emergency teams.
(15) The person responsible for the BA ECP should ensure the provision of any additional
equipment that might be needed by BA emergency teams and ensure that it is ready for
immediate use.
(16) The BA emergency team must be provided with the equipment considered to be
suitable and sufficient to meet the needs of all reasonably foreseeable emergency
events, including:
(i) Radio communications
(ii) Means of providing a supplementary air supply to a BA wearer
(iii) Any other specialist equipment
(iv) Drag mats
(v) Breaking-in gear
(17) As part of ensuring BA wearers’ welfare and physiological readiness for deployment,
account should be taken of ambient temperatures and weather conditions when
deciding on the standard of dress and other provisions necessary for the BA emergency
team on standby.
(18) There must be at least as many BA wearers in BA emergency teams as in the largest
team deployed or likely to be deployed from the BA ECP to the risk area.

(19) Minimum requirements for each BA emergency team:
(i) Two BA wearers
(20) Consideration must be given to:
(i) Numbers in the BA emergency team, taking into account the working
environment
(ii) Distance from the BA entry control point
(iii) Size of the BA team requiring assistance
(21) The person responsible for the BA ECP is responsible for activating emergency
procedures and the deployment of emergency teams, including BA emergency team
support arrangements. This person is also responsible for all other BA entry control
procedures relating to BA emergency team deployment, including:
(i) Briefing and debriefing BA emergency teams
(ii) Maintaining a suitable record of all relevant operational and risk information,
decisions made and tasks given to BA emergency teams
(22) BA emergency team call signs must identify the BA ECP they are being deployed from
and their emergency team status. For example, emergency BA team, Alpha 1,
emergency BA team, Alpha 2, etc.
(23) Before deployment to the risk area, the person responsible for the BA ECP should brief
BA emergency teams, providing:
(i) Any relevant information, for example the BA team size, route, tasks, last known
location
(ii) All hazards identified during the risk assessment process
(iii) Control measures to be used for the protection of BA emergency teams
(iv) Specific details of their tasks
(24) The brief should be repeated by the BA emergency team leader and acknowledged by
the person giving the briefing to ensure that the whole BA team understands the
details.
(25) Following the deployment of any BA emergency team, arrangements must be made
immediately for replacement BA emergency teams.
(26) Breathing apparatus wearers should indicate that they are in distress by activating their
distress signal unit. When in distress the BA wearer or the BA team leader should carry
out the following actions:
(i) Inform the BA entry control point, including the phrase ‘BA emergency’, of the
nature of the distress, current location and intentions

(ii) Retrace steps to the BA entry control point. If this is not possible, locate an
alternative exit (for example window or door) in the immediate vicinity, then
attempt to attract attention or decide to remain at the current location or
relocate to a safe waiting area
(iii) Inform the BA entry control operative of each BA wearer’s cylinder pressures; in
some cases, telemetry equipment will deliver this information automatically
(iv) Where necessary, adopt ‘entrapped procedures’ to conserve air while awaiting
rescue Activate the distress signal unit of the affected BA wearer; in the unlikely
event that a distress signal unit fails to activate, the device of another BA team
member should be activated
(v) Where a distress signal unit has activated accidentally, the BA team leader should
inform the BA entry control point. A decision should then be made on whether
the BA team should return to the BA ECP or whether another BA team should be
deployed to the risk area to reset the unit with a distress signal unit key.
(27) BA teams will:
(i) Inform the BA ECP that a distress signal unit alarm is audible
(ii) Follow the revised brief issued by the person responsible for the BA ECP
(rendering assistance to a BA team in distress should take precedence over
existing tasks unless the tasks are risk-critical and could compromise the safety of
other BA wearers if not carried out)
(iii) Not take unnecessary risks, such as entering large or complex areas if unable to
retrace their steps
(28) BA emergency teams will:
(i) If possible, confirm the nature of the emergency with distressed BA wearers
(ii) Inform the BA entry control operative that distressed BA wearers have been
located and request further assistance (if required)
(iii) Take gauge readings of distressed BA wearers’ cylinders Take gauge readings of
BA emergency team cylinders Render any required on-scene emergency
assistance
(iv) Implement a safe rescue plan to remove distressed BA wearers from the risk area
following a risk assessment
(29) The incident commander will:
(i) Ensure that a BA emergency message is communicated to the aerodrome rescue
and firefighting service control room at the earliest opportunity

(ii) Request the resources required to resolve the emergency situation
(30) On receipt of a BA emergency message, watchroom control will:
(i) Mobilise a minimum of one further pumping appliance
(ii) Arrange for the ambulance service to attend
(31) The BA entry control operative will:
(i) Immediately inform the person responsible for the BA entry control point; if
unavailable, they will notify the incident commander and aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service control room
(ii) Take whatever practicable action possible in the circumstances
(iii) If Stage 2 BA entry control procedures are in use, inform all other BA entry
control points
Entrapped procedure
(a) The aim of the entrapped procedure is to maximise the duration of available air in BA sets
where BA wearers are trapped or unable to withdraw from the risk area.
(b) Partial breathing apparatus set removal is an additional technique for self-rescue available to
BA wearers in extreme circumstances where no safe means of egress from the risk area is
available or where adopting entrapped procedure presents an intolerable risk to the safety of
the BA team.
(c) In those rare circumstances where a BA wearer has become trapped and the dangers are too
great to await rescue, partial BA set removal may be deemed the only technique available.
(d) Before commencing partial BA set removal to negotiate any obstruction or restriction on
egress from a risk area, the BA team leader should seek further guidance, additional
instructions and details of other actions being undertaken from the BA entry control point.
The BA team leader should also investigate the availability of any safe alternative exit routes
and consider adopting the entrapped procedure.
(e) Partial BA set removal is a technique available to BA wearers for self-rescue in extreme
circumstances, where:
(1) Egress is through a restricted opening and no other safe means of egress is available
(2) Adopting entrapped procedures presents an intolerable risk to the safety of the BA
team
(f) The technique is carried out systematically under supervision and with assistance from other
BA wearers

(g) The BA team leader should consider the physiological and psychological effects of the
environment and the increased air consumption of wearers during partial BA set removal.
Frequent gauge checks must be undertaken and, where possible, communicated to the BA
entry control point.
(h) The BA team leader should:
(1) Consider the physiological and psychological effects of the environment and the
increased air consumption of wearers during partial BA set removal
(2) Carry out frequent gauge checks and communicate with the BA entry control operative
(3) Consider the availability of safe alternative exit routes and adopting entrapped
procedure
(4) Ask the BA entry control operative for further guidance and details of other actions
being undertaken from the BA entry control point
(i) The BA wearer should:
(1) Ask the BA team leader for further guidance and details of other actions being
undertaken from the BA entry control point
Breathing Apparatus set failure and reporting procedure
(a) Incidents may occur when a breathing apparatus set fails, resulting in distress to the wearer.
(b) The term malfunction does not include leakage into a facemask due to poor face fit or a
failure arising from an external source such as falling debris or entanglement.
(c) All ‘distress to wearer’ situations should be properly investigated.
(d) When impounding a BA set, the incident commander must:
(1) Impound the BA set
(2) Record the  cylinder pressure before closing the cylinder valve
(3) Record the exact number of turns required to close the cylinder valve
(4) The time the wearer entered the incident
(5) Record the time the wearer left the incident
(6) Record all other information from the BA entry control board
(7) Record any other obvious information regarding the condition of the set without
carrying out a detailed inspection
(8) Record any remarks made by the wearer or other members of the BA team
(9) Record witness statements
(10) Place the BA set, BA tally, facemask, cylinder, service log book into a plastic bag which
should then be sealed, labelled and secured in a safe place

(11) Inform the watch/control room
(12) Complete any administration relevant to the investigation
(13) Ensure a full investigation is carried out by a competent person
Interoperability and intraoperability
(a) There will be occasions when breathing apparatus wearers from aerodrome rescue and
firefighting services are required to work alongside teams from other fire and rescue services
and with personnel from other mutual-aid emergency services.
(b) The BA command and control procedures of aerodrome rescue and firefighting services
should provide a common framework for safe and effective systems of work when working
with other mutual-aid emergency services and, where necessary, other public, private and
commercial fire and rescue organisations.
(c) Subject to prior arrangement, planning, exercising and validation of arrangements between
fire and rescue services, BA teams may work together where:
(1) Methods for identifying BA entry control points are compatible
(2) BA wearers from different fire and rescue services are wearing the same specification
BA equipment and follow the same procedures
(3) BA wearers ensure that the person responsible for the BA ECP is fully informed of their
maximum cylinder capacity and duration, to ensure the correct duration table is used to
plan the time of whistle or low-pressure warning device
(4) Radio communications are compatible between all BA wearers in a BA team and the BA
entry control point, and at least between the BA team leader and the BA entry control
point.
(5) BA wearers from different fire and rescue services using the same specification BA sets
and associated equipment may insert their BA tallies (where used) into each other’s BA
entry control boards at an incident.
(d) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services should comply with appropriate locally agreed
protocols for safe work procedures based on this guidance and developed for interoperability
with the other fire and rescue services.
5. OPERATIONAL TECHNIQUES
Air Management
(a) Breathing Apparatus wearers should return to the BA entry control point:
(1) Before their low pressure warning device or whistle activates
(2) Before the pre-determined return time specified in the BA team briefing

(3) Where a BA team member displays symptoms likely to affect their welfare, such as a
heat- related condition.
(b) The only exceptions are in the event of a:
(1) Set malfunction
(2) BA wearer becoming trapped
(3) Situation where a BA wearer’s air supply has to be augmented
(c) Air consumption rate tables should be used to provide a predicted exit time for BA wearers.
However, the person responsible for the BA ECP should be aware that BA wearers consume
air at different rates.
(d) Each wearer will consume air at a different rate. These differences will be determined by a
number of factors including:
(1) Body mass
(2) Individual levels of fitness Work rate
(3) Tasks undertaken Environmental conditions
(4) Personal protective equipment in use
(5) Psychological stress
(e) To maintain an accurate record of air consumption each BA wearer must read their own
gauge, make their own calculations, and inform the BA team leader of the pressure at which
they will need to start exiting the risk area.
(f) BA team leaders should regularly update the BA entry control operative about the air
consumption of the BA team.
Calculating Turn-around Pressure
(a) Where the use of a turn-around pressure might be appropriate, the following methods may
be considered:
(1) Method 1: Making progress. This is used for tasks such as making steady progress into a
hazard area. The wearer notes their gauge pressure as they book in with the BA ECP and
start up their BA set. They then calculate their turn-around pressure by dividing their
full duration by two, then adding half the safety margin. This is a basic calculation but
will ensure that, if they begin to exit when this pressure is reached, they will exit before
their low-pressure warning device or whistle activates. For example:
Method 1 example: Making progress
Entry pressure = 200 bar Divide by two = 100 bar

Half safety margin (60÷2) = 30 bar Add the two = 100 + 30
Turn-around pressure = 130 bar

(2) Method 2: Working at a location. This is a more accurate method and can be used when
a BA team enters a risk area and will be working for some time. For example, if team 1
were sent into a risk area to relieve team 2, they would need to calculate the initial
turn-around pressure on entry and take gauge readings regularly along the route. Once
team 1 reached team 2, they would take another reading and calculate the pressure
they had used to reach that point. Team 1 can then safely stay with the branch until the
pressure drops to the point where they have sufficient air to exit back along the same
route without entering their safety margin.
(3) When using Method 2, the BA team will have more time to complete a task. This can
make fire and rescue operations more effective and may mean that fewer BA wearers
will be required.
Method 2 example: Working at a location
Entry pressure = 200 bar
Gauge reading on reaching objective = 160 bar Air used to reach objective = 40 bar
Air required to exit = 40 bar + safety margin (i.e. 60 bar) Turn-around pressure = 100 bar

Landmarking
(a) While navigating through the risk area, identifiable locations such as a change of level or
direction, doorways and large obstacles, can act as prompts for gauge checks. By checking at
regular intervals using these landmarks, any unexpectedly high levels of air consumption or
loss of air should be identified. In particular, the team will be able to determine the amount of
air and the pace required to exit the risk area.
Rescue of a Casualty
(a) Where a BA team plans to exit with a casualty, it is essential that a gauge reading is taken and
a calculation made on the air required to leave the incident unless they are already close to an
exit. If there is an insufficient air supply to exit with the casualty, the team should request
additional assistance from the BA entry control operative.
(b) On exiting the risk area, further gauge readings should be taken when reaching familiar
landmarks. By referring to earlier calculations, team members will be able to determine
whether they can leave the incident with the casualty or progress as far as possible before

having to leave the casualty with another BA team. The team must remain in communication
with the BA entry control operative so that appropriate support and additional risk control
measures can be introduced where necessary.
Close Personal Contact

(a) Close personal contact is defined as maintaining visual, verbal communication and/or physical
contact (touching distance) with breathing apparatus team member/s at all times within the
risk area to ensure the safety of personnel and for the exchange of information within the BA
team. This can be achieved in a number of ways, including:
(1) Attachment by short personal line
(2) Constant physical contact between each BA team member
(3) Remaining within touching distance
(b) In circumstances where all BA team members are in contact with a hose reel, delivery hose or
casualty, personnel are deemed to be in physical contact, providing they maintain visual (line
of sight) and verbal contact (not radio communication).
(c) BA team members will maintain close personal contact when performing personal safety
techniques, such as hand and foot sweeping.
Entrapped Procedure

(a) When the breathing apparatus wearer is unable to escape from the risk area, they should:
(1) Contact the BA ECP by radio (if possible)
(2) Operate the distress signal unit
(3) Relax as much as possible in the circumstances by assuming a reclined or seated
posture
(4) Breathe calmly and gently to minimise air usage.
(b) Any supplementary air supply should not be operated and the cylinder valve should not be
adjusted other than to check that it is fully open.
(c) Once the safety margin has been reached, the low-pressure warning device or whistle will
activate. In the case of an air-operated whistle device, the air consumed is minimal; electronic
low pressure warning devices do not use any air.
Compartment Search and Rescue Procedures
(a) With this method of search, each compartment is mapped out systematically as the breathing
apparatus search and rescue teams’ progress. The team progresses around the room using
either a left or right hand search pattern (identified to the BA team as part of their brief prior
to entry). As they do so each door encountered is checked and swept for casualties,
immediately visible or within touching distance, from the doorway.
(b) Once a full circuit of the compartment has been carried out the team progresses into the first
door they encountered on their search to carry out this procedure again. This promotes the
concept of fully searching compartments before progressing on to the next identified
compartment, enabling accurate recording of the search and assists crews with orientation
whist operating in low visibility conditions. Compartment search procedures can also assist

with the efficient management of firefighting hose due to the fact that hose is always returned
to the initial compartment after subsequent compartment searches have been carried out.
(c) This procedure is suitable for a range of structures, particularly multi-compartmented
structures which may have interconnecting rooms.

and sweeping doorways, using the compartment search procedure.

Below is a progressive example of a BA team performing a left-hand compartment search

Directional Search Procedure
(d) This method of search is particularly suitable for smaller buildings, where compartments have
standard and recognisable layouts; the procedure is practical to adopt and compartments can
be cleared as the directional search progresses, often making the procedure time efficient.
(e) This procedure is easier to perform as a BA wearer, however there is an increased risk of  BA
teams inadvertently missing a fire compartment or risk area (depending upon the building
layout), which could compromise their means of escape should the incident develop.
Additionally, firefighting hose management may be more difficult due to the fact that steps
must be retraced throughout the search route to retrieve it or to exit. Search and rescue
operations should therefore be comprehensively co- ordinated, with an effective search plan
and recording process.
Below is a progressive example of a BA team performing as left-hand directional search

 Searching Large Compartment
(a) In larger compartments, multiple teams will need to be committed in a co-ordinated way to
ensure the compartment is thoroughly searched and team safety is maintained. The
directional search procedure does not necessarily mean that a team will clear a compartment
before moving on to the next compartment.
(b) It may not be possible to search large compartments entirely using conventional search
procedures, as BA teams may not be able to access the centre of the compartment safely,
whilst maintaining contact with a fixed reference point. When large compartments are
encountered, additional control measures may need to be implemented to enable a complete
search. This may include the use of thermal imaging equipment, tactical ventilation and BA
guidelines.
Below is a progressive example of a BA team performing a left-hand directional search of large
compartments

 Left/right-hand Orientation
(a) Both compartment and directional search procedures will employ a left- or right-hand
orientation. This means that in larger compartments, multiple teams will need to be
committed in a co-ordinated way to ensure the compartment is thoroughly searched and
team safety is maintained. The directional search procedure does not necessarily mean that a
team will clear a compartment before moving on to the next compartment.
(b) It may not be possible to search large compartments entirely using conventional search
procedures, as BA teams may not be able to access the centre of the compartment safely,
whilst maintaining contact with a fixed reference point. When large compartments are
encountered, additional control measures may need to be implemented to enable a complete
search. This may include the use of thermal imaging equipment, tactical ventilation and BA
guidelines.
(c) The team leader will use and follow the left- or right-hand wall as their fixed reference point
to ensure the search is orientated and systematic. This left- or right-hand orientation will
apply as soon as a BA team passes through the point of entry and throughout their time in the
risk area.
(d) Other than under the most extreme and exceptional circumstances, when visibility is poor or
deteriorating the BA team leader should remain in contact with the wall or with fittings

integral to the wall at all times. Maintaining the wall as a fixed reference point, either by touch
or vision, is a cornerstone of the safety and effectiveness of these procedures.
Breathing Apparatus Guideline
(a) The term ‘guideline’ refers to a special line that is used either as a main guideline, to carry out
an initial search and indicate a route between an BA ECP and the scene of operations, or as a
branch guideline, used where is it necessary to traverse or search more than 6 metres off a
main guideline. The same methods and guidance apply to both types of line.
(b) BA guideline containers should be securely fitted to the set of the BA team leader, in a way
that allows them to be detached easily in an emergency. When extended penetration into a
large or complex structure is required, the team should carry an additional BA guideline.
(c) BA guideline must be stowed so that the running end pays out first.
(d) A main guideline leading from a BA ECP should be designated ‘A’ or ‘B’ using the tallies
provided for this purpose. Any main guideline tally must be attached securely to the line
before the BA team enters the risk area.
(e) Unless the BA guideline is to be used to extend a main guideline or form a branch guideline, it
should be secured to an immovable object outside the risk area in safe air, before the BA team
enters the risk area.
(f) No more than one guideline may be laid along a search side (i.e. two BA guidelines cannot be
laid along the same wall). However, two lines may be laid near to the point of entry to a
structure, either side of a route, before they split into defined left/right search patterns.
(g) Guidelines should not cross over each other inside a structure or share tie-off points. Should
two guidelines converge, one should be terminated and secured to a tie-off point a minimum
of two metres from where the lines would have met.
(h) When the guideline is being extended, the BA team leader must inform the BA entry control
operative, who will then inform the sector, operations or incident commander. This will
ensure a suitable and sufficient record is maintained.
Securing a Breathing Apparatus Guideline

way that allows them to be detached easily in the event of an emergency. Examples are set
out in the following photographs:

points as necessary. The line should be kept off the floor, preferably between shoulder and waist
height, and secured to the side of the search area. Where no other means of securing the line are
available, the following methods may be considered.

the loop
(c) The loop is slid between the door and the jamb with a knot on both sides of the hinge
(d) The door can now be closed and the line held above the hinge

Using a high tie-off point

(b) The loop is tied off around the high object using a round turn and two half-hitches

 Negotiating a vertical ladder:
(a) When a guideline route involves a vertical ladder, a tie-off point must be created at the
bottom and the top of the ladder. BA teams should take into account the position of these

Example of negotiating a vertical ladder

Encountering doorways and openings
(a) When laying a guideline, teams should not pass closed doors without first investigating
around the doorway. The door sweep procedure may be adopted following an appropriate
dynamic risk assessment and in conjunction with normal fire fighting and /or fire-gas
suppression techniques for protecting BA teams. The firefighting BA teams supporting the
guideline-laying team should undertake these checks and techniques.
(b) As well as establishing landmark features for the BA team and checking for casualties behind
doorways, these techniques will:
(1) Contribute to maintaining safe access and egress for that team and subsequent BA
teams
(2) Assist in identifying and dealing with any fire compartments.
Encountering small rooms/compartments
(a) Tying off the guideline unnecessarily consumes a significant amount of time. When searching
rooms that are known or discovered to be small, the guideline should therefore be gathered
up and taken out of the room. The advantage here is that:
(1) The guideline can be used more effectively for extending further into the incident
(2) Time will be saved when exiting as only the most direct route will be marked
(3) If exiting carrying casualties, there will be fewer tie-off points and doorways to
negotiate
Extending a guideline
(a) A BA guideline can be extended by clipping the snap-hook of another line onto the looped
end, then unclipping it from the container.

Example of extending a guideline

 Withdrawing from the risk area
(a) If a BA team laying a guideline needs to withdraw before they reach their target, the BA team
leader should first ensure that they are clipped to a secured section (between the last two tie-
off points) of the guideline by their personal line before releasing the guideline container. The
BA team can then retrace their steps from the risk area by following the guideline. This
procedure should also be adopted for emergency withdrawals.
(b) If possible, the guideline container should be secured to a tie-off point before withdrawal. BA
teams can either create a new tie-off point or retrace their steps to the last tie-off point,
gathering the slack line. Their decision will be based on the distance they have travelled from
the last tie-off point and the length of line to be gathered. Any gathered slack line should be
attached to the container with a half- hitch, and the container should be secured to the
nearest tie-off point so subsequent teams can find it.
(c) Where it is not possible to secure the guideline container to a tie-off point before withdrawal,
the withdrawing BA team should inform the BA entry control operative.
BA teams meeting on a guideline
(a) BA teams leaving the incident area always take precedence over incoming teams because the
exiting team leader will have calculated turn-around pressure to ensure exit before activation
of the team’s low pressure warning devices or whistles.
(b) To pass on a BA guideline, incoming teams should kneel as close to the guideline as possible,
with the team leader holding their personal line karabiners. If individual team members are
clipped to the line, their karabiners will need to be pushed together. The outgoing team
leader can then negotiate the incoming team’s karabiners as they would a tie-off point.

Example of passing on a BA guideline

 Purpose of a personal line
(a) A personal line is a special line, a maximum of six metres in length, secured to the breathing
apparatus set of the wearer. The personal line allows all members of a BA team to either
attach themselves individually to a guideline or for team members to attach to each other
with the standard 1.25m length of line. A BA team member may attach their personal line to a
BA guideline (main or branch) to so they can search up to 1.25 metres off it or up to the
extended limit of six metres.

 Branch guidelines
(a) Branch guidelines are used where the distance of the search area from the main guideline is
greater than the length of one personal line.
(b) Branch guidelines are designated numerically, ‘1’, ’2’, ’3’ or ‘4’, by the BA entry control
operative, with the number of holes in the tally representing the branch guideline number. It

is essential that once deployed, all references to branch guidelines are related to their tally
number, not to their numerical position in relation to the BA entry control point.
(c) One method of attaching the tally is to tie an overhand knot on the bight, approximately one
metre from the snap-hook, and attach the branch guideline tally to the loop created by the
knot. This should be done before the BA team enters the risk area.

 Attaching and laying a branch guideline
(a) A branch guideline must be securely attached to the main guideline, away from any tie-off
points.
(b) The branch guideline should be tied off as soon as possible after attaching it to the main
guideline. This prevents the main guideline being deflected down the route of the branch
guideline.
(c) To avoid potential confusion, branch guidelines are not normally extended. However, an
extension may be required in certain circumstances following a risk assessment. The BA team
leader should seek permission from the incident commander to extend a branch guideline
where this is necessary.

(d) When leaving a main guideline and joining a branch guideline, the BA team leader should
inform the BA ECP to record that this transition has occurred.
(e) When re-joining a main guideline from a branch guideline, the BA team leader should check
the first set of tabs encountered to make sure they are travelling in the correct direction and
then, for recording purposes, inform the BA ECP that this transition has occurred.
(f) At all times, the BA team leader must maintain close communication with the BA entry control
point.

6. HEAT-RELATED CONDITIONS
Hyperthermia
(a) Hyperthermia results from an elevated body temperature caused by external or internal heat
stress and/or heat loading. This leads to failure of the body’s thermoregulatory systems and
can be categorised into the following six conditions:
(1) Heat exhaustion
(2) Heat faint
(3) Heat oedema
(4) Heat rash (prickly heat)
(5) Heat cramp
(6) Heat stroke
Heat Exhaustion
(a) Heat exhaustion is a mild response to exposure to hot environments. It results from a
combination of thermal and cardiovascular strain, where the body is unable to maintain
normal function owing to loss of fluids and salts. Symptoms include:
(1) A feeling of being unwell
(2) Tiredness/irritability
(3) Headaches

(4) Dizziness
(5) Nausea
(6) Vomiting
(7) Breathing difficulties (shallow, rapid respiration)
(8) Rapid pulse, which may be bounding or weak
(9) Extreme thirst and mouth dryness
(10) Muscle cramps, particularly affecting the stomach and legs
(11) Poor control over movements/stumbling/weakness
(b) This leads to two forms of heat exhaustion: salt depletion and, more likely in firefighting
situations, water depletion. Heat exhaustion usually responds positively to prompt treatment
but may predispose the firefighter to heat stroke.
Heat faint (Syncope)
(a) Heat faint is caused by a reduction in blood flow to the brain. It is more likely to occur in non-
acclimatized people during early exposure to heat. Symptoms include:
(1) Headache
(2) Dizziness
(3) Weakness
(4) Tunnel vision/blurring of vision
(5) Pale, sweaty skin
(6) Weak, slow pulse
(7) Loss of consciousness
Heat Oedema
(a) Oedema usually occurs among those not acclimatised to heat. It is unlikely to be encountered
in the sporadic exposure conditions of firefighting. Symptoms include swelling of the hands,
feet and ankles
Heat rash (Prickly heat)
(a) Prickly heat appears in red papules on the skin, usually in areas where clothing is restrictive. It
gives rise to a prickling sensation, particularly as sweating increases. It occurs in skin that is
persistently wetted by unevaporated sweat, possibly because the sweat ducts become
blocked.
(b) The papules may become infected unless they are treated. Heat rash is not dangerous.
However, it may result in patchy areas of skin that are temporarily unable to produce sweat,

which may adversely affect evaporative heat loss and thermoregulation. Prickly heat has been
shown to decrease tolerance to heat and to reduce work capacity. Sweating capacity has been
to shown to recover within three to four weeks. If heat rash is likely, the individual should be
referred for a medical opinion.
Heat cramp
(a) Heat cramps (painful muscle spasms) may occur in individuals working in the heat. These are
caused by salt deficiency, when salt is lost during severe sweating and large amounts of water
are taken in without replacing the salt. The condition may have a delayed onset and is most
likely in people who are unacclimatised to hot work or have a low dietary salt intake. Cramps
usually occur in the muscles principally used during work (limbs) or stomach. Adequate salt
intake with food should prevent this occurring.
Heat stroke
(a) If the total heat load (environmental conditions and metabolic heat generation) is such that
sufficient body heat cannot be lost to the environment, core temperature will rise. If this
continues, body temperature may exceed its controllable limits.
(b) In wet humid conditions, sweating may reduce due to the sweat glands swelling and blocking
sweat glands. Although normally associated with humid external environments, the humid
microclimate inside a firefighter's clothing can also create the conditions for heat stroke.
Alternatively, sweating may cease because of depletion of body water. This decrease in
sweating promotes a further, often rapid, rise in core temperature to beyond 38-39°C, where
collapse may occur, and to above 41°C (rectal temperature) where heat stroke may occur.
(c) With heat stroke, there is a major disruption of the central nervous function. At body
temperatures above about 40°C, a person's mental functions are disturbed and sweating
often stops. Normal temperature control mechanisms are lost and a further rapid
temperature rise occurs.
(d) The condition can have a sudden onset with no warning, or may be preceded by headache,
dizziness, confusion, faintness, restlessness or vomiting (symptoms of heat exhaustion). The
change from normal aches or tiredness to serious symptoms may not be obvious to the casual
observer.
(e) The transition from moderately elevated body temperature to heat stroke can be very rapid.
For this reason, no one should work alone or unsupervised in potential heat stress conditions.
If work performance deteriorates, this is usually a reliable indication that significant

physiological strain has already occurred. This is a life-threatening emergency. Symptoms may
include:
(1) Headache Dizziness
(2) Muscle weakness/cramps
(3) Being hot, dry and flushed with a high pulse and a core temperature probably in excess
of 41°C
(4) Failure of central nervous thermoregulation and sweating
(5) Mental confusion
(6) Convulsions Unconsciousness
Treatment
(a) After a period of heat exposure, a significant amount of heat will be trapped in the body and
clothing of the firefighter. Their highly insulated clothing will now act to retain that heat,
preventing its dissipation into the environment. The simple act of unfastening a tunic can help
to speed up the cooling process. In some circumstances, without this, body temperature can
continue to rise as heat in working muscles continues to be distributed around the body.
(b) Where appropriate, and following a dynamic risk assessment and review, ‘dressing down’ of
personal protective equipment to allow body heat to vent and reduce the resulting
physiological burden, should be a normal procedure pre- and post-deployment
(c) Where a heat related condition is identified or likely, the individual(s) should dress down and
drink cool water. If possible, warm, not cold, water should be sprayed onto the affected
individual(s) and they should be fanned to aid the process of cooling by evaporation.
(d) Managing hyperthermia by carrying out the following steps should be considered:
(1) Moving the casualty to a cool (shaded) environment
(2) Cooling: this can be rapid but monitor temperature to prevent hypothermia
(3) Removing heavy clothing
(e) If heat stroke is likely, urgent medical assistance must be sought, stating clearly that this is a
likely case of heat stroke. The individual should then be treated following the guidance
contained within this section, and the incident should be reported according to service policy.
(f) Faints (syncope) can be helped if the person lies down with their legs raised above the level of
their head.
(g) Special consideration should be paid to head cooling. Wrist cooling with cool water using
plunge buckets will also aid core temperature cooling but acts more slowly than the methods
identified above.

(h) Rehydration reverses most of the adverse effects of heat exposure, which stem from
dehydration as the body loses copious quantities of sweat in an attempt to regulate its
temperature. Fluid replacement is therefore an important aspect of restoring the thermal and
physiological equilibrium.
(i) Similarly, although a few mouthfuls of water may be enough to remove the immediate
sensation of thirst, it is not sufficient to restore thermal balance. Adequate fluid replacement
is particularly important for those who may be exposed to elevated temperatures for longer
periods.
(j) Only still water should be permitted for rehydration purposes. Cool (10-15°C) rather than cold
water is preferable. The direct cooling effect of any fluid is minimal and, if a drink is too cold, it
may cause local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in the stomach resulting in a slower rate
of absorption.
(k) Despite the importance of fluid, firefighters should be discouraged from drinking copious
quantities too rapidly. Rapid absorption of large volumes of water can result in excessive
dilution of blood ions (salts), with adverse effects.
(l) If in any doubt, seek medical advice.
(m) Further considerations
(1) Heat intolerance can be caused and exacerbated by a number of factors including
medication, diet and general wellbeing. These will influence a person’s ability to deal
with heat-related conditions.

(3) Benches and tables Lighting

8. BREATHING APPARATUS TELEMETRY SYSTEM

(a) Breathing apparatus telemetry system equipment should comply with relevant national and
international standards.
(b) The power of a radio frequency signal diminishes over distance. It will also be affected as the
radio wave passes through solid objects such as walls and floors of buildings, natural terrain,
basements tunnels, etc.
(c) To maximise the signal power of a radio frequency transmission, aerodrome rescue and
firefighting services should follow telemetry system provider guidance and may consider,
where appropriate, enhancing signal strength by using a leaky feeder and/or repeater units.
(d) Siting of the telemetry BA entry control board or unit should take into account the optimal
position for maximising the effective range of telemetry. It will therefore have a bearing on
the location of the BA ECP (BA entry control point).
(e) The procedures to be followed by individual aerodrome rescue and firefighting services in the
event of a loss of contact or breakdown in telemetry communications must take into account
the availability of other means of communication with BA teams, such as radio, thermal image
camera feed, cable communications and even direct speech.
Emergency total evacuation procedures
(a) Where two or more telemetry BA entry control boards or units are in use at the same incident
and an emergency total evacuation is required, each telemetry BA entry control board or unit
at the scene will initiate this level of evacuation.
(b) After transmitting an emergency total evacuation signal, an acknowledgement signal must be
sent from each telemetry radio unit to the telemetry BA entry control board or unit. In the
event of the acknowledgement signal not being received by the telemetry BA entry control
board or unit, the emergency total evacuation signal must be repeated.
(c) After sending an emergency total evacuation signal, it is imperative that the person
responsible for the BA ECP checks to ensure that all BA wearers committed to the risk area
through their BA entry control board are in telemetry. If this is not the case, the person
responsible for the BA ECP should try to establish radio communications with all BA wearers
committed to the risk area.
(d) If it is not possible to establish communications with BA crews, BA emergency procedures
should be considered.
Emergency Selective Evacuation Procedures
(a) Emergency selective evacuation is an integral emergency feature available when telemetry is
employed. It allows the person responsible for the BA ECP to evacuate specific BA teams in an

emergency while leaving other BA teams in place. For example, in certain circumstances it
may be necessary to ensure that an escape route remains protected while an evacuation takes
place, or to evacuate a BA team/s from an unacceptably hazardous situation.
(b) An emergency selective evacuation signal is an emergency procedure and must not be used
for any other purpose.
(c) Only those in specific command roles may decide that it is necessary to implement the
emergency selective evacuation procedure. The nominated person, under the overall
command of the incident commander, should decide which BA teams should be evacuated by
this method.
(d) After transmitting an emergency selective evacuation signal, an acknowledgement signal must
be sent from each telemetry radio unit to the telemetry BA entry control board or unit. In the
event of the acknowledgement signal not being received by the telemetry BA entry control
board or unit, the emergency selective evacuation signal must be repeated.
(e) After sending an emergency selective evacuation signal, it is imperative that the person
responsible for the BA ECP checks to ensure that all BA wearers committed to the risk area
through their BA entry control board are in telemetry. If this is not the case, the person
responsible for the BA ECP should try to establish radio communications with BA wearers
committed to the risk area.
(f) If it is not possible to establish communications with BA crews, BA emergency procedures
should be considered
BA Wearer Emergency-initiated Withdrawal in relation to BA Telemetry System
(a) BA Telemetry system gives each BA wearer the ability to initiate a signal indicating that they
are withdrawing from the risk area. The decision on whether or not to signal that withdrawal
rests with the BA wearer. When that withdrawal signal is activated, all members of that BA
team must withdraw from the risk area together.
(b) If the BA entry control operative receives a withdrawal signal from a BA wearer or wearers
committed to the risk area, they will acknowledge receipt of the signal and report this directly
to the person responsible for the BA entry control point. An immediate assessment of risk
should be undertaken to identify the subsequent actions to be taken.
Distress Alarm – Automatic and Manual in relation to BA Telemetry System
(a) In the event of a distress alarm (either manual or automatic) being sounded, as a minimum, a
signal will be transmitted to the relevant telemetry BA entry control board or unit.

(b) Only wearers in distress should activate a manual distress alarm. This will allow the BA ECP to
determine how many BA wearers require assistance.
(c) Note: In circumstances where the alarm of a BA wearer in distress cannot be activated, the
distress alarm belonging to another member of the team should be operated.
(d) If the BA entry control operative receives a distress signal (automatic or manual) from a BA
wearer committed to the risk area, they will acknowledge receipt of the signal and report this
through the command line to the incident commander or sector commander and other BA
entry control points.
(e) Following acknowledgement of the distress signal (automatic or manual), the person
responsible for the BA ECP will be expected to follow normal procedures on whether to
commit a BA emergency team immediately.
(f) If enquiries indicate that a distress signal (automatic or manual) does not originate from a
telemetry radio unit that is logged on, the incident commander must be notified, with a view
to passing the information to watchroom control so that checks can be initiated with
neighbouring incidents or fire and rescue services.
BA Telemetry System Communications Signal Failure
(a) There are various reasons for a loss of telemetry. The most likely is that the telemetry radio
unit is temporarily out of range of the telemetry BA entry control board or unit.
(b) Users of telemetry should be aware that, like any device that relies on radio transmissions,
telemetry radio units could be out of range because of their distance from the control board
or unit or owing to physiological conditions at the incident inhibiting effective radio broadcast.
(c) There may be locations where a Site-Specific Risk Assessment indicates that signal broadcast,
and therefore telemetry, will not be achieved. At these locations and/or risk premises,
aerodrome rescue and firefighting services should establish alternative control measures to
maintain effective BA command and control in the absence of telemetry.
7. BREATHING APPARATUS FACEMASK DONNING PROCEDURE AND SEAL TESTING
Facemask donning procedure
(a) This donning procedure is appropriate to all occasions that BA is worn, including training,
operational incidents and when taking over a set at the start of a shift or other time as
appropriate.
(b) Correct facemask fit is essential if the best possible face seal is to be achieved. The ideal fit is
achieved when all straps are tensioned and the chin and temple straps of the mask run in the

direction of the mask strap tongues. In order to get the best possible fit the following points
should be taken into account.
(c) Loosen all head harness straps, including the centre head strap, to their full extent.
(d) Place the facemask against the face by sliding it up to ensure that the chin is securely placed in
the chin cup. Ensure that hair does not compromise the facemask seal area. This may be more
easily achieved if the wearer leans forward whilst fitting the mask.
(e) Where multiple adjustable straps are fitted, adjust the bottom and middle straps progressively
and evenly in pairs to ensure that the head harness is ‘square’ on the back of the head,
finishing with the top strap. The fit should be secure and comfortable but not over-tight.
(f) BA wearers should visually check that each team members’ head harness is positioned
correctly on the head, with the straps in line with the mask tongues and evenly tensioned,
before fire hoods and helmets are donned. Repeat steps (c) to (e) if necessary.
Facemask seal test
(a) It is appropriate that the effectiveness of the facemask seal is tested on every occasion that
BA is donned with the intention of breathing from it. However, in some operational situations
it may be necessary to conduct an assessment of risk to establish the practicality of carrying
out the full-face seal test.
(b) The rigorous application of this test when taking over a set at the start of a shift, or other time
as appropriate, will ensure that the wearer is satisfied that they can achieve an effective seal
with that particular facemask.
(c) Procedures for testing the facemask seal are as follows:
(1) Hold breath and turn off the air supply to the mask keeping a hand on the cylinder
(2) valve.
(3) Observe the pressure gauge for approximately eight seconds whilst moving the head up
and down and side to side. There should be no discernible movement of the pressure
gauge. (The purpose of this is to ensure that the mask is properly fitted to the face.)
NOTE: Extreme movement of the head may cause some leakage, but this should cease once the
head is returned to a more central position and/or the head movement is less severe.
(4) Breathe steadily to exhaust the residual air in the system while observing the pressure
gauge until the gauge shows empty and noting the activation of the low-pressure
warning whistle/device.
(5) Turn the cylinder valve back on and take two or three normal breaths.

(6) Hold breath and again turn off the air supply to the mask keeping a hand on the cylinder
valve.
(7) Breathe steadily until the air is exhausted and inhale to cause the mask to collapse onto
the face.
(8) Hold the breath for approximately eight seconds to ensure that the facemask remains
firmly ‘sucked down’ onto the face. If there is a defect with the facemask or a poor fit
between the face and the mask, the wearer will be unable to generate a vacuum inside
the mask, thereby preventing the continued collapse onto the face.
(9) Turn on the air supply and breathe normally.
(d) If a leak is identified during any part of these tests, the facemask should be re-fitted with
particular attention to correct adjustment of the harness but without over-tightening the
harness and the tests re-applied.
Positive pressure protection
(a) Provided that BA facemasks are donned correctly and the facemask seal test are fully applied,
positive pressure can be expected to provide compensation for any slight mismatch between
the face seal and the face during use and will thus ensure adequate protection to the wearer.
(b) In the event that a gross facemask seal leak is identified, despite rigorous application of the
above procedures, aerodrome rescue and firefighting services should seek to provide an
alternative mask (e.g. different model, size, design, etc) that provides an adequate fit for the
individual.
(c) If a suitable alternative mask is not readily available, aerodrome rescue and firefighting
services should consult with their BA supplier to seek a suitable modification to the mask (e.g.
alteration to the mould, insert, etc). Should this option prove necessary, quantitative fit
testing of the individual, using appropriate apparatus is recommended to demonstrate the
improvement in fit.
Monitoring
(a) All existing BA wearers should be assessed to ensure that they can achieve an effective face
fit.
(b) It is recommended that a suitable record of completing this donning procedure, and gaining a
satisfactory facemask seal test result, be made on the first occasion that it is formally
undertaken by each employee and whenever the wearer experiences facial changes (weight
change, surgery, etc).

(c) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting services must ensure that appropriate systems are in place
to establish that the above procedures are fully applied on every occasion that BA is donned
with the intention of breathing from it.
New BA Wearer
(a) For the purpose of this guidance, new BA wearers are considered to be new employees, inter-
service transfers, personnel returning to operational duties after a significant period of time
involved in non- BA duties, personnel whose facial features have altered significantly through
weight change, dental work or similar and where the Aerodrome rescue and firefighting
service’s BA supplier changes.
(b) Sufficient training shall be provided to ensure that individuals can apply the facemask donning
procedure correctly. Each individual shall then complete the facemask seal test identified in
this guidance. All such training shall be recorded in the individual's personal training record.
(c) Should a gross facemask seal leak remain despite rigorous application of the above
procedures the process as detailed in 9.11 and 9.12 (Positive pressure protection) must be
applied.
Training
(a) The guidance provided on facemask donning procedures and facemask seal testing must be
formally incorporated into initial, refresher and BA instructor training.
8. WORKING ABBREVIATINS FOR USE ON BREATHING APPARATUS ENTRY CONTROL BOARDS
(b) It is recommended that aerodrome rescue and firefighting services use the following
abbreviations on breathing apparatus entry control boards to achieve consistency across BA
entry control points and fire and rescue authorities. All personnel at an incident should use
the same abbreviations.
(c) It is important to note that whilst working abbreviations may be deemed appropriate for use
on the BA entry control board at an incident, for brevity, speed of completion in time-critical
situations and due to space constraints on the BA board, any additional BA records
maintained at the BA ECP or at BA sector command should be written in full.

title: Fire prevention
text:
AERODROME FIRE PREVENTION
(a) An aerodrome operator shall establish and implement a power of entry for rescue and
firefighting service for the sole purpose of preventing or extinguishing a fire or protecting life
or property in a building, facility or aircraft at an aerodrome;
(b) An airside fire prevention programme shall be implemented at the aerodrome including:
(1) implementation of fire prevention measures during aircraft fuelling operations;
(2) prohibition of smoking within the aircraft movement area, other operational areas of
the aerodrome, or areas of the aerodrome where fuel or other flammable material is
stored;
(3) prohibition of display of an open flame or undertaking of an activity that would create a
fire hazard within:
(i) areas of the aerodrome where fuel operation takes place or other flammable
material is stored; and
(ii) the movement area or other operational areas of the aerodrome, unless
authorised by the aerodrome certificate holder;
(4) provision of sufficient fire extinguishing equipment suitable for an initial intervention in
the event of fuel fire including personnel trained in its use, are readily available during
the ground servicing of an aircraft;
(5) provision of a means of quickly summoning the rescue and firefighting service in the
event of a fire or fuel spillage is provided on the apron areas; and
(c) A landside fire prevention programme shall be implemented including terminal buildings and
other facilities at the aerodrome.

title: Fire prevention
text:
1. POWER OF ENTRY
(a) An officer of an aerodrome rescue and firefighting service should be authorised, in writing, for
the officer to do anything the officer reasonably believes to be absolute necessary within the
aerodrome boundary, to take the following actions:
(1) if the officer reasonably believes a fire to have broken out or to be about to break out,
for the purpose of extinguishing or preventing the fire or protecting life or property;
(2) if the officer reasonably believes a road traffic accident to have occurred, for the
purpose of rescuing people or protecting them from serious harm;

(3) if the officer reasonably believes an emergency of another kind to have occurred, for
the purpose of discharging any function conferred on the rescue and firefighting service
in relation to the emergency;
(4) for the purpose of preventing or limiting damage to property resulting from action
taken as mentioned in paragraph (1), (2) or (3).
(b) The authorised officer of the rescue and firefighting service, operating within the aerodrome
boundary, should consider the following actions:
(1) enter premises or a place, by force, if necessary, without the consent of the owner or
occupier of the premises, place or aircraft;
(2) move or break into a vehicle in airside without the consent of its owner;
(3) close an airside roadway, baggage tunnel or a premise;
(4) stop and regulate airside traffic; and
(5) restrict the access of unauthorised persons to premises, place or aircraft.
2. GATHERING INFORMATION AND CONDUCTING SAFETY INVESTIGATION
(a) When entering a building, facility or aircraft within the aerodrome boundary at any
reasonable time, the authorised officer may take the following actions:
(1) for the purpose of obtaining information needed for the discharge of an aerodrome
rescue and firefighting service’s functions under this section; or
(2) if there has been a fire in the building, facility or aircraft, for the purpose of conducting
a safety investigation for determining the root cause, corrective and preventive actions.
3. SUPPLEMENTARY POWERS
(a) When exercising a power of entry, the authorised officer may:
(1) take any other persons, and any equipment, that the officer considers necessary; and
(2) require any person present on the building, facility or aircraft to provide the officer with
any facilities, information, documents or records, or other assistance, that the officer
may reasonably request.
(3) inspect any documents or records on the building, facility or aircraft; and
(4) carry out any inspections, measurements and testing in relation to the building, facility
or aircraft, that the officer considers necessary.

title: Fire prevention
text:
PROVISION OF POWER OF ENTRY
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) The establishment and implementation of a formal power of entry for authorized officers of
the Aerodrome Rescue and Firefighting Service (ARFFS) is a critical requirement for ensuring
effective emergency response and operational readiness. Due to the statutory nature of
aerodrome operations, ARFFS officers must have the legal authority to enter all areas of the
aerodrome, and, where necessary, offsite locations, to perform their duties.
(b) This guidance document provides aerodrome operators with a structured approach to
establishing this power of entry. This includes formal agreements with local fire, police, and
security agencies, and the creation of robust internal policies and procedures to support
ARFFS operations. The guidance ensures that ARFFS officers can act swiftly and lawfully in
emergency situations, inspections, and other operational activities while adhering to the
highest standards of safety, security, and legal compliance.
2. REGULATORY AUTHORITY AND LEGAL CONSIDERATIONS
(a) Aerodrome operators are responsible for ensuring that the power of entry granted to ARFFS
officers is legally grounded in civil aviation regulations. This includes compliance with relevant
public safety legislation that governs emergency response and security protocols at
aerodromes. Operators must review statutory provisions to identify the specific legal basis for
granting ARFFS personnel the authority to enter restricted areas, both during emergencies
and in routine operations.
(b) This power of entry is essential for carrying out rescue, firefighting, and fire safety inspections,
as well as responding to hazardous situations. However, this power must be exercised in strict
accordance with legal guidelines to avoid misuse. Aerodrome operators must also ensure that
ARFFS officers are trained in the scope and limitations of their power of entry and that
appropriate oversight mechanisms are in place.
3. FORMAL AGREEMENTS WITH EXTERNAL AGENCIES
(a) To facilitate the effective exercise of power of entry, aerodrome operators must establish
formal agreements with relevant external agencies, including local fire services, police, and
security forces.
(b) These agreements should clearly define the conditions under which ARFFS personnel can
enter secured or restricted areas, ensuring that their legal authority is recognized and

supported by all stakeholders. For instance, agreements with local fire services should outline
protocols for joint emergency responses and access to offsite areas that may be necessary
during certain incidents. Similarly, police and security agencies must agree on procedures for
ARFFS officers to gain access to secure areas quickly during emergencies, without undue
delays caused by security protocols.
(c) These agreements should also establish communication channels and joint operational
procedures to ensure seamless coordination during incidents requiring interagency
cooperation.
4. ESTABLISHING INTERNAL POLICIES AND PROCEDURES
(a) Aerodrome operators must develop and implement comprehensive internal policies that
govern the exercise of power of entry by ARFFS personnel. These policies should clearly
articulate the situations in which entry may be required, including during emergency
responses, safety inspections, and hazard assessments. Additionally, operators must establish
clear procedural guidelines for notifying relevant stakeholders, such as air traffic control or
aerodrome management, when ARFFS officers exercise their power of entry. Every instance of
entry must be documented, recording the purpose of the entry, the personnel involved, and
any actions taken. This ensures accountability and provides a basis for auditing and
compliance checks. To avoid compromising aerodrome security, ARFFS personnel must carry
identification that verifies their authority to enter restricted areas and follow all relevant
safety and security protocols.
(b) Furthermore, aerodrome operators must ensure that all ARFFS personnel authorized to
exercise the power of entry are properly trained. This training should cover both the legal
framework that governs their authority and the operational procedures that they must follow
when entering restricted areas. Competency assessments should be conducted regularly to
ensure that officers remain fully qualified to exercise their powers, particularly in high-
pressure emergency situations where swift action is required.
5. MONITORING AND COMPLIANCE MECHANISMS
(a) To ensure that the power of entry is exercised responsibly and within the confines of the
regulations, aerodrome operators must implement rigorous monitoring and compliance
mechanisms. Regular audits should be conducted to review the use of power of entry by
ARFFS personnel, ensuring that each instance is properly documented and that statutory
provisions are adhered to. Aerodrome management should also establish a system for

reviewing all reports related to the exercise of power of entry, enabling them to identify any
areas where improvements are necessary.
(b) In the event of any misuse or failure to comply with established procedures, a formal
investigation must be conducted to determine the root cause and take appropriate corrective
action. This may include disciplinary measures for personnel involved, as well as revisions to
existing policies or procedures to prevent future occurrences. Incident reviews should be part
of a broader effort to continuously improve operational efficiency and safety at the
aerodrome.
6. REVIEW OF PROVISIONS
(a) The power of entry for ARFFS personnel is a vital component of aerodrome emergency
management and operational readiness. It enables authorized officers to carry out their duties
effectively, ensuring the safety of aerodrome operations and responding rapidly to
emergencies. To support this authority, aerodrome operators must establish formal
agreements with external agencies, develop robust internal policies, and implement
comprehensive training and oversight procedures. By doing so, they will ensure that ARFFS
officers are empowered to act within the bounds of the law, while maintaining the highest
standards of safety, security, and operational effectiveness.
(b) All aerodrome operators are urged to review their current practices and ensure that they are
in compliance with this regulatory guidance to enhance their emergency response capabilities
and maintain legal compliance.

title: Fire prevention
text:
FIRE PREVENTION PLANNING ARRANGEMENTS
(a) A competent person should be appointed with the authority and responsibility to manage the
fire prevention programme at the aerodrome.
(b) A fire prevention planning committee administered by the aerodrome operator should be
established with the following responsibilities:
(1) oversee all aspects of fire prevention programme within the aerodrome;
(2) review the effectiveness of the programme in compliance with relevant fire safety
regulations;
(3) develop appropriate strategies, policies and procedures to manage fire risks and
hazards; and

(4) review results of fire prevention inspection and fire investigation for improvements to
the programme.

title: Fire prevention
text:
COMPETENT PERSON
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) The objective of this guidance material is to ensure that aerodrome operators appoint a
competent person who possesses the appropriate knowledge, skills, experience, and
delegated authority to effectively manage the aerodrome’s fire prevention programme. The
appointed individual is responsible for leading fire risk assessments, developing and
maintaining fire safety controls, ensuring compliance with applicable codes, and promoting a
culture of fire safety across all operational areas of the aerodrome.
(b) Due to the size and complexity of aerodrome operations, it may be necessary for aerodrome
operators to form a dedicated fire prevention team lead by the competent person.
2. DESIGNATION AND AUTHORITY OF THE COMPETENT PERSON
(a) The Aerodrome Fire Prevention Programme Manager (AFPPM) or equivalent, is responsible
for the development, implementation, and continual improvement of the aerodrome’s fire
prevention programme. The designation will be issued in writing, signed by the accountable
manager or equivalent executive authority, and clearly state the scope of responsibilities,
reporting structure, and delegated authority of the individual.
(b) The appointed competent person is integrated within the aerodrome’s operational safety
framework and be granted sufficient autonomy and access to enforce fire prevention
protocols. This includes the authority to conduct inspections, halt unsafe operations, mandate
corrective actions, and liaise directly with RFFS, engineering and maintenance, airside
operations, and tenant organizations.
3. COMPETENCY AND QUALIFICATION CRITERIA
(a) The competent person must meet minimum competency requirements to ensure they are
capable of discharging their fire prevention duties in a safe, effective, and compliant manner.
The minimum qualifications include:
(1) A recognized qualification or certification in fire safety engineering, fire science, or fire
prevention;
(2) Completion of formal training in fire risk assessment, hazard identification, and control
strategies applicable to aerodrome environments;

(3) Demonstrated knowledge of fire safety guidance, national codes, and fire risk scenarios
unique to airport operations;
(4) At least three (3) years of relevant experience in fire safety or fire risk management,
with preference for aviation-related contexts.
(b) The competent person must demonstrate key competencies in hazard recognition, risk
mitigation, incident analysis, and emergency planning. The ability to prepare detailed fire risk
reports, conduct stakeholder briefings, and participate in the safety management system
(SMS) functions is essential. Ongoing professional development shall be encouraged to ensure
the individual remains informed of new fire prevention technologies and evolving risk profiles.
4. ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
(a) The competent person must develop, implement, and regularly update a formal Fire
Prevention Programme (FPP) for the aerodrome. This programme must be risk-based, scalable
to the complexity of the aerodrome, and integrated with the overall safety and emergency
preparedness frameworks.
(b) The key responsibilities of the competent person must include, but are not limited to:
(1) Conducting systematic fire risk assessments across all operational areas of the
aerodrome;
(2) Inspecting facilities, infrastructure, equipment, and operational practices to identify
potential fire hazards;
(3) Recommending and verifying the implementation of corrective or preventive fire safety
measures;
(4) Coordinating fire drills, awareness programmes, and tenant engagement activities on
fire prevention;
(5) Monitoring compliance with fire safety requirements and preparing periodic reports for
aerodrome management;
(6) Supporting investigations into fire incidents or near misses and tracking follow-up
actions;
(7) Liaising with the Rescue and Firefighting Services to ensure alignment between fire
prevention and emergency response strategies.
5. ORGANISATIONAL INTEGRATION
(a) The competent person must ensure the fire prevention programme integrates into the
aerodrome’s Safety Management System (SMS) and may serve as a member of the
Aerodrome Safety Committee or Emergency Planning Committee. They should maintain

regular coordination with the accountable manager, the safety manager, and the chief of the
RFFS.
(b) The competent person also acts as a focal point for interactions with national fire authorities,
civil defense departments, and other regulatory entities to ensure alignment with statutory
fire safety obligations.
