title: Fire prevention
text:
FIRE PREVENTION PLANNING COMMITTEE
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) This guidance material provides aerodrome operators with structured approach on the
establishment of an Aerodrome Fire Prevention Planning Committee (FPPC) to enhance
oversight, coordination, and continual improvement of the aerodrome’s fire prevention
programme. The committee is a strategic mechanism that brings together relevant internal
and external stakeholders to ensure that fire risks are effectively managed, and fire safety
objectives are consistently achieved in alignment with national regulations and provisions.
(b) The complexity of modern aerodrome facilities and environments necessitates a collaborative
and integrated approach to fire prevention. The FPPC provides a formal platform for
oversight, decision-making, and performance review concerning fire safety matters affecting
the entire aerodrome, including airside, terminal, landside, cargo, maintenance, fueling, and
tenant areas.
2. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
(a) The purpose of the FPPC is to serve as the primary governance structure responsible for the
strategic direction and operational oversight of the fire prevention programme at the
aerodrome. The committee functions as a sub-body of the aerodrome’s overall safety
governance framework and report to the Safety Management Review Board or equivalent
forum.
(b) The scope of the committee encompasses all aerodrome-controlled infrastructure and tenant
operations where fire hazards may arise. This includes oversight of compliance with applicable
fire safety legislation, codes of practice, regulatory guidance, and the aerodrome operator’s
fire safety policies and procedures.
3. COMMITTEE ESTABLISHMENT AND ADMINISTRATION
(a) The Fire Prevention Planning Committee is established by formal directive of the aerodrome
operator. The committee is chaired by a senior management representative from the

aerodrome’s operations, safety, or engineering division. The Fire Prevention Programme
Manager (FPPM) acts as the Secretary to the committee and is responsible for agenda
preparation, records of decisions, and follow-up actions.
(b) Membership of the committee should be multidisciplinary and may include representatives
from:
(1) Rescue and Firefighting Services (RFFS)
(2) Aerodrome Safety Management Unit
(3) Engineering and Maintenance Services
(4) Terminal or Facilities Management
(5) Airside and Apron Operations
(6) Fuel Handling and Storage Operators
(7) Cargo and Ground Handling Agents
(8) Tenant Safety Representatives
(9) Third-party or contracted organizations
(10) National or Local Fire Authority (where applicable)
(c) The committee convenes on a bi-annually basis, or more frequently as required by operational
needs or regulatory findings. Meeting records are retained in accordance with the
aerodrome’s documentation retention policy.
4. RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE COMMITTEE
(a) The Fire Prevention Planning Committee is responsible for the following core functions:
(1) Oversight of Fire Prevention Programme
(i) The committee provides strategic oversight over all aspects of the aerodrome’s
fire prevention programme. This includes reviewing programme design, risk
prioritization, implementation effectiveness, and alignment with organizational
safety objectives.
(ii) The committee ensures that sufficient resources, personnel, training, and
monitoring mechanisms are in place to support the ongoing implementation of
the fire prevention programme.
(2) Review of Programme Effectiveness and Regulatory Compliance
(i) The committee monitors the performance of the fire prevention programme in
terms of compliance with national fire safety legislation, and aerodrome operator
policies.

(ii) This includes ensuring that corrective actions arising from fire inspections,
internal audits, or external authority reviews are tracked, implemented, and
closed within acceptable timelines.
(3) Strategy and Policy Development
(i) The committee develops and updates appropriate strategies, policies, and
procedures to manage fire hazards and reduce fire risk across aerodrome
operations.
(ii) These strategies are informed by fire risk assessments, operational feedback,
emerging hazards, new technologies, and industry best practices.
(4) Review of Fire Inspections and Investigations
(i) The committee reviews the results of all scheduled and unscheduled fire
prevention inspections, including visits, facilities inspections, and tenant premises
walkthroughs.
(ii) The committee also reviews findings of fire-related safety investigations and
ensure that systemic lessons learned are applied to enhance the fire prevention
programme and related emergency preparedness measures.
5. PERFORMANCE MONITORING AND CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT
(a) The committee must establish key performance indicators (KPIs) and fire safety performance
targets to measure the effectiveness of the fire prevention programme. Regular trend
analyses of inspection findings, near misses, incident reports, and audit outcomes must be
conducted.
(b) Opportunities for improvement must be identified and included in a rolling action plan. The
committee also support the development of fire safety awareness campaigns and training
initiatives across the aerodrome community.
6. COORDINATION WITH THE SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
(a) The FPPC functions within the framework of the aerodrome’s Safety Management System
(SMS), supporting hazard identification, safety risk management, safety assurance, and safety
promotion in the domain of fire safety and fire prevention.
(b) The committee contributes to the safety reporting culture by promoting the open and timely
reporting of fire hazards, unsafe conditions, and non-compliances.

title: Fire prevention
text:
AIRSIDE FIRE PREVENTION PROGRAMME

(a) A fire prevention programme for the control of smoking or other operational activities that
may cause fire hazards at airside should be established and implemented at the aerodrome,
including:
(1) provision of adequate procedures, personnel, resources and equipment to implement
the plan;
(2) adoption and use of mitigating measures, when necessary, activities (e.g. maintenance,
fuelling, hot works, etc.) which might involve fire hazards need to be authorised;
(3) authorisation of activities that may not include smoking within the movement area,
other operational areas of the aerodrome, or areas of the aerodrome where fuel or
other flammable material are stored;

board or embark/disembark during refuelling operations;

(6) fire prevention promotional plans and procedures to educate airside community;

title: Fire prevention
text:
AIRCRAFT FUELLING PRACTICES
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) The aerodrome operator, the aircraft operator and the fuel supplier have respective
responsibilities in respect of the safety measures to be taken during fuelling operations. Some
guidance on these safety measures is given below. It is important to note that this material is
not intended to replace fuel supplier operator procedures which are usually developed to
meet requirements imposed by special equipment, national regulations, etc. The material
includes the following subjects:
(1) general precautionary measures to be taken during fuelling operations; and
(2) additional precautionary measures to be taken when passengers remain on board or
embark/disembark during refuelling operations.
(b) The term fuelling encompasses both refuelling and defueling operations at airside.

(c) Further information on internationally accepted petroleum and aviation industry fuel
practices, including fuel quality control and operations, can be found in the Manual on Civil
Aviation Jet Fuel Supply (Doc 9977).
2. GENERAL PRECAUTIONARY MEASURES TO BE TAKEN DURING AIRCRAFT FUELLING OPERATIONS
(a) The following general precautionary measures should be taken during aircraft fuelling
operations:
(1) aircraft fuelling operations should be done outdoors; and
(2) bonding and/or grounding, as appropriate, should be done;
(3) aircraft fuelling vehicles should be positioned so that:
(i) accessibility to aircraft by RFF vehicles is not interrupted;
(ii) a cleared path is maintained to permit rapid removal of fuelling vehicles from an
aircraft in an emergency;
(iii) they do not obstruct evacuation from occupied portions of the aircraft in the
event of a fire; and
(iv) the vehicle engines are not under the wing;
(4) all vehicles performing aircraft servicing functions other than fuel servicing (e.g.
baggage trucks, etc.) should not be driven or be parked under aircraft wings while
fuelling is in progress;
(5) open flames and lighted open flame devices should be prohibited on the apron and in
other locations within 15 m of any aircraft fuelling operation. Included in the category
of open flames and lighted open flame devices are the following:
(i) lighted cigarettes, cigars, pipes;
(ii) exposed flame heaters;
(iii) welding or cutting torches, etc.; and
(iv) flare pots or other open flame lights;
(6) cigarette lighters or matches should not be carried or used by anyone while engaged in
aircraft fuelling operations;
(7) extreme caution should be used when fuelling during lightning and electrical storms.
The fuelling operations should be suspended during severe lightning disturbances in the
immediate vicinity of the aerodrome;
(8) when any part of an aircraft undercarriage is abnormally heated, the aerodrome rescue
and firefighting service should be immediately notified and fuelling should not take
place until the heat has dissipated; and

(9) portable fire extinguishing equipment suitable for at least initial intervention in the
event of fuel fire and personnel trained in its use shall be readily available, and there
shall be a means of quickly summoning the rescue and firefighting service in the event
of a fire or major fuel spill. It should be ensured by regular inspection and maintenance
that this equipment is maintained in a fully serviceable condition.
3. ADDITIONAL PRECAUTIONARY MEASURES TO BE TAKEN WHEN PASSENGERS REMAIN ON
BOARD OR EMBARK/DISEMBARK DURING REFUELLING OPERATIONS
(a) Because of the importance of reducing transit times and for security reasons, aerodrome
operator in consultation with the aircraft operator, after conducting a fire risk assessment,
may allow passengers to remain on board during refuelling operations while others allow
passengers to embark and disembark. However, an aircraft should not be refuelled when
passengers are embarking, on board or disembarking unless it is properly staffed by qualified
personnel ready to initiate and direct an evacuation of the aircraft by the most practical and
expeditious means available.
(b) When aircraft refuelling operations take place while passengers are embarking, on board or
disembarking, ground equipment should be positioned so as to allow:
(1) the use of a sufficient number of exits for expeditious evacuation; and
(2) a ready escape route from each of the exits to be used in an emergency.
(3) The following additional precautions should be observed during refuelling operations
while passengers remain on board or embarking/disembarking:
(4) passengers should be warned that refuelling will take place and that they should not
smoke, operate switches or otherwise produce sources of ignition;
(5) the illuminated “No smoking” signs and exit lighting should be switched on;
(6) aircraft equipped with integral stairs should have them deployed, or if aircraft stairways
are used, these should be positioned at each of the main doors normally used for
passenger embarkation or disembarkation which should be open or ajar and free from
obstruction.
(7) if, during refuelling, the presence of fuel vapour is detected in the aircraft interior, or
any other hazard arises, refuelling and all cleaning activities using electrical equipment
within the aircraft should be immediately stopped until safe conditions permit
resumption; and

(8) where passengers are embarking or disembarking during refuelling, their route should
avoid areas where fuel vapours are likely to be present and this movement should be
under the supervision of a responsible person.

title: Fire prevention
text:
LANDSIDE FIRE PREVENTION PROGRAMME

1. GENERAL.
(a) The intent of this guidance material is to help the aerodrome operator in establishing and
implementing minimum requirements to prevent fires and to protect aerodrome employees
and public from the hazards of fires, and establishes the Aerodrome Fire Prevention
Programme (AFPP).
(b) This guidance acts as a complementary material and does not supersede the UAE Fire and Life
Safety Code of Practice (UAE Fire Code). Where there is a doubt or conflict, the UAE Fire Code
takes precedence.
2. AIM AND OBJECTIVES.
(a) The aim of the Aerodrome Fire Prevention Programme (AFPP) is first to prevent fires, and,
second, should fire break out, to ensure that fires create no threat to the public or hazards to
employees. Property damage from fire should be held to a minimum, as should the impact of
fire and related perils on the programme.
(b) The primary objective of the AFPP is to allow critical aerodrome building or facility to continue
during a fire emergency for a sufficient time to safely transition prior to a facility becoming
inoperable or untenable for human occupancy. In order to achieve this objective, specific
operations will require additional protection to that specified by applicable laws, regulations
or standards. Such operations will rely on early detection of a fire incident, effective
protection for critical operations, as well as planning and training of aerodrome personnel to
accomplish this objective. As a minimum, all critical aerodrome buildings and facilities should
be designed and operated to achieve the objective of the AFPP.
(c) The AFPP requires adherence to and compliance with all applicable UAE laws, orders,
regulations, codes, standards, guidelines, policies, and good practices pertaining to fire
prevention and protection. In many cases, local fire regulations will require the major
attention.
(d) To ensure the efficacy of the AFPP in meeting its intended aim and objectives, it may be
necessary for the aerodrome operator or a delegated suitable competent service
provider/person to be designated as an Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) for all fire and life
safety prevention programmes within the aerodrome. An AHJ status may require an
acceptance or authorisation from the national fire authority or other relevant government
agency.
(e) A sample aerodrome fire prevention manual template is provided below.

INTRODUCTION
The purpose of this template is to provide a sample for developing a comprehensive airport fire
prevention manual. Each section should be elaborated with specific details relevant to the
particular airport, its operations, and infrastructure. Regular updates and adherence to local UAE
fire code regulations and align with key NFPA standards such as NFPA 409 (Aircraft Hangars),
NFPA 407 (Aircraft Fuel Servicing), and NFPA 403 (Aircraft Rescue and Fire-Fighting Services at
Airports). The framework should be comprehensive, covering everything from risk assessment to
emergency response and training.

title: APPENDICES
text:
• Emergency Contact Information: List of essential contacts (civil defense, ARFFS,
management).
• Forms and Checklists: Standard forms for reporting, risk assessments, and inspections.
• Reference Materials: Additional resources for in-depth understanding of specific
topics.

DEFINITIONS.
(a) Authority Having Jurisdiction. An AHJ is an organization, office, or individual who is responsible
for enforcing the requirements of a code or standard, or for approving equipment, materials, an
installation, or a procedure.
(b) Automatic fire detection device. A device designed to detect automatically the presence of fire
by heat, flame, light, smoke or other products of combustion.
(c) Fire emergency plan. A plan for a workplace, or parts thereof, describing what procedures the
employer and employees should take to ensure employee safety from fire or other emergencies.
(d) Emergency exit route. The route that employees are directed to follow in the event they are
required to evacuate the workplace or seek a designated refuge area.
(e) Fire extinguishing system. A permanently installed system that either extinguishes or controls a
fire at the location of the system.
(f) Hazardous materials. Those materials presenting dangers beyond the fire problems relating to
flash point and boiling point. These dangers can arise from, but are not limited to, toxicity,
reactivity, instability, or corrosivity.
(g) Means of egress. A continuous and unobstructed way of exit travel from any point in a building
or structure to a public way and consists of three separate and distinct parts: the way of exit
access, the exit, and the way of exit discharge. A means of egress comprises the vertical and
horizontal ways of travel and shall include all intervening room spaces, doorways, hallways,
corridors, passageways, balconies, ramps, stairs, enclosures, lobbies, escalators, horizontal exits,
courts, and yards.
(h) National Fire Codes. National Fire Codes are published by the National Fire Protection
Association (NFPA), and provide guidance on fire safety issues (e.g., NFPA 101). UAE Fire and Life
Safety Code of Practice also adopted these National Fire Codes, although they may supplement
them where local circumstances so warrant.
(i) Sprinkler system. A system of piping designed in accordance with fire protection engineering
standards and installed to control or extinguish fires. The system includes an sufficient and
reliable water supply and a network of specially sized piping and sprinklers which are
interconnected. The system also includes a control valve and a device for actuating an alarm
when the system is in operation.
BASIC ELEMENTS OF AN AERODROME FIRE PREVENTION PROGRAMME.
(a) The aerodrome operator should ensure an AFPP is developed which includes the appointment in
writing of an Aerodrome Fire Prevention Programme Manager (AFPPM) – a competent person

responsible to oversee and manage the AFPP. Depending on the size and complexity of the
aerodrome, the AFPPM should be supported by a team of professionals who have
responsibilities dealing with the application of fire safety, protection, prevention, and
suppression technologies, which may include:
(1) facility managers;
(2) fire risk managers,
(3) loss control specialists,
(4) fire marshals,
(5) fire safety inspectors / investigators,
(6) fire protection designers,
(7) fire protection engineers, and
(8) fire code enforcers.
(b) The AFPP should be coordinated with the aerodrome emergency plan, and it should be
consistent with the provisions of the aerodrome emergency plan. The use of other contingency
plans (e.g., the business continuity plan) is acceptable provided that all relevant elements of the
AFPP are included. The AFPP should contain the following elements as a minimum:
(1) Fire Protection Plan. There shall be a written fire protection plan for all aerodrome facilities.
Individual and specific plans shall be developed for normally staffed facilities. Facilities that
are not normally staffed can be included in a more generic fire protection plan developed by
AFPPM or facility type. Each facility shall develop a list of the major fuel source fire hazards
and applicable storage and handling procedures. The plan shall also identify potential
ignition sources (such as welding and smoking) and the appropriate fire protection
procedures and equipment that will control a fire involving these sources. Where the
aerodrome operator  has leased space or facilities, or facilities with joint or multi-
occupancies, every effort shall be made to determine all fuel source fire hazards and ignition
sources, including those outside of aerodrome operator  ownership and control. In addition,
where the aerodrome operator  has leased space, responsibility for fire prevention shall be
negotiated with the building owner as appropriate and expressed in writing. The names or
regular job titles of those aerodrome personnel responsible for maintenance of equipment
and systems used to prevent or control ignitions or fires should be listed, as well as the
names of those responsible for fuel source hazards.
(2) Emergency Procedures. Responsible organizations within each facility should establish a
written emergency action plan that addresses the types of personnel evacuation to be used
in emergency circumstances, and the alarm system that is to be used to notify occupants of

the evacuation. The written plan should be kept at the workplace and made available for
employee review.
(3) Fire emergency plan (FEP). A FEP addresses those specific actions aerodrome employees
and contract personnel should take to ensure safety from fire and other emergencies. The
following elements, at a minimum, should be included in the FEP:
(i) Emergency escape procedures and emergency exit route assignments.
(ii) Procedures to be followed by employees who are to remain at their duties to
operate critical operations before they evacuate.
(iii) Procedures to locate and account for all employees and contract employees after
emergency evacuation has been completed.
(iv) Rescue and medical duties for those employees or other employees (by contract or
other agreement) who may be requested as volunteers or required to perform
them.
(v) The preferred means of reporting fires and other emergencies.
(vi) Procedures to be followed to assist disabled employees during evacuation.
(vii) Names or regular job titles of persons or organizational units who can be contacted
for further information or explanation of duties under the FEP.
(4) Evacuation Procedures and Means of Egress. The FEP should address the methods and
routes of evacuation to be used by employees in emergency circumstances and be
coordinated with existing emergency plans and orders. All such exits should never be used
for storage of any materials, and have non-combustible surface finishes with appropriate
surface burning and flame-spread classification. The plan should reflect the following
requirements:
(i) Every building or structure designed for human occupancy should be provided with
sufficient exits to permit the prompt and safe escape of occupants, including
persons with disabilities (PWD), in case of fire or other emergency.
(ii) In every building or structure, exits should be so arranged and maintained as to
provide free and unobstructed egress from all parts of the building or structure at
all times when it is occupied. Special accommodations should be made for PWD’s.
(iii) Every exit should be clearly visible or the route to reach it should be conspicuously
indicated so that every occupant of the building or facility knows the direction of
escape. Any door, passage, or stairway that is neither an exit nor a way of exit
access, and that is located or arranged so that it is likely to be mistaken for an exit,
should be identified by a sign reading “NO EXIT.”

(iv) Means of egress in buildings or structures should, as a minimum, meet the
requirements of the UAE Fire Codes.
(5) Training. Before implementing the FEP, the aerodrome operator should ensure sufficient
personnel are trained and designated to assist in the safe and orderly emergency evacuation
of employees, and should review the plan with each employee covered by the plan initially
when the plan is developed, at least annually thereafter, and whenever the plan or the
employee’s responsibilities or designated actions under the plan change.
(6) Housekeeping. Sufficient responsible personnel are assigned to control accumulations of
flammable and combustible waste materials and residues so that they do not contribute to a
fire emergency. The housekeeping procedures should be included in the written fire
prevention plan.
(7) Maintenance. Sufficient responsible personnel are assigned to regularly and properly
maintain, according to established procedures, all equipment, fire, and life safety systems.
The maintenance procedures should be included in the written fire prevention plan.
FIRE PROTECTION EQUIPMENT.
(a) Fire Extinguishing Equipment. Three basic options exist at the time of a fire emergency. First,
office holders may choose to evacuate all employees from the workplace at the time of a fire
emergency. In this case, requirements regarding manual fire extinguishing equipment are mainly
not applicable. Second, there are those workplaces where office holders have chosen to permit
certain employees to fight fires with portable fire extinguishers, and to evacuate all other non-
essential employees at the time of a fire emergency. Third, there may be those workplaces
where office holders have chosen to permit all employees in the workplace to use portable fire
extinguishers to fight fires.
(1) Portable Fire Extinguishers. Where the office holders have chosen to partially evacuate the
workplace or the affected area at the time of a fire emergency, and has permitted certain
designated employees to remain behind to operate critical operations or to fight fires with
extinguishers, those employees who will be remaining to perform incipient stage firefighting
should be trained in the principles of fire extinguisher use and the hazards involved with
incipient stage firefighting. The AFPPM is responsible for the proper selection and
distribution of fire extinguishers. The selection and distribution of fire extinguishers should
reflect the type and class of fire hazards associated with a particular workplace or facility.
(2) Standpipe Systems (Fire Hoses). Fire hoses may be substituted for portable fire
extinguishers. Any substitution should provide the same coverage that portable fire

extinguishers provide, and should be readily accessible with the hose attached and ready for
service.
(b) Fire Detection, Suppression, and Alarm Systems. Fire detection systems should be designed by
knowledgeable engineers or other professionals with expertise in fire detection systems, and
should be maintained in compliance with UAE Fire Codes in an operable condition except during
repairs or maintenance. When systems are out of service for repair or maintenance, an alternate
means of detection and alarm should be provided (e.g., fire watch). A trained person
knowledgeable in the operations and functions of the system should perform maintenance and
testing of fire detection systems, including cleaning and necessary sensitivity adjustments.
(c) Automatic Sprinkler Systems. Automatic sprinkler systems are the best fire protection system
for the workplace.
(1) All automatic sprinkler designs in aerodrome facilities should provide the necessary
discharge patterns, densities, and water flow characteristics for complete coverage in a
particular workplace or zoned subdivision of the workplace.
(2) The AFPPM should assure that only code and systems-accepted equipment and devices are
used in the design and installation of automatic sprinkler systems.
(d) Evacuation Alarms. If required by code, an alarm system should be installed to provide warning
for necessary emergency action as called for in the FEP, or for reaction time for safe escape of
employees from the workplace or the immediate work area, or both. All alarm systems should
be maintained in operating condition except when undergoing repairs or maintenance, and
should be tested for reliability and adequacy at least monthly. When systems are going to be
down for repair or maintenance, an alternate system is required.
AERODROME FACILITIES & OPERATIONS.
(a) Facility Control. Managers of facilities should ensure the following:
(1) That employees have been trained and understand their fire prevention and protection
responsibilities within the work environment.
(2) That the facility is in a fire safe condition at all times.
(3) That occupant load information for assembly facilities is maintained in the AFPPM’s office.
Every room constituting assembly occupancy and not having fixed seats should have the
occupant load of the room posted in a conspicuous location near the main exit from the
room.

(b) Aerodrome Traffic Control Towers (ATCT). Requirements for plans concerning emergency
action, fire prevention, and fire drills should be referred to US Standard 29 CFR 1960.20,
Alternate Standard for Fire Safety in Aerodrome Traffic Control Towers (ATCT).
(c) Aircraft Ground Operations. Aircraft ground operations should meet the requirements of the
NFPA 407, Aircraft Fuel Servicing; NFPA 409, Aircraft Hangars; and NFPA 410, Aircraft
Maintenance.

FIRE RISK ASSESSMENT
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) The purpose of an aerodrome fire risk assessment is to identify the fire hazards, identify
people at risk, evaluate, remove or reduce the risks, record findings, prepare an emergency
plan and provide training and review and update regularly.
(b) The qualified fire risk assessor will reference a question template when completing the
assessment, the completed report or survey can document the following examples.
(2) Electrical sources of ignition
(3) Smoking
(4) Arson/wilful fire raising
(5) Portable heaters and heating installations
(6) Cooking
(7) Lightning
(8) Housekeeping
(9) Hazards introduced by outside contractors and builders
(10) Dangerous substances
(11) Other significant fire hazards
(12) Means of escape from fire
(13) Measures to limit fire spread and development
(14) Emergency escape lighting
(15) Fire safety signs and notices
(16) Means of giving warning in case of fire
(17) Manual fire extinguishing appliances
(18) Relevant automatic fire extinguishing systems
(19) Other relevant fixed systems and equipment
(20) Management of fire safety procedures and arrangements

(21) Training and drills
(22) Testing and maintenance
(23) Records
1. DETAILS OF THE BUILDING
(a) Including responsible person, competent persons, floors, lifts, basements and stairwells.
2. FIRE PROTECTION
(a) Including firefighting facilities, fire alarm system, extinguishers, fire blankets, fire hoses,
sprinkler systems and extract systems.
3. FIRE HAZARDS
(a) Including sources of ignition, sources of fuel and sources of oxygen.
4. PEOPLE AT RISK
(a) Including numbers of employees, guests, visitors, customers, contractors, patients and tenants
and considerations made for mobility impairment, vision impairment, hearing impairment, lone
workers, elderly persons, language, substance abuse, cognitive disability and young persons
5. MEANS OF ESCAPE
(a) Including measurements and travel distances.
6. RISK RATINGS
(a) It is common for an assessor to use a matrix for calculating risk in their report.
7. SIGNIFICANT FINDINGS
(a) Including any problems identified and recommendations for fixing.
8. PHOTOGRAPHS AND SUPPORTING EVIDENCE
(a) A fire risk assessor may ask for documents or take pictures while on your premises.
(b) For fire risk assessment guidance and recommended methodology, aerodrome operator  may
refer to BS PAS 79 Fire Risk Assessment or NFPA 551, Guide for the Evaluation of Fire Risk
Assessments.
9. FIRE SAFETY RISK ASSESSMENT
The risk assessment process involves an inspection of the premises to identify potential fire
hazards, to ensure adequate measures to stop fire starting and that adequate fire protection
measures are in place to protect everyone in the building. See Figure-28 on the 5 key steps and fill
in the checklist. See Table 45 on sample fire safety risk assessment checklist template.

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
AERODROME WORKS SAFETY
(a) In accordance with CAR AGA PART ADR ADR.OPS.B.070, an aerodrome operator shall
establish and implement procedures to ensure that:
(1) aircraft safety is not affected by aerodrome works;
(2) aerodrome works safety is not affected by aerodrome operational activities; and
(3) airfield work permit system is established and implemented involving all relevant stake
holders.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:

(a) General requirements on aerodrome works safety is detailed in CAR AGA AMC1
ADR.OPS.B.070

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
RFFS RESPONSE CAPABILITY ASSESSMENT
(a) An assessment should be conducted, as part of the initial design study of the aerodrome
works, to determine the extent to which aerodrome works is likely to affect the response
capability or operational performance of the rescue and firefighting service and other
emergency services in the event of emergencies at an aerodrome or work site.

(b) Suitable mitigation measures including notification of all relevant agencies of the measures
should be developed, where the proposed aerodrome works may impact the response
capability of the rescue and firefighting service and other emergency services.
(c) Where necessary, changes to the aerodrome emergency plan and/or operational procedures
should be made, prior to the commencement of the aerodrome works
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

text:

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
SUPPLEMENTARY WATER SUPPLY ASSESSMENT
(a) Notwithstanding the requirements mentioned in AMC2 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.020(a) Rescue and
firefighting, an assessment should be conducted to determine impact to supplementary water
supply requirements at an aerodrome arising from the aerodrome works.
(b) Where there is an impact to the airport supplementary water supply, additional requirements
to support the aerodrome works in case of emergencies should be determined.
(c) Where required, additional supplementary water supply systems, facilities and equipment
should be provided.
(d) Where there are changes to the supplementary water supply systems, facilities and
equipment at the aerodrome, the following actions should be taken:
(1) notify rescue and firefighting service and/or other emergency services; and
(2) develop appropriate contingency measures.

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
FIRE RISK ASSESSMENT
(a) Fire risk assessments of the aerodrome works should be conducted, reviewed and maintained.

(b) Suitable fire prevention measures should be established including control of no-smoking, hot
works, use of flammable/combustible materials, fuelling, emergency response and
evacuation, etc;
(c) A fire prevention programme of the aerodrome works should be established and
implemented.
(d) Where necessary, changes to the aerodrome emergency plan and/or operational procedures
prior to the commencement of the aerodrome works should be developed.

title: Provision of services and/or activities
text:
PROVISION OF SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) The services and/or activities under this SUBPART shall be provided at the aerodrome by the
aerodrome operator either directly or indirectly.
(b) Where the services contained in this SUBPART are provided by a third party either fully or
partially, an aerodrome operator shall establish and implement safety oversight of the
provisions, in accordance with the aerodrome operator’s safety management system, to
ensure compliance with the requirements contained in this Regulation.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Provision of services and/or activities
text:
PROVISION OF SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) The services and/or activities contained in this SUBPART need to be provided at an
aerodrome. In some cases, these services and/or activities are not directly provided by the
aerodrome operator, but by a third-party organisation or combination of both. However, the
aerodrome operator, being responsible for the operation of the aerodrome should have
arrangements and interfaces with the third party to ensure that these services and/or
activities are provided according to the legal requirements. The method described above
meets with the intention of an integrated Safety Management System that helps the
aerodrome operator to ensure the safety objective of the provision is being met.

title: Emergency planning
text:
AERODROME EMERGENCY PLANNING
(a) An aerodrome operator shall:
(1) establish and implement an aerodrome emergency plan that is in accordance with
aerodrome certification requirements stated in CAR AGA PART ADR;
(2) ensure the emergency plan commensurate with the aircraft operations and other
activities conducted at the aerodrome;
(3) ensure the emergency plan provide for the coordination of the actions to be taken in an
emergency occurring at an aerodrome or in its vicinity;
(4) ensure the emergency plan coordinate the response or participation of all existing
agencies which, in the opinion of the aerodrome operator, could be of assistance in
responding to an emergency; and
(5) ensure the emergency plan observe human factors principles to ensure optimum
response by all existing agencies participating in emergency operations.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
AIM AND OBJECTIVES
(a) Aerodrome emergency planning is the process of preparing an aerodrome to cope with an
emergency occurring at the aerodrome or in its vicinity.
(b) The objective of aerodrome emergency planning is to minimize the effects of an emergency,
particularly in respect of saving lives and maintaining aircraft operations.
(c) The aerodrome emergency plan sets forth the procedures for coordinating the response of
different aerodrome agencies (or services) and of those agencies in the surrounding
community that could be of assistance in responding to the emergency.

(d) Guidance in establishing aerodrome emergency plan can refer to GM1
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

(a) Examples of emergencies are: aircraft emergencies, sabotage including bomb threats,
unlawfully seized aircraft, dangerous goods occurrences, building fires, natural disaster and
public health emergencies.

(b) Examples of public health emergencies are increased risk of travellers or cargo spreading a
serious communicable disease internationally through air transport and severe outbreak of a
communicable disease potentially affecting a large proportion of aerodrome staff.
(c) Guidance in developing aerodrome emergency plan document can refer to GM1 AMC2

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY COMMAND FACILITIES
(a) A fixed emergency operations centre and a mobile command post should be available for use
during an emergency at the aerodrome.
(b) The emergency operations centre should be part of the aerodrome facilities and is responsible
for the overall coordination and general direction of the response to an emergency.
(c) The mobile command post is a facility capable of being moved rapidly to the site of an
emergency, and should undertake the local coordination of those agencies responding to the
emergency;
(d) A person should be assigned to assume control of the emergency operations centre and
another person at the mobile command post.

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCY EXERCISES
An aerodrome operator shall:
(a) ensure the emergency plan contain procedures for periodic testing of the adequacy of the
plan and for reviewing the results in order to improve its effectiveness.
(b) ensure the emergency plan is tested by conducting:
(1) a full-scale aerodrome emergency exercise at intervals not exceeding three years and
partial emergency exercises in the intervening year to ensure that any deficiencies
found during the full-scale aerodrome emergency exercise have been corrected; or
(2) a series of modular tests commencing in the first year and concluding in a full-scale
aerodrome emergency exercise at intervals not exceeding four years; and
(3) reviewed thereafter, or after an actual emergency, so as to correct any deficiency found
during such exercises or actual emergency.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
PLANNING AND CONDUCTING EMERGENCY EXERCISES
(a) Procedures for planning and conducting aerodrome emergency exercises should be
established and implemented.
(b) Results of emergency exercises should be reviewed and addressed in order to improve the
effectiveness of the emergency plan.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
FULL-SCALE AND PARTIAL EMERGENCY EXERCISES
(a) Testing and exercising the emergency plan should commensurate with the types of aircraft
operations and operational activities.
(b) Emergency exercises should be sufficiently planned and managed with clear aims and
objectives.

(c) Participation of on and off aerodrome agencies and its associated personnel and resources as
per emergency plan should be included.
(d) Where an aerodrome operates aircraft movement and other major operational activities at
night, emergency exercises should be conducted during the hours of darkness.
(e) Records of emergency exercises should be maintained and readily available for audit and
inspection by the GCAA.
(f) The GCAA should be notified, at least, 1-month before the planned full-scale emergency
exercise.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
FULL-SCALE AND PARTIAL EMERGENCY EXERCISES
(a) It may be appropriate to test some parts of the emergency plan in isolation, provided
satisfactory assurance of overall effectiveness of the emergency plan can be achieved.
(b) The GCAA may attend exercise pre-briefing, testing or debriefing, or choose to attend
emergency exercises conducted at the aerodrome.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
PURPOSES OF EMERGENCY EXERCISES
(a) The purpose of a full emergency exercise is to ensure the adequacy of the plan to cope with
different types of emergencies.
(b) The purpose of a partial emergency exercise is to ensure the adequacy of the response to
individual participating agencies and components of the plan, such as the communications
system.
(c) The purpose of a table-top emergency exercise is to test the integration and capability of
emergency response resources without the expense and disruption of services incurred by a
partial and full emergency exercise.
(d) Guidance on planning and managing aerodrome emergency exercises refer to GM3 AMC1
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
MODULAR TESTING
(a) The purpose of modular tests is to enable concentrated effort on specific components of
established emergency plans.
(b) Guidance on planning and conducting a modular test can refer to GM AMC2
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
REVIEWING EMERGENCY PLAN AFTER EXERCISE OR ACCIDENT
(a) The emergency plan should be reviewed after emergency exercises and aircraft accident at
the aerodrome.
(b) Findings and improvement areas resulting from emergency exercises and aircraft accident
should be recorded and addressed for the purpose of continuous improvements to the
emergency plan.
(c) Records of emergency exercises should be retained for at least five years for audit and
inspection by the GCAA.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:

title: Emergency planning
text:
DEFERRING EMERGENCY EXERCISE AFTER AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT

(a) Following an aircraft accident or serious incident at the aerodrome, the aerodrome operator
may request for a deferment of the planned emergency exercises. Any deferment request
should be submitted, in writing to the GCAA by providing an assessment of all actions taken
during the accident against the relevant emergency orders and instructions contained in the
emergency plan.
(b) Where a deferment is successful, partial and full-scale emergency exercises should be
conducted no later than 24-months or as determined by the GCAA.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
DEFERMENT OF EMERGENCY EXERCISE AFTER ACCIDENT/INCIDENT
(a) An assessment for exercise deferment includes all actions taken during the aircraft accident
against the applicable references of the emergency plan and supporting evidences i.e.,
incident reports, transcripts, recordings, logs, etc.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCIES IN DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENTS
(a) An aerodrome operator shall ensure the emergency plan include the ready availability of, and
coordination with, appropriate specialist rescue services to be able to respond to emergencies
where an aerodrome is located close to water and/or swampy areas and where a significant
portion of approach or departure operations takes place over these areas.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Emergency planning
text:
EMERGENCIES IN DIFFICULT ENVIRONMENTS
(a) At those aerodromes located close to water, and/or swampy areas, or difficult terrain, the
emergency plan should include the establishment, testing and assessment at regular intervals
of a predetermined response for the specialist rescue services.
(b) For a water aerodrome, the emergency plan should consider the particular hazards associated
with seaplane operations, including:
(1) passenger evacuation into a further life-threatening environment, e.g., deep water; the
onset of hypothermia, and its associated effects, during and following prolonged
immersion in cold water; and
(2) the immediate toxicity and respiratory effects on survivors in the water following the
ingestion of floating fuel and oils and their associated vapours, and fire suppressant
foams, powders and gases;

(3) contain sufficient provisions for water rescue and fire response; and
(c) An assessment of the approach and departure areas within 1 000 m of the runway threshold
should be carried out to determine the options available for intervention.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

text:

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROVISION OF SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) No person or organisation shall provide rescue and firefighting services, activities, facilities
and equipment to civil aviation within the United Arab Emirates except under the authority of
the GCAA and in accordance with the provisions contained under this Regulation.
(b) An aerodrome operator shall ensure rescue and firefighting services, activities, facilities and
equipment are provided at the aerodrome.
(c) Where an aerodrome is located close to water/swampy areas, or difficult terrain, and where a
significant portion of approach or departure operations takes place over these areas, an
aerodrome operator shall ensure specialist rescue services and firefighting equipment
appropriate to the hazard and risk are made available.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROVISION OF RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING SERVICE
(a) Rescue and firefighting service should come under the administrative control of the
aerodrome operator, that is responsible for ensuring that the service provided is organised,

equipped, staffed, trained and operated in such a manner as to fulfil its proper function and
achieve compliance with this regulation.
(b) Additional quantities of extinguishing agents, personnel and equipment should be determined
accordingly if rescue and firefighting service is required to response to domestic and non-
aircraft related incidents at an aerodrome, where required.
(c) Information on the provision of rescue and firefighting services, facilities and equipment
should be provided in the Aerodrome Manual.
(d) The GCAA should be immediately notified of any changes to the provision of rescue and
firefighting services, facilities and equipment.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROVISION OF SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) Public or private organizations, suitably located and equipped, may be designated to provide
the rescue and firefighting service if the requirements contained in this Regulation are
complied with.
(b) It is intended that the fire station housing these organizations be normally located on the
aerodrome, although an off-aerodrome location is not precluded provided the response time
can be met.
(c) Requirements for a rescue and firefighting service to deal with domestic incidents involving
building, fuel storage facility and other non-aircraft related emergencies at an aerodrome are
not included in this Regulation.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
SPECIAL RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING EQUIPMENT
(a) Special rescue and firefighting equipment need not be provided for water areas; this does not
prevent the provision of such equipment if it would be of practical use, such as when the
areas concerned include reefs or islands.
(b) The objective is to plan and deploy the necessary life-saving flotation equipment as
expeditiously as possible in a number commensurate with the largest aeroplane normally
using the aerodrome.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
LEVEL OF PROTECTION
(a) An aerodrome operator shall:
(1) provide the level of protection at an aerodrome for rescue and firefighting appropriate
to the aerodrome category irrespective of the number of aircraft movements;

(2) determine the aerodrome category based on the longest aeroplanes using the
aerodrome and their fuselage width;
(3) ensure, if after selecting the category appropriate to the longest aeroplane’s overall
length, that aeroplane’s fuselage width is greater than the maximum width in Table 47,
column 3, for that category, then the category for that aeroplane is one category
higher; and
(4) ensure, during anticipated periods of reduced activity, the level of protection available
is no less than that needed for the highest category of aeroplane planned to use the
aerodrome during that time irrespective of the number of movements.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) An aerodrome operator shall:
(1) provide the amounts of water for foam production and the complementary agents on
the rescue and firefighting vehicles in accordance with the aerodrome category
determined, except that for aerodrome categories 1 and 2 up to 100 per cent of the
water may be substituted with complementary agent;
(2) ensure for the purpose of agent substitution, 1 kg of complementary agent is taken as
equivalent to 1.0 L of water for production of a foam meeting performance level A;
(3) ensure, at aerodromes where operations by aeroplanes larger than the average size in a
given category are planned, the quantities of water are recalculated and the amount of
water for foam production and the discharge rates for foam solution are increased
accordingly;
(4) ensure the quantity of foam concentrates separately provided on vehicles for foam
production is in proportion to the quantity of water provided and the foam concentrate
selected;
(5) ensure the discharge rate of the foam solution is not less than the rates shown in Table
48; and
(6) ensure the complementary agents comply with the appropriate specifications of the
International Organization for Standardization (ISO).
(b) From 1 July 2026, provisions of environmental-sustainable extinguishing agents shall apply to
new builds or replacement of existing systems or part thereof.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) Both principal and complementary agents should be provided at the aerodrome.

(b) Principal extinguishing agent should be either a foam meeting the minimum performance
level B or C.
(c) Complementary extinguishing agent should be a dry chemical powder suitable for
extinguishing hydrocarbon fires.
(d) The amount of foam concentrate provided on a rescue and firefighting vehicle should be
sufficient to produce at least two loads of foam solution.
(e) Supplementary water supplies should be provided for the expeditious replenishment of
rescue and firefighting vehicles at the scene of an aircraft accident.
(f) The discharge rate of complementary agents should be no less than the values shown in Table
48.
(g) Dry chemical powders should only be substituted with an agent that has equivalent or better
firefighting capabilities for all types of fires where complementary agent is expected to be
used.
(h) Reserve supplies of principal and complementary agent, equivalent to 200 per cent of the
quantities identified in Table 48, should be maintained on the aerodrome for vehicle
replenishment purposes.
(i) Sufficient propellant gas should be included to utilize this reserve complementary agent.
(j) RFF categories 1 and 2 aerodromes that have replaced up to 100 per cent of the water with
complementary agent should hold a reserve supply of complementary agent of 200 per cent.
(k) Where there a major delay in the replenishment of the supplies is anticipated, the amount of
reserve supply should be increased as determined by a risk assessment.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EXTINGUISHING AGENTS
(a) When selecting dry chemical powders for use with foam, care should be exercised to ensure
compatibility.
(b) Alternate complementary agents having equivalent firefighting capability may be utilized
provided practical testing and assessment are conducted.
(c) The amounts of water specified for foam production should be predicated on an application
rate of 8.2 L/min/m2 for a foam meeting performance level A, 5.5 L/min/m2 for a foam
meeting performance level B and 3.75 L/min/m2 for a foam meeting performance level C.
(d) When any other complementary agent is used, the substitution ratios should be checked and
recalculated.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE OBJECTIVES
(a) An aerodrome operator shall ensure the rescue and firefighting service achieve the
operational response time objective to any point of each operational runway and movement
areas, in optimum visibility and surface conditions
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE TIME
(a) For land aerodromes:
(1) the operational objective of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding three minutes to any point of each operational runway, in
optimum visibility and surface conditions;
(2) the operational objective of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding four minutes to any other part of the movement area, in
optimum visibility and surface conditions; and
(3) ensure any vehicles, other than the first responding vehicles(s), required to deliver the
amounts of extinguishing agents specified in Table 48 should ensure continuous agent
application and arrive no more than four minutes from the initial call.
(b) For water aerodromes:
(1) the operational objective of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding four minutes to any point of each operational runway, in
optimum visibility and surface conditions;

(2) the operational objective of the rescue and firefighting service should be to achieve a
response time not exceeding five minutes to any other part of the movement area, in
optimum visibility and surface conditions; and
(3) ensure any vessels, other than the first responding vessel(s), required to deliver the
amounts of extinguishing agents specified in Table 48 should ensure continuous agent
application and arrive no more than five minutes from the initial call.
(c) To meet the operational objective as nearly as possible in less than optimum conditions of
visibility, especially during low visibility operations, suitable guidance, equipment and/or
procedures for rescue and firefighting services should be provided.
(d) A system of preventive maintenance of rescue and firefighting vehicles/vessels should be
established and implemented to ensure effectiveness of the equipment and compliance with
the specified response time throughout the life of the vehicle.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESPONSE TIME
(a) Response time is considered to be the time between the initial call to the rescue and
firefighting service, and the time when the first responding vehicle(s) is (are) in position to
apply foam at a rate of at least 50 per cent of the discharge rate specified in Table 48.
(b) Optimum visibility and surface conditions are defined as daytime, good visibility, no
precipitation with normal response route free of surface contamination, e.g. water or sand.
(c) Guidance on conducting response time verification can refer to GM2 AMC1
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EMERGENCY ACCESS ROADS AND GATES
(a) Emergency access roads should be provided at the aerodrome where terrain conditions
permit their construction, so as to facilitate achieving minimum response times.
(b) Particular attention should be given to the provision of ready access to approach areas up to
1,000 m from the threshold, or at least within the aerodrome boundary.

(c) Where the airport is fenced, access to outside areas should be facilitated by the provision of
emergency gates or frangible barriers.
(d) Emergency access roads should be capable of supporting the heaviest vehicles which will use
them, and be usable in all weather conditions.
(e) Roads within 90 m of a runway should be surfaced to prevent surface erosion and the transfer
of debris to the runway.
(f) Sufficient vertical clearance should be provided from overhead obstructions for the largest
rescue and firefighting vehicles.
(g) When the surface of the road is indistinguishable from the surrounding area, or in areas
where sand or scrubs may obscure the location of the roads, edge markers should be placed
at intervals of about 10 m.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
EMERGENCY ACCESS ROADS AND GATES
(a) Aerodrome service roads may serve as emergency access roads when they are suitably
located and constructed.
(b) Guidance on provision of emergency access roads and gates can refer to GM AMC3
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
FIRE STATIONS
(a) A fire station should be provided to accommodate rescue and firefighting personnel, vehicles
and equipment at the aerodrome.
(b) Satellite fire station should be provided, whenever the response time cannot be achieved
from a single fire station.
(c) The fire station should be strategically located so that the access for rescue and firefighting
vehicles into the runway area is direct and clear, requiring a minimum number of turns.
(d) A watchroom, should be provided at the fire station, where necessary.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
FIRE STATIONS
(a) Where a purpose-built fire station is not available, a suitable facility to accommodate rescue
and firefighting vehicles, personnel and equipment may be provided at the aerodrome.

(b) Guidance on fire station/s and facilities can refer to GM AMC6 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.020 Rescue
and firefighting.

text:
COMMUNICATION AND ALERTING SYSTEMS
(a) A discrete communication system should be provided linking a fire station with the control
tower, any other fire station on the aerodrome and the rescue and firefighting vehicles.
(b) An alerting system for rescue and firefighting personnel, capable of being operated from that
station, at a fire station, any other fire station on the aerodrome and the aerodrome control
tower, should be provided.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING PERSONNEL
 An aerodrome operator shall:
 ensure all rescue and firefighting personnel are properly trained to perform their duties
in an efficient manner and participate in live fire drills commensurate with the types of
aircraft and type of rescue and firefighting equipment in use at the aerodrome, including
pressure-fed fuel fires;
 ensure the rescue and firefighting personnel training programme includes training in
human performance, including team coordination; and
 provide all responding rescue and firefighting personnel with protective clothing and
respiratory equipment to enable them to perform their duties in an effective manner.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECKS REQUIREMENTS
(a) Training and proficiency checks requirements for rescue and firefighting personnel are
specified in CAR AGA PART TRAINING.
(b) Fires associated with fuel discharged under very high pressure from a ruptured fuel tank are
known as “pressure-fed fuel fires”.
(c) Guidance material to design training programmes on human performance and team
coordination can be found in the ICAO Doc 9683 Human Factors Training Manual.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING PERSONNEL
(a) Sufficient trained and competent personnel including supervisors and/or managers, should be
readily available to ride the rescue and firefighting vehicles and to operate the equipment at
maximum capacity.

(b) These personnel should be deployed in a way that ensures that minimum response times can
be achieved and that continuous agent application at the appropriate rate can be fully
maintained.
(c) Consideration should be given for personnel to use hand lines, ladders and other rescue and
firefighting equipment normally associated with aircraft rescue and firefighting operations.
(d) The minimum number of rescue and firefighting personnel including supervisors and/or
managers, should be determined and documented in the Aerodrome Manual.
(e) Where the GCAA determines that the staffing level is insufficient to meet the promulgated
level of protection, the aerodrome operator should review the current staffing arrangements
and implement the required number of personnel including supervisors and/or managers.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
ESTABLISHING MINIMUM STAFFING LEVEL
(a) At aerodrome holding a landing area acceptance, it is possible that personnel performing full-
time facilities management, aircraft maintenance, etc, may be assigned to perform additional
rescue and firefighting duties in the event of an aircraft accident. However, this arrangement
must not compromise the capability of these personnel to respond to an aircraft accident at
an aerodrome safely and efficiently.
(b) Aerodrome operator may refer to Table 50 for guidance on minimum staffing levels. Further
guidance on establishing the minimum level of rescue and firefighting personnel for different
aerodrome categories can refer to GM2 AMC1 ACM.OPS.CERT.E.005(a) Rescue and
firefighting.

title: Rescue and firefighting
text:
PROTECTIVE CLOTHING AND RESPIRATORY EQUIPMENT
(a) The aerodrome operator should ensure:
(1) rescue and firefighting personnel are provided with fit for purpose protective clothing
and respiratory equipment to enable them to perform the assigned operational duties
safely and effectively;

(2) rescue and firefighting personnel are trained and competent in the use and operations
of these equipment;
(3) safety procedures are established and implemented in the use of these equipment at
operational incidents and training activities; and
(4) facilities for the storage, maintenance and cleaning of these equipment are provided at
the aerodrome.

title: Fire prevention
text:
AERODROME FIRE PREVENTION
(a) An aerodrome operator shall establish and implement a fire prevention programme at airside
including:
(1) appropriate fire prevention measures are taken during aircraft fuelling operations;
(2) prohibition of smoking within the movement area, other operational areas of the
aerodrome, or areas of the aerodrome where fuel or other flammable material is
stored;
(3) prohibition of display of an open flame or undertaking of an activity that would create a
fire hazard within:
(i) areas of the aerodrome where fuel operation takes place or other flammable
material is stored; and
(ii) the movement area or other operational areas of the aerodrome, unless
authorised by the aerodrome holder;
(4) ensure sufficient fire extinguishing equipment suitable for an initial intervention in the
event of fuel fire including personnel trained in its use, are readily available during the
ground servicing of an aircraft; and

(5) a means of quickly summoning the rescue and firefighting service in the event of a fire
or fuel spillage is provided on the apron areas.
(b) An aerodrome operator shall establish, implement and maintain a fire prevention programme
at landside including new builds at an aerodrome.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-ACM - AERODROME CRISIS MANAGEMENT - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Fire prevention
text:
AIRSIDE FIRE PREVENTION
(a) Policies and procedures including provide sufficient personnel, resources and equipment, for
the control of smoking or activities that may cause fire hazards at airside should be
established and implemented at the aerodrome.
(b) Policies and procedures should address the adoption and use of mitigating measures, when
necessary, activities (e.g. maintenance, etc.) which might involve fire hazard need to be
authorised.
(c) Authorised activities should not include smoking within the movement area, other operational
areas of the aerodrome, or areas of the aerodrome where fuel or other flammable material
are stored;
(d) Precautionary measures should be taken during fuelling operations and when passengers
remain on board or embark/disembark during refuelling operations.
(e) Sufficient portable fire extinguishing equipment suitable for at least initial intervention in the
event of fire or major fuel spill at airside including trained personnel should be readily
available.
(f) A means of quickly summoning the rescue and firefighting service in the event of a fire at
airside should be provided.

title: Fire prevention
text:
LANDSIDE FIRE PREVENTION
(a) A fire prevention programme for all buildings and facilities, commensurate with the level of
fire risks and hazards at an aerodrome should be established and implemented.
(b) A competent person with the authority and responsibility to oversee and manage the
programme should be nominated.

(c) The programme should comply with the applicable requirements of the UAE fire code
regulations.

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
AERODROME WORKS SAFETY
 In accordance with CAR AGA PART ADR ADR.OPS.B.070, an aerodrome operator  shall
establish and implement procedures to ensure that:
 aircraft safety is not affected by aerodrome works;
 aerodrome works safety is not affected by aerodrome operational activities;
 airfield work permit system is established and implemented involving all relevant stake
holders.

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
RFFS RESPONSE CAPABILITY ASSESSMENT
(a) The extent to which aerodrome works is likely to affect the response capability or operational
performance of the rescue and firefighting service and other emergency services in the event
of emergencies at an aerodrome or work site should be assessed.

(b) Suitable control measures should be developed if the aerodrome works may impact the
response capability of the rescue and firefighting service and other emergency services.

SUPPLEMENTARY WATER SUPPLY ASSESSMENT

(1) impact to supplementary water supply arising from the aerodrome works is assessed;
and
(2) suitable control measures are developed to mitigate the impact to supplementary
water supply.

event of aircraft emergencies at an aerodrome only. Additional quantities need to be
calculated to support the aerodrome works.
(b) Guidance on supplementary water supply assessment can refer to GM AMC3

title: Aerodrome works safety
text:
FIRE RISK ASSESSMENT
(a) The aerodrome operator should ensure:
(1) assessment of the fire hazards and risks relating to the aerodrome works is conducted;
and
(2) suitable control measures are developed to prohibit smoking, managing hot works, use
of flammable/combustible materials, fuelling, emergency response and evacuation.

FOREWORD
PURPOSE
(a) Federal Act No. 20 (1991) promulgating the Civil Aviation Law and Federal Law No.(4) of 1996, of
the United Arab Emirates, establish the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA) as the Competent
Authority with respect to civil aviation activities.
 Note.- A Competent Authority is any person or organization that has the legally delegated or
invested authority, capacity, or power to perform a designated function. Similarly, once an
Authority is delegated to perform a certain act, only the Competent Authority is entitled to take
accounts therefrom and no one else.
(b) The GCAA is required, under article 6 of the General Civil Aviation Law, to implement international
agreements in the field of aviation, and by article 7 of the same Law, to promulgate policy for civil
aviation and propose laws and regulations.
(c) As the Competent Authority, the GCAA has implemented CAR AGA for the provision of
aerodrome design and operations in the areas for which the UAE has jurisdiction.
(d) The CAR AGA is divided into the following parts:
(1) PART-ADR
(2) PART-ACM
(3) PART- VFI
(4) PART - TRG
These regulations represent the minimum requirements designed to achieve an acceptable level of
safety, considering the various nature of operations within the UAE. Aerodrome Operators are
required  to meet or exceed the regulations.
(e) Where relevant the requirements of SUBPART ADR.DEF, SUBPART ADR.OR and SUBPART ADR.OPS
are applicable to land and water aerodromes.

INTERPRETATION

Term Meaning
May The term ‘may’ is used in the GCAA regulation to give permission to do or not to do
something
Shall  in IR The term ‘shall’ is used in the GCAA regulation to impose an obligation or a
requirement or a prohibition.
Should in an AMC The term ‘should’ is used to indicate any specification which is recognized as
necessary in the interest of safety unless an alternative is accepted by the GCAA.
Shall in CS The term ‘shall’ is used in a CS to define basic technical specifications required by the
GCAA for certification purposes. In this case, deviation from the CS cannot be
permitted unless an ELOS is accepted by the GCAA
Should in CS  The term ‘should’ is used in a CS to define supporting technical specifications provided
by the GCAA for certification purposes. In this case, compliance with the CS will be
checked, only if the operator adopts it.

(a) The terms ‘Competent Authority’, or ‘GCAA’, is used to refer to the General Civil Aviation Authority
of the United Arab Emirates.
(b) The interpretation of some of the specifications used in this CAR requires the exercising of
discretion, and /or the taking of a decision. In both the cases, the discretion or decision of the GCAA
is binding.

(a) Implementing Rules (IR) may be supported by one or more Acceptable Means of Compliance (AMC)
and/or one or more Guidance Material (GM).
(b) Each IR is designed in a manner that it addresses one or more safety objective(s), through creating
or limiting rights, creating or limiting duties and responsibilities.
(c) Compliance is mandatory, unless a waiver has been granted by the GCAA. IRs are binding in
their entirety and used to specify a high and uniform level of safety and uniform conformity
and compliance.

(a) Certification Specifications (CS) are technical standards adopted by the GCAA. CS shall be used by
the Aerodrome Operators to establish their compliance/non-compliance register.
(b) Should an Aerodrome Operator  not meet the CS, they may propose an equivalent level of safety
that demonstrates how they meet the intent of the CS.

(a) AMCs are standards (but not necessarily the only standards) adopted by the GCAA to illustrate
means to establish compliance with the CARs. Compliance with AMC is mandatory unless an
alternative means of compliance has been accepted by the GCAA.
(b) Where multiple AMC exist for an IR then all AMC are applicable unless specified otherwise.
IMPLEMENTING RULES (IR)
CERTIFICATION SPECIFICATION (CS)
ACCEPTABLE MEANS OF COMPLIANCE (AMC)

(c) Aerodrome operators, if unable to comply with the AMC, must comply using other means  that are
accepted by the GCAA. Organisations may propose ‘Alternative Means of Compliance’ to an
existing AMC, but this is subject to review and approval by the GCAA. Alternative Means of
Compliance proposals shall be accompanied with evidence of the ability to meet the intent of the
IR.
(d) Once an Alternative Means of Compliance is  accepted by the GCAA, compliance therewith is
mandatory.

GMs are non-binding explanatory and interpretation material on how to achieve the requirements
contained in the IRs, CS and the AMCs. It contains information, including examples, to assist the user in
the interpretation and application of the requirements.
