operational status of related facilities and report on matters of operational significance, whether
of a temporary or permanent nature, to the relevant air traffic services providers and aeronautical
information services providers as applicable.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator  shall carry out regular inspections of the movement area and its related
facilities including the runway strip, RESA and other associated safety area.
(c) Aerodrome operator shall maintain records of all routine, non -routine inspections, which shall be
carried out by competent staff only.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
GENERAL
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should establish a monitoring and inspection program of the movement
area which is commensurate with the traffic expected at the aerodrome in order to identify any
irregularity or potential hazards to the safety of aircraft or aerodrome operations. Such
programmes should be established in coordination with the relevant air traffic service provider.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator , during excessive weather events (excessive heat, following a significant
storm, etc.) should be conducting extra inspections of paved areas to check for pavement hazards
and debris that could damage aircraft, or cause pilots to lose directional control.
(c) Inspections must also be carried out under the following circumstances:
(1) as soon as practicable, after any aircraft accident or incident;

(2) during any period of construction or repair of the aerodrome facilities or equipment that is
critical to the safety of aircraft operation;
(3) at any other time when there are conditions at the aerodrome that could affect aviation
safety;
(4) whenever the runway surface conditions may have changed significantly due to
meteorological  conditions;
(5) special air reports received from pilots;
(6) upon request from air traffic services.
(d) Surface inspection should be conducted following any significant maintenance activity (e.g. surface
enrichment course, large scale repairs, repainting of markings) conducted on the area and before
it is returned to service.
(e) When there are indications that the serviceability of a runway may be reduced because of poor
drainage, additional assessment should be conducted. This assessment differs in that water depths
in the poorly drained areas are normally greater in local rain conditions. The results are thus more
appropriate to identify problem areas having poor drainage values that could induce hydroplaning.

Monitoring and inspecting of movement area and related facilities
REQUIREMENTS AND PROCEDURES FOR MOVEMENT AREA INSPECTIONS
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should designate the personnel responsible for carrying out movement
area inspections.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator  should ensure that all vehicles on the manoeuvring area are in radio
contact with the appropriate air traffic services either directly or through an escort.
(c) In order to prevent runway incursions, the Aerodrome Operator  should have procedures in
place, which have been coordinated with the air traffic services unit, for conducting runway
inspections, communication procedures, actions in case of radio communication or transponder
failure or vehicle breakdown, stop bars crossing, including in cases of stop bar unserviceability,
runway crossings, etc. Runway inspections should be conducted in the opposite direction to
that being used for landing or taking off and without interruption, unless it is operationally
not feasible.

(d) The Aerodrome Operator  should ensure that personnel conducting movement area inspections
should be trained in, at least, the following areas:
(1) aerodrome familiarisation, including aerodrome markings, signs, and lighting;
(2) aerodrome Manual;
(3) aerodrome Emergency Plan;
(4) Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) initiation procedures;
(5) aerodrome driving rules;
(6) procedures for radiotelephony, phraseology and ICAO phonetic alphabet;
(7) aerodrome inspection procedures and techniques;
(8) procedures for reporting inspection results and observations;
(9) basic understanding of air traffic services procedures on the movement area; and
(10) low-visibility and adverse weather procedures.
(e) Personnel conducting runway surface condition assessments, in addition to the training specified
above, should be trained in, at least, the following areas:
(1) procedures for completion/initiation of RCR;
(2) type of runway contaminants and reporting;
(3) awareness   of   the   impact   of   runway   surface   condition   assessment   on   aircraft
performance.
Following the successful completion of the theoretical training, the practical part of the training to be
provided should consider the individual needs of the trainees, and should include the practical application
of the theoretical training. After the completion of the practical training, a competency assessment
should take place.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
VISUAL CHECK FOR OBSTACLES
(a) Aerodrome operators should include visual checks of aerodrome’s immediate vicinity and
surroundings (within line of sight) to identify objects that may pose a hazard to operations and if so
report to the designated persons or organisations for their immediate intervention.
(b) All authorised obstacles should be checked for proper lighting and marking.
(c) Any unauthorised obstacles should be reported to the designated persons or organisations for
their immediate intervention, including removal of the obstacle.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
REQUIREMENTS FOR MOVEMENT AREA INSPECTIONS
(a) Aerodrome operator should use checklists covering the various inspection areas. Unless other
acceptable methods are used, a sketch of the aerodrome should accompany the checklist so that
the location of problems can be marked for easy identification.
(b) Person(s) conducting the inspections should review the most recently completed checklist from
the previous inspection cycle prior to beginning the inspection.
(c) If construction or works are in progress, person(s) conducting the inspections should be familiar
with the safety plan of the construction or works.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
VEHICLE USED FOR INSPECTION
During the inspection of the runway a sterile environment should be adopted with only essential
communication conducted within the vehicle, with clearance, co-ordination and co-operation from ATC.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
FOLLOW-UP OF INSPECTIONS
Arrangements should exist for reporting the results of inspections, and for taking prompt follow-up
actions to ensure correction of unsafe conditions. These arrangements could include, depending on
the result or observation, notification to air traffic services and aeronautical information services,
removal of FODs, wildlife control, recording of events for further analysis according to the Aerodrome
Operator’s SMS requirements, etc.

title: Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related
text:
facilities
FREQUENCY OF INSPECTION
(a) Inspections of the movement area covering items such as the presence of FOD, the status of
visual aids, wildlife and current surface conditions, should be carried out each day, as stated
below:
(1) at least once where the aerodrome reference code number is 1 or 2 and at least twice
where the aerodrome reference code number is 3 or 4; and
(2) for the  runway(s):

(i) inspections in addition to  (a)(1)  whenever  the  runway surface  conditions  may
have  changed significantly due to meteorological conditions; and
(ii) Where the total number of movements is 250 or more, then not less than four
inspections in a day should be carried out.
(b) Inspections covering other items such as other lighting systems required for the safety of
aerodrome operations, pavements and adjacent ground surfaces, drainage and storm water
collection systems, fencing and other access control devices, the movement area environment
inside the aerodrome boundary and outside the aerodrome boundary within line of sight, should
be carried out, at least, weekly.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
FREQUENCY OF INSPECTION
(a) The frequency of aerodrome inspections should commensurate with the level of risk identified
in the  aerodrome safety management system (SMS) , however not less than the requirem ents
of AMC1 ADR.OPS.B.015(a)(b) .
(b) Where the number of movement is more than 250 then the minimum number of inspection of
movement area excluding runways should be increased by one.

title: Monitoring and inspection of movement area  and related
text:
facilities
TIER INSPECTION SYSTEM
Apart from daily routine inspections, Aerodrome operator should carry out regular focused supervisory
inspections which will include management, operations post holder or their delegated representative(s)
and senior management personnel. Therefore, a three-level inspection system should be carried out.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
TIER INSPECTION SYSTEM
Arrangements should be made by the Aerodrome Operator  to carry out
(1) Tier 1 – Airfield Operations Inspections

 These inspections consist of the daily routine inspections of the movement area. These inspections
should also cover the strips and other safety area associated with the runways and taxiways
,RESA(s), aprons, aircraft stands, associated infrastructure, and include a basic AGL check and apron
lighting check.
 Each inspection should be recorded. Records of the inspections should be reviewed daily by the
airfield Duty Manager. Any item that requires rectification, identified defect or unserviceability
should be reported to the concerned appropriate department fo r the necessary action and/or
rectification.
(2) Tier 2 – Airside Surface Inspections
 These are more detailed inspections of the movement area. The movement area should be divided
into smaller areas with the whole airfield covered over a 4-week period. These inspections are best
carried out on foot. The inspection should be recorded on the 2nd tier inspection report forms
which should mention the details of defects/deficiencies and actions arising from the inspection.
(3) Tier 3 – Airside Operations Management Inspections
 Tier 3 inspections are carried out by the Senior Operations Management Team, any other relevant
management personnel covering the entire movement area at least twice a year. The inspections
are best carried out on foot. The inspection should be recorded on the 3-tier inspection report
forms which should mention the details of defects/deficiencies and actions arising from the
inspection.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
The inspection procedures should also cater to allow a full runway inspection, including area between
side strip and the runway side of the holding position to be carried out preferably without interruption,
and should address the need to effectively inspect unidirectional lights.

Monitoring and inspection of movement area and related facilities
INSPECTION RECORDS AND LOGS
The Aerodrome Operator  should keep a log for all routine and non-routine inspections of the movement
area and related facilities.
The inspection log should include:

(a) details of inspection intervals and times;
(b) names of persons carrying out the inspection; and
(c) results and observations, if any, including requirement for  maintenance intervention be indicated,
the location, extent, and results should be recorded.
 All appropriate records, including completed checklist of inspections are kept for a period as mentioned
in AD.OR.D.035 from the date of inspections.

title: Foreign Object Debris (FOD) control programme
Foreign object debris control programme
text:
GENERAL
(a) The FOD control programme should be actively supported by the senior management   of  the
Aerodrome Operator  and of the other organisations operating or providing services at the
aerodrome.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator  should designate an individual within the aerodrome organisation to
manage the aerodrome’s FOD control programme.

title: Foreign object debris control programme
text:
FOD PREVENTION MEASURES
The Aerodrome Operator  should identify activities that may be associated with the generation of FOD,
as well as measures that should be taken in order to prevent this from happening. A record of the
analysis made should be maintained.

title: Foreign object debris control programme
Foreign object debris control programme
text:
FOD ANALYSIS — CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT
(a) FOD identified and collected on the aerodrome should be recorded, analysed and evaluated. To
record the location of the FOD, When needed, an investigation should be carried out to identify the
source of the FOD. The sources of FOD, including their location  and the activities generating FOD
on the aerodrome, should be identified, recorded and analysed to identify trends and problem
areas as well as to focus the efforts of the FOD control programme. Relevant records, including of
the actions taken, should be maintained.
(b) The FOD control programme should be periodically reviewed to assess and continually improve its
effectiveness. The programme should be updated based on the feedback received, data analysis
results and trends identified through the evaluation of FOD collected at the aerodrome.

AMC1 ADR.OPS.B016(b)Foreign object debris control programme
FOD PREVENTION
(a) Personnel awareness
Personnel should be kept aware through appropriate activities of the existence of the FOD control
programme, and should be actively encouraged to identify and report potential FOD hazards, act
to remove observed FOD, and propose solutions to mitigate related safety risks.
(b) Personnel training
The FOD training programme should aim at increasing the personnel awareness of the causes and
effects of FOD damage and to promote their active participation in eliminating FOD during the
performance of daily work routines.
(1) The theoretical part of the initial FOD training programme should cover the following areas:
(i) safety of aircraft, personnel and passengers as they relate to FOD;
(ii) overview of the FOD control programme in place at the aerodrome;
(iii) causes and principal contributing factors of FOD creation;
(iv) the consequences of ignoring FOD, and/or the incentives for preventing FOD;
(v) practicing ‘clean -as-you-go’ work habits and the general cleanliness and inspection
standards of work areas;
(vi) FOD detection procedures, including the proper use of detection technologies (if
applicable);
(vii) requirements and procedures for the regular inspection and cleaning of movement
areas;
(viii) FOD removal procedures;
(ix) proper care, use, and stowage of material and component or equipment items used
around aircraft while in servicing, maintenance or on aerodrome surfaces;
(x) control of debris in the performance of work assignments;
(xi) control over personal items and equipment;

(xii) proper control/accountability and care of tools and hardware;
(xiii) how to report FOD incidents or potential incidents; and
(xiv) continuous vigilance for potential sources of FOD.
The theoretical training should  be  followed  by  an assessment  of  the trainees .
(2) Following the successful completion of the theoretical training, the practical part of the
training to be provided should consider the individual needs of the trainees, according to the
responsibilities/tasks of the personnel, and, as a minimum, should inc lude familiarisation
with the tools/equipment used for the removal/containment/prevention of FOD, and the
implementation of the relevant aerodrome operating procedures related to the programme.
Following the completion of the practical training, a  compete ncy  assessment  should  take
place.

title: Foreign object debris control programme
text:
FOD PREVENTION MEASURES
FOD may be produced by many activities and may be generated by personnel, aerodrome
infrastructure (pavements, lights and signs), the environment (e.g. wind, heavy rain), aircraft, vehicles, or
other equipment operating at the aerodrome. The elements below have also the potential to become
sources of FOD on an aerodrome.
(a) Aircraft servicing and maintenance activities
During the activities related to the aircraft servicing, various types of FOD may be generated
and be left or transferred on the apron, service roads, and other operational areas. Such items
may include small luggage parts, cabin waste, plastic or metallic items, etc. FOD may also be
generated by vehicles or the equipment that operates in these areas.
To control this type of FOD, measures need to include securing and removing cabin waste from the
aircraft stand. Cabin waste would not be left unattended on the apron, especially near aircraft
stands.
Moreover, cabin waste need not be disposed of using the FOD containers provided, as cabin
waste may attract wildlife. To this end, the handling of cabin waste should be organised so that a
damage of the rubbish bag is not likely to attract wildlife on the apron.

Similarly, during aircraft maintenance, FOD may be generated either in the form of waste or
small items inadvertently left on the apron such as rivets, bolts, tools, etc. Procedures to address
this may include measuring of tools, use of toolboxes, checklists, removal of waste produced
upon the completion of the maintenance activities, etc.
Inspection of the aircraft stand or other areas that may have been used for aircraft servicing or
maintenance, before and after the departure of the aircraft is an effective measure. The secure
installation of suitable FOD bins, in appropriate locations, for depositing FOD is also an effective
preventive measure.
(b) Cargo areas
 In a cargo area, there is a high potential for blowing debris such as cargo strapping and plastic
sheeting. Procedures to contain such debris, possibly by installing (and monitoring) catch
fencing where appropriate, may help to control the environment. FOD trapped by such fences
should be removed regularly.
(c) Construction activities
During construction activities, several materials (rocks, tools, vehicle parts, etc.) have the
potential to become FOD if transferred by vehicles, weather phenomena, etc. on the movement
area or other operational areas. For this reason, specific FOD prevention procedures need to be
established and employed for each construction project. These procedures would be based on the
proximity of the construction activities to the movement area and other operational areas, but in
general would stress containment and regular cleaning of construction debris.
Aerodrome pre-construction planning would include means for controlling and containing FOD
generated by the construction. This is especially true in high-wind environments where debris is
more likely to become airborne.
The designated routes of construction vehicles on the movement area need to be planned so as
to avoid or minimise crossing in critical areas of aircraft operations. If high-risk crossings cannot
be avoided, subsequent provisions such as an increased frequency of FOD inspections could be
implemented.

Contractors need to understand and comply with the requirements regarding the control and
removal of FOD. To facilitate compliance with these requirements, the Aerodrome Operator
should consider drafting FOD control guidance for all construction projects taking place within the
movement area or nearby areas. Standard and project-specific FOD measures include:
(1) requiring contractors to cover all loads;
(2) requiring contractors to secure any loose items that could easily blow away or control
dust  through spraying of water;
(3) ensuring the proper functioning of storm drains throughout the construction;
(4) specifying whether any mechanical FOD removal devices will be required;
(5) specifying how monitoring for FOD hazards will be accomplished; and
(6) requirements for inspecting and removing FOD from tyres prior to traversing operational
 areas.
(d) Aerodrome maintenance operations
Maintenance operations routinely disturb the vegetation and soil in areas adjacent to those used
aircraft. Therefore, procedures to remove this debris, such as the use of an assigned aerodrome
sweeper or personnel on foot using shovels to repair vegetation and soil, need to be implemented.
Aerodrome lighting, pavement, and marking maintenance operations may generate
concrete/asphalt debris as well as increase the potential for dropped repair parts, tools, and
other items stored on the maintenance vehicles. Corrective procedures may include the use of
aerodrome sweepers and the inspection of the worksite after maintenance is completed.
(e) Pavements and other aerodrome surfaces may be prone to generating FOD
(1) Pavements
(i) Deteriorating pavements can exhibit spalling or cracks. For example, pieces of
concrete can break loose from pavements or FOD can develop from fatigue corner
cracks.
(ii) The service roads that cross taxiways may generate FOD from the vehicles using
them, especially in the case of construction operations.

(iii) Special attention should be paid to the cleaning of cracks and pavement joints.
(iv) Asphalt and concrete pavements may be the most common source of FOD on an
aerodrome; therefore, effective pavement maintenance practices are important for
the prevention of FOD.
(2) Other aerodrome surfaces
Grass areas and ditches may collect and hold large amounts of light debris such as paper,
cardboard, plastic and various containers that can originate from terminal aprons, cargo
ramps and hangar ramps. This debris can blow back into areas used by aircraft unless
collected in a timely manner.
Unpaved areas adjacent to pavements may require compaction, as appropriate, to
prevent FOD from jet wash.
FOD fences may collect debris on windy days. This FOD should be collected before the
wind increases or changes direction and the debris that blows back on to areas used
by aircraft.
(f) Vehicle operational activities
Vehicles used for operational reasons, e.g. preventive maintenance, wildlife management, and
which may need to frequently move on surfaces that contain material that could be FOD in the
movement area. Thus, procedural (e.g. inspection/cleaning of tyres) or technical (development of
surfaces at predetermined points that help the removal of FOD from tyres) measures may be taken
to address this potential FOD source.

title: Foreign object debris control programme
text:
FOD DETECTION AND REMOVAL
FOD detection
(a) In addition to the standard inspections, personnel on the movement area need to employ a ‘clean-
as-you-go’ technique, by looking for FOD during their regular duties.
(b) When inspections occur at night, additional lights/lighting systems on vehicles are beneficial to
better detect FOD.

(c) Whenever possible, vehicles involved in FOD detection activities, are only driven on clean, paved
surfaces. If a vehicle needs to be driven on unpaved surfaces, the driver needs to ensure that the
vehicle’s tires do not transport FOD (e.g. mud or loose stones) back onto the pavement.
(d) Encouraging the participation of the personnel of other organisations such as air operators, ground
handling companies, air traffic services providers in inspections may reinforce the concept that FOD
control is a team effort and demonstrates the Aerodrome Operator’s commitment to a FOD -free
environment. This practice may help increase familiarity with local aerodrome conditions, and
promotes effective communication between the Aerodrome Operator  and its stakeholders.
FOD removal
(a) FOD may be removed either manually or by using mechanical equipment, such as sweepers,
vacuum systems, jet air blowers, magnetic bars, FOD ‘sweeping carpets’, etc.
(b) FOD containers need to be able to withstand strong winds and be of a ‘closed-type’ to prevent the
wind from dislodging their content. Suggested locations for FOD containers are: near all entry points
to the apron area, in hangars, aircraft maintenance area s, near aircraft stands and baggage areas.
Clearly identified FOD storage locations increase the likelihood that collected debris will be
deposited by personnel. Access to the FOD containers should not be blocked.

title: Foreign object debris control programme
Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
(a) In coordination with the Appropriate Authority and /or local planning authority  the Aerodrome
Operator  shall:
(1) assess the wildlife hazard on, and in the surrounding, of the aerodrome; and the
assessments are carried out by competent personnel;
(2) establish and implement a Wildlife Hazard Management Plan to minimise or eliminate
wildlife hazards;
(3) establish means and procedures to minimise the risk of collisions between wildlife and
aircraft, at the aerodrome.
(b) Aerodrome operator shall notify the GCAA of all wildlife strike.
(c) Aerodrome operator shall Notify the GCAA and Appropriate Authority(ies) if a wildlife assessment
indicates conditions in the surroundings of the aerodrome  are conducive to a wildlife hazard
problem.
(d) The wildlife strike hazard on, or in the vicinity of, an aerodrome shall be assessed through:
(1) the establishment of a procedure for recording and reporting wildlife strikes to aircraft;
(2) the collection of information from aircraft operators, aerodrome personnel and other
sources on the presence of wildlife on or around the aerodrome constituting a potential
hazard to aircraft operations.

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
WILDLIFE RISK ASSESSMENT
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should:
(1) conduct a risk assessment using strike data for each species, as well as information on the
presence of species, the number of individuals, and their biology, and update this
regularly;
(2) take into account the number of strikes for each species and the severity of damage
arising from those strikes; and
(3) target actions on those species which are present with the highest frequency and create the
greatest damage.
(b) Wildlife risk assessments should be made by qualified personnel.
(c) Procedures on the management of wildlife hazards on and in the vicinity of an aerodrome, including
the establishment of a wildlife hazard management programme (WHMP), wildlife risk assessment,
land-use management and personnel training, are specified in th e PANS-Aerodromes (Doc 9981),
Part II, Chapters 1 and 6. Further guidance is given in the Airport Services Manual (Doc 9137), Part 3.

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
TRAINING FOR WILDLIFE CONTROL PERSONNEL
(a) The aerodrome wildlife control personnel should receive formal training prior to their initial
engagement as wildlife controllers.
(b) Training for aerodrome wildlife control should be documented and records of it should be
retained to satisfy periodic reviews, audits, and competence checks.
(c) Training of aerodrome wildlife control personnel should be conducted by qualified aerodrome
wildlife control personnel, or specialists with proven experience in this field.
(d) Wildlife control initial training should, at least, address the following general areas:
(1) an understanding of the nature and extent of the aviation wildlife management problem, and
local hazard identification;

(2) an understanding of the national and local regulations, where applicable,  standards, and
guidance material related to aerodrome wildlife management programs (use of best-
practice models);
(3) appreciation of the local wildlife ecology and biology, including (where applicable) the
importance of good airfield grass management policies, and the benefits they can deliver to
wildlife control;
(4) the importance of accurate  wildlife identification and observations, including the use of
field guides;
(5) local and national laws and regulations relating to rare and endangered species, and
species of special concern, and the Aerodrome Operator s’ policies relating to them;
(6) wildlife strike remains collection, and identification policies and procedures;
(7) long-term (passive) control measures, including on and off aerodrome habitat
management, including identification of wildlife attractions, vegetation policies, air
navigation aids protection, and drainage system, and water body management
practicalities;
(8) short-term (active) tactical measures, using well established effective wildlife removal,
dispersal, and control techniques;
(9) documentation of wildlife activities and control measures, and reporting procedures (the
aerodrome wildlife management plan);
(10) use of personal protective equipment; and
(11) wildlife strike risk assessment and risk management principles, and how these programs
  integrate with the aerodrome’s safety management system.
(e) Wildlife control staff should be fully aware of the conditions and terms of the operations of the
aerodrome environment.
(f) It should be ensured that wildlife control staff maintains competence in the role. This could
 be achieved either by training or another system of monitoring. The maintenance of competence
should include the areas in (d) and (e) above,
and also include:

(1) Reviewing the use of wildlife deterrent tools ;
(2) changes in the local environment;
(3) changes in risk management policy;
(4) recent wildlife events at the aerodrome;
(5) improvements in active and passive measures; and
(6) any other matters the Aerodrome Operator  deems appropriate.

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
GENERAL
The Aerodrome Operator  should:
(a) participate in the  relevant national committees  ;
(b) establish procedures to record and report wildlife strikes to aircraft occurred at the aerodrome, in
close cooperation with organisations operating, or providing services at the aerodrome;
(c) ensure that wildlife hazard assessments are made by competent personnel; and
(d) establish, implement and maintain a wildlife risk management programme.

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
Wildlife strike hazard reduction
Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
WILDLIFE RISK MANAGEMENT PROGRAMME
The wildlife risk management programme should cover an area of at least 13 km (7 NM) from the
aerodrome reference point, and should include, at least, the following elements:
(a) assignment of personnel:

(1) a person who is accountable for developing and implementing the wildlife risk
programme;
(2) a person who oversees the daily wildlife control activities, and analyses the collected data and
carries out risk assessments in order to develop and implement the wildlife risk
management programme; and
(3) trained and qualified staff who detect and record the birds/wildlife, and assess the
bird/wildlife hazard, and expel hazardous birds/wildlife.
(b) a process to report, collect, and record data of struck and living birds/wildlife;
(c) a process to analyse the data and to assess the bird/wildlife hazard to develop mitigation,
 proactive, and reactive measures. This should include a risk assessment methodology;
(d) a process of habitat and land management both on, and in its surroundings, whenever possible, in
 order to reduce the attractiveness of the area to birds/wildlife;
(e) a process to remove hazardous birds/wildlife;
(f) a process for liaison with non-aerodrome agencies and local landowners, etc. to ensure the
aerodrome is aware of developments that may contribute to creating additional bird hazards
within the surrounding of the aerodrome’s infrastructure, vegetation, land use and activities (for
example crop harvesting, seed planting, ploughing, establishment of land or water features,
hunting, etc. that might attract birds/wildlife).

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
REPORTING OF WILDLIFE STRIKE
In the event of a wildlife strike (including bird strike), the Aerodrome Operator  shall use the ROSI system
and/ or any other system as established by the GCAA to make mandatory reports to the GCAA.

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
RECORDING AND REPORTING OF WILDLIFE STRIKES AND OBSERVED WILDLIFE
(a) It is necessary to maintain a record of all wildlife activity or ‘bird/wildlife log’. The log should
include, at least, the following information:
(1) numbers, species, and location of birds/wildlife seen; and

(2) actions taken to disperse birds/wildlife, and the results of these actions.
(b) The log should be completed at regular intervals by the wildlife control staff.
(c) The log should be analysed to identify which species represent a hazard, at which times of day or
year, or under which weather conditions, etc.
(d) The Aerodrome Operator  should have a system in place to collect bird/wildlife strike reports in
close cooperation with data owners, like aircraft operators, air navigation service providers,
aircraft engine maintenance departments, etc.

title: Wildlife strike hazard reduction
text:
Procedures on the management of wildlife hazards on and within the vicinity of aerodromes, including
the establishment of a wildlife hazard management programme (WHMP), wildlife risk assessment, land-
use management and personnel training, are specified in the PANS -Aerodromes (Doc 9981), Part II,
Chapters 1 and 6. Further guidance is given in the Airport Services Manual (Doc 9137), Part 3.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
(a) the driving of a vehicle on any part of the movement area  or other operational areas of an
aerodrome shall require an authorisation (Airside Driver Permit –ADP), issued to the driver by the
operator of that aerodrome.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator  shall establish and implement a driving training programme for drivers
who operate on the airfield, , the training programme shall:
(1) be appropriate to the characteristics and operation of the aerodrome, the driver’s functions
and tasks to be performed, and the areas of the aerodrome that drivers may be authorised
to operate;
(2) include theoretical and practical training of adequate duration., in at least the area as
included in  CAR AGA PART TRG;
(3) assess the competency of the drivers.
(c) Aerodrome operator shall ensure that they have in place a system for the promulgation of
Information to all ADP holders regarding any changes on the airfield that may impact upon airside
driving.

(d) The Aerodrome Operator  in coordination with the air traffic services,  shall establish a system of
allocating RTF call signs to be used by vehicles, so that the potential for confusion between vehicles
and aircraft is minimized. This is particularly impor tant at aerodromes where the RTF frequency
used by vehicles is the same as that used by aircraft, or where the RTF frequency used by vehicles
is re-broadcast on the RTF frequency used by aircraft.
(e) Notwithstanding ADR.OPS.B.024 (a) the Aerodrome Operator  may permit a person to temporarily
drive a vehicle on the movement area or other operational areas if:
(1) that person holds a valid driving licence, and any other licence required for the operation of
specialised vehicles; and
(2) that vehicle is escorted by a vehicle driven by a driver authorised in accordance with point
(a).

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
DRIVER AUTHORISATION
(a) Except as provided for in point ADR.OPS.B.024 (e). The driving authorisation should  be issued to a
person who:
(1) is employed with an organisation authori sed to operate at the aerodrome and is allocated
tasks that involve driving in such areas;
(2) holds a valid UAE driving licence, and any other licence required  for  the  operation  of
specialised vehicles;
(3) has successfully completed a relevant driving training programme and demonstrated his or
her competence in accordance with (c);
(4) has demonstrated language proficiency in accordance with point ADR.OPS.B.029, if that
person intends to drive a vehicle on the manoeuvring area;
(5) has received training by their employer on the use of the vehicle intended to operate at the
aerodrome;
(6) Medically fit to drive.
(b) An Aerodrome Operator should establish a system to define the validity period of driving
authorization, specify the conditions for their renewal, circumstances under which a permit will
cease to be a valid and requirements for surrender of the driver’s authorisation.

(c) A driving authorisation issued should specify the parts of the movement area or other operational
areas on which the driver is allowed to drive and shall remain valid as long as:
(1) the requirements of points (a)(1) to (a)(6) are met;
(2) the holder of the driving authorisation:
(i) undergoes and successfully completes training  and proficiency checks in accordance
with the requirements of this CAR .
(ii) where applicable, continues to demonstrate the required language proficiency in
accordance with point ADR.OPS.B.029 – Language proficiency.
(f) The Aerodrome Operator  shall:
(1) establish a system and implement procedures for:
(i) for issuing and revoking airside driver permits.
(ii) temporarily permitting the driving of vehicles;
(iii) ensuring that drivers to whom a driving authorisation has been issued, continue to
maintain their competencies;
(iv) monitoring the compliance of drivers with any driving requirements applicable at the
aerodrome and for taking appropriate action, including the suspension and revocation
of driving authorisations or permissions to temporarily drive a vehicle.
(2) maintain relevant records.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
GENERAL - ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
(a) Aerodrome operator
It is the responsibility of the Aerodrome Operator  to establish and implement procedures for the
training, assessment and authorisation of all drivers operating and for vehicles permitted on the
movement area. These procedures are required to be documented within the Aerodrome Manual
and should include:
(1) details of the applicable traffic rules (including speed limits and the means of enforcement
of the rules);

(2) details of  vehicle serviceability requirements;
(3) a description of the method for issuing driving permits for operating vehicles in the
Movement Area; and
(4) a description of the method for issuing vehicle permits/authorisation for vehicles and ground
service equipment. Special attention needs to be given for the types of vehicles/equipment
that will remain airside;
(b) Nominated Person
 The Post Holder Operations, as the process owner, is responsible to ensure the implementation,
maintenance and enforcement of the aerodrome’s airside driving permit scheme. Further, the Post
Holder Operations is responsible to ensure that the safety manag ement system principles and
procedures of the Aerodrome Operator  are applied to the continuous improvement and
development of the aerodrome’s ADP scheme.
(c) Stakeholders
Stakeholders are responsible for ensuring that the company and its drivers meet the criteria stated
in the ADP Scheme document issued by the Aerodrome Operator s, and that its drivers hold a valid
ADP.
 Stakeholders are also responsible for ensuring that any change to the company or drivers’
circumstances that may have an effect on any of the requirements of the ADP scheme is
communicated to the Aerodrome Operator  in a timely manner.
(d) Airside Driver Permit Holder
 All applicants for an ADP should hold a current UAE Driver’s License applicable to the vehicle they
intend to operate, and be fully conversant with the relevant rules, procedures and instructions of
the aerodrome(s) where they drive, whilst ensuring they meet all requirements as stated.
 The ADP procedure should include recognition of a “Certificate of Competence” for specialist
vehicles such as ground handling equipment, e.g. aircraft tugs and high loaders, in addition to the
UAE driving licence.

 Any change to the driver’s circumstances that may have an effect on their ADP should be
communicated to their company in a timely manner. It is also the driver’s responsibility to notify
their company if their UAE Driver’s License is suspended or disqualified.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit –
ADP)
SPECIFIC TRAINING OF DRIVERS ON THE USE OF VEHICLES OR EQUIPMENT
(a) A driver needs to receive specific training on the use of any vehicle or equipment, they  will be using
during their duties, e.g. special vehicle, tug, high loader, coach, etc. The aerodorme operator shall
have access to these records for audit purposes  upon request.
(b) If the driver is to be assigned a new vehicle type following the issuance of the authorisation, the
process of point (a) should be repeated prior to allowing the driver to operate the new vehicle.

Authorisation airside of vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit –
ADP)
MEDICAL REQUIREMENTS
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should implement medical standards as part of the criteria for holding
an ADP.  As a minimum the medical requirements should require the items listed below:
(1) an initial and renewal medical declaration to include eyesight, colour perception.
(2) medical assessments to relate to occupational age limits; and
(3) the requirement for a review following a driving accident or incident at work.
(b) Renewal and Monitoring
Airside driver’s health standard should be monitored within the period specified by the Aerodrome
Operator  or in accordance to the employees own company policy, and where necessary,
examinations should be carried out by suitably qualified staff.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit –
ADP)
MEDICAL REQUIREMENTS
(a) It is the responsibility of the Aerodrome Operator  to decide what additional specific factors there
might be about the workplace and vehicles which may impose additional medical fitness
requirements over and above those required for driving on the public roads. This should be based
on a local risk assessm ent by the Aerodrome Operator , which may include organisations that
operate airside, and should relate to local procedures, environment, infrastructure, topography,
and the complexity of the aerodrome and aircraft operations.  Medical fitness should also i nclude
the  ability of the driver to distinguish between colours associated with signage, ground markings
and lighting.
(b) A driver should be required to disclose to the Aerodrome Operator  and their employer, any existing
or new medical condition or prescribed medication which may affect their ability to drive safely.
Where a health professional places a condition or restriction on a driver, this should be declared to
and considered by the employer and medical advice obtained. The employer should inform the
Aerodrome Operator  of any such condition or restriction who should take appropriate action which
may involve the suspension or removal of the ADP.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
VALIDITY AND REVALIDATION REQUIREMENTS
(a) Revalidation requirements
 Aerodrome operators should ensure that drivers continue to hold the correct categories of licence
for the public roads at all times.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator  should establish a system ensuring that drivers maintain competence in
their driving rules, duties and procedures in those areas where they are permitted to drive.
(c) ADP validity and renewal
(i) Duration: up to two years; and
(ii) Renewal: competence should be maintained. This may be confirmed/assessed by a
maintenance of competency scheme or refresher training, but in either case, must include
appropriate assessments.

(d) In order  for the ADP to be renewed :
Apart from the requirements of (c) (ii)  the driver holds a current and valid UAE licence .
(e) Records of training and assessments should be retained. Third party trainers/assessors must ensure
that records are available for audit by the Aerodrome Operator .

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
TRAINING OF DRIVERS - RADIOTELEPHONY
In addition to the requirements of CAR AGA  PART TRG , drivers who are expected to operate on the
manoeuvring area of the aerodrome should also receive training in Radiotelephony , which should include
as a minimum:
(a) hierarchy of message priority :message priorities, and understanding of distress, alerting, control
and information messages.
(b) phonetic alphabet: correct pronunciation of letters, words, and numbers.
(c) standard phraseology
(1) emphasis on the need for drivers to use standard phraseology; and
(2) the need for caution with certain phrases such as ‘cleared’.

(d) call signs for aircraft, ATC, and vehicles
(1) an understanding of terminology and acronyms used by ATC and pilots;
(2) knowledge of the airline call signs used at the aerodrome; and
(3) knowledge of vehicle call signs, and that they should be appropriate to their function.
(e) read back procedures : The need for vehicle drivers to use standard readback, in the same manner
as pilots, for instructions such as ‘enter/cross the runway’, and if conditional clearances are used.
(f) readability scale: Understanding and use of the readability scale from 1 to 5.
(g) lost or uncertain of position: Understanding of local procedures for vehicle drivers are lost or
uncertain of their position on the manoeuvring area.
(h) vehicle breakdown
(1) local procedure for vehicle breakdown on runways and taxiways; and
(2) procedure for notifying ATC of vehicle failure.
(i) radio failure
(1) understanding of the local procedure if radio failure occurs while on the runway or taxiway;
and
(2) understanding of the light signals that can be used by ATC to pass instructions to vehicles.
(j) transmitting techniques and use of RTF
(1) understanding the reasons for listening out prior to transmitting;
(2) use of standard phraseology and ICAO air-ground radiotelephony communications
procedures;
(3) words and sounds to be avoided;
(4) correct positioning of microphones to avoid voice distortion;
(5) avoidance of ‘clipped’ transmissions;
(6) awareness of regional accents and variations of speech; and

(7) speed of delivery of RTF phraseology.
(k) portable radios
(1) correct use of radios;
(2) effective range and battery life;
(3) screening/shielding effects on the aerodrome; and
(4) use of correct call signs, either related to a vehicle or a person.
(l) safety while using radios
(1) local instructions regarding the use of portable radios and hand-held microphones while
driving a vehicle; and
(2) local instructions on the use of mobile telephones while operating airside.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
PRACTICAL TRAINING- RADIO TELEPHONY
In this phase, the training should cover the use of fixed and portable radio communication devices, and
the practical use of the theoretical knowledge acquired in the previous phase of the training, through the
implementation of the aerodrome’s communication procedures.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
AERODROME OPERATING AREAS
The Aerodrome Operator  should separate the airside area into distinct operating areas, each operating
area requiring a separate category of ADP.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
AERODROME OPERATING AREAS FOR ADP
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should separate the airside area into distinct operating areas, each
operating area requiring a separate category of authorisation. It is recommended that the airside is
split into a minimum of 2 areas, the first area comprising the airside road system and aprons, while
the second area consists of the taxiways and runways (the manoeuvring area).
(b) Depending on the complexity of the aerodrome, the manoeuvring area may be further split into
that area excluding the runways, and that area including the runways.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
(a) A separate ADP Category may be issued for each of the operating areas established with the
recommended ADP categories as follows:
(1) ‘Airside Roads and Aprons’
The airside roads and apron permits are the initial permit awarded to a new driver who has
successfully completed a local training course and assessment. The permit allows a driver to
operate on airside roads and aprons, which may include controlled and uncontrolled taxiway
crossings. The awarding of the permit allows the holder to progress their training to operate
on the manoeuvring area, excluding runways.
(2) ‘Manoeuvring Area excluding Runways’
The manoeuvring area (excluding runways) permit allows a driver to operate on the
manoeuvring area but excludes operation on the runway. It is a pre -requisite for the
candidate to successfully complete a radiotelephony course, prior to obtaining this permi t.
The holder of the permit should maintain competence in RTF throughout the validity period
of the permit. RTF competence checks should be completed by persons approved by the
Aerodrome Operator : this may be a training provider, their employer or the Aerodrome
Operator  itself.
(3) ‘Manoeuvring Area including the Runway’
The manoeuvring area (including runways) permit allows a driver to operate on runway(s)
once the RTF training course is successfully completed.

 Where only a single ADP category is required for operating on the manoeuvring area, the
training and assessments should be based on requirements of CAR AGA, Part- TRG .
(b) If the Aerodrome Operator  permits free ranging on the manoeuvring area, the authorizations and
scope needs to be defined and be part of the ADP licensing and training scheme. Any assessment
or consideration to ‘free ranging’ should be documented through the LRST and be coordinated with
aerodrome control tower. It should be made very clear, if ‘free ranging’ exists that at no time does
this allow the entry onto a runway without aerodrome control tower authorization.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
TEMPORARILY PERMITTING THE DRIVING OF VEHICLES
(a) When permitting temporarily the driving of a vehicle, the period for which the permit is valid and
the areas in which the driver will be allowed to operate under escort should be specified.
(b) The escort of a vehicle whose driver has been issued a temporary driving permit should only be
performed by the Aerodrome Operator  or any other driver(s) authorised for this purpose.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
TEMPORARILY PERMITTING THE DRIVING OF VEHICLES
(a) ADR.OPS.B.024 in general addresses the case of authorisation of drivers whose nature of work and
activities involves regular presence and driving within the aerodrome environment.
(b) However, there are cases where it may be necessary to temporarily allow the driving of a vehicle
on the movement area  or other operational areas of the aerodrome for other reasons (e.g. a
contractor’s vehicle that needs to enter the movement area for maintenance activities taking place
at the aerodrome, etc.).
(c) In cases where the driving on the movement area or other operational areas is necessary but for a
limited period of time, the Aerodrome Operator  may permit such driving without requiring the
driver to undergo the process for the issuance of an authorisation for the driving of this vehicle. It
is expected, however, that before being permitted to operate in such areas, such drivers will be
adequately briefed about their obligations while operating within the aerodrome perimeter, and
that the Aerodrome Operator  has developed procedures to be implemented during this type of
operations.

(d) In any case, the issuance of such a permit for such a driver does not waive the obligation of the
Aerodrome Operator  to ensure:
(1) the condition of the vehicle that this driver may be temporarily driving into the aerodrome
area, in accordance with ADR.OPS.B.024.
(2) that this vehicle will in any case be escorted; and
(3) that the operation of this vehicle on the manoeuvring area is subject to the  applicable
provisions of ADR.OPS.B.025 and ADR.OPS. B.026.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
PROCEDURES FOR ISSUANCE OF DRIVING AUTHORISATIONS (ADP) AND TEMPORARILY PERMITTING
DRIVING OF VEHICLES, AND RELEVANT MONITORING ACTIVITIES
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should clearly identify responsibilities for:
(1) issuing driving authorisations and temporary driving permits;
(2) ensuring that the prerequisites for maintaining a driving authorisation valid continue to be
met;
(3) monitoring the compliance of the drivers with the driving rules applicable at the aerodrome,
and taking appropriate action as the case may be. Such actions should include the possibility
of suspension or revocation of the ADP or of temporary driving permit.
(b) Issuing such authorisations, temporarily permitting the driving of vehicles and ensuring that the
prerequisites for maintaining a driving authorisation should be a controlled activity.
(c) Irrespective of the organisational set -up chosen, it should be ensured that information regarding
drivers who:
(1) do not continue to meet the requirements for maintaining the validity of the relevant driving
authorisation; or
(2) violate the driving requirements,
is forwarded to the aerodrome unit(s) responsible for the issuance/revocation of the driving
authorisations, in a timely manner, to take appropriate action depending on the case.

(d) The established procedures should clearly indicate how cases of violations of the applicable driving
requirements at the aerodrome are dealt with. They should especially take into account the
seriousness of each violation and also address cases of repeated violations of the applicable driving
requirements. The cases where a driver should be required to undergo additional training should
also be addressed in the procedures.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit – ADP)
RECORD KEEPING
(a) Records of training and assessments for the airside driving permits should be retained. Third-party
trainers/assessors must ensure that records are available for audit by the Aerodrome Operator .
(b) A suitable means should be provided for the secure storage of information relating to ADPs.

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers (Airside Driver Permit –
ADP)
DRIVING AUTHORISATION FORMAT
There are various solutions for issuing an ADP. A combination of the driving authorisation with the badge
issued to personnel or the issuance of a separate card are some of the possible solutions. In any case, it is
important that the privileges  of the holder are clearly contained in the authorisation.

title: Airside Driving Rules
text:
(a) Aerodrome operators shall
(1) establish and implement airside driving rules;
(2) ensure all airside drivers are made aware of the rules;
(3) monitor that the driving rules are always adhered to.
(b) The driver of a vehicle on the movement area shall comply with all mandatory instructions  and
 information conveyed by aerodrome visual aids .
(c) The Aerodrome Operator  shall ensure that the movement of vehicles on the movement area  is
safely managed.
(d) The Aerodrome Operator  shall include rules and procedures to manage driving behaviour.
(e) An emergency vehicle responding to an emergency should be given priority over all other surface
movement traffic.

title: Airside Driving Rules
Airside Driving Rules
text:
RIGHT OF WAY
(a) A vehicle operating on an apron should give way to vehicle as mention in ADR.OPS.B.25(e ) and:
(1) an aircraft taxiing, about to taxi, or being pushed or towed;
(2) to other vehicles in accordance with local airport regulations.

title: Airside Driving Rules
text:
Airside driving rules should include details such as:
(a) Speed
Aerodrome Operator s must establish speed limits based on their assessment of various factors,
including road conditions, proximity to aircraft, type of vehicle / equipment expected to use the
road etc., The driver of a vehicle should follow strictly all speed limits, indict ed by road signs and
markings.
(b) Service road
(1) Primary service roads (also known as inner GSE roads)
these are roads normally located front of aircraft parking stands and are meant for the
movement of vehicles and equipment to individual aircraft stands without having to proceed
on apron areas.
(2) Secondary service roads (also known as outer GSE roads )
(i) these roadways are normally located behind aircraft parking stands between the
aircraft stand and the aircraft stand taxilane, and are usually painted with two solid
white lines on the road edge that is nearer to the taxilane / taxiway.
(ii) drivers should maintain the correct speed and look out and give way to all taxing
aircraft and aircraft moving onto or off a stand or being towed.
(iii) when an aircraft is approaching, the driver should immediately take evasive action .
The driver should visually check that the area is clear of aircraft movement before
proceeding.

(iv) A driver should not use secondary service road as a short cut or to overtake.
(3) Perimeter service roads
these are roadways normally located near the fence surrounding the airport boundary and
away from the apron areas.
(c) Service roads crossing taxiways
(1) where service roads cross taxiways the driver should keep a constant look out and give way
to aircraft at all times.
(2) drivers are required to adhere to any safety instructions when approaching a taxiway for
crossing  it. It is  common to see a “Give Way to Aircraft” sign or marking warning drivers of
taxiway crossing ahead and potential aircraft movement. Drivers should stop at the “STOP”
marking and visually check that the area is clear of aircraft movement before moving onto
the crossing.
(3) if there are light signals at the service road crossing, driver should check that the signals
indicate that it is clear to proceed. The driver should still visually check that the area is clear
of aircraft movement before proceeding.
(4) to prevent obstruction to aircraft movement, the driver should not stop on any part of the
crossing.
(d) Apron boundary line
 the apron boundary line indicates the boundary between the aircraft stand and the secondary
service roads. Represented by a double white or yellow line, crossing this line requires permission
from ATC and a driving permit authorising to diver in that area.
(e) Fuel hydrant pits
 fuel hydrant pits are usually demarcated with a red box or circle. Drivers should not drive or park
over fuel hydrant pits.
(f) Passenger Boarding Bridge (PBB) safety area

 Safety area is usually indicated by a red hatched area and this area should be kept clear of any
movements at all the time for the safe operations of the P BB. Vehicles and equipment are not
permitted to enter and/or park within the PLB safety area at any time. All drivers should alert the
PLB operator if anything is obstructing the safety area before PBB operations begin.
(g) Equipment restraint area
 the Equipment Restraint Area is demarcated by a solid red and white line. The Equipment Restraint
Area of an aircraft stand to be kept clear for the safe movement of an aircraft operating in and out
of the stand. Drivers should not park or position any vehicle or ground Servicing equipment within
the Equipment Restraint Area at all times, unless they are servicing an aircraft after its arrival or
prior to its departure of the aircraft.
(h) Pedestrian crossings
 all Drivers should look out for pedestrian crossing signs and slow down when approaching a crossing
and be prepared to stop and give way to pedestrians.
(i) Safe distance from Aircraft
The Aerodrome Operator  in coordination with the respective ground handlers/airlines should
define minimum safety distances to be kept during the servicing of an aircraft.
(j) Safe distance from taxing aircraft
No driver should cross the movement area in front of the path of a taxing aircraft or an aircraft on
tow or pushback. A driver should remain vigilant to the hazards of jet blast and a safety distance,
as defined by the Aerodrome Operator , should be maintained behind a taxing aircraft.
(k) Driving Equipment
All drivers should be authorised and trained to operate the specific type and kind of equipment
such as forklifts, boom lifts and scissor lifts as applicable. Pre-start checks should be conducted prior
to operating the equipment to ensure it is fully operational. While driving, the driver should watch
out for any height limit surrounding structures and when approaching any blind area, the driver
should drive with caution.
(l) Driving Inside Aircraft Parking Stand

(1) drivers should not enter or park in an aircraft parking stand unless they are required for
ground operations of the aircraft and possess an AVP/ADP with access to aircraft stand.
(2) while waiting in the Equipment Staging Area to service an arriving aircraft, drivers should
park their vehicle with the handbrake engaged. When aircraft are entering the aircraft stand,
the driver should stay clear of the Equipment Restraint Area and may o nly enter the
Equipment Restraint Area after the aircraft chocks have been positioned and if it is safe to
do so.
(3) a marshaller should assist the driver while reversing towards the aircraft.
(4) drivers should not drive or park under the wing or fuselage of an aircraft unless the vehicle is
engaged in refuelling and maintenance service.
(5) during pushback, the driver  of other vehicles  should again stay clear of the Equipment
Restraint Area to ensure the safe movement of the aircraft.
(m) Vehicle refuelling
(1) vehicle refuelling should only carried out at dedicated vehicle refuelling locations declared
by the Aerodrome Operator .
(2) to avoid vehicle breakdowns in operationally critical areas, drivers should complete a vehicle
serviceability check prior to using the vehicle which should include a fuel level check.
(3) in the event that a vehicle does run out of fuel, the vehicle should be immediately towed to
a designated location for refuelling.
(4) in the event of a fuel spillage the driver should follow airport reporting and cleaning
procedures immediately.
(n) Vehicle height limits in the airside
a driver driving /operating/ towing tall equipment should take note of any overhanging building
structures and height limit signs displayed and not use roads with a height limit lower than that of
the equipment under tow.
(o) Use of seat belts
all vehicles should be installed with seat belts for the driver and, if applicable, passengers. All drivers
and passengers should wear their seat belts while the vehicle is in motion.

title: Airside Driving Rules
text:
DRIVING DURING LOW VISIBILITY
(a) During Low Visibility Conditions the Aerodrome Operator  is required to ensure that persons and
vehicles operating on the movement area are restricted to the essential minimum.
(b) Aerodrome operators should put in place specific training and authorisations for those drivers that
may be required to operate on the manoeuvring area during Low Visibility conditions.
(c) All non-essential traffic should remain off the aprons until the low visibility conditions have cleared
and have been officially terminated unless necessary for the imminent movement/servicing of an
aircraft.
(d) Unless absolutely necessary, drivers should be required to stay on the service roads and not drive
between stands or behind aircraft and all movement from one stand to another should be restricted
to the service roads.
(e) Vehicles operating airside during low visibility should display, as a minimum, head lights and the
flashing beacon.
(f) Speed limits on the service roads should be reduced and drivers required to take all precautions.

title: Airside Driving Rules
text:
GENERAL DRIVING CONDUCT
Aerodrome operator’s general driving conduct should include the following requirements also:
(a) drivers should be required to carry their ADP at all times while operating on airside and be required
to show it upon request from the Aerodrome Operator .
(b) no person under the influence of alcohol; medicine or drugs should be permitted to operate a
vehicle or equipment at airside.
(c) no driver or passenger should consume any form of food while on airside.
(d) smoking should be strictly prohibited airside.

(e) use of mobile phone while driving airside should be prohibited. Where it is necessary to
communicate using a mobile phone, i.e. where there is a communication failure with ATC or
essential communication with the Aerodrome Operator  or the driver’s company is required, the
driver should park the vehicle in an area that is safe from aircraft movements.
(f) never drive or walk in front of or behind an aircraft with its engine is running.
(g) never drive or park under aircraft wings unless involved in aircraft servicing.
(h) never leave vehicle unattended with the engine running.
(i) never reverse vehicle near an aircraft without a marshaller.
(j) never park equipment so that other vehicles are obstructed.
(k) never park within the fuel zone during the refuelling process unless involved in refuelling activity.
(l) never work close to the filling or ventilation openings of the aircraft fuel tanks during refuelling.

(m) report all fuel, oil and other chemical spillages.
(n) keep the movement area clean of FOD.

title: Airside Driving Rules
text:
MANOEUVRING AREA AND RADIOTELEPHONY
The movement of vehicles on the manoeuvring area is generally subject to authorization by aerodrome
control tower.  Depending on the complexity of the aerodrome, aerodrome control tower may operate a
number of radio frequencies. Typically, in these cases, the aerodrome ground controller will be
responsible for all ve hicles operating on the taxiways, and the air controller will be responsible for all
vehicles wishing to enter or cross the runway(s). It is essential that all vehicles required to be under
positive control on the manoeuvring area are equipped with the appropriate radio communication
devices tuned to the appropriate frequencies.

title: Airside Driving Rules
Authorisation of airside vehicles
text:
(a) The operation of vehicles on the movement area  or other operational areas shall require
authorisation issued by the Aerodrome Operator (Airside vehicle  Permit – AVP). The authorisation
may be issued if the vehicle is used in activities related to the operation of the aerodrome, have a
justifiable reason to be on airside, and:
(1) is serviceable and fit for the intended operation;
(2) complies with the marking and lighting requirements of point ADR.OPS.B.080- Marking and
lighting of vehicle and other mobile objects;
(3) is equipped with a radio allowing two -way communication on the appropriate air traffic
services frequency and any other frequency necessary, if it is intended to be operated on
either of the following areas:
(i) the manoeuvring area;
(ii) other operational areas where communication with the air traffic services unit or other
operational units of the aerodrome is necessary;

(4) is fitted with a transponder or other equipment that supports surveillance, if it is intended to
be operated on the manoeuvring area, and the aerodrome is equipped with a surface
movement surveillance system whose operation requires the use of a transponder or other
equipment supporting surveillance fitted on the vehicles.
(b)  The Aerodrome Operator  shall:
(1) establish and communicate to stake holders the processes and procedures for the application
of an Airside Vehicle Permit (AVP) and;
(2) limit the number of vehicles authorised to operate on the movement area  and other
operational areas to the minimum number required for the safe and efficient operation of
the aerodrome.
(c) An authorisation issued in accordance with point (a) shall:
(1) specify the parts of movement area or other operational areas where the vehicle may be
operated;
(2) remain valid as long as the requirements of point (a) are met.
(d) The Aerodrome Operator  shall assign a call sign to a vehicle authorised in accordance with point
(a) to operate at the aerodrome, if that vehicle is required to be radio -equipped. The call sign
assigned to a vehicle shall:
(1) not cause confusion regarding its identity;
(2) be appropriate to its function;
(3) for vehicles that operate in the manoeuvring area, be coordinated with the air traffic services
unit, and disseminated to the relevant organisations at the aerodrome.
(e) By derogation from point (a), the Aerodrome Operator  may permit:
(1) a vehicle authorised to operate  in the airside where it is needed to be equipped  with a radio
equipment  and a transponder in accordance with (a)(3), (a)(4), to be occasionally operated
in the areas referred to in (a)(3) and (a)(4), provided:

(i) that vehicle is escorted, at all times, by an authorised vehicle meeting the requirement
of (a)(3) and, if necessary, (a)(4);
(ii) the escorting vehicle complies with the marking and lighting requirements of

title: Authorisation of airside vehicles
text:
EQUIPAGE OF VEHICLES - GENERAL
(a) An updated copy of the movement area chart of sufficient size, including hot spots, as well the
visual aids configuration on the aerodrome, and areas to be safeguarded, should be readily
available in the vehicle intended to be operated in the manoeuvring area. If a vehicle is not to be
operated in the manoeuvring area, the copy of the chart may be customised to provide only
relevant information of the area in which the vehicle is to be operated, along with informa tion of
the adjacent areas, to improve the situational awareness of the driver.
(b) The Aerodrome Operator , in coordination with the air traffic services provider and the apron
management services provider ( where applicable ), should assess in which areas of the aerodrome
a vehicle needs to be equipped with a radio ,apart from the manoeuvring area.
 The radio with which the vehicle is equipped should allow two -way communication with the air
traffic services unit frequency, and any other unit that the driver of the vehicle may need to
establish contact with.
 Updated information regarding the frequencies of each unit should be readily available in the
driver’s cabin, as well as the frequencies that may need to be used at different areas of the
aerodrome. Moreover, the call-sign of the vehicle should be displayed  at a prominent place.

title: Authorisation of vehicles
text:
VEHICLE’S FITNESS TO USE IN THE AIRSIDE
(a) The applicant or employer applying for an Airside Vehicle Permit should be responsible for the safe
operation and condition of the vehicle / equipment used airside and should be required to certify:
(1) that the vehicle/equipment for which an Airside Vehicle Permit has been issued is, on a
regular basis, properly inspected, maintained and serviced by an appropriately qualified
person;
(2) the applicant or employer should be required to retain inspection and maintenance records
and make them available to the airport operator upon request.
(b) The vehicle’s fuel and hydraulic systems should be free of leaks.

(c) Ensure systems are in place to prevent fire including the following:
(i) regular vehicle maintenance and daily checks, especially for older vehicle;
(ii) fire extinguisher is available in the vehicle at all times;
(iii) vehicle/equipment engine are be switched off before leaving the vehicle;
(iv) checking the vehicle for leakage of fluid before starting the engine.

title: Authorisation of vehicles
text:
LIMITING THE NUMBER OF VEHICLES
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  should limit vehicular activity to what is necessary, in order to ensure
 the safety of operations, but also taking into account the need to ensure the proper and smooth
 functioning of the aerodrome.
(b) In this respect, vehicle use may be limited to those vehicles which are necessary to support the
ground servicing and handling of aircraft cargo/mail and passengers, aerodrome maintenance and
operations, including aerodrome emergency services, aerodrome security  services, and
State authorities’ vehicles.
(c) Vehicles on the manoeuvring area should be limited to those absolutely necessary, especially on
the runway. Vehicles allowed to operate on the runway should include only those necessary for
operational activities such as inspections and maintenance, and em ergency vehicles. It is strongly
advised not to increase runway use by other vehicles such as those involved in ground operations,
e.g. aircraft towing, etc. unless there is no alternative route.
AMC1 ADR.OPS. B.026(c)(1) Authorisation of airside vehicles
DISPLAY OF VEHICLE AUTHORISATION
A vehicle authorisation should be displayed at a prominent place on the vehicle, in a position that
minimizes obstruction to the driver’s view while driving.

title: Authorisation of airside vehicles
text:
AIRSIDE VEHICLE PERMIT
(a) Vehicles required to access the airside should be controlled by Aerodrome Operator  through the
use of an Airside Vehicle Permit (AVP) scheme and all vehicles should display an AVP whilst airside.
Exceptions may be made for visiting vehicles performing maintenance or other services but these
vehicles should be escorted by a holder of an ADP.
(b) An AVP does not confer the right of entry and does not identify the driver or passengers. An AVP
serves to identify the vehicle and is an acknowledgment by the a erodrome  operator that the
vehicle is permitted to be used in the controlled or restricted areas specified on the permit when
on official use.
(c) Depending on the number of vehicles and the complexity of the aerodrome, the use of colour -
coded vehicle authorisations is a solution that may be considered, to facilitate the control of the
vehicles.

title: Authorisation of vehicles
text:
TEMPORARILY PERMITTING VEHICLE OPERATION
Vehicles may be authorised only if they are used in activities related to the operation of the aerodrome.
However, from time to time, and for various reasons, it may be necessary to allow a vehicle to enter the
aerodrome area and to be operated on the movement area or other operational areas, for a limited period
of time (e.g. transportation of supplies, maintenance activities, transportation of patients, etc.). In such
cases, the Aerodrome Operator  may issue a temporary permit for the entry of the vehicle  into the
aerodrome and its operation in the area necessary.
In such situations, a visual inspection of the vehicle is necessary, for obvious damages or malfunctions of
the vehicle (e.g. leakages, braking system, condition of tyres, lights, etc.) to determine the serviceability
of the vehicle.
Temporary Airside Vehicle Permit should be valid for a specific period of time for a specific vehicle. A
temporary AVP should be issued to vehicles that require short term access to perform a specific task, such
as contractors delivering construction material.

title: Authorisation of vehicles
text:
CONDITION FOR ISSUE OF VEHICLE AUTHORISATION
(a) The following conditions should apply when issuing an Airside Vehicle Permit:
(1) a permit should be subject to a signed declaration by the applicant, indicating that the details
provided are accurate.
(2) the permit should be issued to a specific vehicle.
(3) the Airside Vehicle Permit should be non -transferable between vehicles, companies or
persons and serve only to identify the vehicle, not the driver or passengers within.
(4) the vehicle should have a current UAE vehicle registration (if applicable) with valid and airside
specific insurance clause coverage as required by the Aerodrome Operator .
(5) the applicant should be responsible for returning an Airside Vehicle Permit to the relevant
airport department management for cancelations in the following circumstances:
(i) when the purpose for which the pass was issued has ceased; and
(ii) when the vehicle ownership changes or when the vehicle permanently ceases
operation airside.

title: Authorisation of vehicles
text:
VEHICLE CALL SIGNS
(a) The use of similar call signs may lead to call sign confusion, which is one of the factors associated
with runway incursions. To avoid call sign confusion, when assigning a call sign to a vehicle, careful
consideration needs to be given to the call signs used by aircraft operating at the aerodrome, as
well as the call signs of other vehicles.
(b) Ways to reduce the possibility of call sign confusion include:
(1) use of call signs which are appropriate to the function of the vehicle (e.g. ‘Operations’,
‘Fire’). Where more than one vehicle is used in the same function, then a numbering
policy may be used, such that the call sign is followed by a number, e.g. ‘Operations 1’.
(2) use of unique numbers or identification call signs for each vehicle.

(c) At aerodromes where the number of vehicles and the aircraft traffic is high, before assigning a
call sign to a vehicle, it is recommended that the Aerodrome Operator , apart from the
coordination with  the air traffic services provider, consults also the other organisations
operating vehicles at the  aerodrome. As soon as a call sign is assigned to a vehicle, this needs to
be known to at least the air  traffic services provider.

title: Authorisation of vehicles
Authorisation of vehicles
text:
OCCASIONAL OPERATION OF AUTHORISED VEHICLES WITHOUT RADIO, TRANSPONDER OR OTHER
MEANS SUPPORTING SURVEILLANCE
(a) The Aerodrome Operator  may decide to permit the occasional operation of vehicles, which have
been authorised to be operated on the aerodrome but which are not equipped with a radio, in
areas where vehicles are required, by ADR.OPS. B.026 (a)(3). The same applies with regard to
authorised vehicles, which are not equipped with a transponder or other equipment supporting
surveillance as foreseen in ADR.OPS. B.026 (a)(4).
(b) Characteristics of escorting vehicles
A vehicle mentioned in points (a)  above, needs to be escorted by a vehicle equipped with a radio,
in accordance with ADR.OPS. B.026 (e)(1)(i) or ADR.OPS. B.026 (e)(2)(ii) Authorisation of airside
vehicles, if it is to be operated:

(1) on the manoeuvring area; or
(2) in other areas where vehicles are required to be equipped with a radio (see also point (b) of
AMC1 ADR.OPS. B.026(a)(1) ;(3)).
(3) In addition, If the escorted vehicle is to be operated on the manoeuvring area, the escorting
vehicle would also need to be fitted with a transponder or other equipment supporting
surveillance, if so required for the operation of the SMGCS of the aerodrome (see ADR.OPS.
B.026(a)(4)).
(4) Moreover, the escorting vehicle needs to meet at all times the respective marking and
lighting requirements for the area(s) where the escorted vehicle will be operating (see
ADR.OPS.B.080).
(5) In this way, occasional unforeseen operational needs that may arise in the context of the
operation of the aerodrome may be satisfied, given that such vehicles are not intended to be
operated in such areas.
(c) Operational considerations
If the vehicle(s) mentioned in points (a) above are intended to be operated on the manoeuvring
area, care is to be  taken to ensure that this is done in compliance with ADR.OPS. B.026 (e)(1)(iii)
Authorisation of airside vehicles or ADR.OPS. B.026 (e)(2)(iii), Authorisation of airside vehicles  as
the case may be, as well as the relevant procedures.
(d) Particular attention needs to be paid to the cases where two or more vehicles are temporarily
entering the aerodrome, and especially the manoeuvring area, forming a convoy. In such cases, the
escorting vehicles should be  in positions that allow the monitoring of all escorted vehicles at all
times, to ensure that all vehicles comply with the instructions of the air traffic services unit. In
addition, attention is necessary to the way s and means that the communication between the
escorting and the escorted vehicle will be taking place.
(e) In any case, temporarily permitting the use of the vehicle in accordance with ADR.OPS.B.026 (e)(2),
or permitting the operation of an already authorised vehicle in accordance with ADR.OPS.B.026
