SUBPART - CERTIFICATION SPECIFICATIONS AND GUIDANCE MATERIAL FOR WATER AERODROMES
(PART WCS-ADR-WDSN)

title: Applicability
text:
Applicability
The water aerodrome criteria are designed to cater for day, Visual Flight Rules (VFR) operations only; they
do not cater for night, Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC).

title: Applicability
text:
(a) All aircraft on water shall comply with requirements of the International Regulations for Preventing
Collisions at Sea, harbour regulations and local byelaws that are not addressed in this document.
(b) Operations on water differ significantly from those conducted on land and as such, the criteria for
land aerodromes maybe inappropriate in some areas.  Although based on the existing land
aerodrome criteria, the different operational and safety risks when operating onto and from water,
particularly in more challenging environments have to be addressed.

title: Aerodrome Reference Point (ARP)
text:
The Aerodrome Reference Point (ARP) shall be established.  The ARP shall be located near the initial or
planned geometric centre of the aerodrome.

title: Aerodrome Reference Elevation
text: An Aerodrome Reference Elevation shall be determined at the ARP.

title: Aerodrome Reference Elevation
text:
(a) The Aerodrome Reference Elevation is located at the planned geometric centre of the Manoeuvring
Area or of the main one if more than one is provided.
(b) The Aerodrome Reference Elevation  should be determined from the chart height, or from the
lowest recorded water level, converted to an elevation in feet above the local datum established
by the emirate in which the aerodrome is located.

title: Movement Area
text:
Aerodrome operators shall determine the area of any land and water on which seaplane operations may
take place.  It is this area that shall be declared as the movement area.
One or more Manoeuvring Area(s) shall be established within the movement area from which all seaplane
operations requiring the use of an aerodrome shall take place.

title: Manoeuvring Area
text:
The available manoeuvring area shall be large enough to provide a choice of take -off and landing
direction, dependent upon prevailing water surface and weather conditions.

The manoeuvring area shall encompass all parts of the water surface intended for the taking off and
landing of seaplanes.

title: Manoeuvring Area
text:
(a) The manoeuvring area(s) should be square, rectangular or rhomboidal in shape.
(b) In other cases, such as on a narrow inlet, it may be more appropriate to provide a Manoeuvring
Area that caters for take -off and landing in one direction and its reciprocal only, in a direction
parallel to the longer sides of the Manoeuvring Area.

title: Number and Orientation of water runways
text:
The number of water runways at a water aerodrome and their orientation should be such that, for a large
percentage of time as practicable but for not less than 95 percent there is at least one water runway for
which the surface wind velocity component at r ight angles to its longitudinal axis will not preclude the
landing or taking off of seaplane that the water aerodrome is intended to serve.

title: Number and orientation of water runways
text:
The number of usable water runways at a water aerodrome and their geographic orientation should
minimize the effect of the local surface wind direction, velocity component, existing obstacles and noise
pollution to neighbouring human habitat as much as possible.

title: Length of water runways
text:
The length of the water runway to be provided should be adequate to meet the operational requirements
(take-off and landing) of  the critical seaplane for which the runway is intended and should be not less
than the longest length determined by applying the corrections for local conditions to the operations and
performance characteristics of the relevant seaplanes.

title: Width of water runways
text: The width of the water runway should be not less than 60 m wherever practicable.

title: Water Depth
text:
The depth of the water measured at low water level in the water runway should not be less than 1.8 m (6
ft.) or less than 0.3 m below the hull or floats when the seaplane is stationary and loaded to maximum
take-off weight.

title: Water runway strip
text:
A protective buffer should extend on each side from the edge of the water runway to a distance of not
less than 30 m (100 ft.) and on each end of the water runway to a distance of 60 m wherever practicable.

No fixed object should be permitted on a water runway or on a water runway strip unless it is being used
for aeronautical purposes.

title: Turning basins
text:
Turning basins should be provided at the end of the water runway, whenever necessary.
When turning basins are provided it shall have:
(a) A diameter measured at low water level of not less than twice the specified minimum width of the
corresponding water runway;
(b) The depth of turning basins measured at low water level should be at least that of the
corresponding water runway; and
(c) A horizontal obstruction clearance between the edge of the turning basin and the nearest obstacle
of no less than 15 m (50 ft.).

title: Taxi channels
text:
(a) Taxi channels should be provided to permit the safe, orderly and expeditious handling of
aerodrome traffic. Where provided, the taxi channels shall have a width of not less than 45 m ,
wherever practicable.
(b) Wingtip to wingtip clearance for passing seaplanes (dual directional taxi channels) should  be not
less than of 15 m (50 ft.) .
(c) The depth of the water measured at low water level in the taxi channel should not be less  than
1.8 m (6 ft.) or less than 0.3 m below the hull or floats when the seaplane is stationary  and
loaded to maximum take-off weight.

title: Mooring areas
text:
Mooring areas should be provided, whenever necessary, for the mooring of seaplane and to permit the
embarkation and disembarkation of passengers, loading and unloading of cargo and mail without
interfering with the aerodrome traffic.
When mooring areas are provided:
(a) The size of the mooring areas should be adequate to permit expeditious handling of the peak hour
traffic.
(b) The depth of water at the mooring area measured at low water level should be at least that of the
corresponding taxi channel.

(c) The mooring area shall be designed in such a manner as to provide a minimum clearance of 15 m
(50 ft.) between any part of the seaplane and any object it could come into contact with depending
on water level.

title: Shore facilities
text:
A platform (fixed or floating), ramp or beach should be provided to permit the embarking and
disembarking of passengers and crew, loading and unloading of cargo and refueling.
(a) Where a platform is provided it shall:
(1) be in a condition that permits constant use without causing injury to persons or damage to
aircraft;
(2) be attached or anchored in a manner that prevents it from shifting position or becoming
detached;
(3) have access from the shore that provides for the safe movement of crew and passengers;
and
(4) have at least two bull rails or provision for appropriate number of tie -down cleats at each
seaplane parking position to secure the seaplane.
(b) Where a ramp or beach is provided it shall be:
(1) built 1.5 times the width of floats or landing gear of the largest seaplane intended to
 use the facility;
(2) located in such a manner as to provide a minimum clearance of 1.8 m (6 ft.) between a
seaplane wing and any object it could come into contact with;
(3) constructed with a slope not steeper than 8:1.

(c) When a seaplane is normally secured in a position where any seaplane component overhangs the
platform and constitutes a hazard to the movement of crew and passengers, the hazard shall be
clearly indicated by means of:
(1) cones; and/ or
(2) hashed red and white markings; and
(3) in a manner easily identifiable to crew and passengers.

title: Obstacle limitation surfaces
text:
(a) The following OLS shall be established for non-instrument water aerodromes
(1) a take-off climb/approach surface;
(2) a transitional surface; and
(3) an inner horizontal surface
(b) Declaration of the Obstacle Limitation Surfaces shall be made by the Aerodrome Operator  and
shall be supported by an Aeronautical Study.

title: Obstacle limitation surfaces
text:
(a) When determining the extent of the Obstacle Limitation Surfaces, account should be taken of all
factors that significantly affect the performance of the largest seaplane likely to operate from the
water aerodrome;
(b) Factors that significantly affect performance include, but are not limited to: maximum certificated
take-off mass, operating procedures, temperature, wind, water surface condition and constrains
by property boundaries or topographical features;
(c) When it is  not be possible or practicable in some locations to establish an inner horizontal surface
due to terrain or local factors, procedures could be established to ensure an acceptable level of
safety.

title: Take-off climb and Approach surfaces
Straight-in take-off climb / Approach Surface
text:
Where the slope is designed for a straight -in approach the divergence of the take -off climb/approach
surface shall be set at 10% starting from the inner edge.

title: Curved take-off climb / Approach Surface
text:
(a) Where established, a curved take -off climb/approach surface shall not contain more than one
curved portion.
(b) A curved portion of a take-off climb/approach surface shall not allow a change of direction greater
than 90 degrees.
(c) Where a curved portion of take-off climb/approach surface is provided:
(1) the straight portion originating at the inner edge shall not be less than 1300 m (4265 ft.); and
(2) the radius of arc defining the centre line of the take -off climb/approach surface shall not in
any portion of the take -off climb/approach surface be less than 736 m (2415 ft.) in
accordance with the figure below.
(d) A take-off climb/approach surface incorporating a curved portion shall be established only where
guidance, such as, geographical points or other visual references are available.
Note. — An offset curved approach is normally established at a non -instrument water runway
where it is necessary to avoid obstacles, terrain, noise sensitive areas, or to utilise the airspace
above public lands (e.g. freeways, rivers, golf courses).

title: Displaced Threshold
text:
(a) Where the integrity of the approach surface cannot be maintained due to fixed or mobile obstacles,
a landing threshold shall be displaced from the normal threshold.
(b) This displacement shall be established so that the new approach surface, starting at the
displacement, will clear all obstacles.
(c) Where a threshold has been displaced, the inner edge of approach surface shall be located at 60 m
from the point of displacement.

title: Objects and obstacles
text:
(a) No fixed object shall be permitted on a water runway or on a water runway strip.

(b) Fixed objects or structures that are located within the water aerodrome boundary shall not
penetrate OLS unless:
(1) those structures are for air navigation purposes; or
(2) are essential to the safety of aircraft operation;
(3) are marked, in accordance with CAR AGA Part ADR;
(4) are frangible.
(c) A mobile object shall not penetrate take -off climb/approach surfaces, unless procedures are in
place to ensure the object is removed during approach and departure operation

title: Other objects
text:
(a) Where an aeronautical study (safety risk assessment) indicates that an object is hazardous to
seaplane located on the movement area  or in the air in the immediate vicinity of the water
aerodrome, it shall be:
(1) removed; or
(2) marked; and/or
(3) lighted in accordance with CAR AGA, Part ADR.
(b)  The water Aerodrome Operator  shall conduct a safety risk assessment to establish the required
clearances to be used above waterways, lagoons, or harbor.

title: Wind direction indicator
text:
(a) Unless the direction of the wind can be obtained by radio, at least one wind direction indicator shall
be installed.
(b) Where a wind direction indicator is installed it shall be:
(1) of an international orange, orange and white or red and white colour; and
(2) in the form of a truncated cone.
(c) The wind direction indicator should be:
(1) visible at a height of 300 m (1000 ft.) above the water runway; and
(2) visible from any portion of the manoeuvring area.

title: Markings –Platform/ Dock identification marking
text:
(a) Platform / Dock identification markings shall consist of:
(1) triangle;

(2) painted bull rails.
Both markings shall be affixed to the upper surface of the dock so as to be visible from 300 m (1000 ft.)
above the water runway.
(b) Bull rails
Where bull rails are installed they shall be painted in alternated bands of international orange and
white stripes.
(c) Gangways shall be painted red or signage provided indicating seaplane access only.

title: Markings – Marker buoys
text:
Marker buoys should be in accordance with International Maritime Organisation (IMO) standards and be
visible to aircraft:
(a) manoeuvring on the surface of water; and
(b) 300 m (1000 ft.) above the water runway.

title: Water runway markers
text:
(a) Except as specified in (b) at water aerodromes where there is no conflict with marine  traffic
or marine regulations:
(1) Both ends of the take-off and landing area shall be marked with floating markers.
(2) The markers shall be visible from a distance greater than 2 nautical miles.
(3) Each marker shall be :
(i) of international orange in color; or
(ii) alternating international orange and white.
 (b) Where it is impracticable to mark the water runway as specified in (a):
(1) guidance such as geographical points and/or other visual references shall be provided to
designate the take-off and landing area; and
(2) these visual references shall be identified and published.

title: Displaced threshold markers
text:
Where a threshold is displaced permanently or temporarily:
(a) the threshold displacement shall be marked with floating markers;

(b) the markers shall be visible from a distance of at least 2 nautical miles; and
(c) each  marker  shall  be  international  orange  or  the  markers  shall  be  alternating international
orange and white.

title: Hazardous area markers
text:
(a) Where shoals or other hazards could endanger a seaplane, marker buoys shall be installed to clearly
indicate the hazardous area.
(b) Marker buoys for delineating hazardous area shall be distinctly marked from water runway markers
in colour and shapes.

title: Prohibition sign
text:
(a) A sign shall be provided and displayed on the dock restricting the dock to seaplane operations only.
(b) A sign shall be displayed on the dock restricting passengers from the docking area until all seaplanes
and propellers have come to a complete stop.

title: Strobe lights
text:
Strobe lights should be provided to delineate water aerodrome facilities wherever necessary.

Where installed, the strobe lights shall be:
(a) white, quick flashing; and
(b) located in an area that is easily and constantly seen by both marine and air traffic.

title: Visual Aids to denote obstacles
text:
(a) Fixed objects
(1) Objects that are conspicuous by their shape, size or colour need not be marked.
(2) Except as covered under the Marine Act, objects shall be marked in accordance with (b).
(b) Marking of objects
(1) Except as specified in (a) all fixed objects shall be marked in a conspicuous colour.
(2) Where it is not possible to colour the objects, markers or flags shall be displayed on or above
the objects.
(c) The colour and form of marking displayed on objects shall be in accordance with CAR AGA, Part
ADR.
(d) Use of markers
(1) markers displayed on or adjacent to objects shall be:

(i) located in conspicuous positions so as to retain the general definition of the object;
and
(ii) recognizable in clear weather from a distance of:
(A) 1000 m for an object to be viewed from the air; and
(B) 300 m for an object to be viewed from the ground in all directions in which a
seaplane is likely to approach the object.
(2) The shape of the markers shall be:
(i) distinctive to the extent necessary to ensure that they are not mistaken for markers
employed to convey other information; and
(ii) such that the hazard presented by the object they mark is not increased.
(3) The colour selected shall contrast with the background against which it will be seen.

title: Visual Aids
text:
(a) Water aerodrome identification and maneuvering area lighting should be provided for reduced
visibility conditions wherever necessary.
(b) A lighted water aerodrome can be identified by a beacon alternating white and yellow flashes at
the rate of 12 to 30 flashes per minute.
(c) In water traffic congested areas, a radio activated strobe beacon may be used to alert mariners and
other airman that a seaplane will be arriving or departing within a short time.
(d) Floodlights or spotlights should be installed on the shore to illuminate aprons, floats, ramps, and
piers wherever necessary. Care must be taken in locating and aiming floodlights to preclude
affecting the vision of pilot's landing or taking off or creating distracting reflections.

SUBPART – ORGANISATIONAL REQUIREMENTS (TRG.OR)

title: Provision of training services and/or activities
text:
PROVISION OF TRAINING SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) The training services and/or activities stated under this SUBPART shall be provided to all
personnel by the aerodrome operator, either directly or indirectly.
(b) Where the training services and/or activities contained in this SUBPART are provided by a
third party either fully or partially, aerodrome operator shall establish and implement safety
oversight of the provisions, in accordance with the aerodrome operator’s safety management
system, to ensure compliance with the requirements contained in this Regulation.

title: Provision of training services and/or activities
text:
PROVISION OF TRAINING SERVICES AND/OR ACTIVITIES
(a) Unless otherwise specified, the generic term “aerodrome” refers to both aerodrome and
vertical flight infrastructure (i.e., heliport, helideck and vertiport).
(b) The training services and/or activities contained in this SUBPART need to be provided at an
aerodrome. In some cases, these training services and/or activities are not directly provided
by the operator, but by a third-party organisation or combination of both. However, the
operator, being responsible for the operation of the aerodrome should have arrangements
and interfaces with the third party to ensure that these services and/or activities are provided
according to the legal requirements. The method described above meets with the intention of
an integrated Safety Management System that helps the operator to ensure the safety
objective of the provision is being met.

title: Provision of training services and/or activities
Establishing and implementing safety oversight of third party
text:
ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING SAFETY OVERSIGHT OF THIRD PARTY
Refer to CAR SMS for guidance on establishing and implementing safety oversight.

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
text:
TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECK PROGRAMMES
(a) Aerodrome operator shall establish and implement a training programme for personnel
involved in the operation, maintenance and management of the aerodrome, to ensure their
continued competence, and that they are aware of the rules and procedures relevant to
operation of the aerodrome and the relationship of their functions and tasks to the
aerodrome operation as a whole.
(b) The training referred to in point (a) shall:
(1) include initial, recurrent, refresher and continuation training;
(2) be appropriate to the functions and tasks for the personnel
(3) include the applicable operational procedures and requirements of the aerodrome, as
well as driving when required.
(c) Aerodrome operator shall establish and implement a proficiency check programme for
personnel referred to in point (a), that they have demonstrated their capabilities in the
performance of their tasks, in accordance with a proficiency check programme, in order to
ensure:
(1) their continued competence; and
(2) that they are aware of the rules and procedures relevant to their functions and tasks.
(d) Aerodrome operator shall ensure that:
(1) adequately qualified and experienced instructors for the provision of training and
assessors for the assessments and the proficiency checks are used; and
(2) suitable facilities, means and equipment are used for the provision of the training and,
where applicable, for the conduct of the proficiency checks.

(e) Aerodrome operator shall establish and implement procedures for the implementation of the
training and proficiency check programmes and shall:
(1) maintain appropriate qualification, training and proficiency check records to
demonstrate compliance with this requirement;
(2) upon request, make such records available to its personnel concerned.

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
text:
TRAINING OF PERSONNEL — GENERAL
(a) The training programme should cover all personnel:
(1) involved   in   the   operation, maintenance, and management of the aerodrome
(supervisors, managers, senior managers, and the accountable manager); and
(2) operating unescorted on the movement area, and other operational areas of the
aerodrome, and which are related to the Aerodrome operators, regardless of their level
in the organisation.
(b) The training programme should include safety management system training whose level of
detail should be appropriate to the individual’s responsibility and involvement in the safety
management system and should also include human and organisational factors.
(c) The training programme should consist of the following:
(1) a process to identify training standards, including:
(i) syllabi, duration, and frequency for each type of training and area of activity for
the persons mentioned in point (a), including for the instructors and assessors;
(ii) method(s) for delivery of training and competency assessment;
(iii) minimum performance to be achieved by trainees; and
(iv) track completion of required training;
(2) a validation process that measures the effectiveness of training;
(3) initial job-specific training;
(4) practical training;
(5) recurrent training;
(6) refresher training; and
(7) continuation training.
(d) The training programme should identify training responsibilities and contain procedures:
(1) for training and competency assessment of the trainees; and

(2) to be applied in the event that personnel do not achieve or maintain the required
standards.
(e) Training contents, syllabi and duration should comply with the operational requirements
prescribed in PART ADR, PART ACM and PART VFI.
(f) A training file should be developed for each employee, including management, and a system
should be in place to assist in identifying and tracking employee training requirements, and
verifying that personnel have received the required/planned training.
(g) Information related training standards and the related syllabi and frequency, should be
included in the aerodrome -related operations manual.

title: Training of personnel — general
text:
TRAINING OF PERSONNEL — GENERAL
(a) Aerodrome personnel
(1) The purpose of the training programme is to ensure the initial and continued
competence of the Aerodrome operators’ personnel to perform their duties,
irrespective of their level in the organisation. This is to be achieved by ensuring that
each person receives initial, recurrent, and if necessary, refresher training (as a result of
absence from duties), and other ad hoc training (e.g., due to the planned/implemented
change to the aerodrome system, etc.), which is relevant to his or her function and
tasks.
(b) One method to achieve this is by identifying the tasks of the employees and ensuring that
each one of them receives the training that corresponds to such tasks.
(c) For example, an employee whose tasks involve driving would need to undergo the relevant
driving training (depending on the area of the aerodrome that he or she will operate in the
course of his or her duties). Moreover, if the duties of that person involve also conducting
inspections of the movement area, then the training plan for that employee would also need
to include relevant training for that area.
(d) Moreover, apart from this specific type of training, one would also consider the need for all
personnel to undergo a safety management system training relevant to their duties.
(e) As part of the process of the development of the training programme, there are also other
issues that need to be considered, such as:
(1) the content and duration of the courses;
(2) the minimum performance required by the trainees;

(3) the method to be used for the delivery of the training;
(4) the way the competency assessments of the trainees will be performed; and
(5) the development of the relevant procedures to ensure that the training programme
achieves its objectives and covers circumstances that may occur (e.g., the case where
an employee fails to achieve the required competency level).

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
text:
INITIAL TRAINING
(a) Theoretical training
(1) A suitable method (or suitable methods) for the delivery of each part of the required
training should be identified and specified in the training programme;
(2) The theoretical training should be delivered at appropriate training facilities, and the
delivery of the training should be supported by means and equipment which are
suitable for the training area covered;
(b) After the initial training, the acquired competency should be assessed. The competency
assessment should be accomplished by using identified method(s), appropriate to the training
element to be assessed. Assessment procedures should be established, addressing, as a
minimum, location(s), identity check and invigilation, and assessment discipline. Computer-
based systems may be used for the assessment of the trainees.
(c) Practical training
(1) The practical training, where applicable, should follow the successful completion of the
theoretical training and   should   be   provided   by   an   instructor   nominated   in
accordance with AMC1 TRG.OR.A.005(d);
(2) A practical competency assessment should be conducted by an assessor nominated in
accordance with AMC1 TRG.OR.A.005(d), following the completion of each practical
training provided.

title: Initial training
text:
INITIAL TRAINING
Computer-based training may also be used, where interaction of the trainee(s) with other persons is
not necessary and where the training material has been prepared, reviewed and updated by an
instructor nominated in accordance with AMC1 TRG.OR.A.005(d). Where provided, such training

should consider human factors principles, and, as a minimum, should also cater for the possibility for
the trainees to ask questions and receive clarifications, as well as to provide feedback.

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
text:
RECURRENT, REFRESHER AND CONTINUATION TRAININGS
(a) Recurrent training
(1) The recurrent training may be only theoretical and should cover the areas addressed in
the initial theoretical training provided.  The recurrent training should be designed to
review, reinforce or enhance the existing knowledge and skills of the trainees, and
should also take into account the changes that have taken place in the content of the
subjects covered by the initial training.
(2) Upon completion of the recurrent training, an assessment of the trainee should be
conducted.
(b) Refresher training
(1) The refresher training may be only theoretical, and shorter than the recurrent training,
and its content should consider the length of the person’s absence and the magnitude
of the relevant changes that may have taken place during the period of absence of the
employee.
(2) Upon completion of the refresher training, an assessment of the trainee should be
conducted.
(c) Continuation training
(1) Continuation training should be provided in the following cases:
(i) A person is assigned new/different tasks;
(ii) In the case a person is to be assigned to different/additional tasks, an appropriate
theoretical and practical training which covers any differences between his or her
previous and future tasks should be completed. This differences training should
be determined based on a comparison between the training required for the new
tasks, and the training already completed by that person, as documented in his or
her training records;
(iii) The provision of training should be followed by relevant competency assessment;
and

(iv) A change is introduced to the operating environment of a person, which is of
such nature and/or magnitude that it requires the training of the personnel (e.g.
a new system to be used by the personnel concerned).
(d) A method should be established and documented to be used for determining the need (or
not) for, as well as the type(s) (theoretical, practical, or both) of, training to be provided
following changes. The provision of training should be followed by a relevant competency
assessment.

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
text:
PROFICIENCY CHECKS
(a) Aerodrome operator should establish a system for ensuring that their employees maintain
their competencies in those areas which they are operating.
(b) The proficiency check programme should:
(1) include a process to identify the frequency of proficiency checks, including for the
instructors and assessors, and track completion of the required checks;
(2) identify checking responsibilities and relevant checking methods and procedures;
(3) include procedures to be applied in the event that personnel do not achieve the
required standards; and
(4) include a validation process that measures the effectiveness of the programme.
(c) Information related to the proficiency check programme should be included in the aerodrome
-related operations manual.

title: Proficiency checks
text:
PROFICIENCY CHECKS
(a) The purpose of the proficiency check is to establish the ability of an individual to perform
satisfactorily, in accordance with applicable requirements and the content of the aerodrome -
related operations manual as they relate to his or her tasks.
(b) In particular, the proficiency checks of the Aerodrome operators’ personnel should determine
the performance of an individual regarding the tasks assigned to him or her.
(c) To this end, the elements that each proficiency check should be identified and documented.
(d) A proficiency check does not need to cover all associated elements at the same time;
however, all elements of a proficiency check should be covered within the period as
mentioned in (g) or lesser determined by the Aerodrome operators.

(e) Depending on the situation, specialty and element checked, and provided that it will not affect
the quality and completeness of the proficiency check, a single proficiency check may be used
to cover more than one person. The person(s) to be checked should be made aware prior to
the proficiency check.
(f) The methods to be used for the checking of the trainees could include:
(1) practical demonstration;
(2) computer-based assessment;
(3) oral or written tests;
(4) or combinations of such methods, as appropriate.
(g) Unless otherwise specified in this Part and Part-ADR.OPS, PART ACM and PART VFI,
Aerodrome operator should ensure that persons referred to in point TRG.OR.B.005 (a) -
Training and proficiency check programmes, undergo proficiency checks at intervals not
exceeding 24 months since the completion of their initial training.

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
text:
INSTRUCTORS AND ASSESSORS
(a) Aerodrome operator should nominate instructors and assessors to be used for the
implementation of the training and proficiency check programmes.
(b) Instructors
(1) Theoretical instructions should be given by appropriately qualified instructors.  They
should have:
(i) appropriate level and depth of knowledge in the field where instruction is to be
given;
(ii) documented ability to use appropriate instructional techniques; and
(iii) adequate experience in the subject where instruction is to be given.
(iv) Instruction on practical skills should be given by appropriately qualified
instructors who:
(A) meet the theoretical knowledge, and the working experience
requirements appropriate to the instruction being given;
(B) have demonstrated the ability to instruct, and to use appropriate
instructional techniques;
(C) are proficient in instructional techniques in the areas in which it is
intended to provide instruction; and

(D) receive relevant training, in accordance with the training programme, to
ensure that the instructional competencies are maintained.
(c) Assessors
(1) The persons who are responsible for assessing the competence of the personnel should:
(i) have demonstrated the ability to assess the performance of, and conduct tests
and checks in the areas covered by the training;
(ii) receive relevant training, in accordance with the training programme, to ensure
that the assessment standards are maintained up to date; and
(iii) meet the theoretical knowledge requirements appropriate to the instruction
being given and have adequate working experience in the area of instruction.

title: Training and proficiency check programmes
Training and proficiency check programmes
Training and proficiency check programmes
Proficiency check records
text:
PROFICIENCY CHECK RECORDS
Proficiency checks may be conducted at shorter intervals following, for example, an occurrence or to
ensure that the person is able to apply in practice knowledge acquired due to updated training.

title: Airside driving personnel
text:
AIRSIDE DRIVING PERSONNEL
(a) Aerodrome operator shall establish and implement training and proficiency checks
programmes for airside vehicle drivers at the aerodrome.

title: Airside driving personnel
text:
TRAINING OF DRIVERS — GENERAL

(a) Aerodrome operator should ensure that all airside drivers have successfully completed
theoretical and practical training of adequate duration, at least in the following areas:
(1) regulatory framework and personal responsibilities;
(2) vehicle standards, aerodrome operational requirements and procedures;
(3) safety of operating vehicles and equipment on the airside
(4) communications and radiotelephony, for drivers that operate in the manoeuvring area;
(5) human performance limitations;
(6) aerodrome layout and familiarisation with the operating environment;
(7) aerodrome rules including right of way and emergency procedures;
(8) aerodrome marking, signs and lighting.
(b) The training programme that drivers need to follow should depend on the areas where they
need to be operating. The following two training programmes should be developed:
(1) General driving training programme
(i) This training should cover the needs of all drivers operating on the apron area
and other operational areas of the aerodrome. The successful completion of this
training grants a driver the authorisation to operate unescorted, a vehicle on
aprons and other operational areas of the aerodrome, except on the
manoeuvring area.
(2) Manoeuvring area training programme
This training should cover the additional specific needs of the drivers who will be
operating on the manoeuvring area. A driver is granted the authorisation to operate
unescorted on the manoeuvring area subject to the:
(i) provisions of ADR.OPS. B.024(a)(4)- Language proficiency;
(ii) successful completion of the general driving training programme; and
(iii) successful completion of the manoeuvring area training programme.
(c) Each of the above-mentioned training programmes (general driving training programme and
manoeuvring area training programme) should consist of the following parts:
(1) Theoretical training
(i) The theoretical training should be of a defined and adequate duration, supported
by suitable educational means and material.
(ii) The theoretical training should be followed by an assessment of the trainees (see
AMC1 ADR.OR.D.017(e)). Once the theoretical part has been successfully
completed, the driver should undertake practical training.

(2) Practical training
(i) During the phase of the practical training, which needs to be of a defined and
adequate duration, the trainees should be provided with adequate practical
training and familiarisation with the aerodrome facilities and its procedures by
the nominated instructors, in day and, if relevant, night conditions.
(ii) Following the delivery of the practical training, the competence of the trainees
should be assessed, in practical terms, by the nominated assessors (see AMC1
ADR.OR.D.017(e)). This assessment should aim at assessing the ability of the
trainees to apply, in practice, the knowledge and skills they have acquired
through the theoretical and practical training.
(3) Upon the successful completion of the practical training, and provided that the driver
has received training on the use of a vehicle (see AMC1 ADR.OPS. B.024(a)(5)), a driving
authorisation may be issued.
(d) Instructors and assessors should be suitably qualified and competent.
(e) The aerodrome operator should conduct continuous oversight of the content and quality of
the training.
(f) Where the responsibility for vehicle driver training (apron and manoeuvring area) and RTF
training is delegated to a third-party provider, the aerodrome operator should institute an
oversight programme as part of its safety management system to ensure that agreed
standards are being maintained.
(g) Aerodrome operator should regularly review their vehicle driver training programmes.

title: Training of drivers — general
text:
TRAINING OF DRIVERS — GENERAL
(a) Generally, operations at an aerodrome are dependent on air traffic controllers, pilots and
vehicle drivers using visual observations to estimate the respective relative position of aircraft
and vehicles. Pilots and vehicle drivers rely on visual aids (lighting, markings and signage) to
guide them along their assigned routes and to identify intersections and holding positions.  As
part of the Surface Movement Guidance and Control System (SMGCS) the aerodrome
operator should establish and train aerodrome users on the characteristics and meaning of
the standardized markings and signage implemented at the aerodrome. These should include,
but are not limited to:
(1) Markings

(i) Boundary of responsibility line
(ii) Stand safety line
(iii) Stand-by areas – restricted for aircraft manoeuvres
(iv) Stand-by areas – height restricted
(v) Stand divide line
(vi) Tractor pushback line and pushback limit line
(vii) Equipment staging area
(viii) Air bridge wheel position
(ix) Underground services including fuel hydrant markings
(x) Service road
(xi) Vehicle limit line
(xii) Stand identification on service road
(xiii) Taxiway and taxi lane crossing
(xiv) Pedestrian crossing
(xv) Pedestrian guide line
(2) Apron Signs
(i) Stand identification sign for aircraft
(ii) No-entry sign for aircraft
(iii) Sign attention to crossing aircraft for vehicles
(iv) Jet blast sign for vehicles
(v) Examples of road and other traffic signs
(vi) Examples of emergency signs
(vii) FOD Bin
(b) The theoretical training should be supported by material which provides up-to-date, adequate
and suitable information regarding the aerodrome, in the form of presentations, maps,
diagrams, videos, booklets, checklists, etc. as appropriate

title: Recurrent, refresher and continuation training
text: RECURRENT, REFRESHER AND CONTINUATION TRAINING

Training and proficiency check programmes regulates the provision of training
following the completion of the initial training, as part of the aerodrome operator’s training
programme.

title: Airside driving personnel
Airside driving personnel
Airside driving personnel
text:
TRAINING OF DRIVERS — RADIOTELEPHONY
In addition to the training requirements listed in AMC1 ADR.OPS.B.024(c) and AMC2

Authorisation of airside vehicle drivers , drivers who are expected to operate on
the manoeuvring area of the aerodrome should also receive training in Radiotelephony , which
should include as a minimum:
(a) hierarchy of message priority: message priorities, and understanding of distress, alerting,
control and information messages.
(b) phonetic alphabet: correct pronunciation of letters, words, and numbers.
(c) standard phraseology
(1) emphasis on the need for drivers to use standard phraseology; and
(2) the need for caution with certain phrases such as ‘cleared’.
(d) call signs for aircraft, ATC, and vehicles
(1) an understanding of terminology and acronyms used by ATC and pilots;
(2) knowledge of the airline call signs used at the aerodrome; and
(3) knowledge of vehicle call signs, and that they should be appropriate to their function.
(e) read back procedures: The need for vehicle drivers to use standard readback, in the same
manner as pilots, for instructions such as ‘enter/cross the runway’, and if conditional
clearances are used.

(f) readability scale: Understanding and use of the readability scale from 1 to 5.
(g) lost or uncertain of position: Understanding of local procedures for vehicle drivers are lost or
uncertain of their position on the manoeuvring area.
(h) vehicle breakdown
(1) local procedure for vehicle breakdown on runways and taxiways; and
(2) procedure for notifying ATC of vehicle failure.
(i) radio failure
(1) understanding of the local procedure if radio failure occurs while on the runway or
taxiway; and
(2) understanding of the light signals that can be used by ATC to pass instructions to
vehicles.
(j) transmitting techniques and use of RTF
(1) understanding the reasons for listening out prior to transmitting;
(2) use of standard phraseology and ICAO air-ground radiotelephony communications
procedures;
(3) words and sounds to be avoided;
(4) correct positioning of microphones to avoid voice distortion;
(5) avoidance of ‘clipped’ transmissions;
(6) awareness of regional accents and variations of speech; and
(7) speed of delivery of RTF phraseology.
(k) portable radios
(1) correct use of radios;
(2) effective range and battery life;
(3) screening/shielding effects on the aerodrome; and
(4) use of correct call signs, either related to a vehicle or a person.
(l) safety while using radios
(1) local instructions regarding the use of portable radios and hand-held microphones while
driving a vehicle; and
(2) local instructions on the use of mobile telephones while operating airside.

title: Airside driving personnel
text:
THEORITICAL TRAINING — RADIO TELEPHONY

(a) All drivers of vehicles operating on the manoeuvring area should have an appropriate level of
competence with respect to the use of RTF phraseology.
(b) The theoretical training should emphasise on the following areas:
(1) categories of messages
(i) message categories and priorities; an understanding of distress, alerting; and
(ii) control and information messages.
(2) test procedures including readability scale
(i) understanding and use of the readability scale from 1 to 5.
PRACTICAL TRAINING — RADIO TELEPHONY
(a) In this phase, the training should cover the use of fixed and portable radio communication
devices, and the practical use of the theoretical knowledge acquired in the previous phase of
the training, through the implementation of the aerodrome’s communication procedures.

title: Aerodrome rescue and firefighting personnel
text:
AERODROME RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING PERSONNEL
(a) An aerodrome operator, except vertical flight infrastructure, shall:
(1) ensure all rescue and firefighting personnel are properly trained to perform their duties
in an efficient manner and participate in live fire drills commensurate with the types of
aircraft and type of rescue and firefighting equipment in use at the aerodrome,
including pressure-fed fuel fires;
(2) establish and implement training and proficiency check programmes for rescue and
firefighting personnel including training in human performance and team coordination;
and
(3) ensure training and proficiency check programmes for rescue and firefighting personnel
including initial and subsequent changes to the programmes are managed in
accordance with the operator’s safety management system.

title: Aerodrome rescue and firefighting personnel
text:
AERODROME RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING PERSONNEL

(a) As the success of any rescue and firefighting operations relies very much on teamwork, the
importance of building mutual trust and team coordination among RFF personnel during
training cannot be overstressed. Training must therefore be suitably designed to guide RFF
personnel towards achieving these objectives.
(b) In order for rescue and firefighting training to be as realistic as possible, live fire training is
crucial in helping RFF personnel acclimatize to a heated and smoke-filled environment, so that
in the event of an actual emergency, RFF personnel will be able to execute their tasks more
confidently and effectively. Where possible, simulators replicating different facades of rescue
and firefighting operations (e.g., vehicle driving and operations; command and control, etc.)
should be made available for RFF personnel to be trained in a controlled, safe and realistic
environment.
(c) Fires associated with fuel discharged under very high pressure from a ruptured fuel tank are
known as “pressure-fed fuel fires”. The rupture of fuel tanks in an aircraft crash and the
consequent spillage of highly volatile fuels, and other flammable liquids used by aircraft,
present a high degree of probability of ignition if these liquids come into contact with hot
metal parts of the aircraft or because of sparks caused by the movement of wreckage or
disturbance of the electrical circuit.
(d) The most important factors bearing on effective rescue in a survivable aircraft accident is the
training received, the effectiveness of the equipment and the speed with which personnel and
equipment, designated for RFF purposes, can be deployed.

title: Aerodrome rescue and firefighting personnel
text:
TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECK PROGRAMMES ARRANGEMENTS
(a) A competent person should be formally appointed with the authority and responsibility for
establishing and implementing training and proficiency check programmes for rescue and
firefighting personnel at the aerodrome.
(b) A training standardisation and development committee should be established to:
(1) ensure consistency of assessment decisions and associated records;
(2) provide continuous improvement of the overall training and proficiency check
programmes;
(3) review and implement changes to requirements as appropriate; and
(4) consider the learning that arises from aircraft accidents or other similar events.

title: ARFFS training competent person
text:
1. DEFINITION OF COMPETENT PERSON
(a) A competent Person is defined as an individual who possesses the requisite qualifications,
knowledge, experience, and authority to manage and oversee the training and proficiency of
RFF personnel. This person is formally appointed by the aerodrome operator and is overall
responsible for establishing, implementing, and maintaining training and proficiency check
programmes to ensure compliance with regulatory and operational requirements.
2. QUALIFICATIONS AND EXPERIENCE
(a) The competent person should, at least, have the following qualifications and experience:
(1) recognised qualifications in RFFS management, emergency management, or a related
field;
(2) experience in a supervisory or managerial role within a RFFS or equivalent emergency
services environment;
(3) instructor and assessor qualifications in the development and delivery of training
programmes and proficiency assessments, including understanding of adult learning
principles and assessment methodologies; and
(4) knowledge of relevant GCAA, ICAO SARPs, national regulations, and industry best
practices related to RFFS operations and training.
3. AUTHORITY AND RESPONSIBILITY
(a) The competent person should have the authority to:
(1) establish and implement training programmes for all ARFFS personnel, including initial,
recurrent, and specialised training.
(2) develop and administer proficiency check programmes to ensure that personnel
maintain the required level of competency.
(3) authorise and conduct assessments, evaluations, and acceptance of ARFFS personnel’s
performance.
(4) monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of training programmes and make necessary
adjustments to improve training outcomes and operational readiness.
(5) report to senior management and the regulatory authority on the status and
effectiveness of training and proficiency check programmes.
4. APPOINTMENT OF THE COMPETENT PERSON

(a) The aerodrome operator should formally appoint the competent person through an official
appointment letter, specifying the authority, responsibilities, and accountability of the role.
This appointment should be recorded in the aerodrome’s official documents and
communicated to all relevant stakeholders, including the regulatory authority.
(b) The competent person’s appointment, qualifications, and experience should be documented
and maintained in the aerodrome’s personnel records. These records should be readily
available for inspection by the regulatory authority upon request.
5. RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE COMPETENT PERSON
(a) The competent person is responsible for the following key functions:
(1) Initial Training: Develop comprehensive training programmes for new ARFFS personnel,
covering all core competencies, including fire suppression, rescue operations,
emergency medical response, and operational procedures.
(2) Recurrent Training: Ensure ongoing training for all ARFFS personnel to maintain and
update skills and knowledge, in line with changing operational requirements and
regulatory standards.
(3) Specialised Training: Implement specialised training for specific operational roles or
equipment, such as breathing apparatus operations, hazardous materials response, and
incident command.
(b) Implementing Proficiency Check Programmes
(1) Annual Proficiency Checks: Develop and administer annual proficiency checks for all
ARFFS personnel to verify their ability to perform required tasks and responsibilities.
(2) Scenario-Based Assessments: Conduct scenario-based assessments to evaluate
personnel’s performance under realistic and challenging conditions.
(3) Remedial Training: Identify areas of deficiency during proficiency checks and implement
remedial training to address gaps in knowledge or skills.
(c) Maintaining Training Records
(1) Training Logs: Maintain accurate and up-to-date training logs for all ARFFS personnel,
documenting training activities, proficiency checks, and acceptances.
(2) Assessment Records: Keep detailed records of all assessments and proficiency checks,
including performance evaluations and any corrective actions taken.
(d) Continuous Improvement

(1) Programme Review: Regularly review and update training and proficiency check
programmes to reflect changes in regulations, industry standards, and operational
needs.
(2) Feedback Mechanism: Establish a feedback mechanism to collect input from ARFFS
personnel and use this information to improve training and assessment processes.
(e) Compliance Monitoring
(1) The competent person should ensure that all training and proficiency check
programmes comply with GCAA standards, national regulations, and any additional
requirements set by the aerodrome operator.

title: ARFFS training standardisation and development committee
text:
RFFS TRAINING STANDARDISATION AND DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE
1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
(a) The purpose of the training standardisation and development committee (TSDC) is to maintain
the integrity of the training and proficiency checks programmes by:
(1) consistency of assessment decisions: Maintain uniformity in the evaluation of ARFFS
personnel's performance and the associated documentation.
(2) continuous improvement of training programmes: Enhance the quality and
effectiveness of training programmes through regular review and updates.
(3) implement changes to requirements: Monitor and adapt training programmes and
requirements in response to regulatory updates, industry best practices, and
operational needs.
(4) learning from aircraft accidents and similar Events: Analyse and integrate lessons
learned from incidents, accidents, and other significant events to improve training and
operational readiness.
(b) The scope of this guidance applies to all aerodromes within the regulatory jurisdiction and is
intended for use by aerodrome operator, ARFFS training managers, and training providers
overseeing ARFFS training standards.
2. ESTABLISHMENT OF THE TRAINING STANDARDISATION AND DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE (TSDC)
(a) The TSDC should consist of a diverse group of stakeholders, including but not limited to:
(1) Chief Fire Officer: Chairperson responsible for coordinating committee activities.
(2) Training Manager: acts as the secretariat to the committee

(3) Senior ARFFS Personnel: Experienced members who can provide insight into
operational challenges and training needs.
(4) Training Instructors and Assessors: Individuals directly involved in delivering and
assessing training programmes.
(5) Safety and Compliance Officer: Ensures alignment with regulatory requirements and
safety standards.
(6) Human Resources Representative: Supports the integration of training outcomes with
personnel development and competency frameworks.
(7) External Experts: As needed, individuals with specialised knowledge in training, safety,
or emergency response.
(b) Roles and Responsibilities of the TSDC include the following key functions:
(1) Develop and implement standardised assessment tools and criteria to ensure
uniformity in evaluating ARFFS personnel.
(2) Conduct regular calibration sessions for assessors to align their understanding and
application of assessment standards.
(3) Review assessment records to verify the consistency and accuracy of evaluation
decisions.
(4) Conduct periodic reviews of training programmes to identify areas for enhancement
and update content based on feedback and emerging trends.
(5) Analyse training outcomes and assessment data to identify gaps and opportunities for
improvement.
(6) Implement revised training methodologies and resources to address identified needs
and improve training effectiveness.
(7) Monitor changes in regulatory requirements, industry standards, and operational needs
that impact ARFFS training.
(8) Develop and recommend modifications to training programmes and requirements to
ensure compliance and relevance.
(9) Communicate and implement approved changes within the training framework and
ensure that all stakeholders are informed and trained accordingly.
(10) Review reports and findings from aircraft accidents, incidents, and other significant
events to identify lessons relevant to ARFFS training.
(11) Develop training modules or updates that incorporate these lessons to improve
preparedness and response capabilities.

(12) Facilitate scenario-based training and simulations that reflect real-world events to
reinforce learning and enhance operational readiness.
3. COMMITTEE OPERATIONS
(a) The TSDC should meet at least annually to review training outcomes, discuss emerging issues,
and plan future activities.
(b) Additional meetings may be convened as necessary in response to significant events,
regulatory changes, or urgent training needs.
(c) Agendas and minutes of meetings should be documented and retained for audit and review
purposes.
(d) Decisions within the TSDC should be made by consensus wherever possible. If consensus
cannot be reached, decisions will be made by a majority vote of committee members.
(e) Any proposed changes to training programmes or assessment criteria should be documented,
reviewed, and approved by the committee before implementation.
(f) The TSDC is responsible for producing regular reports on its activities, including
recommendations for changes to training programmes, assessment findings, and continuous
improvement initiatives.
(g) All records of committee meetings, decisions, and actions should be maintained in a secure
and accessible format for review by regulatory authorities and senior management.
4. IMPLEMENTATION AND COMMUNICATION
(a) Approved changes to training programmes or assessment processes should be implemented
in a structured manner, with clear timelines and responsibilities assigned.
(b) Training instructors, assessors, and RFF personnel should be informed of changes through
formal communication channels, and additional training or briefings should be provided as
needed.
(c) The TSDC should maintain open communication with all stakeholders, including RFFS
personnel, management, and regulatory authorities, to ensure transparency and collaboration
in the development and implementation of training initiatives.
(d) Feedback from stakeholders should be actively sought and considered in the committee’s
ongoing review and development activities.
5. EVALUATION AND REVIEW

(a) The TSDC should conduct an annual review of its activities, including an evaluation of the
effectiveness of implemented changes and the overall impact on training and operational
performance.
(b) This review should include an assessment of the committee’s processes, the relevance of
training content, and the quality of assessment decisions.
(c) Based on the findings of the annual review, the TSDC should identify areas for improvement
and develop an action plan to address these areas.
(d) The committee should remain proactive in identifying and responding to emerging challenges
and opportunities within RFFS training and development.
6. COMPLIANCE AND ACCOUNTABILITY
(a) The TSDC should ensure that all training programmes and assessment processes comply with
applicable GCAA standards, national regulations, and industry best practices.
(b) Regular audits and inspections should be conducted to verify compliance and address any
identified issues promptly.
(c) The TSDC is accountable to the aerodrome operator and the regulatory authority for ensuring
the integrity and effectiveness of RFFS training and assessment.
(d) Any issues or concerns regarding the committee’s activities or decisions should be reported to
the appropriate authority for resolution.

title: Aerodrome rescue and firefighting personnel
text:
ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECK PROGRAMMES
(a) Suitable training facilities, resources and equipment should be provided to rescue and
firefighting personnel including availability of instructors and assessors for the
implementation of the training and proficiency check programmes.
(b) Rescue and firefighting personnel should actively participate in live fire drills commensurate
with the types of aircraft, types of vehicles, vessels and equipment, and types of principal and
complementary extinguishing agents in use at the aerodrome, including pressure-fed fuel
fires.
(c) Training and proficiency check programmes for rescue and firefighting personnel should
include training in human performance, including team coordination.
(d) Training and proficiency check programmes for RFF personnel should include competency-
based training and assessment plan consisting of:

(1) structured learning programme (SLP) for the initial acquisition of knowledge, skills and
understanding for each role/rank;
(2) maintenance of competence (MOC) for maintaining the necessary knowledge, skills and
understanding for each role/rank, not exceeding four years; and
(3) proficiency checks (PFC) conducted at intervals not exceeding 12 months after
completing the SLP.

title: Establishing and implementing competence-based training and
text:
assessment programmes

ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING COMPETENCE-BASED TRAINING AND ASSESSMENT
PROGRAMMES
A. AERODROME RFFS COMPETENCE STANDARDS
(a) This guidance outlines the requirements for an aerodrome operator to establish, implement
and maintain training and proficiency checks programmes for aerodrome rescue and
firefighting personnel employed at aerodrome in the United Arab Emirates, which include:
(1) a structured learning programme (SLP) for RFF personnel to achieve an initial
acquisition of knowledge, skill, and understanding (KSU) in a particular set of tasks
according to their assigned roles and responsibilities as operational, supervisory and
managerial personnel;
(2) a maintenance of competence (MOC) plan for RFF personnel to maintain the acquired
knowledge, skill and understanding (KSU) in accordance with their assigned roles and
responsibilities not exceeding four years; and
(3) proficiency checks (PFC) conducted at intervals not exceeding 12 months since the
completion of the structured learning programme.
B. ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING COMPETENCE-BASED TRAINING AND ASSESMENT
FRAMEWORK FOR ARFFS PERSONNEL AT AERODROME S.
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) The principal objective of an aerodrome rescue and firefighting service is to save lives in the
event of an aircraft accident or incident occurring at, or in the immediate vicinity of, an
aerodrome. The RFF service is provided to create and maintain survivable conditions, to
provide egress routes for occupants and to initiate the rescue of those occupants unable to
make their escape without direct aid. The most important factors bearing on effective rescue
in a survivable aircraft accident is:

(1) the training received;
(2) the effectiveness of the equipment; and
(3) the speed with which personnel and equipment, designated for RFF purposes, can be
deployed.
(b) Personnel whose duties consist solely of the provision of RFF services for aircraft operations
are infrequently called upon to face a serious situation involving lifesaving at a major aircraft
fire. They will experience a few incidents and a larger number of standbys to cover
movements of aircraft in circumstances where the possibility of an accident may reasonably
be anticipated but will seldom be called upon to put their knowledge and experience to the
test. It follows, therefore, that only by means of a most carefully planned and rigorously
followed programme of training can there be any assurance that both personnel and
equipment will be capable in dealing with a major aircraft fire should the necessity arise.
2. DESIGNING COMPETENCY-BASED APPROACH TO TRAINING AND ASSESSMENT PROGRAMME
(a) The development of competency-based training and assessment is based on ICAO
instructional system design (ISD) methodology approach whereby competencies and their
standards are defined, training is based on the competencies identified, and assessments are
developed to determine whether these competencies have been achieved.
(b) Competency-based approaches to training and assessment should include at least the
following features:
(1) the justification of a training need through a systematic analysis and the identification
of indicators for evaluation;
(2) the use of a job and task analysis to determine performance standards, the conditions
under which the job is carried out, the criticality of tasks, and the inventory of
knowledge, skills and attitudes;
(3) the identification of the characteristics of the trainee population;
(4) the derivation of training objectives from the task analysis and their formulation in an
observable and measurable fashion;
(5) the development of criterion-referenced, valid, reliable and performance-oriented
tests;
(6) the development of a curriculum based on adult learning principles and with a view to
achieving an optimal path to the attainment of competencies;
(7) the development of material-dependent training; and

(8) the use of a continuous evaluation process to ensure the effectiveness of training and
its relevance to line operations.
Note. — A detailed description of the ICAO course development methodology, a competency-based
approach to training and assessment and an example of an ISD methodology is provided in the
attachment to ICAO Doc 9868 Chapter 2.
(c) A training provider should develop general requirements concerning the management of
instructors, assessors and provide guidance on:
(1) the selection of instructors, assessors and description of competency-based assessment
training;
(2) the performance criteria to be considered by assessors when assessing each
competency; and
(3) the tolerances applicable to all competency-based tests.
The Competency Framework
(d) The competency framework consists of competency units, competency elements,
performance criteria, evidence and assessment guide and range of variables. Competency
units, competency elements and performance criteria are derived from job and task analysis
and are describe observable outcomes.
The ICAO Course Development Methodology
(e) The ICAO course development methodology, like any other ISD methodology, uses a
systematic approach to training development. It therefore constitutes a quality assurance tool
for accepted training providers that supports compliance with requirements and the
development of appropriate training activities. It does so by identifying the key competencies
that need to be achieved, determining the most effective way of achieving them and
establishing valid and reliable assessment tools to evaluate their achievement.
(f) Such a tool, however, cannot be effectively implemented without the support of all
stakeholders. Stakeholders include personnel involved in management, instruction design,
instruction delivery, instruction assessment, operations and, of course, trainees. Successful
implementation of competency-based training and assessment depends to a large extent on
the support of this systematic approach at all levels of a training provider.
(g) The ICAO course development methodology has three broad categories — analysis, design
and production, and evaluation — which can be subdivided into nine phases. A brief

description of the specific outputs of the nine phases is summarized in Table D-1 and a more
detailed description of each phase’s process is provided below.

3. COURSE DEVELOPERS, ASSESSORS AND INSTRUCTORS
Course Developer Qualifications
(a) Course developers should have demonstrated that they possess the competencies described
in this guidance and that they have successfully achieved the ability to develop training in
accordance with the features of a competency-based approach to training.
Assessor and Instructor Qualifications

(b) All assessors and instructors should hold or have held appropriate qualifications and
experiences commensurate with the level of training programme for which the privilege to
assess or instruct is being sought.
(c) Qualified assessors and instructors may be assigned to carry out specific assessment, training,
checking, testing and/or auditing duties to determine that all required performance standards
have been satisfactorily achieved. These performance standards may have been established
as a final objective or required to be met on a continuous basis. In either case, the assessors
and instructors are responsible for making a determination of the actual standards attained
and any recommendation for immediate remediation, if necessary.
(d) Prior to a training provider authorizing the provision of instruction within holistic competency-
based training environments, assessors and instructors should undergo a selection process
designed to ensure the individual’s motivation and disposition are suitable for the assessor’s
and instructor’s role.
(e) Training programmes for the assessor and instructor role should focus on development of the
competencies listed in the attachment to this guidance, in the following areas:
(1) manage safety;
(2) prepare the training environment;
(3) manage the trainee;
(4) conduct training;
(5) perform trainee assessment;
(6) perform course evaluation; and
(7) continuously improve performance.
(f) All assessors and instructors should successfully complete a formal assessor and instructor
competency assessment during the conduct of practical training. The final assessment of
assessor and instructor competence should be made against the competency.
(g) All assessors and instructors should receive refresher training, and be reassessed using a
documented training and assessment process acceptable to the appropriate authority,
implemented by a certificated or accepted provider, or at appropriate intervals. Such
refresher training and reassessment intervals should not exceed three years.

5. ESTABLISHING AN ARFFS CBTA PROGRAMME
(a) Scope
(1) In order to establish and implement an effective CBTA programme, the training
provider should consider a systematic approach which is based on the following phases:

(i) Establish competence maps for each identified rank
(ii) Carry out a task analysis for each rank
(iii) Complete a training needs analysis
(iv) Establish a training syllabus
(v) Establish a proficiency check programme
(vi) Establish a validation and review programme
(b) Establish competence maps for each identified role
(1) Competence-maps have been established within this guidance for the generic roles of:
(i) ARFFS Operational personnel – Watchroom attendant, Firefighter and Senior
Firefighter
(ii) ARFFS Supervisory personnel – Crew, Watch and Station Commanders
(iii) ARFFS Managerial personnel – Unit Commander, Deputy and Chief Fire Officer
(c) Competence-mapping refers to the collection of tasks grouped together, defining the activities
relevant to a particular grade. Within the tasks are critical functions which have to be carried
out to ensure the objective is achievable.
(d) The ARFFS may choose to adopt their own specific terms within the generic terminology of
Supervisor and Manager. There is no such thing as a “typical” Firefighter, as all roles at
aerodrome can vary due to a number of factors such as risk, resource availability, and
organisational structure.
(e) Competence-maps provide a tool against which performance can be assessed and measured
in order to plan for the four stages of development, namely:
(1) Learning and development.
(2) Achievement of competence.
(3) Maintenance of competence.
(4) Continuous Professional Development (CPD).
6. CONDUCTING A TRAINING ANALYSIS
(a) Training Needs Analysis
(1) A training needs analysis should be conducted to identify the underpinning knowledge,
understanding and skills required to carry out the tasks of ARFFS personnel in relation
to their roles, i.e., Operational, Supervisors and Managers. This analysis will also include
an evaluation process which measures the outcomes of the training provided by the

aerodrome, against the published aims and objectives of the training programme to
ensure that these are being achieved.
(2) It is important to understand that completion of a training course does not, in isolation,
determine that someone is competent. Competence can only be assessed and
confirmed when there is sufficient and satisfactory evidence of consistent workplace
performance.
(b) Training Frequency Analysis
(1) Upon the formulation and completion of the task and training needs analysis the next
fundamental element of this scheme is to determine how many times specific
tasks/functions have to be carried out in the workplace to ensure that operational
competency is maintained at all times.
(2) This training frequency analysis is based on an assessment of four areas relating to the
training for competency.
(i) Change: i.e. does the subject change much over time?
(ii) Repetition: i.e. how often is the subject/skill practised in normal work?
(iii) Complexity: i.e. how difficult is the subject/skill?
(iv) Risk: i.e. what are the consequences of poor performance?
(c) Training Facilities Analysis
(1) A detailed assessment needs to be carried out on what appropriate training simulator
and training aids will be required, to ensure that the ARFFS maintains its operational
competency in relation to the type and frequency of aircraft operations.
(2) Training facilities and equipment should commensurate with the level of aerodrome
rescue and firefighting protection provided at the aerodrome. Where an aerodrome
operator manages multiple aerodrome rescue and firefighting services, the provision of
a centralised training facility can be considered provided that the facility provides the
necessary training simulations catering to the specific needs of the RFF personnel
employed at these aerodromes.
(3) The provision of kerosene-based fuel can be considered for live fire trainings to provide
the necessary realism and exposure to RFF personnel. Where the use of such fuel is
prohibited or restricted due to environmental laws and regulations, a suitable
alternative fuel or a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) may be selected provided it delivers
sufficient characteristics to a kerosene-based fuel in terms of radiant heat and
performance. Where an alternative training fuel is selected, RFF personnel should be

informed of the differences in firefighting and the use of such fuel should not create
additional hazards and risks to RFF personnel.

title: Competence standards for ARFFS personnel
text:
COMPETENCY STANDARDS FOR ARFFS PERSONNEL
Introductory Note.
Competency standard: An authoritative benchmark that defines the expected levels of performance,
skills, knowledge, and behaviours required for individuals to perform their roles effectively within a
specific industry or profession. It serves as a definitive guideline for both training and assessment,
providing a clear framework for what constitutes proficiency in a given occupation or task.
Competency standards are meticulously developed to ensure that individuals are equipped to meet
the demands of their roles, particularly in high-stakes environments where precision, expertise, and
adherence to best practices are crucial. They are widely used in sectors such as aviation, healthcare,
emergency services, and technical industries, where the consequences of inadequate performance
can be significant.
Competency Unit: A specific area of performance relevant to the role. For example, in the aviation
industry, competency units might include "Response to Aircraft Emergencies," "Fire Suppression
Techniques," and "Emergency Medical Care."
Performance Criteria: Each competency unit includes detailed performance criteria that define what
an individual should achieve to be considered competent. These criteria are measurable and specific,
outlining the quality and quantity of performance expected in various tasks or scenarios.
Knowledge Requirements: Competency standards specify the theoretical understanding necessary to
perform tasks effectively. This may include knowledge of industry regulations, operational
procedures, safety protocols, and technical information related to specific equipment or systems.
Skills and Abilities: The standard identifies the practical skills and abilities that individuals should
demonstrate. This includes technical skills such as operating equipment, as well as cognitive skills like
problem-solving and decision-making in complex situations.

Behavioural Attributes: Competency standards often include behavioural attributes that reflect
professional conduct. This can encompass teamwork, communication, leadership, and adherence to
ethical and safety standards, all of which are critical in high-pressure environments.
Assessment Guidelines: Competency standards provide guidance on how to assess an individual’s
performance against the defined criteria. This can include both formative (ongoing) and summative
(final) assessments, practical demonstrations, simulations, and theoretical examinations.
1. INTRODUCTION
(a) This guidance document establishes the competency standards for Aerodrome Rescue and
Firefighting Services (ARFFS) personnel employed in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), including
operational, supervisory, and managerial roles. These standards are designed to ensure that
all ARFFS personnel possess the necessary skills, knowledge, and behaviours to perform their
duties effectively, maintaining high levels of safety, operational readiness, and compliance
with UAE General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA) regulations and international best practices.
2. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
(a) The purpose of this document is to:
(1) Define the competency requirements for ARFFS personnel across different roles,
including operational firefighters, supervisory staff, and managerial positions.
(2) Provide a framework for training, assessment, and professional development to ensure
that all personnel meet the required competency standards.
(3) Support aerodrome operator in maintaining a high standard of safety and performance
within their ARFFS units.
(b) This guidance applies to all aerodromes and heliports within the UAE that employ ARFFS
personnel and is intended for use by aerodrome operator, ARFFS managers, training
providers, and regulatory bodies overseeing ARFFS operations.
3. COMPETENCY STANDARDS OVERVIEW
(a) Table 6 details each competency unit includes competency elements and performance criteria
that define the expected skills, knowledge, and behaviours including assessment ratio
required for each ARFFS personnel.
Table 6: Competency standards for ARFFS personnel
Competency Unit 1: Operational Communication

This competency unit outlines the required competency elements, performance criteria, and the
skills, knowledge, and behaviour needed for effective operational communication for ARFFS
personnel in ensuring clear, concise, and effective communication during routine operations and
emergency situations.
Skill Development: The unit emphasises real-time application of communication skills, particularly
in emergency contexts where ARFFS personnel should react swiftly and accurately.
Behavioural Expectations: Given the high-stakes nature of ARFFS operations, effective
communication behaviour, such as maintaining calm under pressure, adhering to protocols, and
showing cultural sensitivity, is crucial to the safety and success of the mission.
Assessment Ratio: The recommended split between theoretical knowledge and practical
application reflects the critical importance of both the understanding and hands-on use of

Competency Unit 4: Don Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
This competency unit is designed to ensure ARFFS personnel possess the necessary skills,
knowledge, and behaviours to properly use, maintain, and manage personal protective equipment
(PPE). PPE is critical for safeguarding ARFFS personnel during emergency operations, and
maintaining readiness through proper PPE management is essential for operational safety and
effectiveness.
Skill Development: This unit ensures that ARFFS personnel can competently select, inspect,
maintain, and use PPE, ensuring their safety during routine and emergency operations, particularly
in environments where hazardous materials or high temperatures are involved.
Behavioural Expectations: Personnel are expected to demonstrate a high level of responsibility
and discipline in the use and maintenance of PPE. Proactive management of PPE readiness,
coupled with adherence to safety protocols, is essential for maintaining operational safety and
effectiveness.

Assessment Ratio: The emphasis on practical assessment recognises that hands-on proficiency in
the use of PPE is critical to ARFFS operations. Theoretical knowledge provides a foundation for
understanding the technical aspects and proper management of PPE, while practical assessments
ensure personnel can apply this knowledge in real-world situations.

emergency scenarios. Theoretical understanding provides a foundation for system functionality,
