This competency unit is designed to ensure ARFFS (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Services)
personnel possess the required skills, knowledge, and behaviours to effectively deploy and
operate firefighting equipment during emergency situations. This unit covers the operational
readiness, use, and maintenance of essential firefighting tools and equipment to ensure a safe,
efficient, and coordinated response.
Skill Development: This unit focuses on developing the ability of ARFFS personnel to deploy,
operate, and maintain firefighting equipment effectively during various emergency scenarios.
Critical skills include hose management, extinguisher use, equipment coordination, and post-
operation maintenance.
Behavioural Expectations: Personnel are expected to demonstrate responsibility, precision, and
teamwork during the deployment and operation of firefighting equipment. A proactive attitude
towards equipment maintenance and readiness is essential for maintaining safety and operational
effectiveness.
Assessment Ratio: The balance between theoretical and practical assessment reflects the
importance of understanding the technical aspects of firefighting equipment while ensuring
personnel are proficient in their practical use during high-stress situations. Emphasis is placed on
hands-on application to simulate real-world operations.

them effectively in real-world firefighting scenarios (practical). Practical assessments are
prioritised to ensure personnel can deploy and operate extinguishing media with precision.

focusing on the understanding of aircraft systems, emergency scenarios, and ICAO regulations.

triage principles, emergency medical care, and coordination with medical responders to ensure
effective and life-saving interventions.

communication, and precision in administering medical care. A proactive and organised approach
to casualty management is critical to ensuring the best possible outcomes in emergency situations.

with practical application in real-world scenarios. Theoretical assessments focus on understanding
triage systems, medical interventions, and communication protocols, while practical assessments
emphasise the execution of triage, medical care, and coordination during mass casualty events.

leadership are required to ensure that hazards are addressed promptly and safely, maintaining
operational continuity.

identify, assess, and mitigate hazards in real-time situations. Theoretical understanding is essential

control.

This competency unit ensures ARFFS (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Services) personnel are
equipped with the knowledge, skills, and behaviours necessary to understand and apply
aerodrome emergency planning effectively. This unit covers the key components of aerodrome
emergency plans (AEP), the coordination of resources and stakeholders, and the execution of
emergency response procedures to ensure a rapid, organised, and effective response to any
emergency incident at the aerodrome.

coordination, incident command, and communication. Personnel are trained to manage both the
development of aerodrome emergency plans and the execution of these plans during actual
emergencies or drills.

effective communication throughout the planning, activation, and management of aerodrome
emergency responses. The ability to collaborate with multiple agencies and continuously improve
emergency plans is essential.
Assessment Ratio: This unit balances theoretical understanding with practical application,
ensuring personnel are well-versed in both the regulatory requirements of aerodrome emergency
planning and the real-time implementation of emergency procedures. Theoretical assessments
ensure comprehension of GCAA and national regulations, while practical assessments focus on
applying emergency plans and coordinating responses.

equipped with the knowledge, skills, and behaviours necessary to understand and apply human
factors principles during emergency operations. The unit covers the impact of human factors on

are expected to apply these principles to enhance operational effectiveness, safety, and
coordination during emergency responses.

communication, leadership, and stress management skills, ensuring that personnel can apply
human factors principles to improve safety, teamwork, and operational efficiency.
Behavioural Expectations: Personnel are expected to demonstrate strong leadership, effective
communication, and proactive management of human factors that influence performance. A
commitment to situational awareness, teamwork, and continuous improvement is critical for
operational success.
Assessment Ratio: The balance between theoretical and practical assessments ensures personnel
have a deep understanding of human factors principles and can apply them in real-world
scenarios. Theoretical assessments focus on the ICAO framework and cognitive factors, while
practical assessments emphasise the application of these principles during emergency operations.

This competency unit ensures ARFFS (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Services) personnel are
proficient in responding to incidents involving dangerous goods (hazardous materials). The unit
covers hazard identification, risk assessment, containment procedures, and coordination with
specialised response teams to mitigate the risks posed by dangerous goods incidents, ensuring the
safety of personnel, the environment, and airport operations.

communication, and decontamination. Personnel are expected to manage dangerous goods
incidents safely, minimising risks to people, the environment, and operations.

during dangerous goods incidents. Effective communication, quick decision-making, and
leadership in hazardous environments are critical to operational success.
Assessment Ratio: Theoretical and practical assessments are balanced to ensure personnel are
proficient in both understanding the regulations and classifications of dangerous goods and
applying real-time response strategies. Theoretical assessments focus on regulations, risk
identification, and planning, while practical assessments focus on containment, mitigation, and
coordination with external response teams.

COMPETENCY UNIT 28: RESPONSE TO DOMESTIC INCIDENTS AT AERODROMES
This competency unit ensures ARFFS (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Services) personnel are
proficient in responding to domestic incidents at aerodromes, such as fires in terminal buildings,
hangars, fuel storage areas, or other facilities. This unit covers fire suppression, evacuation
procedures, coordination with internal and external agencies, and the management of domestic
incidents to ensure the safety of personnel, passengers, and infrastructure.
Skill Development: This unit focuses on key skills such as fire suppression, evacuation
management, risk assessment, and incident command. Personnel are trained to manage domestic
incidents within aerodromes effectively, ensuring the safety of personnel, passengers, and
infrastructure.
Behavioural Expectations: Personnel are expected to demonstrate calmness under pressure,
effective communication, and leadership throughout the incident. A proactive approach to risk
assessment and hazard management is critical for ensuring the safety and success of the
response.
Assessment Ratio: Theoretical assessments focus on understanding the types of domestic
incidents and the regulatory requirements for responding to such incidents. Practical assessments
emphasise fire suppression techniques, evacuation procedures, and coordination with internal
and external response teams.

COMPETENCY UNIT 29: RESPONSE TO UNLAWFUL INTERFERENCE INCIDENTS AT AERODROMES
This competency unit ensures ARFFS (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Services) personnel are
equipped to respond effectively to incidents of unlawful interference at aerodromes, including
hijacking, sabotage, terrorism, and unauthorised access. This unit covers threat identification,
coordination with security agencies, containment, and mitigation strategies to ensure the safety
of passengers, personnel, and critical infrastructure.
Skill Development: This unit develops critical skills in threat assessment, coordination with
security agencies, incident command, and public safety management. Personnel are trained to
manage unlawful interference incidents effectively while prioritising safety and compliance with
security protocols.
Behavioural Expectations: Personnel are expected to demonstrate strong leadership, effective
communication, and adaptability in managing high-pressure situations involving unlawful
interference. Vigilance, coordination, and a focus on safety are essential to the successful
resolution of these incidents.
Assessment Ratio: This unit balances theoretical understanding of ICAO Annex 17, threat
identification, and coordination protocols with practical application in real-time responses to
unlawful interference incidents. Theoretical assessments focus on regulatory requirements and
security protocols, while practical assessments emphasise coordination, communication, and
threat mitigation.

COMPETENCY UNIT 30: RESPONSE TO MEDICAL EMERGENCIES AT AERODROMES
This competency unit ensures ARFFS (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting Services) personnel are
proficient in responding to medical incidents and public health emergencies at aerodromes,
including first aid, casualty management, and the containment of infectious diseases or other
health-related crises. This unit covers emergency medical response, coordination with healthcare
providers, and the application of public health protocols to ensure safety and well-being at the
aerodrome.
Skill Development: This unit develops critical skills in medical assessment, first aid, public health
emergency management, and coordination with medical teams and public health authorities.
Personnel are trained to respond effectively to medical incidents and public health emergencies,
ensuring safety and compliance with international guidelines.
Behavioural Expectations: Personnel are expected to demonstrate calmness, effective
communication, and leadership during medical emergencies. A proactive approach to public
health risks and a commitment to safety and compliance are essential.

Assessment Ratio: This unit balances theoretical knowledge of medical and public health
response protocols with practical application, focusing on immediate medical interventions,
communication with health authorities, and public safety management. Theoretical assessments
focus on understanding health regulations, while practical assessments emphasise medical
response, evacuation, and containment procedures.

Module 1 – Vehicle familiarisation

Module 2 - Demonstrate basic driving skills
• Correctly manage hazards using various observational skills, with safe and accurate use of

• Make suitable progress while positioning the vehicle safely and correctly, in relation to

• Understand the appropriate corrective action to take, based on the type of vehicle being

• Day and night practical driving skills
• Practical firefighting exercises/drills

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR LAA AERODROME ARFFS OPERATIONAL PERSONNEL

AIM
• The aim of the structured learning programme is to train new ARFFS operational
personnel and to provide refresher for current personal employed at landing area
acceptance aerodrome in both the technical and practical skills for the effective
deployment to deal with an aircraft incident utilising the ‘safe person concept’.
• This SLP focuses on critical modules essential for ARFFS personnel at landing area
acceptance aerodromes, designed for completion over 6 weeks, with 8 hours of
instructions per weekday.
ATTENDANCE CRITERIA
• Candidates should attend this SLP before they operate as a competent ARFFS firefighter
or as a refresher for current ARFFS firefighters
• Candidates should be accepted medically and physically fit by an accepted occupational
medical person or provider.
• A minimum of 80% attendance is eligible for an award of certificate of competence.

operations will assist with this intensive programme. If candidates are able to carry out
pre-study, they should concentrate on study notes covering the technical subjects.
PROGRAM STRUCTURE AND MODULES
Module 1: Firefighting Fundamentals
• Fire Science Basics: Understanding fire behaviour.
• Suppression Techniques: Use of various fire suppression agents.
• Firefighting Equipment: Operation, maintenance, and safety.
• Practical Exercises: Conducting drills with different fire scenarios.
Module 2: Aircraft Rescue Techniques
• Aircraft Structure and Access: Techniques for gaining access to aircraft during
emergencies.
• Evacuation Procedures: Safe methods for evacuating passengers and crew.
• Hazardous Materials Handling: Managing dangerous substances found in aircraft.
• Practical Drills: Simulated rescue operations.

Module 3: Medical Response and First Aid
• Basic First Aid: Addressing aviation-specific injuries, such as burns and fractures.
• Triage and Casualty Management: Prioritising and managing multiple casualties.
• Emergency Medical Services Coordination: Working effectively with local EMS.
• Hands-On Practice: Realistic medical scenarios.
Module 4: Emergency Response Planning
• Developing Response Plans: Tailoring emergency response plans to specific aerodromes.
• Risk Assessment: Identifying and mitigating potential hazards.
• Scenario Planning: Creating and practising response scenarios.
• Practical Drills: Execution of emergency response plans.
Module 5: Communication and Coordination
• Communication Protocols: Effective use of communication tools during emergencies.
• Teamwork and Leadership: Managing teams and making decisions under pressure.
• Interagency Coordination: Working with other emergency services and aerodrome
personnel.
• Simulation Exercises: Practising communication and coordination in simulated scenarios.

• The SLP should be heavily biased to practical mentored instruction. Clear, concise and
relevant notes should be provided to underpin the subject areas with the emphasis on
practical acquisition and development of skills.
• Blended learning delivery method and use of virtual reality simulations to demonstrate
mastery of theoretical knowledge can be considered.
ASSESSMENTS
• Written, oral and practical assessments against the requirements should be carried out
and recorded.

• A minimum of 240 instructional hours (excluding breaks, assessment and additional
training hours).
VALIDITY

• Upon successful completion of this SLP, a certificate of competence should be issued with
a validity of three years, during which continued competence and regular proficiency
checks should be maintained.

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR LAA AERODROME ARFFS SUPERVISORY PERSONNEL
AIM

landing area acceptance aerodromes. By focusing on key subject areas, the SLP ensures

capacity to absorb technical information and the physical capability to participate in all
practical aspects of the programme.

• A minimum of two years operational experience serving as a competent ARFFS
operational personnel or as per organisational policies.

PRE-STUDY

assist with this intensive programme.

PROGRAM STRUCTURE AND MODULES
Module 1: Advanced Firefighting Tactics and Strategy (80 weeks)
• Fire Behaviour Analysis: In-depth understanding of complex fire scenarios.
• Fire Suppression Strategy and Tactics: Developing and implementing advanced
suppression tactics.
• Resource Management: Efficient use of personnel and equipment during firefighting
operations.
• Initial Incident Command: Role and responsibilities of a supervisor in managing
firefighting operations.
• Practical Exercises: Scenarios focused on strategic decision-making in firefighting
situations.
Module 2: Leadership and Team Management (60 hours)
• Leadership Skills: Developing leadership qualities crucial for ARFFS supervision.
• Team Dynamics: Understanding and managing team behaviour and morale.
• Decision-Making Under Pressure: Techniques for making sound decisions in high-stress
situations.
• Conflict Resolution: Handling disputes and ensuring team cohesion during operations.
• Simulation Exercises: Leadership scenarios to practice and refine management skills.
Module 3: Emergency Planning and Risk Management (40 hours)
• Emergency Plan Development: Creating and implementing aerodrome-specific emergency
plans.
• Risk Assessment and Mitigation: Identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks at non-
certificated aerodromes.
• Crisis Management: Supervising the response to large-scale incidents and coordinating
with external agencies.

• Practical Planning Exercises: Developing and testing emergency response plans in
simulated environments.
Module 4: Communication and Interagency Coordination (40 hours)
• Advanced Communication Techniques: Enhancing communication skills for effective
leadership.
• Coordination with External Agencies: Working with local emergency services, law
enforcement, and other relevant agencies.
• Interagency Drills: Coordinated exercises with other agencies to practice communication
and joint operations.
Module 5: Regulatory Compliance and Reporting (20 hours)
• Understanding Regulations: Knowledge of local and international regulations relevant to
non-certificated aerodromes.
• Compliance Strategies: Ensuring that ARFFS operations comply with regulatory
requirements.
• Incident Reporting: Accurate and timely reporting of incidents and actions taken.
• Audit Preparation: Preparing for audits and inspections by regulatory bodies.
DELIVERY METHOD
• The course should cover the technical content in the classroom followed by the
application of tactics and techniques and their supervision by practical exercises.
• Blended learning delivery method and use of virtual reality simulations to demonstrate
mastery of theoretical and practical knowledge can be considered.
ASSESSMENTS
• Candidates will be assessed through written, oral questioning and observation of
performance in a simulated command role
LENGTH OF COURSE
• A minimum of 240 instructional hours (excluding breaks, assessment and additional
training hours).
VALIDITY

• Upon successful completion of this SLP, candidates will be issued with certificate of
competence with a validity of four years, during which continued competence and regular
proficiency checks should be maintained.

personnel

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR LAA AERODROME ARFFS MANAGERIAL PERSONNEL
Table D-15 provides minimum training syllabus to training providers in delivering structured learning
programmes for ARFFS managerial personnel employed at landing area acceptance aerodrome in
the United Arab Emirates.

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR LAA AERODROME ARFFS MANAGERIAL PERSONNEL
AIM
• The aim of this SLP is designed to equip Aerodrome rescue and firefighting Services
(ARFFS) managers at landing area acceptance aerodromes with the advanced skills and
knowledge necessary to oversee and enhance ARFFS operations. The program focuses on
key managerial competencies, including leadership, strategic planning, and regulatory
compliance.
ATTENDANCE CRITERIA
• Candidates nominated to attend this SLP will have been selected for the role of landing
area acceptance aerodrome ARFFS managers through a rigorous recruitment programme.
This programme should ensure that the candidate has the capacity to absorb technical
information and the physical capability to participate in all practical aspects of the
programme.
• Completed a landing area acceptance ARFFS Supervisor course or equivalent
• A minimum of three years operational experience serving as a competent ARFFS
supervisor or as per organisational policies.
• Candidates should be accepted medically and physically fit by an accepted occupational
medical person or provider.
• A minimum of 80% attendance is eligible for an award of certificate of competence.
PRE-STUDY

• Extensive knowledge of RFF service management and operations is essential and will
assist with this intensive programme.
• If candidates are able to carry out pre-study, they should concentrate on study notes
covering the technical subjects.
PROGRAM STRUCTURE AND MODULES
Module 1: Leadership and Management (80 hours)
• Leadership in Crisis: Strategies for leading ARFFS teams during high-pressure situations.
• Management Principles: Key concepts in managing teams, resources, and operations
effectively.
• Vision and Strategy Development: Crafting a long-term vision for ARFFS operations and
aligning team efforts.
• Decision-Making Frameworks: Approaches to making informed and strategic decisions
under pressure.
• Case Studies: Analysis of real-world incidents and the application of leadership strategies.
Module 2: Advanced Emergency Planning and Risk Management (60 hours)
• Comprehensive Emergency Planning: Developing robust emergency response plans
tailored to non-certificated aerodromes.
• Risk Management Strategies: Identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks at a managerial
level.
• Crisis Management Coordination: Leading large-scale emergency responses and
coordinating with multiple agencies.
• Business Continuity Planning: Ensuring operational resilience and recovery post-incident.
• Practical Workshops: Developing and testing emergency plans through tabletop exercises
and simulations.
Module 3: Regulatory Compliance and Organisational Governance (40 hours)
• Regulatory Frameworks: Understanding the legal and regulatory environment governing
ARFFS operations.
• Compliance Management: Strategies for ensuring all operations meet regulatory
requirements.
• Organisational Governance: Implementing governance structures that support
compliance and ethical operations.

• Audit and Inspection Preparedness: Preparing for and managing external audits and
inspections.
• Reporting and Documentation: Best practices for incident reporting, record-keeping, and
communication with regulatory bodies.
Module 4: Resource Management and Operational Efficiency (40 hours)
• Human Resource Management: Recruiting, training, and retaining skilled ARFFS
personnel.
• Financial Management: Budgeting and financial oversight for ARFFS operations.
• Operational Efficiency: Optimising the use of equipment, technology, and other resources.
• Supply Chain and Logistics: Managing the logistics of equipment and supplies to ensure
readiness.
• Continuous Improvement: Implementing processes for ongoing operational improvement.
Module 5: Stakeholder Engagement and Public Relations (20 hours)
• Stakeholder Mapping: Identifying and prioritising key stakeholders in ARFFS operations.
• Engagement Strategies: Building and maintaining relationships with internal and external
stakeholders.
• Community Engagement: Developing programs that enhance community safety and
awareness.
• Crisis Communication: Best practices for communicating during an emergency, ensuring
clarity and trust.
DELIVERY METHOD
• The course should cover the technical content in the classroom followed by the
application of tactics and techniques and their supervision by practical exercises.
• Blended learning delivery method and use of virtual reality simulations to demonstrate
mastery of theoretical and practical knowledge can be considered.
ASSESSMENTS
• Candidates will be assessed through written, oral questioning and observation of
performance in a simulated command role
LENGTH OF COURSE

• A minimum of 240 instructional hours (excluding breaks, assessment and additional
training hours).
VALIDITY
• Upon successful completion of this SLP, candidates will be issued with certificate of
competence with a validity of four years, during which continued competence and regular
proficiency checks should be maintained.

title: Direct entry personnel
text:
DIRECT ENTRY PERSONNEL
(a) Direct entry scheme
(1) Direct entry is used as a mechanism to fill ARFFS operational, supervisory and
managerial grades by attracting external candidates who possess sought after and
valuable management and leadership skills; this approach can run alongside the
development of internal employees to managerial roles and transfers in from other
aerodrome rescue and firefighting services or non-aerodrome fire rescue services.
(2) Direct Entry can be an effective way to help increase current talent pool by allowing
candidates to enter the organisation at a higher operational level than the entry level
role of a Firefighter, any predicted shortages in supervisors and managers that are
identified through workforce planning activities, can help to be addressed.
(3) Direct entry can, therefore, be used as part of recruitment policies and procedures to
positively impact and support the aerodrome operator’s ability to deliver its strategic
aims. Where training providers do not have the appropriate aerodrome rescue and
firefighting service experience, an initial assessment should be conducted to determine
role suitability. Once selected, sector related knowledge and skills can be acquired
through an intensive training and development programme.
(4) Careful consideration should be given to training providers who have not been
maintaining their competencies or trying to join the fire rescue industry after long
absence. Where their competence are in doubt, these training providers should attend
full structured learning programmes appropriate to the role they are applying for.
(5) Personnel recruited or selected via direct entry scheme should be meet the competency
standards appropriate to the grades detailed in this regulation.

(b) Career advancements
(1) All grades of ARFFS personnel should re-qualify by competence assessments following
attendance on further courses appropriate to their grades. Candidates with long-term
career prospects should be encouraged to undertake more advanced training to
prepare them for their future grades.

title: Integration of incident command with operational core competence
text:
INTEGRATION OF INCIDENT COMMAND WITH OPERATIONAL CORE COMPETENCE
(a) Incident command
(1) In the realm of aerodrome rescue and firefighting services, Incident Command is a
critical framework. It ensures structured, systematic, and coordinated command,
control, and communication during emergency responses. This methodology is pivotal
in managing resources, decisions, and strategies during incidents, ranging from small-
scale emergencies to large-scale accidents.
(b) Core Operational Competence
(1) Core operational competence in aerodrome rescue and firefighting services
encompasses the essential skills, knowledge, and abilities required for effective
emergency response. This includes expertise in fire suppression, rescue operations,
hazard identification, risk assessment, and emergency medical care. These
competencies are fundamental in ensuring that fire and rescue personnel can
effectively mitigate risks and protect lives and property.
(c) Integration of Incident Command with Operational Competence
(1) The integration of Incident Command and Control with core operational competence is
vital for efficient and effective aerodrome rescue and firefighting operations. This
integration allows for a seamless transition from strategic planning to tactical
execution. Incident Commanders utilize their understanding of operational
competencies to make informed decisions and deploy resources strategically.
Meanwhile, operational responders, equipped with robust operational skills, can adapt
to the dynamic requirements of the incident, guided by the command structure. This
synergy ensures a cohesive response, minimizing risks and enhancing the safety of both
the public and the responders. Effective integration also fosters continuous
improvement, as lessons learned from incidents feed back into training and

development, further strengthening operational competencies. See Figure D-1 below
showing the integration of incident command with operational core competencies.
Figure D-1: Integration of operational core competencies with incident command competencies.

title: Vertical flight infrastructure operations personnel
text:
VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE OPERATIONS PERSONNEL
(a) A vertical flight infrastructure operator shall establish and implement training and proficiency
check programmes for its operational personnel including training in human performance and
team coordination.
(1) ensure its personnel are trained and competent to perform their duties in safe and
efficient manner; and
(2) ensure personnel assigned for rescue and firefighting duties participate in live fire drills
commensurate with the types of aircraft, rescue and firefighting vehicles and
equipment in use at the vertical flight infrastructure, including pressure-fed fuel fires.

title: Vertical flight infrastructure operations personnel
text:
VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE OPERATIONS PERSONNEL
(a) As the success of any rescue and firefighting operations relies very much on teamwork, the
importance of building mutual trust and team coordination among RFF personnel during
training cannot be overstressed. Training must therefore be suitably designed to guide RFF
personnel towards achieving these objectives.
(b) In order for rescue and firefighting training to be as realistic as possible, live fire training is
crucial in helping RFF personnel acclimatize to a heated and smoke-filled environment, so that
in the event of an actual emergency, RFF personnel will be able to execute their tasks more
confidently and effectively. Where possible, simulators replicating different facades of rescue
and firefighting operations (e.g., vehicle driving and operations; command and control, etc.)
should be made available for RFF personnel to be trained in a controlled, safe and realistic
environment.
(c) Fires associated with fuel discharged under very high pressure from a ruptured fuel tank are
known as “pressure-fed fuel fires”. The rupture of fuel tanks in an aircraft crash and the
consequent spillage of highly volatile fuels, and other flammable liquids used by aircraft,
present a high degree of probability of ignition if these liquids come into contact with hot
metal parts of the aircraft or because of sparks caused by the movement of wreckage or
disturbance of the electrical circuit.
(d) The most important factors bearing on effective rescue in a survivable aircraft accident is the
training received, the effectiveness of the equipment and the speed with which personnel and
equipment, designated for RFF purposes, can be deployed.

title: Vertical flight infrastructure operations personnel
Structured learning programme for VFI operations manager
text:
STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR VFI OPERATIONS MANAGER

programme for an operations manager employed at a vertical flight infrastructure in the United Arab

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR VFI OPERATIONS MANAGER
Aim and Objectives
The aim and objectives of this training programme are to equip the delegate with the initial
knowledge, understanding and skills required to perform the roles of an operations manager at a
vertical flight infrastructure safely and effectively.
Learning Outcomes
(a) To successfully complete this training programme, delegates should be able to know and
understand:
(1) GCAA regulations on heliports, helidecks or vertiports
(2) Planning considerations
(3) Design considerations
(4) Obstacle Control
(5) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting
(6) Emergency planning

(7) Safety management system
ACCEPTANCE PROCESS AND REQUIREMENTS
Performance Assessment
(a) Delegates will be assessed against the learning outcomes specified using written questions and
direct observation as appropriate.
(b) Debriefs should be conducted with participating delegates on the completion of practical
exercises.
Duration and Timing
(a) The duration for this training programme is a minimum of 40 hours excluding lunch and
breaks, delivered over consecutive days. Where a blended learning method is provided, the
total duration should not exceed 3 weeks.
(b) An approximate ratio of 70% theory to 30% practical is appropriate for this training
programme.
(c) Practical and theory sessions should contain adequate breaks for delegate welfare.
(d) The total programme day includes the delegate enrolment and acceptance process, contact
time, welfare breaks, meal breaks and where applicable, travel between sites.
Training Pre-requisites
(a) Delegates should have successfully completed the landing officer training programme.
Module 1 – Planning Considerations
(a) Status of ICAO, GCAA and other international regulations for heliport planning and design
(b) Legal binding principles
(c) ICAO standards and recommended practices on heliport requirements
(d) Types of heliports (surface-level heliports, elevated heliports, helidecks and shipboard
heliports)
(e) Heliport data
(f) Acceptance of helicopters
(g) Helicopter flight characteristics, aerodynamics of rotor systems
(h) Relevant helicopter performance parameters (performance classes 1, 2 and 3) and
classification of helicopters
(i) Geometric dimensioning of helicopters (overall length, rotor diameter, undercarriage
width/length)

(j) Declared distances (TODAH, RTODAH, LDAH)
Module 2 – Design considerations
(a) Heliports, helidecks, vertiports and aerodromes
(b) Final approach and take-off area (FATO)
(c) Clearways
(d) Safety area
(e) Touchdown and lift-off area (TLOF)
(f) Ground taxiways and ground taxi-routes
(g) Air taxiways, air taxi-routes and air transit routes
(h) Aprons
(i) Visual Aids - markings and markers
Module 3 – Obstacle Control
(a) Regulations regarding obstacle limitation surfaces and sectors subject to type and usage of
heliport
(b) Control of obstacles at heliports
Module 4 - Rescue and firefighting
(a) Levels of protection at on-shore heliports and off-shore helidecks
(b) Types and quantities of extinguishing agents (principal & complementary agents)
(c) Portable and fixed foam application systems
(d) Personnel requirements (task resource analysis)
(e) Consideration of response areas (on and off heliport area)
(f) Testing and inspection of aerodrome rescue and firefighting equipment
Module 5 - Emergency planning
(a) Developing an emergency plan
(b) Coordination with agencies
(c) Accident investigation
(d) Disabled helicopter removal plan
(e) Planning and conducting exercises/drills
Module 6 - Safety management system
(a) Safety policy and objectives

(b) Safety risk management
(c) Safety assurance including quality assurance
(d) Safety promotion
(e) Planning and conducting audits/inspections

Structured learning programme for VFI landing officer and assistant

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR VFI LANDING OFFICER AND ASSISTANT
Table E-2 provides minimum training syllabus to training providers in delivering a structured learning
programme for landing officer and assistant employed at a vertical flight infrastructure in the United
Arab Emirates.
Table E-2: Structured learning programme for VFI landing officer and assistant.
STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR VFI LANDING OFFICER AND ASSISTANT
Aim/ Objectives
(a) The aim and objectives of this initial training programme are to equip the delegates with the
initial knowledge, understanding and skills required to perform the roles and responsibilities
as a Landing Officer or Assistant at a vertical flight infrastructure safely and effectively.
Learning Outcomes
(a) To successfully complete this training programme, delegates should be able to know and
understand:
(1) Key parts of relevant operations regulations and guidelines
(2) Physical characteristics
(3) Obstacle-free requirements
(4) Operational equipment and systems
(5) Meteorological requirements for vertical flight infrastructure operations
(6) Typical hazards associated with vertical flight infrastructure operations.
(7) The role and key responsibilities of the VLO and VLA
(8) Main vertical flight infrastructure team responsibilities and required actions,
including:
(i) 30 minutes before helicopter ETA;
(ii) 10 minutes before helicopter ETA;
(iii) Immediately before helicopter lands;

(iv) After landing: rotors running turnaround;
(v) After landing - engines shut down and rotors not running;
(vi) Helicopter/VCA tie-down, engine blanks and covers fitted; and
(vii) Helicopter/VCA start-up
(9) For offshore helideck, the structure and terms in a typical pre-flight weather report
and floating installation (or vessel) data required by helicopter pilot.
(10) For offshore helideck, typical team requirements for Normally Unattended
Installations (NPAIs).
(11) Correct use of handheld radios and radio checks, complying with radio
communications protocol and correct use of appropriate hand signals if radio
communications are ineffective.
(b) To successfully complete this training programme, delegates should be able to demonstrate:
(1) Checking landing area for contamination, debris or damage before and after take-off.
(2) Performing communication checks, checking equipment status, safety nets, security
and stowage of equipment.
(3) Performing team brief prior to helicopter/VCA landing at appropriate times during
helicopter/VCA operations.
(4) Wearing of appropriate PPE during helicopter/VCA operations
(5) Ensuring VFI team are in required locations during helicopter operations.
(6) Using handheld radios and radio checks
(7) Conducting and responding to required vertical flight infrastructure protocols during
helicopter/VCA operations, to include: safe-to-approach, helicopter/VCA anti-collision
lights switched off and ‘thumbs-up’ from pilot (as agreed by operating company).
(8) Checking passenger and freight manifests.
(9) As a landing officer, supervising landing assistants during passenger, freight and
baggage handling:
(i) Loading, unloading and securing of life saving equipment;
(ii) Load and unload passenger baggage correctly;
(iii) Load and unload freight correctly – using correct manual handling techniques
and within freight loading limitations and requirements;
(iv) Identify dangerous goods during helicopter/VCA loading and unloading; and

(v) Assist with passenger safe egress and access on the vertical flight
infrastructure, to and from the helicopter/VCA.
(10) Complying with vertical flight infrastructure protocols and procedures during
helicopter/VCA operations
(11) Complying with helicopter/VCA danger areas rules.
Performance Assessment
(a) Delegates should achieve a minimum of 80% attendance to be eligible for performance
assessment.
(b) Delegates should attain a minimum of 80% score to be awarded with a certificate of
competence.
(c) Delegates will be assessed against the learning outcomes specified in learning outcomes
using direct observation and oral and/or written questions as appropriate.
(d) Debriefs should be conducted with participating delegates on the completion of practical
exercises.
Duration and Timing
(a) The duration for this programme is a minimum of 40 hours excluding lunch and breaks. This
programme should be delivered over consecutive days or where blended learning method is
provided; the entire programme should not exceed 3 weeks.
(b) An approximate ratio of 60% theory to 40% practical is appropriate for this training
programme.
(c) Practical and theory sessions should contain adequate breaks for delegate welfare.
(d) The total programme day includes the delegate enrolment and acceptance process, contact
time, welfare breaks, meal breaks and where applicable, travel between sites.
MODULE 1 - Regulations and Guidelines
(a) Overview of UAE regulations and guidelines
(1) GCAA aviation regulations and safety management system
(2) GCAA dangerous goods regulations
(3) Emergency response requirements
(4) Operating procedures
(5) Acceptance criteria
MODULE 2 - Hazards and Management Systems
(a) Landing areas

(1) Physical characteristics, to include: ‘D value’, MTOW, access and escape routes,
friction properties across the landing area
(2) Visual aids, marking and lights, to include: landing lights are fully serviceable and
emergency power back-up is operational, installation obstacle lighting
(3) Obstacle-protected surfaces, to include:
(i) 210-degree Obstacle-Free Sector
(ii) 150-degree Limited Obstacle Sector
(iii) Clear Zone below Helideck Level - 5:1 falling gradient
(iv) Maximum height limit across the entire helideck
(4) Landing area and perimeter safety nets – purpose and requirements
(5) Landing areas and winching areas on vessels.
(b) Equipment and systems
(1) Main helicopter/VCA types used in region of operations including:
(i) Emergency exits
(ii) Seat configurations
(iii) Types of doors and hold openings
(2) Systems, to include:
(i) Visual aids (markings and lighting systems)
(ii) Wave-off and status lights.
(iii) TD/PM lighting
(3) Location and motion characteristics (floating installations)
(4) Acceptance limitations:
(5) Standard plant and equipment and uses; to include:
(i) Plant and equipment for routine and non-emergency response operations
(ii) Aerodrome rescue and firefighting equipment – guidance on when and where
to use various media
(iii) Principal media requirements: foam type, delivery and testing
(iv) Complementary media requirements
(v) Portable and/or fixed foam application system: overview-only required.
(vi) Tie-down points. Prohibited landing marker
(6) Meteorological systems and minimum meteorological equipment requirement for
region of operations.

(7) Typical systems routine checks.
(8) Reporting systems defects to appropriate person e.g., Accountable manager,
Operations Manager, OIM, Helicopter Operator, etc
(c) Hazards
(1) Human factors that may affect the safety of helicopter/VCA operations, to include the
following categories: the job/task, the individual and the organisation.
(2) Helicopter/VCA danger areas.
(3) Rotors running – personnel contact with main or tail rotors while on deck.
(4) Adverse weather effect on helicopter operations, to include: excessive wind
turbulence, wave height, trigger lightning
(5) Poor visibility effect on helideck operations.
(6) Process thermal affects e.g., turbine exhausts and normal or emergency process
venting.
(7) Helicopter/VCA engine or cabin fire.
(8) Electrical hazards.
(9) Mobile installations stability hazards during landing and take-off.
(10) Dangerous goods transfer to/from helicopter/VCA by the (c) Vertical flight
infrastructure team.
(11) Helicopter refuelling/VCA charging operations: spillages and faulty equipment.
(12) Loose items (baggage, freight, netting etc.) being sucked into rotor area or air intake.
(13) Flying debris e.g. disintegrating rotor hitting personnel following a crash.
(14) Crane operations: crane work to cease during helicopter/VCA operations.
(15) Obstacles on deck.
(16) Noise hazard – ear protection requirement.
(17) Helicopter/VCA shutdown and start-up hazards
(18) Unfamiliarity with helicopter/VCA type
(19) Wrong deck landing
(20) Downdraft forces from helicopter/VCA creates in and around the vertical flight
infrastructure areas
(d) Helicopter refuelling or VCA charging equipment
Note: Due to the technical nature of managing and quality assurance of helicopter refuelling or VCA
charging, Helicopter refuelling or VCA charging training and acceptance should be provided

through specialist training. This element provides a simple overview of the equipment a delegate
may find onboard for the purpose of helicopter refuelling or VCA charging.
(1) Typical hazards during helicopter refuelling/ VCA charging, including:
(i) Spillage and ignition
(ii) Vapours
(iii) Hoses
(iv) Fuel handling / VCA charging
(2) Typical helicopter refuelling / VCA charging equipment, including:
(i) Tanks
(ii) Dispensing Unit
(iii) Hose
(iv) Delivery nozzle types
(v) Bonding
(3) Key roles and responsibilities relating to maintenance and quality checks, including:
(i) Quality Checks and record keeping – (Person who has been trained, accepted
and competent in the task of helicopter refuelling offshore).
(ii) Maintenance (Appropriately trained and competent maintenance technicians)
MODULE 3 - Responsibilities during Landing and Departure
(a) The roles and key responsibilities of landing officer and assistant
(1) The role, key responsibilities and accountabilities of a landing officer during routine
helicopter/VCA operations
(2) The role, key responsibilities and accountabilities of landing assistant during routine
helicopter/VCA operations.
(b) Checks, procedures and communications during helicopter/VCA operations
(1) How the landing officer is identifiable to the helicopter crew.
(2) Typical helicopter/VCA operational procedures prior to landing, helicopter-on-deck
and take off, to include:
(i) 30 minutes before helicopter/VCA ETA
(ii) 10 minutes before helicopter/VCA ETA
(iii) Immediately before landing
(iv) After landing - rotors running turnaround
(v) After landing - engines shut down and rotors not running

(vi) Helicopter/VCA tie-down, engine blanks and covers fitted - under the direction
of the helicopter/VCA crew.
(vii) Helicopter/VCA start-up.
(3) Pre-flight weather report templates (typical) and standard weather report terms.
(4) Adverse weather helicopter/VCA operation limits.
(5) Floating installations and vessels data request by pilot, to include: inclination, heave-
rate and heading.
Delegates to practice the role of landing officer:
(6) Ensuring duties and responsibilities are clearly understood during landing and
departure.
(7) Briefing the assistants prior to operations, to include a ‘tool-box-talk’.
(8) Ensuring the assistants are in the correct location and stations during helicopter/VCA
landing, take-off and preparing for helicopter/VCA emergencies.
(9) Ensuring assistants are equipped with appropriate PPE.
(10) Safety protocols e.g. safe-to-approach, helicopter/VCA anti-collision lights switched
off and ‘thumbs-up’ from pilot (as agreed by operator).
(11) Effective communications, to include:
(i) Communications with all relevant personnel e.g. admin personnel, pilot, crane
operator, standby vessel, fire crews, HLA/VLAs/VLAs, loaders and passengers
(simulated)
(ii) Landing officer and flight crew radio transmissions restricted to essential
dialogue.
(iii) Using standard radio comms protocols, to include landing assistants’ radios set
to ‘receive-only’ (landing assistants’ should only transmit in the event of an
emergency)
(iv) How to ensure that the correct and agreed protocol for “clear to lift” signal to
the pilot is understood on the specific fixed or mobile installation the landing
officer is operating on.
(v) Landing officer-to-pilot comms protocols are conducted correctly, to include
‘deck available’ or ‘do not land’ call to pilot.
(vi) Handover procedure to installation radio Aerodrome operators
(vii) Limitation of radio comms and correct use of hand signals

(12) Helicopter/VCA type identification.
(13) Monitoring of environmental conditions and change in conditions
(14) Radio communications system checks, to include two-way radio checks between
landing officer and radio operator and/or admin.
(15) Checking VFI equipment availability.
(16) Landing officer to ensure that the VFI surface is free from any contamination, debris
or damage after take-off.
Delegates to practice the role of landing assistant:
(17) Identifying and reporting hazards that the landing officer may not be aware of.
(18) Effective communications, to include:
(i) Confirming completion of tasks to the landing officer
(ii) Using standard radio protocols
(iii) Limitation of radio comms and correct use of hand signals - landing assistants’
radios set to ‘receive-only’ during helicopter/VCA operations (landing
assistants) should only transmit in the event of an emergency)
(iv) Radio communication protocols during helicopter/VCA operations.
(19) Helicopter/VCA type identification prior to landing – for helicopter/VCA-specific
passenger, cargo loading and emergency response requirements.
(20) Assisting with monitoring of weather and environmental conditions.
(21) Assisting landing officer with communications system checks.
(22) Assisting landing officer with checking helideck equipment status and safety nets.
(23) Assisting landing officer with security and stowage of equipment - helicopter and heli-
deck.
(24) Landing assistants are in a safe location adjacent to the helideck during helicopter
landing, take-off and preparing for helicopter emergencies.
(25) Ensuring appropriate landing assistants’ PPE are worn during helicopter operations.
MODULE 4 - Cargo and Passenger Handling
(a) Cargo Handling
(1) Helicopter/VCA freight loading limitations and requirements and how these will vary
for different types of helicopters/VCAs.
(2) Underslung loads: hazards and typical procedures including risk assessment
requirements.

(3) Importance of understanding and complying with company VFI operations
procedures.
(4) VFI protocols including ‘safe to approach the helicopter/VCA’, anti-collision lights
switched off and ‘thumbs-up’ from pilot.
Delegates to practice the role of a landing officer:
(5) Checking freight manifests (inbound and outbound)
(6) Preparing for, and supervising, correct loading and unloading of freight and baggage.
(Landing officers should not become involved in manual activity, such as carrying
bags, at the expense of their supervisory role).
(7) Supervising correct manual handling techniques during freight loading and unloading.
(8) Supervising passenger baggage reclamation from VFI or designated area
(9) Dangerous goods identification.
(10) Dangerous goods management; preparing for, and correct handling of dangerous
goods according to GCAA regulations.
(11) ‘Notification to Captain’ of dangerous goods - NOTOC
Delegates to practice the role of a landing assistant:
(12) Responding to ‘safe to approach the helicopter/VCA’ from the landing officer.
(13) Complying with helicopter/VCA danger areas rules
(14) Assisting with preparations for, and correct handling of, freight and baggage.
(15) Correct manual handling techniques during freight loading and unloading.
(16) Asking for assistance from other landing assistants with heavy cargo.
(17) Dangerous goods identification.
(b) Passenger Handling
Delegates to practice the role of a landing officer:
(1) Checking and interpreting information on passenger manifest and routing plans
(2) Receiving incoming manifest from pilot and handing over outgoing manifest to pilot.
(3) Supervising passenger safe access and egress on vertical flight infrastructure.
(4) Supervising passenger entry into helicopter/VCA.
(5) Supervising passenger exit from helicopter/VCA.
(6) Conducting passenger checks, to include: checking that passengers are wearing
required transit suits and lifejackets for region of operations, ear protection and seat
belt harnesses are secure.

Delegates to practice the role of a landing assistant:
(7) Interpreting information on passenger manifests.
(8) Assisting with passenger safe egress and access on vertical flight infrastructure
(9) Assisting with passenger entry into helicopter/VCA.
(10) Assisting with passenger exit from helicopter/VCA.
(11) Being alert to changing events and conditions while assisting passengers.
MODULE 5 – Not Permanently Attended Installations
(a) Landing officer and assistant responsibilities on an NPAI
This element is about briefly explaining to the delegates how landing officer and assistant
responsibilities on an NPAI differ from those on the main installation or vessel.
(1) Types of NPAIs
(2) Typical NPAI-specific hazards, to include guano infestation
(3) Landing officer first to disembark from helicopter/VCA.
(4) Disembarkation: NPAI status check by landing officer and decision to disembark
helicopter/VCA passengers.
(5) Embarkation: landing officer is responsible for ensuring that all passengers have
boarded the helicopter/VCA prior to take-off and landing assistant to assist landing
officer in ensuring that all passengers have boarded the helicopter/VCA prior to take-
off.
(6) Landing assistant to assist landing officer with the following, (where applicable):
(i) Bird exclusion devices are switched on
(ii) All equipment (fire extinguishers, firefighting clothing, chocks etc.) positioned
on the vertical flight infrastructure and surrounding areas is correctly stored
and secured.
(7) The importance of understanding and following individual company procedures for
individual NPAIs.

Structured learning programme for VFI RFF team leader and member

STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR VFI RFF TEAM LEADER AND MEMBER
Table E-3 provides minimum training syllabus to training providers in delivering a structured learning
programme for rescue and firefighting team leader and member employed at a vertical flight
infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates.

Table E-3: Structured learning programme for VFI RFF team leader and member
STRUCTURED LEARNING PROGRAMME FOR VFI RFF TEAM LEADER AND MEMBER
Aim and Objectives
(a) The aim of this training programme is to equip personnel assigned to perform rescue and
firefighting duties at a vertical flight infrastructure with the knowledge, understanding and
skills required to perform as a team leader and member.
(b) The main objectives are for delegates to fully understand the role and responsibilities of
rescue and firefighting team leader (RTL) and member (RTM) and practice responding to a
variety of helicopter/VCA firefighting and non-firefighting emergency scenarios in a training
environment.
Learning Outcomes
Delegates should be able to know and understand:
(a) Module 1
(1) The key role and key responsibilities of the RTL and RTM.
(2) The main elements of emergency response plan.
(3) Types of potential helicopter/VCA emergencies.
(4) Helicopter/VCA firefighting tactics and techniques.
(5) The purpose of typical emergency systems and controls.
(6) Casualty handling techniques – first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation
(7) Personal protective clothing – benefits and limitations
(8) Breathing apparatus – benefits and limitations
(9) Rescue equipment – ladders, hoses, nozzles, forcible entry,
(b) Module 2
(1) The main differences between vertical flight infrastructure emergency response on a
main fixed or floating installation and a not permanently attended installation (NPAI).
(c) Module 3
Delegates should be able to demonstrate:
(1) Emergency access and egress to and from vertical flight infrastructure including clear,
concise and effective communications with RTL and RTM.
(2) RFFTM updating RFFTL on progress against the emergency response plan at
appropriate times.

(3) Responding appropriately to direction during emergencies including the correct
selection of appropriate fire-fighting equipment for the incident.
(4) Under direction from the RFFTL approaching the incident area in a controlled manner
continually assessing how the changes in the emergency could impact on the safety of
other RFF members, maintaining a means of escape from the incident area.
(5) Effective execution of emergency response tasks.
(6) Conducting helicopter incident firefighting operations, to include responding to a
helicopter engine fire using a CO2 media extended applicator.
(7) Correct donning and use of breathing apparatus (BA)
(8) Perform search and rescue (SAR) principles and techniques – on or close to the
vertical flight infrastructure, locating, extracting and handling missing personnel and
casualties following a helicopter incident.
(9) Appropriate response to non-firefighting operations during helicopter/VCA incident.
(10) Effective use of firefighting fixed, portable and mobile systems, including fixed fire
monitors, dry chemical and CO2 fire extinguishment and control media
(11) Responding to an NPAI vertical flight infrastructure fire (with limited firefighting
equipment).
(12) Working with back-up RFF teams – where required to do so.
(13) Correct casualty handling and rescue techniques
(14) Hose-running techniques and associated hazards
Performance Assessment
(a) Delegates should be assessed medically fit by a qualified medical person due to high physical
nature of this training programme.
(b) Delegates should achieve a minimum of 80% attendance to be eligible for performance
assessment.
(c) Delegates should attain a minimum of 80% score to be awarded with a certificate of
competence.
(d) Delegates will be assessed against the learning outcomes specified in learning outcomes
using direct observation and oral and/or written questions as appropriate.
(e) Assessments results should be recorded and maintained.
Duration and Timing

(a) This duration of this programme is a minimum of 32 hours excluding lunch and breaks,
delivered over consecutive days. Where a blended learning method is provided, the total
duration should not exceed 3 weeks.
(b) An approximate ratio of 30% theory to 70% practical is appropriate for this training
programme.
(c) Practical and theory sessions should contain adequate breaks for delegate welfare.
(d) The total programme day includes the delegate enrolment and acceptance process, contact
time, welfare breaks, meal breaks and where applicable, travel between sites.
MODULE 1 Emergency Response Preparedness
(a) Emergency response pre-planning
(1) The role and key responsibilities of a RFFTL and RFFTM.
(2) The requirement for emergency response pre-planning.
(3) The main elements of a emergency response plan.
(4) Examples of emergency scenarios involving helicopter operations and typical
response requirement of RFFTM to the emergency, to include:
(i) Helicopter/VCA incident resulting in crash/overturned aircraft involving fire/no
fire
(ii) Engine fire
(iii) Fuel Spill during refuelling operations resulting in fire/no fire
(iv) Emergency/precautionary landing
(v) Responding to Class A fires caused by helicopter/VCA incident
(vi) Responding to Class B/E fires (flammable liquid spill, leaking fuel fires, electric
fires, etc) caused by helicopter/VCA Incident
(vii) Rescue from an overturned aircraft
(viii) Internal fire fighting
(ix) Responding to a helicopter incident off the vertical flight infrastructure
(x) Loss of fire water main/pressure
(5) Events that may severely impact on flight safety, to include:
(i) Aviation fuel contamination
(ii) Obstructed vertical flight infrastructure
(iii) Wrong deck landing (wrong installation)
(iv) Installation, MODU or vessel status changes with helicopter/VCA on deck.

(6) General firefighting safety goals and objectives and how to achieve them.
(7) Helicopter/VCA emergency response practice: Fire and non-fire training drills and
practices.
(b) Emergency systems and controls
(1) Typical firefighting equipment and systems, to include foam producing equipment
performance requirements:
(i) Speed of response of producing foam
(ii) Reliability– through weekly tests and maintenance routines
(iii) Coverage
(iv) Quality of the foam
(v) Performance Standards
(2) Portable foam application system
(3) Fixed foam application system (DIFFS, FMS and RMS)
(4) Mobile firefighting equipment and systems
(5) Rescue equipment
(6) Helicopter/VCA emergency systems and controls that can be initiated by the RFFTMs
under the direction of the RFFTL, to include helicopter/VCA:
(i) engine shutdown
(ii) fuel isolation
(iii) fixed firefighting and protection systems (onboard helicopters/VCAs)
MODULE 2 - Aerodrome rescue and firefighting Team Leader (RFFTL) and Member (RFFTM)
(a) Response in helicopter/VCA emergencies
(1) Human factors during emergency response including:
(i) stress affecting decision making
(ii) physical limitations
(iii) Sources of assistance available during emergency events
(2) Potential helicopter/VCA hazards during the emergency response, to include:
(i) fire
(ii) electrical
(iii) helicopter/VCA composition materials
(iv) dangerous goods cargo
(v) flotation devices

(3) PPE requirements
(4) How different helicopter/VCA types can affect the emergency response.
(5) Emergency response arrangements.
(6) Breathing apparatus operation and control procedures.
(7) Search and rescue (SAR) principles and techniques – on or close to the helideck,
following helicopter/VCA incident on vertical flight infrastructure.
(8) Relevant equipment and controls - vertical flight infrastructure and helicopter/VCA
(9) Firefighting equipment: guidance on when and where to use various media.
(10) Monitoring of environmental conditions and how they may impact on the emergency
response
(11) Awareness and understanding of back up crew during protracted incident.
(b) Practical Aerodrome rescue and firefighting Exercises
(1) Emergency access and egress to and from vertical flight infrastructure including clear,
concise and effective communications with RFFTL and RFFTMs.
(2) RFFTM updating RFFTL on progress against the emergency response plan at
appropriate times.
(3) RFFTM responding appropriately to RFFTL direction during emergencies including the
correct selection of appropriate fire-fighting equipment for the incident.
(4) Under direction from the RFFTL: RFFTM approaching the incident area in a controlled
manner – continually assessing how the changes in the emergency could impact on
the safety of other RFFTMs, maintaining a means of escape from the incident area.
(5) Effective execution of emergency response tasks.
(6) Conducting helicopter/VCA incident firefighting operations, to include responding to
a helicopter/VCA engine fire using a CO2 media extended applicator.
(7) Correct donning and use of breathing apparatus (BA) (all delegates to practice
donning and using BA).
(8) Effective search and rescue (SAR) principles and techniques – on or close to the
vertical flight infrastructure, locating, extracting and handling missing personnel and
casualties following a helicopter incident on the vertical flight infrastructure.
(9) Appropriate response to non-firefighting operations during helicopter/VCA incident.
(10) Effective use of firefighting fixed, portable and mobile systems, including fixed fire
monitors, dry chemical and CO2 fire extinguishment and control media

(11) Responding to an NPAI fire (with limited firefighting equipment).
(12) Working with back-up emergency response teams – where required to do so.
(13) Correct casualty handling techniques including first aid and cardiopulmonary
resuscitation
(14) Hose-running techniques and associated hazards
(15) Using appropriate combinations of all of the following scenarios:
(i) Helicopter/VCA incident resulting in crash/overturned aircraft involving fire/no
fire
(ii) Engine fire
(iii) Fuel Spill during refuelling operations resulting in fire/no fire
(iv) Emergency/precautionary landing
(v) Responding to Class A fires caused by helicopter incident
(vi) Responding to Class B/E fires (flammable liquid spill, leaking fuel fires, electrical
fires) caused by helicopter/VCA Incident
(vii) Rescue from an overturned aircraft
(viii) Internal fire fighting
(ix) Responding to a helicopter/VCA incident off the facility
(x) Loss of fire water main/pressure
Note 1. - Classes B/E fires: For environmental purposes, smoke suppression or clean-burn systems
are acceptable for reducing smoke during Class B fire exercises.
Note 2. - All delegates to practice in the role of the RFFTM during emergency response exercises.
Note 3. - Training Centres should provide a role-playing RFFTL during these exercises (this could be
one of the instructors).
MODULE 3 - NPAI emergency Response
(a) NPAI emergency response requirements
(1) Planning for emergencies on an NPAI with limited emergency response capability, to
include:
(i) Helicopter/VCA on deck, and
(ii) no helicopter/VCA on deck.
(2) NPAI Rescue, firefighting equipment and extinguishant media requirements.
(3) Typical limited NPAI accommodation – if personnel onboard NPAI have to stay
beyond expected duration.

(4) First aid arrangements on NPAI.
(5) Evacuation from NPAI if no helicopter/VCA is available.
(6) Importance of understanding and following individual company procedures relating
to NPAI
(7) Emergency response requirements

title: Vertical flight infrastructure operations personnel
text:
FREQUENCY OF TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECKS
(a) Initial training should be completed by all newly appointed personnel to develop the
minimum skills and knowledge required for their roles before assuming their duties, ensuring
they are competent and fully prepared to perform their tasks safely and efficiently. Where
current personnel have been absent from their duties for a prolonged period or where major
competency deficiencies are discovered following an incident, they should attend initial
training.
(b) Refresher training should be conducted not exceeding four years to ensure personnel stay up-
to-date with regulatory changes, technological advancements, and operational best practices.
Additional refresher training may be required when there are significant changes to
operational procedures, equipment, or regulations.
(c) Proficiency checks should be conducted annually for all operational personnel to validate their
ongoing competency in both routine and emergency tasks. Additional proficiency checks
should be carried out whenever personnel are transferred to new roles or responsibilities,
after extended periods of leave, or following the introduction of new equipment or
procedures. Proficiency checks should evaluate both theoretical knowledge and practical
skills. The assessment should include:
(1) Normal operations: Ensuring personnel can perform their day-to-day tasks efficiently
and safely.
(2) Emergency scenarios: Testing responses to simulated incidents, such as aircraft fires,
emergency landings, or hazardous material spills.
(3) Communication and coordination: Evaluating the ability to communicate clearly and
effectively with other team members, operations management, and external agencies.
(4) Each proficiency check should be conducted by a qualified assessor using a standardised
checklist, ensuring consistency and fairness in evaluations. All personnel should achieve
a satisfactory performance rating to continue in their operational roles.

title: Vertical flight infrastructure operations personnel
text:
COMPETENCY-BASED TRAINING AND ASSESSMENT (CBTA) PROGRAMME

(a) Training and proficiency checks programmes should include competence-based training and
assessment plan that are designed to ensure that all personnel including associated facilities
and equipment are at all times fully efficient. In addition, the programmes should also be
designed to build cohesiveness in order to deliver a consistent level of proficiency.
(b) To ensure a high standard of operational readiness, an operator should develop a competency
audit framework to assess the effectiveness of the programmes at both individual and team
levels
