text:
ESTABLISHING AND IMPLEMENTING COMPETENCE STANDARDS
Guidance on establishing and implementing competence standards for RFF personnel can refer to

title: Vertical flight infrastructure operations personnel
text:
MANAGING TRAINING AND PROFICIENCY CHECKS PROGRAMMES
(a) Policies and procedures should be implemented for managing changes to the training and
proficiency checks programmes, according to the aerodrome operator’s safety management
system, including:
(1) a systematic process to review, revise, and validate the programmes;
(2) a documentation control process;
(3) quality assurance and audit process; and
(4) an approval process by the Accountable Manager or a delegated executive.

title: Training provider
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER
(a) No entity shall provide trainings to aerodrome rescue and firefighting and vertical flight
infrastructure operations personnel without an acceptance from the GCAA.
(b) Where an entity including its associated facilities is located outside the United Arab Emirates,
the entity shall bear all costs for the initial regulatory acceptance and continued oversight
activities, in accordance with GCAA policies and procedures.

(c) The entity shall comply with the application training and proficiency checks requirements, in
accordance with TRG.OR.B.005 Training and proficiency check programmes.

title: Training provider
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER – GENERAL
(a) A training provider mentioned in this Section can either be:
(1) a holder of GCAA aerodrome certificate or landing area acceptance;
(2) a holder of GCAA vertical flight infrastructure (heliport, helideck or vertiport) certificate
or landing area acceptance; or
(3) a person or organisation with a trade license located within or outside the United Arab
Emirates.

title: Training provider — acceptance requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — PRE-ACCEPTANCE REQUIREMENTS
(a) Interested person or organisation (applicant) should submit a formal application to the GCAA
via our website (https://www.gcaa.gov.ae/en/), including the following information:
(1) the registered name of the applicant, including trade license;
(2) the address of the applicant and its associated training facilities;
(3) the intended scope of acceptance;
(4) the name and signature of the accountable manager; and
(5) the date of application.
(b) The applicant should:
(1) arrange all logistics, transportation and other miscellaneous activities for site
inspections by the GCAA, including bearing any costs arising from the regulatory
activities;
(2) grants full and unrestricted access to the GCAA to its training documents, personnel,
facilities, equipment, including contracted activities and services; and
(3) provide the appropriate personal protective equipment to the GCAA, where necessary.
TRAINING PROVIDER — POST-ACCEPTANCE REQUIREMENTS
(a) Where the applicant has successfully demonstrated compliance with the relevant
requirements, a training provider acceptance certificate is issued and will remain valid for a
period of three (3) years from the date of issue, subject to the following conditions:

(1) the training provider demonstrates continued compliance with this regulation, in
accordance with the provisions related to managing non-compliances, as specified in
this regulation;
(2) the training provider grants full and unrestricted access to the GCAA to its training
personnel, facilities, equipment, etc, including contracted activities and services, to
determine continued compliance with the requirements; and
(3) the training provider certificate is not surrendered or revoked.
(b) Where the training provider decides to surrender or revoke the acceptance certificate, the
GCAA should be immediately notified in writing and the certificate should be returned to the
GCAA.

title: Training provider — acceptance requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — POST-ACCEPTANCE REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider may surrender the acceptance certificate when it decides not to or
unable to comply with the applicable requirements contained in this SUBPART.
(b) The acceptance certificate may be revoked by the GCAA if it is determined that there are
serious and major non-compliances against the applicable requirements contained in this
SUBPART, which have directly affected the safe delivery of the training and proficiency check
programmes.

title: Training provider — acceptance requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — PRE-ACCEPTANCE REQUIREMENTS
(a) The pre-acceptance processes consist of the following phases:
(1) Phase 1 (Initial) – Upon receiving the application, the GCAA will meet with the training
provider to understand its intention and overall requirements
(2) Phase 2 (Inspection) – The GCAA will conduct site inspections of personnel, training
documents, facilities, resources and equipment, including contracted activities and
services
(3) Phase 3 (Evaluation) – The GCAA will conduct evaluations of the design, delivery, and
control of training and assessments programmes, including attending theoretical and
practical lessons (if required).
(4) Phase 4 (Final review) – The GCAA will conduct a full review of the submission.

(5) Phase 5 (Acceptance) – Upon satisfactory completion of all phases, the GCAA will issue
acceptance certificate.
(b) The applicant will be formally notified after each phase. Completion of each phase is
dependent on compliance with the training requirements. The GCAA may conduct more site
inspections, if necessary.
(c) The applicant is given up to 3 months or as determined by the GCAA, to address the non-
compliances and/or observations raised by the GCAA during the acceptance process. If no
satisfactory response is received thereafter, the GCAA will cancel the application. The
applicant may request for an extension subject to the acceptance of the GCAA. If the applicant
decides to withdraw the application, the GCAA should be formally notified in writing.

Training provider — acceptance from other training accredited body or
organisation

ACCEPTANCE FROM OTHER TRAINING ACCREDITED BODY OR ORGANISATION
(a) Where the applicant has received prior acceptance or approval from national or international
accredited training body or organisation recognised by the GCAA, the pre-acceptance
requirements stated in AMC1 TRG.OR.F.005 Acceptance requirements may be reduced or
omitted.
(b) The applicant should submit a complete assessment to the GCAA to demonstrate compliance
against the applicable requirements stated in this SUBPART. The GCAA will review the
submission and notify the applicant on the status of the training provider application.
(c) Upon successful issuance of the training provider acceptance certificate, the post-acceptance
requirements stated in AMC1 TRG.OR.F.005 Acceptance requirements apply.

title: Training provider — personnel requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — PERSONNEL REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider should ensure:
(1) an accountable manager is appointed who is responsible in ensuring that the
organisation has adequate resources, staffing, facilities and financed to comply with this
regulation.
(2) a training post holder is appointed who will be responsible for managing the overall
delivery of the training programs in accordance with these requirements.

(3) sufficient resources and staffing to plan/perform knowledge and practical training,
conduct examinations and assessments in accordance with these requirements, which
include but not limited to instructor and assessor.
(4) sufficient numbers of instructors and assessors:
(i) the experience and qualifications of instructors and assessors are appropriate to
the training provided and established in accordance with the applicable
requirements;
(ii) instructors and assessors are specified in the organisation manual for the
acceptance of such staff;
(iii) instructors and assessors maintain their competencies, at least, every 2 years
relevant to current technology, practical skills, human factors and the latest
training techniques appropriate to the knowledge being trained or examined; and
(5) depending on the size and complexity of the organisation, additional staff such course
developers, maintenance team, administrative, safety, quality, etc, are made available.
(b) The training provider should ensure:
(1) records of all instructors and assessors are maintained;
(2) records reflect the experience and qualification, training history and any subsequent
trainings undertaken;
(3) terms of reference should be drawn up for all instructors and assessors;
(4) the following minimum information relevant to the scope of activity are kept on record
in respect of each instructor and assessor:
(i) Name
(ii) Date of Birth
(iii) Personnel Number
(iv) Experience
(v) Qualifications
(vi) Training history (before entry)
(vii) Subsequent Training
(viii) Scope of activity
(ix) Starting date of employment/contract
(x) If appropriate – ending date of employment/contract.
(5) records are kept in any format but should be under the control of the organisation’s
quality management system; and

(6) records on any persons authorised to access the records are maintained at a minimum
to ensure that records cannot be altered in an unauthorised manner or that such
confidential records become accessible to unauthorised persons.

Training provider — aerodrome rescue and firefighting facilities requirements

TRAINING PROVIDER — AERODROME RESCUE AND FIREFIGHTING FACILITIES REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider should ensure:
(1) training facilities and its supporting infrastructures are safely designed and constructed
commensurate with the types of training and proficiency checks programmes for RFF
personnel;
(2) a single integrated facility or a combination of multiple structures within the same
facility is provided to demonstrate that the intended training objectives are achieved;
(3) an analysis is conducted to determine the appropriate training facilities, resources and
equipment required to deliver the training and proficiency checks programmes;
(4) facilities are suitably equipped, including ancillary structures for effective delivery of
training programmes, protection from the prevailing weather and safe operation of all
planned training and assessment for rescue and firefighting personnel; and
(5) a preventive maintenance programme is established and implemented for all training
facilities, including associated vehicles and equipment.

title: ARFF training facility design, construction, and operation
text:
ARFF TRAINING FACILITY DESIGN, CONSTRUCTION, AND OPERATION
(a) Live fire training facilities should make provision for RFF personnel to practice the strategy,
tactics and techniques for the control and extinguishment of aviation fuel fires including
pressure fed fires.
(b) Ideally live fire training should involve Class B liquid fires. However, taking into account the
various requirements and sources of guidance, the use of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) may
be considered as a suitable alternative to the use of Class B liquid fuels. This is based on the
principles that:
(1) LPG can enhance safety during training due to its controllability
(2) Environmental constraints can restrict the use of Class B liquid for fire training at
aerodromes
(3) Generating high volumes of black smoke may not be acceptable at an aerodrome

(c) It is important that, if LPG is used during live fire drills, ARFFS personnel are provided with
suitable training to enable them to recognise the differing characteristics of LPG as opposed to
class B fires when used to simulate realistic fire training.
(d) Provision should also be made for ARFFS personnel to periodically practice the application of
the types of extinguishing agent available at the aerodrome onto a Class B liquid fire.
(e) The frequency of live fire drills, and the periodic application of firefighting agent to control
and extinguish a Class B fire, should be determined through a suitable decay analysis.
(f) The aircraft simulator should make provision for ARFFS personnel to practice:
(1) Vehicle manoeuvring
(2) Command and control sectorisation
(3) Aircraft external fires – engines, undercarriage, fuselage, fuel tanks, wings, etc.
(4) Aircraft internal fires – flight deck, cabin, lavatory, pantry, cargo, etc.
(5) Gaining entry
(6) Search and rescue
(7) Specialist equipment drills e.g. HRET, aerial appliances, rescue/emergency stairs
(g) The ARFFS training simulator should be designed in accordance with the relevant standards
and is subject to a suitable inspection and maintenance programme by a competent authority.
(b) System Description
(1) Types. There are two main types of ARFF training facilities that use two main types of
fuel. ARFF training facilities can be either “fixed” or “mobile.” Fixed systems may use
Flammable Liquid Hydrocarbons (FLHs) or LPG as the training fuel, while mobile systems
use only LPG.
(2) Components. ARFF training facilities contain the following functional units (See Figure F-
1):
(i) Burn area
(ii) Vehicle manoeuvring area
(iii) Aircraft mock-up
(iv) Control station
(v) Support systems:
(vi) Fuel delivery / collection
(vii) Water delivery / collection
(viii) Electrical
(c) System Components

(1) Burn Area Structure. The burn area structure, or fire area, is the focal point of the
training facility. It is designed to create a realistic aircraft accident fire environment and
to contain training substances. Its size is a function of the typical aircraft serving the
airport.
(2) Vehicle Manoeuvring Area. This area physically surrounds the burn area structure and
should be large enough to allow for the tactical operation of ARFF vehicles as they
approach the burn area structure and the realistic deployment of personnel using hand
lines.
(3) Aircraft Mock-up. A structure of a configuration and size that represents the typical
aircraft servicing the airport. The mock-up is capable of presenting a variety of realistic
exterior, component, and interior aircraft fires if specified. The mock-up may either be
of a fixed or mobile type.
(4) Control Station. A system that allows an operator to configure and control the live-fire
exercises of the training facility. The station may utilize either manual or automatic
control systems to control the simulation variables.
(5) Support Systems. Support systems comprise the functional units needed for a training
facility to function properly and implement the simulation of various types of aircraft
fires. Each support system contains individual support components that make up the
system (e.g., the fuel distribution system consists of a storage tank, pumps, associated
piping, etc.). These systems include:
(i) Fuel delivery / collection.
(ii) Water delivery / collection.
Figure F-1: Basic components of aircraft aerodrome rescue and firefighting training facility

(d) Training providers should consider the benefits of VR simulation in support of training and
proficiency checks.
(e) Training providers should provide suitable hygiene and welfare facilities for both males and
females (if required), which may include:
(1) Toilets and showers
(2) Changing areas
(3) Rest areas
(4) Smoking areas where appropriate
(5) First aid
(6) Dirty / clean areas for equipment servicing / exercise briefings
(f) Fully enclosed appropriate accommodation separate from other facilities should be provided
for the instruction of theory and the conduct of knowledge examinations.

(1) The maximum number of students undergoing knowledge training during any training
course should be defined.
(2) The size of accommodation for examination purposes should be such that no student
can read the paperwork or computer screen of any other student from his/her position
during examinations.
(3) The accommodation environment should be maintained such that students are able to
concentrate on their studies or examination as appropriate, without undue distraction
or discomfort.
(4) In the case of a practical training, facilities separate from training classrooms should be
provided for practical instruction appropriate to the planned training course. If,
however, the organisation is unable to provide such facilities, arrangements may be
made with another organisation to provide such workshops and/or maintenance
facilities, in which case a written agreement should be made with such organisation
specifying the conditions of access and use thereof. The GCAA requires full access to
any such contracted organisation and the written agreement should specify this access.
(5) The maximum number of students undergoing practical training during any training
course should be safely determined. Where a high-risk practical training is involved e.g.,
live fire evolution training, the maximum number should not exceed 7 students per
instructor or assessor. If a trained assistant is provided, a maximum number of students
should not exceed 3 per assistant.
(6) Office accommodation should be provided for instructors and assessors of a standard to
ensure that they can prepare for their duties without undue distraction or discomfort.
(7) Secure storage facilities should be provided for assessment papers and training records.
The storage environment should be such that documents remain in good condition for
the retention period of a minimum of 5 years. The storage facilities and office
accommodation may be combined, subject to adequate security.
(g) Preventive maintenance programme for the training facilities including associated vehicles
and equipment should be in accordance with OEM recommendations and/or other
internationally-accepted standards.
(h) Guidance on the design, construction, and operation of aircraft aerodrome rescue and
firefighting (ARFF) training facilities can be refer to US Federal Aviation Administration
Advisory Circular 150/5220-17B Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) Training Facilities.

title: Training provider — vertical flight infrastructure facilities requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE FACILITIES REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider should ensure:
(1) training facilities and equipment are safely designed and constructed commensurate
with the types of training and proficiency checks programmes for VFI personnel;
(2) surface and elevated training structures are provided for the common type of
helicopter/VCA operating at onshore and offshore facilities;
(3) a single integrated facility or a combination of multiple structures within the same
facility is provided to demonstrate the intended training objectives are achieved;
(4) an analysis is conducted to determine the appropriate training facilities, resources and
equipment required to deliver the training and proficiency checks programmes;
(5) facilities are suitably equipped, including ancillary structures for effective delivery of
training programmes, protection from the prevailing weather and safe operation of all
planned training and assessment for VFI personnel; and
(6) a preventive maintenance programme is established and implement for all training
facilities including associated vehicles and equipment.

title: Vertical flight infrastructure training facilities and equipment
text:
VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE TRAINING FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT
(a) For surface-level training facility (see Figure F-2):
(1) a diameter of FATO/TLOF based on a helicopter having D-value of not less than 12-m or
a VCA having a D-value of not less than 8-m;
(2) adequate safety area of not less than 15-m is provided for the free movement of
vehicle, personnel and equipment during trainings; and
(3) all supporting structures and rest areas are located outside the safety area.
(b) For an elevated training structure (see Figure F-3):
(1) elevation from ground level should be no less than 2.5-m from ground level.
(2) have stair-access wide enough for RFF teams to manoeuvre aerodrome rescue and
firefighting equipment to and from the landing area.
(3) Landing Area: Minimum helicopter D-value of 12-m or VCA D-value of 8-m.
(4) The structure should contain at least two helicopter/VCA wells and should:
(i) be of sufficient depth below the deck so that RFF personnel can take cover from
flying debris in the event of a helicopter/VCA crash on deck;

(ii) have sufficient space to allow at least two people to move freely
(iii) have a safety railing around the helicopter/VCA well
(iv) provide at least two fire monitors, preferably more, typical of the type used on
elevated or offshore facility;
(v) be accessible by grated walkways and /or stairs; and
(vi) have stair (with handrails) access to the landing area.
(c) Training facility should capable of replicating Class A, B and E fires expected of a helicopter or
VCA accident.
(d) Wind sock.
(e) Portable and fixed foam application system equipment should be of adequate performance
and be suitably located to ensure an effective application of foam to any part of the VFI
landing area irrespective of the wind strength/direction or accident location.
Figure F-2: Example of a surface level training facility

Figure F-3: Example of an elevated training facility

1. LANDING AREA MARKINGS
(a) Makings should be typical of marking used onshore and offshore VFIs (see Figure F-4 for an
example of helicopter landing area markings and Figure F-5 for an example of VTOL-capable
aircraft landing area markings).
Figure F-4: Example of helicopter landing area markings

Figure F-5: Example of VTOL-capable aircraft landing area markings

2. VFI TRAINING SIMULATOR
Internal configuration
(a) The cockpit (basic simulation of helicopter/VCA cockpit);
(b) A realistic baggage and freight compartment, including door or hatch and handle operational
arrangements as found on onshore and offshore helicopters/VCAs; and
(c) Passenger seating arrangement as found in onshore and offshore helicopters/VCAs, to
simulate seating arrangements for passengers
Helicopter/VCA Firefighting Simulator
(a) Helicopter/VCA Simulator Shape and Size
(1) Although the fire and emergency response simulator doesn’t have to be an exact size
and shape of a real helicopter for transporting passengers offshore, it should have a
shape of a helicopter and reasonably realistic size. (See Figure F-6 for an example of a
helicopter simulator and Figure F-7: Example of VTOL-capable aircraft simulator)
Figure F-6: Example of a helicopter simulator

Figure F-7: Example of VTOL-capable aircraft simulator

(b) The helicopter/VCA simulator should accommodate the following:
(1) search, rescue and retrieval of passenger casualty simulators by the RFF team using
breathing apparatus

(2) facility for Classes A, B and C fires inside helicopter/VCA simulator
(3) passenger seating
(4) capable of being smoke-logged (Cosmetic smoke can be used during casualty
extraction)
(5) window arrangement typical of a type used on an transport helicopter/VCA
(6) helicopter/VCA baggage hold
(7) capability/arrangement for RFF team to enter the helicopter/VCA simulator for
helicopter/VCA crash on deck exercise i.e., fuselage top entry.
(8) facility to enable simulation from an overturned helicopter.
(9) facility to accommodate the extinguishing of a simulated engine fire by a CO2 or other
gaseous extended applicator.
Firefighting
(a) Fire Classes
 Fire Scenario Fire Classification
1 Fuel spill fire Class B- flammable liquid
2 Leaking fuel fire Class B- flammable liquid
3 Internal fires Class A
4 Engine fire Class B-flammable liquid OR Class C-flammable gas
5 Battery fire (thermal
runway)
Class E- electric
Note 1. — Flammable liquid that has similar combustion characteristics of aviation fuel.
Note 2. — For environmental purposes, smoke suppression or clean-burn systems are acceptable for
reducing smoke during Class A, B & C fire exercises.
(b) Firefighting Equipment
(1) Firewater Hydrants – for attaching fire hoses
(2) Hand adjustable foam-producing fire monitors capable of cross-arcing over the helideck
(3) Mobile foam and dry powder CO2 cart/trolley
(4) Portable extinguishers:
(i) Water
(ii) Dry powder
(iii) Foam

(iv) CO2
(5) Fire hoses
(6) Variety of branches: aspirated and non-aspirated
(7) Foam inductors
(8) CO2 extended applicator for extinguishing engine fires
(9) Water fire hose reel
(10) Fire-lighting equipment for lighting fires.
Firewater Reservoir Tank/Vessel
(a) Firewater pumping capacity adequate to supply practical fire exercise areas at full training
capacity.
(b) Firewater pumping system back-up capability to supply adequate pressurised water to the
exercise area in the event of the main pump/s failure.
(c) Adequate controls and safety arrangements to shut off fuel to fires in event of fire water
failure.
(d) Low firewater pressure alarm.
3. RESCUE EQUIPMENT AND PERSONAL PROTECTIVE CLOTHING
Helicopter Crash Rescue equipment
(a) The provision of at least one set of helicopter crash rescue equipment is required in order to
support firefighting and rescue activities (see rescue equipment list stated in PART VFI).

(b) The equipment should be easily accessed by the RFF team, kept in complete and serviceable
condition, and be ready for use in the vicinity of the training structure.
(c) The equipment stored in the Crash Box should cover the items recommended in applicable
documentation in accordance with PART VFI.
(d) Medical and first aid equipment – sufficient types and quantities for the training
(e) Casualty manikins – various sizes and weights

(f) Protective clothing and respiratory equipment should be fit for purpose for RFF teams.
(g) Resuscitation equipment for training delegates.
4. PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE
(a) Preventive maintenance programme for the training facilities including associated vehicles
and equipment should be in accordance with OEM recommendations and/or other
internationally-accepted standards.

title: Training provider — instructional equipment requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — INSTRUCTIONAL EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider should ensure:
(1) each classroom has appropriate presentation equipment of a standard that ensures
students can easily read presentation text/drawings/diagrams and figures from any
position in the classroom. Presentation equipment shall include representative
synthetic training devices to assist students in their understanding of the particular
subject matter where such devices are considered beneficial for such purposes;
(2) training facilities have all tools and equipment necessary to perform the accepted scope
of training. Training facilities should, at least, include physical & virtual simulators,
personal protective equipment, aerodrome rescue and firefighting equipment,
respiratory protection, smoke chambers, firefighting simulators. Additional tools and
equipment should be added where relevant;
(3) practical training facilities have appropriate selection of aircraft simulations including
fuselage, engines, cabin parts, rotary components and avionics equipment at both dry
and wet practical training areas. All students should be provided with appropriate
personal protective equipment for all practical trainings. Where training involves
working in smoke environment, respiratory protective equipment (breathing apparatus)
should be provided to all students. Appropriate safety briefing should be conducted
before each practical training including use of PPE and/or RPE; and
(4) a preventive maintenance programme is established and implemented for all simulators
and instructional equipment.

title: Training provider — training materials requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — TRAINING MATERIALS REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider should ensure:

(1) training course material should be provided to all students, which, at least, include:
(i) a training syllabus consisting of a full training programme, lesson plan, instructor
guide, student notes, assessment, presentation materials; and
(ii) type of course content for each structured learning programme.
(2) training course notes, diagrams and any other instructional material are accurate.
(3) all records are maintained including student training, examination and assessment
records for a minimum of 5 years.
(b) The training provider should establish and implement:
(1) sufficient procedures to ensure proper training standards and compliance with all
relevant requirements.
(2) management systems which, at least, contain:
(i) safety and quality management procedures;
(ii) implementation of a management of change of the full training processes;
(iii) an independent audit function to monitor training standards, the integrity of
knowledge examinations and practical assessments, compliance with and
adequacy of the procedures;
(iv) evaluation of training effectiveness e.g., course evaluation, customer
engagement, industry visit, etc; and
(v) a feedback system of audit findings to the person(s) and ultimately to the
accountable manager to ensure, as necessary, corrective and preventive actions
(3) the independent audit procedure ensure that all aspects of compliance are checked at
least annually and may be carried out as one complete single exercise or subdivided
over a 12-month period in accordance with a scheduled plan.
(4) Where the training provider is also accepted to conduct training based on another
GCAA regulation requiring a quality management system, then such system may be
combined.
(c) Where training activities and/or services are contracted to a third-party organisation, the
training provider should ensure:
(1) a pre-audit procedure is established whereby the training provider audits a prospective
third party to determine whether the contracted activities or services meet the intent
of this regulation;
(2) internal audit of the contracted activities or services is conducted at least once every 12
months to ensure continuous compliance with this regulation; and

(3) third party audits of the contracted activities or services are maintained and corrective
and preventive actions plan.
(4) independency of the third party audit to ensure that audits are not conducted by
personnel directly responsible for the function or procedure being checked.

title: Training provider — training delivery requirements
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — TRAINING DELIVERY REQUIREMENTS
(a) The training provider should ensure all students meet the necessary training pre-requisites
requirements. Where practical training is involved, the fitness status of the students should be
verified by the organisation.
(1) If the fitness status of a student is in doubt, he/she should be temporarily removed
from the training course to seek the advice of a qualified occupational medical person
to confirm the suitability of the student to continue with the training. Where in doubt,
students should submit a fit for duty declaration form.
(2) Certain practical trainings may require above average fitness levels. Training providers
should determine the appropriate fitness levels for different practical trainings.
(b) Training facilities should be regularly checked prior to the delivery of the training course.
Where practical training is involved, a safety inspection should be conducted around the
training area. Safety briefing including walk around and equipment induction should be
conducted, where necessary, to familiarise students with the training area, facility and
equipment.
(c) Safe management procedures should be implemented including use of personal protective
equipment, health and safety arrangements, where practical training involves:
(1) the use of flammable liquids, liquefied gases or alternative fuels including
determination of safe allowable quantity and exposure limit;
(2) working at height;
(3) working in confined spaces;
(4) working in smoke;
(5) manual handling; and
(6) working in heat and humidity.
(d) The training provider should ensure the validity and security of the overall training system
including:

(1) knowledge examinations and practical assessment can either be computerised or hard
copy or a combination of both; and
(2) the methodologies to be used in a particular examination and assessment are
determined by the assessors

title: Training provider — continued validity
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — CONTINUED VALIDITY
(a) The training provider should ensure training and proficiency checks programmes are delivered
in accordance with the requirements stated in the acceptance certificate issued by the GCAA.
(b) Where the training providers are deemed of not meeting the requirements mentioned in (a)
above, the GCAA may restrict or revoke the delivery of training and proficiency checks
programmes. The training and proficiency checks programmes may resume once the GCAA is
satisfied that the training provider has ensure that the programmes are acceptable for gaining
or maintaining the conditions according to the acceptance certificate.
CHANGES IN THE SCOPE OF THE ACCEPTANCE
(a) Training is a dynamic activity, and it is likely that training provider will ask regularly for a
change in the scope of their acceptance; for instance, they may want to provide new training
or change a training programme to take advantage of new training equipment or facilities. In
such a case, the training provider should notify the GCAA and provide a management of
change assessment against the applicable requirements in this Regulation, its requirements
and the relevant parts of this guidance material. An amendment to the acceptance certificate
should be issued by the GCAA after a satisfactory assessment.
(b) Major changes in management personnel, training facilities, equipment or modifications to
safety critical structures that may affect the conditions stated in the acceptance certificate,
should be immediately reported to the GCAA, in writing, to ensure that any required
acceptances are obtained without delay.
CONTINUED SURVEILLANCE AFTER THE ACCEPTANCE
(a) The training provider is subjected to continued surveillance by the GCAA to ensure that the
training provider is operating within the terms of the conditions stated in the certificate.
(b) The acceptance certificate may be suspended, curtailed or revoked where the GCAA has
determined that there are serious non-compliances or major diversions from the terms of the
certificate conditions conducted by the training provider.

(c) No changes to training and proficiency checks programme syllabi, personnel, facilities and
resources without the approval of the GCAA.
(d) The GCAA reserves the right to review the syllabus content and practical trainings, as and
when required.

title: Training provider — documentation requirements
text:
DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS
1. TRAINING AND COMPETENCY MANUAL
(a) The training provider should develop a training and competency manual describing the
training and proficiency checks programme being offered and the way in which the training
provider conducts its activities. It is an essential document for the training provider because it
provides the management and line personnel with clear guidance on the policy of the training
provider as well as the procedures and processes which are used to provide training. It is also
an essential document for the GCAA. During the acceptance process, it allows the GCAA to
assess whether the way in which a training provider is planning to operate is in line with
existing requirements and accepted practices. Once the training provider is accepted, a large
part of the surveillance activities of the GCAA is to ensure that the training provider is
following the training and procedures manual.
(b) It is important that the contents of the training and competency manual be consistent with
other operational documents, regulations and manufacturer’s requirements. The manual
should also be user-friendly. It is also necessary to ensure that the manual is used consistently
across all Departments within the training provider. This can be achieved through an
integrated approach that recognizes operational documents as a complete system.
(c) This chapter explains how the training and competency manual should be developed,
implemented and managed.
2. DOCUMENTATION MANAGEMENT
(a) The training and competency manual should be issued in separate parts if the training
provider find it too cumbersome to have all the required content appear in a single document.
It also mandates that these documents be maintained to ensure their continued relevancy
and compliance with applicable regulations.
(b) An effective quality system requires robust policies, processes and procedures for
documentation management and record keeping. Since shortcomings in documentation
management eventually lead to poor standardization and a diminished quality of training,

training provider should be vigilant of weaknesses in this area by including it in their internal
assurance programme.
3. CONTENT
(a) The content of the training and competency manual should provide a more detailed
breakdown of the content of the manual and includes additional requirements for training
provider that are engaged in aerodrome rescue and firefighting training. Depending on the
size, complexity and scope of the training provided by the training provider, some of the
elements contained in the list can be reduced, combined or expanded further.
4. STRUCTURE OF MANUAL
(a) The training and competency manual should be organized according to criteria relating to the
information, its importance and use. The information should be structured and sequenced so
that operational personnel can access it easily. This principle will help determine whether to
issue the manual as a single document or in separate parts. When the training and
competency manual is organized into separate parts, it should include a master index to help
users locate information included in more than one part. The master index should be placed in
the front of each part.
(b) The manual should describe accurately the training provider’s policies, processes and
procedures.
(c) The structure of the manual should be easy to understand, appropriate for the information
and clearly identified through headings and other formatting devices. An explanation of the
manual elements such as the headings, numbering scheme, main parts of the document and
other sources of coding or groupings should be provided at the beginning of the manual.
(d) Precise language should be used wherever possible. Terms for common items and actions
should be consistent throughout the manual and should be clear and easily understood.
(e) Writing style, terminology, formatting and use of graphics and symbols should be consistent
throughout the document, including the location of specific types of information and use of
units of measurement and codes.
(f) The manual should contain a glossary of definitions and significant terms including a list of
acronyms and/or abbreviations. The glossary should be updated on a regular basis to ensure
access to the most recent terminology.
(g) For ease of amendment and distribution, an appropriate revision process should be defined
and established when designing the manual.

(h) The training and competency manual should comply with the requirements of the training
provider’s quality assurance practices.
5. VALIDATION
(a) The training and competency manual should be reviewed and tested under realistic conditions
before its operational release. The validation process should include using the critical aspects
of the information contained in the manual to verify its effectiveness. Routine interaction
among groups within the training provider should be included in the validation process.
(b) A final review of the manual should ensure that all required topics have been addressed with
an appropriate level of detail for users. The final review should also confirm compliance with
safety regulations, manufacturers’ recommendations and the training provider’s policies,
procedures and processes.
6. DEPLOYMENT AND FEEDBACK
(a) The training provider should maintain and update as necessary the training and competency
manual after its initial release. This will ensure appropriate and realistic use of the manual,
based on the current operational environment, in a way that is operationally relevant and
appropriate for the users for whom it is intended.
(b) In order to gather information for updates of the manual, a formal feedback system should be
established to obtain input from principal users and others who would be affected by a new
or revised policy, procedure or process.
7. AMENDMENT
(a) The training provider should develop an effective information gathering and review system to
process information obtained from all sources relevant to the provider, such as the GCAA,
safety regulators, training clients, manufacturers and equipment vendors, as well as a
distribution and revision control system.
Note. — Manufacturers provide information on the operation, handling and maintenance of
specific equipment, vehicles and components thereof, which emphasizes the equipment or
systems and procedures under conditions that may not fully match the requirements of the
training provider. Training providers should ensure that such information meets their specific
needs and those of the GCAA.

(b) The training provider should also develop an information review, distribution and revision
control system to process information resulting from changes that originate within the
training provider. This includes changes to:
(1) the training provider’s policies, processes, procedures and practices;
(2) respond to operating experience;
(3) the scope of training provided;
(4) the content of training programmes;
(5) results stemming from the installation of new equipment;
(6) an acceptance document or certificate requested by the training provider and issued by
the GCAA; and
(7) maintain standardization of training delivery and performance criteria.
(c) The manual should be reviewed in association with other operational documents that form
the training provider’s document control system:
(1) on a regular basis (at least once a year);
(2) after major events such as mergers, acquisitions, rapid growth or downsizing;
(3) after technology changes, e.g. the introduction of new equipment;
(4) after changes to safety regulations;
(5) after changes to key operational personnel (e.g. Head of Training); and
(6) after changes to the scope of training provided.
(d) Permanent changes to the training and competency manual should be communicated through
a formal amendment process.
(e) Distribution of amendments and revisions should have a tracking system. The tracking system
should include some form of log combined with a procedure to ensure that all amendments
are furnished promptly to all providers or persons to whom the manual has been issued.

title: Training provider — quality assurance
text:
QUALITY ASSURANCE
Note 1. — The objective of quality assurance (QA) is to ensure the achievement of results that
conform to the standards set out in the training provider’s manuals and in requirements and
documents issued by the GCAA. The effective application of QA principles will aid the training
provider in meeting all regulatory requirements.

Note 2. — Quality is an outcome of a number of processes: establishing standards; planning activities
and documenting procedures to support such activities and standards; training the personnel
involved before implementing the documented procedures; and measuring the outcomes of the
activities to ensure that they meet the standards and expected results. If any non-conformities are
found, corrective actions are taken to improve processes and procedures.
Note 3. — It is to be emphasized that, to be truly effective in delivering the very best possible
products and services, training providers need to implement proactive as well as reactive processes.
Note 4. — The instructions and information contained in the following paragraphs provide guidance
on the QA that each training provider needs to establish.
1. ELEMENTS OF QUALITY ASSURANCE
(a) The following QA elements should be clearly identifiable in the training and competency
manual:
(1) the training provider’s training policy (for its own personnel and others);
(2) training standards;
(3) allocation of responsibility;
(4) resources, provider and operational processes;
(5) procedures to ensure conformity of training with the training policy;
(6) procedures for identifying deviations from training policy and standards, and for taking
corrective action, as necessary; and
(7) the evaluation and analysis of experiences and trends concerning policy and training
standards, in order to provide feedback into the system for the continual improvement
of the quality of training.
2. QUALITY ASSURANCE AND THE QUALITY SYSTEM OF THE TRAINING PROVIDER
(1) FACILITIES
(a) A training provider should provide facilities appropriate to the size and scope of the intended
operations provided in an environment conducive to learning. These facilities should include:
(1) general areas which consist of sufficient:
(i) office space for training provider’s managerial, administrative and training staff;
(ii) study and examination rooms and reference/library facilities; and
(iii) storage areas, including secure areas for training and personnel records;

(2) classroom areas which are suitably equipped to effectively deliver the theoretical
elements of the training programme in accordance with the training and procedures
manual; and
(3) practical training areas which are designed and equipped to ensure the attainment of
end-state competencies. These facilities should include, whenever applicable:
(i) operations, planning and briefing rooms;
(ii) simulation and training areas;
(iii) trainees changing and rest areas;
(iv) workshop and maintenance facilities; and
(v) equipment storage areas.
(2) TRAINING COURSEWARE AND EQUIPMENT
(a) A training provider should ensure that all courseware and equipment required by the training
programme, as specified in the training and competency manual, are available and in good
working order.
(b) Changes to working conditions and any temporary “work-around” solutions should be
discussed prior to continuing with the scheduled training.
(3) ACCEPTANCE OF TRAINING FACILITIES AND DEVICES
(a) With the rapid improvements in technology, an increasing number of simulation training
devices for training personnel within the aviation industry are entering the marketplace. Some
training programmes even use web-based simulation to such an extent that full accreditation
for successful programme completion is achieved without the trainees ever having to leave
their normal place of work or, in some cases, their residence.
(b) Each training device that is intended for training, testing or checking in an accepted training
programme and for which credit is being sought needs to be made available to the applicable
Authority, prior to initial use, for determination of its suitability.
(c) In addition to meeting the obligations of national regulations, the training provider should
implement at least the following for all training devices:
(1) a routine maintenance programme to ensure that the training devices continue to
function properly and, when applicable, continue to accurately replicate any
component, system or equipment for which training, checking or testing credits are
being sought; and

(2) a record-keeping process for each training device to be established and maintained,
which accurately records the device’s use and lists any discrepancies with respect to its
functionality or intended performance characteristics that may impact training.

title: Training provider — third party
text:
TRAINING PROVIDER — THIRD PARTY PROVIDER
1. COURSEWARE
(a) As training programme design becomes more sophisticated, training providers may consider
engaging outside assistance - third party provider in the development of courseware. This is
particularly true with competency-based programmes that require a relatively short-term
increase in manpower during the development phase.
(b) Whether or not a training provider engages outside assistance in designing and providing
courseware, the training provider should be accountable for the quality and suitability of its
courseware. The work being performed by the third-party provider should therefore be
subjected to the same quality assurance (QA) practices that the training provider is expected
to apply to its own work.
2. FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT
(a) Frequently the aviation training industry runs in cycles, during which training providers may be
operating below capacity for long periods of time only to suddenly find themselves inundated
by demands that exceed their ability to deliver. A training provider may also need equipment
for some parts of the training which may not be economically viable to own. To mitigate the
impact of not being able to effectively respond and thus potentially lose valued clients,
training providers frequently have standing agreements with other institutions to lease
facilities and equipment.
(b) The temporary use of another provider’s facilities and equipment can present challenges in
terms of the QA processes of the training providers. Under these circumstances, a breakdown
in vigilance can cause serious damage to the integrity and quality of the training. To mitigate
this, training providers should develop contingency plans in their quality manual for instances
when training levels are such that the use of another institution’s facilities and equipment is
required.
3. PERSONNEL

(a) The most frequent outsourcing practice of training providers is the hiring of temporary
instructional personnel. It is during these times in particular that a robust quality system will
protect the integrity and quality of an training provider’s training programmes and the
training provider’s reputation for delivering quality products and services.
(b) Despite their best intentions and qualifications, temporary employees elevate the risk of non-
standardized delivery of training and of a decrease in the level of service provided to the
training provider’s clients. Detailed, documented policies, processes and procedures that are
easy to understand and uniformly applied, combined with initial indoctrination training, will
go a long way to mitigating this risk.
(c) Besides training its regular staff, training providers should ensure that refresher training is
implemented on a scheduled basis for part-time or temporary instructional personnel prior to
commencing their duties after a specified period of inactivity. Re-familiarization with the
training providers’ quality system and expected levels of service should be included in this
training scheme. Besides the contingency plan, the training provider’s quality manual should
include policies, processes and procedures for the employment of temporary instructional
staff.
4. RECORD KEEPING
(a) Keeping accurate and complete training records is an important aspect of complying with the
acceptance requirements. It is also an essential tool for the training providers to ensure the
continuity and consistency of its training. The qualifications required for training personnel
and trainees should be recorded in the record-keeping system to ensure that those
qualifications are monitored and current.
(b) The record-keeping system of an training provider should have the following characteristics:
(1) Completeness. The records kept by the ATO should be sufficient to provide
documentary evidence of each training action and allow the reconstruction of the
training history of each student or instructor in the TRAINING PROVIDER;
(2) Integrity. It is important to maintain the integrity of records, ensuring that they are not
removed or altered. A backup of the records is also necessary to ensure continuity in
case of a major disaster; and
(3) Accessibility. Records of both instructional personnel and trainees should be readily
accessible.

(c) Each training provider should also establish rules for archiving personal employment and
training records that are non-active.
(d) Training records should be archived for at least 5 years.

title: Training provider — oversight activities
Training provider — overseas acceptance and oversight activities
text:
OVERSEAS ACCEPTANCE AND OVERSIGHT ACTIVITIES
(a) For the acceptance and oversight activities of the training provider located outside of the
United Arab Emirates, the training provider should:
(1) bear all travel, accommodation, logistics, transportation and other miscellaneous costs
in accordance with GCAA per diem policies and procedures; and
(2) ensure initial acceptance and continued regulatory oversight activities e.g., audits and
inspections by the GCAA include all contracted services and/or activities.

title: Scope
text:
(a) Heliport/helideck/vertiport operator or the PAO shall not provide a service to civil aviation, within the UAE except under the authority of, and
in accordance with the provisions of, a valid Certificate, PAO Acceptance or Heliport Certificate of Registration issued by the GCAA under this
regulation.
(b) This regulation establishes the common requirements, unless specifically mentioned, to be followed by an operator with respec t to its
Certification, PAO acceptance or Heliport Certificate of Registration, management, manuals and other responsibilities.
Note:
For the purpose of this regulations, the generic term “operator” will be used to denote Holders of or applicant for Certificate, PAO Acceptance
or Heliport Certificate of Registration.

title: Means of compliance
text:
(a) The operator shall comply with the scope and conditions that are endorsed in the Certificate, PAO acceptance or Heliport Certificate of
Registration.
(b) The operator shall provide all the relevant evidence to demonstrate compliance with the applicable requirements of this regulation at the
request of the GCAA.
(c) When The operator wishes to use an alternative means of compliance to the Acceptable Means of Compliance (AMC ), they shall, prior to
implementing the alternative means of compliance, provide the GCAA with a full description of the alternative means of compliance.
The description shall include a clear justification for the need for alternative, any revisions to manuals or procedures that may be relevant, as
well as an assessment demonstrating that the implementing rules are met.

(d) The operator shall implement alternative means of compliance subject to prior approval by the GCAA and only upon receipt of s uch
notification.

text:

title: Demonstration of compliance
text:
(a) The operator shall:
(1) perform and document all actions, inspections, tests, safety assessments or exercises necessary, and shall demonstrate to the GCAA:
(i) compliance with the requirements of this CAR, any safety decision, as appropriate;
(ii) that the VFI, as well as its obstacle limitation and protection surface and other areas associated with the heliport/helideck/
vertiport, have no features or characteristics making it unsafe for operation.
(2) provide to the GCAA the means by which compliance has been demonstrated.
(b) Relevant design information, including drawings, inspection, test and other relevant reports, shall be held and kept by the o perator at the
disposal of the GCAA, in accordance with the provisions of VFI.OR.G.035 - Record keeping, and provided on request to the GCAA.
AMC1.OR. A.020(a)(b) Demonstration of compliance
GENERAL- USE OF THIRD PARTIES TO DEMONSTRATE COMPLIANCE
While performing the necessary actions, inspections, tests, safety assessments, or exercises necessary to demonstrate compliance, the operator
may also use contracted third parties. In any case, the declaration of compliance and responsibility remains with the operator.
GM1.OR. A.020(a)(b) Demonstration of compliance
Operators should maintain a compliance register that should include all the certification specification requirements pertaini ng to all the
heliport/helideck/vertiport that is under their management/oversight. The compliance register should provide status o f their compliance to all the
relevant certification specification.

title: Personnel requirements - Certified VFI
text:
(a) An operator prior to the grant of a certificate and on an on-going basis shall engage, employ or contract:
(1) sufficient and qualified personnel for the planned tasks and activities to be performed related to the operation, maintenance and
management of the heliport/vertiport in accordance with the applicable requirements and the operator’s training programme; and
(2) sufficient number of supervisors to defined duties and responsibilities, considering the structure of the organisation.

(b) The operator shall nominate an Accountable Manager, acceptable to the GCAA, who has the authority for ensuring that all a ctivities can be
financed and carried out in accordance with the applicable requirements. The Accountable Manager shall be responsible for est ablishing and
maintaining an effective management system. Therefore, the Accountable Manager shall:
(1) have full cont rol of the resources, final authority over operations under the certificate/acceptanc e of the organisation and ultimate
responsibility and accountability for the establishment, implementation and maintenance of management systems, policies, and
resolution of all safety issues;
(2) have the final responsibility for all safety issues;
(3) ensure that all necessary resources are available to operate the heliport/  vertiport in accordance with the applicable requirements and
the heliport/ vertiport manual;
(4) ensure that if there is a reduction in the level of resources or abnormal circumstances which may affect safety, the required  reduction
in the level of operations at the heliport / vertiport is implemented;
(5) ensure the establishment, implementation, and promotion of the safety management system;
(6) ensure the establishment of a just culture which encourages safety reporting.
(c) The operator, shall nominate the operations Post Holder, acceptable to the GCAA, who is responsible for the management and supervision of
operations and safety critical aspects.
(d) The operations Post Holder shall have direct access to the Accountable Manager.
(e) The operator shall ensure that personnel involved in the operation, maintenance and management of the heliport/ vertiport are adequately
trained in accordance with the training programme.
(f) The operator shall determine the number of personnel needed to carry out planned tasks.

(a) The term ‘qualified’ denotes fitness or fit for the purpose.  This may be achieved through fulfilment of the necessary conditions such as
completion of required training, or acquisition of a diploma or degree, or through the gaining of suitable experience.  It, a lso, includes the
ability, capacity, knowledge or skill that matches or suits an occasion, or makes someone eligible for a duty, office, position, privilege or status.

(b) Certain posts may, by nature, be associated with the possession of certain qualifications in a specific field ( e.g., rescue and firefighting, civil,
mechanical or electrical engineering, wi ldlife biology, etc.).  In such cases, the person occupying such a post is expected to possess the
necessary qualifications.

title: Personnel requirement - Certified VFI
text:
RESPONSIBILITIES
(a) Operations Post Holder:
Should be responsible for all aspects of the heliport/helideck/vertiport operations as applicable and maintenance, rescue and firefighting,
where necessary and for the issuing and cancelling of Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP) and Notice to Airmen  (NOTAMs). The post
holder is also responsible for development, implementation of and compliance with the heliport and/or vertiport requirements including:
(1) emergency response;
(2) safety plan;
(3) manoeuvring area access and control procedures;
(4) apron management where applicable;
(5) disabled helicopter/VCA removal plan;
(6) other environmental, security and safety programs as required; and
(7) oversight to ensure compliance with certification regulatory obligations.
(b) Landing Officer (LO)
(1) for the day-to-day management of the heliport/vertiport, associated operations and supervision of the Assistants and support staff.

(2) exercise immediate and effective control of all persons who are engaged in helicopter/VCA operations, or who are on or near t he
helicopter/VCA landing area.
(3) report any form of deviation on heliport/vertiport to his immediate superior/installation manager, so that the helicopter/VCA operator
may be informed of the situation.
(4) Ensuring pre-operational and post-operational checks are carried out.
(5) Ensuring that on receipt of radio information regarding helicopter/VCA arrivals, facilities are ready to receive the helicopter/VCA.
(6) Ensuring the safe movement of passengers, baggage, freight and correct loading.
(7) Initiating fire-fighting and rescue procedures on the heliport/vertiport, and ensuring that members of the heliport/vertiport crew carry
out their duties.
(8) Liaison with the installation fire teams and ensuring that backup fire-fighting and rescue procedures are implemented to assist after the
initial stage of an emergency.
(9) Briefing the team on helicopter/VCA handling and other relevant tasks.
(10) Ensuring the management, are kept aware of helicopter/VCA movements.
(11) Ensuring that the 210° OFS is clear of obstructions before giving a helicopter/VCA clearance to land, where applicable.
(12) Ensuring that the flood lighting controls are accessible to and controlled by the LO (or Radio Operator).
(13) Ensuring that the charging/ refuelling procedures are implemented as applicable.
(14) Ensuring necessary steps are taken to deny unauthorised persons access to the helicopter deck prior to take-off and landing.
(15)  Ensuring the deck is cleared of loose objects, inflammable substances, etc.
(16)  Ensuring necessary personnel are present and at a state of readiness.
(17)  All equipment and instruments are in place and in full working order.
(18)  Passengers are held in the safe zone during landing/take off and that they are given guidance during disembarkation and embarkation.
(19) The LO shall be positioned to be able to observe as best as possible, and closely monitor, landing and take -off of helicopters/VCAs. The
LO shall immediately inform the pilot via radio or visually if any abnormal situation occurs.
(c) Landing Assistant (LA):
The responsibilities of the Landing Assistant should include but not be limited to:
(1) Assisting the LO in the operation.
(2) Directing passengers to and from the helicopter/VCA.
(3) Operation of fire-fighting and rescue equipment under the di rection of the LO and assisting the LO in checking fire -fighting and rescue
equipment.

(4) Undertaking other duties around the facility as required by the LO.
(5) Passenger and freight control before departure and on arrival.
(6) liaison with the LO, Radio Operator on helicopter movements and requirements.
(d) Radio Operator (RO):
(1) The RO should provide information and advice for the purpose of assisting the safe and efficient operation of aircraft. This should include:
(i) information when available on other known traffic;
(ii) weather information;
(iii) information regarding radio and navigational aids;
(iv) landing area conditions and associated facilities;
(v) alerting service; and
(vi) any other information likely to affect safety.
(2) Coordinate with other agencies as required, including:
(i) other ATS and AFIS units,
(ii) meteorological services providers,
(iii) operators of aircraft and landing platforms,
(iv) rescue and fire-fighting emergency services,
(v) search and rescue authorities, and
(vi) UAE armed forces and/or police as applicable.
(3) RO’s duties may include passing Weather Status Reports to the helicopter/VCA operator, estimated times of arrival, and revisi ons, to
the LO, confirmation that the deck is ready for arriving helicopters, sending arrival message s, and obtaining flight plan and load details
etc.
(4) RO’s emergency preparedness includes having  an emergency procedures checklist which clearly displays Alerting Service actions
involving overdue or missing aircraft.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-VFI - VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Personnel requirement - Certified VFI
text:
RADIO OPERATOR
(a) Continuous two-way radio communications should be available between the helicopter/VCA pilot and the operator or an appropriate agent.
While not always possible, it is highly desirable to have a three -way communications link between the helicopter pilot, t he off-shore facility,
and a land-based facility.

(b) Radio Operators should be aware of helicopter/VCA operations within the vicinity and should be prepared to pass on relevant information to
the pilots.
(c) On most facilities, the radio operator (RO) is the ini tial and final point of contact between flight crew and the facility. However, as final
approach to the landing area is established, personnel (LOs and LAs) with portable aeronautical headsets, may be available fo r guidance to
the pilot as to the status of the landing area. When such personnel are utilised, the use of this equipment requires that they should be suitably
trained.
(d) Major advantage of having a radio -equipped person is that they can maintain visual as well as radio communication during the circu it, final
approach and landing, so assisting the helicopter/VCA crew with further positive identification of the facility and thereby r educing the
incidence for a landing on an incorrect location. A radio -equipped person is also in a good position to warn of any developing issues to the
helicopter / VCA crew.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-VFI - VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE - ISSUE 02.pdf

(b) The system should have a mechanism to verify that the information has reached the intended recipient.

title: Personnel requirements - PAO
text:
(a) A PAO prior to the grant of an acceptance and on an on-going basis shall engage, employ or contract:
(1) sufficient and qualified personnel for the planned tasks and activities to be performed related to the management , oversight, and
operation of the helideck in accordance with the applicable requirements and the operator’s training programme; and
(2) sufficient number of supervisors to defined duties and responsibilities, considering the structure of the organisation.
(b) The PAO shall nominate an Accountable Manager, acceptable to the GCAA, who has the authority for ensuring that all activities can be financed
and carried out  in accordance with the applicable requirements. The Accountable Manager shall be responsible for establishing and
maintaining an effective management system. Therefore, the Accountable Manager shall:
(1) have full control of the resources, final authority ove r operations of the organisation and ultimate responsibility and accountability for
the establishment, implementation and maintenance of management systems, policies, and resolution of all safety issues;
(2) have the final responsibility for all safety issues;
(3) ensure that all necessary resources are available to operate the helideck in accordance with the applicable requirements and the manual;

(4) ensure that if there is a reduction in the level of resources or abnormal circumstances which may affect safety, the r equired reduction
in the level of operations at the helideck is implemented;
(5) ensure the establishment, implementation, and promotion of the safety policy;
(6) ensure compliance with relevant applicable requirements, the organisation’s safety management system, as well as its quality assurance
programme;
(7) ensure the establishment of a just culture which encourages safety reporting;
(8) ensure the establishment, implementation and maintenance of the organisation’s competence to learn from the analysis of data
collected through its safety reporting system and others Safety Data Collection and Processes Systems (SDCPS) in place; and
establishment of safety objectives and safety targets.
(c) The PAO, shall nominate the following Post Holders, acceptable to the GCAA, who are responsible for the management and supervision of
safety critical aspects, for the helidecks under their management and/or oversight, as below:
(1) operations–operations Post Holder;
(2) quality assurance- quality Post Holder;
(3) safety management system- safety Post Holder; and
(d) The Post Holders shall have direct access to the Accountable Manager.
(e) The aerodrome operator shall appoint personnel responsible for the management and supervision of the following areas:
(1) ARFF; and
(2) maintenance of the aerodrome.
(f) The PAO shall determine the number of personnel needed to carry out planned tasks.
(g) The PAO shall ensure that their personnel are adequately trained to carry out their responsibilities.
(h) The PAO shall update its manual including the organisational structure with respect to the accepted Post Holders.

title: Personnel requirements - PAO
text:
(a) PAO should carry out an analysis to compare their existing and planned oversight activities with the requirement to ensure sufficient numbers
of auditors are available to carry out their compliance monitoring activities.

title: Personnel requirements - PAO
text:
PAO’S INTERNAL AUDIT TEAM
(a) PAO should have sufficient number of qualified personnel to perform compliance monitoring and quality assurance and have the necessary
knowledge, experience, initial, on-the-job and recurrent training to ensure continuing competence.
(b) PAO’S internal audit team should consist of Audit team leader and Member(s).
(c) PAO should maintain a list of trained and competent internal auditors who are tasked to internally audit their facilities.
(d) The PAO’s audit team should be sufficiently staffed, taking into consideration the following:
(1) The number of facilities under their management and/or supervision;
(2) The geographical layout of the facilities under their management and/or supervision;
(3) The requirement to ensure that the audit program is satisfied.

title: VFI manual
text:
(a) Following details should be provided in the VFI manual.
(1) PART A. – GENERAL
(i) Purpose and scope of the manual.
(ii) Legal requirements for the manual as prescribed in SUBPART B - (VFI.OR).
(iii) Conditions for use of the VFI  by its users.
(iv) The obligations of the operator; rights of the GCAA and guidance to staff on how to facilitate audits/inspections by the GCAA.
(v) Systems for amendments and revisions of the manual.
(2) PART B. -  VFI MANAGEMENT SYSTEM, QUALIFICATION, AND TRAINING REQUIREMENTS
(i) Description of the organisational structure.
(ii) Names, authorities and duties of nominated accountable manager, operations post holder, LO, LA, RO.
(iii) Description of the SMS – policy, aviation focused hazard identification and risk assessment process, safety reporting, investigation,
change management process, description of compliance monitoring process, procedure to report to the GCAA.
(iv) Training details of the personnel.
(v) Description of internal compliance monitoring process.
(3) PART C. - PARTICULARS OF THE VFI  SITE
(i) Name of the VFI .
(ii) The location of the VFI.
(iii) The name of the operator and contact details (including telephone numbers) of the operator at which may be contacted at all
times.
(iv) Details of the infrastructure, visual aids, wind direction indicator.
(v) Type of the operations that VFI is approved for.
(vi) Details of FATO,  declared D-Value, load bearing capability,  safety areas, clearways, TLOF, Taxiways, Taxi routes, parking stands,
obstacle environment, level of RFF protection.
(vii) The geographical coordinates of the reference point determined in terms of the World Geodetic System — 1984 (WGS -84)
reference datum.
(viii) The elevation.

(ix) Declared distances.
(x) Visual aids, slope indicators.
(xi) Helideck limitations in a Helideck Limitations List (HLL), where applicable, mentioning all limitations- applicable for PAO.
(xii) Limitations, warnings, cautions or other comments of operational importance.
(4) PART D. OPERATING PROCEDURES AND SAFETY MEASURES
(i) Movement area inspection.
(ii) Access to movement area.
(iii) Works safety.
(iv) Safeguarding.
(v) Wildlife hazard management.
(vi) Occurrence reporting.
(vii) Rescue and firefighting.
(viii) Emergency planning.
(ix) Maintenance procedures – landing surface, electrical, visual aids.
(x) Procedure for stand allocation in case of multiple parking stands.
(xi) FOD prevention.
(xii) Obstacle control and monitoring.
(b) If a particular element is not included in the manual is not applicable to the heliport/vertiport then the operator should state in the manual:
(1) that the particular element is not applicable; and
(2) why the particular element is not applicable.

title: PAO Documentation
text:
The PAO shall:
(a) establish and maintain a Safety and Quality management system manual which is a fundamental requirement for its acceptance;
(b) maintain documented agreement between the Primary Accountable Organisation and the named helideck operating companies for the
system of safety oversight.
(c) establish process by which the Primary Accountable Organisation ensures that their audit team are sufficiently trained and qualified for the
planned tasks and activities to be performed.

title: PAO Documentation
text:
The PAO’s quality system should include the following documented procedures:
(a) for the internal audit process (i.e., audit scope, audit periodicity; audit plan; audit programme; definition of findings).
(b) for the follow-up process on audit findings, (i.e. actions to be taken for safety critical issues; identifying causal factors and corrective actions;
agreement on action plans; agreement on timescales).
(c) for notification of safety critical issues / findings to stakeholders and the GCAA.
(d) for document control of audits, reports and records.

title: Application for a Heliport Certificate of Registration
text:
(a) Pursuant to the United Arab Emirates Federal Act No. 20 (1991) Promulgating The Civil Aviation Law Article 27 and to the Civi l Aviation
Regulations (CARs) for the time being in force , a Heliport Certification of Registration  may be granted  by the GCAA, if it is satisfied that an
applicant is competent, having regard to the applicant’s previous conduct and experience, the equipment, organisation, staffing, maintenance
and other arrangements, to ensure that the heliport/helideck and airspace are safe for use by aircraft.
(b) The requirement for Heliport Certificate of Registration is as follows:
Heliports that are used for domestic flight operations within the UAE, including commercial (for air services) and non-commercial, including
but not limited to transport, hospitality, tourism, filming, and HEMS operating bases.
Note:
(a) A heliport operator , who meets the requirement for a Heliport certificate of Registration , may choose to apply for a heliport certificate  in
accordance with SECTION C2 - CERTIFICATION (VFI.OR.C2), in which case the applicable requirements of CAR AGA PART VFI  shall be met and
maintained and will be subject to oversight by the GCAA.
(b) Holders of heliport Certificate of Registration, when intending to accommodate VCA operations, shall apply and obtain a Heliport /vertiport
certificate that is applicable for hybrid operations.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-VFI - VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: Application for a Heliport Certificate of Registration
text:
REGISTRATION OF THE ORGANISATION
(a) The owner and operator must both ensure their organisations are registered on the GCAA website.
(b) The heliport must be registered with the GCAA.
(c) The Operator is responsible for maintaining the currency of the details on the registration record.
(d) The Operator is responsible for renewing the Heliport Certificate of Registration  no less than three months prior to any expiratio n date
included on the Heliport Certificate of Registration.
(e) The Operator shall not operate outside the parameters provided to the GCAA and as indicated on the Heliport Certificate of Registration.
(f) Applicants should provide evidence of their identity such as establishment / trade license documentation and official documents as required
during the registration process.

(g) Applicant should provide all documents and information as including the following:
(1) Legal and Administrative Details
(i) Operator name and corporate registration;
(ii) Contact details;
(iii) Proof of site control.
(2) Technical Documentation
(i) Location;
(ii) Elevation;
(iii) Details for each FATO and TLOF including civil characteristics, visual aids, fuelling/charging facilities and emergency equipment;
(iv) Azimuths for approach paths.
(3)  Operational Information
(i) Intended operations;
(ii) Provisions for emergency response;
(iii) Declared restrictions or limitations.
(4) Supporting Files
(i) Site map;
(ii) Engineering drawings or plans;
(iii) Photographs of the heliport;
(iv) Other related approvals;
(v) Evidence of required third part agreements;
(vi) Signed declaration of regulatory compliance.
(h) Applicants should have secure access to the GCAA e-Services, available on the GCAA’s website: www.gcaa.gov.ae. Applicants who do not have
access to the GCAA’s e-Services must make an initial request through GCAA’s customer service channels.
(i) Applicants should obtain r equired approvals from other Appropriate Authorities ( i.e., municipalities, civil defence, local departments of civil
aviation.
(j) Applicants should apply for other certificates or approvals from the GCAA; this will be dependent upon the scale and type of operations the
heliport/vertiport intended to be used. Other areas that require certification or approval are:
(1) Air Navigation Services:

For the purposes of arrangements for Air Navigation services.
(2) Airspace:
 For the purpose of ensuring the suitability of the proposed site from an airspace perspective, taking into consideration the proximity of
the aerodrome to other aerodromes and landing sites, including military aerodromes, obstacles and terrain, any excess ive operational
restriction requirements, any existing restrictions such as – special use airspace, controlled airspace; and any existing flight procedures.
(3) Aviation Security:
Security clearance to confirm that supporting resources and facilities required by aviation security services are made available at facilities
serving civil aviation.
(k) There may also be other bodies that the applicants should inform in their own interests and it is the responsibility of the heliport operator to
obtain the appropriate approvals. The application for planning/building permissions and the request for a certificate are not  interdependent
and are required to be made separately.
(l) The physical characte ristics and design of the heliport/ helideck should consider, where appropriate, land -use and environmental control
measures.
source_file: CAR-AGA - PART-VFI - VERTICAL FLIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE - ISSUE 02.pdf

title: (c) Application for a Certificate of Registration
text:
INFORMATION REQUIRED IN THE APPLICATION
(a) Legal and Administrative Details should include details of both the owner and the operator (if not the owner) as well as evidence of
ownership or right to use.  Heliport contact for operational enquiries should be provided.  The heliport name and any designators should be
